messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] two yes/no questions on ERGM in R (fwd)
messages.body_plain:
John Paolillo wrote:
> (1) R uses approximately 8 bytes per cell of a numeric matrix, not 
> counting any row and column labels and/or other descriptive vectors 
> (partitions from cluster analyses, etc.) This means that the 1k*1K 
> matrix you describe consumes 8MB of memory. So this is not at all a 
> problem on modern machines.

This is true.  Also, note that network objects are stored as edge lists 
(with some indexing and other mojo), so sparse graph storage will not 
scale quadratically in the number of vertices.  (There's some overhead, 
but it's linear.)  Whether this is honored by the various statnet 
routines varies: ergm keeps the network in edgelist form (although some 
term initialization routines might not), but current sna routines 
convert network objects to matrix form prior to analysis.  Such are the 
joys of legacy code.

> 
> (2) Data objects that R works with must be entirely in memory. Most 
> systems will use some form of virtual memory (on disk) if you exceed the 
> available physical memory, but when your computer starts swapping R 
> objects in and out of memory, things start to really bog down. Treat the 
> available physical memory as an upper limit on what you should use.

Also, be aware that the Windows implementation of R seems to have some 
low ceilings on memory allocation.  Those of us in the Linux world 
remain happily immune to this, but we hear of it from our students....

> 
> (3) Many operations in R require copying an entire object. For example, 
> changing the value of a cell in a matrix by assignment (e.g. m[96,42] <- 
> 7) requires copying the entire matrix.

Not always true -- this depends on how the appropriate assignment method 
  is written.  IIRC, most of the standard data types support in-place 
modification, so long as the dimensions of the object are not changed. 
This is also true of network objects, which are almost always modified 
in place.

> If you do this in a loop for 
> several elements, that's one entire copy of the matrix for each 
> assignment. This is costly both in space and time. In loops, the issue 
> generally is time. Use R's vectorized computations (including 
> assignment) to advantage if at all possible, to minimize this problem. 
> Other times the issue is (or rapidly becomes) space. For example if you 
> conduct a cluster analysis of your matrix, you may have a distance 
> matrix that you compute and want to save. This will be true for each 
> version of distance you use and want to keep for later. If these objects 
> are saved in your .RData file, then they all must live in memory 
> together at the same time. This becomes an issue as you iterate through 
> solutions to a problem.

Again, this varies -- R's garbage collection system recaptures most of 
this memory, and many assignments are implemented without copying. 
Because of this, loops are not always faster than the *apply methods, 
despite folk wisdom to the contrary.  However, you are right that R's 
loops are generally pretty slow, and are in some cases space 
inefficient.  Backending can often accelerate highly iterative 
calculations, especially those which would require a lot of object 
handling if performed in the interpreted code.  (My sense, however, is 
that the latter is the real culprit in most of these cases -- working 
with the .Call interface for a while gives one a sense of the vast 
amount of overhead which is involved in supporting R's friendly, 
object-oriented interface.)

> 
> (4) Some R functions do very bad things when it comes to memory usage, 
> at least when large data sets are being used. For example, glm() and 
> lm() create entire copies of your data that are obligatorily saved into 
> an object that is returned. Since you often need to save these for 
> future use, you may be saving multiple copies of the data unnecessarily. 
> I don't know if the ergm package does this, but I wouldn't be surprised 
> if it does as this is something of an R convention. Also, analyses can 
> create very large data objects that are not copies of the data, and 
> these can also get out of control.

This is a very common trope -- it allows secondary methods to perform 
"smart" diagnostics on analysis objects, but does consume a lot of 
memory in some cases.  Similarly, most high-level analysis routines 
perform a number of handy subsidiary calculations which are useful for 
end users, but which consume processor time.  If you are dealing in huge 
data sets, or if you simply need to repeat a specific calculation many 
times (e.g., as do the netlm qap tests), then you should avoid using the 
high-level routines.  Instead, you should employ a function which is 
more appropriately tailored to your particular time/space constraints -- 
most of these routines have back-end components which can be used for 
this purpose.

> 
> (5) Plotting can be very inefficient in R, depending on the package 
> used. Again, there are data copying issues (a copy is made to represent 
> in the output device), but I know less of the specifics here, just that 
> certain reasonable things can work out pretty badly if care is not 
> exercised. For example, plotting an hclust object with 1000 leaves can 
> be reasonably fast, but the same analysis cast as a dendrogram object 
> plots exceedingly slowly. I believe this is because of the 
> hierarchically structured representation of the dendrogram object, as 
> opposed to hclust, which is flatter (for the exact same information). 
> Since ergm/statnet/network packages adopt a structured representation of 
> their data object, there may be similar performance problems, but I 
> wouldn't know for sure.

Well, plot.network (which is a clone of gplot) still coerces its input 
to matrix form for certain purposes, so you'll take a hit there; that's 
rarely a major constraint, however.  IIRC, a bigger issue is the 
overhead involved in creating the polygons to represent the 
edges/vertices, and in having R print them.  I don't worry about this 
too much, however -- by the time this becomes a problem, one's network 
has usually become too large to visualize without more exotic methods 
(especially on a low-resolution display).  A sparse 1000 node network 
should be no problem, in any event.

> 
> Some general guidelines of use would be, (i) use a utility such as 
> Activity monitor (mac) or top (unix) to keep an eye on the memory usage 
> as you work, (ii) force garbage collection if you need to with gc(), 
> though keep in mind this may not always free up memory, and (iii) save 
> out objects that you are not immediately working with to separate RData 
> files. If you don't do these, in the worst case you can hang your 
> system. Most OS's will allow you to kill the offending process if you 
> get stuck (R), but doing so loses your changes in the data since your 
> last save as well as your command history, so do everything to avoid 
> this and you will be happier.
> 
> If you have a system with, say, 2 GB of ram (reasonably standard these 
> days) then for 1M cell matrices you probably will not run into too many 
> problems with memory within R, would be my guess. At the same time, 
> someone from the statnet team should comment on the memory use and time 
> complexity of statnet-specific functions.

FWIW, I don't think that memory is going to be a major constraint for 
most operations on a 1k network (with certain exceptions, such as 1000+ 
parameter models).  I've run diffusion models in R on sparse networks of 
over 100,000 nodes on an Athlon w/2GB of RAM, and nothing was in 
imminent danger of crashing.  Of course, many functions would not be 
feasible on such a network....common sense applies, and YMMV.  The 
statnet library has to balance the disparate demands of versatility, 
performance, and ease-of-use, and users whose requirements push very 
hard on the performance end may find it worthwhile to code something 
more narrowly focused on their specific application.  Of course, no 
software on earth is going to change the fact that many interesting 
network analytic calculations are intrinsically expensive, and you may 
not have enough Time*Iron to get the answer you desire.  Still, 
optimization can sometimes have benefits, if done properly.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] two yes/no questions on ERGM in R (fwd)
messages.body_plain:
> 1. My network is very large and I heard that ERGM is computation- 
> intensive.
> Is ERG modeling in R feasible for networks of 1000x1000 or larger?

I can't speak to Statnet in specific, but 1000*1000 may or may not be  
large depending on what you are trying to do. If the goal is a  
statistical analysis in R, it is not too large although one should be  
aware of the way R uses memory. If you're trying to plot such a  
thing, or use certain forms of analysis, then you need to be even  
more careful.

Things to be alert to are:

(1) R uses approximately 8 bytes per cell of a numeric matrix, not  
counting any row and column labels and/or other descriptive vectors  
(partitions from cluster analyses, etc.) This means that the 1k*1K  
matrix you describe consumes 8MB of memory. So this is not at all a  
problem on modern machines.

(2) Data objects that R works with must be entirely in memory. Most  
systems will use some form of virtual memory (on disk) if you exceed  
the available physical memory, but when your computer starts swapping  
R objects in and out of memory, things start to really bog down.  
Treat the available physical memory as an upper limit on what you  
should use.

(3) Many operations in R require copying an entire object. For  
example, changing the value of a cell in a matrix by assignment (e.g.  
m[96,42] <- 7) requires copying the entire matrix. If you do this in  
a loop for several elements, that's one entire copy of the matrix for  
each assignment. This is costly both in space and time. In loops, the  
issue generally is time. Use R's vectorized computations (including  
assignment) to advantage if at all possible, to minimize this  
problem. Other times the issue is (or rapidly becomes) space. For  
example if you conduct a cluster analysis of your matrix, you may  
have a distance matrix that you compute and want to save. This will  
be true for each version of distance you use and want to keep for  
later. If these objects are saved in your .RData file, then they all  
must live in memory together at the same time. This becomes an issue  
as you iterate through solutions to a problem.

(4) Some R functions do very bad things when it comes to memory  
usage, at least when large data sets are being used. For example, glm 
() and lm() create entire copies of your data that are obligatorily  
saved into an object that is returned. Since you often need to save  
these for future use, you may be saving multiple copies of the data  
unnecessarily. I don't know if the ergm package does this, but I  
wouldn't be surprised if it does as this is something of an R  
convention. Also, analyses can create very large data objects that  
are not copies of the data, and these can also get out of control.

(5) Plotting can be very inefficient in R, depending on the package  
used. Again, there are data copying issues (a copy is made to  
represent in the output device), but I know less of the specifics  
here, just that certain reasonable things can work out pretty badly  
if care is not exercised. For example, plotting an hclust object with  
1000 leaves can be reasonably fast, but the same analysis cast as a  
dendrogram object plots exceedingly slowly. I believe this is because  
of the hierarchically structured representation of the dendrogram  
object, as opposed to hclust, which is flatter (for the exact same  
information). Since ergm/statnet/network packages adopt a structured  
representation of their data object, there may be similar performance  
problems, but I wouldn't know for sure.

Some general guidelines of use would be, (i) use a utility such as  
Activity monitor (mac) or top (unix) to keep an eye on the memory  
usage as you work, (ii) force garbage collection if you need to with  
gc(), though keep in mind this may not always free up memory, and  
(iii) save out objects that you are not immediately working with to  
separate RData files. If you don't do these, in the worst case you  
can hang your system. Most OS's will allow you to kill the offending  
process if you get stuck (R), but doing so loses your changes in the  
data since your last save as well as your command history, so do  
everything to avoid this and you will be happier.

If you have a system with, say, 2 GB of ram (reasonably standard  
these days) then for 1M cell matrices you probably will not run into  
too many problems with memory within R, would be my guess. At the  
same time, someone from the statnet team should comment on the memory  
use and time complexity of statnet-specific functions.

Hope this helps,

John Paolillo
Informatics, Indiana University

messages.subject: [statnet_help] question about ERGM terms
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Hank -

Hank Green wrote:
> hi statnet team:
>  
> i'm working on some model hypotheses and wonder if you might point me in 
> the direction of the terms that would best summarize indedgree and 
> outdegree centralization. i'm interested in both network-wide and 
> differential centralization metrics. i've been through the ergm-terms 
> document and am not entirely sure which (if any) of the terms best suit 
> my needs.
>  
> i thought i'd appeal to the masters for guidance.
>  
> thanks for any help...
>  
> and happy fall semester to all reading this.
>  
> hank

All Freeman centralization measures can be written in the (unnormalized) 
form:

C(G) propto cmax(G) - cmean(G)

where cmax is the maximum observed centrality score among the vertices 
of G (under whatever centrality measure is being used), and cmean is the 
corresponding observed mean centrality score.  (I use this trick 
extensively in a soon-to-appear Social Networks piece on density-based 
bounds for degree centralization, but the result applies to any 
centrality measure.)  This means that you can capture centralization 
effects by a statistic which weights the difference between the maximum 
and mean centrality score within the network in question.  In the case 
of degree, this can be re-expressed in terms of the maximum degree and 
density, both of which admit easily computed changescores.

As of right now, there is not a specific ergm term which tracks this 
statistic.  However, ergm was designed to accept user-generated terms, 
and it wouldn't be too hard to hack something like that together. 
Otherwise, this is the kind of thing which will probably get added to 
the main package eventually (since the UCI group is also interested in 
centrality-related questions); AFAIK, however, it's not a priority 
development target in the immediate near-term.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
Dear Statnet List,

I'm finally embarking on a simulation study of the statistical properties
of ERGMs as implemented in statnet. I'm setting up the code to run these
simulations, but as I did so, I noted some strange things.

I simulated (sparse) networks of 100 nodes, with an edge parameter of -6.
Fitting a model with only edges to this worked fine (estimates fell around
the true value), but when I fitted a model that also included triangles,
estimates of the triangle parameter followed a bimodal distribution;
57/100 simulations had triangle estimates of -12 to -13 (so, effectively
zero on the antilog scale), whereas 43/100 simulations had triangle
parameters greater than 0. In addition, the LRT test statistic between the
null and the alternative model was larger than I expected:

> sum(unlist(lldiff)*2>3.84)
[1] 16
> summary(unlist(lldiff)*2)
     Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean   3rd Qu.      Max.
 0.005212  1.253000  2.704000  3.217000  3.429000 26.660000

Has anyone had any similar experiences with simulated data?

Thanks
Simon

messages.subject: [statnet_help] generating a predicted network
messages.body_plain:
Dear Brian,

Thanks for the question.

As your model is dyad independence you can obtain an expression analytically
using the coefficients in the same way as you do for logistic regression.
That is, in this case the conditional and unconditional probabilities are
the same.

It is easier to use the simulate command to generate, e.g., 1000 networks
from the fitted model and take the average sociomatrix from them. This is a
consistent estimate of the probabilities, and will work for an arbitrary
"ergm" model to boot.

I hope this helps.

Mark

messages.body_plain:
Note that most of statnet is coded in C.  The user interface in in R, but 
not much of the computation -- so the well known limitations of R in 
general do not hold.

best,
mm


On Tue, 27 Mar 2007, John Paolillo wrote:

>> 1. My network is very large and I heard that ERGM is computation-intensive.
>> Is ERG modeling in R feasible for networks of 1000x1000 or larger?
>
> I can't speak to Statnet in specific, but 1000*1000 may or may not be large 
> depending on what you are trying to do. If the goal is a statistical analysis 
> in R, it is not too large although one should be aware of the way R uses 
> memory. If you're trying to plot such a thing, or use certain forms of 
> analysis, then you need to be even more careful.
>
> Things to be alert to are:
>
> (1) R uses approximately 8 bytes per cell of a numeric matrix, not counting 
> any row and column labels and/or other descriptive vectors (partitions from 
> cluster analyses, etc.) This means that the 1k*1K matrix you describe 
> consumes 8MB of memory. So this is not at all a problem on modern machines.
>
> (2) Data objects that R works with must be entirely in memory. Most systems 
> will use some form of virtual memory (on disk) if you exceed the available 
> physical memory, but when your computer starts swapping R objects in and out 
> of memory, things start to really bog down. Treat the available physical 
> memory as an upper limit on what you should use.
>
> (3) Many operations in R require copying an entire object. For example, 
> changing the value of a cell in a matrix by assignment (e.g. m[96,42] <- 7) 
> requires copying the entire matrix. If you do this in a loop for several 
> elements, that's one entire copy of the matrix for each assignment. This is 
> costly both in space and time. In loops, the issue generally is time. Use R's 
> vectorized computations (including assignment) to advantage if at all 
> possible, to minimize this problem. Other times the issue is (or rapidly 
> becomes) space. For example if you conduct a cluster analysis of your matrix, 
> you may have a distance matrix that you compute and want to save. This will 
> be true for each version of distance you use and want to keep for later. If 
> these objects are saved in your .RData file, then they all must live in 
> memory together at the same time. This becomes an issue as you iterate 
> through solutions to a problem.
>
> (4) Some R functions do very bad things when it comes to memory usage, at 
> least when large data sets are being used. For example, glm() and lm() create 
> entire copies of your data that are obligatorily saved into an object that is 
> returned. Since you often need to save these for future use, you may be 
> saving multiple copies of the data unnecessarily. I don't know if the ergm 
> package does this, but I wouldn't be surprised if it does as this is 
> something of an R convention. Also, analyses can create very large data 
> objects that are not copies of the data, and these can also get out of 
> control.
>
> (5) Plotting can be very inefficient in R, depending on the package used. 
> Again, there are data copying issues (a copy is made to represent in the 
> output device), but I know less of the specifics here, just that certain 
> reasonable things can work out pretty badly if care is not exercised. For 
> example, plotting an hclust object with 1000 leaves can be reasonably fast, 
> but the same analysis cast as a dendrogram object plots exceedingly slowly. I 
> believe this is because of the hierarchically structured representation of 
> the dendrogram object, as opposed to hclust, which is flatter (for the exact 
> same information). Since ergm/statnet/network packages adopt a structured 
> representation of their data object, there may be similar performance 
> problems, but I wouldn't know for sure.
>
> Some general guidelines of use would be, (i) use a utility such as Activity 
> monitor (mac) or top (unix) to keep an eye on the memory usage as you work, 
> (ii) force garbage collection if you need to with gc(), though keep in mind 
> this may not always free up memory, and (iii) save out objects that you are 
> not immediately working with to separate RData files. If you don't do these, 
> in the worst case you can hang your system. Most OS's will allow you to kill 
> the offending process if you get stuck (R), but doing so loses your changes 
> in the data since your last save as well as your command history, so do 
> everything to avoid this and you will be happier.
>
> If you have a system with, say, 2 GB of ram (reasonably standard these days) 
> then for 1M cell matrices you probably will not run into too many problems 
> with memory within R, would be my guess. At the same time, someone from the 
> statnet team should comment on the memory use and time complexity of 
> statnet-specific functions.
>
> Hope this helps,
>
> John Paolillo
> Informatics, Indiana University
>
>> 2. Does ERGM in R enable correcting for underselection of non-existing ties
>> in the way rare event logit (relogit) does it in Stata?
>> 
>> Knowing this would help me a lot. Please advise.
>> 
>> Sincerely,

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Wald test P values vs. AIC/LRTs
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Wald test P values vs. AIC/LRTs
messages.body_plain:
A quick comment --

> I've noticed that interpretation of statistical significance in ERGM
> terms can be extremely different depending on whether you use the Wald
> test (at least, that's what I think they are) P values reported in the
> model summary or compare AICs of nested models; sometimes the addition
> of an extra term contributes virtually nothing to improving the
> likelihood, but the se of the term is very low. Has anyone done any
> simulations for different kinds of dataset in order to come up with
> guidelines?

FWIW, the method used to approximate the log-likelihood is (unless it 
has changed recently) generally less stable than the method used to 
obtain approximate standard errors.  Thus, the log-likelihood estimates 
can be pretty noisy in some cases.  On the other hand, the reported 
standard errors are based on the hessian of the (approximate) 
log-likelihood surface at the MLE, and may or may not represent true SEs 
for the parameters in question.  (Size asymptotics apply in the case of 
independent dyads, but otherwise there are no guarantees -- then again, 
asymptotics don't come with finite-sample guarantees anyway, so you may 
not be losing much.)

The pessimistic view is thus that you have a choice between a noisier 
estimate of a number which has a principled interpretation, or a cleaner 
estimate of a number which has an unprincipled interpretation.  The fact 
that the two choices can lead to different test results is not too 
surprising (although this is cold comfort from a practical standpoint). 
  There is reason to expect that both the noise and the quality of the 
asymptotic approximation will become worse as dyadic dependence 
increases, so taking action to reduce excess dependence (e.g., by using 
covariates where possible) may help.  You can also improve the quality 
of the log-likelihood estimate by increasing the number of simulation 
draws, as well as the number of refinement iterations which are 
performed (see the ergm help).

An alternative to both approaches is to employ a parametric bootstrap, 
as suggested in the recent Hunter and Handcock JCGS paper (unless they 
took it out of the final version).  This is computationally expensive, 
but avoids the assumption of an asymptotically log-quadratic likelihood 
surface.  You can also employ approximate Bayesian inference, e.g., by 
using posterior mode approximations as described in Gelman et al. 
(2004).  I've not done these with ERGMs yet, but have had good luck with 
a related family of models.

That doesn't exactly solve your problem (such is the nature of life at 
the bleeding edge), but perhaps it provides some useful background.  Now 
that we're finally getting a handle on how to parameterize and fit these 
models, I expect that more attention will be turned to problems such as 
these....

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Simulation issues
messages.body_plain:
sdfrost@ucsd.edu wrote:
> Dear Statnet List,
> 
> I'm finally embarking on a simulation study of the statistical properties
> of ERGMs as implemented in statnet. I'm setting up the code to run these
> simulations, but as I did so, I noted some strange things.
> 
> I simulated (sparse) networks of 100 nodes, with an edge parameter of -6.
> Fitting a model with only edges to this worked fine (estimates fell around
> the true value), but when I fitted a model that also included triangles,
> estimates of the triangle parameter followed a bimodal distribution;
> 57/100 simulations had triangle estimates of -12 to -13 (so, effectively
> zero on the antilog scale), whereas 43/100 simulations had triangle
> parameters greater than 0. In addition, the LRT test statistic between the
> null and the alternative model was larger than I expected:
> 
>> sum(unlist(lldiff)*2>3.84)
> [1] 16
>> summary(unlist(lldiff)*2)
>      Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean   3rd Qu.      Max.
>  0.005212  1.253000  2.704000  3.217000  3.429000 26.660000
> 
> Has anyone had any similar experiences with simulated data?
> 

The former is a known phenomenon (at least, if I understand your setup 
correctly).  It is easiest to describe using some simple notation: let G 
be the random graph whose distribution is the ERG defined by parameter 
vector theta and sufficient statistic vector t.  (I'll ignore the 
support for now, since it's mostly irrelevant...take the support of G to 
be all graphs on N vertices, if you like.)  Now, define the mean value 
parameter, tau, as follows:

tau(theta) = E(t(G)|theta)

where E(a|b) is the conditional expectation of a given b.  Clearly, for 
any choice of theta and t on a fixed support, there will be one value of 
tau; what's not so obvious (but true, nonetheless) is that every 
realizable value of tau corresponds to one value of theta.  That is, 
there's a 1:1 mapping between the vector of mean values of the 
sufficient statistics, and the vector of model parameters.

This observation sometimes leads to the misapprehension that the 
distribution of t(G) (here, the edge and triangle counts) will be 
concentrated about tau(theta).  As you have observed, this is not the 
case -- it is possible to get multimodal distributions for t(G) which do 
not cluster tightly about the mean.  In fact, things are worse than 
that: there is no guarantee that _any_ substantial probability mass will 
be found near the tau(theta)!  This is quite striking in the case of the 
MLE, since (for regular families, at least), the MLE satisfies the relation

tau(thetahat) = t(G_obs)

where thetahat is the MLE of theta, and G_obs is the observed network. 
The MLE, then, effectively sets the expected statistics equal to the 
observed statistics under the model (assuming the MLE exists, of 
course).  This is a very nice feature, but is not quite so beneficent as 
it might appear; this is because the model can "cheat," by producing a 
distribution whose mean matches the data, but which nearly always 
generates graphs whose properties are unlike the observed graph.  This 
has been studied extensively by Mark Handcock, who has looked in detail 
at some of the properties which lead models to produce this sort of 
behavior.  It's well worth looking at his work on model degeneracy, if 
you want additional details.

Anyway, what does this have to do with your case?  If I correctly 
understand your strategy, you are taking a model with parameter theta, 
simulating draws from it, and then finding the MLEs for the simulated 
networks.  From the above, it is quite possible that your model produces 
a bimodal distribution of triangle/edge count vectors (triangle terms 
are infamous for this).  Fitting the model to this bimodal graph 
distribution is likely to generate a bimodal distribution of MLEs, whose 
  modes correspond to the modes of the distribution of input statistics. 
  It is also likely that you will get some simulated networks whose 
statistics are on the boundary of the convex hull of possible 
statistics.  In that case, the MLE won't exist at all for some draws.  I 
would also note that some granularity may be expected in the MLE 
distribution when on the edge of the convex hull (especially for small 
graphs), because the "jump" from an expectation of, say, 1 triangle to 
an expectation of 2 triangles may involve a larger shift in the 
parameter space than the jump from 100 triangles to 101 triangles. 
IIRC, Mark has also looked at this, although I can't recall exactly what 
was found.

Hopefully, that helps shed some light on the phenomenon.  Mark and the 
others should certainly chime in if I've mischaracterized the State 'O 
Knowledge on the matter....

-Carter

Dear Statnet Help,

I've noticed that interpretation of statistical significance in ERGM
terms can be extremely different depending on whether you use the Wald
test (at least, that's what I think they are) P values reported in the
model summary or compare AICs of nested models; sometimes the addition
of an extra term contributes virtually nothing to improving the
likelihood, but the se of the term is very low. Has anyone done any
simulations for different kinds of dataset in order to come up with
guidelines?

Best

messages.body_plain:
Martina Morris wrote:
> 
> ---------- Forwarded message ----------
> Date: Sun, 24 Dec 2006 20:37:30 -0800
> From: Denis Trapido <dtrapido@stanford.edu>
> To: morrism@u.washington.edu
> Subject: two yes/no questions on ERGM in R
> 
...
> 1. My network is very large and I heard that ERGM is computation-intensive.
> Is ERG modeling in R feasible for networks of 1000x1000 or larger?

Depends on the terms you employ.  Some of the AddHealth networks are 
larger than that, and I've also run models on some large 
interorganizational interaction networks.  The main issues are:

   1. Making sure you pick terms whose changescores scale well.  Most 
which are in current use are constant or linear time, but this isn't the 
case for all terms (e.g., cycles).

   2. Making sure that the number of parameters and statistics remains 
constrained.  Optimization on 1000+ fixed effects is not pleasant; nor 
are computations for curved models with 1000+ statistics going to scale 
well (unless the way those calculations are internally performed has 
changed recently).

Otherwise, ergm should work just fine -- especially if the graph is sparse.

> 
> 2. Does ERGM in R enable correcting for underselection of non-existing ties
> in the way rare event logit (relogit) does it in Stata?
> 

I don't see that this would be relevant here, but Mark or Dave might 
have other ideas.  (BTW, these are not logit models, except in the case 
of independent dyads.  Or, if you like, the whole thing is a huge 
multinomial logit with one observation, but that's another matter...)

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Computational time required by netlogit
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Paola -

Criscuolo, Paola wrote:
> Dear statnet users,
> 
> I am trying to estimate a QAP model with a binary network as a dependent 
> variable using the command netlogit with the double semi-partialling 
> method. I have 435 nodes and 9 independent variables. I have estimated 
> the same model using UCINET routine for the same permutation method and 
> the valued network as dependent variable. The computation time in UCINET 
> was around 1 hour with 2000 permutations but the netlogit estimation is 
> taking more than 5 hours with 1000 permutations.
> Is this normal? Would you advice me to use a different permutation 
> method with netlogit?
> 

That kind of procedure is always going to be slow on a 10x435x435 array, 
and the netlogit routine is not built for speed.  In terms of alternate 
permutation methods, there's not much theory at this point (of which I 
am aware) on the properties of these test procedures in the logistic 
regression case; so, caveat emptor.  I would probably opt for a network 
permutation model (see the netperm package) under these circumstances, 
myself, but it depends on what you want to infer....

-Carter

> i have read over the set.vertex.attributes help file, but am still not 
> sure exactly how to do this type of work from a file...
> (i assume i use the read.table function in some way, but i'm not 
> entirely sure)
>  
> thanks for the help, sorry i'm being dense...

Here's one way to do it:

dat<-read.table("myfile",header=T)
for(i in 1:NROL(dat))
   mynet%v%names(dat)[i]<-dat[,i]

This assumes that you have a header row in "myfile" and that your 
network is called "mynet."  Other variants are possible.  (In fact, you 
can do this in one line, using an apply function....)

Hi, Caroline -

Caroline Buckee wrote:
> Dear Statnet help,
> 
> I have been having a problem with network visualization while using 
> statnet and I can't find any threads on R postings that are relevant so 
> I thought I would ask you, even though it might be a network package 
> problem.
> 
> Whenever I try to plot networks with different edge colours, given as a 
> matrix, the edges are suddenly pastel shades and a different style. Even 
> if I try plot(network, edge.col=matrix, edge.lty=0) the edges will be 
> pastel colors. I have looked in the documentation and can't find why 
> this is and the edge.lty and edge.lwd commands don't seem to work. Have 
> you come across this problem and do you know how I could fix it?
> 
> I'm running R Version 2.4.0 GUI 1.17 (3868), network package Version 
> 1.1-1, sna version 1.3, and statnet Version 1.0-11, on a Mac PowerBook G4.
> 
> Thank you. I'd really appreciate some advice...
> 

I haven't seen this problem before; it doesn't seem to be affecting my 
installation.  Can you post a snippet of the offending code?

Thanks,

-Carter

PS. The lty argument to plot.network/gplot controls the line type for 
the border of the edge, not the edge itself.  (Edges are actually drawn 
as very thin polygons, for fascinating but suitably arcane reasons which 
need not concern us here.)  In some cases, however, the polygons may be 
so thin that only the outer line is visible -- thus can one obtain the 
effect of dotted edges without actually drawing them as such.  In any 
event, lty=0 does not mean "draw no edges," at least not since sna 
version 0.5 or thereabouts (when the new gplot was introduced).  Those 
who are interested should take a look at gplot.arrow/network.arrow and 
polygon to see how the code is written.

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] is there a statnet version compiled for a 64 bit linux machine?
messages.body_plain:
Hank Green wrote:

> hi statnet team...

>  

> i'm trying to set up statnet on our new 64 bit Linux machine and run 

> into this error:

>  

> "Error: package 'statnet' was built for i686-pc-linux-gnu"

> 

> is there a solution? we considered installing a 32 bit version of R so 

> that we can use statnet but wondered if there was another solution. for 

> example, is there a statnet version compiled for 64 bit machines?

>  



In principle, there is no obstacle to using statnet on a 64-bit machine. 

  However, you'll need to install the package from source, rather than 

use the 32-bit binary package (whence came the error).  I've 

successfully installed sna from source on an Opteron, and IIRC there 

weren't any complications.  I don't think I installed the other statnet 

components at that time, but they should work in the same manner.



To install packages from source under Linux, you'll need to use the command



R CMD INSTALL mypackagefile



where "mypackagefile" is the file containing the source package. 

Assuming you want to do this for the whole system, you'll need root 

access; you can install to a local library directory, however, if you're 

acting as a regular user.  (See R CMD INSTALL --help and/or the R man 

page for details.)  It is also possible to do this with install.packages 

from within R, and indeed that is the default option (where available). 

  Usually, this process is entirely transparent, although things can 

occasionally go wrong (e.g., the compiled code turns out not to be fully 

portable to your platform).  The statnet backends are pretty vanilla 

ANSI stuff, and hence I expect few problems.



Let us know if you need those source packages, and we should be able to 

hook you up....



-Carter



PS. Clearly, we "need" a new 64-bit server....for testing purposes only, 

of course!  ;-)

messages.body_plain:
Brian Rubineau wrote:

> Dear Statner Sages,

> I'm attaching my network as an R-image.

> It has 105 nodes and 1337 edges (density=0.245), and is named ta2.

> when i run:

> ta_plain<-ergm(ta2~edges)

> the resulting coefficient is -2.062.

> Turning this into a probability:

> 

> Shouldn't the coefficient for this ergm yield a

> probability equal to the network density?

> 

> What am i missing?

>

Based on your density calculations, I am assuming that this is an 

undirected graph?  In that case, you need to be sure to set 

directed=FALSE when creating your network object; the results you are 

now obtaining appear to be consistent with what you would expect for a 

digraph of order 105 with 1337 edges (which is what you'll get if you 

leave directed=TRUE).  Check this, and let us know if the issue persists.



BTW, it would be helpful if petitioners would 1) report the versions of 

R and the statnet packages they are using, and 2) include a short R 

script which will regenerate the problem.  Please do _not_ include large 

attachments (e.g., Rdata files), since this will flood readers' inboxes 

and anger various eldritch powers who must not be named.



Hope that helps,



-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] FAQ: Installing and Updating "statnet" procedure.
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,



This posting is describes the procedure to install and update to the current

version of "statnet".



A new installation involves two main steps: downloading R, and then

installing the "statnet" package within R.  Those of you who already have

the most recent version of R (2.3.1) may skip over Step 1 of the

instructions. Those with a previous version of R, please be sure to follow

Step 1 in order to update.



****************************************

Step 1.  Downloading R version 2.3.1:



a.  Go to http://cran.r-project.org/, and select Mirrors from the left-hand

menu.



b.  Select a location near you.



c.  From the "Download and Install R" section, select the link for your

operating system.  Follow the instructions on the relevant page.  Note that

you need to download only the base distribution, not the contributed

packages.



d.  Once you've downloaded the installation file, follow the instructions

for installation.





****************************************

2.  Downloading and installing "statnet":



a.  Open the version of R that you've just installed (method varies by

platform but is fairly typical on each).



b.  First you need to install the "statnet" installer. At the R cursor,

type:



install.packages("updatestatnet",

contriburl="http://csde.washington.edu/statnet")



c.  Now, and in the future, you can update "statnet" at any point using the

installer. To do this, at the R cursor, type:



library(updatestatnet)



d.  Follow the directions; feel free to say no to any optional

(recommended) packages, although we recommend saying yes.





****************************************

3.  If you have time, we recommend that you familiarize yourself with the

basics of R, although this is not required.  A good place for doing so is

by using any one of the many R tutorials at:



http://cran.r-project.org/other-docs.html



****************************************

There is much more information available on the "statnet" website:



http://csde.washington.edu/statnet



****************************************

If you have problems installing, or other issues arise, email

"statnet_help at u.washington.edu"



The "statnet" team



Mark S. Handcock <handcock at stat.washington.edu>

David R. Hunter <dhunter at stat.psu.edu>

Carter T. Butts <buttsc at uci.edu>

Steven M. Goodreau <goodreau at u.washington.edu>

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Feature Request
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

Thanks for the suggestions. We are in the process of adding a lot of
features in preparation for the Workshop at this year's Sunbelt Conference
in Corfu (http://nicomedia.math.upatras.gr/conf/Sunbelt2007).

These are good ideas and we have updated "statnet" to version 1.0-14 to
accommodate them. Explicitly:

1) To force the use of the MCMC algorithm for dyad independence models, give
the option "force.mcmc" e.g.,

fit <- ergm(flomarriage ~ edges, algorithm.control=list(force.mcmc=T))

2) There is a new summary command called "Summary.ergm" that returns all the
objects it prints. For example,

# The usual summary
Summary.ergm(fit)
# Save the results
out <- Summary.ergm(fit)
names(out)
out$aic
out$asycov

out

This will be made the default is an upcoming version.

To get the new version, as usual, enter:

library(updatestatnet)

Mark

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Simulation issues - the curse of degeneracy
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Simulation issues - the curse of degeneracy
messages.body_plain:
Hi Simon, I'll add a little to Carter's great response.  Yes, it sounds to 
me like you're running into the classic degeneracy problem, as Carter 
pointed out.  In my own simulations I've found that the triangle 
parameterization almost always leads to degeneracy in anything but the 
smallest of networks.  Mark Handcock's book chapter and working paper on 
degeneracy are the places to start for a deeper understanding (to find 
them, searching on Handcock and degeneracy in Google Scholar should get 
you to everything).

It is precisely this problem that led to the development of new 
parameterizations for network statistics that can capture triangle closure 
and other dyadic-depedent processes, but in a non-degenerate way.  These 
are explained in an article by Snijders et al that just came out in 
Sociological Meythodology.  Hunter and Handcock have a Penn State 
Statistics working paper that further develops them, and then there's a 
special issue of Social Networks coming out with a cluster of papers that 
explains and applies them to some examples.  So no shortage of stuff to 
read on the topic - just very little that's already appeared in the 
literature, unfortunately!

Most of the relevant unpublished articles appear as working papers either 
at UW, Penn State, Melbourne, or Gronigen.  Which suggests to me that we 
really should have an up-to-date page that links to all of them from the 
Statnet webpage.

Hope that helps,
Steve

  * Steven M. Goodreau / Assistant Professor / Dept. of Anthropology     *
  * University of Washington / Denny Hall 140 / Campus Box 353100        *
  * Seattle WA 98195 / 1-206-685-3870 (phone)/ 1-206-543-3285 (fax)      *
  * http://faculty.washington.edu/goodreau                               *

On Sat, 27 Jan 2007, Carter T. Butts wrote:

> sdfrost@ucsd.edu wrote:
>> Dear Statnet List,
>> 
>> I'm finally embarking on a simulation study of the statistical properties
>> of ERGMs as implemented in statnet. I'm setting up the code to run these
>> simulations, but as I did so, I noted some strange things.
>> 
>> I simulated (sparse) networks of 100 nodes, with an edge parameter of -6.
>> Fitting a model with only edges to this worked fine (estimates fell around
>> the true value), but when I fitted a model that also included triangles,
>> estimates of the triangle parameter followed a bimodal distribution;
>> 57/100 simulations had triangle estimates of -12 to -13 (so, effectively
>> zero on the antilog scale), whereas 43/100 simulations had triangle
>> parameters greater than 0. In addition, the LRT test statistic between the
>> null and the alternative model was larger than I expected:
>> 
>>> sum(unlist(lldiff)*2>3.84)
>> [1] 16
>>> summary(unlist(lldiff)*2)
>>      Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean   3rd Qu.      Max.
>>  0.005212  1.253000  2.704000  3.217000  3.429000 26.660000
>> 
>> Has anyone had any similar experiences with simulated data?
>> 
>
> The former is a known phenomenon (at least, if I understand your setup 
> correctly).  It is easiest to describe using some simple notation: let G be 
> the random graph whose distribution is the ERG defined by parameter vector 
> theta and sufficient statistic vector t.  (I'll ignore the support for now, 
> since it's mostly irrelevant...take the support of G to be all graphs on N 
> vertices, if you like.)  Now, define the mean value parameter, tau, as 
> follows:
>
> tau(theta) = E(t(G)|theta)
>
> where E(a|b) is the conditional expectation of a given b.  Clearly, for any 
> choice of theta and t on a fixed support, there will be one value of tau; 
> what's not so obvious (but true, nonetheless) is that every realizable value 
> of tau corresponds to one value of theta.  That is, there's a 1:1 mapping 
> between the vector of mean values of the sufficient statistics, and the 
> vector of model parameters.
>
> This observation sometimes leads to the misapprehension that the distribution 
> of t(G) (here, the edge and triangle counts) will be concentrated about 
> tau(theta).  As you have observed, this is not the case -- it is possible to 
> get multimodal distributions for t(G) which do not cluster tightly about the 
> mean.  In fact, things are worse than that: there is no guarantee that _any_ 
> substantial probability mass will be found near the tau(theta)!  This is 
> quite striking in the case of the MLE, since (for regular families, at 
> least), the MLE satisfies the relation
>
> tau(thetahat) = t(G_obs)
>
> where thetahat is the MLE of theta, and G_obs is the observed network. The 
> MLE, then, effectively sets the expected statistics equal to the observed 
> statistics under the model (assuming the MLE exists, of course).  This is a 
> very nice feature, but is not quite so beneficent as it might appear; this is 
> because the model can "cheat," by producing a distribution whose mean matches 
> the data, but which nearly always generates graphs whose properties are 
> unlike the observed graph.  This has been studied extensively by Mark 
> Handcock, who has looked in detail at some of the properties which lead 
> models to produce this sort of behavior.  It's well worth looking at his work 
> on model degeneracy, if you want additional details.
>
> Anyway, what does this have to do with your case?  If I correctly understand 
> your strategy, you are taking a model with parameter theta, simulating draws 
> from it, and then finding the MLEs for the simulated networks.  From the 
> above, it is quite possible that your model produces a bimodal distribution 
> of triangle/edge count vectors (triangle terms are infamous for this). 
> Fitting the model to this bimodal graph distribution is likely to generate a 
> bimodal distribution of MLEs, whose  modes correspond to the modes of the 
> distribution of input statistics.  It is also likely that you will get some 
> simulated networks whose statistics are on the boundary of the convex hull of 
> possible statistics.  In that case, the MLE won't exist at all for some 
> draws.  I would also note that some granularity may be expected in the MLE 
> distribution when on the edge of the convex hull (especially for small 
> graphs), because the "jump" from an expectation of, say, 1 triangle to an 
> expectation of 2 triangles may involve a larger shift in the parameter space 
> than the jump from 100 triangles to 101 triangles. IIRC, Mark has also looked 
> at this, although I can't recall exactly what was found.
>
> Hopefully, that helps shed some light on the phenomenon.  Mark and the others 
> should certainly chime in if I've mischaracterized the State 'O Knowledge on 
> the matter....
>
> -Carter

messages.body_plain:
Hi Simon,

I have noticed similar effects like this at times, and have considered 
that I should at some point explore it more deeply.  Others on the statnet 
team can probably answer this more rigorously, but in my own casual use I 
tend to be more interested in the p-values than in the AIC or other model 
likelihood measures, since the former seem to be more stable across 
multiple repeated runs on the same data, for what seem like reasonable 
chain lengths.  We're looking at other measures of goodness of fit in 
terms of the degree to which models capture various network statistics 
that are not includedin the model.  However, I'm not aware of anyone 
delving very deeply into the question you asked specifically.  Perhaps you 
could take the first stab?

Cheers,
Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ergm(net~edges) is not yielding density
messages.body_plain:
Hi Brian,



Thanks for the message. 



The problem appears to be that the network was created from a 
sociomatrix

with diagonal 1's. That is, all actors have self-ties, but the "loops" 
option to network is not set. Thus the network object is not stored in a 
self-consistent way.



To fix it you can do something like:



ta2.loops <- ta2[,]

diag(ta2.loops) <- 0

ta2.noloops <- network(ta2.loops, directed=F)



and then add the covariates back.



I hope this helps!



Mark

eln <- network(el)

On Tue, 2006-10-31 at 09:32, Steven Goodreau wrote:
> Hi Simon,
> 
> I have noticed similar effects like this at times, and have considered 
> that I should at some point explore it more deeply.  Others on the statnet 
> team can probably answer this more rigorously, but in my own casual use I 
> tend to be more interested in the p-values than in the AIC or other model 
> likelihood measures, since the former seem to be more stable across 
> multiple repeated runs on the same data, for what seem like reasonable 
> chain lengths.

I'm just not used to seeing Wald test P values that are soooo different
from doing LRTs (e.g. P<0.0001 for Wald, and P>0.1 for LRT). It might be
nice to tweak profile() in MASS to work with ergm objects to investigate
this further.

> We're looking at other measures of goodness of fit in 
> terms of the degree to which models capture various network statistics 
> that are not includedin the model.  However, I'm not aware of anyone 
> delving very deeply into the question you asked specifically.  Perhaps you 
> could take the first stab?

play with some simulated data to characterize type I and type II errors
for different kinds of network. We've got a ton of computing power down
here, so we could probably do a reasonable job. The tricky part is

messages.subject: [statnet_help] setting attributes of a single edge
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] setting attributes of a single edge
messages.body_plain:
As Mark pointed out, this is an internal development question.  However, 

I will cc: the response to statnet_help, since I suspect that some of 

the folks there will find some of this to be of use.  In general, 

development questions should be kept out of statnet_help, to avoid 

deluging everyone with a lot of inside baseball.  :-)



Skye Bender-deMoll wrote:

> hi folks,

>   Ok, maybe this is a stupid question, but if I want to set an attribute 

> of an edge between vertices i and j is the only way to do it:

> 

> set.edge.attribute(myNetwork,"myAttribute",value=myValue,get.edgeIDs(myNetwork,i,alter=j)) 

> 



That's the direct way, but not the only way to accomplish this.



> 

> 

> I realize that it is a complicated operation because there may be 

> directed and/or multiple edges between i and j, but maybe we should have 

> a basic default form?  It is confusing when you can assign to all edges 

> with

> 

>  myNetwork%e%"myAttribute" <- myVal

> 

> Something that uses the same conventions as the myNetwork[i,j] 

> assignment?  Or maybe we just need to add an example and some more 

> explanation to the attribute methods man page.  The edge ID lookup makes 

> sense once you understand it, but it isn't clear from looking at the man 

> for set.edge.attribute how you can discover the edge ids.

> 

> thoughts?

> 



Well, I am sure that it wouldn't hurt to add more docs to the man page 

re: dealing with edge IDs.  You are correct that they are needed because 

of multiplex networks (since there is no other way to keep track of 

which edge is which)....their usage can be a bit arcane, and it is 

possible that the current documentation does not provide enough detail 

on the matter.  I'll add that to my TODO file for the next release.



That said, I should note that you do not have to use the long-form 

syntax to achieve this goal in most settings.  The syntax



g[i,j,names.eval="boo"]<-val



will assign val to an attribute named "boo" for every i,j edge in g.  By 

default, this will not add new edges to the graph, although this 

behavior can be changed using the add.edges argument.  (See the 

network.extraction man page for details.)  This syntax can be adapted in 

the usual manner to, say, set values for all edges incident upon a given 

vertex, and so forth.  I suspect that this will solve your problem.



> P.S.  maybe we should also add an example and a "see also" for get.edge 

> to the main network man page.  It is a little hard to find without 

> looking through the whole package listing.



I like Mark's "getting started" page for statnet...it seems to me that 

something of that form might be added for the next release.  Such a page 

would be the appropriate spot for pointers of the form you suggest.



Again, apologies to the statnet_help folks for the development 

discussion (though I think that some will appreciate the names.eval 

trick).  Follow-ups should go off-list.



Enjoy,



-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] MPLE and large networks/models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kevin.  Just wanted to give you an update.  I hope you don't mind  
I'm forwarding this to the list; I thought others might find this  
discussion helpful.  (A bit of background for others:  Kevin is trying  
to fit an ERGM with 71 terms on a directed network with 736 nodes.   
Four of the 71 terms are "gw" terms like gwidegree etc.)

One problem that your example was causing is that it could not even  
fit an MPLE.  This is because it is a large network and you are using  
a large number of terms.  The former means means that the number of  
dyads is large; and the combination of the two means that number of  
unique rows in the matrix of change statistics (when considering a  
change in every single dyad in the network) is also very large.  We  
had written a very simplistic algorithm -- really only meant as a  
stopgap but then forgotten about, sort of like what caused the whole  
Y2K problem :) -- to check for unique rows, and it was getting  
completely bogged down by your model / network combination.  We also  
had placed a ceiling on the max number of rows, 100K, which your model/ 
network combo was exceeding and this is what I think was part of what  
led to the errors you obtained.  (Note:  Now the ceiling is a miillion  
but this can be adjusted using control.ergm(maxNumDyadTypes=xxx))

Pavel has now replaced the old row-checking algorithm, so now it works  
much faster.  However, the problem still remains that with your  
network and the model you have chosen, almost each of the 500K+  
possible dyad changes gives a unique value for the 71-dimensional  
change statistic vector.  As a result, the logistic regression used to  
find the MPLE (which is then used as the starting value for the MCMC  
MLE routine) has to deal with an enormous covariate matrix.

Actually, it turns out that there are "only" 458362 unique rows (out  
of 736*735 = 540960 possible), which means that the covariate  
(predictor) matrix for the logistic regression is 458362 x 71.  To  
find the MPLE, we use the "glm" function of R.  It turns out that this  
function is not very good with very large covariate matrices, so just  
trying to find the MPLE made my machine choke.  This is not a problem  
with ergm, which found the 458362 x 71 matrix very quickly with the  
new code; it is (I think) the fact that glm can't seem to handle a  
matrix this large.  So I guess this is sort of bad news -- we don't  
plan to rewrite "glm", which would be a lot of work, so we have to  
live with its limitations in the absence of something better.

Note, however, that simplifying the model makes a big difference in  
the number of unique rows.  For instance, can you do without some of  
the four GW terms?  These really increase the number of rows  
dramatically, since their change statistics are real-valued variables  
(as opposed to integers, which allow for lots of duplication).

Alternatively, you could try avoiding the MPLE altogether by giving an  
explicit starting value for the parameters via the "theta0" argument  
to ergm, but this is pretty hard to do without any guidance.  One  
thing that might work, though:  Fit an MPLE using all but the four gw  
terms.  Then take those parameter estimates, tack on four zeros for  
the gw terms, and use the resulting vector as the starting value for  
the MCMC MLE routine.  This should avoid the big problems with glm.  I  
tried this, and in fact it seemed to work, or at least it ran (I  
didn't check the results too thoroughly).  I'll send you the code I  
used in a separate email.

Dave

PS.  Of course, this code assumes ergm 2.0-7, a beta version of which  
(source code only) is at http://www.stat.psu.edu/~dhunter/code/

tools apparently lack a Fortran compiler. Here is some text from the
JAGS 0.90 manual (http://www-fis.iarc.fr/~martyn/software/jags/manual.pdf):


> A.2.4 Mac OS X: instructions from Bill Northcott If trying to build
> software on Mac OS X you really need to use Tiger (10.4.x) or Panther
>  (10.3.x). The open source support has improved greatly in recent
> releases. You also need the latest version of Apple?s Xcode
> development tools. These are available as a free download from 
> http://developer.apple.com. You need to set up a free login to ADC.
> The Apple developer tools do not include a Fortran compiler. Without
> Fortran, you will not be able to build libRmath. The GNU g77 Fortran
> compiler is included in the R binary distribution available on CRAN.
> Install the R binary and select ?GNU Fortran?, and ?Tcl/Tk? from
> the optional components in the customize step of the installer. 
> IMPORTANT for Tiger (10.4.x) users: The default C/C++ compiler for
> Tiger is gcc-4. This is not compatible with g77. Before trying to
> build anything using g77, the default compiler must be changed with
> the command sudo gcc_select 3.3. (It won?t hurt to do this on Panther
>  as well.) gcc-4 uses a new Fortran compiler known as gfortran. This
> should be usable in the near future, but for the moment some hacking
> would be required.

I don't know if this is still true but it would explain why you can't 
load statnet.so, and you are using gcc 4.0...

messages.subject: [statnet_help] interpreting GWESP
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kevin,

A wonderful question.  Interpretation of GWESP can be complex and subtle - 
every time I work with it for a sustained period, I find new ways of 
thinking about it.  At some point, if I ever find the time (ha!) I'd love 
to write it all out (along with my thoughts on GWDSP and perhaps GWD) into 
a paper.

In the meanwhile, it's important to note that the interpretation is not as 
straightforward as you lay out. The number of triangles that the edge will 
close matters, so one component of the change in log-odds involves this. 
But one needs to think of things from the point of view of the other two 
ties in each of those triangles that will be close.  The number of 
triangles that each of them is in will also change, and that will affect 
the log-odds of the first tie as well.  Ive never sat down and put it all 
into a single formula for specifying the logodds as a function of these 
different quantities, but it shoulnd't be complicated. Unfortunately, 
it'll never be quite as straightforward as many other commonly used 
statistics.

I hope that helps!
Steve




> greetings,
>
> i am wondering if there is a straightforward formula that can be used to 
> interpret the GWESP coefficient, together with the weight parameter, in more 
> commonsense language? in other words, i am looking for a way to interpret the 
> coefficient in a manner that is comparable to the other terms in the model, 
> by saying, for instance, that if a tie closes a SINGLE triangle, then the 
> log-odds of that tie forming increases by X, if a tie closes only TWO 
> triangles, then the log-odds of that tie forming increases by Y, etc etc 
> (thus, i would be able to directly compare the likelihood of such ties to, 
> say, a tie that symmetrizes a dyad or a tie that is racially homophilous). is 
> there an easy way to determine such log-odds, then, as a function of a) the 
> coefficient, b) the weight parameter, and c) the number of triangles that the 
> tie will form? (as goodreau et al. do in 'birds of a feather,' i think- 
> hunter 2007 also includes something comparable.)
>
> thanks greatly!
>
> -kevin
>
> --

messages.subject: [statnet_dev] RE: [statnet_help] Degeneracy problem
messages.body_plain:
Hello Jichao,

Yes, from my own experience, I find that as a whole models do seem to be more 
likely to experience degeneracy when applied to larger networks than smaller 
ones.  I personally would only suggest selecting out subsets of your data if 
you have a valid scientific reason for doing so; otherwise I'd recommend 
thinking of degeneracy as a sign that your model is not appropriate to the 
data, and keep hunting.

The degeneracy warning that sometimes appears at the end of an ergm is a bit of 
a blunt instrument, and we're working to refine it.  A much better way to 
diagnose degeneracy at this point is to examine the MCMC diagnostics. 
Instructions for doing so, and how to interpret the resulting plots, can be 
found in Section 6 of the statnet tutorial that is now published in JSS:

http://www.jstatsoft.org/v24/i09

Good luck!
Steve

On Wed, Feb 20, 2008 at 12:08 PM, Steven Goodreau <goodreau@u.washington.edu>
wrote:

>
> Hi Jenine,
>
> Because your model contains only "dyadic-independence" terms,
> interpretation is relatively straightforward. I will outline it below, but
> you should definitely turn to the Social Networks special issue (Vol 29,
> issue 2) or the JoSS special issue (currently available as the "Online
> Users Guide" at statnetproject.org) for more background.
>
> The ERGM model is a logit model, so that coefficients are interpretable as
> additions to the logodds.  The ERGM model can be interpreted either in
> terms of the probability of a given edge or arc existing, or in terms of
> the probability of an entire network being observed; let's use the former,
> since it's generally more intuitive.
>
> In this framework, to get the logodds of a given edge/arc (given the rest
> of the network), you multiply each "change statistic" by its corresponding
> coefficient, and then add these terms together.  A "change statistic" is
> the amount by which any of the statistics in your model changes when you
> add the new edge/arc.
>
> So, for instance, your model is:
>
> > y ~ edges + nodefactor(grade) + nodefactor(age group) +
> nodematch(gender)
>
> If I make up coefficient values of
>
> edges = -5.1
> nodefactor.grade08 = 0.3
> nodefactor.grade09 = 0.2
> nodefactor.agegroup01 = 0.4
> nodefactor.agegroup02 = 0.8
> nodematch.gender = 2.1
>
> Then, the logodds of an edge or arc (in either direction) between a
> male/grade8/agegroup1 and a female/grade8/agegroup2 would be:
>
> -5.1(1) + 0.3(2) + 0.4(1) 0.8(1) = -3.3
>
> since by forming this edge/arc, the total number of edges/arcs increases
> by 1, the total degree for all grade 8 actors increases by 2, the total
> degree for age group 1 actors increases by 1, and the total degree for all
> age group 2 actors increases by 1.
>
> If the same two actors had been of the same sex instead of different
> sexes, then the logodds would increase by 2.1 (since the number of
> same-sex edges would increase by 1), bringing the logodds to -1.2.
>
> The probabilities corresponding to logodds of -3.3 and -1.2 are .036 and
> .23, respectively.
>
> If you have a dyadic dependence model (i.e. with terms like triangle or
> degree), then interpretation gets slightly more complex, because you need
> to know about the other edges/arcs in the network to know how likely a
> given edge/arc is.
>
> I hope this helps.
>
> Cheers,
> Steve
>
>
>
>

Sent: Friday, April 18, 2008 4:50 PM
To: Zembower, Kevin

Subject: Re: [statnet_help] Newbie: doubled edges in undirected network?

Zembower, Kevin wrote:
> Is my confusion just due to my inexperience with SNA and modern
> definitions of terms like 'degree' and the way the sna package is
> deliberately designed, or should the output above for Medici be 6?

Per the man page, the degree() command returns the total (aka "Freeman")

degree by default; as also noted on the man page, 
indegree=outdegree=total degree/2 for simple graphs.  Thus, the output 
for Medici is correct.  If you want to get the graph theoretic degree, 
you can either choose "indegree" or "outdegree," or else divide the 
return value by 2.

With respect to "doubled edges" with usecurv=T, this is just the way 
that the curved edge option handles mutual dyads: they are always 
displayed with an arc going in each direction, to emphasize the fact 
that the dyad is mutual.  In an undirected graph, of course, all dyads 
are either mutual (arc in each direction) or null (no arcs) -- the way 
this is drawn is a display convention, and doesn't suggest anything deep

or mysterious about your structure.  Generally, there's no reason to use

usecurv with undirected graphs, but the option is left available for 
those who prefer to display their structure in this manner.

Hope that clarifies things,

-Carter

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] How to asses convergence a possible bug
messages.body_plain:
> Can anyone give me quick pointers on how to asses it the convergence of the 
> ergm model is good. I have used the function mcmc.diagnostics, but am not

Hello Ales,

A great question.  It turns out that we (the statnet development team) are 
in the process of putting together a special journal issue on statnet, and 
there will be some more guidance in there on assessing model convergence 
(as well as many other topics - stay tuned!)

My own personal set of heuristics for considering model convergence is as 
follows:

(1) Using the verbose=T argument in ergm, check to see whether the density 
of the returned network is roughly the same as the density of the initial 
network for each iteration of the fitting algorithm.  If the network is 
heading towards an empty or full network, this will be a sure sign of 
problems.  Of course if you are using an MCMC proposal that fixes density, 
this is not an option.

(2) Check the MCMC diagnostic plots.  The plots on the left should have no 
sustained trend away from their original value.  There will certainly 
be short-term trends (such is the nature of MCMC) but in the long-term it 
should vary around the oringial value.  The plots on the right should be 
centered around the original value, and will generally be unimodal if all 
is well.

(3) Check the log-likelihood ratio that is printed out with each iteration 
of the fitting algorithm.  A small value (often less than 1) is good.  If 
it starts creeping up towards 20 (which is where the software caps 
estimating it) then there is likely to be a problem.

(4) Within the verbose output, look for the summary of the simluation.  In 
the later iterations, the values for "mean" should be close to zero, and 
the std. t units should also be low, or at least declining with successive 
iterations.  This tells you how far away your simulated statistics are 
from your observed statistics.

Generally I find that the results from these different measures have a 
high degree of concordance - if one shows a problem, they all do.  So one 
doesn't necessarily have to check all, but collectively they can give you 
a very good sense whether your model convergence is good or not.

> Are there any other options. Are there any suggestions what can be done 
> besides selecting better starting values, increasing MCMC sample size and 
> selecting terms that are not correlated?

I am a big fan of using TNT for the proposal type instead of 
constantedges.  That plus a large MCMC sample size, should help in most 
cases where the model is a good one.  The new version of statnet to be 
released soon will have additional aids to convergence as well.

> Somethimes, when I run "mcmc.diagnostics", I get "NaN" for some terms in the 
> correlations and the convergence statistics is missing for these terms. These 
> are the same terms that have NA for MCMC s.e. in summary output.  What does 
> this mean.

Could you send an example?

> Aslo, when I sepcify theta0 (starting values that are therefore not estimated 
> using maximum pseudo-likelihood ), I get the following error when I run the 
> summary on ergm object:
> "Error in -object$mplefit$hessian : invalid argument to unary operator"
> Probably because the ergm object does not have the element "mplefit".

Thanks for letting us know - we'll look into it and fix any bugs.

Cheers,
Steve

Hi Jenine,

A great question.  We really should make some tweaks to the print.gofoject 
function so that it only prints the lines up until everything equals 0. 
We don't need you to see 1,877 lines to know that none of the nodes in 
your simulations have degrees above 10 or so!

In the meanwhile, you can do it yourself by using the command:

gofobject$summary.nameofgofstat[linestoinclude,]

for any gof statistic of interest.  You can get the names of the gof stats 
by typing "print.gofobject" in R to look inside the print.gofobject 
function.

So for instance, if you just want to see the first 20 lines of the degree 
distrubtions, and your gof object is named model11gof, type:

model11gof$summary.deg[1:20,]

Cheers,
Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Re: degeneracy with new version ERGM
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Re: degeneracy with new version ERGM
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Art -

Art Poon wrote:
> Dear Statnet developers and users,
> 
> We are trying to analyze an epidemiological network that is somewhat 
> sparse and highly clustered.  Using a previous version of Statnet, we've 
> obtained reasonably good fits with only 'edges' and 'triangle' terms in 
> the model (validated via network simulation) that we sought to improve 
> by implementing new user terms.
> 
> However, using the recent build of ergm and R, the same model now 
> exhibits tremendous degeneracy.  Has anyone else experienced apparently 
> 'worse' performance with the newer package?  We are secretly hoping that 
> this is simply due to 'growing pains' in the current iteration of 
> statnet, instead of being sent back to square one.
> 

The parameter space of the edge/triangle model has a very small 
non-degenerate region, so it is plausible that your issues stem from 
being close to the boundary of a phase transition (where tiny deviations 
due to numerical or other factors can produce substantial differences in 
behavior).  I would strongly recommend simulating draws from the model 
for a gridded region in the vicinity of your estimate(s), and examining 
the qualitative behavior of the system -- for instance, by plotting the 
mean edge and triangle statistics -- across the region of interest. 
(Mark has some nice plots of this kind in his degeneracy papers, and the 
approach is sadly underutilized.)  If your data falls near a region of 
degeneracy, then you should consider the possibility that the model is 
too unstable to be socially realistic -- unless, of course, you are 
willing to posit a sort of "fine tuning" hypothesis for your social 
system.  (There are probably circumstances in which such a hypothesis 
would be appropriate, but I doubt this is one of them.)

As a side note, I would also suggest checking (if you haven't already) 
to be sure that your MCMC is mixing properly, and that it has burned in 
adequately.  Mixing can slow down drastically when one approaches a 
region of "frozen" behavior, and initially salubrious results are 
sometimes found to be the result of insufficient burn-in.  By analogy, 
think of putting hot water in a freezer at 0 degrees Celsius: if you 
check on it after only a few minutes, you will find it to be quite 
liquid; a few hours later, however, it is frozen solid.  A very naive 
observer making only the former observation (and lacking the means to 
inspect the water temperature directly) might erroneously conclude that 
water does not freeze at 0 degrees Celsius -- the error, of course, 
would result from the fact that the system was initially far from 
equilibrium, and was observed before equilibrium was reached.  In the 
ERG case, the "hot water" corresponds to the initial network state, 
which may in fact be very "hot" relative to the MLE for the proposed 
model.  (Since the ERG parameters are essentially inverse temperatures, 
the analogy is quite close.)  As the MCMC evolves, the initially "hot" 
state may then "cool," in extreme cases locking into a very narrow range 
of configurations (which we experience as "degeneracy").  A degenerate 
model is "frozen" in equilibrium, but this equilibrium still takes time 
to reach; if we observe the state of the system before the MCMC has 
burned in, we may find that the system still exhibits quite a lot of 
non-degenerate behavior, and may thus erroneously conclude that the 
model is not actually degenerate.  As with our thought experiment, 
drawing the right conclusion depends on first allowing the system to 
equilibrate.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] actor specific random effects
messages.body_plain:
Hello dear all,

I want to estimate a logit model of link formation in the random  
effects tradition. I assume that when actor-specific effects (e.g. a_i  
is effect for actor i) are given, link formation becomes independent  
from the rest of the network. The actor-specific effects are assumed  
to be uncorrelated with covariates. The LOGIT MODEL can be written as:

Prob(y_ij = 1|x_ij,beta,a_i,a_j) = exp(x_ij' %*% beta + a_i + a_j)/ (1  
+ exp(x_ij' %*% beta + a_i + a_j))

, where y_ij = y_ji = 1 if i has link with j, x_ij dyad covariates,  
beta are coefficients and the actor specific effects a_i are  
distributed iid Normal(0,sig^2).

The usual way is to integrate out the a's for estimation. This case is  
special because integration needs to be done over the whole quality  
function not only the contribution of one observation (one firm-pair).

As OPTIMIZATION EXAMPLE take MLE, where the likelihood of one network would be

L(Y | X,beta,a_1,...,a_n) = Product_(i=1)_(n-1) ( Product_(j=i+1)_(n)  
( Prob(y_ij = 1|x_ij,beta,a_i,a_j)))

and optimization should be done for L(Y | X,beta,sig_a), which is an  
integral of L(Y | X,beta,a_1,...,a_n) with respect to a_1..a_n.

THE PROBLEM is that neither in the statnet package nor any other  
package I found an appropriate function to estimate the model.

1. Is anybody aware of such a function????
2. If not, which algorithms would you suggest to solve the problem?  
(B.t.w. the network consists of 240 nodes.)

Thank you very much
Moritz Mueller

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] gof results too long to print
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jenine.  Sorry about the insane version of print.gofobject that was  
in ergm.  I don't know if this addresses your question completely, but  
try copy-and-pasting the code below after loading statnet.  This will  
create a new version of print.gofobject and summary.gofobject (these  
will be in ergm 2.0-7, which should be on CRAN in a few days, after  
which time it won't be necessary to copy and paste!).  This version  
prints only the rows in which the stats aren't all zero.

Dave

##COPY AND PASTE STARTING HERE:
print.gofobject <- function(x, ...){
   all.gof.vars <- ergm.rhs.formula(x$GOF)
   # match variables
   goftypes <- matrix( c(
       "model", "model statistics", "summary.model",
       "distance", "minimum geodesic distance", "summary.dist",
       "idegree", "in-degree", "summary.ideg",
       "odegree", "out-degree", "summary.odeg",
       "degree", "degree", "summary.deg",
       "espartners", "edgewise shared partner", "summary.espart",
       "dspartners", "dyadwise shared partner", "summary.dspart",
       "triadcensus", "triad census", "summary.triadcensus"),
                       byrow=TRUE, ncol=3)
   for(i in seq(along=all.gof.vars)){
     all.gof.vars[i] <- match.arg(all.gof.vars[i], goftypes[,1])
   }
   for(statname in all.gof.vars){
     r <- match(statname, goftypes[,1])  # find row in goftypes matrix
     cat("\nGoodness-of-fit for", goftypes[r, 2],"\n\n")
     m <- x[[goftypes[r, 3] ]] # get summary statistics
     zerorows <- m[,"obs"]==0 & m[,"min"]==0 & m[,"max"]==0
     print(m[!zerorows,])
   }
   invisible()
}

summary.gofobject <- function(object, ...) {
   print.gofobject(object, ...) # Nothing better for now
}

## THAT"S ALL TO COPY AND PASTE!

messages.body_plain:
Hi Kevin.  The fact that you're seeing a symmetric matrix when you  
type 'net3' is no cause for alarm; this is merely how undirected  
networks are represented:  Even though you see twelve ones in the  
matrix, each pair represents only a single edge in the matrix.  Of  
course, only the lower triangle is relevant, so one might well ask  
what is the point of seeing a symmetric matrix other than simple  
aesthetics.  One answer to this is that it's sometimes of interest to  
study the eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix, which are guaranteed to  
be real because it's a real symmetric matrix.

As for the plot, you may have found a bug here -- I've never used  
edge.curve before (cool!), but it does appear that something fishy is  
going on here.  I'll leave this one for Carter...

Dave
