messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] "subscript out of bounds" error in simulate.sisnetwork
messages.body_plain:
Hi Rodolfo.  I found what I think are a couple bugs in the  
simulate.sisnetwork function:  I believe that the line

     mat[1:nrow.nonnull, 1:ncol.nonnull] <- matrix(s$newmat,
         ncol=ncol.nonnull)[,order(order.col.sums)]

is incorrect and that it should be replaced by these lines:

     mat[1:nrow.nonnull, 1:ncol.nonnull] <- matrix(s$newmat,
         ncol=ncol.nonnull)
     mat <- mat[,order(order.col.sums)]

in two different places.  Also, the  line
   mat <- matrix(0, nrow=nrow, ncol=ncol)

should be moved just inside the for loop.  If you "source" the  
attached file (which contains these modifications), then your code  
should run.  You might also read the help file for simulate.sisnetwork  
just to make sure this is actually what you want -- i.e., a network  
whose marginals are exactly the same as the one you passed.

One further issue:  If you were expecting 10 different networks, your  
code won't produce that -- there is something I don't understand about  
the way the "simulate.network" function processes its "save.networks"  
argument that prevents using it to simulate multiple networks  
(possibly another bug?).  If you want 10 different networks then the  
following code should do it:

  tmp <- as.sociomatrix(Cong110.g2)
  tmp2 <- list(rows=rowSums(tmp), cols=colSums(tmp))
  class(tmp2) <- "sisnetwork"
  sim=simulate.sisnetwork(tmp2, n=10, save.networks=T)

Hope this helps.
Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] questions about statnet
messages.body_plain:
Hi Elena,

I can't help you with the first question, but I can tell you how I 
solved the second.

Say you have a graph called "net" and two vectors (the length of which 
corresponds to the number of vertices in your graph): "gpa" and "race". 
  Set these as vertex attributes:

set.vertex.attribute(net,"gpa",floor(gpa)+2) # gpa=1 => triangle
set.vertex.attribute(net,"race", race)

Now you can plot the graph:

plot(net,
      vertex.col="race",
      vertex.sides="gpa"
      edge.lwd=1)

You can do more tweaking, but that's the general idea.  You can rig your 
colors to be something more mnemonic using palette().  Type this command 
at the R prompt and you will see what the default color order is. Either 
set the race such that they correspond to the colors you want or change 
the order in palette() -- just remember what you did to change it!

Hope this helps.

Cheers,

Jamie

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Re: bug in revisetheta0
messages.body_plain:
Dear Statnet developers and users,

I've come across a possible bug in ergm() when fitting the "altkstar"  
term with an arbitrary lambda value and 'fixed' = FALSE, which causes  
the process to abort before entering the MCMC run:

 > Error in newoverlap[j] = m$terms[[i]]$params[[j]] :
 >  nothing to replace with


It turns out that the theta0 names do not match the model term names.   
This can be fixed by replacing the following line:

InitErgmTerm.R: 169:	coef.names = paste("altkstar", lambda, sep="."),  
#coef.names: required

with
InitErgmTerm.R: 169:	coef.names = "altkstar",  #coef.names: required


Making this substitution restores normal functionality to fitting the  
altkstar term without a constraint on the lambda parameter.

Best,
- Art.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ale?,

I looked at the files and I can see the problem:

1) You did not create a network from the data table. e.g.
     cheyenne<-network(cheyenne, directed=TRUE)
   The package works with networks stored as network objects.
2) The term for transitive triples is "ttriple" and not "transitive".

Once these changes are made all works out well.
Here is the core result:

Monte Carlo MLE Results:
        Estimate Std. Error MCMC s.e.  p-value
mutual   0.97964    0.45899     0.022 0.034418 *
istar2   0.39096    0.13470     0.004 0.004254 **
ostar2   0.43154    0.12422     0.001 0.000668 ***
ttriple -0.07544    0.09745     0.001 0.440039
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

In answer to your question:
"What is the meaning of the MCMC s. e. in the statnet output (next to the
parameter estimates and standard errors). I assume that s.e. stands for
standard error, but what are then the "standard errors" (just before them)."

The "Std. Error" is the usual standard error of the coefficient. The "MCMC
s.e." is the amount of the standard error that results from the use of the
approximate MLE rather than the true MLE. The MLE is approximate because it
is estimated using simulation. I believe "statnet" is the only package that
estimates this. It helps the user because if the uncertainty in the
estimation method is a non-negligible contributor to the overall uncertainty
the algorithm should be refined (e.g., by increasing the MCMCsamplesize or
interval arguments). In this case the contribution is small.

The second question is not relevant is a network is created first.

I have added a few more diagnostic plots in the attached code and figures.
They are fun to see, especially the triad census diagnostics.

Enjoy!

Mark

for the "statnet" team

messages.subject: [statnet_help] TNT MCMC Sampler
messages.body_plain:
Hi Robert.   Nice catch -- you're correct about the case of moving  
from the empty graph to the one-edge graph and vice-versa.  We will  
fix this in the next release of ergm.

Incidentally, this bug is as you point out almost never an issue in  
practice, but it is possible to construct an example specifically to  
reveal it:
x <- network(1-diag(3),dir=F)
s <- simulate(x~edges, nsim=1e+4, theta0=-2, interval=100, statsonly=T)

In this example of an undirected 3-node network, the expected number  
of edges is 3*exp(-2)/(1+exp(-2)), which is
 > 3*exp(-2)/(1+exp(-2))
[1] 0.3576088

Yet what I get from the simulation is consistently too high.
 > mean(s)
[1] 0.5404

I suspect this may be due to the bias introduced by the Hastings ratio  
problem.

Dave


On Apr 18, 2009, at 4:23 PM, Goudie, Robert wrote:

> Hi David. Many thanks for your emails clearing up my question about  
> the sampler.
>
> For the sampler implemented, I think there may be a problem with a  
> minor edge case. (Again, it is very possible I am not fully  
> understanding the C.) The case involves proposals to and from the  
> empty graph - so clearly in practice this isn't an important issue.
>
> Suppose current graph y. Draw proposal y' from proposal density Q.  
> Suppose y has 1 edge, and y' is the empty graph. Then,
>
> Q(y |y') = 1/ndyads [rather than (1-comp)/ndyads, since can't remove  
> an edge from an empty graph]
> Q(y'|y ) = comp/nedges + (1 - comp)/ndyads = comp + (1 - comp)/ndyads
>
> Hastings factor
> = 1/(comp * ndyads + (1 - comp))
> != nedges/(odds * ndyads + nedges)
> = 1/(odds * ndyads + 1)
>
> The case when y is the empty graph, y' is a graph with 1 edge is  
> similar.
>
> Thanks again,
>
> Robert Goudie
>
> --
> Ph.D. Student

Hi Thomas.  I've written some comments below.  I apologize in advance  
that they're a bit on the vague side.

On Feb 5, 2009, at 1:28 PM, Thomas House wrote:

> Hello,
>
> I was wondering if this list could help me with a couple of questions
> related to some work I am doing with the aim of modelling infectious
> disease. While I'm new to both R and statnet, I would much rather
> contribute to an existing (particularly open-source) project than  
> write
> things from scratch.
>

Hear, hear! :)

> 1) I would like to generate undirected networks with a certain  
> number of
> nodes, edges, triangles, 4-loops and other 4-motifs. Most of the  
> statnet
> documentation assumes that there is a comparator 'real' dataset, but  
> is
> there a simple way to construct networks a priori? (Data on
> epidemiological rather than social connections is less often a  
> detailed
> study of a small group and more often population-level measurements or
> inference on local structure.)
>

I think that the answer is no -- there is not an easy way to do this  
and in general (i.e., for general types of motifs that you'd like to  
see) I think this is a research-level question -- though perhaps  
someone else on the list can supply a more complete answer.

code in that package, particularly in the files InitErgmTerm.users.R  
(see the comments at the top) and changestats.h.  However, in the not-

messages.body_plain:
Dear Jef,

Sorry for the delay...

For me, it was a question of memory handling (RAM and swap). Because, 
when you have to estimate a Curved exponantial family model, memory is 
very soon a problem.

My questionning was: what is the max memory handled by the OS per 
process. Because if your OS cannot handle more than 2.5Gb per process, R 
won't be able to pass this limit.

Debian (and Linux in general) are known to be more efficients with 
memory handling than The OS of Microsoft (windows server entreprise or 
more expensive could also be ok).

If you have to handle a lot of memory, a good idea is to install a Linux 
64bit version or the Debian bigmem kernel. The memory is better handled 
by the OS with this 2 solutions.

Best regards,
Victorin Luisier

Hi David.  I'm not sure why you're getting an error about trying to  
allocate an object of 158.7 Mb, which doesn't seem that large to me,  
but nonetheless one suggestion I have is to use "fixed=TRUE" (perhaps  
with several values of the parameter) as in Section 7 of the JSS  
article you mention instead of "fixed=FALSE".  It is MUCH more  
computationally intensive to do "fixed=FALSE" because the ergm routine  
is trying to fit a complicated curved exponential family model,  
whereas with "fixed=TRUE" the model is actually just a standard ergm.

Hope this helps,
Dave

> I am a graduate student at the Stanford School of Education, running
> ergms using Add Health data. I have two questions.
>
> 1. I would like to include a parameter which adds a statistic for all

> ever seen an error like this?

Hi Elena,

My first guess would be that you have an NA for at least one student's 
parental education level in your data.  Is that right?  I do believe that 
smalldiff as written does not handle missing attribute values.

If that's the problem, then you might consider somehow imputing your 
missing values. Better, more model-based approaches to handling missing 
data in ergms are in development, but I would consider starting there.

If that's not the problem, let me know and I'll brainstorm some more.

Steve

messages.body_plain:
Hi Martin.  Try the following.  First is a simplistic function (beware  
-- no error-checking!) that changes an edgelist into a "named  
edgelist" where the integers 1 through n are replaced by the vertex  
names.  Then, you can stack two such edgelists using the "rbind"  
function and convert to a network:

named.edgelist <- function(x)
matrix((x %v% "vertex.names")[as.edgelist(x)], ncol=2)

# Now "stack" the two networks created below, called g1 and g2, and  
change to a network:
g12 <- network(rbind(named.edgelist(g1), named.edgelist(g2)))

# See the result:
as.matrix(g12)

   A B C D
A 0 1 0 0
B 0 0 1 0
C 1 0 0 1
D 0 1 0 0

Hope this helps.

Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ergm
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for your help (David Hunter, Martina Morris, Carter T. Butts).

following on your comments, I have another question.

I've looked into Lubbers & Snjiders 2005 SNA; Lubbers 2003 SN and Snijders &
Baerveldt 2003 JMS and they use meta-analytical procedures to summarize
findings over different networks (i.e. weighted least squares estimators of
each parameter). Although not comparing parameters, basically an average
value (with some corrections) is being computed. Following your line of
argument, than this meta-analytical procedure raises some questions. Am I
thinking straight or making no sense at all?

Thanks
Jo?o

On Thu, Jul 31, 2008 at 7:16 AM, Carter T. Butts <buttsc@uci.edu> wrote:

> David Hunter wrote:
>
>> Hello Jo?o.  It is not generally possible to do this kind of comparison,
>> especially in a way that allow things like hypothesis tests (is the
>> transitivity effect significantly different?).  That said, there are some
>> methods that people do use from time to time to make such comparisons in
>> logistic regression models, and perhaps someday in the not-too-distant
>> future we'll have an easy generalization to the ERGM case...
>>
>
> Just to elaborate on Dave's point, the problem here is that many parameters
> have practical implications which are difficult to interpret when the
> support (i.e., the set of possible graphs) is changed.  There is a technical
> sense in which one can ask whether the MLE for the triangle parameter of
> graph A is larger than that of graph B, and it does have a conditional
> log-odds interpretation...however, this is very unlikely to map in a simple
> way to your scientific intuition about a "stronger" effect.  Thus, the
> conservative answer is that parameter comparison is not well-understood at
> this time, and probably should be avoided.
>
> That said, there are some cases in which parameters have clear
> size-independent interpretations, and comparison can be fairly intuitive.
>  For instance, if your model leads to dyadic independence, most reasonable
> effects (e.g., edge covariates) can be interpreted in a size-independent
> fashion.  (Of course, this assumes that the model is correct, or at least
> that you are interpreting the parameters in the correct marginal way.)
>
> Ultimately, the real problem is that the kinds of social ``forces''
> parameterized by standard models (especially in the general case) have
> effects which scale in a non-obvious way with graph size.  A triangle
> parameter of 0.1 says, in essence, that the conditional log-odds of an edge
> are increased by 0.1 for every triangle which would be added by that edge's
> appearance.  In a small graph, there are not many possible triangles, and
> the impact of this parameter on triangle formation is fairly small (in a
> practical sense).  In a large graph, however, there are many ways to attain
> a very large number of ``pre-triangles,'' and the same 0.1 ``triangulation
> force'' will lead the entire structure to collapse with large probability
> into a clique.  (This is the degeneracy problem -- see David Strauss's 1986
> SIAM review paper for an early technical argument, or Mark Handcock's work
> for a more recent take.)  To use an alternate (but technically justifiable!)
> metaphor, the ``freezing point'' of a large graph (vis a vis triangle
> temperature) is much higher than the freezing point of a small graph, and
> thus the former will become degenerate at temperatures at which the latter
> would be in a ``fluid'' state.  One could thus find a small graph with a
> large triangle parameter (i.e. at lower temperature) and a large graph with
> a small triangle parameter (at higher temperature), and simultaneously
> observe a much greater manifested tendency towards triangulation in the
> latter than the former.
>
> This apparent contradiction could lead one to assert any of the following:
> (1) larger social structures really do have something which reduces the
> strength of ``social forces'' like the triangle effect, as compared to
> smaller structures; (2) one's real measure of ``strength'' should not be the
> natural parameter value, but the corresponding mean value parameter (or some
> such); or (3) the triangle model (and others of its ilk) are not modeling
> ``social forces'' in an appropriate way (at least for large graphs).  All of
> the above have been kicked around by workers in the field, and each is
> probably meritorious in particular empirical contexts.  This is a
> fundamentally _theoretical_ problem, and has to be resolved by close
> attention to the properties of the process you are trying to capture -- it's
> not some little artifact which can be automagically ``corrected'' or
> otherwise brushed under the rug.
>
> And now you know why Dave simply told you, "don't do it."  :-)
>
> As far as other means of graph comparison, I discuss some of the
> alternatives in my recent AJSP review paper.  There are actually two
> ERGM-like ways to compare graphs at present, but both require the graphs to
> be on the same vertex set.  (One of these is supported in the netperm
> package, if you'd like to try it out -- it also works with valued data.)
>  Kathleen Carley and I have also used distance-based methods to compare
> graphs on different vertex sets, but the kind of comparison this gives is an
> omnibus notion of similarity (i.e., it does not separate out different kinds
> of underlying structural biases) and it is purely data analytic in
> character.
>
> That's a long answer to a short question; hope it helps,
>
> -Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] problem with cug.test
messages.body_plain:
In using a function I've written to compute the Watts-Strogatz
clustering coefficient, I get different observed values when using it
in cug.test versus using it alone.

g = rgraph(10)
clusteringCoefficientWS(g) # see function below
[1] 0.4638095
cug = cug.test( g, FUN = clusteringCoefficientWS, mode = "graph",
cmode = "edges" )
cug

Univariate Conditional Uniform Graph Test

Conditioning Method: edges
Graph Type: graph
Diagonal Used: FALSE
Replications: 1000

Observed Value: 0.431746
Pr(X>=Obs): 0.748
Pr(X<=Obs): 0.252

# Function:
clusteringCoefficientWS = function( g ) {
	total = 0
	nodesUsed = 0
	for( iteration in 1:length( g[1,] ) )  {
		# Retrieve the ego network
		egonetwork = ego.extract( g, iteration, neighborhood = "combined" )
		# If ego has neighbors, calculate the clustering coefficient for this node
		if ( dim( egonetwork[[1]] )[1] < 3 ) {
			# Clustering coefficient is undefined
			next
		} else {
			# Get the neighbor network ( ego is the first row/col )
			neighbornetwork =
					egonetwork[[1]][ 	2:nrow( egonetwork[[1]] ),
										2:ncol( egonetwork[[1]] ) ]
			# Get the degree of ego
			degree = nrow( neighbornetwork )
			# Get the number of edges
			numEdges = sum( upperTriangle( neighbornetwork , diag = FALSE ) )
			C_i = numEdges / ( degree * ( degree - 1 ) / 2 )
			total = total + C_i
			nodesUsed = nodesUsed + 1
		}
	}
	clusCoef = total / nodesUsed
	return( clusCoef )
}


Brian Riordan
Postdoctoral Fellow
Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences
Indiana University

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Change statistics
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jef,

I don't have an answer to your question exactly, but I have something that 
may or may not come close enough to be useful to you. That is, how to get 
a count of the number of i,j pairs that have each value of a change 
statistic in a network. That you can find with:

tempfit <- ergm(my.network~statistic.of.interest,MPLEonly=T)
cbind(tempfit$glm$y,tempfit$glm$data,tempfit$glm$prior.weights)

The resulting table has three columns:

- The first gives the value of i,j, in the network

- The second gives the change statistic for the statistic you included in 
the first line of code. Here change stat means the value by which the 
statistic would change if i,j went from 0 to 1, regardless of whether it 
is currently 0 or 1.

- The third column gives the number of i,j pairs that meet the first two 
criteria.

Hope that helps!
Steve

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jef.  One way is to use a "brute-force" approach on a tabular  
summary of the attribute.  If the network is undirected, then simply  
calculating k-choose-2 for each count k of network attribute counts  
should do the trick.  For instance, using the faux.mesa.high dataset  
of the ergm package, we have:

 > library(ergm)
  ...
 > data(faux.mesa.high)
 > choose(table(faux.mesa.high %v% "Race"),2)

Black  Hisp NatAm Other White
    15  5886  2278     6   153

These numbers could be doubled for a directed network of course.  Hope  
this helps.
Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Hypothesis Testing/Graph Comparison
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sean.  Hope you don't mind I'm responding to the group; this topic  
seems interesting to a few others.

Yes, you're exactly right -- it would be defensible, and in fact this  
is exactly the observation that Carter Butts made yesterday to me  
offline.  (Thanks, Carter!)
The analogy would be to a 2-sample t-test with unequal variances, in  
which the two estimated variances (or in this case, approximated  
covariance matrices) are summed to give the variance of the  
difference, which would have mean zero under the null hypothesis of  
equality.

Dave


On May 20, 2009, at 9:14 AM, Sean L. Simpson wrote:

> Hi Dave,
>
> For instance, if we appealed to the asymptotic normality of MLEs to  
> construct an ?approximate? 2-sample z-test of difference, would this  
> rudimentary approach seem defensible in this context?
>
> Thank you,
> Sean
>
> From: David Hunter [mailto:dhunter@stat.psu.edu]

> Subject: Re: [statnet_help] Hypothesis Testing/Graph Comparison
>
> Hi Sean.  Interesting question.
>
> In that case the parameters would be comparable, though I'm not  
> exactly sure what comparing based on likelihood theory would mean.   
> You could certainly do things like compute confidence intervals and  
> then conclude if the intervals do not overlap that the parameters  
> are significantly different, though this is not usually such a good  
> way to run tests (the power is low and if the intervals do overlap  
> then you can't conclude that the test shouldn't reject the null  
> hypothesis).
>
> Dave

> The "Std. Error" is the usual standard error of the coefficient. The "MCMC

> approximate MLE rather than the true MLE. The MLE is approximate because it

> estimation method is a non-negligible contributor to the overall
> uncertainty
> the algorithm should be refined (e.g., by increasing the MCMCsamplesize or
> interval arguments). In this case the contribution is small.
>
> The second question is not relevant is a network is created first.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] TNT MCMC Sampler
messages.body_plain:
Hi David. Many thanks for your emails clearing up my question about the sampler.

For the sampler implemented, I think there may be a problem with a minor edge case. (Again, it is very possible I am not fully understanding the C.) The case involves proposals to and from the empty graph - so clearly in practice this isn't an important issue.

Suppose current graph y. Draw proposal y' from proposal density Q. Suppose y has 1 edge, and y' is the empty graph. Then,

Q(y |y') = 1/ndyads [rather than (1-comp)/ndyads, since can't remove an edge from an empty graph]
Q(y'|y ) = comp/nedges + (1 - comp)/ndyads = comp + (1 - comp)/ndyads

Hastings factor 
= 1/(comp * ndyads + (1 - comp))
!= nedges/(odds * ndyads + nedges)
= 1/(odds * ndyads + 1)

The case when y is the empty graph, y' is a graph with 1 edge is similar.

Thanks again,

Robert Goudie

--

University of Warwick

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jef.  Mark Handcock noticed that your "female" variable contains  
all zeros, which is causing a couple problems that will be fixed if  
you drop all the "female" terms:

First, it means that nodematch("female") is always equal to "edges"  
for any network.  Thus, you have a problem including both of those  
terms in your model.

Second, it means that nodeifactor("female") and nodeofactor("female")  
don't make sense -- and this is what is actually causing the error.   
In fact, you seem to have found a bug in ergm:  nodeifactor and  
nodeofactor weren't written to be robust enough to deal with calls  
like this in which the user tries to define a factor on a variable  
with only a single value.  Oops!  I'll add this to the to-do list, and  
thanks for the heads up.

Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Using mutuality in an interaction term
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Using mutuality in an interaction term
messages.body_plain:
Hi David.   First, I have to say I'm not sure what is creating the  
error you're getting since I think that the model is okay from a  
mathematical perspective.  This could potentially be a bug, though I'd  
have to look into that more.

However, I'm afraid that your code does not produce the interaction  
you are looking for.  In fact, I don't know of a way to do what you  
want currently in ergm.  The reason your code does not do this is that  
the CovMat.DxM matrix is *fixed* according to mutuality status of the  
original network and thus the corresponding coefficient is actually  
measuring something like the additional edgecov effect for those dyads  
that were mutual in the original network, not those that are mutual in  
the current network.

Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Blockmodeling in R
messages.body_plain:
Dear Phill,

I was looking around for solutions for your problem a few months ago and 
have found no satisfactory solution, at least not for the problem of 
your size.

For my problem, which was only about 90 by 260 matrix, I then used my 
package for blockmodeling (with sum of squres approach and complete 
blocs, which run the fastest) , which is available at 
http://www2.arnes.si/~aziber4/blockmodeling, but I doubt it will be of 
use to you, as it would simply take to long, if nothing else goes wrong.

When I was looking at the literature, the 2-mode clustering algorithms 
seemed promising (for review see Van Mechelen, Bock and De Boeck, 2004), 
but none of those or similar algorithms seem to be implemented in R. I 
would be very happy if somebody pointed something out.

So my suggestion for now would be that you do cluster separately each 
mode (as when analyzing classical, non network data) and then form 
two-mode blockmodel from that. If you find some at lest reasonably fast 
algorithm, you can try it to optimize this solution.

Best regards,
Ales Ziberna

Iven Van Mechelen, Hans-Hermann Bock and Paul De Boeck (2004): Two-mode 
clustering methods: astructuredoverview. Stat Methods Med Res 2004; 13; 
363, DOI: 10.1191/0962280204sm373ra

Phil Murphy pravi:

> options and limitations of the blockmodeling algorithm that is 
> available on R?
>
>  
>
> I have a good deal of experience with blockmodeling in Pajek and the

list of packages.  You'll find a couple pre-compiled binaries along  
with the source code (the latter is in a tarred and gzipped file; see  
below).

If you're using a PC, then Duncan Murdoch's website at http://www.murdoch-sutherland.com/Rtools/ 
  is a must-read if you're going to play with source code.

If you're on a mac or linux, you can type
tar xfz XXX.tar.gz
in a terminal window in order to expand a tarred and gzipped directory  
called XXX.tar.gz.  If you're on windows, then I think you'll be able  
to do the same thing from a DOS window after you install the tools at  
Murdoch's website.

Hope this helps.
Dave

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jef.  Sending this to the list in case it's helpful to others too.

Oops -- take a look at the "note" when you type help(diag).  This  
occurs for a few functions in R ('sample' is another) and I've been  
caught by this before.  The remedy is given in that same note:  Change  
the 'f' function as follows:

f <- function(v) (outer(v,v)-diag(v, nrow=length(v)))/2

and then the previous answer will work even for attributes with a  
single value.

Dave

> Miko?aj Hnatiuk wrote:
>
>> Hi,
>> im newbie to ERGM. Im doing research for my project. My problem is somehow
>> complicated one. I have network with 2 kinds of relations, one is
>> dichotomous, the other one valued. I have a reason to belive that strength
>> of the tie on 2nd network influences the appareance of the tie in the first
>> one. The network contains 2467 nodes. Ive read some articles on logistic
>> regression in networks, but didn't figure out how to do it on such large
>> networks - i've tried to use "netlogit" (using quadtratic assigment-
>>  nullhyp="qap" )  function from SNA package, following Krackhardt article in
>> Social Networks (*Krackhardt, David "Predicting with Networks: A Multiple
>> Regression Approach to Analyzing Dyadic Data." Social Networks, 10
>> (December): 359-381.)   , but after approximately 20h of computation i gave
>> up and decided to post on the list. My question is: Is it possible to do
>> logistic regression on 2 networks using just some kind of "sample" of  a
>> network and by doing such - obtain significant results? Or is there a way
>> around this, possibly including usage of ERGMs ? Im really desperate to do
>> this.
>>
>>
> netlogit will do it, but the computations for the QAP replications are very
> expensive; you should expect it to take quite a while.  One can run such an
> analysis in ergm, but the tests it gives you will be essentially the
> equivalent of the classical test option in netlogit (which will be faster,
> but will not help in the case of autocorrelation).  Another option is
> netperm (an optional package within statnet), which fits the network
> permutation models from my 2007 Sociological Methodology paper.  I've never
> tried fitting anything that large using netperm, but it will probably be
> faster than a logistic QAP (though you may need to tweak the parameters to
> get good performance).
>
> Hope that helps,
>
> -Carter

            linksamp[k,l] <- links[s[k],s[l] ]
            comsamp[k,l] <- commat[s[k], s[l] ]
            }

        }
        linksamp.net <- as.network(linksamp)
        comsamp.net<- as.network(comsamp)
        logity[i] <- netlogit(linksamp.net ~comsamp.net, nullhyp=c("qap",
         "classical") )

      }

messages.subject: [statnet_help] meta analysis and ergm-models
messages.body_plain:
Dear statnet team,

 

I have a question about the implementation of erg models.

I'm trying to fit a erg model on a very large social network dataset,
containing 80 different schools in Belgium. It has about 15.000 respondents.
In particular I'm looking for ethnical and gender homophily , and structural
homophily (class, school and education type).

 

( model2 <- ergm(vlo13 ~ edges + transitive + nodematch("class") +
nodematch("ethnicity") + nodematch("EducType") + nodematch("gender"),
verbose = TRUE) )

 

 

Because it is such a large data set, would it be a good idea to split the
dataset by school? I would than look for a model that fits all the 80
networks, and perform a meta analysis to check whether the model has a good
fit for all the different school networks.

So I would split the dataset because:

-          I have to deal with smaller datasets, so it takes less longer to
do the calculations. This makes experimenting with the model much easier. 

-          It is structural impossible to have a relationship with someone
from a different school (because of the geometric distance), so there would
be very large homophily for the variable 'school' when I would do my
analysis on the whole network.

-          There is no theoretical issue when I split the network up by
school, because of this structural restraint. 

 

I hope you understand my question. 

 

Many thanks,

 

Jef

messages.body_plain:
Hi Robert.  Coincidentally, I was just looking at that same patch of  
code with a grad student.  You are correct:  The TNT proposal does not  
choose an empty dyad with probability 1/2; in fact, this probability  
is actually somewhat less than 50% in the current implementation.  It  
would certainly be possible to modify this code (by allowing the  
function to change the value of the "comp" variable) so that the  
probability is exactly 50%, but when comp=0.5 as it is presently set,  
your description below is correct.

For a sparse graph, the probability of choosing an empty dyad is close  
to 50%, but nevertheless the description in the article is not accurate.

Sorry we did not catch that error in the article!

Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Possible bug w/centralization function?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Natalie -

Natalie C. Cotton wrote:
> Hi Statnet Help,
> 
> I'm trying to get the betweenness centralization scores for some 
> undirected networks, and have run into a problem.  The result of the 
> command (centralization(NetworkObj, betweenness, mode="graph", 
> normalize=TRUE)) on my data is incorrect.  It is exactly half of what it 
> should be when I calculate betweenness centralization by hand.
> 
> I have discovered that if I instead use the command for a directed 
> network (centralization(NetworkObj, betweenness, mode="digraph", 
> normalize=TRUE)) it does give the right number.  But, that shouldn't be, 
> since I do not have a directed network.
> 
> By contrast, when I run the two commands on an older version of R (with 
> older versions of SNA and Network), the results are correct.  Is this a 
> bug in the new version?

Looks like the new version introduced an inconsistency in how 
directedness is handled in the centralization normalization for 
betweenness when cmode is left at its default value ("directed").  You 
can force the expected behavior with

centralization(NetworkObj, betweenness, mode="graph",
cmode="undirected")

(However, you can get the same answer by treating the network as 
directed, since this multiplies the numerator and the denominator by the 
same amount.  So centralization(NetworkObj,betweenness) will also work 
for undirected data.)

Thanks for the bug report.  A fix will go out in the next revision,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] meta analysis and ergm-models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jef,

When one has data on multiple settings in which it is impossible for 
people to nominate those in other settings, then I would strongly 
recommend modeling them as separately.  Otherwise one is confounding two 
different processes.

> -          It is structural impossible to have a relationship with someone
> from a different school (because of the geometric distance), so there would
> be very large homophily for the variable 'school' when I would do my
> analysis on the whole network.

Yes, in this case the MLE for a school-homophily parameter would be 
positive infinity. We know this without having to actually model it 
directly, and doing so won't tell you anything in addition.

Jef, I will forward you a manuscript in which we analyzed multiple schools 
independently, so you can get a sense for how we did it.

Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ergm
messages.body_plain:
David Hunter wrote:
> Hello Jo?o.  It is not generally possible to do this kind of comparison, 
> especially in a way that allow things like hypothesis tests (is the 
> transitivity effect significantly different?).  That said, there are 
> some methods that people do use from time to time to make such 
> comparisons in logistic regression models, and perhaps someday in the 
> not-too-distant future we'll have an easy generalization to the ERGM 
> case...

Just to elaborate on Dave's point, the problem here is that many 
parameters have practical implications which are difficult to interpret 
when the support (i.e., the set of possible graphs) is changed.  There 
is a technical sense in which one can ask whether the MLE for the 
triangle parameter of graph A is larger than that of graph B, and it 
does have a conditional log-odds interpretation...however, this is very 
unlikely to map in a simple way to your scientific intuition about a 
"stronger" effect.  Thus, the conservative answer is that parameter 
comparison is not well-understood at this time, and probably should be 
avoided.

That said, there are some cases in which parameters have clear 
size-independent interpretations, and comparison can be fairly 
intuitive.  For instance, if your model leads to dyadic independence, 
most reasonable effects (e.g., edge covariates) can be interpreted in a 
size-independent fashion.  (Of course, this assumes that the model is 
correct, or at least that you are interpreting the parameters in the 
correct marginal way.)

Ultimately, the real problem is that the kinds of social ``forces'' 
parameterized by standard models (especially in the general case) have 
effects which scale in a non-obvious way with graph size.  A triangle 
parameter of 0.1 says, in essence, that the conditional log-odds of an 
edge are increased by 0.1 for every triangle which would be added by 
that edge's appearance.  In a small graph, there are not many possible 
triangles, and the impact of this parameter on triangle formation is 
fairly small (in a practical sense).  In a large graph, however, there 
are many ways to attain a very large number of ``pre-triangles,'' and 
the same 0.1 ``triangulation force'' will lead the entire structure to 
collapse with large probability into a clique.  (This is the degeneracy 
problem -- see David Strauss's 1986 SIAM review paper for an early 
technical argument, or Mark Handcock's work for a more recent take.)  To 
use an alternate (but technically justifiable!) metaphor, the ``freezing 
point'' of a large graph (vis a vis triangle temperature) is much higher 
than the freezing point of a small graph, and thus the former will 
become degenerate at temperatures at which the latter would be in a 
``fluid'' state.  One could thus find a small graph with a large 
triangle parameter (i.e. at lower temperature) and a large graph with a 
small triangle parameter (at higher temperature), and simultaneously 
observe a much greater manifested tendency towards triangulation in the 
latter than the former.

This apparent contradiction could lead one to assert any of the 
following: (1) larger social structures really do have something which 
reduces the strength of ``social forces'' like the triangle effect, as 
compared to smaller structures; (2) one's real measure of ``strength'' 
should not be the natural parameter value, but the corresponding mean 
value parameter (or some such); or (3) the triangle model (and others of 
its ilk) are not modeling ``social forces'' in an appropriate way (at 
least for large graphs).  All of the above have been kicked around by 
workers in the field, and each is probably meritorious in particular 
empirical contexts.  This is a fundamentally _theoretical_ problem, and 
has to be resolved by close attention to the properties of the process 
you are trying to capture -- it's not some little artifact which can be 
automagically ``corrected'' or otherwise brushed under the rug.

And now you know why Dave simply told you, "don't do it."  :-)

As far as other means of graph comparison, I discuss some of the 
alternatives in my recent AJSP review paper.  There are actually two 
ERGM-like ways to compare graphs at present, but both require the graphs 
to be on the same vertex set.  (One of these is supported in the netperm 
package, if you'd like to try it out -- it also works with valued data.) 
  Kathleen Carley and I have also used distance-based methods to compare 
graphs on different vertex sets, but the kind of comparison this gives 
is an omnibus notion of similarity (i.e., it does not separate out 
different kinds of underlying structural biases) and it is purely data 
analytic in character.

That's a long answer to a short question; hope it helps,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] gof p-values
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kevin.  The idea behind the MCMC p-value is simply that you  
calculate what proportion of the "null" distribution (in this case,  
represented by the 100 simulated values) is at least as extreme as the  
observed statistic.  Here, I believe that "at least as extreme" means  
"at least as far from the sample mean", which would give essentially a  
2-sided hypothesis test of the null that says the observed came from  
the same distribution as the simulations, though I'm not 100% sure  
that's the exact method of calculation.

You are therefore correct that large p-values in this instance are  
"good", in the sense that they give no evidence that the null  
hypothesis is false (i.e., no evidence that the observed stat comes  
from a different distribution than the simulated stats).

Hope this helps.

Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] longitudinal analyses
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kevin,

Sorry it has taken so long to respond to your email.  The short answer is 
that the development team is hard at work developing a fully dynamic 
modeling capacity in statnet.  Some of this is functional now in our 
development code, and the rest is likely to be within the next 6-9 months.

There are two types of dynamics in networks: dynamics that govern ties 
(formation, dissolution, attribute changes) and dynamics that govern nodes 
(entry, exit, attribute changes).  We've been calling these "tie dynamics" 
and "vital dynamics" respectively.

We have a working version of a simple tie dynamic process up and running 
now in our development version of statnet.  It uses an ERGM model to 
govern tie formation, and one or more duration parameters to govern tie 
dissolution.  The size and composition of the network are fixed.  We have 
used this model to simulate an epidemic over a network where the ties form 
and dissolve over time, preserving a set of mean statistics (defined by 
the ERGM terms) and a duration distribution (both estimated from data). 
A paper that uses this model this will be published in the American 
Journal of Public Health in June 2009.

One of our graduate students, Pavel Krivitsky, is currently working on 
developing the modeling framework for vital dynamics in his dissertation. 
The fundamental question for the model is: what stays invariant as network 
size and composition change?  The answer depends in part on what kind of 
data you have.  Even cross sectional network data can be used to drive a 
fully dynamic network simulation, if you are willing to make assumptions 
about the parts of the process that you do not observe.  Pavel is 
presenting a paper up at the NIPS conference (today!) that presents one 
approach to that topic.

Making the network fully dynamic (tie and vital) also requires reworking 
some of the data storage and retrieval aspects of the code.  We have been 
developing the specifications for that over the past month, and hope to 
have the framework settled by the end of January.

If you (or others) are interested in more discussion about this, let us 
know.  If there are specific kinds of functionality that you would like to 
see implemented, it's a good time to speak up.  We can't promise to make 
it happen in the first pass, but if it is easy to incorporate, we will.

best of the season to all,
Martina

messages.body_plain:
Miko?aj Hnatiuk wrote:
> Hi,
> im newbie to ERGM. Im doing research for my project. My problem is 
> somehow complicated one. I have network with 2 kinds of relations, one 
> is dichotomous, the other one valued. I have a reason to belive that 
> strength of the tie on 2nd network influences the appareance of the tie 
> in the first one. The network contains 2467 nodes. Ive read some 
> articles on logistic regression in networks, but didn't figure out how 
> to do it on such large networks - i've tried to use "netlogit" (using 
> quadtratic assigment-  nullhyp="qap" )  function from SNA package, 
> following Krackhardt article in Social Networks (*Krackhardt, David 
> "Predicting with Networks: A Multiple Regression Approach to Analyzing 
> Dyadic Data." Social Networks, 10 (December): 359-381.)   , but after 
> approximately 20h of computation i gave up and decided to post on the 
> list. My question is: Is it possible to do logistic regression on 2 
> networks using just some kind of "sample" of  a network and by doing 
> such - obtain significant results? Or is there a way around this, 
> possibly including usage of ERGMs ? Im really desperate to do this.
>

netlogit will do it, but the computations for the QAP replications are 
very expensive; you should expect it to take quite a while.  One can run 
such an analysis in ergm, but the tests it gives you will be essentially 
the equivalent of the classical test option in netlogit (which will be 
faster, but will not help in the case of autocorrelation).  Another 
option is netperm (an optional package within statnet), which fits the 
network permutation models from my 2007 Sociological Methodology paper. 
  I've never tried fitting anything that large using netperm, but it 
will probably be faster than a logistic QAP (though you may need to 
tweak the parameters to get good performance).

Hope that helps,

-Carter

Dear Gurus,

My goal is to choose (and justify the choice) a model
(including terms for individual differences, homophily, and closure)
giving the best prediction of ties to use in creating a predicted-tie 
network.
In the ergms I'm estimating, I find no clear favorite, and need help
to choose appropriately.

Sample ERGMs:
Model1 <- ergm(net ~ edges + nodefactor(foo) + nodematch(foo))
Model2 <- ergm(net ~ gwesp(fixed=F) + edges + nodefactor(foo) + 
nodematch(foo))
Model3 <- ergm(net ~ gwesp(fixed=F) + edges + nodefactor(foo) + 
nodematch(foo), theta0=c(0,Model1$coef))
 
Model1
Pro: no MCMC / precise SEs,  non-degenerate
Con: no closure term, terrible GOF

Model2
Pro: much better GOF, AIC & BIC < Model1
Con: degenerate, suspect standard errors

Model3
Pro: non-degenerate, much better GOF
Con: AIC & BIC more than twice those of Model1

Since my goal is prediction and not hypothesis testing,
wouldn't Model2 be best even with the degeneracy?
Does degeneracy affect confidence in coefficient point estimates in 
addition to SEs?
If degenerate models should not be used predictively,
Model2 is better in terms of GOF, but horrible in terms of AIC & BIC.
I'd prefer to stick with models with good GOF,
but the huge increases in AIC & BIC give me pause.

Alternatively, are there other things I should be doing in structuring 
my ergms to reduce the likelihood of degeneracy?

Thanks very much for your help and advice!
Best,
Brian

-- 
Brian Rubineau
Assistant Professor, Organizational Behavior       146K Ives Hall
School of Industrial and Labor Relations         ph. 607.255.3048
Cornell University                              fax. 810.963.2738
Ithaca, NY 14853                            brubineau@cornell.edu

messages.subject: [statnet_help] plot.network() with colored edges
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Jamie -

James Holland Jones wrote:
> Hi all,
> 
> I'm worried that I'm just being dumb here, but I seem to be stuck.  I'm 
> trying to draw a network in which edges are colored according to some 
> vertex attribute.  Specifically, I have a sexual contact network with 
> sero-status measured for the vertices. I want all edges connecting to a 
> positive vertex to be colored, say, red. I seem to be missing something 
> about the sort order for the edge list.  I think this simple code 
> reproduces the problem I'm having with real data.  I create a network 
> object from a simulated edge list.  I then arbitrarily infect nodes 17, 
> 22, and 44. I create a dummy vector (which I also attach as an edge 
> attribute) indicating whether or not an edge is incident with an 
> infected vertex.  When I plot the network, the coloring does not come 
> out the way I expected it to.
> 
<snip>
> 
> I hope someone can help illuminate what I'm doing wrong here.

The %e% operator is a front-end to set.edge.value, which expects edges 
to be listed in their adjacency matrix order.  To adjust edge attributes 
in edge ID order, you need to use set.edge.attribute.  In your case,

set.edge.attribute(net,"edge.status",edge.status+1)
plot(net,vertex.col=1+status,edge.col="edge.status")

seems to produce the desired result.  (Note that edge.col uses matrix 
order, too, but can also take attributes as arguments.)

> 
> A somewhat related question: is there a way to extract an edge list as 
> one sees when summarizing a network, summary(net)?

Yes:

as.matrix(net,matrix.type="edgelist")

Hope that helps,

-Carter

enough memory can be allocated.  The code I'm using and the
corresponding error message are included below.

statnet tutorial in the Journal of Statistical Software.  I'm using the

includes only nodematch terms.  I've increased the memory available to R

doesn't appear that the network is too large or that there are too many
rows or terms in the model.  I'm using version 2.1 of statnet and
version 2.8 of R.

David

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ergm
messages.body_plain:
Hello Jo?o --

This is a very fundamental problem in network analysis:  are there size 
invariant parameters that can be estimated for network processes.  That 
is, parameters that govern the generative process of tie formation that 
are independent of the size (and composition) of the network.

The problem is easy to understand even with a simple Bernoulli random 
graph.  The single ergm parameter in that case measures the log-odds of a 
tie -- essentially, a scaled version of network density.  So the question 
is what happens to network density as the size of the network increases 
(or decreases)?  One possibility is that the mean degree remains fixed. 
So, for example, as the population increases, people do not have 
increasingly more friends, they probably max out at a certain point. 
That would be the fixed parameter of interest -- the parameter that is 
invariant to network size.

You can estimate a fixed parameter like this, but it clearly depends on 
what you think should remain fixed. If you were to posit a simple model 
like the mean degree remains constant as network size increases, you can 
fit this with something like an offset term to control for the expected 
decline in network density.

There is no one-size-fits-all here, though.  It will depend on the type of 
network and process that you are trying to represent.

We are working on these types of models now, for an application in network 
epidemiology.  The capabilities will be added to statnet when they're 
working.

best,
Martina

> logistic regression models, and perhaps someday in the not-too-distant future 
> we'll have an easy generalization to the ERGM case...
>
> Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Hypothesis Testing/Graph Comparison
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sean.  Interesting question.

In that case the parameters would be comparable, though I'm not  
exactly sure what comparing based on likelihood theory would mean.   
You could certainly do things like compute confidence intervals and  
then conclude if the intervals do not overlap that the parameters are  
significantly different, though this is not usually such a good way to  
run tests (the power is low and if the intervals do overlap then you  
can't conclude that the test shouldn't reject the null hypothesis).

Dave

Hi Hannu.  In general, the question comes down to what you mean by  
"similar statistical characteristics".  It turns out that this phrase  
is not always so easy to define in terms of the only thing that  
matters about a network in the context of a specific ERGM, namely, the  
vector of network statistics.  Thus, your question is best answered  
with another question:  What do you mean precisely by "the same ERGM  
model characteristics"?

(I should add that this question is sometimes fairly easy to answer  
satisfactorily, sometimes not!)

Dave

messages.body_plain:
Hi Tait,

As you know, the gof command automates the comparison of network 
statistics from an original network to a set of simulated networks.  In 
the process it compiles the statistic across all the runs, calcuates a 
p-value, and creates plots.  Gof is only implemented for a short list of 
network statistics; however, the steps involved are straigthforward, and 
can easily be implemented by the interested user for any other network 
statistic of interest, either by adding code to their copy of gof, or by 
writing a few new lines of independent code. Reading through the gof code 
is a good way to see examples of the syntax one might use for this. We 
also have an example doing this for triangles in Section 8 of the statnet 
tutorial paper.

http://www.jstatsoft.org/v24/i09/paper

In terms of calculating your statistic of interest on any given network, 
you may be able to use a function within sna or ergm if it exists, or else 
you'll have to write it.

Yours,
Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] sna, large networks, and the network data structure
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] sna, large networks, and the network data structure
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Alex -

Alex D'Amour wrote:
> Hello all,
> 
> I'm working on a project the requires generating social network
> metrics on a graph with a set of vertices on the order of 10^5 to 10^6
> nodes. I'm able to represent the network using the "network" data
> structure from the network package, but when I try to run sna
> functions on my network, I get the following error:
> 
> Error in matrix(0, nr = network.size(x), nc = network.size(x)) :
>   too many elements specified
> 
> The reason is that R is only able to create matrices with 2^31-1
> because a matrix is really a vector with a dim attribute, and this
> vector is indexed by a signed integer (this property is independent of
> system architecture -- running on a 64-bit system will not help).
> Since all of the sna functions start by coercing whatever data type
> it's handed (including the network data type) into a full matrix, this
> puts a hard limit on the size of graphs that sna can analyze at 46,340
> vertices.
> 
> It seems like the network package was developed specifically to keep
> this type of thing from happening. The network C API gives all of the
> necessary power to construct all the measures that are currently
> inefficiently calculated in sna. Have the sna developers considered
> overhauling sna to use the network data structure as the primary data
> structue instead of the sociomatrix?
> 
> I've started to modify the underlying C code to use the network API so
> that I can run some of the analyses that I need on graphs with
> millions of nodes, and I've had a lot of success. I would be happy to
> contribute the work that I've done to the sna project, but want to
> make sure that I'm not duplicating effort. Who can I talk to to start
> contributing?

What you are running into is the grand old phenomenon of "legacy code." 
  When sna was first being accumulated in the late 1990s, a "large" 
social network data set had 50-100 nodes.  Sparse-graph performance was 
a not a major issue at that time, nor was support for truly huge graphs. 
  For the most part, this is still the case: despite the "bigger is 
better" push of recent years, most social network data sets are still no 
more than 1-2k nodes, and are handled just fine by adjacency matrices.

That said, an important and growing body of users have much larger data 
sets, and supporting those is also a goal.  As you note, this was one of 
the factors behind the development of the network package, and has been 
considered to a greater or lesser degree in other modern statnet 
components.  The issue, then, is with migrating the old (but useful) 
routines to support the new data structures.

The first step in this process (taken a while back) was to make sure 
that sna and network were functionally interoperable, in the basic sense 
that calling an sna routine with a network object should yield 
reasonable results.  To get to this first milestone, we simply used the 
expedient of transparently coercing network objects (and other 
reasonable data) to adjacency form, and passing this to the existing 
code.  This works, but obviously does not convey any of the other 
advantages of the network package to sna -- in particular, none of the 
scalability advantages apply.

What I've been working on recently is "phase two" of the transition. 
This involves:

   1. Introducing a new interim edgelist standard, which is simple 
enough not to require additional package support (e.g., network), but 
which keeps the scalability/sparsity advantages.
   2. Modifying the internal coercion routines to recognize and use this 
format, and introducing a new (internal) coercion routine to efficiently 
convert existing sparse data objects (network objects and SparseM 
matrices) thereto.
   3. Gradually converting extant routines to natively and transparently 
employ edgelists where feasible.

Although I could use the network API for this purpose, I elected to take 
this route as the interim solution to a full network-based migration. 
This is for three reasons: first, sna has historically been a standalone 
option, and I am inclined to keep that possibility for the time being; 
second, the development path is easier with the interim step (which can 
be more quickly rolled out than a full makeover); and third, there are 
various ways in which the interim step will facilitate the final 
migration to native network object support.  I won't go into all the 
details here, but it basically boils down to the fact that sna is a big 
and fairly stable package, and I can't pull the rug out from under it. 
Luckily, that's not necessary to give folks most of what they want (at 
least, in increments)!

Since this is rapidly getting into a deeper development discussion, I 
don't want to spam the list with too much more of it.  However, if 
you're interested in helping out, that would be great -- the primary 
limitation on progress right now is my own time, which is sliced very 
thinly these days.  (I'm also working on some further updates to 
network, including enhanced dynamic data support, so there are lots of 
irons in the fire!)  I need to get the current development version of 
sna somewhat more stabilized, but at that point I should be in a 
position to highlight specific code contributions which would be 
especially welcome.  I am targeting mid-March for the next release, in 
part since I want to use the updated version in my Spring methods class. 
  :-)

For those of you who are reading this with confusion and trepidation 
(or, alternately, hope and excitement), let me add a few observations 
about the new version:

1. It will not break any existing code.  Your current sna-based scripts 
should work just fine.
2. The new edgelist form will be a new "low-tech" option for those who 
want it, but will not be mandatory.  (Objects like networks and SparseM 
matrices will be automagically handled, as before, but now without 
adjacency matrix conversion in most cases.)
3. Not every routine will immediately see efficiency gains from this 
process, although several have been targeted for the initial update.  As 
routines are re-written, various things will suddenly run much faster 
and/or with much less memory for large, sparse graphs.
4. Users working with ordinary-scale data won't notice much of a change. 
  (But the new release does have some new functions and other goodies 
that may be of interest.)

Hopefully this gives an initial cut at the answers to your questions. 
Volunteers for the conversion effort should contact me directly, and 
I'll send out some additional information over the next few days.

Thanks!

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] A question about ERGMs and simulating networks with an arbitrary number of nodes
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] A question about ERGMs and simulating networks with an arbitrary number of nodes
messages.body_plain:
Hi Hannu.  The answer to your question is yes, it is possible (and  
very easy, in fact, using ergm) to do exactly what you're suggesting:

initialfit <- ergm(network ~ edges + <otherterms>)
parameterestimates <- initialfit$coef
simulate(newnetwork ~ edges + <otherterms>, theta0=parameterestimates)

However, doing this is perilous.  The reason it's perilous is that it  
is not clear that doing the above gives you "statistically similar"  
results.  In fact, it's rather clear that in many cases it does not.

Consider the simplest of all ergms:  The "edges" ergm, where the only  
statistic is the number of edges.  This gives the well-known Erdos- 
Renyi graph model in which each edge has the same probability of  
forming, independent of all others.  If you fit this ergm on a network  
with n nodes, you will obtain as a parameter estimate exactly the  
following quantity:
   log(p) - log(1-p),
where p equals the density of the network, i.e., the proportion of the  
n-choose-2 pairs of nodes that share an edge in your n-node  
(undirected) network.  If you now simulate a new network on m nodes  
with the same ergm and the same parameter estimate, you will recreate  
the same density in your new network, on average.  However, note that  
this does NOT give you the same number of edges on average.  For  
instance, if m = 2n, then the same proportion will produce on average  
more than four times as many edges (because m-choose-2 is a bit more  
than 4 times n-choose-2 when m=2n).  So it is necessary here to be  
very clear about what you mean by "statistically similar".  If you  
mean that you want the same number of edges on average, then you  
cannot merely use the same parameter value obtained using an "edges"  
model.  Perhaps it's more realistic to define "statistically similar"  
in this case to mean "same mean degree", but even in this case the  
"edges" parameter must be adjusted when the number of nodes changes.   
Then again, if "statistically similar" means that you want the same  
network density on average, then it's fine to use the same "edges"  
parameter for different-sized networks.

Now consider using the "density" term instead of "edges" in an ergm.   
The density term equals edges divided by n-choose-2, so it is  
equivalent to the edges term AS LONG AS n REMAINS FIXED, since in this  
case density is simply a constant multiple of edges.  In other words,  
using density alone gives you an Erdos-Renyi graph just as using edges  
alone does.  But if you intend to change the size of the network while  
keeping the network "statistically similar", then once again it is  
necessary to be very specific about defining "statistically similar".   
In particular, using the same parameter value in a new m-node network  
will not give the same density on average (remember, it's the *edges*  
parameter that does this).

If the story is so complicated for even the simplest of ergms, imagine  
what happens for more complicated ones!

I hope this helps.
Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] statnet and igraph function masking
messages.body_plain:
I received this in reply to a similar query yesterday. It suggests that
the last-loaded package controls the definition of a given function
foo() in R.

My question was about the network() function, which is defined
differently by each package {statnet} and {igraph}.

    Ben,

    I believe that the reason for this is that both packages define
    functions with the same name and the 'network' package does not have a
    NAMESPACE.

    A possible workaround is to load the 'igraph' package first, and then
    'statnet' (which loads 'network', etc.) next. At least

    library(igraph)
    library(statnet)
    example(network)

    works fine. Best,
    Gabor

    Dear R users:
    >
    > There appears to be a conflict between the statnet package and the
    > igraph package.
    >
    > With igraph loaded into memory, the network() function of statnet
    > failed, returning the error to the effect that the matrix being
    > converted was "not a graph object." Removing igraph from memory restored
    > statnet to proper function.
    >
    > Apologies if this is redundant. I could not find this documented in the
    > help archives or in the docs for either package.
    >
    > Best,
    > Ben

HI all,

We have developed a model which we think represents our data well, however,
in writing up our results we are finding significant odds ratios (confidence
intervals do not include 1) for some of the estimates which are shown as
non-significant in our output. We are aware that large standard errors can
be the culprit in cases of Type II error, but this typically happens when
the estimate is large and the Wald test is used to determine significance.
This doesn't seem to be the case for us. Any thoughts on this would be great
--- should we interpret the statnet output as a Type II error, or are we
doing something wrong with our OR/CI calculations? Or neither of these?

As an example, the estimate in the output pasted below for LocalRegion.2 is

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chanung,

It sounds like what you have is nodal attribute data (like gdp) and you 
want to model the potential impact of these on tie formation.  This is 
effectively a question about selective mixing based on nodal attributes. 
While you can think about this at the dyadic level, it really is a 
property of the (two) nodes.

Why do you want to model it as a dyadic covariate rather than a nodal 
covariate (using, for example, the absdiff ergm term)?

best,
Martina

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Dave -

dnolin wrote:
> A further question I have on this subject is, What is the appropriate Null
> model to use for these types of comparisons? The null deviance in the ergm
> output appears to be based on an Erdos-Renyi random graph with p = 0.5.
> However, the literature I've been reading on standardizing logistic
> regression coefficients appears ambiguous on what is meant by the "null"
> model. In some cases, it appears to mean the model with the theoretical
> maximum deviance; in other cases the null model is described as a model
> fitted "without parameters", but apparently including an intercept term
> (i.e. edges, in the ergm case). (For an example of this ambiguity, see
> Nagelkerke's (1991) generalized R-squared.)

As is always the case, your null should be based on the baseline process 
against which you wish to test.  The null on which the ergm() parameter 
p-values are based is a model in which all parameters but the indicated 
one are fixed at their MLEs, with the indicated parameter being fixed at 
0 (i.e., the associated statistic is not in the model).  As far as the 
null _deviance_, this is indeed based on the uniform random graph 
(conditional on number of vertices).  Nothing prevents one, however, 
from comparing one's fitted model to other baselines, such as the 
maximum likelihood homogeneous Bernoulli graph (i.e., the model with 
only an edge term), a degree distribution model, etc.  Indeed, Holland 
and Leinhardt's original paper suggests the use of the p1 family as a 
null model against which to test a hypothesis of excess triangulation 
(something that could not be estimated directly at the time, although 
they discuss the possibility).  Note that they suggest performing this 
test in the mean value space, not the natural parameter space, since (as 
noted) they could not fit models with dyadic dependence.

Testing in the mean value space is also the logic behind conditional 
uniform graph tests, and the use of general ERGMs as nulls in this 
manner is a natural extension to this philosophy (and, indeed, can be 
thought of generalized baseline models in a "pure" Mayhewan sense, since 
they maximize entropy given the support and mean stats).  The model 
adequacy checks in ergm.gof() can be viewed in this light.  Choosing an 
appropriate baseline model is as much a matter of substantive theory as 
statistics per se, and your choice should reflect your knowledge of the 
system under study (e.g., through the "obvious" baseline effects that 
are known to be present, and which must be discounted before concluding 
that something more interesting is afoot).  For this reason, there can 
be no universally "correct" null.

In general, my sense is that one is better served by reasoning about 
these models from first principles, than by trying to directly import 
ideas from the logistic regression world sans attention to context. 
That's not to say that no such concepts can be brought over -- after 
all, the logistic case is a special case of the discrete exponential 
family framework -- but techniques developed for a world of independent, 
non-relational variables can often be misleading and/or useless when 
dealing with network data.  Start with what you know and what you want 
to measure.  If this leads you back to a problem for which a known (and 
applicable) solution exists in the logistic/GLM literature, great!  If 
not, then trying to apply an inapplicable technique from conventional 
regression is probably going to get you in trouble.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
> However, I do not fully understand what is captured by the scaling parameter 
> alpha (or lambda?). If I do not fix this parameter (i.e. the default 
> setting), the model fit as indicated by AIC and BIC is quite good, but the 
> graphical goodness of fit assessment does *not* look very nice. If I fix the 
> parameter at 0 or 0.1, the gof is really good, but AIC and BIC are much

Hello Philip,

This is a good (and common question) - thanks for asking it, and sorry for the delay in response.

This parameter and its interpretation is discussed in a few of our group's papers, but generally only very briefly.  Moreover, its parameterization has varied from paper to paper so it can be particularly confusing.  One way I like to think of it is as follows - we believe there is a tendency for triangles to close (assuming we're testing for a positive coefficient here, as we usually are).  Or, equivalently, we believe there is a tendency for those with shared partners to become tied.  We might imagine that this effect is stronger the greater the number of shared partners two people have.  That effect could be linear in the number of shared partners, or it could take some other parametric or non-parametric form.  GWESP assumes a parametric form in which there are declining marginal returns to tie probability across different numbers of shared partners.  The scaling parameter that you asked 
about controls that rate of declining marginal returns; the GWESP coefficient controls the overall strength of triad close given that rate.

It helps to think of the extremes. When the scaling parameter equals 0, nothing beyond the first shared partner matters; thus, the statistic becomes equivalent to the number of edges that are in at least one triangle. When it approaches in finity, there is no decline; all triangles matter equally no matter how many other triangles two of their actors are in, and the statistic approaches three times the number of triangles. In general, the lower the value of the scaling parameter, the less likely the model is to be degenerate.

One can allow ergm to estimate the parameter from the data (using fixed=FALSE), although this generally greatly increases the estimation time one needs in order to ensure convergence.  Or, one can can use fixed=TRUE and simply estimate the coefficient for a single scaling parameter, if one either has a priori information about what the scaling parameter should be, or is willing to make an assumption.  In practice I have found that it seems to matter relatively little what specific value I use in the range of 0-1.5 or so on a variety of networks.

As for your observation that the AIC and BIC get better when the GOF plots get worse. I don't have much specific insight on that, other than to say that they are measuring different features of model fit (the GOF plots are generally focusing on more global features depending on which you are using) and we still have a long way to go to understand all of the ways that global structure emerges from local network process. If you have more information to help us understand your specific case, I'd love to hear it.

Cheers,
Steve

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] A question about running ergm on 2-mode networks
messages.body_plain:
Moses,

If I understand correctly, you want to create a social network of objects, where the relationship defining a link is their shared value of an attribute in A.  You then want to create a second social network of objects, where the relationship defining a link is their shared value of an attribute in B.  Then, you want to see if one the two networks is a significant predictor of link formation in the other.

To create a network, where the relationship is based on their shared attribute, take the vector of length O consisting of attributes A (we'll call this X).  Take the dot product of X.Xtranspose.  This will create a social network of size O by O, where there is a link if two nodes share the same attribute in A.  Repeat the same process for O and B.

To see if one network is significant in the ergm model for another, use edgecov().  

Depending on the nature of the attribute, it may be more interesting to see how different they are.  For example if your O by A vector was {2,5,9}, you could take differences to get the network {0,-3,-7}{3,0,-4}{7,4,0} or something.

If you want to see how similar two objects are across multiple attributes, then Ox(A,B)*(A,B)xO will give you an OxO where the link weight is the shared number of attributes.  This is what I typically do for homophily.

Best of luck.

Ian

You definitely don't want to mix igraph and the statnet suite -- they 
sometimes don't play nice together.  There is a betweenness routine in 
sna, a package that is part of the statnet suite.

that if your graphs are sizable, you might want need to write some more 
specialized code.  The voltage matrix is a computational beast and we 
had to write parallelizable code to run on a big Linux cluster to 
perform community structure calculations on 3000-node graphs.

Hope this helps.

Cheers,

Jamie

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] ERGM, missing data, and dyadcov and edgecov terms
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a Statnet-ERGM question that I suspect has been asked and  
answered, but so far my search of the archives has not yielded an  
answer.

I am working with a directed graph. A small number of actors in my  
population have missing data for their edges.  However, I have a rich  
set of attribute data for these actors, which leads me to retain dyads  
in which they are alters for models w/ nodematch terms, etc.

Certain ERGM terms (e.g., edgecov) require that the dataset analyzed  
consist of all possible edges in the data along with values for  
whatever edge covariates are of interest.  In my case, given missing  
data, all possible edges (possible = possibly observed) would not be a  
square matrix, because only actors with alter data can be egos, while  
all actors can be alters.

I assume the edgecov term expects a square matrix anyway.  If so, I  
seem to have two options:

1) Reduce my data to only edges in which ego and alter both are  
complete in terms of tie data.
2) Provide ERGM with the full square matrix, including edges that I  
can't observe.

If #2, to the extent I have a node attribute indicating whether the  
node's edges were missing rather than null, are there additional  
statements that can be made to capture that only certain directed  
edges can be observed?

As a reminder (from the JOSS ERGM article):

"The x argument is either a square matrix of covariates, one for each  
possible edge in the network, covariates, or a network; if the latter,  
optional argument attrname provides the name of the quantitative edge  
attribute to use for covariate values (in this case, missing edges in  
x are assigned a covariate value of zero). "

It appears to call for the square matrix, but that doesn't feel quite  
right.

Any suggestions, best practices, readings, or considerations are  
appreciated....

Thanks!

Matthew

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Re: help with edge attributes & network extraction
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Re: help with edge attributes & network extraction
messages.body_plain:
Hi statnet group,

I got a response that indicated that my question was a problem that  
others have run into, so I thought I'd present my solution. I wrote a  
function that takes a network and a vector of edge attributes, and  
returns a 3 column matrix with the edgelist of the network's largest  
component plus the corresponding edge attributes. This can be easily  
read back into a network object or into tnet, a package I've been  
playing with.

Disclaimer: I am not a programmer and have self-taught myself R so I  
make no claims that this is great code but it appears to be working  
for me.Any advice on how to improve would be great! Hopefully some  
part of it might help others out there and save some time.

Second disclaimer: I wrote the function for undirected networks, if  
you're working with directed networks then you will have to change a  
few minor things.

-Michael

#largest.component.edgeattr(net, edgeattr)
#Takes a network object and a vector of edge attributes for that  
network, and returns
#an edgelist for the largest component of that network with a 3rd  
column containing
#the edge attributes;

largest.component.edgeattr <- function(net, edgeattr){

#Get edgelist from network, attach attribute
edgelist <- as.matrix.network(net, matrix.type = "edgelist",  
directed=FALSE)
edgelist <- cbind(edgelist, edgeattr)

#Initialize weighted adjacency matrix
numnodes <- network.size(net)
zeros <- rep(0, numnodes^2)
edgeattr_mat <- matrix(zeros, nrow = numnodes, ncol = numnodes)
#Add in edge weights for each tied node pair to matrix edgeattr_mat
for(x in 1:network.edgecount(net)) {
	i <- edgelist[x,1]
	j <- edgelist[x,2]
	edgeattr_mat[i,j] <- edgelist[x,3]
	#If network is undirected, symmetrize the assignments
	edgeattr_mat[j,i] <- edgelist[x,3]
	}

#Create a new edgelist for the largest subcomponent, in addition to a  
vector comp_names
	#comp_names = a crosswalk between node IDs in the largest  
subcomponent and the network such that
	#if i is the index of a node in the subcomponent, comp_nodes[i] =  
node index in the network
comp <- as.network(component.largest(net, connected="weak", result =  
"graph"), matrix.type = "adjacency", directed = FALSE)
comp_names <- as.numeric(comp %v% "vertex.names")
comp_edgelist <- as.matrix.network(comp, matrix.type = "edgelist")

#initializing edgeattr_comp = edge attributes vector for largest  
component edges
edgeattr_comp <- vector(mode = "integer",  
length=network.edgecount(comp))

#Extract the attribute for each edge in the largest subcomponent from  
edgeattr_mat above, using the
#crosswalk vector comp_names to translate node names between the two  
networks
for(x in 1:network.edgecount(comp)) {
	i <- comp_names[comp_edgelist[x,1]]
	j <- comp_names[comp_edgelist[x,2]]
	edgeattr_comp[x] <- edgeattr_mat[i,j]
	}

#comp_edgelist is the weighted edgelist
comp_edgelist <- cbind(comp_edgelist, edgeattr_comp)
return(comp_edgelist)
}

messages.body_plain:
Hello Richard.  The problem appears to be R fussiness about how a  
data.frame is handled.  Essentially, your "as.vector" commands are not  
doing what you think they're doing; since a data.frame is a fancy  
list, applying as.vector to the whole thing (rather than to an  
individual element in the list, which is a column in the data.frame)  
doesn't actually do anything.

You are not the only one to have had a similar problem recently, by  
the way!

There are several ways to correct this.  Perhaps the most elegant is  
to use "scan" in place of "read.table", in which case the "as.vector"  
commands will be unnecessary, as in:

grov <- scan ("gro.txt")
etc.

But the easiest and probably the most instructive fix to your existing  
code (I'm not sure it will work, since I can't be sure I'm replicating  
your errors) would be as follows:

gro <- read.table("gro.txt")
grov <- as.vector(gro[,1])
etc.

I hope this helps.
Dave
