messages.subject: [statnet_help] Numbered IDs create massive problems
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Dai -

The issue here is that the edgelist->network conversion assumes that 
your data is given in the form of vertex IDs (since you are using a 
numeric matrix).  Vertex IDs are not names, but the sort order of the 
vertex; thus, you can't have an ID (in the sense of the network package) 
of 112998 on a 43-node network.  You can, of course, have a vertex that 
carries this number as a name (or other attribute).

As this suggests, one approach is to renumber your edgelists prior to 
conversion.  E.g., something like this:

#Let el be your edgelist matrix
uvert<-sort(unique(c(el[,1],el[,2])))
el[,1]<-match(el[,1],uvert)
el[,2]<-match(el[,2],uvert)

This will keep your network vertex IDs in the same order as your own ID 
numbers (names).  Then, set the vertex names (or any other attribute) 
equal to uvert; you can retrieve the original names in the usual fashion 
using %v% or get.vertex.attribute.

If you don't like that road, another option is to convert your numbers 
to fixed-width character strings with leading zeros.  (formatC will do 
this.)  That ensures that the sort order matches the numeric order of 
your vertex names.  Finally, you could just create the network as usual, 
and then permute the vertices into your desired order using 
permute.vertexIDs (with the order identified by 
order(as.numeric(vertex.names(mynet))) or some such).

Any of these should work, but I recommend the first, FWIW.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Valued networks in network package
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Alex -

Alexander H. Montgomery-Amo wrote:
> It seems that the network package doesn't actually preserve valued 
> relations when coercing matricies into networks. For example:
> 
>  > m <- matrix(c(0,2,2,0),nrow=2)
>  > n <- network(m)
>  > degree(n)
> [1] 2 2
>  > degree(m)
> [1] 4 4
> 
> Does the network package assume that networks are not valued? Or am I 
> missing something else here?
> 

Network objects can contain arbitrary edge metadata (including numeric 
values).  To include this information, you need to either tell the 
network constructor how to store it, or else add it later (using, e.g., 
the %e% operator or add.edge.attribute).  Here's a simple example:

#Create a test matrix
library(sna)
library(network)
mat<-rgraph(5)*matrix(1:25,5,5)
mat

#Create a network object, storing the edge values in "value"
net<-network(mat,ignore.eval=FALSE,names.eval="value")
summary(net)

#Retrieve the original form using as.sociomatrix
all(as.sociomatrix(net,"value")==mat)

Note that, since network objects can in theory contain any number of 
edge attributes of any type (including lists, complex objects, etc.), 
most functions try not to make too many assumptions about them.  Some of 
the shortcuts (e.g., %e%) are made specifically to handle standard 
vector types (characters, numerics, etc.), but the core functions (e.g., 
add.edge.attribute) have to be able to work with much more general data 
types.  Thus one needs to specifically tell commands like network() what 
you want to do with any available metadata.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
Hello again,
The problem all boiled down a line of code in robust.inverse.  This
line in question reads:
        Hsvd <- svd(H)
In my call to ergm, I was (mis)using the dyadcov term in a way that
caused a row of NAs in the Hessian matrix.  This caused svd to fail.
As it so happens, this line of code has been updated in the ergm
binaries and source currently available on cran to:
     Hsvd <- try(svd(H), silent=TRUE)
The version number (2.2-1) of ergm hadn't changed from what I had
installed to the present, but there must have been some minor
modifications.  I've also noticed another issue.  When I load ergm
directly the robust.inverse function is correct (with try(svd...)
while if I load ergm via statnet, the older chunk (where svd is being
used without try) is being used for robust.inverse.  That's not an
error per se, but having statnet load an older version of ergm did
lead to some confusion.
Hopefully this is helpful to others confronting this issue.  To the
statnet team, the suite of packages rules and the documentation
(especially the JSS special edition) is great!
Ben

Hi all,

I'm working on a project looking a referral network of cancer services
organizations for low-income cancer patients (what predicts organization A
referring a patient to organization B). One of the predictors of referrals
that I am using is a network of distance (in minutes) on public
transportation between the organizations. I am using the dyadcov term in my
ERGM to predict the presence of a referral tie between two organizations
based on how far apart they are. My question is: How would I interpret the
following:

dyadcov.minutes.mutual       -28.44480    0.06961        NA  < 1e-04 ***
dyadcov.minutes.utri         -15.46894    0.11195        NA  < 1e-04 ***
dyadcov.minutes.ltri         -15.42000    0.10858        NA  < 1e-04 ***

The first row appears to be the reduction in likelihood of a tie for a 1
unit increase in minutes between organizations when A refers to B and B
refers to A (there are referral links going both directions).

The upper triangle is then likely to be the reduction in the likelihood of a
tie for a 1 unit increase in minutes when A refers to B (but B does not
refer to A)

The lower triangle is the reduction in the likelihood of a tie for a 1 unit
increase in minutes when B refers to A (but A does not refer to B)

I gather from the statnet tutorials that each dyad only falls into one of
these categories....mutual, upper, or lower

Does this sound like an appropriate interpretation of these results?

Thanks in advance for any thoughts on this.

Jenine

messages.subject: [statnet_help] interpreting GWDSP?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jenine,

I don't know if you got a response to this question, and I just ran 
across something that might help, so thought I'd send it to you.
Danny Wyatt (from here at UW) sent us a short description, and I made up a 
little excel spreadsheet to see if I could get some intuition (attached).

Briefly, these terms (GWESP, GWDSP, and GWDEG) fit a 2 parameter curve to 
the histogram of the number of shared partners, or degree.  The two 
parameters, alpha and w, define the shape of this curve.  The alpha term 
acts a bit like an intercept (in a non-linear way), and the coefficient 
(w) acts a bit like a slope (again, in a non-linear way)

Danny's explanation below.  Hope this helps.

best,
Martina

> Anyhow, have you read this paper by David Hunter?
> Curved exponential family models for social networks, Social Networks
> 29(2). 216-230.
> http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.socnet.2006.08.005
>
> It helped me understand the GW* features a lot better.  In particular
> Eqn. 16 in that papers works it out so that you can interpret your
> parameters as the log odds of a node increasing its degree from k to
> k+1---or for GWESP the log odds that a pair will change their number
> of shared partners from k to k+1.
>
> The general form of that is
> w * (1 - exp(-alpha))^k
> where w is the regular non-alpha parameter.
>
> So if you've fixed alpha=0.2, then it's just w * (0.181)^k.  You could
> plot that out for k from 0 to N-2 (if you've got N people) and it'll
> show you how the log odds of adding a new shared partner decreases as
> you have more shared partners.
>
> Actually, if you exp it to get the odds it'll approach 1 and you can
> find the point where it's close enough to 1 for you and then say "this
> is the point at which its no longer beneficial for two people to keep
> adding mutual friends."

On Thu, 6 Aug 2009, Jenine Harris wrote:

> Hi,
> 
> I was wondering if anyone has an example of how a GWDSP term would be interpreted in somewhat lay terms. From my understanding GWDSP

messages.subject: [statnet_help] the vertex.attributes option of network()
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Victorin -

Victorin Luisier wrote:
> Dear Statnet team,
> 
> I think that the "vertex.attributes" option of network() doesnt work 
> (sorry if this problem is already known, or if i'm wrong :-) :
> 
> library(statnet)
> resp2<-paste("subj",1:220,sep="") #list of respondant
> t<-c(182,170,150,180,100,170,220)
> h<-c(1,1,2,2,3,3,3)
> el2<-matrix(c(t,h),ncol=2) #numeric edglist
> n2<-network(el2,vertex.attrnames=resp2)
> n2 %v% "vertex.names" # the vertex.attrnames option appears not to work
> 
> n2<-network(el2,vertex.attr=list(vertex.names=resp2))
> n2 %v% "vertex.names" # seems to work now
> 
> 
> Anyway, thanks a lot for your work,
> Victorin Luisier
> 

Your first call uses the vertex.attrnames argument incorrectly.  This 
argument supplies a list of attribute name vectors (or something that 
can be sensibly coerced to this.  If you wanted to make such a call, you 
would do it like so:

n2<-network(el2,vertex.attrnames=rep("vertex.names",220),vertex.attr=list(as.list(resp2)))

This is cumbersome (though flexible), which is why we do not recommend 
it for general use.  A more obvious thing to do would be

n2 %v% "vertex.names" <- resp2

after having created n2.  In any event, this appears to be a non-error.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] are ergm's parameters and change statistics standardized?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Guido,

I was looking at this very same problem this past week. There are a number
of different methods for standardizing log-odds coefficients. Most of these
require information about the standard deviation of the independent
variable, the dependent variable, or both. The problem with ergm models is
that we do not know the standard deviation of the network-structural
independent variables of the model.

Menard (2004) has proposed an information-based method for standardizing
log-odds coefficients. The advantage of using this method with ergm
coefficients is that it does not require an estimate of the standard
deviation of the independent variable, just the log-likelihood values from
the set of all possible nested models. The disadvantage is that with even
modest numbers of covariates the number of models that must be run can
become cumbersome.

Perhaps someone more versed in ergm statistics will respond on the
appropriateness of this method for ergm coefficients.

A further question I have on this subject is, What is the appropriate Null
model to use for these types of comparisons? The null deviance in the ergm
output appears to be based on an Erdos-Renyi random graph with p = 0.5.
However, the literature I've been reading on standardizing logistic
regression coefficients appears ambiguous on what is meant by the "null"
model. In some cases, it appears to mean the model with the theoretical
maximum deviance; in other cases the null model is described as a model
fitted "without parameters", but apparently including an intercept term
(i.e. edges, in the ergm case). (For an example of this ambiguity, see
Nagelkerke's (1991) generalized R-squared.)

Cheers,
Dave

Menard, Scott. 2004. Six approaches to calculating standardized logistic
regression coefficients. The American Statistician, 58: 218-223.

Nagelkerke, N.J.D. 1991. A note on a general definition of the coefficient
of determination. Biometrika, 78: 691-692.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] commented and edited code from last post
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] commented and edited code from last post
messages.body_plain:
Last post on this thread - there was a bug in my function and it  
wasn't very well commented, so here it is. If anyone can think of  
something simpler and faster, that would be great! This is a pretty  
time consuming little function.

-Michael

******

#Function returning nbddensity, a matrix of egocentric neighborhood  
densities for
#each node in a network from distance 1 to "distance"
nbd_density <- function(net, distance) {	
	# Initializing objects
	size <- network.size(net)
	nbddensity <- matrix(nrow = size, ncol = distance)
	
	#Get neighborhoods
	nbd <- neighborhood(net, distance, neighborhood.type="total",  
mode="graph", return.all=TRUE, partial = FALSE)
	
	#Nested loop which creates adjancency matrix for each node in a  
network, then calculates
	#its density and deposits the value in a matrix. Repeated for each  
order up to supplied value distance
	for (i in 1:distance) {
		for (j in 1:size) {
			adj_m <- as.matrix(net[c(nbd[i,j,]==1),c(nbd[i,j,]==1)])
			ifelse (length(as.vector(adj_m)) == 1, nbddensity[j,i] <- 0, #If  
isolate, density = 0, not 1
				nbddensity[j,i] <- network.density(as.network.matrix(adj_m,  
matrix.type="adjacency")))
			}
		}	
	nbddensity	 #return nbddensity matrix,
}

messages.subject: [statnet_help] GWESP - parameter setting
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Steve.  Just to chime in on this -

Steven Goodreau wrote:
> As for your observation that the AIC and BIC get better when the GOF 
> plots get worse. I don't have much specific insight on that, other than 
> to say that they are measuring different features of model fit (the GOF 
> plots are generally focusing on more global features depending on which 
> you are using) and we still have a long way to go to understand all of 
> the ways that global structure emerges from local network process. If 
> you have more information to help us understand your specific case, I'd 
> love to hear it.

In my experience, that's usually a sign of poor mixing.  The AIC/BIC are 
based on the estimated likelihood, which is fairly sensitive to the size 
and quality of the MCMC sample.  A poorly mixed sample can lead to an 
erroneously high likelihood, but tends to show itself in the diagnostics 
(both ours and the MCMC diagnostics one gets from e.g., coda).  Adding a 
high-dependence statistic can thus lead to an apparent improvement in 
fit, due not to an actual impact on model performance, but to the fact 
that it cripples the underling Markov chain.  Careful attention to the 
diagnostics is, as always, the best defense.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

PS. Of course, the GOF plots are also sample-dependent, so it is 
important to inspect those MCMC diagnostics as well.  One would hate to 
propose a good model, only to accidentally reject it due to skimping on 
the validation sample!

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGM with Loops
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jared,

Ergm was not written to handle loops, so it ignores that information.  If you want to consider the presence of a loop on a node as a fixed attribute and a predictor of other ties, you could code it as a binary nodal attribute.  But unfortunately there's no way to have nodal loops be an outcome of the stochastic process of tie formation in ergm.

Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] interpreting GWDSP?
messages.body_plain:
On Thu, 6 Aug 2009, Jenine Harris wrote:

> I was wondering if anyone has an example of how a GWDSP term would be
> interpreted in somewhat lay terms. From my understanding GWDSP accounts for
> the distribution of shared partnership for each dyad in a network, but I'm
> not sure how to go about interpreting a negative signficant GWDSP
> coefficient of -0.25 in an actual ERGM model. What does this say about the
> distribution and how does it influence the likelihood of a tie?


Hi Jenine,

A great question.  Yes, I do think GWDSP is a bit trickier than interpret 
than any of the other terms we commonly work with.  I can give you my own 
idiosyncratic approach.

First, as technical background: As you probably know, GWDSP is a 
parametric summary measure of the tendency for two actors to have x 
partners in common, regardless of whether the two actors themselves are 
tied.  GWESP is the same measure, but only counted across two actors who 
are tied.  The two are comparable to the "alternating 2-paths" and 
"alternating k-triangles" that Snijders et al discuss in a series of 
papers. The two measures, combined with a third (GW degree, or the 
comparable alternating k-stars) are derived in those papers by placing a 
parametric constraint on three sets of statistics that emerge when making 
a very sociologically reasonable set of assumptions about relational 
dependence.  The three parametric stats are also seen to work well in 
practice at modeling real-world social networks and avoiding degeneracy 
when doing so.

So, on to interpretation.  As I said, I agree that GWDSP is the hardest to 
interpret.  In fact, I personally never use a GWDSP term without also 
using a GWESP term. And once I combined the two, I always find that the 
GWDSP coefficient is close to zero, and non-significant. Let me see if I 
can give good intuition as to why.

GWESP has some relatively clear interpetations (which I discuss in a few 
of my papers). In real-world data of friendship or collaboration or 
similar kinds of networks, it is generally significantly positive. This 
means that those who are tied are more likely than chance to have multiple 
shared partners.

GWDSP tells whether shared partners tend to clump together, regardless of 
whether two people are tied or not.  For example, whether or not you and I 
are friends, if we have one friend in common, are we more likely than 
expected by chance to have a second friend in common?  And so on.  If yes, 
the GWDSP coefficient will be positive.  If it is zero, then we are as 
likely as chance to have one in common; if negative, then less.

If one only uses GWDSP and not GWESP, then it's hard to know whether an 
observed non-random shared partner distribution is driven by pairs who are 
themselves tied, pairs who are not tied, or both.  If you include both 
GWESP and GWDSP, then it becomes clear - GWDSP is the base effect (which 
now isolates the effect for those not tied only); GWESP occurs on top of 
this base, and isolates the effect for those who are tied.  And what I 
have always found is that the GWESP effect is then strong and significant, 
and the GWDSP is tiny and insignificant.  It may be that in different 
kinds of data GWDSP would be significant itself, though.

My questions for you are: is your GWDSP term significant? Does it remain 
so when GWESP is added?  If the answer to both questions is yes, then you 
have something particuarly interesting (and unprecendented, at least for 
me) on your hands. If it remains negative and significant, then that says 
that people who are not tied tend not to have multiple shared partners. 
Once two unconnected people have one shared partner, they're less likely 
than chance to have a second; if they do have a second, they're less 
likely than chance to have a third, and so on. I can't think of a type of 
social relationship I would anticipate this pattern for, but it could just 
be that I've never thought about the kind of relaitonship that you're 
studying, and it makes perfect sense to you.

My other quesiton would be what your alpha is; that changes the fine 
quantitative details of the interpretation, but not the general 
qualitative interpretation. Unless your alpha is either essentially 0 or 
very very high, in which case it would change the latter as well. If it's 
in the 0.1 - 2.0 range, I don't think it would.

I hope that helps!
Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Edges as a Constraint or a Parameter?
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Edges as a Constraint or a Parameter?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I had a question that I am hoping someone here with more experience  
with ERG models might have some input.

Background on Project: I am using ERG models to examine the patters of  
advice networks in traditional settings related to acquiring  
skills/knowledge. I am interested in empirically testing if a variety  
of attributes (perceived skill, age, gender, etc.), suggested by  
analytical modeling to be important, are related to the patterns of  
these networks and the number of nominations that an individual  
receives. The way that the data was collected, we allowed individuals  
to nominate at most 5 other people, which I am including as a  
constraint in all models.

I am unsure whether to include edges as a constraint or as a parameter  
to estimate.  When I include it as a parameter, all my main effects  
parameters (nodeicov) are strongly correlated (above .8) with the  
edges parameter (and with each other). When I constrain the simulated  
networks to match the number of edges present in the observed data, I  
no longer have this problem, but the parameter estimates are different  
(same direction, but different magnitudes).

Theoretically, I think that varying the number of total ties present  
in the network is important, since there are reasons to think that  
this might happen in the real world.  However, the correlation between  
this parameter and all the main effects is troubling.

Does anyone have any thoughts on what is more important, not having  
strong correlations between predictors, or having a model that is  
allowed to vary in ways that are similar to what we might expect in  
reality?

Any input is appreciated,

James Broesch

PhD Candidate
Department of Anthropology
Emory University

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Valued networks in network package
messages.body_plain:
You want to use the network.adjacency option to create a valued adjacency matrix

m = matrix(c(0,2,2,0),nrow=2)
n = network(m)
degree(n)
network.adjacency(m,n)
degree(n)
degree(m)

If you're familiar with R you'll a little confused by the syntax for
network.adjacency, where m is the adjacency matrix that defines the
values of the ties in n. The function (I think) takes care of the
assignment itself.

Hope that helps,
Sam Stewart

> Here are some details about the file format:
>
> The ##d file:
> - the 'data' file which contains all the cell entries of the adjacency
> matrix. They are not separated by any character. Each cell entry is encoded
> as a 32 bit float number according to the IEEE-754 standard and with little
> endian encoding. For example, a weight in the adjacency matrix of '3' is
> saved as the hex value '00 00 80 3F'.
>
> The ##h file:
> - the header file which contains the row and column labels
> - starts with the hex value '05'
> - then '44 41 54 45 3A' (which means 'DATE:' in ASCII)
> - then some code I haven't been able to figure out yet (probably a date...,
> perhaps the authors of Ucinet are able to help here)
> - then the row labels as ASCII code (separated by '00 00' in hex code)
> - and finally the network label in ASCII.
> - of course, the structure may be different if we are talking about
> two-mode networks etc.
>
> If anyone in the statnet team or elsewhere is interested in writing a
> read.ucinet function (which is probably something many people would be

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Simulate and estimate ERGM with missing edges?
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Simulate and estimate ERGM with missing edges?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Randall.  Have you verified that you are getting the correct mean 
stats (i.e., that your simulated mean statistics match the observed 
statistics) for your model _without_ adding the missing data?  If your 
model is borderline-degenerate (as most regular models based on 
triangles/k-stars are), then this could be the root of your problem. 
Alternately, the algorithm may not have converged closely enough for 
your needs.  MCMC diagnostics are helpful here, but are not a substitute 
for making sure that you have convergence in mean value space; if not, 
you may need to increase the number of iterations of the fitting 
procedure.  (Remember that the likelihood surface is being approximated 
via a finite-sample Monte Carlo procedure, and even a "clean" sample 
will leave some approximation error, especially if the starting value 
was far from the true MLE.)

Some current work by Arthur Asuncion appears to suggest that greatly 
increasing the number of fitting iterations (the ergm maxit argument) 
can result in improved performance, even if the quality and size of each 
MCMC sample is reduced.  This is still an area of active research, but 
my informal experimentation with this type of approach has been pretty 
consistent with his initial findings.  If you want to experiment with 
this approach, try greatly reducing the burn-in, thinning, and sample 
size parameters, and increase maxit correspondingly (e.g., on the order 
of 100-500).  Purely anecdotally, my experience was that this worked 
surprisingly well at getting close to the MLE, but that getting 
high-precision convergence required boosting the MCMC sample quality 
back up.  (There are good reasons to expect this kind of behavior, as 
Arthur has pointed out.)  Also, bear in mind that for goodness-of-fit 
assessment, you really need a high-quality sample.

To sum up:

1. If your model doesn't work in the complete data case, it is unlikely 
to work otherwise.  So check that first, if you haven't already.

2. If your MCMC samples are good, then the problem may be that you need 
more "outer" iterations of the fitting procedure to get convergence to 
the true MLE.  If the mean stats from a high quality MCMC sample at the 
estimated MLE don't closely match your observed stats, the model has not 
converged.

3. On the other end of things, it is possible to get MCMC samples that 
appear to have converged based on casual inspection, but have that are 
still far from equilibrium.  (Note that I am speaking of the Markov 
chain per se, not the entire MLE estimation process.)  Increasing 
burn/thin/sample size parameters can help with this, as might switching 
to another MCMC proposal distribution.  See also any good applied MCMC 
text (e.g., Gilks et al.) for advice on convergence assessment/improvement.


Oh, one other thing: given a draw, g, from an ERG(theta) distribution, 
there is no guarantee that MLE(g) exists.  (Indeed, for graphs of finite 
order, there will usually be a positive probability that the MLE will 
not exist.)  That's because there is a positive probability of drawing 
some g that is on the edge of the convex hull of possible values for the 
sufficient statistics (as opposed to being in the relative interior), 
and the MLE in this case will diverge for some or all of the model 
parameters.  For some models, this contingency is remote: the 
probability of drawing a "defective" g is so tiny that you'll never run 
into one.  (E.g., a pure edges model with parameter 0 on a graph of 
order >>10.)  For models with "extreme" choices of theta, for which the 
underlying statistics interact in funny ways, or for very small graphs, 
this can happen much more often.  If you are finding that your 
simulate/refit process usually works, but occasionally produces models 
with divergent MLEs, this could be the culprit.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] are ergm's parameters and change statistics	standardized?
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] are ergm's parameters and change statistics	standardized?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Guido -

Guido Conaldi wrote:
> Dear all,
> 
> I have a basic question about the parameters and the change statistics
> returned respectively by ergm and ergmMPLE. Are they standardized?

No.

> 
> My take is that they are not, and I would need them both standardized in
> order to replicate Faust and Skvoretz (2002) and compare networks using
> their predictors.
> 
> If I am correct and they are not standardized, what is the correct way
> of standardizing ERGM's parameters and change statistics? Especially
> parameters seem tricky to me to standardize.

You will need to clarify the sense in which you want them to be 
"standardized."  One can, e.g., "standardize" them in the sense of 
approximate z-scores by dividing the coefficient by its approximate 
standard error; if, on the other hand, you want to "standardize" an 
effect by reparameterizing it in such a manner that e.g., it maintains a 
fixed scaling relationship with some given statistic (e.g., N), then a 
different approach will be needed.

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
Thanks a lot, it helped me a lot!

Carter T. Butts a ?crit :
> Hi, Victorin -
> 
> Victorin Luisier wrote:
>> Dear Statnet users,
>>
>> I have discovered a potential problem with the network command. Here 
>> is an example code:
>>
>> library(statnet)
>> resp1<-c("Victorin","Alice","Gabrielle","Jonas","Thibault", "Nad?ge")
>> x<-c("Victorin","Alice","Gabrielle","Jonas","Thibault","Nad?ge","Nad?ge","Gabrielle","Victorin","Victorin") 
>>
>> y<-c("Alice","Victorin","Victorin","Victorin","Jonas", 
>> "Jonas","Victorin","Jonas","Alice","")
>> el1<-matrix(c(x,y),ncol=2) #charactere edgelist
>> n1<-network(el1,matrix.type="edgelist")
>> n1
>>
>> As I discovered, the charactere edgelist in n1 is ranked in 
>> alphabetical order and not in the order of appearance of el1. For me 
>> it's a problem because you cannot easily add other variables (like 
>> vertex variables) in n1 and you will probably have corrupted data.
> 
> This is standard behavior: vertices are coded in sorted ID order for 
> edgelist entry, not by the (arbitrary) order they may happen to appear 
> in your edgelist.  If you want a different vertex order, then I 
> recommend either naming them in the desired order or permuting them ex 
> post facto (see permute.vertexIDs).  The more natural thing to do, 
> however, is to sort your vertex covariates in the order of the vertices 
> prior to entry.
> 
> I should also point out, by the way, that edges _are_ stored within the 
> network object in the order of entry, as you can verify by using 
> as.matrix(n1,"edgelist").  Thus, any edge covariates can be entered in 
> the same order as the original edges, without ill effect.
> 
> Hope that helps,
> 
> -Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] memory limit
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone -

Another question: I'm working with a set of networks ranging from  
~400-5000 nodes. I'm running a simple program to calculate basic node- 
level stuff, just three different centrality measures. When I run my  
program on my office's UNIX server, the program inevitably crashes  
with the error "memory exhausted{limit reached?)". I've checked the  
memory limits on the server and they are all "unlimited" except for  
stacksize which is 10240 kbytes. Any suggestions? I'm pasting my code  
below in case maybe it's my code's fault.

-Michael

#APSC_nodes = list of nodes and attributes for each subnetwork in  
APSC_comp
#APSC_comp = list of networks (which are largest components of other  
networks)

APSC_centrality <- list()	

for (i in 1) {
	size <- network.size(APSC_comp[[i]])
	
	#Component nodes indexing
	comp_nodes <- APSC_nodes[[i]][APSC_comp[[i]] %v% "vertex.names",1]
	
	#Precalc geodesic distance matrix
	gd <- geodist(APSC_comp[[i]], predecessors = TRUE)
	
	#PCP node level statistics
	degree <- degree(APSC_comp[[i]], gmode = "graph")
	degree_cent <- degree/(size-1)
	
	#Centrality measures
	between_std <- betweenness(APSC_comp[[i]], nodes = NULL, gmode =  
"graph", cmode = "undirected", geodist.precomp = gd)
	between_std_norm <- 2*between_std/((size-1)*(size-2))
	close <- closeness(APSC_comp[[i]], nodes = NULL, gmode = "graph",  
cmode = "undirected", geodist.precomp = gd)

	
	#Collate into list of dataframes for all nodes and PCPs
	APSC_centrality[[i]] <- cbind(APSC_nodes[[i]][comp_nodes,], degree,  
degree_cent, between_std, between_std_norm, close) 	
}

)

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Use of network() with a charactere edgelist: the edgelist is ranked in alphabetical order in the network object.
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Victorin -

Victorin Luisier wrote:
> Dear Statnet users,
> 
> I have discovered a potential problem with the network command. Here is 
> an example code:
> 
> library(statnet)
> resp1<-c("Victorin","Alice","Gabrielle","Jonas","Thibault", "Nad?ge")
> x<-c("Victorin","Alice","Gabrielle","Jonas","Thibault","Nad?ge","Nad?ge","Gabrielle","Victorin","Victorin") 
> 
> y<-c("Alice","Victorin","Victorin","Victorin","Jonas", 
> "Jonas","Victorin","Jonas","Alice","")
> el1<-matrix(c(x,y),ncol=2) #charactere edgelist
> n1<-network(el1,matrix.type="edgelist")
> n1
> 
> As I discovered, the charactere edgelist in n1 is ranked in alphabetical 
> order and not in the order of appearance of el1. For me it's a problem 
> because you cannot easily add other variables (like vertex variables) in 
> n1 and you will probably have corrupted data.

This is standard behavior: vertices are coded in sorted ID order for 
edgelist entry, not by the (arbitrary) order they may happen to appear 
in your edgelist.  If you want a different vertex order, then I 
recommend either naming them in the desired order or permuting them ex 
post facto (see permute.vertexIDs).  The more natural thing to do, 
however, is to sort your vertex covariates in the order of the vertices 
prior to entry.

I should also point out, by the way, that edges _are_ stored within the 
network object in the order of entry, as you can verify by using 
as.matrix(n1,"edgelist").  Thus, any edge covariates can be entered in 
the same order as the original edges, without ill effect.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

On Tue, Aug 18, 2009 at 10:22 AM, Steven Goodreau <goodreau@u.washington.edu
> wrote:

>
> On Thu, 6 Aug 2009, Jenine Harris wrote:
>
>  I was wondering if anyone has an example of how a GWDSP term would be
>> interpreted in somewhat lay terms. From my understanding GWDSP accounts
>> for
>> the distribution of shared partnership for each dyad in a network, but I'm
>> not sure how to go about interpreting a negative signficant GWDSP
>> coefficient of -0.25 in an actual ERGM model. What does this say about the
>> distribution and how does it influence the likelihood of a tie?
>>
>
>
> Hi Jenine,
>
> A great question.  Yes, I do think GWDSP is a bit trickier than interpret
> than any of the other terms we commonly work with.  I can give you my own
> idiosyncratic approach.
>
> First, as technical background: As you probably know, GWDSP is a parametric
> summary measure of the tendency for two actors to have x partners in common,
> regardless of whether the two actors themselves are tied.  GWESP is the same
> measure, but only counted across two actors who are tied.  The two are
> comparable to the "alternating 2-paths" and "alternating k-triangles" that
> Snijders et al discuss in a series of papers. The two measures, combined
> with a third (GW degree, or the comparable alternating k-stars) are derived
> in those papers by placing a parametric constraint on three sets of
> statistics that emerge when making a very sociologically reasonable set of
> assumptions about relational dependence.  The three parametric stats are
> also seen to work well in practice at modeling real-world social networks
> and avoiding degeneracy when doing so.
>
> So, on to interpretation.  As I said, I agree that GWDSP is the hardest to
> interpret.  In fact, I personally never use a GWDSP term without also using
> a GWESP term. And once I combined the two, I always find that the GWDSP
> coefficient is close to zero, and non-significant. Let me see if I can give
> good intuition as to why.
>
> GWESP has some relatively clear interpetations (which I discuss in a few of
> my papers). In real-world data of friendship or collaboration or similar
> kinds of networks, it is generally significantly positive. This means that
> those who are tied are more likely than chance to have multiple shared
> partners.
>
> GWDSP tells whether shared partners tend to clump together, regardless of
> whether two people are tied or not.  For example, whether or not you and I
> are friends, if we have one friend in common, are we more likely than
> expected by chance to have a second friend in common?  And so on.  If yes,
> the GWDSP coefficient will be positive.  If it is zero, then we are as
> likely as chance to have one in common; if negative, then less.
>
> If one only uses GWDSP and not GWESP, then it's hard to know whether an
> observed non-random shared partner distribution is driven by pairs who are
> themselves tied, pairs who are not tied, or both.  If you include both GWESP
> and GWDSP, then it becomes clear - GWDSP is the base effect (which now
> isolates the effect for those not tied only); GWESP occurs on top of this
> base, and isolates the effect for those who are tied.  And what I have
> always found is that the GWESP effect is then strong and significant, and
> the GWDSP is tiny and insignificant.  It may be that in different kinds of
> data GWDSP would be significant itself, though.
>
> My questions for you are: is your GWDSP term significant? Does it remain so
> when GWESP is added?  If the answer to both questions is yes, then you have
> something particuarly interesting (and unprecendented, at least for me) on
> your hands. If it remains negative and significant, then that says that
> people who are not tied tend not to have multiple shared partners. Once two
> unconnected people have one shared partner, they're less likely than chance
> to have a second; if they do have a second, they're less likely than chance
> to have a third, and so on. I can't think of a type of social relationship I
> would anticipate this pattern for, but it could just be that I've never
> thought about the kind of relaitonship that you're studying, and it makes
> perfect sense to you.
>
> My other quesiton would be what your alpha is; that changes the fine
> quantitative details of the interpretation, but not the general qualitative
> interpretation. Unless your alpha is either essentially 0 or very very high,
> in which case it would change the latter as well. If it's in the 0.1 - 2.0
> range, I don't think it would.
>
> I hope that helps!
> Steve

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] interpretation of the utriangle,	ltriangle terms in dyadcov
messages.body_plain:
I would actually recommend using edgecov.  You can run the command, ergm(refer~edgecov(dist)), where refer and dist are the referral network and distance network respectively.  A significant finding will tell you that there is a relationship between distance and referral.  A negative coefficient on the estimate would suggest that as distance increases, the likelihood of referral decreases.  The dist network can remain as a weighted network.

Ian McCulloh

Subject: [statnet_help] interpretation of the utriangle, ltriangle terms in dyadcov

Hi all,

I'm working on a project looking a referral network of cancer services organizations for low-income cancer patients (what predicts organization A referring a patient to organization B). One of the predictors of referrals that I am using is a network of distance (in minutes) on public transportation between the organizations. I am using the dyadcov term in my ERGM to predict the presence of a referral tie between two organizations based on how far apart they are. My question is: How would I interpret the following:

dyadcov.minutes.mutual       -28.44480    0.06961        NA  < 1e-04 ***
dyadcov.minutes.utri         -15.46894    0.11195        NA  < 1e-04 ***
dyadcov.minutes.ltri         -15.42000    0.10858        NA  < 1e-04 ***

The first row appears to be the reduction in likelihood of a tie for a 1 unit increase in minutes between organizations when A refers to B and B refers to A (there are referral links going both directions).

The upper triangle is then likely to be the reduction in the likelihood of a tie for a 1 unit increase in minutes when A refers to B (but B does not refer to A)

The lower triangle is the reduction in the likelihood of a tie for a 1 unit increase in minutes when B refers to A (but A does not refer to B)

I gather from the statnet tutorials that each dyad only falls into one of these categories....mutual, upper, or lower

Does this sound like an appropriate interpretation of these results?

Thanks in advance for any thoughts on this.

Jenine

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Convert network adjacency matrix to indexed matrix
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Convert network adjacency matrix to indexed matrix
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Rico-

Rico Leuthold wrote:
> Hi,
> 
> I would like to extract the adjacency matrix from a network object, to 
> use it as the tprob parameter in the rgraph function. The command -  
> as.matrix(net,matrix.type="adjacency") - gets the matrix, unfortunately 
> with named columns and rows, which is obviously not accepted in the 
> tprob parameter. Is there a way to convert a "named" matrix to an 
> indexed one?
> 
> I tried the following which doesn't work:
> as.matrix(net_obj,matrix.type="adjacency", 
> dimnames=list(c(1:network.size(net)),c(1: network.size(net))))

The rgraph tprob parameter ignores dimnames, so this will not affect the 
results.  In fact, here's a (working) example:

library(network)
library(sna)
data(emon)
g<-rgraph(network.size(emon[[1]]),tprob=as.matrix(emon[[1]])*0.8+0.1)

Check to be sure that you are passing the right size parameter to 
rgraph, and that your matrix output is a full adjacency matrix (i.e., 
that this is not a bipartite matrix).  These are the more likely errors 
in your case.

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Version 2.2-3 of ergm on CRAN
messages.body_plain:
Hi all.  A new version of ergm (version 2.2-3) just went up on CRAN.   
This version has a few new features that might be of interest:

(1) There are new simulate.formula and simulate.ergm functions that  
allow a bit more control over output of simulated networks and that  
should increase efficiency if only network statistics are desired.   
Mostly, this change will be invisible, but if you simulate random  
network statistics using statsonly=TRUE then you may notice an  
improvement in speed.

(2) In response to a couple of requests from this list, there is now a  
function, called ergmMPLE, that will return the response and  
predictors (the latter is sometimes called the matrix of change  
statistics) that can be plugged into a logistic regression routine to  
obtain the MPLE (maximum pseudolikelihood estimate).  Check ?ergmMPLE  
for details.

(3) There is a new algorithm for fitting ERGMs, called "stepping",  
that is implemented as a 'style' in the control.ergm function.  See ? 
control.ergm for details.  This algorithm is described in a tech  
report:  http://www.stat.psu.edu/~dhunter/papers/step.pdf

(4) Assorted odds and ends, used for various and sundry purposes:   
Check out ?is.inCH, ?wtd.median, ?ecoli


Already, there are a few bugs that I did not fix before uploading the  
new version.  Thus, another new version (2.2-4) will go up in just a  
few days.  So I'm curious:  Are there bugs that we've missed, or  
simple additions that would be helpful?  If so, I might be able to  
fix / add them before the next release.

Thanks in advance,
Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Question about statnet
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jacob.  Since you didn't provide an example to test, I invented  
one.  This might explain the problem:

 > nw=network.initialize(5)
 > nw[1,2]=nw[3,4]=nw[4,5]=1
 > slfctrl_s <- c(1, 1, 2, 2, NA)
 > nw %v% "slfctrl_s" <- slfctrl_s
 > ergm(nw~nodecov("slfctrl_s"))
Error in ergm.pl(Clist = Clist, Clist.miss = Clist.miss, m = m,  
theta.offset = theta.offset,  :
   NA/NaN/Inf in foreign function call (arg 11)

This (above) appears to be the same error you got.  However, note that  
your fix does not work:

 > slfctrl_s[is.na(slfctrl_s)] <- mean(slfctrl_s, na.rm = TRUE)
 > ergm(nw~nodecov("slfctrl_s"))
Error in ergm.pl(Clist = Clist, Clist.miss = Clist.miss, m = m,  
theta.offset = theta.offset,  :
   NA/NaN/Inf in foreign function call (arg 11)

The reason is that you did not change the vertex attribute in the nw  
object.  The code below does this and fixes the error:

 > nw %v% "slfctrl_s" <- slfctrl_s
 > ergm(nw~nodecov("slfctrl_s"))
Newton-Raphson iterations:  4

MLE Coefficients:
nodecov.slfctrl_s
           -0.5485


Hope this helps!



Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Numbered IDs create massive problems
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Dai,

I had the same problem with a network of 69 vertices from a dorm with
subject ID numbers assigned from earlier analyses, which I wanted to
keep, but that ranged up to 109.  The network function filled in the
missing vertices  with isolates, so  after I created the network object
in the usual manner, I simply deleted those isolates like this:

dorm <- delete.vertices(dorm, isolates(dorm))

It seems to work just fine, retaining all the correct vertexIDs, edges,
and their attributes.  Incidentally, if anyone sees a flaw in my
approach, please let me know.

Thanks,

David M. Ouellette, PhD

messages.subject: [statnet_help] FAQ entry on ERGM with missing or sampled data
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] FAQ entry on ERGM with missing or sampled data
messages.body_plain:
Dear David,

statnet does recognize missing data on vertex attributes. For example, 
they can be stored as NA in the vectors:

> a <- slmiss %v% "group"
> a[4] <- NA
> slmiss %v% "group" <- a
> slmiss %v% "group"
  [1] "Loyal"    "Loyal"    "Loyal"    NA         "Loyal"    "Loyal"
  [7] "Loyal"    "Turks"    "Turks"    "Turks"    "Turks"    "Turks"
[13] "Turks"    "Turks"    "Outcasts" "Outcasts" "Outcasts" "Outcasts"

However this version of the ergm() function does not adjust for missing 
data on vertex attributes - it only adjusts for missing values on the 
tie values. It is possible to do and we have worked out the statistical 
theory to do it, but have not implemented it in the public version. I 
expect it will appear in a major future release and we will communicate 
it to this forum.

Best,

Mark	

for the "statnet commons" team

On 11/8/09 12:52 PM, David Schaefer wrote:
> Thank you for providing that information, Mark.  If I could just ask for one clarification.  Does the statnet package also handle missing data on vertex attributes?
> Thanks,
> David
>
> ________________________________________
> From: statnet_help-bounces@mailman2.u.washington.edu [statnet_help-bounces@mailman2.u.washington.edu] On Behalf Of Mark S. Handcock [handcock@stat.washington.edu]
> Sent: Sunday, November 08, 2009 1:25 PM
> To: statnet_help@u.washington.edu
> Subject: [statnet_help] FAQ entry on ERGM with missing or sampled data
>
> Hi statnet users,
>
> A frequent question on this forum is how to use "statnet" to estimate
> ERGM parameters from networks with sampled or missing data and how to
> simulate networks for the fitted models.
>
> Here is a brief FAQ to that.
>
> 1) To represent missing entries in the adjacency matrix use a NA
> (instead of a 0 or a 1). "network" and "ergm" recognize that the dyad
> has not been observed.
>
> e.g. Suppose y is a network object with missing values in it. You can
> set the missing via e.g.:
>
> y[1,3]<- NA
>
> 2) To fit models, just do the regular thing.
>
> e.g.
>
> fit<- ergm(y ~ ...)
>
> 3) To simulate from the model conditional on the observed dyads (i.e.,
> simulate only the NAs but respectful to the observed data and model) use
> the "simulate command". That is,
>
> sim<- simulate(fit, constraints=~observed)
>
> If you want an unconditional simulation (i.e., from the model but not
> conditional on the observed data itself) use the usual, e.g.,
>
> sim<- simulate(fit)
>
> I have attached some example code using Sampson's liking network among
> monks. It should be helpful.
>
> In general, missing and sampled network methods have been embedded into
> "statnet" as seamlessly as we can.
>
> I hope you enjoy using it :-)
>
> Best,
>
> Mark
>
> for the "statnet commons" team

messages.subject: [statnet_help] memory limit
messages.body_plain:
Michael,

I've run into memory problems in the past as well, albeit on a Windows rather 
than unix platform. You've probably already looked at this info, but here are 
some helpful pages:

help(Memory) #note this is case sensitive
help(memory.limit)
help("Memory-limits")

I can't speak for unix platforms, but for Windows platforms memory limits appear 
to be a combination of both OS and R limitations: apparently 32-bit
Windows by default caps user processes at 2G, and R by default requests 1/2G
less than the max; 64-bit Windows caps at 4G by default, and again R by default
requests 1/2G less. The user can increase the available memory using 
memory.limit(size=####) up to the maximum allowed by the OS.

Hopefully someone with unix experience can offer more helpful advice specific to 
your problem.

My work-around has been to split my simulations into smaller batches, extract 
the information I need, and concatenate the results into a new workspace.

Cheers,
David

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Numbered IDs create massive problems
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I had a number of potential solutions to my problem. There were two
particularly good solutions (by Dr. Carter Butts, no surprisingly)... So I'm
going to post here my problem and the two solutions for anyone who might
encounter this issue in the future. I apologize for the long post.

The problem: unique ID numbers get interpreted by statnet as a continuous
parameter. So, when trying to turn an edge list composed of these ID numbers
into a network object, it will try to create a node for every possible
number from 1 to the largest ID number. This screws up the data. You can get
around this problem by converting ID numbers to character strings, but when
you have ID numbers that are different numbers of digits, then it will sort
them weirdly when constructing the adjacency matrix. I'm going to
demonstrate the problem with two examples, and then provide the two
suggested solutons. You can just plug the codes into R and try it out if you
are curious.


# problem 1: Here, I am setting up a sample edge list consisting of 5
individuals with unique IDs: 8, 27, 123, 356 and 900. this will produce an
unreasonable network object because it tries to create a node for all values
between 1 and 900

Focal=c(356,123,27,8,900)
Interactor=c(123,8,900,27,356)
el=as.data.frame(cbind(Focal,Interactor))
net=network(el,matrix.type="edgelist",directed=FALSE)
summary(net)

# this yields:
Network attributes:
 vertices = 900
 directed = FALSE
 hyper = FALSE
 loops = FALSE
 multiple = FALSE
 bipartite = FALSE
 total edges = 5
   missing edges = 0
   non-missing edges = 5
 density = 1.235941e-05
... clearly not right.

## problem 2: trying to get around this by changing the IDs to characters
makes the matrix funky:
Focal=as.character(c(356,123,27,8,900))
Interactor=as.character(c(123,8,900,27,356))
el=as.data.frame(cbind(Focal,Interactor))
net=network(el,matrix.type="edgelist",directed=FALSE)
summary(net)

#This yields:
Network attributes:
 vertices = 5
 directed = FALSE
 hyper = FALSE
 loops = FALSE
 multiple = FALSE
 bipartite = FALSE
 total edges = 5
   missing edges = 0
   non-missing edges = 5
 density = 0.5


Network adjacency matrix:
    123 27 356 8 900
123   0  0   1 1   0
27    0  0   0 1   1
356   1  0   0 0   1
8     1  1   0 0   0
900   0  1   1 0   0

#So here, the network is ok, but the resulting adjacency matrix puts the ID
numbers in funky order: (123, 27, 356, 8, 900)


### solution 1: convert IDs to 3-digit string with leading 0s. This way, the
character strings will sort correctly in the adjacency matrix####
Focal=c(356,123,27,8,900)
Interactor=c(123,8,900,27,356)
el=as.data.frame(cbind(Focal,Interactor))
el$Focal=as.character(sprintf("%03d",el$Focal))
el$Interactor=as.character(sprintf("%03d",el$Interactor))
net=network(el,matrix.type="edgelist",directed=FALSE)
summary(net)

The resulting adjacency matrix:
Network adjacency matrix:
    008 027 123 356 900
008   0   1   1   0   0
027   1   0   0   0   1
123   1   0   0   1   0
356   0   0   1   0   1
900   0   1   0   1   0


### solution 2: Re-code the ID into sequential numbers, and then retrieve
the appropriate ID numbers after establishing the network object
Focal=c(356,123,27,8,900)
Interactor=c(123,8,900,27,356)
el=as.data.frame(cbind(Focal,Interactor))
code=sort(unique(c(el[,1],el[,2])))
el[,1]=match(el[,1],code)
el[,2]=match(el[,2],code)
net=network(el,matrix.type="edgelist",directed=FALSE)
network.vertex.names(net)=code
summary(net)

The resulting matrix:
Network adjacency matrix:
    8 27 123 356 900
8   0  1   1   0   0
27  1  0   0   0   1
123 1  0   0   1   0
356 0  0   1   0   1
900 0  1   0   1   0


... I learned a lot from this exercise, so I thought I'd share the
knowledge. Thanks to all those who were kind enough to reply.

Dai
----------
Daizaburo Shizuka
Postdoctoral Researcher
Department of Zoology & Physiology
University of Wyoming
1000 E. University Ave
Laramie, Wyoming 82071


On Tue, Mar 23, 2010 at 7:11 PM, Carter T. Butts <buttsc@uci.edu> wrote:

> Hi, Dai -
>
> The issue here is that the edgelist->network conversion assumes that your
> data is given in the form of vertex IDs (since you are using a numeric
> matrix).  Vertex IDs are not names, but the sort order of the vertex; thus,
> you can't have an ID (in the sense of the network package) of 112998 on a
> 43-node network.  You can, of course, have a vertex that carries this number
> as a name (or other attribute).
>
> As this suggests, one approach is to renumber your edgelists prior to
> conversion.  E.g., something like this:
>
> #Let el be your edgelist matrix
> uvert<-sort(unique(c(el[,1],el[,2])))
> el[,1]<-match(el[,1],uvert)
> el[,2]<-match(el[,2],uvert)
>
> This will keep your network vertex IDs in the same order as your own ID
> numbers (names).  Then, set the vertex names (or any other attribute) equal
> to uvert; you can retrieve the original names in the usual fashion using %v%
> or get.vertex.attribute.
>
> If you don't like that road, another option is to convert your numbers to
> fixed-width character strings with leading zeros.  (formatC will do this.)
>  That ensures that the sort order matches the numeric order of your vertex
> names.  Finally, you could just create the network as usual, and then

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Adolescent Health Network Data and R
messages.body_plain:
I'm a graduate student trying to figure out Add Health's social
network data and I'm hoping that, because it is widely used, someone
on this list could offer a little guidance.  Also, feel free to inform me
if I'm breaking list protocol in any way.

My primary goal is to predict "popularity."  I figured I'd create and
predict multiple measures of centrality and try to think about how
they differ.  I can read the documentation to learn how to create
those measures in general.  But I'm wondering, -here is my first question-
has anyone written up anything specific to manipulating the Ad Health
network data.


That alone would be enormously helpful, but if you want to comment on
another issue that would be great.  Here it is: popularity cannot be
directly measured, and various facts about the way data is collected
are going to bias any measure of popularity I use.  I face the
following questions: what are the ways I expect various measures of
popularity to be biased and how can I correct for them.

One way to categorize biases in the measures would be those that
affect school/grade-level means and those that affect variation within
schools/grades.  Some of the biases I'm thinking about are school
size, fraction absent or otherwise not providing usable data, and
fraction of friends outside the school. Sometimes students nominate
someone that they say is in the school but does not show up on the
roster which indicates the accuracy of the roster could be an issue.

I see two potentially complementary ways to approach correcting for
these biases.  One is to build the correction into my measure of
centrality.  The other is that when I model these influences when I am
predicting the measure of centrality (with some kind of mixed effects
model).  Right now I'm just working with In-Degree so I'm
experimenting with the latter approach but I'd like to consider the
former now that I'm ready to construct new measures of centrality.

I'm sorry this email got so long.  Please don't feel a burden to solve
my research problems, but if you can point me in the right direction
that would be great.

Many thanks,
Mike

Ph.D. Student
Sociology Department
University of Chicago

Hi Dave,

Thanks a lot for your quick, but very precise, reponse.

I had forgotten it, but the use of the summary() fonction is very 
appropriate here and in situations where I'm not sure about a statistic

Best Regards,

David Hunter a ?crit :
> Hi Victorin.  In your attachment, situations 2 through 5 give different 
> answers for esp(2) and dsp(2).  The direction of the arc from node A to 
> node B is important.
> 
> Situation 2:  A 2-esp is counted only if the two 2-paths from A to B go 
> in the same direction as this arc, as in this situation.
> Situation 3:  If both of the 2-paths go in the opposite direction as the 
> arc from A to B, then this counts as a 2-dsp (because B->A is a dyad 
> without an edge) but not a 2-esp.
> Situations 4 and 5: Finally, if the only two 2-paths from A to B go in 
> opposite directions, then there is no 2-esp nor 2-dsp.
> 
> Here is some code that verifies this:
> 
>  > m=matrix(0,4,4);m[1,2]=1   # situation 2
>  > m[1,3]=m[3,2]=m[1,4]=m[4,2]=1;summary(m~esp(2)+dsp(2))
> esp2 dsp2
>    1    1
>  > m=matrix(0,4,4);m[1,2]=1   # situation 3
>  > m[2,3]=m[3,1]=m[2,4]=m[4,1]=1;summary(m~esp(2)+dsp(2))
> esp2 dsp2
>    0    1
>  > m=matrix(0,4,4);m[1,2]=1   # situation 4
>  > m[1,3]=m[3,2]=m[2,4]=m[4,1]=1;summary(m~esp(2)+dsp(2))
> esp2 dsp2
>    0    0
>  > m=matrix(0,4,4);m[1,2]=1   # situation 5
>  > m[2,3]=m[3,1]=m[1,4]=m[4,2]=1;summary(m~esp(2)+dsp(2))
> esp2 dsp2
>    0    0
> 
> 
> Hope this helps.
> Dave

an example code:

library(statnet)
resp1<-c("Victorin","Alice","Gabrielle","Jonas","Thibault", "Nad?ge")
x<-c("Victorin","Alice","Gabrielle","Jonas","Thibault","Nad?ge","Nad?ge","Gabrielle","Victorin","Victorin")

el1<-matrix(c(x,y),ncol=2) #charactere edgelist

n1

order and not in the order of appearance of el1. For me it's a problem 
because you cannot easily add other variables (like vertex variables) in

Feng Luo wrote:
> Dear All:
> 
>  
> 
> Sorry to bother you again!
> 
> I learned a ERGM model from a fully connected network. Is there a way I 
> can guarantee my simulated networks are also fully connected?

Yes: simulate normally, and subsequently filter out only the connected 
graphs (using is.connected or the like to identify those you need to 
keep).  This is a trivial rejection sampling scheme, and will give you 
draws from the model conditional on being connected.

(Note, however, that this is not the same as _fitting_ a model 
conditional on the graph being fully connected (i.e., a model whose 
support is on the connected graphs of order matching the observed 
graph).  For that, you would need to use an MCMC proposal that preserved 
connectedness.  I don't believe we have one of those at present, 
although I could be mistaken.)

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Numbered IDs create massive problems
messages.body_plain:
Just taking a stab:

Solution 1: Paste a leading "b" (for "bird") in front of your ID's so they
import correctly and are labeled with familiar ID's.

Solution 2: Import the ID's as strings (with "" around the ID's), or from R
use encodeString(your.edgelist) before applying as.network, which should
again convert properly without blank nodes.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] FAQ entry on ERGM with missing or sampled data
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] FAQ entry on ERGM with missing or sampled data
messages.body_plain:
Thank you for providing that information, Mark.  If I could just ask for one clarification.  Does the statnet package also handle missing data on vertex attributes?
Thanks,
David

________________________________________
From: statnet_help-bounces@mailman2.u.washington.edu [statnet_help-bounces@mailman2.u.washington.edu] On Behalf Of Mark S. Handcock [handcock@stat.washington.edu]
Sent: Sunday, November 08, 2009 1:25 PM
To: statnet_help@u.washington.edu
Subject: [statnet_help] FAQ entry on ERGM with missing or sampled data

Hi statnet users,

A frequent question on this forum is how to use "statnet" to estimate
ERGM parameters from networks with sampled or missing data and how to
simulate networks for the fitted models.

Here is a brief FAQ to that.

1) To represent missing entries in the adjacency matrix use a NA
(instead of a 0 or a 1). "network" and "ergm" recognize that the dyad
has not been observed.

e.g. Suppose y is a network object with missing values in it. You can
set the missing via e.g.:

y[1,3] <- NA

2) To fit models, just do the regular thing.

e.g.

fit <- ergm(y ~ ...)

3) To simulate from the model conditional on the observed dyads (i.e.,
simulate only the NAs but respectful to the observed data and model) use
the "simulate command". That is,

sim <- simulate(fit, constraints=~observed)

If you want an unconditional simulation (i.e., from the model but not
conditional on the observed data itself) use the usual, e.g.,

sim <- simulate(fit)

I have attached some example code using Sampson's liking network among
monks. It should be helpful.

In general, missing and sampled network methods have been embedded into
"statnet" as seamlessly as we can.

I hope you enjoy using it :-)

Best,

Mark

for the "statnet commons" team

Marc Scott

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Re: help with edge attributes & network extraction
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Re: help with edge attributes & network extraction
messages.body_plain:
Hi statnet group,

I got a response that indicated that my question was a problem that  
others have run into, so I thought I'd present my solution. I wrote a  
function that takes a network and a vector of edge attributes, and  
returns a 3 column matrix with the edgelist of the network's largest  
component plus the corresponding edge attributes. This can be easily  
read back into a network object or into tnet, a package I've been  
playing with.

Disclaimer: I am not a programmer and have self-taught myself R so I  
make no claims that this is great code but it appears to be working  
for me.Any advice on how to improve would be great! Hopefully some  
part of it might help others out there and save some time.

Second disclaimer: I wrote the function for undirected networks, if  
you're working with directed networks then you will have to change a  
few minor things.

-Michael

#largest.component.edgeattr(net, edgeattr)
#Takes a network object and a vector of edge attributes for that  
network, and returns
#an edgelist for the largest component of that network with a 3rd  
column containing
#the edge attributes;

largest.component.edgeattr <- function(net, edgeattr){

#Get edgelist from network, attach attribute
edgelist <- as.matrix.network(net, matrix.type = "edgelist",  
directed=FALSE)
edgelist <- cbind(edgelist, edgeattr)

#Initialize weighted adjacency matrix
numnodes <- network.size(net)
zeros <- rep(0, numnodes^2)
edgeattr_mat <- matrix(zeros, nrow = numnodes, ncol = numnodes)
#Add in edge weights for each tied node pair to matrix edgeattr_mat
for(x in 1:network.edgecount(net)) {
	i <- edgelist[x,1]
	j <- edgelist[x,2]
	edgeattr_mat[i,j] <- edgelist[x,3]
	#If network is undirected, symmetrize the assignments
	edgeattr_mat[j,i] <- edgelist[x,3]
	}

#Create a new edgelist for the largest subcomponent, in addition to a  
vector comp_names
	#comp_names = a crosswalk between node IDs in the largest  
subcomponent and the network such that
	#if i is the index of a node in the subcomponent, comp_nodes[i] =  
node index in the network
comp <- as.network(component.largest(net, connected="weak", result =  
"graph"), matrix.type = "adjacency", directed = FALSE)
comp_names <- as.numeric(comp %v% "vertex.names")
comp_edgelist <- as.matrix.network(comp, matrix.type = "edgelist")

#initializing edgeattr_comp = edge attributes vector for largest  
component edges
edgeattr_comp <- vector(mode = "integer",  
length=network.edgecount(comp))

#Extract the attribute for each edge in the largest subcomponent from  
edgeattr_mat above, using the
#crosswalk vector comp_names to translate node names between the two  
networks
for(x in 1:network.edgecount(comp)) {
	i <- comp_names[comp_edgelist[x,1]]
	j <- comp_names[comp_edgelist[x,2]]
	edgeattr_comp[x] <- edgeattr_mat[i,j]
	}

#comp_edgelist is the weighted edgelist
comp_edgelist <- cbind(comp_edgelist, edgeattr_comp)
return(comp_edgelist)
}

messages.subject: [statnet_help] non-significant estimates but significant odds ratios?
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] non-significant estimates but significant odds ratios?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Jenine,

Thanks for the question.

The issues here is not the model fits, but the various asymptotic
approximations to the test statistics. Specifically, the Normal approximate
CI for the log odds ratio is 0.458518+/-1.96*0.308264 = (-0.146, 1.063).
This is based on the Central Limit Theorem for the log odds ratio. To get a
CI for the odds ratio we can exponential the limits to get (0.864,2.894).
The CI you give for the OR is based on the Normal approximation for the OR.
Typically, the approximation is better for the log OR rather than the OR,
but this is an empirical question.

I hope this helps!

Mark

for the statnet team

mistake in ergm.  Thanks in advance!

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a Statnet-ERGM question that I suspect has been asked and  
answered, but so far my search of the archives has not yielded an  
answer.

I am working with a directed graph. A small number of actors in my  
population have missing data for their edges.  However, I have a rich  
set of attribute data for these actors, which leads me to retain dyads  
in which they are alters for models w/ nodematch terms, etc.

Certain ERGM terms (e.g., edgecov) require that the dataset analyzed  
consist of all possible edges in the data along with values for  
whatever edge covariates are of interest.  In my case, given missing  
data, all possible edges (possible = possibly observed) would not be a  
square matrix, because only actors with alter data can be egos, while  
all actors can be alters.

I assume the edgecov term expects a square matrix anyway.  If so, I  
seem to have two options:

1) Reduce my data to only edges in which ego and alter both are  
complete in terms of tie data.
2) Provide ERGM with the full square matrix, including edges that I  
can't observe.

If #2, to the extent I have a node attribute indicating whether the  
node's edges were missing rather than null, are there additional  
statements that can be made to capture that only certain directed  
edges can be observed?

As a reminder (from the JOSS ERGM article):

"The x argument is either a square matrix of covariates, one for each  
possible edge in the network, covariates, or a network; if the latter,  
optional argument attrname provides the name of the quantitative edge  
attribute to use for covariate values (in this case, missing edges in  
x are assigned a covariate value of zero). "

It appears to call for the square matrix, but that doesn't feel quite  
right.

Any suggestions, best practices, readings, or considerations are  
appreciated....

Thanks!

Matthew

that identifies differences in transitive closure for triads that either 
do or do not include ingroup members?

   If i & j are both members of the target group, then if the "group" is

parties, than I guess I'd expect to see a lot of closed triads:

messages.subject: [statnet_help] solution for egocentric density at any distance
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] solution for egocentric density at any distance
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone -

After my mailing yesterday, I plowed through and wrote a function to  
do what I was looking for. I didn't quite understand the  
neighborhood() function at first, but once I thought more about it, I  
realized that I could do what I was looking for. Here's my code  
(apologies if it's ugly):

#Returns nbddensity, a matrix of egocentric densities for each node in  
a "net" for each distance from 1 to "distance"
nbd_density <- function(net, distance) {	
	
	size <- network.size(net)
	nbddensity <- matrix(nrow = size, ncol = distance)
	nbd <- neighborhood(net, distance, neighborhood.type="total",  
mode="graph", return.all=TRUE, partial = FALSE)
	
	for (i in 1:distance) {
		for (j in 1:size) {
			adj_m <- as.matrix(net[c(nbd[i,j,]==1),c(nbd[i,j,]==1)])
			ifelse (length(as.vector(adj_m)) == 1, nbddensity[j,i] <- 0,
				nbddensity[j,i] <- network.density(as.network.matrix(adj_m,  
matrix.type="adjacency")))
			}
		}	
	nbdensity	
	}

-Michael

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jim.  I didn't know statnet had been removed from CRAN.  As a  
stopgap, you can install individual packages that fall under the  
statnet umbrella.  The most commonly-used of these are network, sna,  
and ergm.  If you install these three packages from CRAN (by using the  
install.packages command exactly as you've done below), you should do  
so in that order, since ergm depends on network.  (Technically, sna  
does not, though it is written to exploit network if network is loaded.)

If there are other statnet packages that you know you want, those too  
can be installed separately, but I believe the three above are the  
most commonly-used.  In fact, the only thing that the statnet  
"package" does -- when it's working -- is to install a series of other  
CRAN packages (including the three above, of course).

Once these are installed you can type 'library(ergm)' or  
'library(network)' or 'library(sna)' to use the packages.

Dave

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] esp and dsp stats with directed networks
messages.body_plain:
Hi Victorin.  In your attachment, situations 2 through 5 give  
different answers for esp(2) and dsp(2).  The direction of the arc  
from node A to node B is important.

Situation 2:  A 2-esp is counted only if the two 2-paths from A to B  
go in the same direction as this arc, as in this situation.
Situation 3:  If both of the 2-paths go in the opposite direction as  
the arc from A to B, then this counts as a 2-dsp (because B->A is a  
dyad without an edge) but not a 2-esp.
Situations 4 and 5: Finally, if the only two 2-paths from A to B go in  
opposite directions, then there is no 2-esp nor 2-dsp.

Here is some code that verifies this:

 > m=matrix(0,4,4);m[1,2]=1   # situation 2
 > m[1,3]=m[3,2]=m[1,4]=m[4,2]=1;summary(m~esp(2)+dsp(2))
esp2 dsp2
    1    1
 > m=matrix(0,4,4);m[1,2]=1   # situation 3
 > m[2,3]=m[3,1]=m[2,4]=m[4,1]=1;summary(m~esp(2)+dsp(2))
esp2 dsp2
    0    1
 > m=matrix(0,4,4);m[1,2]=1   # situation 4
 > m[1,3]=m[3,2]=m[2,4]=m[4,1]=1;summary(m~esp(2)+dsp(2))
esp2 dsp2
    0    0
 > m=matrix(0,4,4);m[1,2]=1   # situation 5
 > m[2,3]=m[3,1]=m[1,4]=m[4,2]=1;summary(m~esp(2)+dsp(2))
esp2 dsp2
    0    0


Hope this helps.
Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] FAQ entry on ERGM with missing or sampled data
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] FAQ entry on ERGM with missing or sampled data
messages.body_plain:
Hi statnet users,

A frequent question on this forum is how to use "statnet" to estimate 
ERGM parameters from networks with sampled or missing data and how to 
simulate networks for the fitted models.

Here is a brief FAQ to that.

1) To represent missing entries in the adjacency matrix use a NA 
(instead of a 0 or a 1). "network" and "ergm" recognize that the dyad 
has not been observed.

e.g. Suppose y is a network object with missing values in it. You can 
set the missing via e.g.:

y[1,3] <- NA

2) To fit models, just do the regular thing.

e.g.

fit <- ergm(y ~ ...)

3) To simulate from the model conditional on the observed dyads (i.e., 
simulate only the NAs but respectful to the observed data and model) use 
the "simulate command". That is,

sim <- simulate(fit, constraints=~observed)

If you want an unconditional simulation (i.e., from the model but not 
conditional on the observed data itself) use the usual, e.g.,

sim <- simulate(fit)

I have attached some example code using Sampson's liking network among 
monks. It should be helpful.

In general, missing and sampled network methods have been embedded into 
"statnet" as seamlessly as we can.

I hope you enjoy using it :-)

Best,

Mark

for the "statnet commons" team

Thanks, Dave.  I didn't even notice the "coef" part at the beginning of 
the command. So yes, to fully clarify, Randall, the syntax for getting 
what you want is:

ergm.object <- ergm(Network~edges+triangle)
summary(ergm.object)

Or, if you really just want to look at it, and not save it, then you can 
just do:

summary(ergm(Network~edges+triangle))

It seems like you're likely a new user.  I would recommend (for you, or 
anyone just beginning to explore ergm) to check out the special issue of 
statnet in the Journal of Statistical Software, accessible fron the 
statnet project webpage (www.statnetproject.org).

Happy networking,
Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] loading data into Statnet (UCI*NET dl List of adjacency pairs)
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] loading data into Statnet (UCI*NET dl List of adjacency pairs)
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

in case someone starts writing a read.dl or write.dl function: It may be 
worthwhile writing a read.ucinet or write.ucinet function instead which 
reads the native (binary) file format of Ucinet (the .##h. and ##d 
files). Here are some details about the file format:

The ##d file:
- the 'data' file which contains all the cell entries of the adjacency 
matrix. They are not separated by any character. Each cell entry is 
encoded as a 32 bit float number according to the IEEE-754 standard and 
with little endian encoding. For example, a weight in the adjacency 
matrix of '3' is saved as the hex value '00 00 80 3F'.

The ##h file:
- the header file which contains the row and column labels
- starts with the hex value '05'
- then '44 41 54 45 3A' (which means 'DATE:' in ASCII)
- then some code I haven't been able to figure out yet (probably a 
date..., perhaps the authors of Ucinet are able to help here)
- then the row labels as ASCII code (separated by '00 00' in hex code)
- and finally the network label in ASCII.
- of course, the structure may be different if we are talking about 
two-mode networks etc.

If anyone in the statnet team or elsewhere is interested in writing a 
read.ucinet function (which is probably something many people would be 
interested in), it might be a good idea to start out with a hex editor 
and reproduce the above steps.

Take care

Philip

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Re: help with edge attributes & network extraction
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Re: help with edge attributes & network extraction
messages.body_plain:
Hi statnet group,

I got a response that indicated that my question was a problem that  
others have run into, so I thought I'd present my solution. I wrote a  
function that takes a network and a vector of edge attributes, and  
returns a 3 column matrix with the edgelist of the network's largest  
component plus the corresponding edge attributes. This can be easily  
read back into a network object or into tnet, a package I've been  
playing with.

Disclaimer: I am not a programmer and have self-taught myself R so I  
make no claims that this is great code but it appears to be working  
for me.Any advice on how to improve would be great! Hopefully some  
part of it might help others out there and save some time.

Second disclaimer: I wrote the function for undirected networks, if  
you're working with directed networks then you will have to change a  
few minor things.

-Michael

#largest.component.edgeattr(net, edgeattr)
#Takes a network object and a vector of edge attributes for that  
network, and returns
#an edgelist for the largest component of that network with a 3rd  
column containing
#the edge attributes;

largest.component.edgeattr <- function(net, edgeattr){

#Get edgelist from network, attach attribute
edgelist <- as.matrix.network(net, matrix.type = "edgelist",  
directed=FALSE)
edgelist <- cbind(edgelist, edgeattr)

#Initialize weighted adjacency matrix
numnodes <- network.size(net)
zeros <- rep(0, numnodes^2)
edgeattr_mat <- matrix(zeros, nrow = numnodes, ncol = numnodes)
#Add in edge weights for each tied node pair to matrix edgeattr_mat
for(x in 1:network.edgecount(net)) {
	i <- edgelist[x,1]
	j <- edgelist[x,2]
	edgeattr_mat[i,j] <- edgelist[x,3]
	#If network is undirected, symmetrize the assignments
	edgeattr_mat[j,i] <- edgelist[x,3]
	}

#Create a new edgelist for the largest subcomponent, in addition to a  
vector comp_names
	#comp_names = a crosswalk between node IDs in the largest  
subcomponent and the network such that
	#if i is the index of a node in the subcomponent, comp_nodes[i] =  
node index in the network
comp <- as.network(component.largest(net, connected="weak", result =  
"graph"), matrix.type = "adjacency", directed = FALSE)
comp_names <- as.numeric(comp %v% "vertex.names")
comp_edgelist <- as.matrix.network(comp, matrix.type = "edgelist")

#initializing edgeattr_comp = edge attributes vector for largest  
component edges
edgeattr_comp <- vector(mode = "integer",  
length=network.edgecount(comp))

#Extract the attribute for each edge in the largest subcomponent from  
edgeattr_mat above, using the
#crosswalk vector comp_names to translate node names between the two  
networks
for(x in 1:network.edgecount(comp)) {
	i <- comp_names[comp_edgelist[x,1]]
	j <- comp_names[comp_edgelist[x,2]]
	edgeattr_comp[x] <- edgeattr_mat[i,j]
	}

#comp_edgelist is the weighted edgelist
comp_edgelist <- cbind(comp_edgelist, edgeattr_comp)
return(comp_edgelist)
}

messages.body_plain:
Hi statnetters,

By way of introduction, I'm a third year PhD student at Northwestern
University in Noshir Contractor's SONIC group. I'm interested in analyzing
team assembly processes in online communities like Wikipedia and massively
multiplayer online games. I'm currently working to analyze a co-authorship
network of Wikipedia articles about breaking news stories and using this
relatively small dataset (as compared with our game networks with >10k
nodes) as an opportunity to migrate to using statistical network analysis
tools in R such as network, statnet, ergm, and RSiena.

I've gone through the tutorials and documentation, but I need help in two
broad areas: (1) learning the syntax to manipulate bipartite relational and
attribute data in the R environment and (2) mapping the ergm-terms onto the
parameters I'm more accustomed to using in the MelNet team's BPNet (pg.
39-40, http://www.sna.unimelb.edu.au/pnet/download/PNet/PNetManual.pdf).

I have an affiliation matrix of 1107 actors and 127 events with 5132 edges
representing editor contributions to Wikipedia articles saved as a space
delimited text file ("network.txt") with 1107 rows and 127 columns. I also
have binary and continuous event attributes as text files separated by new
lines ("binary1.txt").

(1) Syntax problems
I import the network sociomatrix using this workflow adapted from the one
used for one-mode networks:

A <- matrix(scan("network.txt", n=1107*127), 1107, 127, byrow=TRUE)
N <- as.network.matrix(A, matrix.type="adjacency", bipartite=127+1107)

names.eval = en,  :

length!"

  directed = FALSE
