binary1 <- matrix(scan("binary1.txt", n=127), 127, 1, byrow=TRUE)
binary1 <- as.vector(binary1)
set.vertex.attribute(N, "Binary1", binary1, v=1:127)

I suspect something goes profoundly wrong in that final step involving
"set.vertex.attribute" with respect to mapping event/column/article
attributes onto the appropriate events but not actors/rows/editors. However,
no errors print and "Binary1" appears in vertex attribute names.

(2) Parameter specification
It's unclear to me how the parameters corresponding with the "first mode" or
"second mode" map onto the events/columns (Wikipedia articles) or
rows/actors (Wikipedia editors). I specify what I think is a simple model
incorporating an edge/density parameter and a 2-star parameter for both

assume model 1 below is the same as L + Sp2 + Sa2 in MelNet's BPNet

The estimation runs, returns some results with significance but possible
degeneracy, none of which is a game changer since I'm happy to play with
post-estimation diagnoses. I simply want to make sure that I can correctly
specify structural models before adding attribute parameters.

Now I attempt to add the attribute parameters. Again, I don't believe that
the vertex attributes were properly imported in my set.vertex.attribute

Hi Jenine.  The base argument does in fact work with nodemix.  This is  
a bit clunky, but it's not hard to do.  Take a look at this example:

  data(faux.mesa.high)
  summary(faux.mesa.high~nodemix("Race"))
mix.Race.Black.Black  mix.Race.Black.Hisp   mix.Race.Hisp.Hisp  
mix.Race.Black.NatAm
                    0                    8                    
53                   13
  mix.Race.Hisp.NatAm mix.Race.NatAm.NatAm mix.Race.Black.Other   
mix.Race.Hisp.Other
                   41                   46                     
0                    1
mix.Race.NatAm.Other mix.Race.Other.Other mix.Race.Black.White   
mix.Race.Hisp.White
                    0                    0                     
5                   22
mix.Race.NatAm.White mix.Race.Other.White mix.Race.White.White
                   10                    0                    4

Suppose I wanted to omit all pairings involving the "Other" category.   
Notice that in the summary above, there are 15 total positions in the  
vector and "Other" occurs in positions 7, 8, 9, 10, and 14.   
Therefore, I can make these positions the base and get rid of them:

  summary(faux.mesa.high~nodemix("Race", base=c(7,8,9,10,14)))
mix.Race.Black.Black  mix.Race.Black.Hisp   mix.Race.Hisp.Hisp  
mix.Race.Black.NatAm
                    0                    8                    
53                   13
  mix.Race.Hisp.NatAm mix.Race.NatAm.NatAm mix.Race.Black.White   
mix.Race.Hisp.White
                   41                   46                     
5                   22
mix.Race.NatAm.White mix.Race.White.White
                   10                    4


Hope this helps.
Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] two-mode network in StatNet
messages.body_plain:
Hi Rick,

The short answer is yes, statnet can recognize and work with bipartite 
networks.  I'm not sure about whether this happens automatically when you 
import a 2mode Pajek .net file, but you can check by using the summary() 
function on the network object.  If it is bipartite, that will be 
displayed in the summary info at the top.

Modeling with bipartite networks requires using bipartite-specific ergm 
terms.  You can see the terms currently available in the Table of Model 
Terms in the JoSS article on Specification of ERGMS (vol 24 i4), available 
here:

http://www.statnetproject.org/users_guide.shtml

best,
Martina

messages.subject: [statnet_help] 	from network to igraph and back again, and NAMESPACEs
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] 	from network to igraph and back again, and NAMESPACEs
messages.body_plain:
Hi, John -

John Paolillo wrote:
> The point about namespaces is well-made by Michal, but really it
> should have been obvious and best practice would have indicated using
> R namespaces at the outset of the Statnet project. 

This would have been rather difficult, since namespaces were unused 
and/or non-existent when the first bits of statnet were being assembled. 
   Back then, R had a very small community, and we dealt with conflicts 
via the time-honored method of not creating duplicate nomenclature (also 
called "not being a jerk," though circumstances have changed since 
then).  I don't recall when current the R NAMESPACE system first came 
into existence -- I suspect that it postdates sna -- but it was 
essentially unused until just a few years ago.  If the R precognition 
library had been available back then, perhaps we would have done things 
differently.  (Of course, seriously entertaining the idea that R would 
become so popular -- especially among network analysts -- that there 
might be a need for such a thing would have been grounds at that time 
for diagnosis of narcissistic personality disorder.)

If you are new to R, then you will doubtless be mystified by many things 
you find in the older packages.  These are the legacies of a wild, 
frontier age, when the documentation standards were loose, you could use 
generics any way you wanted, and the actual rules for R package 
construction were determined by a complex version of 20 questions. 
(This last is still true, to an extent.)  To those who have grown up 
with sidewalks and indoor plumbing, the free-wheeling designs of this 
earlier period doubtless carry a whiff of the barbaric.  As the heavy 
hand of civilization has descended upon the R community (with an influx 
of new users and developers unencumbered by history), however, many of 
our packages have gradually been subjugated to the useful and the good. 
  Thus are the fruits of the ancient days of R made available to its 
modern, enlightened user base, though they must occasionally cope with 
the narrow streets, blind alleys, and poor sewage treatment that 
accompany legacy code.

> 
> (1) Statnet imposes an unusual modification on the semantics of
> formula objects in R. In no other R package does one write a formula
> in which complex object (i.e. the network, which contains many
> vectors of differing lengths) is expressed in terms of objects
> contained within it.

Why, thank you.  We like to stay ahead of the curve.

> 
> (2) Insistence on C code (ostensibly for speed), to the point of
> incorporating legacy code that duplicates basic functionality of the
> BLAS in R (e.g. eigen decomposition). This actually flies in the face
> of the speed criterion, because the R BLAS is optimized for
> multiple-core architectures (not as common when the Statnet project
> started as they are now), and the legacy code is not (nor is
> specialized Statnet C code like the network layout code necessarily
> multi-processor optimized).

Ah yes, the good ole' days, before C backending.  Back then, you could 
almost compute betweenness on a 100 node network, if your life 
expectancy was high enough.  (But then, you didn't have data sets that 
big, so this was not so horrid as might be imagined.)  You will find 
that nearly everything in some packages is now backended, and none of it 
for the pure joy of writing in C.  If something is backended, there is 
usually a good reason for it -- generally, that reason being that the 
requisite R builtins were non-existent, slow, inapplicable, non-robust, 
etc.  As R evolves, it may gradually become possible to shift from using 
custom backends to R internal functions, and I expect that such things 
will occur.  (Of course, one does not tamper with working code unless 
one has a very good reason to do so, so there would need to be clear 
evidence of performance gains.)

With respect to your specific question re:BLAS, I'm not sure to what 
code you are referring.  I can, however, provide an illustrative case 
study (for those who are curious about how the process works).  A few 
releases ago, I switched the default method for evcent from the standard 
R eigen() method to a customized internal version, since I was able to 
obtain substantial memory and performance improvements on large graphs 
by so doing, and since I had received some requests in that regard.  The 
custom backend generally performs much better for this specific task, 
but is less robust than the backend that R uses; for that reason, and 
for compatibility with legacy code, the option to use the R built-in was 
included.  I certainly wouldn't have bothered with creating a custom 
backend if it wasn't needed, having better things to do with my scarce 
time than reinvent a somewhat lumpy wheel.  In this case, however, there 
was a need, the code resolved that need, and the change was worth 
making.  If you have better backend code that you would like to 
contribute, please feel free -- there is a whole laundry list of things 
in there that could stand to be improved.

> 
> (3) Statnet has dependencies on packages that bear a UW license which
> is NOT compatible with GPL licenses, meaning that Statnet and code
> that uses Statnet packages raise legal complications regarding
> licensing that are likely to surprise many users. Specifically, "for
> profit" uses of some parts of the code potentially require payment of
> royalty fees to UW (the GPL license of R has no such restriction).
> 

As far as I know, there is one optional package (latentnet) that has one 
such dependency on an external R package with a possibly funny license 
(mclust).  The statnet public releases are all GPL (v2 or v3, 
depending), and the core packages have no such dependencies AFAIK. 
Perhaps you would like to expand on the list of "packages" involved? 
(Or, by "dependencies" and "packages," did you mean "dependency" and 
"package?")  I would also be interested to learn what parts of the 
statnet code require payment of royalty fees to UW.  Perhaps this was 
decided at a super-secret meeting to which I wasn't invited.

> The above problems, like the namespace issue, make Statnet not play
> well with other packages, and for this reason any use of Statnet is
> awkward for me. It would be good if the Statnet team could give some
> attention to them, so that it can interoperate better with R and
> other R packages.

Despite all evidence to the contrary, we do love our peeps, and we try 
to evolve our toolkit in response to user input.  This is more like 
steering a tanker than a motorboat, so the salutary effects of 
belligerence are not always immediate; and, of course, there are some 
cases in which well-intentioned suggestions are unwise or infeasible due 
to engineering trade-offs that are not apparent to the person making the 
suggestion.  The R world has changed radically over the past few years, 
as have the kind of data analysis challenges that we and our peers face. 
  (When I wrote the first version of sna, the largest complete network 
data set of which I was aware had about 60 nodes.)  In the face of such 
challenges, our ragtag band of sociologists, anthropologists, and 
statisticians attempts to provide the best free software reasonably 
producible by amateur developers working in their spare time.  So long 
as we and others find it useful, we will continue to do so.

Thanks,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Re: Modifying plot layout parameters (repulse.rad)
messages.body_plain:
Three points:

1. As noted, shrinking plot elements is important with very large 
displays.  You will want to set your vertex.cex to something suitably 
small.  Getting the ideal values for parameters like repulse.rad 
requires some testing in difficult cases; recall that custom coordinates 
can also be specified if needed.

2. R's default plot margins eat a lot of space.  Setting the "mar" 
argument with "par" can help.

3. Semi-transparancy has been supported in gplot/plot.network for as 
long as R has supported it -- it's a standard feature.  (Just pass a 
color with an alpha parameter.)

4. Currently, gplot in sna is slightly more advanced than plot.network. 
  (It lacks some of plot.network's conveniences, however.)

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Blockmodeling 2-Mode data
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Sam -

Sam Stewart wrote:
> Do you mean treat the bipartite network as a standard network?  When I 
> run sedist on a 2-mode network I get this:
> 
> Error in d[1, , ] <- dat : 
>   number of items to replace is not a multiple of replacement length
> 
> The error occurs because the sedist function uses as.sociomatrix.sna to 
> extract the sociomatrix, but then it sets up the dissimilarity matrix (d 
> in the sedist code) to be square, using dim(dat)[1], while the 
> sociomatrix is not square.
> 
> If I set up the 2-mode network as a bipartite network, but didn't 
> actually record it as a bipartite network, then the resulting 
> sociomatrix would be 617x617 (rather than 300x317), with large 0 blocks 
> in the top-left and bottom right.  If I were to run a partitioning on 
> that would it be meaningful?

Yes, you will need to represent your matrix in one-mode form (i.e., as a 
bipartite graph on the union of row and column vertices); you can do 
that an adjacency matrix will work fine here, as will an sna edgelist. 
At that point, sedist and friends will operate normally.  Note that the 
meaning of structural equivalence is the same in one-mode and two-mode 
contexts (i.e., v and v' are structurally equivalent to the extent that 
they have identical neighborhoods in V minus v,v'), and analysis 
proceeds as usual.  (You might interpret the block structure 
differently, however, depending on the meaning of the row and column 
vertices.  When using redist, you might also want to begin by 
differentiating between the row and column vertices in the seed partition.)

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I thought people here might be interested in this:

I created an R package that enables somewhat easier conversion between 
network objects of class 'network' and networks of class 'igraph', from 
the respective packages. It is called 'intergraph'. More information here:

http://brokeringclosure.wordpress.com/2010/08/25/from-igraph-to-network-and-back-again/

The package is still experimental. It may give warnings during some of 
the operations. This happens most often at places where I was not sure 
what is the best default behavior so decided to warn the user about the 
choices made (for example when not copying some network/edge/vertex 
attribute).

*If you try it out I'm very interested in your feedback!*

A related issue:

To be able to build upon the 'network' package reliably I had to patch 
it to add the package namespace. Package namespaces, as definined here

http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/R-exts.html#Package-name-spaces

are a necessary standard for R packages nowadays. I remember discussing 
this issue with Mark when I was visiting Stats dep. at UW in autumn 2008.

*Please seriously consider adding namespaces to all 'statnet' packages.*

The procedure should be very straightforward. For the 'network' package 
you add a NAMESPACE file to the top level of package directory 
containing two lines:

useDynLib("network")
exportPattern("^[^\\.]")

This will export all the R functions defined in the package which names 
do not start with a dot (there are none as far as I remember) and 
register the C functions contained in the package.

The namespaced 'network' package passes R CMD check. Additionally I ran 
all the examples and tests in 'ergm' and some other 'statnet' packages 
to check if it doesn't break something by accident. Everything performed 
seamlessly.


Best,
Michal

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] 	from network to igraph and back again, and NAMESPACEs
messages.body_plain:
The point about namespaces is well-made by Michal, but really it should have been obvious and best practice would have indicated using R namespaces at the outset of the Statnet project. Unfortunately, this is just one of the programming practices that the Statnet project has adopted that runs counter to the R environment that they chose to work within. To the namespace issue may be added at least the following three:

(1) Statnet imposes an unusual modification on the semantics of formula objects in R. In no other R package does one write a formula in which complex object (i.e. the network, which contains many vectors of differing lengths) is expressed in terms of objects contained within it. 

(2) Insistence on C code (ostensibly for speed), to the point of incorporating legacy code that duplicates basic functionality of the BLAS in R (e.g. eigen decomposition). This actually flies in the face of the speed criterion, because the R BLAS is optimized for multiple-core architectures (not as common when the Statnet project started as they are now), and the legacy code is not (nor is specialized Statnet C code like the network layout code necessarily multi-processor optimized). 

(3) Statnet has dependencies on packages that bear a UW license which is NOT compatible with GPL licenses, meaning that Statnet and code that uses Statnet packages raise legal complications regarding licensing that are likely to surprise many users. Specifically, "for profit" uses of some parts of the code potentially require payment of royalty fees to UW (the GPL license of R has no such restriction).

The above problems, like the namespace issue, make Statnet not play well with other packages, and for this reason any use of Statnet is awkward for me. It would be good if the Statnet team could give some attention to them, so that it can interoperate better with R and other R packages.

John Paolillo

> On 08/30/2010 10:20 AM, Carter T. Butts wrote:
>> Michal Bojanowski wrote:

>> run into difficulties; did you also use the C-level API? I entertain
>> some hope of getting the network release out before the curtain of fall
>> quarter descends, so it is possible that this change could be rolled out
>> ere long....
> 
> First of all apologies for a somewhat lengthy e-mail.
> 
> I can understand why S4 is considered by some people an over(haul/kill). But as far as it goes for namespaces: they are very practical, especially in case of multiple name conflicts, like between 'network' and 'igraph'. I do think namespaces will be more and more indispensable given the pace at which the number of packages available through CRAN grows. I also believe that adding namespaces will make extending 'network' and Statnet much easier. Simultaneously, I do not really see any harmful side effects of using namespaces, unless of course somebody feels intimidated by writing two lines of pseudo-code to an extra file.
> 
> To be honest I have somewhat farther-reaching plans as it goes for the 'intergraph' package. Given that 'network' and 'igraph' are two main packages providing data structures for networks ('graph' package following closely) it would be really neat to have a somewhat unified interface to the data in both packages. What I have in mind is something like 'DBI' package in the case of interfacing relational data bases. It defines generic functions for which packages 'RMySQL', 'RSQLite' and others provides methods. DBI is written in S4, but given that both 'network' and 'igraph' are written in S3 it would not be necessary to go for S4. What I had in mind is having generics for, say: as.network, as.igraph, as.matrix, network/edge/vertex attribute get/set methods defined in a separate package like 'intergraph' and specific methods like 'as.matrix.network' in 'network', 'as.matrix.igraph' in 'igraph' and so on.
> 
> I did already quite some work in that direction with positive results. What is important is that the tiny modifications that has to be made to both igraph and network do not change the R API: users will not notice that, and so the exising software depending on either network or igraph should be perfectly OK. I'll be happy to collaborate on that with any volunteers.
> 
> I'm curious what you and other Statnet-ers would think about such a project.
> 
> As for the conversion functions within 'intergraph':
> 
> Apart from the namespace issue I did not really run into any problems. The package is pure R, I did not use C API directly. As both 'network' and 'igraph' use C under the hood I can imagine that it might make sense performance-wise to have the conversion done by some C routines. Currently the conversion does not use adjacency matrices as an intermediate format but data frames: edgelist + edge attributes and vertex data frame with attributes so should be rather efficient.
> 
> One limitation is that 'igraph' is somewhat less general than 'network' in terms of the data model, so hypergraphs for example are not supported (I still have to add some warnings into the code).
> 
> I would definitely welcome namespacing the 'network' and other Statnet packages. Let me know if there is any way I could be of help.
> 
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

Thanks for the code!  It resolved the problem without a hitch.

Best,
David

________________________________
From: statnet_help-bounces@mailman2.u.washington.edu [mailto:statnet_help-bounces@mailman2.u.washington.edu] On Behalf Of David Hunter
Sent: Sunday, June 27, 2010 7:12 AM
To: statnet list
Subject: Re: [statnet_help] ERGM - too many unique dyads

Hi David.  You are correct that this is a memory-related error.  You're getting the error because (a) your network has more than 1 million possible edges; and (b) the model you're using uses quantative variables in such a way that most vectors of "change statistics" (each possible edge gets its own such vector) are completely unique, which means that you're not able to take advantage of ergm's default compression algorithm, which basically stores only the unique change statistic vectors (and keeps a count of the number of times each one is used).  All of this information is fed into the logistic regression solver that returns the MPLE for you.

In any case, the error you're seeing should be pretty easy to fix, though the error message you got should be more informative about how to fix it!  (I'll make a change for the next version of ergm).  The key is changing the default value (which is 1 million) of the control parameter called "maxNumDyadTypes" using the control.ergm function.

I'll use the faux.magnolia.high dataset to demonstrate, since it has 1461 nodes and 1461-choose-2 is just big enough to go over a million.  First, here's what happens before changing the default:

> data(faux.magnolia.high)
> fmh <- faux.magnolia.high
> fmh %v% "quantitative.var" <- rnorm(1461)
> ergm(fmh ~ absdiff("quantitative.var"))
Error in ergm.pl(Clist = Clist, Clist.miss = Clist.miss, m = m, theta.offset = theta.offset,  :
  Too many unique dyads!

Now for the control.ergm function:

> big.enough <- 1461 * 1460 / 2
> ergm(fmh ~ absdiff("quantitative.var"), control=control.ergm(maxNumDyadTypes=big.enough))
Newton-Raphson iterations:  12

MLE Coefficients:
absdiff.quantitative.var
                  -20.49

Hope this helps.

Dave

Hi Jeff,

The "istar" term does not have a "base" argument (according to the manual page for it). That is what is causing the error. However, e.g.,

messages.body_plain:
On 07/28/2010 11:09 PM, Soriani Nicola wrote:
> Hi Michal,
>
> Unfortunatly in Statnet I don't think exist "predict" procedures for a
> ERGM object, but your idea is right. And I used the same idea when I
> started to perform mine personal routines.
>
> After I thought that by simulating networks what you probably obtain is an
> approximation of the conditional probabilities. I mean the probability of
> each Y_ij=1 given the rest of the graph.
>
> So, it is easier and faster to compute directly that probabilities.
>
> I performed some routines for both: (sorry for the Italian terms in the code)
>
> ############
>
> "predict.ergmbysim" follows your idea, so it simulates "nsim" networks in
> according to an ergm model "modello". If you want, you can repeat that
> procedure "nrep" times, and you will have also the standard error.
>
>    ###
>
> predict.ergmbysim<-function(modello,newnetwork=NULL,nsim=100,nrep=1,single=FALSE,burnin=10000,interval=1000){
>
> if(is.null(newnetwork)) rete<-modello$"network"
> else rete<-newnetwork
> n<-network.size(rete)
> iperP<-iperP2<-matrix(0,n,n)
> if(single | nsim>2000){
> for(j in 1:nrep){
> P<-matrix(0,n,n)
> for(i in 1:nsim){
>   obj<-simulate(modello$"formula",
>                    nsim=1,theta0=modello$"coef",
> 			basis=rete,burnin=burnin,interval=interval)
>
> P<-P+as.matrix(obj)
> }
> iperP<-iperP+P/nsim
> iperP2<-iperP2+(P/nsim)^2
> }
> }
> else if(!single&  nsim<2000){
> for(j in 1:nrep){
> P<-matrix(0,n,n)
> obj<-simulate(modello$"formula", nsim=nsim,theta0=modello$"coef",
> 			basis=rete,burnin=burnin,interval=1000)$"networks"
> for(i in 1:nsim){
> P<-P+as.matrix(obj[[i]])
> }
> iperP<-iperP+P/nsim
> iperP2<-iperP2+(P/nsim)^2
> }
> }
> print(paste("Risultati su ", nrep," iterazione/i per rispettivamente ",
> nsim, "reti simulate ad ogni iterarazione"))
> list("P"=iperP/nrep, "Stand.Error"=sqrt(iperP2/nrep-(iperP/nrep)^2))  }
>
>
> #############################
>
> "predict.ergm" is such long because it can predict also the probabilities
> of a new network or for new nodes in the network. But if you want to
> predict the links of the observed network, put "modello" = ( your ergm
> object ) and forget all the other terms.
>
>   ###
>
> predict.ergm<-function(modello,data=NULL,newnetwork=NULL){
> if(is.null(newnetwork)) rete<-modello$"network"
> else rete<-newnetwork
> n<-network.size(rete)
> beta<-modello$coef
>
> if(is.directed(rete)){
> if(is.null(data)){
> eta<- matrix(0, n, n)
>
> for(i in 1:n){
> 	for(j in 1:n){
> 	alternativa<-rete
> 	if(is.na(rete[i,j])){
> 	rete[i,j]<-1
> 	alternativa[i,j]<-1 - rete[i,j]
> 	u1<-summary(safeupdate.formula(modello$formula, rete ~ .))
>    u2<-summary(safeupdate.formula(modello$formula, alternativa ~ .))
> 	delta<-u2-u1
> 	prob<-1/(1+exp(sum(beta*delta)))
>
>   if (rete[i,j]==1) eta[i,j]<- prob
>
> else eta[i,j]<-1-prob
>
> if (i==j) eta[i,j]<-0
> rete[i,j]<-NA
> }
> else{
> alternativa[i,j]<-1 - rete[i,j]
> u1<-summary(safeupdate.formula(modello$formula, rete ~ .))

messages.body_plain:
Hi Professor Morris: 

Thank you very much for your reply. Unfortunately it seems like StatNet doesn't recognize it as a bipartite graph, but there may be a way to got around it. There's probably an easier way but I'll just post what I did here.  Here's the network (pajek format)

*vertices 10 5
1 "a"
2 "b"
3 "c"
4 "d"
5 "e"
6 "u"
7 "v"
8 "w"
9 "x"
10 "y"
*arcs
1 6
1 9
1 10
2 10
2 8
2 7
3 6
4 6
5 6
4 10


net <- read.paj("test.net")
# can check that this is not bipartite
is.bipartite(net)
# FALSE

#This is a bit silly but I'm not sure how else to directly assign the bipartite attribute
temp0 <- as.matrix(net)
net <- as.network(temp0, bipartite = 5)
is.bipartite(net)
# TRUE
# :-)

Rick






----- Original Message ----
From: Martina Morris <morrism@u.washington.edu>
To: Rick L <rick22304@yahoo.com>
Cc: StatNet <statnet_help@u.washington.edu>
Sent: Thu, April 22, 2010 1:48:50 PM
Subject: Re: [statnet_help] two-mode network in StatNet

Hi Rick,

The short answer is yes, statnet can recognize and work with bipartite networks.  I'm not sure about whether this happens automatically when you import a 2mode Pajek .net file, but you can check by using the summary() function on the network object.  If it is bipartite, that will be displayed in the summary info at the top.

Modeling with bipartite networks requires using bipartite-specific ergm terms.  You can see the terms currently available in the Table of Model Terms in the JoSS article on Specification of ERGMS (vol 24 i4), available here:

http://www.statnetproject.org/users_guide.shtml

best,
Martina

messages.subject: [statnet_help] decay for gwidegree
messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

I'm not a big user of the directed gw* terms, but for the undirected ones 
my general rule of thumb is to start low with the decay term.  As a 
general rule of thumb for empirical data, the lower the decay term is, the 
less likely the model is to be degenerate. So I typically start around 
0.25 or so.  For data I've worked with I often find there is little 
diffence in model fit across a range of decay terms, often 0.5 to 1.5 or 
so. But then again, I've only applied these to a specific social network 
domain (adolescent friendship nets) and the details of my experience may 
not be universal.

Cheers,
Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] anyone know how to extract largest connected subnetwork from a netowrk object
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] anyone know how to extract largest connected subnetwork from a netowrk object
messages.body_plain:
I don't know if this was ever satisfactorily answered, but the general
method I use to extract a subnetwork is to create a copy of the source
network using network.copy()*, then delete from the copy the nodes I don't
want. This retains all the attribute data for the sub-network. (*If you use
regular assignment to create a copy of your network then any vertices
deleted from the child network object will also be deleted from the parent
network object for some reason!)

I've included two example functions (below my sig). The firstextracts the
largest component from a network; the second extracts a network consisting
of all nodes sharing a specified vertex attribute value. I think these
functions should be pretty generic, though I've only tested them on two
networks.

Cheers,
Dave
____________________________
David A. Nolin
Postdoctoral Scholar
Carolina Population Center
University of North Carolina


### Function to extract largest component of a network:
### Step 1: Create network copy of source network
### Step 2: Extract node set of largest component
### Step 3: Define a cut set consisting of all other nodes
### Step 4: Delete nodes not in largest component from network copy

extract.lc.net<-function(x){
temp<-network.copy(x)
temp.lc<-component.largest(temp)
cut.set<-row(as.matrix(temp.lc))[temp.lc==F]
temp<-delete.vertices(temp, cut.set)
return(temp)}

### Load example data
data("faux.magnolia.high")

### Extract largest component
fmh.lc<-extract.lc.net(faux.magnolia.high)

### Test: check that new network is same size as largest component
network.size(fmh.lc)
length(component.largest(faux.magnolia.high)[component.largest(faux.magnolia.high)==T])

### Check that attributes are attached
list.vertex.attributes(fmh.lc)


### Function to extract a network of all nodes having a specified attribute
value
extract.att.net<-function(net,att,val){
temp<-network.copy(net)
nodes.having.val<-temp%v%att==val
cut.set<-row(as.matrix(nodes.having.val))[nodes.having.val==F]
temp<-delete.vertices(temp, cut.set)
return(temp)}

### Test: extract seperate networks of all females and males from
faux.magnolia.high
fmh.F<-extract.att.net(faux.magnolia.high, "Sex", "F")
fmh.M<-extract.att.net(faux.magnolia.high, "Sex", "M")

### Check result
network.size(fmh.F)
network.size(fmh.M)
table(faux.magnolia.high%v%"Sex")

### Check that attributes are attached:
list.vertex.attributes(fmh.F)
list.vertex.attributes(fmh.M)

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Comparative study for ERGM vs its rival models
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Hamid.  The term "exponential family random graph model" refers to a 
way of parameterizing models for networks, not for a "kind" of network 
model in the sense that a scientist would use the term.  Thus, to ask 
for a "competing" model is senseless (rather like asking for sonnets 
that compete with the English language).  In the case of the Kronecker 
graph family, for instance, it is necessarily true that (at least the 
versions I have seen) must have an equivalent exponential family 
expression, though that expression may or may not be parsimonious, 
convenient, intelligible, etc.

In a nutshell, you should think of the ERG form as a formal language for 
describing network models.  Choice of language is driven by many 
considerations, and there are certainly cases in which the exponential 
family representation is cumbersome and unhelpful.  (The inhomogeneous 
Bernoulli graphs come to mind.)  One should not, however, confuse choice 
of language with choice of model.

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] results that are too significant
messages.body_plain:
Hi, David -

David Schaefer wrote:
> Hi all,
> 
> I just received a review in which a reviewer suggested that the low
> p-values of an ERGM were possibly an indication of poor convergence
> (in this case, p-values for all effect but one fell below .001).
> When estimating those models, the MCMC diagnostic plots showed no
> signs of degeneracy and the gof plots indicated the model reproduced
> the network well.  To be safe, I reran the models and increased the
> burnin to 10 million, the MCMC sample size to 200,000 and the
> sampling interval to 10,000.  The results don't change; the
> significance levels are just as extreme; and, the MCMC diagnostic
> plots look even better than before.
> 
> Is convergence something that I should be worried about?  If so, is
> there anything else I can do to check for it?  I should mention I am
> using ergm 2.2-4 and R 2.10.1.  I have included the model estimation
> command below.

I have seen that problem before (pseudo-convergence leading to strange 
standard error estimates), usually on large networks with models that 
had substantial dependence.  The fact that something can go wrong does 
not, however, necessarily imply that it has.  If, in this case, (1) the 
chain seems to be mixing well, (2) diagnostics look good, (3) your mean 
stats match closely match the observed statistics, and (4) you get 
consistent results with multiple runs, and (5) you have no particular 
reason to expect that something is amiss, then (given the length of the 
chains) it would seem that you are about as safe as you are likely to 
get.  Getting similar results for the covariate effects with the 
dependence terms removed, assuming you do, would also help rule out some 
sources of algorithmic malfeasance.

Did the reviewer suggest some specific reason to doubt the results?  If 
not, it isn't obvious to me why one would suggest this as a problem.  I 
have on occasion raised similar questions in reviews, but always because 
there was something funny in the results (or in the description of the 
fitting procedure) that suggested poor convergence.  Convergence issues 
are certainly a risk with these sorts of models (and they can be hard to 
detect), but one wouldn't suspect non-convergence simply on the basis of 
low p-values.

This reviewer may or may not have had a good reason for raising this 
issue, but one should be aware that there is a lot of mythology 
surrounding ERGMs these days.  Your reviewer might be an expert, whose 
question arises from a problem they noticed in your analysis, or they 
might be someone who once saw an ERGM talk, and who is now applying 
something they hazily remember having heard during an excessively 
caffeinated exchange between persons whose own expertise consisted of 
having attended an afternoon workshop.  It is wise to respond diligently 
and respectfully to reviewer comments, while also entertaining the 
possibility that some of them do not arise from a position of competence.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] 	from network to igraph and back again, and NAMESPACEs
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] 	from network to igraph and back again, and NAMESPACEs
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Michal -

Michal Bojanowski wrote:
> I can understand why S4 is considered by some people an over(haul/kill). 
> But as far as it goes for namespaces: they are very practical, 
> especially in case of multiple name conflicts, like between 'network' 
> and 'igraph'. I do think namespaces will be more and more indispensable 
> given the pace at which the number of packages available through CRAN 
> grows. I also believe that adding namespaces will make extending 
> 'network' and Statnet much easier. Simultaneously, I do not really see 
> any harmful side effects of using namespaces, unless of course somebody 
> feels intimidated by writing two lines of pseudo-code to an extra file.

It is always possible that I am exaggerating my opposition for purposes 
of humorous effect and/or to distract the reader from considering 
accusations of sloth on my part, though I prefer to let such questions 
remain in the domain of personal speculation.  From an end user 
perspective, the main downside of namespaces is that they reduce the 
transparency of access to code within the interpreter (since you need to 
know what namespace the function is in, and query it correctly).  This 
is not terribly difficult, but is IMHO a lot less obvious for new users 
(and I find it a pain, myself).  From a developer's point of view, the 
only real concern is making sure that there's not some highly 
non-obvious bug in cross-package compatibility that will suddenly arise 
when you add namespaces to your package.  That may seem unlikely, but 
maintaining multiple interdependent packages teaches one the Tao of 
Paranoia.

 From a historical perspective, collision problems used to be avoided by 
not creating packages with duplicate nomenclature.  That was eminently 
doable, even until very recently.  But the R world has changed, the 
number of packages has grown to the point where collisions are a real 
issue, and needs of the network community have become sufficiently 
diverse that multiple R-based toolkits start to make sense.  In this 
environment, I am persuaded that namespaces are a regrettable necessity. 
  (There is still no excuse for American Idol.)

> 
> To be honest I have somewhat farther-reaching plans as it goes for the 
> 'intergraph' package.
 >...
> I'm curious what you and other Statnet-ers would think about such a 
> project.

It's an interesting issue.  Back when we started building statnet per 
se, the idea was to build the network class as a unifying data 
structure.  It works pretty damn well (though it has legacy aspects that 
could be improved), but my sense at this stage is that the increasing 
scale and diversity of network data sets is such that no one structure 
is going to work well for all applications.  There are intrinsic 
engineering tradeoffs involved in choosing one representation over 
another, and nothing makes everyone happy.  As it is, I use adjacency 
matrices when just playing around with simple structures, network 
objects for large/complex networks with rich metadata, and sna edgelists 
for ultra-huge networks with ~1e6 nodes/edges.  (Actually, I've also 
used network objects for the latter, but even the linear costs of 
metadata support start to become a concern when you are squeezing every 
bit of RAM out of your machine.)  We also have projects that are 
starting to require database storage (as you describe), for incompletely 
observed networks of unthinkable size.  Trying to shoehorn all of this 
into one class would require a very special brand of madness.

Given that, the idea of working towards a unified API (or 
``meta-class,'' as it were) to form another abstraction layer between 
the usual class-level data representation and the analysis tools would 
seem to have promise.  Very difficult to do well, however.  In the short 
term, a more systematic scheme for class conversion would doubtless be 
helpful.  (Otherwise, our packages have to know how to decode everyone 
else's classes, which is not practical.  And vice versa.)  Not speaking 
for the other members of the team, I am sympathetic to supporting such a 
lingua franca effort if (1) it's well-designed, (2) doesn't break 
anything, and (3) doesn't create maintenance problems down the road.  I 
have learned the hard way to be very careful vis a vis (2) and (3), and 
do not lightly make changes to the network class.  But persuasion is not 
impossible, and I am open to specific proposals.

Cheers,

-Carter

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Question about measuring associations among a set of	valued networks
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Moses.  To get graph correlations/covariances, try gcor and gcov. 
(gscor and gscov do the same thing for partially labeled structures; see 
also hdist and structdist for distances.)  If passed multiple graphs, 
these will return the appropriate correlation/covariance matrix (and the 
data can be valued).  QAP is a permutation procedure that provides a 
null distribution for bivariate graph statistics (e.g., the graph 
correlation, Hubert's gamma, Hamming distance, etc.), so there's not 
actually such a thing as a "QAP Correlation" per se.  The correlations 
and such obtained from the above can, however, be compared against QAP 
nulls using the qaptest command.  For a related parametric approach, try 
the optional netperm package.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
Hi Sean.  Just to add to what Martina said, the answer to your  
question is technically YES.  However, as she points out, the main  
difference that would be visible to the user is due to the fact that  
the estimates are stochastic.  That said, if you notice any estimates  
that are vastly different than something you obtained before, I'd be  
interested to hear about it.

One thing that you may notice:  If you used a random seed to set the  
random number generator in an effort to make your results *exactly*  
reproducible, then your results probably will have changed anyway from  
version 2.2-2 to 2.2-3.  But again, the change should be small.

Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] converting ergm output into tables
messages.body_plain:
Hi Elena,

A good question...

The coefficients exist as a table in the summary of the fit. So they can be extracted from the summary and written to a CSV file, for example. Here is how I do it:

data(florentine)
gest <- ergm(flomarriage ~ edges + absdiff("wealth"))
summary(gest)
write.table(summary(gest)$coefs,sep=",",file="test.csv")

The file can be read straight into Excel with row and column names intact. Of course, you can also remove the names. See ?write.table for that.

Cheers,

Mark

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Saeed.  That is considered to be an open problem (although there is 
a long line of partial solutions in the research literature).  The short 
answer is that there is no agreed-upon solution in the general case, 
although special-case approaches exist (depending on the kind of 
blockmodel, what you are willing to assume about the data, etc.).  I 
recommend thinking more carefully about what, precisely, you want to 
infer, and then looking to the primary literature for references that 
are germane to that specific problem, before selecting a method.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Re: results that are too significant
messages.body_plain:
I've seen this criticism in econometrics when your dependent variable and
the independent variable in question are mechanically correlated - i.e.
inadvertently derived from the same underlying source of variation, in which
case you by definition will have small standard errors. But that has nothing
to do with convergence, it has to do with your variable choices. I'm an ERGM
rookie myself, so I'm not sure how that would apply to your specific model,
but perhaps this may nudge the discussion in the right direction.

> off the top of my head.  The low p-values indicate small standard errors
> (relative to the values of the coefficient estimates).  These standard
> errors come from estimates of the second derivative matrix (the Hessian) of
> the approximated log-likelihood function -- they are the square roots of the
> diagonal of the inverse of the negative Hessian, to be exact -- and thus
> it's not clear to me how small standard errors (i.e., a very sharply peaked
> approximate likelihood surface at the maximum) might result from "poor
> convergence".  Perhaps someone else on the list can help with the intuition
> here, but it sounds to me as though (a) you have done all you could to try
> to rule out any convergence issues, and (b) there is no reason to suspect
> that low p-values are by themselves evidence of convergence issues.

Hi David.  I have to say, I can't see any basis for the referee's  
suspicion off the top of my head.  The low p-values indicate small  
standard errors (relative to the values of the coefficient  
estimates).  These standard errors come from estimates of the second  
derivative matrix (the Hessian) of the approximated log-likelihood  
function -- they are the square roots of the diagonal of the inverse  
of the negative Hessian, to be exact -- and thus it's not clear to me  
how small standard errors (i.e., a very sharply peaked approximate  
likelihood surface at the maximum) might result from "poor  
convergence".  Perhaps someone else on the list can help with the  
intuition here, but it sounds to me as though (a) you have done all  
you could to try to rule out any convergence issues, and (b) there is  
no reason to suspect that low p-values are by themselves evidence of  
convergence issues.

Does this help?  (And does anyone else see something I'm missing?)

Dave

The ergm fitting procedure has a stochastic component to it (it's MCMC),

estimation, you will get slightly different point estimates.  They should

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Question about latentnet
messages.body_plain:
Saeed,

Indeed, the runtime of latentnet is approximately quadratic in the
number of nodes in the network, so when fitting networks of that size,
so it can take a while, especially with random actor effects. If you
have multiprocessor or multicore hardware, you might want to try running
in multiple threads (by setting the control parameter "threads"). Also,
you can run with verbose=1 to see on what stage of the process it gets
stuck. (If you want, send me the output, off-list.)

                            I hope this helps,
                            Pavel

Hi all,

I just received a review in which a reviewer suggested that the low p-values of an ERGM were possibly an indication of poor convergence (in this case, p-values for all effect but one fell below .001).  When estimating those models, the MCMC diagnostic plots showed no signs of degeneracy and the gof plots indicated the model reproduced the network well.  To be safe, I reran the models and increased the burnin to 10 million, the MCMC sample size to 200,000 and the sampling interval to 10,000.  The results don't change; the significance levels are just as extreme; and, the MCMC diagnostic plots look even better than before.

Is convergence something that I should be worried about?  If so, is there anything else I can do to check for it?  I should mention I am using ergm 2.2-4 and R 2.10.1.  I have included the model estimation command below.

f4<-ergm(coTiesBin2_653~ edges + gwdegree(.5, fixed=TRUE) +
    gwesp(.75, fixed=TRUE) + gwdsp(.75, fixed=TRUE) +   
    nodecov('pop1017') + nodecov('SES') + nodecov('oneparentP') +
    nodecov('nonWhiteP') + nodecov('crimHistory') + nodecov('diffhome') + 
    absdiff('diffhome') + absdiff('SES') + absdiff('oneparentP') + 
    absdiff('nonWhiteP') + absdiff('crimHistory') + 
    edgecov(schoolMat653) + edgecov(logDist653)
    ,burnin=10000000, MCMCsamplesize=200000, interval=10000)

David

messages.subject: [statnet_help] 	from network to igraph and back again, and NAMESPACEs
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] 	from network to igraph and back again, and NAMESPACEs
messages.body_plain:
Hi all.  John has raised some intriguing issues in his post and has  
generated quite a bit of off-list email traffic among the statnet  
team.  To summarize briefly:


Point (3) appears to refer to the fact, alluded to by Michal and  
Magnus and Pavel already, that the latentnet package (in statnet) has  
to date depended on the mclust package (not written by us and not in  
statnet).  This dependency is going away, and in fact Pavel reports  
that a new version of latentnet is already percolating through CRAN.   
Otherwise, all statnet code is, and has always been, GPL; details are  
at http://statnetproject.org/attribution


Point (2) is trickier to parse.  There are undoubtedly some issues of  
legacy code (parts of sna are over 10 years old, after all!) but the  
fact is that there is no way to make statnet packages do what they do,  
as fast as they do it, by writing in R only. Multiple cores do not  
change this fact.  That said, statnet does rely on R for a lot of its  
heavy lifting when possible.  Nothing about the statnet packages is  
unusual, relative to many other R packages, in these regards.


As for (1), it is important to keep in mind that ergms are not glms.   
The "unusual modification" is not a creation of statnet; it is the  
reality of these models.  Thus, there is no way to use completely  
standard glm syntax in formulating an ergm specification; the choice  
is between creating a completely new syntax and bending the existing  
formula structure.  We are still convinced that the latter is by far  
the better choice in terms of consistency with the R paradigm.  (We  
thought very carefully about this issue when the ergm package was in  
its infancy!)

Note that in some cases, an ergm coincides with a logistic regression  
model, which *is* a glm.  In such cases, one could in fact use a more  
traditional glm-like syntax, but even in these cases, the bookkeeping  
necessary to create the traditional predictor matrix is pretty  
complicated and would require its own brand-new syntax since we would  
certainly want to create methods to help the user do this.  Our choice  
of ergm syntax is thus a massive benefit to simplicity.

There is quite a bit more room for discussion of this question, and  
undoubtedly if others have questions/suggestions then this could  
create some more lively discussion on this list.  In particular, if  
novice (or not-so-novice) users are confused about the similarities  
and differences between an ergm, with its inherent auto-dependency,  
and a glm, please ask!  It's a great topic for this list.


Finally, kudos to Michal for what sounds like great work on the  
intergraph package!  I won't address the namespace issue, the only  
real way in which statnet currently doesn't "play well" in my opinion,  
except to say that Michal and Magnus offer very persuasive arguments  
in favor of namespaces and we will probably add them in future statnet  
releases (as others have stated or surmised, namespaces did not exist  
in their current form when we began statnet).



Thanks to all for keeping discussions professional and respectful.

Dave
for the statnet team:  Mark, Carter, Steve, Martina, Pavel




On Aug 30, 2010, at 8:43 AM, John Paolillo wrote:

> The point about namespaces is well-made by Michal, but really it  
> should have been obvious and best practice would have indicated  
> using R namespaces at the outset of the Statnet project.  
> Unfortunately, this is just one of the programming practices that  
> the Statnet project has adopted that runs counter to the R  
> environment that they chose to work within. To the namespace issue  
> may be added at least the following three:
>
> (1) Statnet imposes an unusual modification on the semantics of  
> formula objects in R. In no other R package does one write a formula  
> in which complex object (i.e. the network, which contains many  
> vectors of differing lengths) is expressed in terms of objects  
> contained within it.
>
> (2) Insistence on C code (ostensibly for speed), to the point of  
> incorporating legacy code that duplicates basic functionality of the  
> BLAS in R (e.g. eigen decomposition). This actually flies in the  
> face of the speed criterion, because the R BLAS is optimized for  
> multiple-core architectures (not as common when the Statnet project  
> started as they are now), and the legacy code is not (nor is  
> specialized Statnet C code like the network layout code necessarily  
> multi-processor optimized).
>
> (3) Statnet has dependencies on packages that bear a UW license  
> which is NOT compatible with GPL licenses, meaning that Statnet and  
> code that uses Statnet packages raise legal complications regarding  
> licensing that are likely to surprise many users. Specifically, "for  
> profit" uses of some parts of the code potentially require payment  
> of royalty fees to UW (the GPL license of R has no such restriction).
>
> The above problems, like the namespace issue, make Statnet not play  
> well with other packages, and for this reason any use of Statnet is  
> awkward for me. It would be good if the Statnet team could give some  
> attention to them, so that it can interoperate better with R and  
> other R packages.
>
> John Paolillo
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Annie.  Not silly at all -- in fact, this is a vexing problem that  
we've seen before.

Here's what's happening:  When you read in TestVec, it is created as  
an object of type "data.frame".  Then, when you try to coerce it to  
type "vector", essentially nothing happens.  (In particular, the thing  
you think has happened, has not.)  You can verify this by typing  
class(TestVec), when you'll see that it is STILL a data.frame.  This  
is something of an R quirk.  I'm sure there is a reason for it, but  
I'm not sure what the reason is.

In any case, If you replace your line
TestVec = as.vector(TestVec)

by, say,
TestVec = as.vector(TestVec[,1]) # Convert just the first column in  
the data frame

or alternatively
TestVec = as.vector(as.matrix(TestVec)) # Convert data.frame to matrix  
to vector

then your example should work.

Dave

messages.body_plain:
On 08/30/2010 05:06 PM, Magnus Thor Torfason wrote:
> I think this is a really great endeavor, and am extremely happy to see
> someone take this up. I have used igraph quite a bit, mostly because I
> have been using very large networks. However, statnet and the network
> package have a bunch of really useful functions available. Some get
> ported between the two packages, but many do not. I have ended up
> writing some conversion functions myself, but having them nicely
> encapsulated in an interface package would be really great. For me
> personally, it would probably increase my use of statnet quite a bit.

Indeed, there was quite some porting between 'network' and 'igraph'. 
Especially from 'network' to 'igraph': network layout algorithms for 
plotting for example ported from 'network' or 'sna' into 'igraph'. If 
you look at the source code you can see that the core functionality was 
more or less copy-pasted. Apart from the fact that it might be 
considered as a not a very nice behavior, although not illegal, to me it 
is really counter-productive. Any upgrade or bug-fixing in the original 
code leaves the "ported" copy unchanged.

(Side note: Actually, it is a somewhat strange use of the word "porting" 
as both packages are within the same system: R. It's not porting Fortran 
to C or something...)

The above seems to be another argument for working towards package 
interoperability. If there would be tighter conversion routines or 
interfaces between the two packages no "porting" would be necessary.


> I'm too grateful both to the authors of statnet and igraph to fully
> endorse the somewhat harsh tone of John's email, although all of his
> points seem like things that could improve the attractiveness of statnet
> to a number of audiences. As for licensing specifically, I've personally
> released stuff under non-commercial-only license. I feel that the
> decision of license is a very personal one, and that it is seldom
> reasonable to phrase requests for changes in licensing in terms of
> 'should' (*).

Very true. On CRAN there are many packages that have a non-standard 
licenses, take 'ff' for example. Any author is free to choose licensing 
options that suit him best. But, in the context of 'intergraph' and alike:

1. I don't think licensing actually matters much.

2. Although there are non-GPL Statnet packages, like 'mclust' (thanks 
John!) the 'network' package is under GPL, and so are, I conjecture, all 
its reverse-dependencies.

messages.body_plain:
I think this is a really great endeavor, and am extremely happy to see
someone take this up. I have used igraph quite a bit, mostly because I have
been using very large networks. However, statnet and the network package
have a bunch of really useful functions available. Some get ported between
the two packages, but many do not. I have ended up writing some conversion
functions myself, but having them nicely encapsulated in an interface
package would be really great. For me personally, it would probably increase
my use of statnet quite a bit.

I'm too grateful both to the authors of statnet and igraph to fully endorse
the somewhat harsh tone of John's email, although all of his points seem
like things that could improve the attractiveness of statnet to a number of
audiences. As for licensing specifically, I've personally released stuff
under non-commercial-only license. I feel that the decision of license is a
very personal one, and that it is seldom reasonable to phrase requests for
changes in licensing in terms of 'should' (*).

However, as for using namespaces when writing public packages for R, I am
very close to using the 'should' word, and will second a hearty call to
'please please please' add namespaces to network and related packages.

In the end, we are all trying to help each other out in doing good research
and pushing forward the frontiers of knowledge (**). In this, increased
interoperability between the 'competing' packages helps everyone. However, I
am also very sensitive to the fact that although the open-source licenses
that most of the code is released under allow lots of changes by third
parties, it tends to be most productive to involve all authors/copyright
holder in a constructive relationship.

I look very much forward to seeing the outcome of the intergraph project,
which builds on two great packages.

Best,
Magnus

(*) Re-reading John's email, I see that it could be interpreted as
suggesting that the dependencies be removed, rather than the licenses being
changed. I don't know the code in question well enough to know if it would
be feasible to do so without loosing a lot of functionality, but if the
dependency was very minimal, that would seem like a good idea.

(**) All this talk about helping each other out reminded me that I have been
intending to respond to a request for help on this list for over a month now
:-P Hopefully, I'll be able to address that soon.


On Mon, Aug 30, 2010 at 9:48 AM, Michal Bojanowski <m.j.bojanowski@uu.nl>wrote:

> I did not check it with the history of the R sources nor Statnet
> packages, but it may very well be that when the first Statnet packages
> were written the namespace mechanism was not yet part of R itself. My
> own first R packages did not use namespaces either, I added them later.
> As I wrote in my initial e-mail, the modification to the package is
> really tiny and non-intrusive, it does not affect any other code within
> that package nor in any other packages depending on it.
>
>
>  (1) Statnet imposes an unusual modification on the semantics of
>> formula objects in R. In no other R package does one write a formula
>> in which complex object (i.e. the network, which contains many
>> vectors of differing lengths) is expressed in terms of objects
>> contained within it.
>>
>> (2) Insistence on C code (ostensibly for speed), to the point of
>> incorporating legacy code that duplicates basic functionality of the
>> BLAS in R (e.g. eigen decomposition). This actually flies in the face
>> of the speed criterion, because the R BLAS is optimized for
>> multiple-core architectures (not as common when the Statnet project
>> started as they are now), and the legacy code is not (nor is
>> specialized Statnet C code like the network layout code necessarily
>> multi-processor optimized).
>>
>
> I do not really see any conflict nor interdependence between the the use
> of namespaces and the first two issues you mentioned. The namespace
> can be added to a package irrespectively whether the functions in that
> package use formula objects in a non-standard way, duplicate some
> functionality (whether written in R on in C) in base R or some other
> packages etc. It is just a mechanism enabling the users to, among other
> things, use a consistent way of calling functions with the same names
> that come from different packages.
>
> In fact, if you plan to duplicate a certain functionality, say an R
> function, it may even make more sense to call the new function the same
> way as the original to indicate that it is designed to do the same thing
> and then use the namespace so that the users can choose to import the
> version they prefer.
>
>
>  (3) Statnet has dependencies on packages that bear a UW license
>> which is NOT compatible with GPL licenses, meaning that Statnet and
>> code that uses Statnet packages raise legal complications regarding
>> licensing that are likely to surprise many users. Specifically, "for
>> profit" uses of some parts of the code potentially require payment of
>> royalty fees to UW (the GPL license of R has no such restriction).
>>
>
> Well, this seems to me as a completely different matter. Indeed, I am a
> bit surprised with what you wrote. I just had a look at the sources of
> 'network' and 'ergm' (COPYING and LICENSE files) and they both seem to
> be under GPL (?). Statnet authors, please clarify.
>
> Taking the issue a bit more generally. There are other
> packages in the R World created to work with network data, like 'igraph'
> and 'graph'. Apart from the data structures for networks, they do
> provide a lot of other functionality. I see that functionality
> definitely *complementary* to all the things that were created within
> Statnet. For me as a network modeling person it was always a real pain
> going back and forth between 'igraph' and 'network' while, say, running
> some community detection algorithm in 'igraph' and then fitting some
> ERGMs to the same data set.
>
> It is of course the decision of a package author whether, while writing
> the package, he/she facilitates or impedes using his/her package
> together with other R packages designed to work with the same type of data.
>
> Nevertheless, whatever Statnet's standing about the licensing is, in my
> opinion, it does not have much to do with the "technical" benefits of
> having the packages NAMESPACEd.
>
>
>  The above problems, like the namespace issue, make Statnet not play
>> well with other packages, and for this reason any use of Statnet is
>> awkward for me. It would be good if the Statnet team could give some
>> attention to them, so that it can interoperate better with R and
>> other R packages.
>>
>
> Two thumbs up about that. Although, as I wrote above, the other issues
> (apart from namespaces) do not seem to be that "severe" for
> interoperability with other packages.
>
>
>
>
> --
> -----------------------------
> Michal Bojanowski

> Utrecht University

messages.body_plain:
On 08/30/2010 10:20 AM, Carter T. Butts wrote:
> Michal Bojanowski wrote:
>>
>> *Please seriously consider adding namespaces to all 'statnet' packages.*
>>
>
> I rather despise R namespaces, considering them to be (along with S4
> methods, text messaging, and American Idol) symptomatic of the
> degeneration of our society. However, all the cool kids are using them
> these days, and I expect to yield to peer pressure in upcoming releases.
> My own curmudgeonry aside, I am much cheered by the fact that you didn't
> run into difficulties; did you also use the C-level API? I entertain
> some hope of getting the network release out before the curtain of fall
> quarter descends, so it is possible that this change could be rolled out
> ere long....

First of all apologies for a somewhat lengthy e-mail.

I can understand why S4 is considered by some people an over(haul/kill). 
But as far as it goes for namespaces: they are very practical, 
especially in case of multiple name conflicts, like between 'network' 
and 'igraph'. I do think namespaces will be more and more indispensable 
given the pace at which the number of packages available through CRAN 
grows. I also believe that adding namespaces will make extending 
'network' and Statnet much easier. Simultaneously, I do not really see 
any harmful side effects of using namespaces, unless of course somebody 
feels intimidated by writing two lines of pseudo-code to an extra file.

To be honest I have somewhat farther-reaching plans as it goes for the 
'intergraph' package. Given that 'network' and 'igraph' are two main 
packages providing data structures for networks ('graph' package 
following closely) it would be really neat to have a somewhat unified 
interface to the data in both packages. What I have in mind is something 
like 'DBI' package in the case of interfacing relational data bases. It 
defines generic functions for which packages 'RMySQL', 'RSQLite' and 
others provides methods. DBI is written in S4, but given that both 
'network' and 'igraph' are written in S3 it would not be necessary to go 
for S4. What I had in mind is having generics for, say: as.network, 
as.igraph, as.matrix, network/edge/vertex attribute get/set methods 
defined in a separate package like 'intergraph' and specific methods 
like 'as.matrix.network' in 'network', 'as.matrix.igraph' in 'igraph' 
and so on.

I did already quite some work in that direction with positive results. 
What is important is that the tiny modifications that has to be made to 
both igraph and network do not change the R API: users will not notice 
that, and so the exising software depending on either network or igraph 
should be perfectly OK. I'll be happy to collaborate on that with any 
volunteers.

I'm curious what you and other Statnet-ers would think about such a project.

As for the conversion functions within 'intergraph':

Apart from the namespace issue I did not really run into any problems. 
The package is pure R, I did not use C API directly. As both 'network' 
and 'igraph' use C under the hood I can imagine that it might make sense 
performance-wise to have the conversion done by some C routines. 
Currently the conversion does not use adjacency matrices as an 
intermediate format but data frames: edgelist + edge attributes and 
vertex data frame with attributes so should be rather efficient.

One limitation is that 'igraph' is somewhat less general than 'network' 
in terms of the data model, so hypergraphs for example are not supported 
(I still have to add some warnings into the code).

I would definitely welcome namespacing the 'network' and other Statnet 
packages. Let me know if there is any way I could be of help.



~michal




-- 
-----------------------------
Michal Bojanowski
PhD Candidate
ICS / Department of Sociology
Utrecht University
http://www.fss.uu.nl/soc/bojanowski
http://www.bojanorama.pl

messages.subject: [statnet_help] predicted link probabilities
messages.body_plain:
Hi Michal,

Unfortunatly in Statnet I don't think exist "predict" procedures for a
ERGM object, but your idea is right. And I used the same idea when I
started to perform mine personal routines.

After I thought that by simulating networks what you probably obtain is an
approximation of the conditional probabilities. I mean the probability of
each Y_ij=1 given the rest of the graph.

So, it is easier and faster to compute directly that probabilities.

I performed some routines for both: (sorry for the Italian terms in the code)

############

"predict.ergmbysim" follows your idea, so it simulates "nsim" networks in
according to an ergm model "modello". If you want, you can repeat that
procedure "nrep" times, and you will have also the standard error.

  ###

predict.ergmbysim<-function(modello,newnetwork=NULL,nsim=100,nrep=1,single=FALSE,burnin=10000,interval=1000){

if(is.null(newnetwork)) rete<-modello$"network"
else rete<-newnetwork
n<-network.size(rete)
iperP<-iperP2<-matrix(0,n,n)
if(single | nsim>2000){
for(j in 1:nrep){
P<-matrix(0,n,n)
for(i in 1:nsim){
 obj<-simulate(modello$"formula",
                  nsim=1,theta0=modello$"coef",
			basis=rete,burnin=burnin,interval=interval)

P<-P+as.matrix(obj)
}
iperP<-iperP+P/nsim
iperP2<-iperP2+(P/nsim)^2
}
}
else if(!single & nsim<2000){
for(j in 1:nrep){
P<-matrix(0,n,n)
obj<-simulate(modello$"formula", nsim=nsim,theta0=modello$"coef",
			basis=rete,burnin=burnin,interval=1000)$"networks"
for(i in 1:nsim){
P<-P+as.matrix(obj[[i]])
}
iperP<-iperP+P/nsim
iperP2<-iperP2+(P/nsim)^2
}
}
print(paste("Risultati su ", nrep," iterazione/i per rispettivamente ",
nsim, "reti simulate ad ogni iterarazione"))
list("P"=iperP/nrep, "Stand.Error"=sqrt(iperP2/nrep-(iperP/nrep)^2))  }


#############################

"predict.ergm" is such long because it can predict also the probabilities
of a new network or for new nodes in the network. But if you want to
predict the links of the observed network, put "modello" = ( your ergm
object ) and forget all the other terms.

Hi Carter,

> remain in the domain of personal speculation. From an end user
> perspective, the main downside of namespaces is that they reduce the
> transparency of access to code within the interpreter (since you need
> to know what namespace the function is in, and query it correctly).
> This is not terribly difficult, but is IMHO a lot less obvious for
> new users (and I find it a pain, myself).

I'm not sure if understand correctly, but I guess you are referring to
accessing the code that is within the package namespace and which is not
exported.

Then one way to "grab" is using the triple-colon operator, then indeed
you have to know in what package the function is to get it.
Alternatively, one can also use 'getAnywhere' or 'getS3method' for that.

The namespace I used for 'network' exports everything, so all the code
that is user-visible in the original package is still user-visible in
the namespaced version.

I have made a note about my early experiments with namespaces and name
conflicts between 'igraph' and 'network' here

http://brokeringclosure.wordpress.com/2010/08/31/namespaces-and-name-conflicts/

Perhaps of interest also to others.



> From a developer's point of view, the only real concern is making
> sure that there's not some highly non-obvious bug in cross-package
> compatibility that will suddenly arise when you add namespaces to
> your package. That may seem unlikely, but maintaining multiple
> interdependent packages teaches one the Tao of Paranoia.

Indeed. That is of course the problem as all the changes propagate 
through dependecy and Suggest inter-package network like STD... As there 
may be a lot of unforeseen consequences the only way, I think, is to 
have a lot of testing code.


> From a historical perspective, collision problems used to be avoided
> by not creating packages with duplicate nomenclature. That was
> eminently doable, even until very recently. But the R world has
> changed, the number of packages has grown to the point where
> collisions are a real issue, and needs of the network community have
> become sufficiently diverse that multiple R-based toolkits start to
> make sense. In this environment, I am persuaded that namespaces are a
> regrettable necessity. (There is still no excuse for American Idol.)

I definitely agree on that. I also recall early days of R somewhat
resemble MIT hacker culture. As the community grows collisions are more 
and more likely. Perhaps American Idol should be namespaced too...


> Given that, the idea of working towards a unified API (or
> ``meta-class,'' as it were) to form another abstraction layer
> between the usual class-level data representation and the analysis
> tools would seem to have promise. Very difficult to do well, however.
> In the short term, a more systematic scheme for class conversion
> would doubtless be helpful. (Otherwise, our packages have to know how
> to decode everyone else's classes, which is not practical. And vice
> versa.) Not speaking for the other members of the team, I am
> sympathetic to supporting such a lingua franca effort if (1) it's
> well-designed, (2) doesn't break anything, and (3) doesn't create
> maintenance problems down the road. I have learned the hard way to be
> very careful vis a vis (2) and (3), and do not lightly make changes
> to the network class. But persuasion is not impossible, and I am open
> to specific proposals.

Thanks for the good word. All your 1-3 points are definitely the top 
priority for me too.

~Michal

messages.body_plain:
Hi Balasz.  Good question.  gof does work with directed networks, but  
I see that the documentation is not good for explaining how this  
works.  I ought to fix this in a future version of ergm.

By typing
gof_model_rok1 <- gof(model_rok1)
you are using the default value of the "GOF" argument, which means  
you're essentially typing

gof_model_rok1 <- gof(model_rok1, GOF = ~degree + espartners + distance)

and, as you saw, this generates an error because "degree" is an  
undirected-network statistic.  What you can do is replace "degree" by  
"odegree" and/or "idegree" (outdegree or indegree), or neither, by  
typing, say,

gof_model_rok1 <- gof(model_rok1, GOF = ~idegree + odegree +  
espartners + distance)

Other options are "dspartners" for dyadic shared partners and  
"triadcensus" for a census of the sixteen types of triads possible in  
a directed network.  The explanation of the triads is found under  
"triadcensus" in ?ergm-terms.

Sorry the gof documentation is lacking!

Dave

Hi Feng,

I just tried fitting your formula, with some well-tuned fitting 
parameters, and I was able to get good model estimates in a couple of 
hours.  This was on a unix cluster, though.  The exact call I used was:

formula <- fmh ~ edges + nodefactor("Grade") + nodefactor("Race") + 
nodefactor("Sex")  + nodematch("Grade",diff=T)  + nodematch("Sex",diff=F) 
+ gwdegree(1.0,fixed=T) + gwesp(1.0,fixed=T) + gwdsp(1.0,fixed=T)

fit <- ergm(formula, burnin = 10000, interval = 1000, MCMCsamplesize = 
2500, maxit = 25, control = control.ergm(steplength = .25))

and the diagnostics are attached, so you can see it worked well.

There's a bit of a learning curve behind knowing what ergm fitting 
parameters to tweak to get model convergence as quickly as possible. I 
like taking the general approach I use here with the gw* terms, though; a 
larger sample size, a high maxit, and a smaller steplength; it seems to 
work for me in general.

Try this specific run and see how long it takes for you.  If it doesn't 
converge or takes a really really long time, then you may want to try to 
get access to a more powerful machine somehow.

Cheers,
Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] 	from network to igraph and back again, and NAMESPACEs
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] 	from network to igraph and back again, and NAMESPACEs
messages.body_plain:
I did not check it with the history of the R sources nor Statnet
packages, but it may very well be that when the first Statnet packages
were written the namespace mechanism was not yet part of R itself. My
own first R packages did not use namespaces either, I added them later.
As I wrote in my initial e-mail, the modification to the package is
really tiny and non-intrusive, it does not affect any other code within
that package nor in any other packages depending on it.

> (1) Statnet imposes an unusual modification on the semantics of
> formula objects in R. In no other R package does one write a formula
> in which complex object (i.e. the network, which contains many
> vectors of differing lengths) is expressed in terms of objects
> contained within it.
>
> (2) Insistence on C code (ostensibly for speed), to the point of
> incorporating legacy code that duplicates basic functionality of the
> BLAS in R (e.g. eigen decomposition). This actually flies in the face
> of the speed criterion, because the R BLAS is optimized for
> multiple-core architectures (not as common when the Statnet project
> started as they are now), and the legacy code is not (nor is
> specialized Statnet C code like the network layout code necessarily
> multi-processor optimized).

I do not really see any conflict nor interdependence between the the use
of namespaces and the first two issues you mentioned. The namespace
can be added to a package irrespectively whether the functions in that
package use formula objects in a non-standard way, duplicate some
functionality (whether written in R on in C) in base R or some other
packages etc. It is just a mechanism enabling the users to, among other
things, use a consistent way of calling functions with the same names
that come from different packages.

In fact, if you plan to duplicate a certain functionality, say an R
function, it may even make more sense to call the new function the same
way as the original to indicate that it is designed to do the same thing
and then use the namespace so that the users can choose to import the
version they prefer.

> (3) Statnet has dependencies on packages that bear a UW license
> which is NOT compatible with GPL licenses, meaning that Statnet and
> code that uses Statnet packages raise legal complications regarding
> licensing that are likely to surprise many users. Specifically, "for
> profit" uses of some parts of the code potentially require payment of
> royalty fees to UW (the GPL license of R has no such restriction).

Well, this seems to me as a completely different matter. Indeed, I am a
bit surprised with what you wrote. I just had a look at the sources of
'network' and 'ergm' (COPYING and LICENSE files) and they both seem to
be under GPL (?). Statnet authors, please clarify.

Taking the issue a bit more generally. There are other
packages in the R World created to work with network data, like 'igraph'
and 'graph'. Apart from the data structures for networks, they do
provide a lot of other functionality. I see that functionality
definitely *complementary* to all the things that were created within
Statnet. For me as a network modeling person it was always a real pain
going back and forth between 'igraph' and 'network' while, say, running
some community detection algorithm in 'igraph' and then fitting some
ERGMs to the same data set.

It is of course the decision of a package author whether, while writing
the package, he/she facilitates or impedes using his/her package
together with other R packages designed to work with the same type of data.

Nevertheless, whatever Statnet's standing about the licensing is, in my
opinion, it does not have much to do with the "technical" benefits of
having the packages NAMESPACEd.

> The above problems, like the namespace issue, make Statnet not play
> well with other packages, and for this reason any use of Statnet is
> awkward for me. It would be good if the Statnet team could give some
> attention to them, so that it can interoperate better with R and
> other R packages.

Two thumbs up about that. Although, as I wrote above, the other issues
(apart from namespaces) do not seem to be that "severe" for 
interoperability with other packages.



-- 
-----------------------------

PhD Candidate
ICS / Department of Sociology
Utrecht University

http://www.bojanorama.pl
