messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGM - too many unique dyads
messages.body_plain:
Hi David.  You are correct that this is a memory-related error.   
You're getting the error because (a) your network has more than 1  
million possible edges; and (b) the model you're using uses quantative  
variables in such a way that most vectors of "change statistics" (each  
possible edge gets its own such vector) are completely unique, which  
means that you're not able to take advantage of ergm's default  
compression algorithm, which basically stores only the unique change  
statistic vectors (and keeps a count of the number of times each one  
is used).  All of this information is fed into the logistic regression  
solver that returns the MPLE for you.

In any case, the error you're seeing should be pretty easy to fix,  
though the error message you got should be more informative about how  
to fix it!  (I'll make a change for the next version of ergm).  The  
key is changing the default value (which is 1 million) of the control  
parameter called "maxNumDyadTypes" using the control.ergm function.

I'll use the faux.magnolia.high dataset to demonstrate, since it has  
1461 nodes and 1461-choose-2 is just big enough to go over a million.   
First, here's what happens before changing the default:

 > data(faux.magnolia.high)
 > fmh <- faux.magnolia.high
 > fmh %v% "quantitative.var" <- rnorm(1461)
 > ergm(fmh ~ absdiff("quantitative.var"))
Error in ergm.pl(Clist = Clist, Clist.miss = Clist.miss, m = m,  
theta.offset = theta.offset,  :
   Too many unique dyads!

Now for the control.ergm function:

 > big.enough <- 1461 * 1460 / 2
 > ergm(fmh ~ absdiff("quantitative.var"),  
control=control.ergm(maxNumDyadTypes=big.enough))
Newton-Raphson iterations:  12

MLE Coefficients:
absdiff.quantitative.var
                   -20.49

Hope this helps.

Dave

messages.body_plain:
Hi Michal,

Unfortunatly in Statnet I don't think exist "predict" procedures for a
ERGM object, but your idea is right. And I used the same idea when I
started to perform mine personal routines.

After I thought that by simulating networks what you probably obtain is an
approximation of the conditional probabilities. I mean the probability of
each Y_ij=1 given the rest of the graph.

So, it is easier and faster to compute directly that probabilities.

I performed some routines for both: (sorry for the Italian terms in the code)

############

"predict.ergmbysim" follows your idea, so it simulates "nsim" networks in
according to an ergm model "modello". If you want, you can repeat that
procedure "nrep" times, and you will have also the standard error.

  ###

predict.ergmbysim<-function(modello,newnetwork=NULL,nsim=100,nrep=1,single=FALSE,burnin=10000,interval=1000){

if(is.null(newnetwork)) rete<-modello$"network"
else rete<-newnetwork
n<-network.size(rete)
iperP<-iperP2<-matrix(0,n,n)
if(single | nsim>2000){
for(j in 1:nrep){
P<-matrix(0,n,n)
for(i in 1:nsim){
 obj<-simulate(modello$"formula",
                  nsim=1,theta0=modello$"coef",
			basis=rete,burnin=burnin,interval=interval)

P<-P+as.matrix(obj)
}
iperP<-iperP+P/nsim
iperP2<-iperP2+(P/nsim)^2
}
}
else if(!single & nsim<2000){
for(j in 1:nrep){
P<-matrix(0,n,n)
obj<-simulate(modello$"formula", nsim=nsim,theta0=modello$"coef",
			basis=rete,burnin=burnin,interval=1000)$"networks"
for(i in 1:nsim){
P<-P+as.matrix(obj[[i]])
}
iperP<-iperP+P/nsim
iperP2<-iperP2+(P/nsim)^2
}
}
print(paste("Risultati su ", nrep," iterazione/i per rispettivamente ",
nsim, "reti simulate ad ogni iterarazione"))
list("P"=iperP/nrep, "Stand.Error"=sqrt(iperP2/nrep-(iperP/nrep)^2))  }


#############################

"predict.ergm" is such long because it can predict also the probabilities
of a new network or for new nodes in the network. But if you want to
predict the links of the observed network, put "modello" = ( your ergm
object ) and forget all the other terms.

 ###

if(is.null(newnetwork)) rete<-modello$"network"
else rete<-newnetwork
n<-network.size(rete)
beta<-modello$coef

if(is.directed(rete)){
if(is.null(data)){

prob<-1/(1+exp(sum(beta*delta)))

 if (rete[i,j]==1) eta[i,j]<- prob

else eta[i,j]<-1-prob

if (i==j) eta[i,j]<-0
}
}
}

}
else {

nomi<-names(data)

for(k in 1:length(nomi) ){

	list.vertex.attributes(rete)[list.vertex.attributes(rete)==names(data)[k]]),
data[,k]))
	}
attribute<-data.frame(attribute)
names(attribute)<-nomi

n1<-dim(attribute)[1]
eta <- matrix(0, n1, n1)
MM<-matrix(0,n1,n1)
MM[1:n,1:n]<-as.matrix(rete)
for(s in (n+1):n1) {

	for(i in 1:n){
	nwM<-matrix(0, n+1, n+1)
	nwM[1:n,1:n]<-as.matrix(rete)
  nwM[i,n+1]<-1
	nwM[n+1,i]<-1
	newrete<-network(nwM,vertex.attr=attribute[c(1:n,s),],direct=is.directed(rete))

		alternativa<-newrete
		alternativa[i,n+1]<-alternativa[n+1,i]<-0
		u1<-summary(safeupdate.formula(modello$formula, newrete ~ .))
		u2<-summary(safeupdate.formula(modello$formula, alternativa ~ .))
delta<-u2-u1
		prob<-1/(1+exp(sum(beta*delta)))

		eta[i,s]<-eta[s,i]<- prob
    if(eta[i,s]>0.5 & eta[s,i]>0.5) MM[s,i]<-MM[i,s]<-1
		}}

for(s in (n+1):n1) {

	for(i in (n+1):n1){
	nwM<-MM
  nwM[i,s]<-1
	nwM[s,i]<-1
	newrete<-network(nwM,vertex.attr=attribute,direct=is.directed(rete))

  alternativa<-newrete
  alternativa[i,s]<-alternativa[s,i]<-0
		u1<-summary(safeupdate.formula(modello$formula, newrete ~ .))
		u2<-summary(safeupdate.formula(modello$formula, alternativa ~ .))
delta<-u2-u1
		prob<-1/(1+exp(sum(beta*delta)))
    eta[i,s]<-eta[s,i]<- prob
		}}
diag(eta)<-0
block12<-eta[1:n,-1*1:n]
block21<-eta[-1*1:n,1:n]
block22<-eta[-1*1:n,-1*1:n]
return(c(as.vector(block12),as.vector(block21),as.vector(block22))) }
}

Hi Dalton,

Standard box plots are not CI (see for ex.: 
http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_plot). Thus, I think it's not a good 
idea to suppress these grey lines (representing the CI). If you still 
want to, you could do the following:

1) Put the attached "newfunction.R" file in your working directory 
(where you have your gof object). This file is a lightly modified 
version of the plot.gofobject function.

2) Make sure that you have a functional working environment by plotting 
your gof object.


3) Write the following code in you R console:
source("newfunction.R")
pdf("gof_plots_without_IC.pdf") #redirect output in a pdf
newfunc(<m.gof>,IC=FALSE) # replace <m.gof> with the names of your gof 
object
dev.off() # close the pdf


The pdf "gof_plots_without_IC.pdf" will not contain any IC...


Hope that helps,
Victorin

> Subject: Re: [statnet_help] Goodness of fit
>
> Hi,
>
> I think that that these grey lines represent the 95% confidence
> intervals of the log-odds contributions for different statistics of
> interest. These CI are estimated on the simulated samples.
>
> So, for example, if I take the graph you gave us and am interested in
> the "degree 0" statistic, I would say that:
>
> 1) your observed sample contribute to the log-odds for about -1
> 2) 95% of the simulated samples (during the gof()) contributes approx.
> between -2.1 and -1.1 to the log-odds.
>
> Technically speaking, your question should be documented in the
> "plot.gofobject" and "gof.ergm" documentation pages but is not. However,
> the code of the "plot.gofobject" function indicates that the grey lines
> are drawn using some parts of your gof object (<m.gof>):
>
> <m.gof>$bds.model
> <m.gof>$bds.ideg

> <m.gof>$bds.triadcensus

>

newfunc<-function (x, ..., cex.axis = 0.7, plotlogodds = FALSE, main = "Goodness-of-fit diagnostics", 
    normalize.reachability = FALSE, verbose = FALSE, IC=TRUE) 
{
    color <- "gray75"
    all.gof.vars <- ergm.rhs.formula(x$GOF)
    statsno <- length(all.gof.vars)
    for (i in seq(along = all.gof.vars)) {
        all.gof.vars[i] <- match.arg(all.gof.vars[i], c("distance", 
            "triadcensus", "espartners", "dspartners", "odegree", 
            "idegree", "degree", "model"))
    }
    GOF <- as.formula(paste("~", paste(all.gof.vars, collapse = "+")))
    if (statsno == 0) {
        stop("The gof object does not contain any statistics!\n")
    }
    n <- x$network.size
    for (statname in all.gof.vars) {
        if ("model" == statname) {
            nstats <- length(x$obs.model)
            if (min(x$pval.model[, "MC p-value"]) < 0) {
                pval.max <- max((1:nstats)[x$pval.model[1:nstats, 
                  "MC p-value"] < 1]) + 3
            }
            else {
                pval.max <- max((1:nstats)[x$obs.model[1:nstats] > 
                  0]) + 3
            }
            if (is.finite(pval.max) & pval.max < nstats) {
                model <- c(1:pval.max)
            }
            else {
                model <- c(1:nstats)
            }
            if (plotlogodds) {
                odds <- x$psim.model
                odds[!is.na(odds)] <- log(odds[!is.na(odds)]/(1 - 
                  odds[!is.na(odds)]))
                odds.obs <- x$pobs.model
                odds.obs[!is.na(odds.obs)] <- log(odds.obs[!is.na(odds.obs)]/(1 - 
                  odds.obs[!is.na(odds.obs)]))
                odds.bds <- x$bds.model
                odds.bds[!is.na(odds.bds)] <- log(odds.bds[!is.na(odds.bds)]/(1 - 
                  odds.bds[!is.na(odds.bds)]))
                mininf <- min(min(odds[!is.infinite(odds)]), 
                  min(odds.obs[!is.infinite(odds.obs)]), min(odds.bds[!is.infinite(odds.bds)]))
                maxinf <- max(max(odds[!is.infinite(odds)]), 
                  max(odds.obs[!is.infinite(odds.obs)]), max(odds.bds[!is.infinite(odds.bds)]))
                odds[is.infinite(odds) & odds > 0] <- maxinf
                odds[is.infinite(odds) & odds < 0] <- mininf
                odds.obs[is.infinite(odds.obs) & odds.obs > 0] <- maxinf
                odds.obs[is.infinite(odds.obs) & odds.obs < 0] <- mininf
                odds.bds[is.infinite(odds.bds) & odds.bds > 0] <- maxinf
                odds.bds[is.infinite(odds.bds) & odds.bds < 0] <- mininf
                out <- odds
                out.obs <- odds.obs
                out.bds <- odds.bds
                ylab <- "log-odds for the statistic"
            }
            else {
                out <- x$psim.model
                out.obs <- x$pobs.model
                out.bds <- x$bds.model
                ylab <- "statistic"
            }
            pnames <- names(out.obs)
            ymin <- min(min(out, na.rm = TRUE), min(out.obs, 
                na.rm = TRUE))
            ymax <- max(max(out, na.rm = TRUE), max(out.obs, 
                na.rm = TRUE))
            boxplot(data.frame(out[, model]), xlab = "model statistics", 
                ylab = ylab, names = pnames, cex.axis = cex.axis, 
                outline = FALSE, ylim = c(ymin, ymax), ...)
	    if (IC) {
		  points(seq(along = model), out.bds[1, model], pch = 1, 
		      cex = 0.75)
		  points(seq(along = model), out.bds[2, model], pch = 1, 
		      cex = 0.75)
		  lines(seq(along = model), out.bds[1, model], pch = 18, 
		      lty = 1, lwd = 1, col = color)
		  lines(seq(along = model), out.bds[2, model], pch = 18, 
		      lty = 1, lwd = 1, col = color)
		}
	    points(seq(along = model), out.obs[model], pch = 16, 
		cex = 0.75)
	    lines(seq(along = model), out.obs[model], lty = 1, 
		lwd = 3)
        }
        if ("degree" == statname) {
            if (min(x$pval.deg[, "MC p-value"]) < 0) {
                pval.max <- max((1:(n - 1))[x$pval.deg[1:(n - 
                  1), "MC p-value"] < 1]) + 3
            }
            else {
                pval.max <- max((1:(n - 1))[x$obs.deg[1:(n - 
                  1)] > 0]) + 3
            }
            if (is.finite(pval.max) & pval.max < n) {
                deg <- c(1:pval.max)
            }
            else {
                deg <- c(1:n)
            }
            if (plotlogodds) {
                odds <- x$psim.deg
                odds[!is.na(odds)] <- log(odds[!is.na(odds)]/(1 - 
                  odds[!is.na(odds)]))
                odds.obs <- x$pobs.deg
                odds.obs[!is.na(odds.obs)] <- log(odds.obs[!is.na(odds.obs)]/(1 - 
                  odds.obs[!is.na(odds.obs)]))
                odds.bds <- x$bds.deg
                odds.bds[!is.na(odds.bds)] <- log(odds.bds[!is.na(odds.bds)]/(1 -

                mininf <- min(min(odds[!is.infinite(odds)]),

                maxinf <- max(max(odds[!is.infinite(odds)]), 
                  max(odds.obs[!is.infinite(odds.obs)]), max(odds.bds[!is.infinite(odds.bds)]))
                odds[is.infinite(odds) & odds > 0] <- maxinf
                odds[is.infinite(odds) & odds < 0] <- mininf
                odds.obs[is.infinite(odds.obs) & odds.obs > 0] <- maxinf
                odds.obs[is.infinite(odds.obs) & odds.obs < 0] <- mininf
                odds.bds[is.infinite(odds.bds) & odds.bds > 0] <- maxinf
                odds.bds[is.infinite(odds.bds) & odds.bds < 0] <- mininf
                out <- odds
                out.obs <- odds.obs
                out.bds <- odds.bds
                ylab <- "log-odds for a node"
            }
            else {
                out <- x$psim.deg
                out.obs <- x$pobs.deg
                out.bds <- x$bds.deg
                ylab <- "proportion of nodes"
            }
            pnames <- c(deg) - 1
            ymin <- min(min(out, na.rm = TRUE), min(out.obs, 
                na.rm = TRUE))
            ymax <- max(max(out, na.rm = TRUE), max(out.obs, 
                na.rm = TRUE))
            boxplot(data.frame(out[, deg]), xlab = "degree", 
                ylab = ylab, names = pnames, cex.axis = cex.axis, 
                outline = FALSE, ylim = c(ymin, ymax), ...)
	    if (IC) {
		points(seq(along = deg), out.bds[1, deg], pch = 1, 
		    cex = 0.75)
		points(seq(along = deg), out.bds[2, deg], pch = 1, 
		    cex = 0.75)
		lines(seq(along = deg), out.bds[1, deg], pch = 18, 
		    lty = 1, lwd = 1, col = color)
		lines(seq(along = deg), out.bds[2, deg], pch = 18, 
		    lty = 1, lwd = 1, col = color)
	      }
	    points(seq(along = deg), out.obs[deg], pch = 16, 
		    cex = 0.75)
	    lines(seq(along = deg), out.obs[deg], lty = 1, lwd = 3)
        }
        if ("odegree" == statname) {
            if (min(x$pval.odeg[, "MC p-value"]) < 0) {

                odds[is.infinite(odds) & odds > 0] <- maxinf

                odds.obs[is.infinite(odds.obs) & odds.obs > 0] <- maxinf
                odds.obs[is.infinite(odds.obs) & odds.obs < 0] <- mininf
                odds.bds[is.infinite(odds.bds) & odds.bds > 0] <- maxinf

            }

            if (!plotlogodds) {

            }
            boxplot(data.frame(out[, dist]), xlab = "minimum geodesic distance", 
                ylab = ylab, names = pnames, cex.axis = cex.axis,

messages.subject: [statnet_help] PhD positions in Groningen, The Netherlands
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] PhD positions in Groningen, The Netherlands
messages.body_plain:
Dear colleagues,

as part of its annual recruitment and selection procedure for 
PhD-students, the Interuniversity Center for Social Science Theory and 
Methodology (ICS) in the Netherlands is looking for excellent candidates 
for a couple of four-year-long PhD projects on several network-related 
topics. In particular, we are looking for candidates interested in the 
following projects in statistical network analysis:

    Project "Statistical Models for Three-Way Network Data"
    Examples of three-way social processes are gossip (where two people
    choose a third person, an ?object? to talk about), informal
    mediation (where a colleague might entrust a problem with another
    colleague to a third colleague, who acts as mediator to solve the
    problem), or social cognitive maps (where actors in a dyadic network
    report their perceptions of the whole network). While in dyadic
    network data actors have two roles, as 'sender' and 'receiver', in
    triadic observations they have a third role, for instance as
    'object' (of gossip), as 'mediator' (of problems with colleagues),
    or as 'observer' (of dyadic relations). While older work
    (Krackhardt, 1987) focused on how to summarize triadic data to
    obtain a dyadic network, such data reduction implies a potentially
    severe loss of information. So far, not much work has been done to
    develop statistical models for three-way data (see Bond & Kenny,
    2002, for an exception). This project focuses on the development of
    appropriate statistical models to handle the richness of this type
    of data.

    Project "Validity of Models for Network Structure and Social
    Influence Processes"
    In the past decade, the analysis of social networks with statistical
    models has developed rapidly with the availability of new estimation
    methods, using advanced computational techniques, coupled with new
    insights in the complex structure of social network data. On the one
    hand, these are models explaining the shape of networks as such,
    i.e., the interdependencies between the network actors. On the other
    hand, there are models using networks to explain other phenomena,
    such as (change in) status, performance, or peer influence. Many new
    methods and models have been proposed, one of them being stochastic
    actor-based modeling ("SIENA"), proposed by the project initiators.
    However, there are hardly any studies comparing the different
    approaches.As a consequence, the demarcation of the conclusions that
    can reliably be drawn with the available methods remains an open
    question and guidelines for the selection of appropriate analytical
    methods are lacking. This project aims to fill these gaps.

The two projects will be supervised by Christian Steglich, Marijtje van 
Duijn, Mark Huisman, and Tom Snijders. The recruitment and selection 
procedure for our scholarships starts December 11, 2010. Applications, 
online only, should be delivered through the ICS website before January 
15, 2011. The interviews will be conducted on March 3, 4, 8 and 9, 2011.

More details, also about the other available positions, can be found via 
the website http://www.ics-graduateschool.nl/vacancies/

We very much appreciate your interest and cooperation,
Christian Steglich, Marijtje van Duijn, Mark Huisman, Tom Snijders
on behalf of Rafael Wittek,
Scientific Director ICS

On 9/27/10 9:15 PM, Michal Bojanowski wrote:
> On 09/27/2010 02:32 PM, Wincent wrote:
>> Yup, it is quite complex.
>> Yet, it is deemed to fail in Windows as the dynamic shared object is
>> *.dll rather than *.so. To solve this problem, the following lines may
>> be a possibility.
>>
>> if (.Platform$OS.type=="windows") {
>> library.dynam.unload(paste(pkg, ".dll", sep = ""),inuse)
>> } else {
>> library.dynam.unload(paste(pkg, ".so", sep = ""),inuse)
>> }
>
>
> To intrude into the discussion:
>
> Actually 'library.dynam.unload' is already platform-independent using the default settings (at least in R 2.11 ...). I believe that instead of using 'if' as above, the line 64 of
> "update_statnet.R" could be like:
>
> library.dynam.unload( pkg, system.file(package="pkg") )
>
> The file extenstion is handled by the 'file.ext' argument which has the default (".so"/ ".dll") set depending on the operating system.
>
>
> As a side note (not tested though): I have a hunch that the complicated detach/unload mechanism in 'update_statnet' is no longer needed as calling 'detach' with unload=TRUE and
> force=TRUE should detach the package and unload any DLL/SO's irrespectively whether there are other packages loaded that depend on the package being detached (which I presume was
> the source of errors to be caught by 'capture.output' inside 'really.detach').

messages.subject: [statnet_help] How much steps?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a directed 800 nodes network and not sure how to set the burnin, 
MCMCsamplesize, interval, and maxit arguments.

As far as I know about MCMC is that I have to set the burnin and 
interval arguments very large. If not, I won't simulate independant 
random samples. So I set these 2 arguments to 1e+06!

I didn't see any reasons to change the default value of the 
MCMCsamplesize argument (10000 by default). But I changed the maxit 
argument to 25 (and sometimes 30), because I saw that maxit=5 was not 
sufficient (the estimated improvment of the log-likelihood was still 
very high. At maxit=25, the LL improvment is at ~1.5).

With these settings, my models typically take weeks to be estimated. And 
you,which settings do you use?

Best regards,
Victorin

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Question for MCMCMLE Calculation Time
messages.body_plain:
This is a nice heuristic my experience in retrospect suggests would be true,
but I had never made the explicit connection. Reviewing the Robins,
Pattison, Kalish, Lusher 2007 article (pg. 188), it nevertheless says this
fairly plainly:

"Simulation studies suggest that Markov graph models that contain at least
non-zero three-star parameters tend to exhibit less near degeneracy than
those with two-stars as the highest order non-zero star parameter (Robins et
al., 2005). But the inclusion of three-star parameters often is not
sufficient to remove near degeneracy behavior in Markov graph models,
particularly when attempting to find models that reproduce the high levels
of transitivity often observed in human social structures (there is an
extended discussion in Snijders et al., in press)."

Although it might be empirically heretical to even suggest that entire
sub-classes of models are *non grata*, but might it be useful to document a
list of some of these heuristics in plain language (with appropriate
references) to guide users in building models?

On Sun, Mar 13, 2011 at 4:46 PM, David Hunter <dhunter@stat.psu.edu> wrote:

> Hi Ick Hoon.
> The reason is the presence of the 2-star term in model 1.  The presence of
> this term essentially always makes a model degenerate.
>
> Dave
>
>
>
>
>

>> I have a question for MCMCMLE calculation time.
>> Currently, I am estimating parameters with two different models.
>>
>> Model 1. The model with edge counts, k2-star, and gwesp terms.
>>
>>> form <- X ~ edges + kstar(2) + gwesp(log(2), fixed=TRUE)
>>> m1 <- ergm(formula=form, MPLEonly=TRUE)
>>> m31 <- ergm(formula=form, theta0=m1$coef, maxit=1,
>>>
>> MCMCsamplesize=50000, verb=TRUE)
>> Model 2. The model with edge count, gwdegree, and gwesp terms.
>>
>>> form <- X ~ edges + gwdegree(0.2, fixed=TRUE) + gwesp(0.2, fixed=TRUE)
>>> m1 <- ergm(formula=form, MPLEonly=TRUE)
>>> m31 <- ergm(formula=form, theta0=m1$coef, maxit=1,
>>>
>> MCMCsamplesize=50000, verb=TRUE)
>>
>> In my thought, Model 1 takes shorter time than Model 2 because the

data.mat<-as.matrix(read.table("DATA"))

messages.subject: [statnet_help] examine relationship between betweenness and vertex attributes?
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] examine relationship between betweenness and vertex attributes?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, folks -

Here is a four-part answer to this question:

1. If your goal is to test for marginal (non)association between an NLI 
(e.g., closeness) and a node-level covariate, IMHO the most 
straightforward approach is to use permutation procedures.  If you want 
a quick tutorial, you might check out the associated portion of the 
statnet workshop we gave at this year's Political Networks meeting; the 
URL is 
http://lectopia.oit.duke.edu/ilectures/ilectures.lasso?ut=1065&id=27647, 
and the discussion starts at around 48 minutes.  (Part 1 of the day's 
session is at 
http://lectopia.oit.duke.edu/ilectures/ilectures.lasso?ut=1065&id=27647, 
for those who are interested.)   As I note in response to a question 
from the audience, generalizing this to the multivariate case is 
possible, but one runs into complications that make the approach less 
attractive.  For the simple, bivariate case, however, my sense is that 
permutation tests are often a good starting point.

2. For more complex, parametric versions of the covariate/NLI question, 
the natural approach is to construct a statistic based on an interaction 
of the covariate with the NLI, and employ an ERG model.  (This is 
equivalent to what nodecov does, with the NLI here being degree.)  We 
have talked for years about adding equivalent terms for other centrality 
scores, but I am not sure if anything is implemented at present -- there 
are no special theoretical issues, but the computation can be painful. 
(I regularly hassle my CS colleagues for the algorithmic developments we 
need to make changescore calculation fast for indices like betweenness, 
but am assured that this is a non-trivial research problem.  :-))  I 
spoke with Mark about putting something crude together a few months ago, 
but am not sure if he's had time to make progress on it -- it's clear 
that this would be a very interesting set of terms to be able to 
include.  Having said that, we don't know how stable models built from 
those terms would be, so this might turn out to be harder in practice 
than it seems.

3. A fact little remembered today is that the ERG were introduced in 
part to act as non-trivial null models against which to test for complex 
structural biases.  (See the discussion in Holland and Leinhardt, JASA, 
1981.)  Using the same scheme they suggest, it is possible to conduct 
Monte Carlo tests of association with more complex structure than the 
simple permutation tests by (1) positing a baseline ERGM, (2) fitting it 
to your data, (3) simulating draws from the fitted model, and (4) 
examining the quantiles of the observed NLI/covariate interaction in the 
distribution of equivalent interactions generated by the simulated data. 
  Some properties of these tests are described in the above paper.  In 
practice, there are more ways for this to go wrong than the permutation 
test, and I would tend to favor the latter when feasible.  One case I 
_can_ think of in which the ERG-based test would be preferable would be 
when you want to test for an association of your covariate with a given 
NLI score, controlling for some other interaction of the same covariate 
with the target network (e.g., homophily).  A null of independence does 
not help you here, and a model-based test could prove efficacious.

4. Another, naive alternative would be to try to treat your problem in a 
standard regression framework, and try to patch things up in some 
fashion.  For some NLIs (e.g., degree) on large networks, we may suspect 
that there is relatively little dependence between observations, and the 
first-order properties of OLS are fairly robust in any case.  This is 
essentially the rationale behind network regression (where one typically 
pairs standard least squares estimators of parameters with multivariate 
QAP tests to assess significance), and it can work quite well.  Then 
again, the "patch and pray" approach can also fail, and you may or may 
not be able to tell when the answers you are getting partake heavily of 
fantasy.  I tend to encourage the use of more principled methods, where 
feasible.

That's my take on it, anyway.  My illustrious colleagues may or may not 
agree.

-Carter

PS. For the adventurous, an interesting technique might be to apply the 
permutation model (a la netperm) where the left-hand matrices consist 
entirely of diagonal matrices with individual NLI scores from the 
observed graph, and the right-hand matrices of consist entirely of 
diagonal matrices with individual covariate scores.  This would be a 
"vector" or "linear" version of the permutation model, analogous to the 
LAP versus QAP distinction in Hubert's terminology.  (It may be simpler 
to think of as a generalized location system model using only 
association terms based on node covariates as object features and NLI 
scores as location features, and with the support limited to 1:1 
assignments -- in fact, that's how I would implement it.  See the 
generalized location systems paper in Sociological Methodology (Butts, 
2007) for some idea of what I am prattling on about.)  I think it's safe 
to say that this application of that model family is not much 
explored...meaning that I'm not sure if anyone has tried it.  If someone 
has experimented with this application, I would be interesting in 
hearing about it.

dnolin wrote:
> I am also curious about this problem. More generally, is there a specific
> method that's preferred when regressing node-level network measures against
> other node attributes (or vice versa)? It would seem that non-independence
> of cases would violate OLS assumptions and some adjustment ought to be
> made. For example, are there permutation method similar to QAP whereby you
> could permute the vector of the dependent variable to see how frequently a
> correlation of the observed size arises?
> 
> Thanks,
> Dave
> 
> 
> On Sun, 5 Sep 2010 11:16:54 +0800, Wincent <ronggui.huang@gmail.com> wrote:
>> Dear all, I use betweenness in sna to get the betweenness score, and
>> would like to see what vertex attributes may influence or "determine"
>> the betweenness centrality.
>> I think OLS regression can get the point estimates but the p-value
>> would be problematic.
>> I wonder if there is existing function(s) for such purpose?
>> Thank you very much in advance.
>

messages.subject: [statnet_help] How much steps?
messages.body_plain:
On 2/2/2011 8:13 AM, Victorin Luisier wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> I have a directed 800 nodes network and not sure how to set the burnin,
> MCMCsamplesize, interval, and maxit arguments.
>
> As far as I know about MCMC is that I have to set the burnin and
> interval arguments very large. If not, I won't simulate independant
> random samples. So I set these 2 arguments to 1e+06!
>
> I didn't see any reasons to change the default value of the
> MCMCsamplesize argument (10000 by default). But I changed the maxit
> argument to 25 (and sometimes 30), because I saw that maxit=5 was not
> sufficient (the estimated improvment of the log-likelihood was still
> very high. At maxit=25, the LL improvment is at ~1.5).
>
> With these settings, my models typically take weeks to be estimated. And
> you,which settings do you use?

When I am working with networks in the size range or larger, I usually 
start out at around MCMCsamplesize = 50,000 or 100,000; interval = 1000; 
maxit = 5 or so.  I usually don't bother changing the burnin.  Of course 
every network has different estimation needs, but that's where I usually 
start, and it often works well (as determined from the mcmc diagnostics, 
and by simulating from the fitted model to see if the sufficient 
statistics hold in the simulations).  Sometimes I lower the steplength 
(under control.ergm) and bump up the maxit in parallel, and that takes 
more time.

I just fit an example (for the upcoming Sunbelt tutorial) that has 1,461 
nodes, 974 edges, and a model involving various dyad-independent terms 
plus GWESP.  I used MCMCsamplesize=50k, interval=1000, maxit=5, and the 
default burnin.  It took about 7 minutes on my PC laptop.

A larger interval does get you more independent samples, but as you say, 
it takes a very very long time to run.  The reason why we made the TNT 
proposal the default instead of a simple dyad toggle is that it rapidly 
speeds up mixing, and can get you much closer to independent samples in 
a small interval, especially for sparse networks. So given what you'd 
said I'd drop my interval down a lot, and see what happens.

Good luck!
Steve







>
> Best regards,
> Victorin
>


--

messages.body_plain:
Dear statnet users,

I have a question about whether ERGMs are appropriate to answer the question of whether similarity on a stable attribute can predict network change.  I know SIENA was developed for this purpose; however, for the purposes of a paper I am combining a longitudinal analysis with another analysis that is necessarily cross-sectional.  Because I am writing for a non-network audience I thought it would be more straightforward to use ERGMs for all of the analyses.

Here is the question: is it acceptable to estimate an ERGM that predicts the time 2 network and includes the following predictors: (1) attribute similarity at time 1, (2) the network at time 1 (as a dyadic covariate), and (3) structural effects for the time 2 network?  Would this approach tell me whether similarity on the attribute drives network change (assuming the attribute itself is constant over time)?

Here is the specific syntax:
model6 <- ergm(net2 ~ edges + edgecov(net1) + edgecov(activities) +
    nodematch("educ") + nodematch("sex") + nodematch("race") + nodematch("grade") +
    gwdegree(.25, fixed=TRUE) + gwdsp(.25, fixed=TRUE) + gwesp(.25, fixed=TRUE) )

Is this type of an ERGM approach justifiable in this situation?  Are there other tradeoffs between the two approaches that should be considered?  I have seen this approach used in at least one published piece, but I haven't seen a statistician's take on it.

I appreciate any insight on this issue.

Thanks,
David

Assistant Professor
School of Social and Family Dynamics
Arizona State University
www.public.asu.edu/~schaef/
http://ssfd.clas.asu.edu/cluster

messages.subject: [statnet_help] hamming distance as network statistic
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bernadette.  You're mostly correct:  If one were to include  
"hamming distance from the observed network" as a statistic in an  
ERGM, then the minimum possible value of the statistic (zero) is  
achieved by the observed network.   According to well-established  
exponential family theory, whenever an observed statistic lies on the  
boundary of the convex hull of possible statistics, no maximum  
likelihood estimator exists.  Stated differently, in this case the MLE  
would essentially be negative infinity.

So _if_ one's goal is to obtain a maximum likelihood estimator of ergm  
parameters, then including "hamming distance from the observed  
network" is never a good idea.  However, there are other conceivable  
contexts (e.g., using descriptive statistics to classify networks)  
where it could make sense as a statistic.

I hope this helps.

Dave



On Sep 29, 2010, at 12:24 PM, Wijk, B.C.M. van, (Bernadette) wrote:

> Dear statnet users,
>
> Im trying to understand the use of the Hamming distance as a network  
> statistic (unweighted, and with x as the observed model). To me it  
> seems that optimizing the hamming distance will always (independent  
> of what network you're looking at) result in a network identical to  
> the observed network, as it can also be seen as a goodness of fit  
> measure. In that case, the hamming distance would become zero and  
> the corresponding network parameter goes to infinity (?). Is this  
> the right way of thinking? Would it make sense to include the  
> hamming distance to the observed network as a statistic in the model  
> at all? If so, when and when not?
>
> Any help would be appreciated!
>
> Kind regards,
> Bernadette van Wijk

Le 02/02/2011 06:14 PM, Steven Goodreau a ?crit :
> On 2/2/2011 8:13 AM, Victorin Luisier wrote:
>> Hi all,
>>
>> I have a directed 800 nodes network and not sure how to set the burnin,
>> MCMCsamplesize, interval, and maxit arguments.
>>
>> As far as I know about MCMC is that I have to set the burnin and
>> interval arguments very large. If not, I won't simulate independant
>> random samples. So I set these 2 arguments to 1e+06!
>>
>> I didn't see any reasons to change the default value of the
>> MCMCsamplesize argument (10000 by default). But I changed the maxit
>> argument to 25 (and sometimes 30), because I saw that maxit=5 was not
>> sufficient (the estimated improvment of the log-likelihood was still
>> very high. At maxit=25, the LL improvment is at ~1.5).
>>
>> With these settings, my models typically take weeks to be estimated. And
>> you,which settings do you use?
>
> When I am working with networks in the size range or larger, I usually
> start out at around MCMCsamplesize = 50,000 or 100,000; interval = 1000;
> maxit = 5 or so. I usually don't bother changing the burnin. Of course
> every network has different estimation needs, but that's where I usually
> start, and it often works well (as determined from the mcmc diagnostics,
> and by simulating from the fitted model to see if the sufficient
> statistics hold in the simulations). Sometimes I lower the steplength
> (under control.ergm) and bump up the maxit in parallel, and that takes
> more time.
>
> I just fit an example (for the upcoming Sunbelt tutorial) that has 1,461
> nodes, 974 edges, and a model involving various dyad-independent terms
> plus GWESP. I used MCMCsamplesize=50k, interval=1000, maxit=5, and the
> default burnin. It took about 7 minutes on my PC laptop.
>
> A larger interval does get you more independent samples, but as you say,
> it takes a very very long time to run. The reason why we made the TNT
> proposal the default instead of a simple dyad toggle is that it rapidly
> speeds up mixing, and can get you much closer to independent samples in
> a small interval, especially for sparse networks. So given what you'd
> said I'd drop my interval down a lot, and see what happens.
>
> Good luck!
> Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] missing edges
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nicola,

"ergm" interprets the value of NA for an edge as meaning that information about the presence or absence of that edge is missing.

When an ERGM model is fit, ergm() uses the methods developed by the "statnet" team to find the MLE of the parameters given the observed data. This is detailed in:

"Modeling social networks from sampled data"
Mark S. Handcock and Krista J. Gile
Annals of Applied Statistics, Volume 4, Number 1 (2010), 5-25.
<http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.aoas/1273584445>

In particular, these estimates and models can be interpreted in the same way as those without missing or sampled data.

It is worthwhile noting that "latentnet" also computes estimates that adjust for missing data.

I hope this helps.

Mark

> releases) when in the network there are some NA edges?

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Full CPU performance with statnet on R
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Full CPU performance with statnet on R
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Martin -

Your performance will depend on how dense your network is, how much 
memory you have, etc.  If you are seeing low CPU utilization, you 
probably have a memory issue.  Using the leanest available 
representations can help (e.g., sna edgelists if you don't need 
metadata), but very large graphs (like other large things) are expensive.

In like vein, you will find that certain calculations are intrinsically 
costly for large graphs (unless they are _extremely_ sparse, and 
sometimes even then).  Things like betweenness/closeness calculation, 
clique enumeration, and cycle enumeration, geodesics, etc. are not 
cheap,* however classic they may be.  (kcores and degree are examples of 
cheap computations, however, and if those are running slow then you 
should check your memory utilization.)

If performance is an issue, you might ask yourself why you are trying to 
calculate something like betweenness on this large graph, and whether 
you actually need the entire structure to answer your question. 
Whenever one deals with very large data sets (as is common in fields 
such as, say, GIS), it pays to think about efficiency when approaching 
one's research problem.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

*Although fast _approximate_ algorithms are sometimes available for 
these quantities.  This is an area of active research.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Re: ergm crashes
messages.body_plain:
Hi Iasonas.  The issue (discovered by looking at the code you sent  
separately) is that when you read in a vector using the "read.table"  
command, it becomes an R object of type data.frame.  These objects can  
be a bit tricky to work with.

In your case, you had code like this:

Gender <-  read.table("Gender.csv",    <other stuff clipped out>)
mGender <- as.vector(Gender)
mGender[mGender=="1"]="Boy"
mGender[mGender=="2"]="Girl"
ng <-network(mat,directed=FALSE)
set.vertex.attribute(ng,"Gender",mGender)

The problem with this is that the "as.vector" function does not  
actually turn a data.frame object into a vector.  One way around this  
is to convert the data.frame into a matrix first, then a vector using
mGender <- as.vector(as.matrix(Gender))

But this is a bit clunky.  A slightly more efficient (if somewhat  
ugly) way is to simply grab the first column in the data.frame object,  
which can be done in a couple of different ways that are equivalent  
for data frames:

mGender <- Gender[[1]]
mGender <- Gender[,1]

In other words, your new code would look something like this:
Gender <-  read.table("Gender.csv",    <other stuff clipped out>)
mGender <- Gender[[1]]
mGender[mGender=="1"]="Boy"
mGender[mGender=="2"]="Girl"
ng <-network(mat,directed=FALSE)
set.vertex.attribute(ng,"Gender",mGender)

Of course, you'd do the same for all of your vertex attributes.

Hope this helps,
Dave

-----Original Message-----
From: Victorin Luisier [mailto:Victorin.Luisier@unige.ch] 
Sent: Wednesday, February 02, 2011 9:24 AM
To: statnet_help@u.washington.edu
Subject: Re: [statnet_help] Goodness of fit

Hi,

I think that that these grey lines represent the 95% confidence 
intervals of the log-odds contributions for different statistics of 
interest. These CI are estimated on the simulated samples.

So, for example, if I take the graph you gave us and am interested in 
the "degree 0" statistic, I would say that:

1) your observed sample contribute to the log-odds for about -1
2) 95% of the simulated samples (during the gof()) contributes approx. 
between -2.1 and -1.1 to the log-odds.

Technically speaking, your question should be documented in the 
"plot.gofobject" and "gof.ergm" documentation pages but is not. However, 
the code of the "plot.gofobject" function indicates that the grey lines 
are drawn using some parts of your gof object (<m.gof>):

<m.gof>$bds.model
<m.gof>$bds.ideg
<m.gof>$bds.espart
<m.gof>$bds.triadcensus
<m.gof>$bds.dist
<m.gof>$bds.odeg
<m.gof>$bds.dspart

Hope that helps!
Victorin

P.S: Really sorry for my faulty english, but I come from the french 
speaking area of Switzerland :-)

messages.subject: [statnet_help] gwdsp error
messages.body_plain:
I'm running a bipartite network with 1316 actors against 735 events. The
majority of these are isolated dyads, but there are a few components (no
giant) in the network. This is running on an Amazon EC2 instance with 17gb
of memory, so hopefully memory is not the limiting issue.

I want to use the gwdsp to capture higher-order "clustering" -- the tendency
for the same people to work together on many of the same projects. I specify
a model:

model<-ergm(bp~edges+gwb1degree(.1)+gwb2degree(.1)+b1degree(1)+b2degree(1)+gwdsp(.1))

This will estimate up to Iteration 3 before reporting out:

Error in svd(H) : infinite or missing values in 'x'

I don't know what matrix is being passed to the singular value
decomposition. Would this error suggest that there's something amiss in my
data, my use of the gwdsp term, or the presence or lack of other parameters?

If my interpretations (below) are wildly wacky, please let me know. I hope
not, because without the gwdsp term, the MCMC.diagnostics and GoF have all
been nice.

Edges = density
gwb1degree = tendency for people to work on many projects
gwb1degree = tendency for projects to have many people
b1degree(1) = tendency for there to be people with exactly one project
(control on degree distribution)
b2degree(1) = tendency for there to be projects with exactly one person
(control on degree distribution)
gwdsp = tendency for many people to share several projects (bipartite
clustering)

Thanks!

Brian

--

Ph.D. Student - Media, Technology, & Society
School of Communication, Northwestern University

messages.subject: [statnet_help] 2-Mode Clusters
messages.body_plain:
In case this helps, here is a list of the currently documented 2-mode  
model terms, all of which are available in statnet:

b1concurrent(by=NULL)
b1degree(d, by=NULL)
b1factor(attrname, base=1)
b1star(k, attrname=NULL)
b1starmix(k, attrname, base=NULL, diff=TRUE)
b1twostar(b1attrname, b2attrname, base=NULL)
...and also "b2" versions of all of the above.  (In this context, b1  
refers to mode 1 of a two-mode network, and b2 refers to mode 2.)

See help("ergm-terms") for explanations of what these do.  Also, we  
hope that others might add more terms using the methods described in http://www.stat.psu.edu/~dhunter/papers/ergmuserterms.pdf

Finally, there are a few additional such terms that we hope to add to  
the ergm package in the near future.

Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ergm.userterms package and document
messages.body_plain:
Hi all.  For the few of you who might be waiting for the document  
describing how to write your own terms to use with the statnet  
packages, this is just a quick update:  The article is essentially  
ready to go, but it's become clear that there are a couple of  
substantial changes that should be made to the ergm package prior to  
the article's release.  The reason for the changes is semantics:  We  
want to make sure that we're using terminology consistently throughout  
the internal workings of the ergm package now that we're writing about  
how to add to those internal workings using ergm.userterms.

So, we're sorry for this latest delay, but the article and new  
ergm.userterms package should be available soon.

Happy new year to everyone!
Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Re: Attribute lookup/match and import to network object
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Re: Attribute lookup/match and import to network object
messages.body_plain:
I worked it out and thought I'd share with the rest of the group if only to
help other newbies. If I botched something terribly or missed the boat
entirely on an easier way to do this, now would be a great time to tell me!
:-)
*
### Reading in directed edgelist to network object. The "network" and "ergm"
libraries don't like networks with non-sequential node names, so if you have
unique IDs, we have to turn them into sequential/ordinal IDs ###
**# Create edgelist matrix named "el" from CSV*
el<-read.csv(file.choose(),header=F)
*# "c" creates a single list of column 1 stacked on top of column 2,
"unique" removes duplicates from this single column, "sort" orders this
column of unique IDs, and "code" is an object where this list of original
IDs can be mapped to sequential/ordinal values*
code<-sort(unique(c(el[,1],el[,2])))
*# Match each of the IDs in the first column of the edgelist to their new
sequential/ordinal number in the "code" mapping list*
el[,1]<-match(el[,1],code)
*# Match each of the IDs in the second column of the edgelist to their new
sequential/ordinal number in the "code" mapping list*
el[,2]<-match(el[,2],code)
*# Import this directed edgelist into a network object.*
n<-network(el,matrix.type="edgelist",directed=T)
*# Rename the vertices back to their original names*
network.vertex.names(n)<-code
*# Re-organize the "code" mapping list to be used for importing attribute
data*
code_frame <- data.frame(code)
*# Give this new object a column name*
colnames(code_frame) <- c('real_id')

*### Reading in nodelist of attributes to network object ###
# Create nodelist matrix named "nl" from CSV assuming you don't have
column/header names*
nl<-read.csv(file.choose(),header=F)
*# Create column/header names*
colnames(nl)<- c('real_id','attribute1')
*# Check to make sure column names are the same*
head(nl)
head(code_frame)
*# Join/merge the "code_frame" mapping object with the "nl" nodelist by
shared "real_id"s*
attributes<-merge(code_frame,nl,by.x='real_id',by.y='real_id')
*# check to make sure attribute vector and code_frame vector are the same
size*
tail(attributes)
tail(code_frame)
*# import each attribute from a column in "attribute" matrix into the
network object "n" starting with the second column which is the first non-id
attribute*
set.vertex.attribute(n, "attribute1", attributes[,2], v=1:network.size(n))
*# check to make sure imported attributes are present in network object*
list.vertex.attribute(n)
*# check to make sure attributes properly imported to network object*
get.vertex.attribute(n, 'attribute1')

Hi everyone.  The package called ergm.userterms is now up on CRAN.   
This package is designed to help folks who are interested in extending  
the capabilities of statnet by creating their own terms that can be  
used in an ERGM formula.  There is a paper that comes with the package  
that explains how this works and also gives a bit of a glimpse under  
the hood of the ergm package.

The paper is in the inst/doc directory of the source code, or you can  
download it separately at http://www.stat.psu.edu/~dhunter/papers/ergmuserterms.pdf

Best,
Dave

PS.  If anyone still at Sunbelt is interested in chatting about this,  
try to track down Steve Goodreau, who's still there.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] degeneracy with missing dyads
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

When I try to estimate model for an undirected network with a large number of
dyads set as missing (NA), it returns me degenerate models.

In what I am working on, I need to set as NA the 20% of the dyads. I tried
with Lazega's Lawyers and Kapfter's tailor shop data.

These problems there were not until the version ergm 2.2-5, I think that
it is not a bug but a problem of the algorithm with low density network.

Attached find a toy example:




library(statnet)

###################

getDyad<-function(net){
n<-network.size(net)
pair<-NULL
if(is.directed(net)){
	for(i in 1:(n-1))for(j in (i+1):n) pair<-rbind(pair,c(i,j),c(j,i))
}
else{
	for(i in 1:(n-1))for(j in (i+1):n) pair<-rbind(pair,c(i,j))
}
return(pair)
}

###################################

#### low density

m <- matrix(rbinom(30^2,1,.07),30,30)
diag(m) <- 0
g <- network(m, directed=FALSE)
summary(g)
plot(g)



ERGMa1<-ergm(g~edges
#+gwdegree(.5,fixed=TRUE)
+gwesp(.5,fixed=TRUE)
#+gwdsp(0.25,fixed=TRUE)
,burnin=100000,interval=5000, MCMCsamplesize=10000,maxit=5)




summary(ERGMa1)
plot(ERGMa1)



coppie<-getDyad(g)

m<-dim(coppie)[1]

c<-sample(1:m,40)

prova<-g

prova[coppie[c,]]<-NA


ERGMa2<-ergm(prova~edges
#+gwdegree(.5,fixed=TRUE)
+gwesp(1,fixed=TRUE)
#+gwdsp(0.25,fixed=TRUE)
,burnin=100000,interval=5000, MCMCsamplesize=10000,maxit=5)


summary(ERGMa2)
plot(ERGMa2)


######### large density

m <- matrix(rbinom(30^2,1,.3),30,30)
diag(m) <- 0
g2 <- network(m, directed=FALSE)
summary(g2)
plot(g2)




ERGMb1<-ergm(g2~edges
#+gwdegree(.5,fixed=TRUE)
+gwesp(1,fixed=TRUE)
#+gwdsp(0.25,fixed=TRUE)
,burnin=100000,interval=5000, MCMCsamplesize=5000)


summary(ERGMb1)
plot(ERGMb1)


prova2<-g2

prova2[coppie[c,]]<-NA


ERGMb2<-ergm(prova2~edges
#+gwdegree(.5,fixed=TRUE)
+gwesp(1,fixed=TRUE)
#+gwdsp(0.25,fixed=TRUE)
,burnin=100000,interval=5000, MCMCsamplesize=5000)


summary(ERGMb2)
plot(ERGMb2)





--

On 7 September 2010 13:34, Carter T. Butts <buttsc@uci.edu> wrote:
> Hi, folks -
>
> Here is a four-part answer to this question:
>
> 1. If your goal is to test for marginal (non)association between an NLI
> (e.g., closeness) and a node-level covariate, IMHO the most straightforward
> approach is to use permutation procedures. ?If you want a quick tutorial,
> you might check out the associated portion of the statnet workshop we gave
> at this year's Political Networks meeting; the URL is
> http://lectopia.oit.duke.edu/ilectures/ilectures.lasso?ut=1065&id=27647, and
> the discussion starts at around 48 minutes. ?(Part 1 of the day's session is
> at http://lectopia.oit.duke.edu/ilectures/ilectures.lasso?ut=1065&id=27647,
> for those who are interested.) ? As I note in response to a question from
> the audience, generalizing this to the multivariate case is possible, but
> one runs into complications that make the approach less attractive. ?For the
> simple, bivariate case, however, my sense is that permutation tests are
> often a good starting point.
>
> 2. For more complex, parametric versions of the covariate/NLI question, the
> natural approach is to construct a statistic based on an interaction of the
> covariate with the NLI, and employ an ERG model. ?(This is equivalent to
> what nodecov does, with the NLI here being degree.) ?We have talked for
> years about adding equivalent terms for other centrality scores, but I am
> not sure if anything is implemented at present -- there are no special
> theoretical issues, but the computation can be painful. (I regularly hassle
> my CS colleagues for the algorithmic developments we need to make
> changescore calculation fast for indices like betweenness, but am assured
> that this is a non-trivial research problem. ?:-)) ?I spoke with Mark about
> putting something crude together a few months ago, but am not sure if he's
> had time to make progress on it -- it's clear that this would be a very
> interesting set of terms to be able to include. ?Having said that, we don't
> know how stable models built from those terms would be, so this might turn
> out to be harder in practice than it seems.
>
> 3. A fact little remembered today is that the ERG were introduced in part to
> act as non-trivial null models against which to test for complex structural
> biases. ?(See the discussion in Holland and Leinhardt, JASA, 1981.) ?Using
> the same scheme they suggest, it is possible to conduct Monte Carlo tests of
> association with more complex structure than the simple permutation tests by
> (1) positing a baseline ERGM, (2) fitting it to your data, (3) simulating
> draws from the fitted model, and (4) examining the quantiles of the observed
> NLI/covariate interaction in the distribution of equivalent interactions
> generated by the simulated data. ?Some properties of these tests are
> described in the above paper. ?In practice, there are more ways for this to
> go wrong than the permutation test, and I would tend to favor the latter
> when feasible. ?One case I _can_ think of in which the ERG-based test would
> be preferable would be when you want to test for an association of your
> covariate with a given NLI score, controlling for some other interaction of
> the same covariate with the target network (e.g., homophily). ?A null of
> independence does not help you here, and a model-based test could prove
> efficacious.
>
> 4. Another, naive alternative would be to try to treat your problem in a
> standard regression framework, and try to patch things up in some fashion.
> ?For some NLIs (e.g., degree) on large networks, we may suspect that there
> is relatively little dependence between observations, and the first-order
> properties of OLS are fairly robust in any case. ?This is essentially the
> rationale behind network regression (where one typically pairs standard
> least squares estimators of parameters with multivariate QAP tests to assess
> significance), and it can work quite well. ?Then again, the "patch and pray"
> approach can also fail, and you may or may not be able to tell when the
> answers you are getting partake heavily of fantasy. ?I tend to encourage the
> use of more principled methods, where feasible.
>
> That's my take on it, anyway. ?My illustrious colleagues may or may not
> agree.
>
> -Carter
>
> PS. For the adventurous, an interesting technique might be to apply the
> permutation model (a la netperm) where the left-hand matrices consist
> entirely of diagonal matrices with individual NLI scores from the observed
> graph, and the right-hand matrices of consist entirely of diagonal matrices
> with individual covariate scores. ?This would be a "vector" or "linear"
> version of the permutation model, analogous to the LAP versus QAP
> distinction in Hubert's terminology. ?(It may be simpler to think of as a
> generalized location system model using only association terms based on node
> covariates as object features and NLI scores as location features, and with
> the support limited to 1:1 assignments -- in fact, that's how I would
> implement it. ?See the generalized location systems paper in Sociological
> Methodology (Butts, 2007) for some idea of what I am prattling on about.) ?I
> think it's safe to say that this application of that model family is not
> much explored...meaning that I'm not sure if anyone has tried it. ?If
> someone has experimented with this application, I would be interesting in
> hearing about it.
>

messages.subject: [statnet_help] interaction effects and absdiff term
messages.body_plain:
Hi Markus.

One approach is to code up a whole matrix of "interaction terms" and  
then enter this into the model as a dyadcov term.  However, depending  
on what you wish to put in the "...", there may be a simpler way:  If  
you are only using model terms that result in independence of the  
edges, then the ergm function is really just doing logistic  
regression.  Thus, you can use the ergmMPLE function to give you the  
response and predictors that may be fed into a logistic regression,  
and then you can use the usual interaction-term capability of the glm  
function.  See help(ergmMPLE) for details on this function.

Hope this helps.

Dave

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am working with an undirected network of approximately 54 nodes and have a question about specifying the alpha parameter for the GWD, GWDSP, and GWESP terms. There appear to be two ways to do this --- specify it yourself and select fixed=TRUE for an ERGM or put in some value and select fixed=FALSE for a CEF. The CEF strategy then approximates the appropriate alpha parameter for you according to Hunter 2006 and others. I'm a little confused by this second strategy after having run the same syntax with two different values as my starting guess for alpha and fixed=FALSE and getting two vastly different results even using the same seed to start.

I guess I'm mostly curious about the relationship between the alpha you specify and the alpha that is selected when you run the model with the fixed=FALSE option. It seems to me they must be related somehow since, in the model where the alpha was 0.5 to begin, the three estimated alphas were all near 0.5, while when I began with an alpha of 1.0 the three estimated alphas were close to 1.0.

Other model results were also pretty different with these two alpha values which would seem to indicate that the alpha is important, at least in this case.

The Snijders et al. paper from 2006 used the fixed=TRUE and tested several alpha values as another possible strategy --- any thoughts on this as opposed to using fixed=FALSE?

Thanks in advance for any insight. I'm happy to send along more of my syntax if that would be helpful.

Jenine

Thanks Vic.  I also forgot to copy this list.

ergm version 2.2-7 is now on CRAN, and it is not much different from  
2.2-6 except that it fixes a couple of bugs.  In particular, one  
potentially important bug, which has been in the code since version  
2.2-3, can reverse the direction of ties in simulated directed  
networks.  Thus, I'd strongly recommend updating to 2.2-7 for anyone  
who depends on directed network simulations (including MCMC-based  
maximum likelihood estimation).


Here, in a nutshell, is the old bug in action:
# using version 2.2-6 now to try to simulate a network with many  
outdegree-3 nodes but few indegree-3 nodes
# by putting a huge positive parameter on odegree(3) and a huge  
negative parameter on idegree(3):
library(ergm)
data(sampson)
mynet <- simulate(samplike ~ odegree(3) + idegree(3), theta0=c(+100,  
-100))
summary(mynet~odegree(3) + idegree(3))
odegree3 idegree3
        0       11

# Now for the same example using version 2.2-7:
library(ergm)
data(sampson)
mynet <- simulate(samplike ~ odegree(3) + idegree(3), theta0=c(+100,  
-100))
summary(mynet~odegree(3) + idegree(3))
odegree3 idegree3
       15        0



Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] A toy example for STATNET
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Hamid -

On 10/23/2010 11:54 PM, Hamid Ghofrani wrote:
> Dear All,
> My question is whether there is any asymptotic assumptions for ERGM?

Yes.  (A less general question might yield a less generic answer.)

> Why isn't there any example for small size graphs?

I believe you will find some such examples in the ergm man pages.

> I was trying to create a toy example, an undirected network of 10 nodes
> and created 3 triangles 123, 456, 789 ( according to node labels).
> model <- ergm(m ~
> triangle,control=control.ergm(check.degeneracy=T),maxit=50)
> Every model ended up being degenerate.
> I needed to use a small network so that I would be able to calculate the
> exact value for normalizing constant.
> The dependence structure is very simple, It has only 3 triangles and
> nothing else so What would be the cause for degeneracy?
> Is there any minimum number of nodes we need to have in STATNET package?

The pure triangle model is the textbook case of a degenerate model -- 
see Strauss's 1986 SIAM Review paper for an analysis.  Heuristically, it 
is easy to see why this is so.  Let t be the triangle count in a simple 
graph of order N, and let theta be the associated parameter.  For 
theta>0, the complete graph (K_N) is clearly of maximum probability 
(since graph probability is proportional to exp(theta*t(G)), and this 
has a unique maximum at G=K_N).  Consider the probability ratio for K_N 
versus some other graph, G', under this model.  If G' is not complete, 
it is missing at least one edge; thus, t(K_N)-t(G')>=N-2.  (This is 
because you will break N-2 triangles by removing an edge from a complete 
graph on N vertices.)  Recalling that normalizing factors cancel here, 
the ratio of graph probabilities is

Pr(G')/Pr(K_N) =  exp(theta*t(G'))/exp(theta*t(K_N))
                =  exp(theta*(t(G')-t(K_N)))
                <= exp(-theta*(N-2))

This falls exponentially fast in N -- the probability of observing any 
other graph versus the complete graph rapidly becomes very small.  This 
alone is not a proof of degeneracy, but it should suggest the nature of 
the phenomenon.  From a more pragmatic viewpoint, let us consider an 
MCMC seeking to simulate draws from this model (via a Metropolis 
algorithm with single edge updates), and ask what happens when the 
Markov chain arrives at K_N.  From the above, the probability of 
accepting any proposal (all of which involve a single edge removal) will 
be exp(-theta*(N-2)); the expected waiting time for a move away from K_N 
will then be the reciprocal of this (since the waiting time here is 
geometrically distributed), or exp(theta*(N-2)).  For the chain to move 
freely away from the complete graph, we need this to be reasonably 
small...say, exp(theta*(N-2))<=k, where k is on the order of 10 to 100. 
  That suggests that theta needs to be very small, e.g.

         N=10    N=100   N=1000
k=10    0.288   0.023   0.002
k=100   0.576   0.047   0.005

in order for the chain to mix.  Increasing theta beyond this point will 
lead the waiting times for exit from the complete graph to increase 
exponentially fast (thus effectively killing the MCMC).  Even if N=10, 
that can still ruin your life -- increase your theta from 0.288 to 1, 
and you are now waiting about 3000 iterations for a single exit. 
Increase it further from 1 to 2, and you are waiting for almost 9 
million iterations.  Further increases are clearly contraindicated for 
those with finite life spans.

I've written this somewhat extensive response because I encounter this 
question frequently, and hope that this answer may be of use to others. 
  (Also, the topic is very interesting.)  The general object lessons to 
be drawn include the following:

1. The triangle model is unsafe at any speed (per Strauss).

2. The degenerate models we tend to encounter have bad behavior that 
grows exponentially worse in the parameters.  Thus, even a small graph 
will not always save you -- there is a high-entropy region in which 
things will work, but the system freezes very quickly once one exits 
that region.  (See Handcock's 2003 chapter for a very nice example of 
how small and irregular those regions can be.)  The fact that this 
region itself often shrinks exponentially fast in N just adds additional 
excitement to the problem.

3. One can often gain an intuition for the extent of the degeneracy 
problem by examining the conditional probabilities of edge 
additions/deletions near the mode (or modes, in some cases).  This is 
not perfect, but has the virtue of mapping directly onto MCMC behavior.


One final cautionary: as my colleagues have often noted, degeneracy is 
not simply a problem of the MCMC (although the former tends to wreak 
havoc with the latter, and the latter is often used heuristically to 
identify the former).  The triangle model is still going to concentrate 
its mass on the complete graph when theta>0, and no simulation method is 
going to change that.  Finding simulation methods that let us get better 
performance for near-degenerate models is an active research area, and 
likewise there are ways that existing MCMC schemes can perform poorly on 
otherwise tolerable models (see Snijders 2002 JoSS paper for some of 
these issues); when things really don't seem to work, however, one 
should entertain the possibility that one's model may be too close to 
the degenerate limit to be salvaged by any degree of computational 
wizardry.  Techniques such as heuristic analysis of probability ratios 
(as performed above) can be helpful in determining whether this is in 
fact the case.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Full CPU performance with statnet on R
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Full CPU performance with statnet on R
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Martin -

Martin Klaus wrote:
> Dear Carter,
> 
> thank you for your fast answer. I totaly understand what your saying and 
> I know that the betweenness and closeness are very calculation intensive 
> measures and e.g. degee ist easy and on that way very fast. But I 
> expected my new PC, which by the way has 24 GB of memory, should be fast 
> than e.g a java compiled program like ORA. But ORA was 5 times faster 
> than R and it used the full 99.9% of the CPU for the whole time of 
> calculation. That is why I thought it would be possible to tell R to use 
> more of the possible CPU AND memory ;)
> But the way I understand you it is not possible to adjust theses things 
> in the statnet packge or in R at any other point?!
> Thanks again for your help,

OK, from what has been said, it sounds like your issue may be that you 
are looking at _total_ CPU utilization, not utilization of a specific 
CPU.  Parallel processing is gradually coming into play within R, and 
you can employ it at user-level via libraries like snow and multicore. 
For the most part, however, R is still engineered around a 
single-processor environment.  The simplest way to exploit 
multi-processor capabilities for a problem like yours would be to use a 
package like multicore, and set your various analysis tasks running in 
parallel.  Even if each task is serially executed, the set of tasks will 
be completed more quickly.  (That's one of the tactics I sometimes use. 
  In fact, there are advantages of this strategy in a clustered 
environment, because it's easier to control how many processors I'm 
eating (and how much the other users will resent my presence).)  As 
parallel processing support stabilizes, I think you'll see it used more 
extensively within R generally (and in statnet -- see the help for 
control.ergm for one currently implemented example).

As far as ORA, my understanding is that the important parts are all 
written in C++ (unless they have rewritten it since, which is always 
possible).  (Fun bit of trivia: when I was in Kathleen's lab at CMU, I 
wrote a collection of C routines called "netstat" that ultimately became 
part of the first ORA backend.  All of that code was rewritten long ago, 
of course, and I doubt that ORA today retains any influence from the old 
netstat base.)  If the CMU folks have done their homework (and they 
usually do), ORA _should_ outperform R-based tools on many tasks, since 
it's a custom-built piece of compiled code, while R libraries have large 
chunks of comparatively slow interpreted code.  That's the price you pay 
for ease of use, flexibility, ability to interoperate with other 
libraries, etc.  I'd guess that much of that factor of 5 is a multiple 
core issue, but even so I would not be surprised to find that many tasks 
run somewhat faster in ORA (or any dedicated, standalone application) 
than in R/statnet.  If they didn't, the number of situations in which 
such standalone tools would be at all preferable to general-purpose 
platforms like R would be very circumscribed.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

network simulated from a negative value (test2) has a ton of nodes with 
zero incoming ties but also a considerable number of hubs; whereas the 
network simulated from a positive value (test1) has a much more balanced 
distribution.

any guidance on this would be much appreciated! thanks as always,

-kevin

messages.subject: [statnet_help] BIC interpretation in Latentnet
messages.body_plain:
Dear Statnet users,

I am running latent space models using the package latentnet to quantify spatial networks based on animal movement. I am interested in comparing among models using model selection criteria. Based on my reading of the documentation of latentnet, it is unclear whether BIC is scaled such that 'smaller is better' or 'larger is better'. One of the examples in the latentnet manual suggests that smaller is better (on the summary.ergmm page), but on another page (the ergmm page), under BIC it cites Handcock et al. (2005). In that article (and Handcock et al. 2007), they select the model with the largest BIC. Could someone please clarify if smaller or larger BIC values are better in this package?

Also, I have been unable to find any documentation regarding the component BIC values that are provided (e.g., for latent spacing/clustering, random effects, etc.). I assume that the clustering BIC component comes from Hancock et al. (2007), but it is not clear about how this applies when G=1 and there is only latent space dimensions (and no clustering specified). Should these be used for model selection, or the overall BIC?

Thanks,

Rob Fletcher

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGMs and co-occurrence networks
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Is there anything special I should take care of when fitting an ERGM to 
a co-occurrence network of political actors (via their common ideas)?

There is no model for weighted networks, so I will have to dichotomize 
edge weights at an arbitrary threshold value, right?

There are also many cliques due to the very nature of a co-occurrence 
network. I suppose I could (1) either model this by including GWDSP and 
GWESP terms (because there are essentially subgroups where every dyad 
has multiple shared partners), or I could (2) argue that the choices of 
ideas in the original two-mode network are actually independent (except 
for covariates), so including network terms for the co-occurrence 
network would be a misspecification - in the latter case, I should 
rather model the co-occurrence network in terms of nodemixing (e.g. same 
actor type, same source of funding etc.). But which makes more sense? 
Intuitively, I would follow the second option.

Thanks for your thoughts about this,

Philip

PS: Btw, I collected the data using my Java software Discourse Network 
Analyzer. I have also written an R package called rDNA which can import 
these networks directly into R. More details on my homepage.

-- 
Philip Leifeld
Max Planck Institute for Research on Collective Goods
http://www.philipleifeld.de

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Question for MCMCMLE Calculation Time
messages.body_plain:
Hello, everybody.
I have a question for MCMCMLE calculation time.
Currently, I am estimating parameters with two different models.

 Model 1. The model with edge counts, k2-star, and gwesp terms.
    > form <- X ~ edges + kstar(2) + gwesp(log(2), fixed=TRUE)
    > m1 <- ergm(formula=form, MPLEonly=TRUE)
    > m31 <- ergm(formula=form, theta0=m1$coef, maxit=1,
MCMCsamplesize=50000, verb=TRUE)
 Model 2. The model with edge count, gwdegree, and gwesp terms.
    > form <- X ~ edges + gwdegree(0.2, fixed=TRUE) + gwesp(0.2, fixed=TRUE)
    > m1 <- ergm(formula=form, MPLEonly=TRUE)
    > m31 <- ergm(formula=form, theta0=m1$coef, maxit=1,
MCMCsamplesize=50000, verb=TRUE)

In my thought, Model 1 takes shorter time than Model 2 because the
calculation of statistics in Model 1 are simpler than those in Model 2.
In actual, Model 1 takes much longer time to find their parameter
estimates. Also, Model 1 has model degeneracy problem.
Why the calculation for Model 1 takes much longer time?
More specifically, is there any algorithms excluding a complete network
or an empty network from MCMC samples? (This is my guess.)
Thank you very much.

-- 
Sincerely Yours,

Jin, Ick Hoon
Ph.D. Candidate
Department of Statisitcs
Texas A&M University

To intrude into the discussion:

Actually 'library.dynam.unload' is already platform-independent using 
the default settings (at least in R 2.11 ...). I believe that instead of 
using 'if' as above, the line 64 of "update_statnet.R" could be like:

library.dynam.unload( pkg, system.file(package="pkg") )

The file extenstion is handled by the 'file.ext' argument which has the 
default (".so"/ ".dll") set depending on the operating system.


As a side note (not tested though): I have a hunch that the complicated 
detach/unload mechanism in 'update_statnet' is no longer needed as 
calling 'detach' with unload=TRUE and force=TRUE should detach the 
package and unload any DLL/SO's irrespectively whether there are other 
packages loaded that depend on the package being detached (which I 
presume was the source of errors to be caught by 'capture.output' inside 
'really.detach').

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Statnet and Parallel/Distributed Computing
messages.body_plain:
Patrick,

The development version of "statnet" has been running in parallel for over five years. It uses the "snow" package (e.g. PVM or MPI) to parallelize the MCMC runs. It is stable and 
very effective but requires that the user have access to PVM or MPI on their local cluster (or a multi-processor machine like a Mac with MPI builtin). Because of this we have not 
released it in the public version as yet. We run it on a number of 128 or 200 CPU linux machines bound together and gets essentially linear speedups.

If you have expertise in getting R to run on NVIDIA CUDA GPUs or a Hadoop cluster then it should be easy to extend what we have done to these platforms. It is mostly the R side of 
it it that needs work. The hoops on the "statnet" side has been developed.

I hope this helps?

Cheers,

Mark

messages.subject: [statnet_help] 'thresh' option in gplot
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Philip.  gplot takes its edge values from the input matrix (e.g., an 
adjacency or sna edgelist matrix) that you supply.  If you supply data 
in some other form (e.g., a network object), then gplot will internally 
coerce the data into edgelist form, taking all edges to have a default 
value of 1 (as if the data had been an adjacency matrix, although that 
is not how it is internally represented).

If you want to use thresholding with gplot and a valued network object, 
you will want to coerce it into matrix form first.  See, e.g., 
as.edgelist.sna, or as.sociomatrix (and specifically the "attrname" 
argument).

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Difference Between Edgelist and Sociomatrix
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sam.  It's hard to diagnose without having an example that will  
replicate the same problem, but here's one possibility illustrated by  
a small test case:

 > e = matrix(1:2,5,2,byrow=T)
 > e
      [,1] [,2]
[1,]    1    2
[2,]    1    2
[3,]    1    2
[4,]    1    2
[5,]    1    2

So this edgelist has 5 "edges" even though they're not all unique.  If  
we now create a network from this edgelist, the network will have 5  
edges even though the derived sociomatrix will have only one:

 > network.edgecount(network(e))
[1] 5
 > sum(as.sociomatrix(network(e)))
[1] 1

This is not a bug, by the way; there are certainly cases in which it's  
conceivable that edges could be multiple, and the network package code  
tries to be as flexible as possible.

One way to test whether this is what's causing your behavior is to  
find the number of unique rows in your edgelist as in:
 > NROW(unique(e))
[1] 1

So if you type
NROW(unique(dat[,c('names','thread')])
and get 244, that's almost certainly the explanation.

Hope this helps,
Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] community detection
messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Mark. I've started reading your paper on the latent approach
to clustering and it really seems to me that it is extremely
interesting. However, I'd like to ask you two (perhaps naive)
questions:

In this approach, covariates are link-dependent. But you say that
covariates might be vector valued. Does this mean that you may also
consider actor-dependent covariates?

Is the latent space approach applicable to 2-mode networks? Actually,
as I have already told you on another occasion, I've got a number of
data which form an incomplete 3-mode graph: vertices in the first mode
are connected both to vertices in a second and a third mode (but there
are no direct associations among vertices in the second and the third
mode). Would the latent space clustering method be applicable in such
networks? If yes, any existing references?

Best regards,

--Moses


On Mon, Dec 20, 2010 at 2:26 PM, Mark S. Handcock <handcock@ucla.edu> wrote:
> Hi Moses,
>
> This is an interesting question, one that is best answered by another: What
> is the scientific purpose of the community detection?
>
> If the purpose is to find a categorization of the nodes into relatively
> homogeneous groups then any of the commonly used algorithms can achieve
> this. They can produce useful descriptives.
>
> If the purpose is to detect underlying categorizations in the presence of
> stochastic variation, to test if such categorizations are real, to look at
> other categorizations that have support from the data, etc, then it is
> scientifically better to consider model-based approaches. This also allows
> to define communities adjusted for nodal and dyadic covariates, and to
> adjust for node specific heterogeneity, etc. We have taken this latter
> approach in "statnet".
>
> In particular, I would point you toward "latentnet". It has a latent
> position cluster model that embeds the nodes within a latent social space
> and estimates clusters/communities/groups via a stochastic model. It
> incorporates the statistical uncertainty, especially uncertainty in the
> community identifications. It is a very visual model. One reference is
> <http://www.jstatsoft.org/v24/i05/paper> and a later paper in Social
> Networks.
>
> There are other model-based approaches, but this is a start and well
> supported and developed in "statnet".
>
> I hope this helps.
>
> Cheers,
>
> Mark
>
> ----------------------------------------------------

hi guido and dave,

i've used both pnet and statnet for ERG modeling, and am pretty sure 
that GWESP corresponds to AT-T (transitive closure), while you are right 
that GWDSP corresponds to A2P-T (2-paths) (though, as dave notes, you 
should also check out his article for exactly how the two relate to each 
other... but they will both get the same job done). i do not believe 
that a higher-order term for cyclic closure (or "activity closure" or 
"popularity closure") currently exists in statnet. hope this helps!

-kevin
