messages.subject: [statnet_help] hamming distance as network statistic
messages.body_plain:
Just to expand on Dave's remarks...

> On Sep 29, 2010, at 12:24 PM, Wijk, B.C.M. van, (Bernadette) wrote:
>
>> Dear statnet users,
>>
>> Im trying to understand the use of the Hamming distance as a network
>> statistic (unweighted, and with x as the observed model). To me it
>> seems that optimizing the hamming distance will always (independent of
>> what network you're looking at) result in a network identical to the
>> observed network, as it can also be seen as a goodness of fit measure.
>> In that case, the hamming distance would become zero and the
>> corresponding network parameter goes to infinity (?). Is this the
>> right way of thinking? Would it make sense to include the hamming
>> distance to the observed network as a statistic in the model at all?
>> If so, when and when not?
>>

Typically, one would not use the dependent network as "x" in an 
estimation context (although one might in a _simulation_ context, e.g. 
to generate perturbed data for robustness testing).  The "x" in the 
hamming term is usually some other network (e.g., the same system at an 
earlier time point, or another relation to which we believe that the 
modeled network may be related); its typical usage is thus closely 
analogous to edgecov.  As Dave noted, Hamming distance is also used in 
other contexts as a tool for graph comparison (see, e.g., hdist in sna), 
but that's a somewhat different matter.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I think that that these grey lines represent the 95% confidence 
intervals of the log-odds contributions for different statistics of 
interest. These CI are estimated on the simulated samples.

So, for example, if I take the graph you gave us and am interested in 
the "degree 0" statistic, I would say that:

1) your observed sample contribute to the log-odds for about -1
2) 95% of the simulated samples (during the gof()) contributes approx. 
between -2.1 and -1.1 to the log-odds.

Technically speaking, your question should be documented in the 
"plot.gofobject" and "gof.ergm" documentation pages but is not. However, 
the code of the "plot.gofobject" function indicates that the grey lines 
are drawn using some parts of your gof object (<m.gof>):

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Estimating alpha with "large" network & running out of RAM with MCMC
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Estimating alpha with "large" network & running out of RAM with MCMC
messages.body_plain:
In a nutshell, networks this size are simply way too large to try to  
fit curved EF parameters currently.  This is due to the memory  
requirements (gwdsp with fixed=FALSE requires a huge amount of memory,  
unlike when fixed=TRUE).  Try several different values of alpha in the  
range (say) 0 to 1, then look at the estimated likelihoods and go with  
the value that gives the largest estimated likelihood.  If the  
estimated likelihoods are all pretty close, it probably doesn't matter  
much which alpha you choose since the likelihood estimates themselves  
are subject to MCMC error.

Dave

Standard box plots are not CI (see for ex.:

source("newfunction.R")

Victorin

Hi Elena.  I'm not sure whether this helps, but if you want to capture  
"same race and same education level" then you might consider instead  
defining a new nodal variable, called "raceeduc" or something, that  
merely pastes the race and educ3 variables together.  Then you could  
use nodematch on that new variable.  I believe this variable could  
even be used in combination with nodematch("sex") and  
nodematch("educ3") without collinearity issues (in that case, the  
variable would give an interaction effect for the two main effects).

Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] error installing previous versions of ergm using tar.gz files ~ ideas or zip files available?
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] error installing previous versions of ergm using tar.gz files ~ ideas or zip files available?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all.  Since this is likely to be helpful to others running windows,  
I'll post a quick update:  Jenine was able to get this to work but it  
involved jumping through a few hoops.  Jumping through these hoops  
will allow windows users to install R packages from their source code  
(which is different from downloading the pre-compiled binary versions  
and which is sometimes a very useful thing to be able to do):

(1) Visit http://www.murdoch-sutherland.com/Rtools/ and download and  
install the latest version of Rtools for windows.
(2) open a terminal (DOS) window.  Don't start R yet.
(3) If you have source code for any version of an R package (such as  
ergm_2.0-4.tar.gz in the email below), type the following after cd'ing  
to the directory containing the source code:

Rcmd INSTALL ergm_2.0-4.tar.gz

(4) Start R
(5) Type library(ergm) or library(statnet) or whatever the name of  
your package is.

There are still a few things that can go wrong here -- for instance,  
if you don't have a version of the network package installed, then  
you'll get an error when trying to install ergm -- but if you run into  
trouble, sometimes the following web page can be helpful:
http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/R-admin.html#The-Windows-toolset

Hope this helps,
Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGMs to estimate network change
messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

Your question provoked a bit of discussion behind the curtain, so you 
may get more than one response.  In theory, yes, you should be able to do 
this.  My own guess is that estimation will be pretty unstable unless you 
have a lot of change from t1 to t2.

With respect to the interpretation of the paramters, I'm not sure this 
would be the right way to identify how nodal attributes drive network 
change.  That's because change has 2 components: formation and dissolution 
of ties.  There may be different dynamics driving the two factors, and 
they would be confounded in the approach you're taking.

best,
mm

messages.subject: [statnet_help] statnet Tutorial for ICWSM or CSCW?
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] statnet Tutorial for ICWSM or CSCW?
messages.body_plain:
I enjoyed meeting several of the statnet developers and users at Sunbelt
last week. I apologize if this is an inappropriate forum to broach the
topic, but I wanted to assess the extent to which the statnet and/or
scholarly ERGM community had any interest in "evangelizing" to a
computer+information+social science audience. In my experience attending
conferences like CHI and CSCW, the scholars at the intersection of these
communities desperately need exposure to more than descriptive SNA. If other
more experienced hands are interested in spreading the "good word" with me
as an ambassador, I'd suggest there are two excellent upcoming opportunities
to submit tutorials or workshops.

First, the International Weblog and Social Media conference (aka ICWSM) is
an archival conference sponsored by AAAI and it has an upcoming deadline for
tutorials (due 2/18). The conference itself will be in Barcelona, Spain from
July 17-21 with the pre-conference tutorial presumably occurring on the 16
or 17th depending on how they're counting. http://www.icwsm.org/2011/cft.php

Second, the Computer Supported Cooperative Work conference (aka CSCW) is
also an archival conference sponsored by ACM and has a July 8 deadline for
workshops. The conference will be in Seattle, Washington from February
11-15, 2012. http://www.cscw2012.org/participation/workshops.php

I believe that a proposal that highlighted the analytic benefits of a
generative approach to SNA coupled with examples which highlight the ability
to interrogate social processes which undergird the structures observed in
the blogosphere, Wikipedia, Twitter, etc. would be really powerful and
expose you to an otherwise statistically and theoretically competent
scholarly audience.

-- 
Brian C. Keegan
Ph.D. Student - Media, Technology, & Society
School of Communication, Northwestern University

Science of Networks in Communities, Laboratory for Collaborative Technology

messages.subject: [statnet_help] direct assignment of network object
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Wincent -

On 10/12/2010 07:20 AM, Wincent wrote:
> It seems that direct assignment behaves NOT in the same manner as
> 'network.copy'.  Is it a bug?

Odd -- this was working in earlier R versions, so it seems to be a 
relatively recent break.  Looks like an issue with R's deferred 
evaluation mechanism.  In particular, note that if you modify g or newg 
(e.g., by adding edges) prior to the delete.vertices call, you do not 
get this effect.  I expect that R delays the network.copy operation 
(which, BTW, is what the assignment operator does) too long, and 
delete.vertices thus gets a pointer to the original object, rather than 
to the copy (that has not yet been made).  That would be my initial 
guess, at least.

I'll put in a patch on the latest version (now on CRAN!), but in the 
interim, here is a workaround.  After you generate the new copy, you can 
force it to be evaluated by a command like

newg[1,1]<-0

or even

g[1,1]<-0

This will have no obvious effect, but will force R to evaluate the 
assignment (and hence network.copy), breaking the tie between the 
objects.  Likely, there are many other commands that would also work, 
but this is an easy option.  It works fine on my system, but let me know 
if it doesn't work for you....

Thanks!

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Interpretation of valued edgecov coefficients
messages.body_plain:
Hi Philip.  In brief,

(1) Yes.
(2) No.

The statistic really is the sum of all covariate values for all edges  
appearing in the network.  However, the important thing to keep in  
mind for interpretation is how this statistic CHANGES with the  
addition or removal of a single edge.  In this case, the statistic  
changes by the covariate value for just that pair of nodes.  When this  
happens, the log-odds of the entire network changes by 0.38 times this  
covariate value.  In your two questions, if the covariate increases by  
one, then the log-odds of a particular edge existing (holding  
everything else in the network fixed) increase by an extra 0.38, which  
multiplies the odds by 1.46.

Best wishes,
Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Homophily with absdiff
messages.body_plain:
Dear Richard,

Your interpretation is exactly right:  Since the absolute difference  
of size decreases as the sizes become more homophilous, a negative  
absdiff coefficient points to stronger homophily (after correcting for  
everything else in the model) and vice-versa.

Best wishes,

messages.subject: [statnet_help] community detection
messages.body_plain:
Hi Moses,

This is an interesting question, one that is best answered by another: What is the scientific purpose of the community detection?

If the purpose is to find a categorization of the nodes into relatively homogeneous groups then any of the commonly used algorithms can achieve this. They can produce useful 
descriptives.

If the purpose is to detect underlying categorizations in the presence of stochastic variation, to test if such categorizations are real, to look at other categorizations that have 
support from the data, etc, then it is scientifically better to consider model-based approaches. This also allows to define communities adjusted for nodal and dyadic covariates, 
and to adjust for node specific heterogeneity, etc. We have taken this latter approach in "statnet".

In particular, I would point you toward "latentnet". It has a latent position cluster model that embeds the nodes within a latent social space and estimates 
clusters/communities/groups via a stochastic model. It incorporates the statistical uncertainty, especially uncertainty in the community identifications. It is a very visual model. 
One reference is <http://www.jstatsoft.org/v24/i05/paper> and a later paper in Social Networks.

There are other model-based approaches, but this is a start and well supported and developed in "statnet".

I hope this helps.

Cheers,

Mark

messages.subject: [statnet_help] network v1.6 released
messages.body_plain:
Greetings, all.  This is a quick note to let you know that network v1.6 
is now on CRAN.  This is a minor bugfix release, but resolves two 
annoying issues: the plot.network bug in which edge colors failed if 
specified by a single character string that was not in reference to an 
edge attribute, and the "spooky action at a distance" bug in which 
changing a network object could sometimes modify another object from 
which it had been copied.*

Thanks as always to those who submitted fixes or bug reports -- props 
are given in the ChangeLog.

Enjoy,

-Carter

* The latter is due to what I impertinently regard as a flaw in R's lazy 
evaluation system, coupled with a ban on overloading certain operators 
that were used to avoid the problem in older versions of R.  We now use 
a different workaround.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ergm question
messages.body_plain:
Hello Jorge.  One of the things Carter said reminded me of something:   
In contrasting the "holistic" and "elementwise" conceptions as he  
explains them below, it's important to remember that every  
holistically-defined model leads to a corresponding set of full  
conditionals (the elementwise model), but the converse is not true!   
In other words, one cannot necessarily define a (holistic) probability  
distribution on networks merely by specifying a full set of  
conditional distributions of each edge given the rest of the network.   
I point this out because I *think* it's at some level another reason  
that the usual dependent / independent variable interpretation is not  
applicable to the ERGM situation.

There is some further discussion of the dependent / independent  
question and a comparison with standard generalized linear models in  
Section 3 of http://www.stat.psu.edu/~dhunter/papers/ergmuserterms.pdf

Best,
Dave




On May 2, 2011, at 9:37 PM, Carter T. Butts wrote:

> Hi, Jorge -
>
> Your question raises some important issues that are too deep to  
> address well in email.  But I will take a stab at some of them....
>
> On 05/02/2011 10:08 AM, Jorge M Rocha wrote:
>> From what I understand, the modeling framework of an ERGM treats the
>> observed network as the _dependent variable_ and the specified
>> structural configurations and covariate information about nodes/ 
>> edges as
>> _independent variables_ whose presence/absence increases the
>> log-likelihood for the model.
>
> I think it is important to make some comment on this conceptual  
> issue, because it lies at the core of one's thinking about the  
> modeling process.  (In so doing I will speak ex cathedra -- I trust  
> that my colleagues will not be shy in administering correctives,  
> should they find me to be in error.)  In a standard ERGM without  
> covariate effects, there are no independent variables (in a  
> regression-like sense).  The model is one large stochastic system,  
> and is treated as fully endogenous.  (Exogenous effects come about  
> from the use of covariates, such as vertex attributes.  Of course,  
> these can also be endogenized, but that's a broader model class.)   
> More to the point, the act of writing down an ERGM is the act of  
> writing down a model for the joint probability distribution of a  
> graph (i.e., the system state).  The exponential family form  
> provides the language in which we express that model; the content  
> and the interpretation must come from elsewhere.
>
> Within this context, the role of statistics based on structural  
> configurations is to parametrize the joint distribution of the edge  
> structure.  There are several formally equivalent ways to understand  
> this.  One natural one is to view the parameter associated with a  
> given structural statistic as measuring the tendency of the  
> expectation of that statistic to be higher or lower than what would  
> be observed if the parameter in question were zero (equivalently, if  
> it were not in the model).  From this point of view, all ERGM  
> parameters reflect different sorts of structural "biases" or  
> "deviations" from the behavior of the uniform Bernoulli graph (i.e.,  
> the homogeneous Bernoulli graph in which every edge occurs with  
> equal probability).
>
> Note that this is a "holistic" view of the network as a jointly  
> interacting system -- if you are familiar with the Lagrangian or  
> Hamiltonian formulations of classical mechanics (in which the  
> behavior of a classical system is described by reference to a  
> potential function), this may prove a useful analogy.  In any event,  
> it's very different from the "elementwise" view of networks that  
> many folks are used to.
>
> For the latter, it can be helpful to think in terms of the full  
> conditionals of the model -- the probability of a given edge being  
> present, given the rest of the structure.  This is a "local/ 
> elementwise" view, perhaps loosely analogous to the way that  
> classical mechanics is taught to beginners (with "forces" acting on  
> particles, the conditional behavior of which is defined in terms of  
> the other particle states). This comports better with the intuition  
> of most social scientists, but IMHO has many underappreciated  
> pitfalls.  Chief among these is the fact that one can easily forget  
> that the elements of the system are indeed interacting, and the  
> conditional behavior of one variable is only meaningful within the  
> context of the rest of the network.  (For an example of where this  
> intuition led the field astray, one need only look at the rise and  
> fall of pseudo-likelihood techniques.)  One can also easily confuse  
> conditional edge probabilities with propensities of _individuals_ to  
> create edges (e.g., in a choice context), with which they are _not_  
> always synonymous.  I am thus less sanguine about the "local" view  
> of ERGMs than some of my colleagues, although there is no question  
> that this perspective _can_ be very helpful.
>
> I want to stress that, properly understood, the holistic and  
> elementwise views of the ERGM are both correct -- they are two  
> equivalent ways of describing the same thing.  Nor are these the  
> only ways in which the formalism can be validly interpreted.  (For  
> instance, one can also understand ERGMs in terms of the equilibrium  
> behavior of certain types of Markov chains, an interpretation that  
> has value in dynamic applications.)  But what all valid  
> interpretations of the ERGM framework have in common is that they  
> recognize that one is modeling a system of components, and those  
> components can potentially interact with one another.  As such, my  
> sense is that regression-based thinking can be as much a hindrance  
> as a help when learning about ERGMs, at least for most social  
> scientists.  (Those whose familiarity with statistical exponential  
> families allows them to understand ERGMs within the broader context  
> of "regression-like" models are exempted, but I daresay that this is  
> not standard training for most social scientists.)  That said, I  
> often teach it that way, because the initial approachability of  
> ERGMs as "logistic network regression with independence relaxations"  
> is higher than "potential functions on graphs" for my students.  YMMV.
>
> For an example of the use of the "local" view of ERGMs for model  
> parametrization, I suggest the Goodreau et al. 2009 _Demography_  
> paper.  For a different, "semi-local" view based on dependence among  
> edges, one can find many good examples in the work of Pattison and  
> Robins; their 2002 _Sociological Methodology_ article comes to  
> mind.  (And, of course, there is the classic Frank and Strauss  
> _JASA_ paper, among others.)  The "holistic" view per se is less  
> well-explored, although there are many precursors in structuralist  
> theory.  (The Harary wing of structural balance, for instance,  
> operates entirely from a holistic standpoint.  This is also where I  
> insert my obligatory plug for Bruce Mayhew.)  Mark Handcock's work  
> on degeneracy (see, e.g., his 2003 chapter) has in my opinion very  
> deep substantive implications from the holistic side, and there are  
> some other recent technical contributions (e.g., a recent arXiv  
> paper by Chatterjee and Diaconis) that are likewise promising.  One  
> could accumulate many more examples, of course.
>
>> In other words, what we want to achieve
>> in these models is to gain a better understanding of the types of
>> processes that might have gone into generating a network similar to  
>> the
>> observed one;
>
> That is one use of the framework, and certainly an important one.
>
>> hypotheses are about this or that configuration or
>> node/edge attribute and their effect on the pattern of social
>> interactions represented in the network.
>
> This is where we must be careful: a configuration does not "have" an  
> effect on the network.  One could say, however, that we hypothesize  
> that our process of interest will result in networks in which  
> certain configurations are over or underrepresented.
>
>> If so, how would I go about
>> testing hypotheses concerning the effects of social interactions on
>> nodal attributes (I?m particularly thinking of different types of
>> opinions individuals might tend to have based on their interactions)?
>
> That depends on whether the attributes affect the network.  If the  
> network structure is not affected by the attributes in question  
> (e.g., because the former evolves over much longer time scales than  
> the latter), then one need not model the network at all: one can  
> condition on the network, and model the attributes (or, if one just  
> wants to test a marginal hypothesis, employ an even simpler method  
> such as a permutation test).
>
> If, on the time scale of interest, the network and the attributes  
> both coevolve, then the ERGM language is not expressive enough: you  
> need a joint attribute/network model.  Such extensions do exist,  
> although my sense is that it is difficult to identify such models  
> without longitudinal data.
>
>>
>> What I?ve done so far is kind of arguing backwards (or at least  
>> that is
>> how it feels to me ?maybe because I?m coming from a traditional
>> linear/logit regression background, and probably part of my problem  
>> is
>> thinking in terms of DV and IV).  If the coefficients are significant
>> for some node covariate of my interest in the ERGM estimation, then  
>> I?ve
>> been interpreting this as evidence that it is not unreasonable to  
>> argue
>> that the pattern of social interactions influences the type of  
>> opinion
>> individuals have (I know that if I had longitudinal data this issue  
>> of
>> reverse causality would not be so much of an issue, but so far all I
>> have is cross-sectional data).  How wrong am I on this (the
>> backward-arguing)?
>
> There may be some settings in which this could give you the right  
> answer, but I would discourage it unless you can prove that you are  
> in one of those settings.  If you are dealing with an attribute and  
> a network that are jointly endogenous, then conditioning on the  
> latter and not the former is not going to do what you want.  If you  
> just want to establish marginal association (e.g., those who are in  
> certain positions tend to have certain kinds of opinions), I would  
> lean towards a permutation test or similar procedure.  If you really  
> want to pull things apart, estimate parameters, test more complex  
> hypotheses, etc., my opinion is that you should look for a joint  
> attribute/network model.  (We don't have one in statnet right now,  
> but RSiena or pnet might.)
>
>>
>> Finally, part of my worry is that I?ll be sending the research to a
>> consumer behavior/marketing journal where the familiarity with social
>> network stuff ?let alone ERGM?s?is limited.  Any suggestions on how  
>> to
>> best explain these issues to a non-specialized audience?
>
> Well, my _personal_ advice in your case would be to look closely at  
> your problem, and try to figure out how much of it you can address  
> without using complex network models -- it's going to be much easier  
> to explain, say, permutation or CUG tests to such a readership than  
> ERGMs.  If you really must model the system as a whole, first  
> determine whether you can reasonably approximate one portion (the  
> network or the attribute) as being fixed relative to the other.   
> (Some basic knowledge of your case is important here: do you have  
> access to ethnographic, observational, or other information that  
> might help you evaluate the plausibility of a one-way effect?)  If  
> you _can_ approximate one portion as fixed, model accordingly (e.g.,  
> if the network is fixed, you may want something like a network  
> autocorrelation model, while fixed attributes suggest an ERGM).  If  
> you are stuck with having to model both the network and individual  
> attributes jointly, you have my sympathy -- this is an exciting area  
> of technical research, which generally implies a painful experience  
> for the practitioner.  Getting your hands on a reasonable cross- 
> sectional network/attribute model is then a must, as is learning to  
> use it properly (bearing in mind that, if the model is new, its  
> creators may have only limited experience in that regard).
>
> This email has become both long and polemical, but these are  
> important and frequently encountered questions.  Perhaps these  
> comments will prove helpful to you, and to others here who are  
> struggling with the same issues.
>
> Good luck!
>
> -Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] homemade ergm terms
messages.body_plain:
Forgive me if I'm demonstrating my ignorance of any of the ergm package,
Kevin's request, or bipartite networks generally, but since when does ergm
(the package) support directed bipartite networks? I ask not out of pique,
but as a methodological matter since it obviously changes the types of
questions which can be asked. I would be very interested in seeing other
papers that expand on such an approach.

Second (and again I defer to others' expertise), it always struck me that
modeling sexual interaction networks as bipartite was a complicating rather
than simplifying assumption relative to modeling the network as unipartite
with attributes (wholly apart from the heteronormative implications). I
trust there is an underlying statistical rationale, but perhaps someone
could hold my hand and elaborate for me why a bipartite approach would be
superior to a unipartite with attributes approach which had null male-male,
female-female interactions?

Thanks and apologies for hijacking the thread in advance...

Brian

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ergm question
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have a conceptual question that is probably somewhat na?ve regarding the
analytic logic behind ERGM?s (I?ve been using statnet and its suite of
tools).  If someone in the community could point me in the right direction
literature wise, I would appreciate it.  Now let me try to state my
question/doubt as briefly and clearly as I can:

>From what I understand, the modeling framework of an ERGM treats the
observed network as the dependent variable and the specified structural
configurations and covariate information about nodes/edges as independent
variables whose presence/absence increases the log-likelihood for the model.
In other words, what we want to achieve in these models is to gain a better
understanding of the types of processes that might have gone into generating
a network similar to the observed one; hypotheses are about this or that
configuration or node/edge attribute and their effect on the pattern of
social interactions represented in the network. If so, how would I go about
testing hypotheses concerning the effects of social interactions on nodal
attributes (I?m particularly thinking of different types of opinions
individuals might tend to have based on their interactions)?   

What I?ve done so far is kind of arguing backwards (or at least that is how
it feels to me ?maybe because I?m coming from a traditional linear/logit
regression background, and probably part of my problem is thinking in terms
of DV and IV).  If the coefficients are significant for some node covariate
of my interest in the ERGM estimation, then I?ve been interpreting this as
evidence that it is not unreasonable to argue that the pattern of social
interactions influences the type of opinion individuals have (I know that if
I had longitudinal data this issue of reverse causality would not be so much
of an issue, but so far all I have is cross-sectional data).  How wrong am I
on this (the backward-arguing)?

Finally, part of my worry is that I?ll be sending the research to a consumer
behavior/marketing journal where the familiarity with social network stuff
?let alone ERGM?s?is limited.  Any suggestions on how to best explain these
issues to a non-specialized audience?

In advance, thanks,

 

Jorge M Rocha

EGADE Business School

 

Description: firma smaller

messages.body_plain:
Hello users:

I have some curious results using GWESP and GWDSP is some ERGMs and I'm hoping for some help with interpretation.

My network is one-mode, non-directed data, but it was generated from two-mode data.  The original data is an accounting of individuals in clubs, and the one-mode projection shows individual's joint memberships in an NxN affiliation matrix.  To do the ERGM we dichotomize the data using an zero threshold. In our modeling we have included GWESP and/or GWDSP terms.  At first I was thinking of these a a test of triadic closure, but now I'm not so sure.  In some models the coefficients for these terms are negative. This seems very odd.  If the one-mode project artificially introduces some triadic closure, how could this term be negative?  Is this an indication that the specification is bunk? Or should I interpret these terms as something other than triadic closure?

Thanks!

-Jennifer Victor

>
> i see what you are saying about dyads either being reciprocal or not- but it seems to me that (even with cross-sectional data) one should be able to get at this difference- in a sense by comparing how many male -->  female ties are returned with how many female -->  male ties are returned. if virtually all of the asymmetric ties in a network are male -->  female, for instance- and there are virtually no asymmetric female -->  male ties- wouldn't this suggest that men are more likely to respond to women than women are to men? thus, i was trying to get at this with the transpose/edge covariate effect (we can ignore the additional income complication for the moment).
>
> as it turns out, however, i DO have a timestamp for each tie- and so the network i'm using is actually a collapsed longitudinal network. given this information, i would love to hear any thoughts you might have on how to go about using this in order to disentangle the type of gender*reciprocity interaction i hope to get at :).

>>> possible dyad. to find the answer to my question, my thought is that i

>>> network, and drop all ties from women to men (i.e. keep only ties from men
>>> to women); 2) take the transpose of this network; and 3) code this

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Michal -

On 05/04/2011 05:50 AM, Micha? Bojanowski wrote:
> 1. I recall Carter's talk on Zurich Workshop in 2008 (available online
> here http://videolectures.net/cvss08_butts_mrwsd/) talking about a
> connection between ERGMs and potential games. Have this connection
> been explored in more detail? I'll be excited to read something about
> it.

Yes, although most of the details are sitting in one of those "almost 
complete" papers that has been in the hopper for a while.  (A somewhat 
more developed version was presented at ASA in '09.  Let no one say that 
I publish in excessive haste.)  This reminds me of the need to push that 
forward....

>
> 2. I also recall a "qualitative" passage in Snijders et al (special
> issue of Social Networks, 2010) paper on SIENA models (which do have a
> choice-theoretic foundation). They write that cross-sectional ERGMs
> coincide with SIENA (would have the same parameter estimates), if the
> modeled process is in dynamic equilibrium. Does this have anything to
> do with:
>
>> (For instance, one can also understand ERGMs in terms of the equilibrium
>> behavior of certain types of Markov chains, an interpretation that
>> has value in dynamic applications.)

Yes, it does.  But there seem to be some subtle issues involved in when 
this interpretation is justifiable -- in some cases, one cannot uniquely 
recover utilities from parameter estimates (and, in others, there is no 
obvious way to obtain an analytical expression relating action 
propensities and equilibrium distributions at all!).  The potential game 
formalism I employ provides a sufficient condition for this to work, 
although it can be restrictive.

> BTW, I heard some rumors, corroborated with incomplete references on
> some people's webpages, of an ERGM book coming out soon (i.e. 2011).
> Does people here happen to know any more details?

I know of one project of that sort, but will let Mark comment on that; 
not sure that it would appear this year.  Books have a tendency to take 
longer than one expects, given the lack of time to work on them!  :-)

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
Hi Hugh.  Thanks for your comments on the docs.

First off, "dynamic" draws in this context refer to networks that  
change over time, and that comment is in the docs only to point out  
that the MCMC process itself could be considered to be a time-changing  
(i.e., dynamic) network process.  But it's a bit confusing and I'll  
edit it out.

With regard to your other question about the non-existent "prob"  
argument referred to in the "theta0" explanation, it turns out that  
documentation is a vestige of an earlier version and I'll edit that as  
well.  Sorry about that!

Best,
Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] homemade ergm terms
messages.body_plain:
i believe the model is doing what it's supposed to be doing. when i run a model solely with the edges term, the parameter estimate it gives me is identical to what i would expect if the network was being modeled as bipartite- in other words, the parameter estimate corresponds to the density of a BIPARTITE network (where only a subset of dyads are eligible), not a one-mode network (where all dyads are eligible). to confirm this, i took the exact same network, but converted it into a one-mode network instead- and indeed, when i do this and model the new network, the parameter estimate for "edges" changes and now corresponds to the density of my network when all dyads are considered.

also, i don't see why one-mode terms shouldn't apply to two-mode data. in my network below, the attribute "female" happens to be identical to the partitioning of the network into two modes (according to gender). therefore, this term still tells me that women are more likely to receive ties than men- which, in this case, is identical to saying men send more ties than women.

all this is to say, i believe ergm is indeed modeling my directed, bipartite network, and doing so correctly. which is good news, right? :)

-kevin

From: briankeegan2008@u.northwestern.edu [mailto:briankeegan2008@u.northwestern.edu] On Behalf Of Brian Keegan

To: Lewis, Kevin
Cc: Steven Goodreau; Steven Goodreau; statnet listserv (statnet_help@u.washington.edu)
Subject: Re: [statnet_help] homemade ergm terms

I had been assuming you were using bipartite-specific parameters like b1factor, b1degree, etc. I guess I'm surprised it doesn't return any errors for using directed, one-mode parameters for your data which means it may be taking it as one-mode data despite your bipartite designation. I know some parameters (e.g., edges, 4-cycles, etc.) work across one and two-mode networks, but nodeifactor definitely shouldn't if it was truly bipartite. Maybe the program's been modeling it as one-mode all along unbeknownst to you--which, in light of Steven's comments, would suggest the results are still valid.

From: Steven Goodreau [mailto:goodreau@uw.edu<mailto:goodreau@uw.edu>]
Sent: Thursday, July 14, 2011 2:36 PM
To: Brian Keegan
Cc: Lewis, Kevin; Steven Goodreau; statnet listserv (statnet_help@u.washington.edu<mailto:statnet_help@u.washington.edu>)
Subject: Re: [statnet_help] homemade ergm terms


> Forgive me if I'm demonstrating my ignorance of any of the ergm package,
> Kevin's request, or bipartite networks generally, but since when does
> ergm (the package) support directed bipartite networks? I ask not out of
> pique, but as a methodological matter since it obviously changes the
> types of questions which can be asked. I would be very interested in
> seeing other papers that expand on such an approach.

Thanks, Brian. Indeed you're not demonstrating your ignorance of the
package - I was!  I pretty much never use directed data, so I was
answering Kevin's question more from the perspective of the sort of
model that would in theory make sense given the question he was trying
to answer, rather than what ergm would actually do. A quick double-check
of ergm, via the following code:

a <- network.initialize(10,directed=T,bipartite=5)
b <- simulate(a~edges,theta0=100)
b[,]

indicates that indeed, ergm does not handle networks that are
simultaneously bipartite and directed.  Mea culpa. (Note that the
network package does, however).

> Second (and again I defer to others' expertise), it always struck me
> that modeling sexual interaction networks as bipartite was a
> complicating rather than simplifying assumption relative to modeling the
> network as unipartite with attributes (wholly apart from the
> heteronormative implications). I trust there is an underlying
> statistical rationale, but perhaps someone could hold my hand and
> elaborate for me why a bipartite approach would be superior to a
> unipartite with attributes approach which had null male-male,
> female-female interactions?

My feeling has always been that if you are modeling a system in which
there are two types of nodes, and there is something structural (in the
real world and.or in your model) that dictates that all ties must by
definition be between nodes in the different sets, then it is cleanest
to model it as bipartite.  It doesn't really matter waht consitutes
those classes of nodes, as long as there is a cross-class requirement of
some form or other.  Modeling it as unipartite with cross-class
parameters fixed at -Inf (which is what happens if you send in a network
with no ties across classes for estimation) is statistically equivalent,
so from a practical standpoint I really don't think it matters.  To me
it just seems cleaner.

I'm not sure what domain of data Kevin was modeling, and whether the
requirement from all ties being cross-sex was something implicit in the
phenomenon or a simplifying assumption that he added.  I guess a case
could be made that for the former it's more philosophically reasonable
to model it as bipartite, and for the latter it's more philosophically
reasonable to model it as unipartite with nulls.  But in reality the
distinction between the two is probably pretty fuzzy.

And, in this case, since ergm doesn't handle bipartite directed
networks, it sounds like Kevin is going to have to go the route you
suggest regardless of philosophical preferences!

I'd love to hear others' thoughts on this.

Steve

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mark,

thank you for your reply on my question on the statnet help mail list.

I have some more question about how "ergm", by method="Stepping",
estimates in presence of missing edges in the network.

If I right understood, when the network has some missing data, ergm should
implement the face-value likelihood. This means that the estimating
algorithm stops when the constrained mean are equal the unconstrained
mean.

In the file attached I estimated a model for the "kapfts1" network setting
randomly the 20% of edges as missing. As you can see, simulating 500
networks from the coef. of the estimated model, in one case putting in
simulate.formula the constrain=observed,  the average statistics are not
equal. So I don't think that these coef. are really the maximum face-value
likelihood estimates.

What I think is that  "ergm" consider any NA as a 0. In fact I replicated
ten times the same estimation, on the same data with the same missing
edges, in one case leaving the NA's (Step: col 1,2) and the other setting
the NA's to be 0 (Step_0: col 3,4). As you can see, the values are close.

Maybe there are some bugs on ergm.

Bests,

Nicola

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mark,

thank you for your reply on my question on the statnet help mail list.

I have some more question about how "ergm", by method="Stepping",
estimates in presence of missing edges in the network.

If I right understood, when the network has some missing data, ergm should
implement the face-value likelihood. This means that the estimating
algorithm stops when the constrained mean are equal the unconstrained
mean.

In the file attached I estimated a model for the "kapfts1" network setting
randomly the 20% of edges as missing. As you can see, simulating 500
networks from the coef. of the estimated model, in one case putting in
simulate.formula the constrain=observed,  the average statistics are not
equal. So I don't think that these coef. are really the maximum face-value
likelihood estimates.

What I think is that  "ergm" consider any NA as a 0. In fact I replicated
ten times the same estimation, on the same data with the same missing
edges, in one case leaving the NA's (Step: col 1,2) and the other setting
the NA's to be 0 (Step_0: col 3,4). As you can see, the values are close.

Maybe there are some bugs on ergm.

Bests,

Nicola

I had been assuming you were using bipartite-specific parameters like
b1factor, b1degree, etc. I guess I'm surprised it doesn't return any errors
for using directed, one-mode parameters for your data which means it may be
taking it as one-mode data despite your bipartite designation. I know some
parameters (e.g., edges, 4-cycles, etc.) work across one and two-mode
networks, but nodeifactor definitely shouldn't if it was truly bipartite.
Maybe the program's been modeling it as one-mode all along unbeknownst to
you--which, in light of Steven's comments, would suggest the results are
still valid.

> there are two types of nodes, and there is something structural (in the
> real world and.or in your model) that dictates that all ties must by

> some form or other.  Modeling it as unipartite with cross-class
> parameters fixed at -Inf (which is what happens if you send in a network
> with no ties across classes for estimation) is statistically equivalent,
> so from a practical standpoint I really don't think it matters.  To me
> it just seems cleaner.

> requirement from all ties being cross-sex was something implicit in the
> phenomenon or a simplifying assumption that he added.  I guess a case
> could be made that for the former it's more philosophically reasonable
> to model it as bipartite, and for the latter it's more philosophically
> reasonable to model it as unipartite with nulls.  But in reality the
> distinction between the two is probably pretty fuzzy.
>

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Storing p-values
messages.body_plain:
Hi Thomas,

Actually, p-values are computed each time you ask for a summary of an 
ergm model [summary(my.model)]. Unfortunately, the "summary.ergm" 
function is not designed to store p-values, but a very slight 
modification of this function, like below, is possible:

###  Just copy the code below and then type 
mespval<-pvalergm(<my_ergm_model>) to store your p-values...

pvalergm<-function (object, ...)
{
     pseudolikelihood <- is.null(object$samplesize) || 
is.na(object$samplesize) # si $mcmcsamplesize n'est pas nul ou manquant, 
cela veut dire que l'estimation ne s'est pas faite par pseudolikelihood.
     independence <- is.dyad.independent(object) # mod?le ? ind?pendance 
dyadique?
     if (any(is.na(object$coef)) & !is.null(object$mplefit)) {
         object$coef[is.na(object$coef)] <- 
object$mplefit$coef[is.na(object$coef)]
     } # Si un des estimateurs ML obtenus par MCMC manque, remplace par 
les estimateurs Max pseudolikelihood. 

     if (is.null(object$hessian) && is.null(object$covar)) {
         return()
     }    # si la matrice hessienne ET la matrice des covariances 
estim?es (covar) n'existent pas, ne renvoie rien. La suite s'applique 
aux autres situations:
     nodes <- network.size(object$network)  # nb de nodes
     dyads <- network.dyadcount(object$network) # nb de dyades
     if (is.null(object$covar)) {
         asycov <- try(robust.inverse(-object$hessian), silent = TRUE)
         if (inherits(asycov, "try-error")) {
             asycov <- diag(1/diag(-object$hessian))
         } # si $covar est null, essaie de calculer asycov ? partir de 
$hessian
     } 

     else {
         asycov <- object$covar # si covar existe, asycov en est une copie.
	## Le if qui suit me para?t bizarre, car jamais TRUE? C'est p? une 
ancienne partie de code qui a ?t? d?sactiv?e...
         if (FALSE & !pseudolikelihood & !independence) {
             if (is.directed(object$network)) {
                 mdyads <- nodes * (nodes - 1)
             }
             else {
                 mdyads <- nodes * (nodes - 1)/2
             }
             asycov <- asycov * mdyads/dyads
             object$mc.se <- object$mc.se * sqrt(mdyads/dyads)
         }
     }
     rownames(asycov) <- names(object$coef)
     colnames(asycov) <- rownames(asycov)
     asyse <- diag(asycov) # asyse = variance des param?tres
     asyse[asyse < 0 | is.infinite(object$coef) | object$offset] <- NA
     asyse <- sqrt(asyse) # asyse = ecart-type des param?tres
     if (any(is.na(asyse) & !object$offset) & !is.null(object$mplefit)) {
         if (is.null(object$mplefit$covar)) {
             if (!is.null(object$mplefit$covar)) {
                 mpleasycov <- try(robust.inverse(-object$mplefit$hessian),
                   silent = TRUE)
                 if (inherits(mpleasycov, "try-error")) {
                   mpleasycov <- diag(1/diag(-object$mplefit$hessian))
                 }
                 asyse[is.na(asyse)] <- sqrt(diag(mpleasycov))[is.na(asyse)]
             }
         }
         else {
             mpleasycov <- object$mplefit$covar
             asyse[is.na(asyse)] <- sqrt(diag(mpleasycov))[is.na(asyse)]
         }
     } # Si certains ?carts-types de param?tres ne sont pas disponibles 
(valeur NA, voir ligne 39), remplace les par les ?carts-types trouv?s 
avec la MPLE.
     asyse <- matrix(asyse, ncol = length(asyse))
     colnames(asyse) <- colnames(asycov)

   dyads <- network.dyadcount(object$network)
   nodes <- network.size(object$network)
   if (!is.null(object$Z.mkl)) {
         p <- ncol(object$Z.mkl)
     }
     else {
         p <- 0
     }
   if (!is.null(object$cluster)) {
         df <- length(object$coef) + object$ngroups * (p + 2) -
             1
     }
     else {
         df <- length(object$coef) + (nodes - (p + 1)/2) * p
     }
     rdf <- dyads - df
     tval <- object$coef/asyse
     pval <- 2 * pt(q = abs(tval), df = rdf, lower.tail = FALSE)
     nomsparam<-colnames(pval)
     pval<-as.vector(pval)
     names(pval)<-nomsparam
return(pval)
}


Hope that helps,
Victorin Luisier

messages.body_plain:
Hi Kevin,


> currently, there are terms available for homophily on a certain attribute (nodematch), and one can even break this down by the value of the attribute using diff=TRUE. so
> in my network, i can see if college-educated people tend to contact one another. instead, i want to know if the tendency towards educational homophily varies by gender-
> in other words, i want to see if the tendency for college-educated men to contact college-educated women is different from the tendency of college-educated women to
> contact college educated men. rather than coding a term for this effect, i wonder if instead i could just create an edge covariate (i.e. a new network X) in which, say,
> every possible tie from a college-educated male to a college-educated female is present. then, if i include two terms in the model- nodematch(collegeeducation) and
> edgecov(X)- the former term will essentially indicate educational homophily from women to men, while the latter will indicate educational homophily from men to women. is
> this accurate? (the same reasoning could therefore be extended to any number of scenarios, in which we expect homophily on covariate A to vary by covariate B.)


I think you can do it even more easily.  Define a new nodal attribute called "educ.and.sex" or something like that, with four values (1 = female college, etc.) Then you can use nodemix on that to get a coefficient for each combination.  Or, if you want to parameterize it differently to get a sense of the significance of the interaction effects, have main effects terms (nodefactor) and then also use nodemix with different "base" arguments so that you only keep the interaction terms in there.


> my second question is similar, but instead involves reciprocity (i appreciate the addition of the new ?by? argument, by the way!). one example is that i want to know
> whether women are more likely to reciprocate ties to men with a similar income. let?s say my network is called ?network,? and i have an edge covariate called
> ?absdiffincome? indicating the absolute difference in income between every possible dyad. to find the answer to my question, my thought is that i could 1) begin with
> network, and drop all ties from women to men (i.e. keep only ties from men to women); 2) take the transpose of this network; and 3) code this transpose network with
> values from absdiffincome (i.e. cell-wise multiply the values of [transpose network] with the values of [absdiffincome]), and use this final network as a new edge
> covariate. am i totally off my rocker here, or would this actually produce the type of effect i am looking for? and if all of this happens to work as i think it might,
> are there any drawbacks to doing things this way other than the extra hassle?

This one is harder to understand.  I think we need one more piece of info.  You said your effect of interest is whether "women are more likely to reciprocate ties to men with a similar income."  But do you mean "more like than they are to reciprocate ties to men with different income"?  More like than the overall tendency to reciprocate ties?

messages.subject: [statnet_help] esp change statistic C code
messages.body_plain:
Dave,

You are correct, the names of the L2ut and L2hu counters are backwards.  And
thank you for catching this.  This was caused by a change to the ergm code
in the 2.3 release, which intended to make the ergm and network code
consistent in their naming conventions for the head and tail nodes -
essentially heads and tails were swapped in the ergm code to conform to the
notion that a directed tie is the outedge of the tail node and the inedge of
the head node.  In that change, the "t" in L2ut and the "h" in L2hu should
have been swapped as well.  They weren't.  You are correct though that this
makes no difference in the calculation of the change statistic.
Nonetheless, this issue will be addressed in a future release.

Thanks again.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] esp change statistic C code
messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to make sense of the C source code for the esp change statistic.
Here's my understanding so far:

1) First, it steps through the neighborhood (with members indexed by u) of
the head (h) node of the proposed toggled edge (i) and counts the number of
edges to the tail (t) node of the propsed toggled edge. This gives the
count of two-paths connecting h and t, stored in varible L2ht.

2) For each node u in the neighborhood of h, the neighborhood of u (with
members indexed by v) is then searched for edges back to nodes t or h. This
counts the two-paths follwing u-v-t and u-v-h, which gives the esp count
for edges ut and hu, respectively. These counts are stored in L2ut and
L2hu. (Note that the addition/removal of edge i will increment or decrement
these esp counts through the inclusion of paths u-h-t and u-t-h,
respectively.)

I found a sketch like the following helped me understand the method:


v           v = a node in the neighborhood of u
|           u = a node in the neighborhood of h
/  |  \
?   u   ?       ? = edges whose existence is being queried for the
calculation of
| /   \ |           esp counts that may be affected by the addition/removal
of edge i
/     \ 
t  -i-  h       t & h = the tail and head nodes of proposed toggled edge i


This is the point where I become confused, possibly because the variable
names don't match my intuition of what is being counted:

if(EdgetreeSearch(MIN(v,head),MAX(v,head),nwp->outedges)!= 0) L2ut++;
if(EdgetreeSearch(MIN(v,tail),MAX(v,tail),nwp->outedges)!= 0) L2hu++;

The first of these lines identifies the existence of an edge from v to h
(or vice versa), then increments the variable L2ut; the second does the
same for nodes v and t and increments L2hu. (Note that at this point in the
code edges (h,u), (u, t), and (u, v) are all verified to exist.) Verifying
edge (v,h) establishes a two-path u-v-h, which adds to the esp count for
edge (h,u), yet the variable that is incremented is L2ut--the opposite of
what I would expect. Am I missing something important about the effect of
edge (v,h) on the esp count for edge (u,t)?

In the final step where the change statistics are actually updated, the
code for L2ut and L2hu are treated identically, so the labels make no
difference to the calculation of the change statistic. I just want to be
sure I understand how the code actually works before I proceed to tinker.

Many thanks,
Dave

_____________________________________________
Dr. David A. Nolin, Ph.D.
Postdoctoral Scholar
Carolina Population Center
University of North Carolina

> function is not designed to store p-values, but a very slight 
> modification of this function, like below, is possible:
>
> ### Just copy the code below and then type
> mespval<-pvalergm(<my_ergm_model>) to store your p-values...
>
> pvalergm<-function (object, ...)
> {
> pseudolikelihood <- is.null(object$samplesize) ||
> is.na(object$samplesize) # si $mcmcsamplesize n'est pas nul ou 
> manquant, cela veut dire que l'estimation ne s'est pas faite par
pseudolikelihood.
> independence <- is.dyad.independent(object) # mod?le ? ind?pendance 
> dyadique?
> if (any(is.na(object$coef)) & !is.null(object$mplefit)) { 
> object$coef[is.na(object$coef)] <- 
> object$mplefit$coef[is.na(object$coef)]
> } # Si un des estimateurs ML obtenus par MCMC manque, remplace par les 
> estimateurs Max pseudolikelihood.
> if (is.null(object$hessian) && is.null(object$covar)) {
> return()
> } # si la matrice hessienne ET la matrice des covariances estim?es
> (covar) n'existent pas, ne renvoie rien. La suite s'applique aux 
> autres
> situations:
> nodes <- network.size(object$network) # nb de nodes dyads <- 
> network.dyadcount(object$network) # nb de dyades if 
> (is.null(object$covar)) { asycov <- 
> try(robust.inverse(-object$hessian), silent = TRUE) if 
> (inherits(asycov, "try-error")) { asycov <- 
> diag(1/diag(-object$hessian)) } # si $covar est null, essaie de 
> calculer asycov ? partir de $hessian } else { asycov <- object$covar # 
> si covar existe, asycov en est une copie.
> ## Le if qui suit me para?t bizarre, car jamais TRUE? C'est p? une 
> ancienne partie de code qui a ?t? d?sactiv?e...
> if (FALSE & !pseudolikelihood & !independence) { if 
> (is.directed(object$network)) { mdyads <- nodes * (nodes - 1) } else { 
> mdyads <- nodes * (nodes - 1)/2 } asycov <- asycov * mdyads/dyads 
> object$mc.se <- object$mc.se * sqrt(mdyads/dyads) } }
> rownames(asycov) <- names(object$coef)
> colnames(asycov) <- rownames(asycov)
> asyse <- diag(asycov) # asyse = variance des param?tres asyse[asyse < 
> 0 | is.infinite(object$coef) | object$offset] <- NA asyse <- 
> sqrt(asyse) # asyse = ecart-type des param?tres if (any(is.na(asyse) & 
> !object$offset) & !is.null(object$mplefit)) { if 
> (is.null(object$mplefit$covar)) { if (!is.null(object$mplefit$covar)) 
> { mpleasycov <- try(robust.inverse(-object$mplefit$hessian),
> silent = TRUE)
> if (inherits(mpleasycov, "try-error")) { mpleasycov <- 
> diag(1/diag(-object$mplefit$hessian))
> }
> asyse[is.na(asyse)] <- sqrt(diag(mpleasycov))[is.na(asyse)]
> }
> }
> else {
> mpleasycov <- object$mplefit$covar
> asyse[is.na(asyse)] <- sqrt(diag(mpleasycov))[is.na(asyse)]
> }
> } # Si certains ?carts-types de param?tres ne sont pas disponibles 
> (valeur NA, voir ligne 39), remplace les par les ?carts-types trouv?s 
> avec la MPLE.
> asyse <- matrix(asyse, ncol = length(asyse))
> colnames(asyse) <- colnames(asycov)
>
> dyads <- network.dyadcount(object$network) nodes <- 
> network.size(object$network) if (!is.null(object$Z.mkl)) { p <- 
> ncol(object$Z.mkl) } else { p <- 0 } if (!is.null(object$cluster)) { 
> df <- length(object$coef) + object$ngroups * (p + 2) -
> 1
> }
> else {
> df <- length(object$coef) + (nodes - (p + 1)/2) * p } rdf <- dyads - 
> df tval <- object$coef/asyse pval <- 2 * pt(q = abs(tval), df = rdf, 
> lower.tail = FALSE)
> nomsparam<-colnames(pval)
> pval<-as.vector(pval)
> names(pval)<-nomsparam
> return(pval)
> }
>
>
> Hope that helps,
> Victorin Luisier

messages.subject: [statnet_help] which nodes are which
messages.body_plain:
Hi Deven,

You just need to use the command get.vertex.attribute:

get.vertex.attribute(network_1,"race")
get.vertex.attribute(network_1,"sex")

This will tell you the sex and race of each node, in node order; you'll 
see that the nodes are in the order that you passed the attributes: 
1-2125=white males, etc.

You can also use the handy short-cut version of the same commands:

network_1 %v% "race"
network_1 %v% "sex"

Steve

> summary(undir.net)  # check that the stored number of edges is correct
> summary(undir.net~edges)  # check that the reported number of edges
> matches

messages.subject: [statnet_help] marginal effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi Philip,

That's not quite how the coefficients work.   It is approximately true when the tie has a low probability to begin with, but gets farther and farther away form the truth as ties get more likely.

Since you said that exp(coef) = 1.23, then that means the coefficient you're talking about is about 0.207.  So, imagine a pair of actors, who otherwise have a log-odds of a tie of -10.  That corresponds to a very low probability, exp(-10) / (1+exp(-10))= 0.0000454. Now, if you bump up the covariate by 1 on your statistic of interest, the log-odds of a tie will rise to -10+0.207 = -9.793.  Indeed the probability corresponding to this is 0.0000558, which is 23% higher than before.

But now imagine they have a log-odds of 2, and thus a tie probability of 0.88. Their revised log-odds will be 2.207, for a probability of 0.90; only about 2% higher.

That's the way log-odds work, and it's by design, not a quirk.  It's one way to capture that fact that you can't ever make a claim that some phenomenon has a strict multiplicative effect on probabilities, because then you run the risk of probabilities rising above 1.

Since humans are much better at thinking in terms of probabilities rather than log-odds, it's common when using methods based on log-odds - whether it's for logistic regression, or ergms, or something else - to report the coefficients, and then also report examples of marginal effects, which is what it sounds like your reviewer wants.

Hope that helps,
Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Re: predicted link probabilities
messages.body_plain:
This function was inspired by a long post by Nicola Soriani from July 2010 and is a
feeble attempt to tack unto that archived thread.

This function takes as input an ergm model for an undirected relation and returns
the edge probabilities, analytically, without simulation. It is considerably simpler
than the previously posted code, and less general, but seems to work fine for
undirected graphs anyway.

I would very much appreciate any comments on this code. I bet it could be far
simpler still if I knoew what I were doing.

Would such a fucntion be a reasonable addition to the ergm package, or is that
suggestion ergm heresy?

thanks,
Hugh

# Analytic (non-simulation) edge probability
# after Anderson, Wasserman, Crouch. p* primer (1999), p. 53
# input: x, an ergm model for an undirected relation
# returns real-valued matrix of same dim as x, the edge probabilities
predict = function(x) {
	n <- network.size(x$network)
	z <- summary(x$formula)
	result = matrix(0.0, n, n)
	# alternative ergm model
	xAlt <- x
	xAlt$formula <- ergm.update.formula(xAlt$formula, xAlt$network ~ .)
	# undirected, upper triangle loop
	for(i in 1:(n-1)) {
		for(j in (i+1):n) {
			xAlt$network[i,j] <- !xAlt$network[i,j] # toggle 1 edge
			zAlt <- summary(xAlt$formula)
			# reverse terms to save -1 factor in Anderson et. al.
			if(x$network[i,j])
				d <- zAlt - z
			else
				d <- z - zAlt
			p <- (1.0 / (1.0 + exp(sum(x$coef * d))))
			result[i,j] <- p # undirected
			result[j,i] <- p
			xAlt$network[i,j] <- !xAlt$network[i,j] # restore edge
		}
	}
	return(result)
}

Dear statnet help list,

I'm attempting to calculate a similarity measure among individuals' local networks in statnet.  The network is set up so that:

1) Each node in my network has values stored on five different vertex attributes (called trait1, trait2, trait3, trait4, and trait5.)
2) Each node is directly connected to up to 8 other nodes (but may be connected to fewer). 

For each node, I'd like to create an index measuring their level of similarity to their directly connected neighbors, where the index is calculated by:

number of similarities to neighbors / total possible similarities to neighbors

So, for example, if node A is connected to node B and only B, and A and B have identical values on trait1 and trait2, but not trait3, trait4, and trait5, then A's similarity index would be 2/5.  

If node C was directly connected to node D and node E, and C had the same values on trait1 and trait2 with D, but had no similar values with E, then C's similarity index should be 2/10. 

How would I be able to create this measure for all nodes in the network?  Any help or pointers would be appreciated!

Many thanks,
Jack

Political Science

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Conflicting network indicators
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am using the statnet package to analyze a dataset I collected on different
types of collaborations between organizations. I imported the data as
edgelists, and I want to compare some basic descriptives of these networks
like the number of triads, the number of edges, density and such. However, I
noticed that there is a disparity between the number of edges and triangles
R tells me the dataset has, and the actual number of edges and triangles I
see when plotting the networks. Even worse, using different methods to
retrieve this data gives me different numbers. Using
network.edgecount(network) or gden(network) gives a different number than
using summary(network~ edges + triangles + density), and both numbers are
wrong. Using sum(as.matrix(network))/2 does give the correct number of edges

In the process of creating networks from the edgelists I specified that the
networks are undirected and that they should not contain multiplex edges. In
the original edgelist the data is directed and only part of the edges are
reciprocal. I have the feeling that there's the problem, and by specifying
that the network should not have multiplex edges statnet does not remove the
multiplex edges from the dataset. THis would explain why network.edgecount
gives a number that is too high (by counting the redundant edges), but not
why summary(network~ edges) gives a value that is too low.

So my question is, is it true that creating an undirected network from
edgelists that are directed and partially reciprocal does not remove the
redundant edges, and if so, is there an easy way to remove them from my
edgelists? Also, does anyone understand why using the network.edgecount
method gives a different result from using summary(network ~ edges)?

Thanks in advance for your help!

Edzard Wesselink

messages.body_plain:
I think that bipartite graphs were used originally to model 2-mode 
networks.  In that case, there really is no possibility of a link 
between the nodes within mode.

In this case, it's an empirical question, but it sounds like Kevin's data 
collection ensured that there are no withn-group ties.  If so, this is a 
bipartite (directed) network.

best,
mm

On Thu, 14 Jul 2011, Steven Goodreau wrote:

>
>> Forgive me if I'm demonstrating my ignorance of any of the ergm package,
>> Kevin's request, or bipartite networks generally, but since when does
>> ergm (the package) support directed bipartite networks? I ask not out of
>> pique, but as a methodological matter since it obviously changes the
>> types of questions which can be asked. I would be very interested in
>> seeing other papers that expand on such an approach.
>
> Thanks, Brian. Indeed you're not demonstrating your ignorance of the package 
> - I was!  I pretty much never use directed data, so I was answering Kevin's 
> question more from the perspective of the sort of model that would in theory 
> make sense given the question he was trying to answer, rather than what ergm 
> would actually do. A quick double-check of ergm, via the following code:
>
> a <- network.initialize(10,directed=T,bipartite=5)
> b <- simulate(a~edges,theta0=100)
> b[,]
>
> indicates that indeed, ergm does not handle networks that are simultaneously 
> bipartite and directed.  Mea culpa. (Note that the network package does, 
> however).
>
>> Second (and again I defer to others' expertise), it always struck me
>> that modeling sexual interaction networks as bipartite was a
>> complicating rather than simplifying assumption relative to modeling the
>> network as unipartite with attributes (wholly apart from the
>> heteronormative implications). I trust there is an underlying
>> statistical rationale, but perhaps someone could hold my hand and
>> elaborate for me why a bipartite approach would be superior to a
>> unipartite with attributes approach which had null male-male,
>> female-female interactions?
>
> My feeling has always been that if you are modeling a system in which there 
> are two types of nodes, and there is something structural (in the real world 
> and.or in your model) that dictates that all ties must by definition be 
> between nodes in the different sets, then it is cleanest to model it as 
> bipartite.  It doesn't really matter waht consitutes those classes of nodes, 
> as long as there is a cross-class requirement of some form or other. 
> Modeling it as unipartite with cross-class parameters fixed at -Inf (which is 
> what happens if you send in a network with no ties across classes for 
> estimation) is statistically equivalent, so from a practical standpoint I 
> really don't think it matters.  To me it just seems cleaner.
>
> I'm not sure what domain of data Kevin was modeling, and whether the 
> requirement from all ties being cross-sex was something implicit in the 
> phenomenon or a simplifying assumption that he added.  I guess a case could 
> be made that for the former it's more philosophically reasonable to model it 
> as bipartite, and for the latter it's more philosophically reasonable to 
> model it as unipartite with nulls.  But in reality the distinction between 
> the two is probably pretty fuzzy.
>
> And, in this case, since ergm doesn't handle bipartite directed networks, it 
> sounds like Kevin is going to have to go the route you suggest regardless of 
> philosophical preferences!
>
> I'd love to hear others' thoughts on this.
>
> Steve
>
>
>
>
>
>
>
>> On Thu, Jul 14, 2011 at 12:07 PM, Lewis, Kevin <kmlewis@fas.harvard.edu
>> <mailto:kmlewis@fas.harvard.edu>> wrote:
>>
>>     steve, many thanks!!! re: the first part, i completely hadn't
>>     thought about the nodemix option, which in hindsight is pretty
>>     obvious- sorry for the brain lapse, but thanks for pointing me in
>>     the right direction :). this solution will work perfectly.
>>
>>     re: the second part, i apologize for the ambiguity- i think i was
>>     also jumping the gun a little bit. my original interest is indeed in
>>     whether men are more likely to reciprocate ties than women. i
>>     initially also figured that the "by" option would take care of this-
>>     but then realized that, because my network is bipartite, counting
>>     every mutual tie involving a female is identical to counting every
>>     mutual tie (because all mutual ties by definition involve a male and
>>     a female), and so the mutual term with the "by" option for women is
>>     identical to the generic mutual term by itself.
>>
>>     i see what you are saying about dyads either being reciprocal or
>>     not- but it seems to me that (even with cross-sectional data) one
>>     should be able to get at this difference- in a sense by comparing
>>     how many male --> female ties are returned with how many female -->
>>     male ties are returned. if virtually all of the asymmetric ties in a
>>     network are male --> female, for instance- and there are virtually
>>     no asymmetric female --> male ties- wouldn't this suggest that men
>>     are more likely to respond to women than women are to men? thus, i
>>     was trying to get at this with the transpose/edge covariate effect
>>     (we can ignore the additional income complication for the moment).
>>
>>     as it turns out, however, i DO have a timestamp for each tie- and so
>>     the network i'm using is actually a collapsed longitudinal network.
>>     given this information, i would love to hear any thoughts you might
>>     have on how to go about using this in order to disentangle the type
>>     of gender*reciprocity interaction i hope to get at :).
>>
>>     (happy to also take this offline, unless you think the list would
>>     benefit.)
>>
>>     thanks again!!!
>>
>>     -kevin
>>
>>     p.s. please forgive my complicated initial posing of the question in
>>     terms of the income question- it seems as though if we are able to
>>     get a solution to the basic male vs. female reciprocity issue above,
>>     then i would probably be able to extend this to define additional
>>     interaction effects between gender, reciprocity, and dyadic covariates.
>>

>>     one example
>>      >> is that i want to know
>>      >> whether women are more likely to reciprocate ties to men with a
>>     similar
>>      >> income. let?s say my network is called ?network,? and i have an 
>> edge

>>      >> ?absdiffincome? indicating the absolute difference in income
>>     between every
>>      >> possible dyad. to find the answer to my question, my thought is

>>     "more like

>>       More like

>>
>>     Oops, by the time I got to question 2 I had forgotten this was a

>>     case you did indeed provide enough information.
>>
>>     Defining an absdiffincome dyadic covariate seems like the right

>>     skip the step with the deletion and transpose, and simply use the
>>     mutual term with a "by" argument directly.  You state the question
>>     of interest in terms of women reciprocating ties with men, but
>>     unless you have some form of longitudinal data (which I am assuming
>>     you don't from the way you described it), then really, you only know

messages.subject: [statnet_help] error in ergm with style "Stepping"
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nicola.   Are you familiar with the manuscript that introduces this  
stepping idea?  An earlier version is available at http://www.stat.psu.edu/~dhunter/papers/tr1003.pdf 
  and it will be coming out sometime soon in J Comp Graph Stat.

Even if you are familiar with it, the error might still need a bit of  
explanation.  Ideally, the stepping algorithm uses a series of "steps"  
to gradually close in on the MLE.  When it gets close enough so that  
it appears plain MCMCMLE can be used to get a final estimate, the  
algorithm draws one more large sample for this final estimate.  If,  
for some reason, the observed vector of statistics is not contained  
inside the convex hull of sampled statistics, then the approximate MLE  
will not exist (and somehow the stepping algorithm didn't quite do its  
job even though it believed that it had done so).  The default  
behavior of the code at this point is to throw the error you're seeing.

I hope this explains it.

Best,
Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Newbie Question
messages.body_plain:
I'm brand new to statnet and have a very newbie question.  I'm trying take a
square adjacency matrix with 435 nodes from a csv file into an edge list for
the purposes of plotting and analysis.  The ties are non-directed and
valued.  So far, I haven't be able to pound R into preserving the tie
values.  Here is the code I'm using and I'm hoping someone can point my
(surely obvious) mistake:

defense.csv <- read.csv("defense.csv", row.names=1, header=T )
dim(defense.csv)
defense.csv <- as.matrix(defense.csv)
diag(defense.csv) <- 0
defense.net<-network(defense.csv, directed=F, loops=F, hyper=F, mulitple=F,
bipartite=F,  ignore.eval=F)

If I don't use the "ignore.eval" option, it runs but turns the values in to
1.  If I use it, I get the following error:

"There were 50 or more warnings (use warnings() to see the first 50)"


Also, at some point I'll want to turn the ties into dichotomous ones based
on some threshold.  Is there a handy guide to figuring out the code for that
as well?

Best,

scott

steve and the statnet team, thanks so much for this clarification- really appreciate it! apologies for having confused everyone, but everything now makes perfect sense. hope you have a great weekend,

-kevin

-----Original Message-----
From: Steven Goodreau [mailto:goodreau@uw.edu]
Sent: Friday, July 15, 2011 3:36 PM
To: Brian Keegan
Cc: Lewis, Kevin; Steven Goodreau; statnet listserv (statnet_help@u.washington.edu)
Subject: Re: [statnet_help] homemade ergm terms

Hi all,

So, indeed, ergm should *not* currently be used with networks that are
both bipartite and directed.  This should be consistent with all of the
documentation out there; if anyone knows of documentation that we've
produced that says (or even suggests) otherwise, please point us to it
so we can correct it.

The reason this is, is that the MCMC estimation code treats all
bipartite networks as undirected, and only proposes toggles Yij where i
and j are of different bipartite classes (i.e. of different modes of a
two-mode network), and i<j. It is the last criterion that makes it work
for undirected networks, but not for directed.

Some of the confusion arises from the fact that we put in error messages
to block users from using ergm terms with directed bipartite networks
for some terms and not others.  Specifically, for those terms that are
specific to bipartite networks (e.g. b1degree), we put in checks for
both bipartiteness and for directedness.  However, for those terms that
are not bipartite-specific (nodeifactor), we didn't do a double-check
and block those fitting both criteria. Kevin appears to have only used
terms in the latter category, so didn't get an error.

We will add errors to all terms to make sure they prevent use on
directed bipartite networks in the next update of ergm.

Note again that the network package can handle with directed bipartite
networks. This limitation is specific to ergm, given the complexities of
the MCMC estimation code.

I imagine some of you are wondering if we plan to add capabilities to
ergm for directed bipartite networks in the future.  As far as I know it
hasn't been on the (already long) list of things to do (but other
statnet developers, correct me if I'm wrong on that).  However, a large
show of hands from those who are interested in such capability could
help prioritize it.  If you're in that camp, feel free to email me and
let me know (no need to copy the entire listserv).

Thanks for bringing this up, Kevin, and thanks to Brian for helping to
clarify.

Steve
(+statnet team)
