messages.subject: [statnet_help] ergm question
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Jorge -

Your question raises some important issues that are too deep to address 
well in email.  But I will take a stab at some of them....

On 05/02/2011 10:08 AM, Jorge M Rocha wrote:
>  From what I understand, the modeling framework of an ERGM treats the
> observed network as the _dependent variable_ and the specified
> structural configurations and covariate information about nodes/edges as
> _independent variables_ whose presence/absence increases the
> log-likelihood for the model.

I think it is important to make some comment on this conceptual issue, 
because it lies at the core of one's thinking about the modeling 
process.  (In so doing I will speak ex cathedra -- I trust that my 
colleagues will not be shy in administering correctives, should they 
find me to be in error.)  In a standard ERGM without covariate effects, 
there are no independent variables (in a regression-like sense).  The 
model is one large stochastic system, and is treated as fully 
endogenous.  (Exogenous effects come about from the use of covariates, 
such as vertex attributes.  Of course, these can also be endogenized, 
but that's a broader model class.)  More to the point, the act of 
writing down an ERGM is the act of writing down a model for the joint 
probability distribution of a graph (i.e., the system state).  The 
exponential family form provides the language in which we express that 
model; the content and the interpretation must come from elsewhere.

Within this context, the role of statistics based on structural 
configurations is to parametrize the joint distribution of the edge 
structure.  There are several formally equivalent ways to understand 
this.  One natural one is to view the parameter associated with a given 
structural statistic as measuring the tendency of the expectation of 
that statistic to be higher or lower than what would be observed if the 
parameter in question were zero (equivalently, if it were not in the 
model).  From this point of view, all ERGM parameters reflect different 
sorts of structural "biases" or "deviations" from the behavior of the 
uniform Bernoulli graph (i.e., the homogeneous Bernoulli graph in which 
every edge occurs with equal probability).

Note that this is a "holistic" view of the network as a jointly 
interacting system -- if you are familiar with the Lagrangian or 
Hamiltonian formulations of classical mechanics (in which the behavior 
of a classical system is described by reference to a potential 
function), this may prove a useful analogy.  In any event, it's very 
different from the "elementwise" view of networks that many folks are 
used to.

For the latter, it can be helpful to think in terms of the full 
conditionals of the model -- the probability of a given edge being 
present, given the rest of the structure.  This is a "local/elementwise" 
view, perhaps loosely analogous to the way that classical mechanics is 
taught to beginners (with "forces" acting on particles, the conditional 
behavior of which is defined in terms of the other particle states). 
This comports better with the intuition of most social scientists, but 
IMHO has many underappreciated pitfalls.  Chief among these is the fact 
that one can easily forget that the elements of the system are indeed 
interacting, and the conditional behavior of one variable is only 
meaningful within the context of the rest of the network.  (For an 
example of where this intuition led the field astray, one need only look 
at the rise and fall of pseudo-likelihood techniques.)  One can also 
easily confuse conditional edge probabilities with propensities of 
_individuals_ to create edges (e.g., in a choice context), with which 
they are _not_ always synonymous.  I am thus less sanguine about the 
"local" view of ERGMs than some of my colleagues, although there is no 
question that this perspective _can_ be very helpful.

I want to stress that, properly understood, the holistic and elementwise 
views of the ERGM are both correct -- they are two equivalent ways of 
describing the same thing.  Nor are these the only ways in which the 
formalism can be validly interpreted.  (For instance, one can also 
understand ERGMs in terms of the equilibrium behavior of certain types 
of Markov chains, an interpretation that has value in dynamic 
applications.)  But what all valid interpretations of the ERGM framework 
have in common is that they recognize that one is modeling a system of 
components, and those components can potentially interact with one 
another.  As such, my sense is that regression-based thinking can be as 
much a hindrance as a help when learning about ERGMs, at least for most 
social scientists.  (Those whose familiarity with statistical 
exponential families allows them to understand ERGMs within the broader 
context of "regression-like" models are exempted, but I daresay that 
this is not standard training for most social scientists.)  That said, I 
often teach it that way, because the initial approachability of ERGMs as 
"logistic network regression with independence relaxations" is higher 
than "potential functions on graphs" for my students.  YMMV.

For an example of the use of the "local" view of ERGMs for model 
parametrization, I suggest the Goodreau et al. 2009 _Demography_ paper. 
  For a different, "semi-local" view based on dependence among edges, 
one can find many good examples in the work of Pattison and Robins; 
their 2002 _Sociological Methodology_ article comes to mind.  (And, of 
course, there is the classic Frank and Strauss _JASA_ paper, among 
others.)  The "holistic" view per se is less well-explored, although 
there are many precursors in structuralist theory.  (The Harary wing of 
structural balance, for instance, operates entirely from a holistic 
standpoint.  This is also where I insert my obligatory plug for Bruce 
Mayhew.)  Mark Handcock's work on degeneracy (see, e.g., his 2003 
chapter) has in my opinion very deep substantive implications from the 
holistic side, and there are some other recent technical contributions 
(e.g., a recent arXiv paper by Chatterjee and Diaconis) that are 
likewise promising.  One could accumulate many more examples, of course.

> In other words, what we want to achieve
> in these models is to gain a better understanding of the types of
> processes that might have gone into generating a network similar to the
> observed one;

That is one use of the framework, and certainly an important one.

> hypotheses are about this or that configuration or
> node/edge attribute and their effect on the pattern of social
> interactions represented in the network.

This is where we must be careful: a configuration does not "have" an 
effect on the network.  One could say, however, that we hypothesize that 
our process of interest will result in networks in which certain 
configurations are over or underrepresented.

> If so, how would I go about
> testing hypotheses concerning the effects of social interactions on
> nodal attributes (I?m particularly thinking of different types of
> opinions individuals might tend to have based on their interactions)?

That depends on whether the attributes affect the network.  If the 
network structure is not affected by the attributes in question (e.g., 
because the former evolves over much longer time scales than the 
latter), then one need not model the network at all: one can condition 
on the network, and model the attributes (or, if one just wants to test 
a marginal hypothesis, employ an even simpler method such as a 
permutation test).

If, on the time scale of interest, the network and the attributes both 
coevolve, then the ERGM language is not expressive enough: you need a 
joint attribute/network model.  Such extensions do exist, although my 
sense is that it is difficult to identify such models without 
longitudinal data.

>
> What I?ve done so far is kind of arguing backwards (or at least that is
> how it feels to me ?maybe because I?m coming from a traditional
> linear/logit regression background, and probably part of my problem is
> thinking in terms of DV and IV).  If the coefficients are significant
> for some node covariate of my interest in the ERGM estimation, then I?ve
> been interpreting this as evidence that it is not unreasonable to argue
> that the pattern of social interactions influences the type of opinion
> individuals have (I know that if I had longitudinal data this issue of
> reverse causality would not be so much of an issue, but so far all I
> have is cross-sectional data).  How wrong am I on this (the
> backward-arguing)?

There may be some settings in which this could give you the right 
answer, but I would discourage it unless you can prove that you are in 
one of those settings.  If you are dealing with an attribute and a 
network that are jointly endogenous, then conditioning on the latter and 
not the former is not going to do what you want.  If you just want to 
establish marginal association (e.g., those who are in certain positions 
tend to have certain kinds of opinions), I would lean towards a 
permutation test or similar procedure.  If you really want to pull 
things apart, estimate parameters, test more complex hypotheses, etc., 
my opinion is that you should look for a joint attribute/network model. 
  (We don't have one in statnet right now, but RSiena or pnet might.)

>
> Finally, part of my worry is that I?ll be sending the research to a
> consumer behavior/marketing journal where the familiarity with social
> network stuff ?let alone ERGM?s?is limited.  Any suggestions on how to
> best explain these issues to a non-specialized audience?

Well, my _personal_ advice in your case would be to look closely at your 
problem, and try to figure out how much of it you can address without 
using complex network models -- it's going to be much easier to explain, 
say, permutation or CUG tests to such a readership than ERGMs.  If you 
really must model the system as a whole, first determine whether you can 
reasonably approximate one portion (the network or the attribute) as 
being fixed relative to the other.  (Some basic knowledge of your case 
is important here: do you have access to ethnographic, observational, or 
other information that might help you evaluate the plausibility of a 
one-way effect?)  If you _can_ approximate one portion as fixed, model 
accordingly (e.g., if the network is fixed, you may want something like 
a network autocorrelation model, while fixed attributes suggest an 
ERGM).  If you are stuck with having to model both the network and 
individual attributes jointly, you have my sympathy -- this is an 
exciting area of technical research, which generally implies a painful 
experience for the practitioner.  Getting your hands on a reasonable 
cross-sectional network/attribute model is then a must, as is learning 
to use it properly (bearing in mind that, if the model is new, its 
creators may have only limited experience in that regard).

This email has become both long and polemical, but these are important 
and frequently encountered questions.  Perhaps these comments will prove 
helpful to you, and to others here who are struggling with the same issues.

Good luck!

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Edge Labels in Network Plot
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sam,

I don't know if it is possible to label edges, but I have found a 
combination of edge width and edge color to be acceptable. Try the 
following modification of your code. You can replace k=0.5 and ^3 by 
other values to tweak the result.

Take care

Philip

ex = matrix(c(
   0,1,1,0,
   1,1,1,0,
   0,0,1,1,
   1,0,0,1,
   1,1,0,0
   ),nrow=5,byrow=T)
row.names(ex) <- paste("U",1:5,sep='')
colnames(ex) <- paste("T",1:4,sep='')
ex1 = t(ex)%*%ex
diag(ex1)=0
row.names(ex1) <- colnames(ex1) <- colnames(ex)
ex2 = ex%*%t(ex)
diag(ex2)=0
row.names(ex2) <- colnames(ex2) <- row.names(ex)

exNet = network(as.sociomatrix(ex))
exNet1 = network(as.sociomatrix(ex1))
set.edge.value(exNet1,'number',ex1)
exNet2 = network(as.sociomatrix(ex2))
set.edge.value(exNet2,'number',ex2)

assign.edge.color <- function(x, k=4) {
   colors <- character(length(x))
   mx <- max(x)
   mn <- min(x)
   for (i in 1:length(x)) {
     colors[i] <- gray((1 - (x[i] / mx))^k)
   }
   return(colors)
}

par(mfrow=c(2,2),mar=c(1,1,1,1))
plot(exNet,vertex.col=c(rep(2,5),rep(3,4)),main='Sample 2-mode 
network',vertex.cex=3,displaylabels=TRUE)
plot(exNet2,vertex.col=2,usearrows=FALSE,vertex.cex=3,displaylabels=TRUE,
edge.col=assign.edge.color(get.edge.value(exNet2, "number"), k=0.5),
edge.lwd=get.edge.value(exNet2, "number")^3)
plot(exNet1,vertex.col=3,usearrows=FALSE,vertex.cex=3,displaylabels=TRUE,
edge.col=assign.edge.color(get.edge.value(exNet1, "number"), k=0.5),
edge.lwd=get.edge.value(exNet1, "number")^3)
plot(0,type='n',xlab='',ylab='',axes=F)
legend("center",pch=16,col=2:3,legend=c("Users","Threads"),cex=3)


Am 18.07.2011 15:49, schrieb Sam Stewart:
> Is it possible to label the edges in a network plot automatically?
> I'm trying to create some demo plots of how 2-mode networks can be
> transformed into two 1-mode networks, and scaling the width of the
> edge doesn't really demonstrate the value of the edge sufficiently.
>
> Thanks,
> Sam
>
> Sample Code:
>
> #producing figure 2: example of a two-mode network and the resulting
> 1-mode networks
> ex = matrix(c(
>    0,1,1,0,
>    1,1,1,0,
>    0,0,1,1,
>    1,0,0,1,
>    1,1,0,0
>    ),nrow=5,byrow=T)
> row.names(ex)<- paste("U",1:5,sep='')
> colnames(ex)<- paste("T",1:4,sep='')
> ex1 = t(ex)%*%ex

>
> exNet = network(as.sociomatrix(ex))
> exNet1 = network(as.sociomatrix(ex1))

> exNet2 = network(as.sociomatrix(ex2))

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] how to manage a bipartite network
messages.body_plain:
I've been working with 2-mode networks a fair bit, and statnet isn't design
well for them.

I found the best way was to assign labels to all of them: for my dataset I'm
working with users and discussion threads, so for reading the data in I
pasted a "T" to the front of all my threads, which prevents actor 132
getting confused with thread T132.

Sam

messages.subject: [statnet_help] A Couple of Real Basic Questions
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] A Couple of Real Basic Questions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Philip,

> First, how do I attach covariates to the 10 by 10 matrix?

To attach covariates to an object of class network, you can use the 
set.vertex.attribute() function. For example:

nodeage<-c(10,12,10,11,9,13,14,23,21,21) # age of each node:
set.vertex.attribute(Data.net,"age",nodeage)

Identically, you could use:

Data.net %v% "age"<-nodeage

> The second question is how do I label the vertices in the matrix?

When you list the existing attributes in you network object, you see 
that a "vertex.name" atttribute already exist:

list.vertex.attributes(Data.net) #list existing vertex attributes

> Forgive me if I'm demonstrating my ignorance of any of the ergm package,
> Kevin's request, or bipartite networks generally, but since when does
> ergm (the package) support directed bipartite networks? I ask not out of
> pique, but as a methodological matter since it obviously changes the
> types of questions which can be asked. I would be very interested in
> seeing other papers that expand on such an approach.

Thanks, Brian. Indeed you're not demonstrating your ignorance of the 
package - I was!  I pretty much never use directed data, so I was 
answering Kevin's question more from the perspective of the sort of 
model that would in theory make sense given the question he was trying 
to answer, rather than what ergm would actually do. A quick double-check 
of ergm, via the following code:

a <- network.initialize(10,directed=T,bipartite=5)
b <- simulate(a~edges,theta0=100)
b[,]

indicates that indeed, ergm does not handle networks that are 
simultaneously bipartite and directed.  Mea culpa. (Note that the 
network package does, however).

> Second (and again I defer to others' expertise), it always struck me
> that modeling sexual interaction networks as bipartite was a
> complicating rather than simplifying assumption relative to modeling the
> network as unipartite with attributes (wholly apart from the
> heteronormative implications). I trust there is an underlying
> statistical rationale, but perhaps someone could hold my hand and
> elaborate for me why a bipartite approach would be superior to a
> unipartite with attributes approach which had null male-male,
> female-female interactions?

My feeling has always been that if you are modeling a system in which 
there are two types of nodes, and there is something structural (in the 
real world and.or in your model) that dictates that all ties must by 
definition be between nodes in the different sets, then it is cleanest 
to model it as bipartite.  It doesn't really matter waht consitutes 
those classes of nodes, as long as there is a cross-class requirement of 
some form or other.  Modeling it as unipartite with cross-class 
parameters fixed at -Inf (which is what happens if you send in a network 
with no ties across classes for estimation) is statistically equivalent, 
so from a practical standpoint I really don't think it matters.  To me 
it just seems cleaner.

I'm not sure what domain of data Kevin was modeling, and whether the 
requirement from all ties being cross-sex was something implicit in the 
phenomenon or a simplifying assumption that he added.  I guess a case 
could be made that for the former it's more philosophically reasonable 
to model it as bipartite, and for the latter it's more philosophically 
reasonable to model it as unipartite with nulls.  But in reality the 
distinction between the two is probably pretty fuzzy.

And, in this case, since ergm doesn't handle bipartite directed 
networks, it sounds like Kevin is going to have to go the route you 
suggest regardless of philosophical preferences!

I'd love to hear others' thoughts on this.

Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Measuring Density by Vertex Attribute
messages.body_plain:
Hi Philip,

There are two ways to accomplish this. The first method is based on the 
rDNA package and gives you binary or weighted within- and between-block 
densities. It takes a sociomatrix as input. Unfortunately, it is not 
very efficient. If I have time, I will reimplement it in C at some 
point. The second one is based on statnet. It gives you a mixing matrix 
and does not distinguish between valued and binary edges. But it is 
probably more efficient for larger networks. There you go:


# create a binary 10x10 matrix
mat <- matrix(rbinom(100,1,0.1), ncol=10)

# create a vector with attributes
attributes <- c(1,2,2,3,2,1,1,1,2,3)


### METHOD 1 using rDNA ###

install.packages("rJava")
install.packages("rDNA")
library(rDNA)

# convert attributes into one-column matrix
groups <- matrix(attributes, ncol=1)

# within- and between-block density values:
dna.density(mat, partitions=groups, weighted=FALSE)


### METHOD 2 using statnet ###

library(statnet)
nw <- network(mat)
set.vertex.attribute(nw, "attrib", attributes)
mixingmatrix(nw, "attrib")


Cheers,
Philip

messages.body_plain:
Jorge, Carter and others,

Thanks for raising an interesting issue and even bigger thanks for
providing very informative answers!

There is one thread I wanted to ask about. It's related to the
"choice" interpretation Carter wrote about, which is said to be not
always justified.

1. I recall Carter's talk on Zurich Workshop in 2008 (available online
here http://videolectures.net/cvss08_butts_mrwsd/) talking about a
connection between ERGMs and potential games. Have this connection
been explored in more detail? I'll be excited to read something about
it.

2. I also recall a "qualitative" passage in Snijders et al (special
issue of Social Networks, 2010) paper on SIENA models (which do have a
choice-theoretic foundation). They write that cross-sectional ERGMs
coincide with SIENA (would have the same parameter estimates), if the
modeled process is in dynamic equilibrium. Does this have anything to
do with:

> (For instance, one can also understand ERGMs in terms of the equilibrium
> behavior of certain types of Markov chains, an interpretation that
> has value in dynamic applications.)

?

BTW, I heard some rumors, corroborated with incomplete references on
some people's webpages, of an ERGM book coming out soon (i.e. 2011).
Does people here happen to know any more details?



Thanks,

~michal








On Tue, May 3, 2011 at 3:37 AM, Carter T. Butts <buttsc@uci.edu> wrote:
> Hi, Jorge -
>
> Your question raises some important issues that are too deep to address well
> in email. ?But I will take a stab at some of them....
>
> On 05/02/2011 10:08 AM, Jorge M Rocha wrote:
>>
>> ?From what I understand, the modeling framework of an ERGM treats the
>> observed network as the _dependent variable_ and the specified
>> structural configurations and covariate information about nodes/edges as
>> _independent variables_ whose presence/absence increases the
>> log-likelihood for the model.
>
> I think it is important to make some comment on this conceptual issue,
> because it lies at the core of one's thinking about the modeling process.
> ?(In so doing I will speak ex cathedra -- I trust that my colleagues will
> not be shy in administering correctives, should they find me to be in
> error.) ?In a standard ERGM without covariate effects, there are no
> independent variables (in a regression-like sense). ?The model is one large
> stochastic system, and is treated as fully endogenous. ?(Exogenous effects
> come about from the use of covariates, such as vertex attributes. ?Of
> course, these can also be endogenized, but that's a broader model class.)
> ?More to the point, the act of writing down an ERGM is the act of writing
> down a model for the joint probability distribution of a graph (i.e., the
> system state). ?The exponential family form provides the language in which
> we express that model; the content and the interpretation must come from
> elsewhere.
>
> Within this context, the role of statistics based on structural
> configurations is to parametrize the joint distribution of the edge
> structure. ?There are several formally equivalent ways to understand this.
> ?One natural one is to view the parameter associated with a given structural
> statistic as measuring the tendency of the expectation of that statistic to
> be higher or lower than what would be observed if the parameter in question
> were zero (equivalently, if it were not in the model). ?From this point of
> view, all ERGM parameters reflect different sorts of structural "biases" or
> "deviations" from the behavior of the uniform Bernoulli graph (i.e., the
> homogeneous Bernoulli graph in which every edge occurs with equal
> probability).
>
> Note that this is a "holistic" view of the network as a jointly interacting
> system -- if you are familiar with the Lagrangian or Hamiltonian
> formulations of classical mechanics (in which the behavior of a classical
> system is described by reference to a potential function), this may prove a
> useful analogy. ?In any event, it's very different from the "elementwise"
> view of networks that many folks are used to.
>
> For the latter, it can be helpful to think in terms of the full conditionals
> of the model -- the probability of a given edge being present, given the
> rest of the structure. ?This is a "local/elementwise" view, perhaps loosely
> analogous to the way that classical mechanics is taught to beginners (with
> "forces" acting on particles, the conditional behavior of which is defined
> in terms of the other particle states). This comports better with the
> intuition of most social scientists, but IMHO has many underappreciated
> pitfalls. ?Chief among these is the fact that one can easily forget that the
> elements of the system are indeed interacting, and the conditional behavior
> of one variable is only meaningful within the context of the rest of the
> network. ?(For an example of where this intuition led the field astray, one
> need only look at the rise and fall of pseudo-likelihood techniques.) ?One
> can also easily confuse conditional edge probabilities with propensities of
> _individuals_ to create edges (e.g., in a choice context), with which they
> are _not_ always synonymous. ?I am thus less sanguine about the "local" view
> of ERGMs than some of my colleagues, although there is no question that this
> perspective _can_ be very helpful.
>
> I want to stress that, properly understood, the holistic and elementwise
> views of the ERGM are both correct -- they are two equivalent ways of
> describing the same thing. ?Nor are these the only ways in which the
> formalism can be validly interpreted. ?(For instance, one can also
> understand ERGMs in terms of the equilibrium behavior of certain types of
> Markov chains, an interpretation that has value in dynamic applications.)
> ?But what all valid interpretations of the ERGM framework have in common is
> that they recognize that one is modeling a system of components, and those
> components can potentially interact with one another. ?As such, my sense is
> that regression-based thinking can be as much a hindrance as a help when
> learning about ERGMs, at least for most social scientists. ?(Those whose
> familiarity with statistical exponential families allows them to understand
> ERGMs within the broader context of "regression-like" models are exempted,
> but I daresay that this is not standard training for most social
> scientists.) ?That said, I often teach it that way, because the initial
> approachability of ERGMs as "logistic network regression with independence
> relaxations" is higher than "potential functions on graphs" for my students.
> ?YMMV.
>
> For an example of the use of the "local" view of ERGMs for model
> parametrization, I suggest the Goodreau et al. 2009 _Demography_ paper. ?For
> a different, "semi-local" view based on dependence among edges, one can find
> many good examples in the work of Pattison and Robins; their 2002
> _Sociological Methodology_ article comes to mind. ?(And, of course, there is
> the classic Frank and Strauss _JASA_ paper, among others.) ?The "holistic"
> view per se is less well-explored, although there are many precursors in
> structuralist theory. ?(The Harary wing of structural balance, for instance,
> operates entirely from a holistic standpoint. ?This is also where I insert
> my obligatory plug for Bruce Mayhew.) ?Mark Handcock's work on degeneracy
> (see, e.g., his 2003 chapter) has in my opinion very deep substantive
> implications from the holistic side, and there are some other recent
> technical contributions (e.g., a recent arXiv paper by Chatterjee and
> Diaconis) that are likewise promising. ?One could accumulate many more
> examples, of course.
>
>> In other words, what we want to achieve
>> in these models is to gain a better understanding of the types of
>> processes that might have gone into generating a network similar to the
>> observed one;
>
> That is one use of the framework, and certainly an important one.
>
>> hypotheses are about this or that configuration or
>> node/edge attribute and their effect on the pattern of social
>> interactions represented in the network.
>
> This is where we must be careful: a configuration does not "have" an effect
> on the network. ?One could say, however, that we hypothesize that our
> process of interest will result in networks in which certain configurations
> are over or underrepresented.
>
>> If so, how would I go about
>> testing hypotheses concerning the effects of social interactions on
>> nodal attributes (I?m particularly thinking of different types of
>> opinions individuals might tend to have based on their interactions)?
>
> That depends on whether the attributes affect the network. ?If the network
> structure is not affected by the attributes in question (e.g., because the
> former evolves over much longer time scales than the latter), then one need
> not model the network at all: one can condition on the network, and model
> the attributes (or, if one just wants to test a marginal hypothesis, employ
> an even simpler method such as a permutation test).
>
> If, on the time scale of interest, the network and the attributes both
> coevolve, then the ERGM language is not expressive enough: you need a joint
> attribute/network model. ?Such extensions do exist, although my sense is
> that it is difficult to identify such models without longitudinal data.
>
>>
>> What I?ve done so far is kind of arguing backwards (or at least that is
>> how it feels to me ?maybe because I?m coming from a traditional
>> linear/logit regression background, and probably part of my problem is
>> thinking in terms of DV and IV). ?If the coefficients are significant
>> for some node covariate of my interest in the ERGM estimation, then I?ve
>> been interpreting this as evidence that it is not unreasonable to argue
>> that the pattern of social interactions influences the type of opinion
>> individuals have (I know that if I had longitudinal data this issue of
>> reverse causality would not be so much of an issue, but so far all I
>> have is cross-sectional data). ?How wrong am I on this (the
>> backward-arguing)?
>
> There may be some settings in which this could give you the right answer,
> but I would discourage it unless you can prove that you are in one of those
> settings. ?If you are dealing with an attribute and a network that are
> jointly endogenous, then conditioning on the latter and not the former is
> not going to do what you want. ?If you just want to establish marginal
> association (e.g., those who are in certain positions tend to have certain
> kinds of opinions), I would lean towards a permutation test or similar
> procedure. ?If you really want to pull things apart, estimate parameters,
> test more complex hypotheses, etc., my opinion is that you should look for a
> joint attribute/network model. ?(We don't have one in statnet right now, but
> RSiena or pnet might.)
>
>>
>> Finally, part of my worry is that I?ll be sending the research to a
>> consumer behavior/marketing journal where the familiarity with social
>> network stuff ?let alone ERGM?s?is limited. ?Any suggestions on how to
>> best explain these issues to a non-specialized audience?
>
> Well, my _personal_ advice in your case would be to look closely at your
> problem, and try to figure out how much of it you can address without using
> complex network models -- it's going to be much easier to explain, say,
> permutation or CUG tests to such a readership than ERGMs. ?If you really
> must model the system as a whole, first determine whether you can reasonably
> approximate one portion (the network or the attribute) as being fixed
> relative to the other. ?(Some basic knowledge of your case is important
> here: do you have access to ethnographic, observational, or other
> information that might help you evaluate the plausibility of a one-way
> effect?) ?If you _can_ approximate one portion as fixed, model accordingly
> (e.g., if the network is fixed, you may want something like a network
> autocorrelation model, while fixed attributes suggest an ERGM). ?If you are
> stuck with having to model both the network and individual attributes
> jointly, you have my sympathy -- this is an exciting area of technical
> research, which generally implies a painful experience for the practitioner.
> ?Getting your hands on a reasonable cross-sectional network/attribute model
> is then a must, as is learning to use it properly (bearing in mind that, if
> the model is new, its creators may have only limited experience in that
> regard).
>
> This email has become both long and polemical, but these are important and
> frequently encountered questions. ?Perhaps these comments will prove helpful

steve, many thanks!!! re: the first part, i completely hadn't thought about the nodemix option, which in hindsight is pretty obvious- sorry for the brain lapse, but thanks for pointing me in the right direction :). this solution will work perfectly.

re: the second part, i apologize for the ambiguity- i think i was also jumping the gun a little bit. my original interest is indeed in whether men are more likely to reciprocate ties than women. i initially also figured that the "by" option would take care of this- but then realized that, because my network is bipartite, counting every mutual tie involving a female is identical to counting every mutual tie (because all mutual ties by definition involve a male and a female), and so the mutual term with the "by" option for women is identical to the generic mutual term by itself.

i see what you are saying about dyads either being reciprocal or not- but it seems to me that (even with cross-sectional data) one should be able to get at this difference- in a sense by comparing how many male --> female ties are returned with how many female --> male ties are returned. if virtually all of the asymmetric ties in a network are male --> female, for instance- and there are virtually no asymmetric female --> male ties- wouldn't this suggest that men are more likely to respond to women than women are to men? thus, i was trying to get at this with the transpose/edge covariate effect (we can ignore the additional income complication for the moment).

as it turns out, however, i DO have a timestamp for each tie- and so the network i'm using is actually a collapsed longitudinal network. given this information, i would love to hear any thoughts you might have on how to go about using this in order to disentangle the type of gender*reciprocity interaction i hope to get at :).

(happy to also take this offline, unless you think the list would benefit.)

thanks again!!!

-kevin

p.s. please forgive my complicated initial posing of the question in terms of the income question- it seems as though if we are able to get a solution to the basic male vs. female reciprocity issue above, then i would probably be able to extend this to define additional interaction effects between gender, reciprocity, and dyadic covariates.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Conflicting network indicators
messages.body_plain:
Hi Edzard,

I just tried the same thing with some of my directed data and got the same
results. I created an undirected network object from the directed edgelist,
with parameters directed=FALSE, multiple=FALSE. When I execute
"summary(network)", it shows a number of edges equal to the number of edges
in my original edgelist. However, if I execute "summary(network~edges)" it
shows a number of edges equal to the number of unreciprocated edges in the
original edgelist.

Note that neither figure is the number of edges we expect. Our expectation
is that an undirected network created from directed data where some ties
are reciprocated and others are not should have [(number of reciprocal
ties)/2 + (number of asymmetric ties)] edges.

I think the problem arises from viewing the "network" command as a tool for
data *conversion*, rather than as a function for network *definition*. When
we supply "directed=FALSE" to the network function, we are telling it what
kind of data we are supplying; we are not telling it how we want to convert
the data.

Anyway, try the following and see if it fixes your problem:

dir.net <- network(your.directed.edgelist)  # create a directed network
object using your directed edgelist data
undir.mat <- as.sociomatrix(dir.net) + t(as.sociomatrix(dir.net))  # create
an undirected sociomatrix by cell-wise adding the directed network to its
own transpose
undir.mat[undir.mat == 2] <- 1  # the previous step sets cell values to "2"
for reciprocal dyads; this recodes those cells to "1"
undir.net <- network(undir.mat, directed = FALSE)  # create an undirected
network object from the symmetrical/undirected sociomatrix
summary(undir.net)  # check that the stored number of edges is correct
summary(undir.net~edges)  # check that the reported number of edges matches

There's probably an easier, less cumbersome method but that should do the
trick.

--Dave

messages.body_plain:
greetings,

i have a couple questions i'm hoping someone can help with. i am working specifically with a large bipartite network (men/women), but i believe the questions are generally relevant. i am interested in including a number of effects in my models that aren't currently included in ergm-terms. i know there is a way for me to code up these terms myself (using the ergmuserterms package)- but for those of us whose programming knowledge is basic/non-existent, i'm wondering if other workarounds are available. specifically, i'm interested in the following two scenarios:

currently, there are terms available for homophily on a certain attribute (nodematch), and one can even break this down by the value of the attribute using diff=TRUE. so in my network, i can see if college-educated people tend to contact one another. instead, i want to know if the tendency towards educational homophily varies by gender- in other words, i want to see if the tendency for college-educated men to contact college-educated women is different from the tendency of college-educated women to contact college educated men. rather than coding a term for this effect, i wonder if instead i could just create an edge covariate (i.e. a new network X) in which, say, every possible tie from a college-educated male to a college-educated female is present. then, if i include two terms in the model- nodematch(collegeeducation) and edgecov(X)- the former term will essentially indicate educational homophily from women to men, while the latter will indicate educational homophily from men to women. is this accurate? (the same reasoning could therefore be extended to any number of scenarios, in which we expect homophily on covariate A to vary by covariate B.)

my second question is similar, but instead involves reciprocity (i appreciate the addition of the new "by" argument, by the way!). one example is that i want to know whether women are more likely to reciprocate ties to men with a similar income. let's say my network is called "network," and i have an edge covariate called "absdiffincome" indicating the absolute difference in income between every possible dyad. to find the answer to my question, my thought is that i could 1) begin with network, and drop all ties from women to men (i.e. keep only ties from men to women); 2) take the transpose of this network; and 3) code this transpose network with values from absdiffincome (i.e. cell-wise multiply the values of [transpose network] with the values of [absdiffincome]), and use this final network as a new edge covariate. am i totally off my rocker here, or would this actually produce the type of effect i am looking for? and if all of this happens to work as i think it might, are there any drawbacks to doing things this way other than the extra hassle?

many thanks, and apologies for the lengthy explanation!

-kevin

Cambridge, MA 02138

Hello Simone.  I notice that your edge list:

> 580 1124
> 792 1244
> 424 539
> 784 1275
> 288 1261
> 919 957

... does not have the property that all mode-1 nodes (actors, in many  
contexts) have smaller numbers than all mode-2 nodes (events).  In the  
network package, a bipartite network is specified by a non-NULL value  
of the "bipartite" flag, which then becomes the number of actors.  So  
I think it would be easy to coerce your network to bipartite if you  
first re-numbered all of your nodes so that all of the actors had  
labels 1 through the value of bipartite, then the events were bipartite 
+1 through n.

Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Measuring Density by Vertex Attribute
messages.body_plain:
The network matrix should have row names -- I forgot them in my example, 
sorry! It is also possible just to use a vector of attributes.

Try this:

mat <- matrix(rbinom(100,1,0.2), ncol=10)
rownames(mat) <- c("a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f", "g", "h", "i", "j")
attributes <- c(1,2,2,3,2,1,1,1,2,3)
dna.density(mat, attributes)

The method can also infer the appropriate attribute values from a larger 
attribute list by matching the row names:

mat <- matrix(rbinom(100,1,0.2), ncol=10)
rownames(mat) <- c("a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f", "g", "h", "i", "j")
attributes <- matrix(c(1,2,2,3,2,1,1,1,2,3,1,2,2,3,2,1,1,1,2,3))
row.names(attributes) <- c("a", "g", "b", "f", "l", "c", "m", "p", "d", 
"e", "g", "j", "i", "h", "k", "n", "o", "q", "r", "s")
dna.density(mat, attributes)

The result should look like this:

           1         2         3
1 0.3333333 0.2500000 0.1111111
2 0.3333333 0.4375000 0.2500000
3 0.2222222 0.3333333 0.3333333

Hope this helps,

Philip

Hi Tom,

Using summary(my.ergm)$coefs[,4] will extract the p-values as a vector, 
removing the header info in the process. If the rest of your code with 
all your models is writen as a loop, then you can simply have a line 
saving this vector into a different column of a data.frame (or any other 
similar object type). If you want to pull out the names of the terms as 
well to populate the row names of the data frame, then use 
rownames(summary(my.ergm)$coefs). When you're done you can export the 
full table into a variety of other formats using standard R functions 
(e.g. write.csv).

I hope that helps,
Steve

messages.body_plain:
Hello, everybody.
I have a basic question on the steps in model bilding and fitting. As far as
I could get , I need to get rid of degeneracy first and only after that add
meaningful parameters to my model.

I started from a very simple model: edges + mutual and began increasing
burn-in and MCMCsamplesize (from 100 000 and 10 000 respectively based on
Goodreau 2007 as I have directed network n=1209, e=5555) and got the
following model :

modela<-ergm(soc.net ~ edges + mutual, verbose = TRUE, control =
control.ergm(check.degeneracy = TRUE), burnin=400000, MCMCsamplesize=40000,
interval=1000)

which showed decent results accordint to MCMCdiagnostics. Although the
graphs for traces were not straight horisontal lines, the density started
approximate normal distribution and there were enough samples everywhere.

So, I decided to run the next model from the theta's of this one:

model1c<-ergm(soc.net ~ edges + mutual, verbose = FALSE, theta0 =
modela$coef, control = control.ergm(check.degeneracy = TRUE), burnin=400000,
MCMCsamplesize=40000, interval=1000)

But this one demonstrated worse results on MCMCdiagnostics: even the samples
were not enough.
So, here are my questions:

1) What is the order of steps? Am I doing it right or I should start
fighting degeneracy after entering all the parametres?
2) How increasing burnin and MCMCsamplesize from the model, reported to have
enough of samples for both of them, results lack of samples on the following
models?

Thanks in advance,
Alexander.

Kevin's comment about the relative eligibility of ties is an important
distinction I missed when thinking through the 1vs2 mode approaches.

Regarding the applicability of terms, I'm going off of pages 15 and 16 of
the Sunbelt statnet tutorial which implies that nodeifactor shouldn't apply
to bipartite networks:

http://csde.washington.edu/statnet/Resources/Sunbelt2011/ergm%20tutorial%20sunbelt%202011.pdf

To return to the distinction, I wonder if the nodeifactor is thus
calculating conditioned on all nodes (so that male-male, female-female,
male-female, female-male ties are all considered) rather than just
male-female, female-male nodes which "bipartite edges" appropriately does.

On Thu, Jul 14, 2011 at 3:30 PM, Lewis, Kevin <kmlewis@fas.harvard.edu>wrote:

> i believe the model is doing what it?s supposed to be doing. when i run a
> model solely with the edges term, the parameter estimate it gives me is
> identical to what i would expect if the network was being modeled as
> bipartite- in other words, the parameter estimate corresponds to the density
> of a BIPARTITE network (where only a subset of dyads are eligible), not a
> one-mode network (where all dyads are eligible). to confirm this, i took the
> exact same network, but converted it into a one-mode network instead- and
> indeed, when i do this and model the new network, the parameter estimate for
> ?edges? changes and now corresponds to the density of my network when all
> dyads are considered.****
>
> ** **
>
> also, i don?t see why one-mode terms shouldn?t apply to two-mode data. in
> my network below, the attribute ?female? happens to be identical to the
> partitioning of the network into two modes (according to gender). therefore,
> this term still tells me that women are more likely to receive ties than
> men- which, in this case, is identical to saying men send more ties than
> women.****
>
> ** **
>
> all this is to say, i believe ergm is indeed modeling my directed,
> bipartite network, and doing so correctly. which is good news, right? :)**
> **
>
> ** **
>
> -kevin****
>
> ** **
>
> *From:* briankeegan2008@u.northwestern.edu [mailto:
> briankeegan2008@u.northwestern.edu] *On Behalf Of *Brian Keegan

> *Cc:* Steven Goodreau; Steven Goodreau; statnet listserv (
> statnet_help@u.washington.edu)

>
> ** **
>
> I had been assuming you were using bipartite-specific parameters like
> b1factor, b1degree, etc. I guess I'm surprised it doesn't return any errors
> for using directed, one-mode parameters for your data which means it may be
> taking it as one-mode data despite your bipartite designation. I know some
> parameters (e.g., edges, 4-cycles, etc.) work across one and two-mode

> Maybe the program's been modeling it as one-mode all along unbeknownst to

> -----Original Message-----
> From: Steven Goodreau [mailto:goodreau@uw.edu]
> Sent: Thursday, July 14, 2011 2:36 PM
> To: Brian Keegan
> Cc: Lewis, Kevin; Steven Goodreau; statnet listserv (
> statnet_help@u.washington.edu)
> Subject: Re: [statnet_help] homemade ergm terms

>
> > Forgive me if I'm demonstrating my ignorance of any of the ergm package,
> > Kevin's request, or bipartite networks generally, but since when does
> > ergm (the package) support directed bipartite networks? I ask not out of
> > pique, but as a methodological matter since it obviously changes the
> > types of questions which can be asked. I would be very interested in
> > seeing other papers that expand on such an approach.
>
> Thanks, Brian. Indeed you're not demonstrating your ignorance of the
> package - I was!  I pretty much never use directed data, so I was
> answering Kevin's question more from the perspective of the sort of
> model that would in theory make sense given the question he was trying
> to answer, rather than what ergm would actually do. A quick double-check
> of ergm, via the following code:
>
> a <- network.initialize(10,directed=T,bipartite=5)
> b <- simulate(a~edges,theta0=100)
> b[,]
>
> indicates that indeed, ergm does not handle networks that are
> simultaneously bipartite and directed.  Mea culpa. (Note that the
> network package does, however).
>
> > Second (and again I defer to others' expertise), it always struck me
> > that modeling sexual interaction networks as bipartite was a
> > complicating rather than simplifying assumption relative to modeling the
> > network as unipartite with attributes (wholly apart from the
> > heteronormative implications). I trust there is an underlying
> > statistical rationale, but perhaps someone could hold my hand and
> > elaborate for me why a bipartite approach would be superior to a
> > unipartite with attributes approach which had null male-male,
> > female-female interactions?
>
> My feeling has always been that if you are modeling a system in which
> there are two types of nodes, and there is something structural (in the
> real world and.or in your model) that dictates that all ties must by
> definition be between nodes in the different sets, then it is cleanest
> to model it as bipartite.  It doesn't really matter waht consitutes
> those classes of nodes, as long as there is a cross-class requirement of
> some form or other.  Modeling it as unipartite with cross-class

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ergm question
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
First, thank you all for the comments (by Jacob, Filip, Tom, Carter, Dave &
Johan), they have been quite helpful both in terms of better understanding
the analytic logic(s) of ERGM's and how I could (maybe alternatively) go
about my research.
The distinction between *holistic* and *element-wise* conceptions of an ERGM
that Carter elaborated has been most informative (I'm not familiar with
classical mechanics, but in my past life I did some ecosystem energy-flow
modeling, so I do relate to the notion of a series of equations
stochastically describing the potential function of a system).  Apart from
section 3 of the paper on ERGM terms Dave suggested I don't believe I had
come across any explicit statement of why the usual dependent/independent
variable interpretation can be misleading.  I believe a published
elaboration of these notions would be a very helpful and welcome addition to
the ERGM literature, which to this point has been mostly of a technical
nature -for understandable reasons.
Based on the above, I think I now have a better idea of when it would be
advisable to employ an ERGM on my own research.  There are a couple of my
research interests that would indeed benefit from an ERGM since I do want to
model the whole network.  The particular question I had in mind when I wrote
my post to the forum, however, I now believe would be better addressed by
some form of a network autocorrelation model (I'll have to give it some
thought -some of the node attributes in which I'm interest are dichotomous,
some continuous. And being an anthropologist, I do have ethnographic
information ;-) ).
Again, thanks to all for the help

Jorge

-----Original Message-----
From: statnet_help-bounces@mailman2.u.washington.edu
[mailto:statnet_help-bounces@mailman2.u.washington.edu] On Behalf Of David
Hunter
Sent: Tuesday, May 03, 2011 7:27 AM
To: statnet_help list
Subject: Re: [statnet_help] ergm question

Hello Jorge.  One of the things Carter said reminded me of something:   
In contrasting the "holistic" and "elementwise" conceptions as he explains
them below, it's important to remember that every holistically-defined model
leads to a corresponding set of full  
conditionals (the elementwise model), but the converse is not true!   
In other words, one cannot necessarily define a (holistic) probability
distribution on networks merely by specifying a full set of  
conditional distributions of each edge given the rest of the network.   
I point this out because I *think* it's at some level another reason that
the usual dependent / independent variable interpretation is not applicable
to the ERGM situation.

There is some further discussion of the dependent / independent question and
a comparison with standard generalized linear models in Section 3 of
http://www.stat.psu.edu/~dhunter/papers/ergmuserterms.pdf

Best,
Dave




On May 2, 2011, at 9:37 PM, Carter T. Butts wrote:

> Hi, Jorge -
>
> Your question raises some important issues that are too deep to 
> address well in email.  But I will take a stab at some of them....
>
> On 05/02/2011 10:08 AM, Jorge M Rocha wrote:
>> From what I understand, the modeling framework of an ERGM treats the 
>> observed network as the _dependent variable_ and the specified 
>> structural configurations and covariate information about nodes/ 
>> edges as _independent variables_ whose presence/absence increases the 
>> log-likelihood for the model.
>
> I think it is important to make some comment on this conceptual issue, 
> because it lies at the core of one's thinking about the modeling 
> process.  (In so doing I will speak ex cathedra -- I trust that my 
> colleagues will not be shy in administering correctives, should they 
> find me to be in error.)  In a standard ERGM without covariate 
> effects, there are no independent variables (in a regression-like 
> sense).  The model is one large stochastic system, and is treated as 
> fully endogenous.  (Exogenous effects come about from the use of 
> covariates, such as vertex attributes.  Of course,
> these can also be endogenized, but that's a broader model class.)   
> More to the point, the act of writing down an ERGM is the act of 
> writing down a model for the joint probability distribution of a graph 
> (i.e., the system state).  The exponential family form provides the 
> language in which we express that model; the content and the 
> interpretation must come from elsewhere.
>
> Within this context, the role of statistics based on structural 
> configurations is to parametrize the joint distribution of the edge 
> structure.  There are several formally equivalent ways to understand 
> this.  One natural one is to view the parameter associated with a 
> given structural statistic as measuring the tendency of the 
> expectation of that statistic to be higher or lower than what would be 
> observed if the parameter in question were zero (equivalently, if it 
> were not in the model).  From this point of view, all ERGM parameters 
> reflect different sorts of structural "biases" or "deviations" from 
> the behavior of the uniform Bernoulli graph (i.e., the homogeneous 
> Bernoulli graph in which every edge occurs with equal probability).
>
> Note that this is a "holistic" view of the network as a jointly 
> interacting system -- if you are familiar with the Lagrangian or 
> Hamiltonian formulations of classical mechanics (in which the behavior 
> of a classical system is described by reference to a potential 
> function), this may prove a useful analogy.  In any event, it's very 
> different from the "elementwise" view of networks that many folks are 
> used to.
>
> For the latter, it can be helpful to think in terms of the full 
> conditionals of the model -- the probability of a given edge being 
> present, given the rest of the structure.  This is a "local/ 
> elementwise" view, perhaps loosely analogous to the way that classical 
> mechanics is taught to beginners (with "forces" acting on particles, 
> the conditional behavior of which is defined in terms of the other 
> particle states). This comports better with the intuition of most 
> social scientists, but IMHO has many underappreciated pitfalls.  Chief 
> among these is the fact that one can easily forget that the elements 
> of the system are indeed interacting, and the conditional behavior of 
> one variable is only meaningful within the context of the rest of the 
> network.  (For an example of where this intuition led the field 
> astray, one need only look at the rise and fall of pseudo-likelihood 
> techniques.)  One can also easily confuse conditional edge 
> probabilities with propensities of _individuals_ to create edges 
> (e.g., in a choice context), with which they are _not_ always 
> synonymous.  I am thus less sanguine about the "local" view of ERGMs 
> than some of my colleagues, although there is no question that this 
> perspective _can_ be very helpful.
>
> I want to stress that, properly understood, the holistic and 
> elementwise views of the ERGM are both correct -- they are two 
> equivalent ways of describing the same thing.  Nor are these the only 
> ways in which the formalism can be validly interpreted.  (For 
> instance, one can also understand ERGMs in terms of the equilibrium 
> behavior of certain types of Markov chains, an interpretation that has 
> value in dynamic applications.)  But what all valid interpretations of 
> the ERGM framework have in common is that they recognize that one is 
> modeling a system of components, and those components can potentially 
> interact with one another.  As such, my sense is that regression-based 
> thinking can be as much a hindrance as a help when learning about 
> ERGMs, at least for most social scientists.  (Those whose familiarity 
> with statistical exponential families allows them to understand ERGMs 
> within the broader context of "regression-like" models are exempted, 
> but I daresay that this is not standard training for most social 
> scientists.)  That said, I often teach it that way, because the 
> initial approachability of ERGMs as "logistic network regression with 
> independence relaxations"
> is higher than "potential functions on graphs" for my students.  YMMV.
>
> For an example of the use of the "local" view of ERGMs for model 
> parametrization, I suggest the Goodreau et al. 2009 _Demography_ 
> paper.  For a different, "semi-local" view based on dependence among 
> edges, one can find many good examples in the work of Pattison and 
> Robins; their 2002 _Sociological Methodology_ article comes to mind.  
> (And, of course, there is the classic Frank and Strauss _JASA_ paper, 
> among others.)  The "holistic" view per se is less well-explored, 
> although there are many precursors in structuralist theory.  (The 
> Harary wing of structural balance, for instance, operates entirely 
> from a holistic standpoint.  This is also where I insert my obligatory 
> plug for Bruce Mayhew.)  Mark Handcock's work on degeneracy (see, 
> e.g., his 2003 chapter) has in my opinion very deep substantive 
> implications from the holistic side, and there are some other recent 
> technical contributions (e.g., a recent arXiv paper by Chatterjee and 
> Diaconis) that are likewise promising.  One could accumulate many more 
> examples, of course.
>
>> In other words, what we want to achieve in these models is to gain a 
>> better understanding of the types of processes that might have gone 
>> into generating a network similar to the observed one;
>
> That is one use of the framework, and certainly an important one.
>
>> hypotheses are about this or that configuration or node/edge 
>> attribute and their effect on the pattern of social interactions 
>> represented in the network.
>
> This is where we must be careful: a configuration does not "have" an 
> effect on the network.  One could say, however, that we hypothesize 
> that our process of interest will result in networks in which certain 
> configurations are over or underrepresented.
>
>> If so, how would I go about
>> testing hypotheses concerning the effects of social interactions on 
>> nodal attributes (I'm particularly thinking of different types of 
>> opinions individuals might tend to have based on their interactions)?
>
> That depends on whether the attributes affect the network.  If the 
> network structure is not affected by the attributes in question (e.g., 
> because the former evolves over much longer time scales than the 
> latter), then one need not model the network at all: one can condition 
> on the network, and model the attributes (or, if one just wants to 
> test a marginal hypothesis, employ an even simpler method such as a 
> permutation test).
>
> If, on the time scale of interest, the network and the attributes both 
> coevolve, then the ERGM language is not expressive enough: you need a 
> joint attribute/network model.  Such extensions do exist, although my 
> sense is that it is difficult to identify such models without 
> longitudinal data.
>
>>
>> What I've done so far is kind of arguing backwards (or at least that 
>> is how it feels to me -maybe because I'm coming from a traditional 
>> linear/logit regression background, and probably part of my problem 
>> is thinking in terms of DV and IV).  If the coefficients are 
>> significant for some node covariate of my interest in the ERGM 
>> estimation, then I've been interpreting this as evidence that it is 
>> not unreasonable to argue that the pattern of social interactions 
>> influences the type of opinion individuals have (I know that if I had 
>> longitudinal data this issue of reverse causality would not be so 
>> much of an issue, but so far all I have is cross-sectional data).  
>> How wrong am I on this (the backward-arguing)?
>
> There may be some settings in which this could give you the right 
> answer, but I would discourage it unless you can prove that you are in 
> one of those settings.  If you are dealing with an attribute and a 
> network that are jointly endogenous, then conditioning on the latter 
> and not the former is not going to do what you want.  If you just want 
> to establish marginal association (e.g., those who are in certain 
> positions tend to have certain kinds of opinions), I would lean 
> towards a permutation test or similar procedure.  If you really want 
> to pull things apart, estimate parameters, test more complex 
> hypotheses, etc., my opinion is that you should look for a joint 
> attribute/network model.  (We don't have one in statnet right now, but 
> RSiena or pnet might.)
>
>>
>> Finally, part of my worry is that I'll be sending the research to a 
>> consumer behavior/marketing journal where the familiarity with social 
>> network stuff -let alone ERGM's-is limited.  Any suggestions on how 
>> to best explain these issues to a non-specialized audience?
>
> Well, my _personal_ advice in your case would be to look closely at 
> your problem, and try to figure out how much of it you can address 
> without using complex network models -- it's going to be much easier 
> to explain, say, permutation or CUG tests to such a readership than 
> ERGMs.  If you really must model the system as a whole, first 
> determine whether you can reasonably approximate one portion (the
> network or the attribute) as being fixed relative to the other.   
> (Some basic knowledge of your case is important here: do you have 
> access to ethnographic, observational, or other information that might 
> help you evaluate the plausibility of a one-way effect?)  If you _can_ 
> approximate one portion as fixed, model accordingly (e.g., if the 
> network is fixed, you may want something like a network 
> autocorrelation model, while fixed attributes suggest an ERGM).  If 
> you are stuck with having to model both the network and individual 
> attributes jointly, you have my sympathy -- this is an exciting area 
> of technical research, which generally implies a painful experience 
> for the practitioner.  Getting your hands on a reasonable cross- 
> sectional network/attribute model is then a must, as is learning to 
> use it properly (bearing in mind that, if the model is new, its 
> creators may have only limited experience in that regard).
>
> This email has become both long and polemical, but these are important 
> and frequently encountered questions.  Perhaps these comments will 
> prove helpful to you, and to others here who are struggling with the 
> same issues.
>
> Good luck!
>
> -Carter
> _______________________________________________
> statnet_help mailing list
> statnet_help@u.washington.edu
> http://mailman2.u.washington.edu/mailman/listinfo/statnet_help

messages.subject: [statnet_help] network.update and graphs operators
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

(package ergm 2.3 / windows x64)

The following illustrates some unwanted (?) feature of network.update
when used with simulate.ergm / ergm.getMCMCsample.

------------------------
#initialize network & put some links
nw = network.initialize(5,directed=F)
nw[1,2] = 1
nw[2,3] = 1
# nw has 2 links

#update link lists with smaller vertex 1st
newedgelist.small.ID.1st.col = matrix(c(1,2,3,4,2,3,5,5),ncol=2)
nw.small.1st = network.update(nw,newedgelist.small.ID.1st.col,"edgelist")

#update link lists with larger vertex first
newedgelist.large.ID.1st.col = matrix(c(2,3,5,5,1,2,3,4),ncol=2)
nw.large.1st = network.update(nw,newedgelist.large.ID.1st.col,"edgelist")

#then compute difference
nw.small.1st - nw # -> gives a network with 2 links, as should be
nw.large.1st - nw # gives a network with 4 links...

-------------------------------

It is indeed said in the network.update documentation that when updating
an undirected graph, the smallest IDs should come first. (consistent
with the 1st behaviour).

HOWEVER... ergm.getMCMCsample returns a 'newedgelist' where the larger
IDs are in the first column, and the code in simulate.formula uses
network.update.
This leads to surprises when arithmetic is done on networks obtained by
simulation.

Cheers

messages.subject: [statnet_help] homemade ergm terms
messages.body_plain:
> Forgive me if I'm demonstrating my ignorance of any of the ergm package,
> Kevin's request, or bipartite networks generally, but since when does
> ergm (the package) support directed bipartite networks? I ask not out of
> pique, but as a methodological matter since it obviously changes the
> types of questions which can be asked. I would be very interested in
> seeing other papers that expand on such an approach.

Thanks, Brian. Indeed you're not demonstrating your ignorance of the 
package - I was!  I pretty much never use directed data, so I was 
answering Kevin's question more from the perspective of the sort of 
model that would in theory make sense given the question he was trying 
to answer, rather than what ergm would actually do. A quick double-check 
of ergm, via the following code:

a <- network.initialize(10,directed=T,bipartite=5)
b <- simulate(a~edges,theta0=100)
b[,]

indicates that indeed, ergm does not handle networks that are 
simultaneously bipartite and directed.  Mea culpa. (Note that the 
network package does, however).

> Second (and again I defer to others' expertise), it always struck me
> that modeling sexual interaction networks as bipartite was a
> complicating rather than simplifying assumption relative to modeling the
> network as unipartite with attributes (wholly apart from the
> heteronormative implications). I trust there is an underlying
> statistical rationale, but perhaps someone could hold my hand and
> elaborate for me why a bipartite approach would be superior to a
> unipartite with attributes approach which had null male-male,
> female-female interactions?

My feeling has always been that if you are modeling a system in which 
there are two types of nodes, and there is something structural (in the 
real world and.or in your model) that dictates that all ties must by 
definition be between nodes in the different sets, then it is cleanest 
to model it as bipartite.  It doesn't really matter waht consitutes 
those classes of nodes, as long as there is a cross-class requirement of 
some form or other.  Modeling it as unipartite with cross-class 
parameters fixed at -Inf (which is what happens if you send in a network 
with no ties across classes for estimation) is statistically equivalent, 
so from a practical standpoint I really don't think it matters.  To me 
it just seems cleaner.

I'm not sure what domain of data Kevin was modeling, and whether the 
requirement from all ties being cross-sex was something implicit in the 
phenomenon or a simplifying assumption that he added.  I guess a case 
could be made that for the former it's more philosophically reasonable 
to model it as bipartite, and for the latter it's more philosophically 
reasonable to model it as unipartite with nulls.  But in reality the 
distinction between the two is probably pretty fuzzy.

And, in this case, since ergm doesn't handle bipartite directed 
networks, it sounds like Kevin is going to have to go the route you 
suggest regardless of philosophical preferences!

I'd love to hear others' thoughts on this.

Steve

>     also jumping the gun a little bit. my original interest is indeed in
>     whether men are more likely to reciprocate ties than women. i
>     initially also figured that the "by" option would take care of this-
>     but then realized that, because my network is bipartite, counting
>     every mutual tie involving a female is identical to counting every
>     mutual tie (because all mutual ties by definition involve a male and
>     a female), and so the mutual term with the "by" option for women is
>     identical to the generic mutual term by itself.
>
>     i see what you are saying about dyads either being reciprocal or
>     not- but it seems to me that (even with cross-sectional data) one

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

So, indeed, ergm should *not* currently be used with networks that are 
both bipartite and directed.  This should be consistent with all of the 
documentation out there; if anyone knows of documentation that we've 
produced that says (or even suggests) otherwise, please point us to it 
so we can correct it.

The reason this is, is that the MCMC estimation code treats all 
bipartite networks as undirected, and only proposes toggles Yij where i 
and j are of different bipartite classes (i.e. of different modes of a 
two-mode network), and i<j. It is the last criterion that makes it work 
for undirected networks, but not for directed.

Some of the confusion arises from the fact that we put in error messages 
to block users from using ergm terms with directed bipartite networks 
for some terms and not others.  Specifically, for those terms that are 
specific to bipartite networks (e.g. b1degree), we put in checks for 
both bipartiteness and for directedness.  However, for those terms that 
are not bipartite-specific (nodeifactor), we didn't do a double-check 
and block those fitting both criteria. Kevin appears to have only used 
terms in the latter category, so didn't get an error.

We will add errors to all terms to make sure they prevent use on 
directed bipartite networks in the next update of ergm.

Note again that the network package can handle with directed bipartite 
networks. This limitation is specific to ergm, given the complexities of 
the MCMC estimation code.

I imagine some of you are wondering if we plan to add capabilities to 
ergm for directed bipartite networks in the future.  As far as I know it 
hasn't been on the (already long) list of things to do (but other 
statnet developers, correct me if I'm wrong on that).  However, a large 
show of hands from those who are interested in such capability could 
help prioritize it.  If you're in that camp, feel free to email me and 
let me know (no need to copy the entire listserv).

Thanks for bringing this up, Kevin, and thanks to Brian for helping to 
clarify.

Steve
(+statnet team)

messages.body_plain:
I'm currently delving into the world of writing/modifying my own ergm
terms, and I'm sure I'm not the only one. Steven Goodreau suggested to me

writing their own ergm.userterms. Is anyone else interested in this
possibility?

On 06/15/2011 05:10 PM, Victorin Luisier wrote:
> Hi Thomas,
>
> Actually, p-values are computed each time you ask for a summary of an
> ergm model [summary(my.model)]. Unfortunately, the "summary.ergm"
> function is not designed to store p-values, but a very slight
> modification of this function, like below, is possible:
>
> ### Just copy the code below and then type
> mespval<-pvalergm(<my_ergm_model>) to store your p-values...
>
> pvalergm<-function (object, ...)
> {
> pseudolikelihood <- is.null(object$samplesize) ||
> is.na(object$samplesize) # si $mcmcsamplesize n'est pas nul ou manquant,
> cela veut dire que l'estimation ne s'est pas faite par pseudolikelihood.
> independence <- is.dyad.independent(object) # mod?le ? ind?pendance
> dyadique?
> if (any(is.na(object$coef)) & !is.null(object$mplefit)) {
> object$coef[is.na(object$coef)] <- object$mplefit$coef[is.na(object$coef)]
> } # Si un des estimateurs ML obtenus par MCMC manque, remplace par les
> estimateurs Max pseudolikelihood.
> if (is.null(object$hessian) && is.null(object$covar)) {
> return()
> } # si la matrice hessienne ET la matrice des covariances estim?es
> (covar) n'existent pas, ne renvoie rien. La suite s'applique aux autres
> situations:
> nodes <- network.size(object$network) # nb de nodes
> dyads <- network.dyadcount(object$network) # nb de dyades
> if (is.null(object$covar)) {
> asycov <- try(robust.inverse(-object$hessian), silent = TRUE)
> if (inherits(asycov, "try-error")) {
> asycov <- diag(1/diag(-object$hessian))
> } # si $covar est null, essaie de calculer asycov ? partir de $hessian
> }
> else {
> asycov <- object$covar # si covar existe, asycov en est une copie.
> ## Le if qui suit me para?t bizarre, car jamais TRUE? C'est p? une
> ancienne partie de code qui a ?t? d?sactiv?e...
> if (FALSE & !pseudolikelihood & !independence) {
> if (is.directed(object$network)) {
> mdyads <- nodes * (nodes - 1)
> }
> else {
> mdyads <- nodes * (nodes - 1)/2
> }
> asycov <- asycov * mdyads/dyads
> object$mc.se <- object$mc.se * sqrt(mdyads/dyads)
> }
> }
> rownames(asycov) <- names(object$coef)
> colnames(asycov) <- rownames(asycov)
> asyse <- diag(asycov) # asyse = variance des param?tres
> asyse[asyse < 0 | is.infinite(object$coef) | object$offset] <- NA
> asyse <- sqrt(asyse) # asyse = ecart-type des param?tres
> if (any(is.na(asyse) & !object$offset) & !is.null(object$mplefit)) {
> if (is.null(object$mplefit$covar)) {
> if (!is.null(object$mplefit$covar)) {
> mpleasycov <- try(robust.inverse(-object$mplefit$hessian),
> silent = TRUE)
> if (inherits(mpleasycov, "try-error")) {
> mpleasycov <- diag(1/diag(-object$mplefit$hessian))
> }
> asyse[is.na(asyse)] <- sqrt(diag(mpleasycov))[is.na(asyse)]
> }
> }
> else {
> mpleasycov <- object$mplefit$covar
> asyse[is.na(asyse)] <- sqrt(diag(mpleasycov))[is.na(asyse)]
> }
> } # Si certains ?carts-types de param?tres ne sont pas disponibles

messages.body_plain:
Hi Wang,

Once you have your object of class network, you can use the 
set.vertex.attribute() function to add vertex attributes. You can also 
use the wrapper "%v%". Here is a simple example:

# Initialize an empty network:
net<-network.initialize(7)

# Define a vertex attribute defining the age of each node:
nodeage<-c(10,12,10,11,9,13,14)
set.vertex.attribute(net,"age",nodeage)

#Or identically, you can do:
net %v% "age" <-nodeage

# To list all existing vertex attributes:
list.vertex.attributes(net)

Hope this helps,
Victorin

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Re: Longest path algorithm?
messages.body_plain:
Hello again,

Let me elucidate one point. I know that the longest path problem is
NP-complete, but I was wondering whether there exist any approximate
optimization techniques (like, for instance, on modularity
maximization for community detection, which is also NP-complete).

In any case, I should say that part of my problem is not so general
and perhaps you may be able to suggest to me another idea to deal with
it. As a matter of fact, I am interested in determining pairs of
vertices (let's say in a simple undirected graph) which are joined
together by (possibly multiple) paths having the same length (and
finding this unique path length for each pair of such vertices). In
other words, this is the case when geodesic paths are also maximal
length paths. Notice that I'd also like to include the degenerate case
of closed paths (of length larger or equal to three) between a vertex
and itself, i.e., cycles passing from a vertex. In this particular
case, I'm interested in determining vertices from which at most one
cycle might pass (and the period of these cycles).

My motivation for this computation is to be able to formulate problems
of transitivity (local clustering, small-worldedness, structural holes
etc.) in a more formal way (graph-theoretically) than in the existing
approaches.

Any clues?

Best,

--Moses

> Hello,
>
> I am a new user of statnet and I work on sexual relationship in  
> France with egocentric data.
>
> To be familiar with statnet function,I am trying to build a network  
> of 53 edges by  using the function san(). I have many problems to  
> find the network i expect:
>
> each vertex can have 0 to 3 edges
> relationship can only be heterosexual (reason why I use a bipartite  
> network)
> Vertices can have two different type of edges: regular and occasional
> each vertex can have 1 or 2 regular partner but a vertex with this  
> attribute can have an occasional relationship with a vertex  having  
> the  'regular'  attribute. That is the problem, I have tried to  
> introduce this attribute in many different fonction and I always  
> have problems with my final edge count:
>
> N=network.initialize(100,directed=FALSE,bipartite=50)
>
> sex=c(rep('F',50),rep('M',50))
> nbpart=c(rep(1,40),rep(2,5),3,rep(0,4),rep(1,30),rep(2,10),3,rep(0,9))

> regularF=c(rep('Y',20),rep('N',20),rep('Y',3),rep('N',2),rep('N', 
> 5),rep('N',50))
>
> N %v% 'sex'=sex

> N %v% 'nbpartF'= nbpartF
> N %v% 'nbpartM'= nbpartM
> N %v% 'regular'= regular

> N %v% 'regularM'= regularM
>
>
>

> S=san(N~edges 
> + 
> degree 
> (1 
> : 
> 3 
> ,'sex 
> '),meanstats 
> = 
> c

> ),nsim 
> = 
> 1 
> ,burnin 
> = 
> 4000000 
> ,MCMCsamplesize 
> =2000000,sequential=TRUE,interval=1000,constraints=~bd(maxout=3))
> summary(S~edges+degree(0:5)+degree(0:5,'sex'))
>

I double-checked and the above worked for me too.


> #introducing 'regular' partnership (all vertice with this attribute  
> have an edge with a vertex with this attribute)
>
> S1=san(N~edges+degree(1:3,'sex') 
> + 
> nodematch 
> ('regular 
> ',diff 
> = 
> TRUE 
> ,keep 
> = 
> 2 
> ),meanstats 
> = 
> c 
> (53,40,5,1,30,10,1,24 
> ),nsim 
> = 
> 1 
> ,burnin 
> = 
> 4000000 
> ,MCMCsamplesize 
> =3000000,sequential=TRUE,interval=1000,constraints=~bd(maxout=3))
> summary(S1~edges+degree(0:5)+degree(0:5,'sex')+degree(0:5,'regular'))
> mixingmatrix(S1,'regular')
>

I'm not sure why the degree distributions above are not matching your  
meanstats vector.  I notice that the edges and nodematch statistics do  
match perfectly in my simulations, though, so I'm wondering whether it  
is simply impossible, or at least very difficult, to construct a  
network with the male and female degree(1:3) statistics you specify  
such that there are 24 regular-regular matches.   Can you construct  
such an example by hand?

As far as I can tell, the edgecov method is equivalent to the  
nodematch method.  Do you find the same results using both of them?

I hope this helps for now.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Interpreting Goodness of fit
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

The information on dependence factors, enough burn-in, and enough 
samples is given to you through the CODA library (when you use the 
mcmc.diagnostics() function). This small article will probably help you:

Plummer, M., Best, N., Cowles, K., & Vines, K. (2006). CODA: Convergence 
diagnosis and output analysis for MCMC. R News, 6(1), 7?11.

See also the raftery.diag help page:
library(coda)
?raftery.diag

Best regards,
Victorin

On 02/27/2012 06:00 PM, Weare, Christopher wrote:
> I would appreciate some help on the interpretation of some of the
> details of GOF diagnostics. I have estimated an ERGM on a network of 85
> neighborhood councils, and the results look good. I have statistically
> significant estimates of coefficients, and they remain stable with
> slightly different model specifications. By increasing the MCMC samples
> I have reduced the MCMC standard errors to at least an order of
> magnitude smaller than the estimated standard errors. The GOF
> diagnostics (which are too large to attach) show that 95% bands of the
> simulated networks based on the model are in line with the observed
> network, and the traces of coefficient estimates do not show any trends.
>
> My main concern is the interpretation of the information on dependence
> factors, enough burn-in, and enough samples. In that table, I have many
> coefficients for which I am told there is not enough burn in and not
> enough samples. How should that information affect my interpretation of
> the GOF diagnostics? I have scanned through the archives of this

> thecols <- col(x)[x>0]
