messages.subject: [statnet_help] MCMC standard errors
messages.body_plain:
Hi Pavel,

This perfectly answers both of my questions- thanks so much! And we appreciate your work on the bug.

-Kevin

-----Original Message-----
From: statnet_help-bounces@mailman2.u.washington.edu [mailto:statnet_help-bounces@mailman2.u.washington.edu] On Behalf Of Pavel N. Krivitsky
Sent: Saturday, June 29, 2013 12:12 AM
To: statnet_help@u.washington.edu
Subject: Re: [statnet_help] MCMC standard errors

Hi, Kevin,

> 1. The ergm command currently provides as part of the output "MCMC %."
> Can someone explain precisely what this means? (i.e. I understand that 
> there are two components to the standard error when using MCMC- so 
> does the percentage refer to the proportion of the reported SE that is 
> due to the MCMC process- and therefore the reported SE's and p-values 
> already reflect both types of SE's- or is it an extra percentage that 
> should somehow be "added on"?)

The SE reported includes the MCMC error, and the percentage is the percentage of the *variance* due to MCMC: SEmcmc^2 / (SEmcmc^2 +
SEmodel^2) * 100%.

> Additionally, is there any guidance for how big we should usually 
> expect these %'s to be, or techniques to minimize them? (Other than 
> the standard recommendations in the documentation for improving 
> convergence.)

Other than the standard recommendations --- increase MCMC sample size and/or interval, write a better MCMC sampler, etc. --- I don't have any.

> 2. For some reason, whenever I run a model that includes a coefficient 
> that cannot be estimated (for instance, let's say I am modeling an 
> academic network and I include a nodematch term for sociologists, but 
> there are no ties between sociologists so the parameter is fixed at 
> "-Inf"), all of my MCMC %'s appear as "NA" instead of an actual number.
> Is there a reason for this; and should I be concerned about it? E.g.
> does this mean that the reported SE's are not conservative enough 
> because they don't incorporate the extra MCMC SE?

No, this is a long-standing bug in a rather involved part of ergm, where models with any offset terms (not just the +-Inf ones from dropping) broke the MCMC SE calculation. Having taken another look, I think I know how to fix it, though, so we'll probably have it working in the next release.

                   I hope this helps,
                   Pavel

On Wed, Jul 31, 2013 at 5:45 PM, Steven Goodreau <goodreau@uw.edu> wrote:

> Hello Ngoni,
>
> My guess is that you attached the igraph package to your session after you
> attached statnet.  Unfortunately, when igraph was developed in 2006, the
> author used some function names that were already in use in the network
> package (the latter on CRAN at the time as an independent package, and then
> subsequently part of the statnet suite).  That means that now, if one
> attaches both, then whichever one gets attached later will be the source of
> the functions drawn when they are shared. If you're trying to use statnet
> functionality, this can cause problems, as it is expecting the network
> functionality, but if you attach igraph later it uses igraph functionality.
>
> One piece of evidence that suggests this is that it says
>
>
> Error in is.directed(x) : Not a graph object
>
> package 'network' uses 'network' objects, and package 'igraph' uses
> 'graph' objects.
>
> If you're trying to use statnet functionality (e.g. ergm), I'd recommend
> either sticking with network for your data management, or, if you do want
> some of the additional igraph functionality, to make sure to attach igraph
> before statnet, so that it won't override some of the network functions.
>
> Hope that helps,
> Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] rem.dyad terms in relevent in R
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] rem.dyad terms in relevent in R
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Mark.  You are indeed correct: the P-shift terms relate to the next 
event in the sequence, while the R* terms reflect overall recency in 
terms of events ever received (RRec) or sent (RSnd) by the focal actor.

The statistics associated with these terms are described formally in:

Butts, C.T. (2008). "A Relational Event Framework for Social Action."  
Sociological Methodology, 38(1), 155-200.

Note that, as a general matter, RRecSnd and PSAB-BA involve distinct 
types of reciprocity, and both can be active within the same exchange.  
The former reflects the tendency of ego to send to alters who have most 
recently directed events to him or her (relative to other alters who 
have directed events towards ego); this depends only on ego's incoming 
event history, and not on other activity within the event sequence.  By 
contrast, the latter reflects temporally local turn-taking dynamics (the 
tendency of the next event to be a response from the last receiver to 
the last sender), and is not egocentric in character.  If you are 
dealing with a small-group setting, you will probably find P-shift 
effects (including the AB-BA shift) to be quite important; in a setting 
where actions are not globally observable (e.g., email), such effects 
are typically contraindicated.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

In the current case, the above error results from (a) the class of object referenced in the LHS of the formula passed to the function "summary;" and (b) my confusion regarding the expected class of object returned from a call to networkDynamic::network.extract. messages.subject: [statnet_help] How to interpret ergm results
messages.body_plain:
Dear folks,

I'm reading a tutorial about ergm. It used florentine data and commands as follows:

> set.seed(0)
> flomodel.02<-ergm(flomarriage~edges+triangle)
> summary(flomodel.02)

Then we got the results like this:

Formula:   flomarriage ~ edges + triangle
Iterations:  20 
Monte Carlo MLE Results:
         Estimate Std. Error MCMC % p-value    
edges     -1.6791     0.3523      0  <1e-04 ***
triangle   0.1646     0.5906      0   0.781    
---
Signif. codes:  0 ?***? 0.001 ?**? 0.01 ?*? 0.05 ?.? 0.1 ? ? 1 
    Null  Deviance: 166.355  on 120  degrees of freedom
 Residual Deviance: 108.074  on 118  degrees of freedom
          Deviance:  58.282  on   2  degrees of freedom
 
AIC: 112.07    BIC: 117.65 

I am not sure below:
1) What's the acceptable values and perfect values of AIC and BIC?

2) In the tutorial, it said:
"Conditional log-odds of two actor forming a tie is:
-1.680*change in the number of ties0.169*change in number of trianges"
Where does 0.169 come from? Does "change in number of trianges" equal to 3?

3) The tutorial also had:
If the tie will not add any triangles to the network, its log-odds is -1.680
If it will add one triangle to the network, its log-odds is: -1.680+0.169=-1.510
If it will add two triangles to the network, its log-odds is: -1.680+0.169*2=-1.341
Then the corresponding probalilities are 0.157, 0.181, and 0.207
How do we calculate these probalilities?

Any help would be highly appreciated. Thank you very much in advance:)

Best,
Shupin

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Network Layout For Valued Networks
messages.body_plain:
That's not a mistake - there is no general way to alter a layout based 
on edge values, and thus this is not done by default.  Particular layout 
routines, however, may accept such information, and you can of course 
add your own quite easily; see ?network.layout and ?gplot.layout (in 
sna) for details.  For layouts that support edge value information (e.g. 
Kamada-Kawai) you can pass it via the layout.par argument.  The exact 
syntax will depend on the layout function, and should be found in the 
above man pages.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] missing data on node attributes
messages.body_plain:
Hi, David.  Missing data on attributes makes certain kinds of 
changescores indeterminate; there are ways to deal with that, but IIRC 
they're not currently built into ergm.  (The main exceptions are some 
categorical terms that by default treat NA as if it were a distinct 
category.)  I was actually under the impression that ergm _always_ 
produced an error when the changescore was poorly defined, so if you 
were able to fit those models before, that might have been due to a bug 
that was fixed.  :-)

Mark and Ian have been thinking about this problem more than I have, and 
so may have a grander suggestion than my pragmatic one. My short-term 
suggestion would be to estimate your model via a two-stage procedure: 
first, impute your missing attribute data using a standard imputation 
method; and second, fit the ergm given the imputed data.  (It would 
probably be wise to create multiple imputed data sets in this manner, 
and examine the distribution of estimates across imputed values.)  This 
is not 100% ideal, but will probably work well so long as the results 
are not very sensitive to the missing values.  If the results _are_ 
sensitive to the missing values (something you can determine by looking 
at the distribution of estimates across imputed data sets), then you are 
likely in a bad spot regardless, and no method is going to be entirely 
trustworthy.  (See also, "you can only get a loan when you don't need it.")

By contrast, if you have missing data in the edges, ergm will indeed 
handle that.  (Or, at least, it will try.  You may still lack the power 
needed to answer your question of interest!)  The approach employed is 
the latent missing data technique developed by Gile and Handcock.

Hope that helps!

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] commands from ergm tutorial take too long to complete
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] commands from ergm tutorial take too long to complete
messages.body_plain:
Hello Szabolcs,

Indeed, with that set of versions you had, it appears that the tutorial 
does go into silence for a long time there.  As you figured out, this is 
a result of the fact that this case is pathological, although the way it 
was handled then was not ideal.

The good news it that with the latest versions of the packages (which 
just went up on CRAN a week ago) we have instituted some more 
informative checks on degeneracy that return much faster.  If you 
install those, you'll see that after just 5-10 seconds you'll get an error:

Error in ergm.MCMLE(init, nw, model, initialfit, control = control, 
MHproposal = MHproposal,  :
   Number of edges in a simulated network exceeds that in the observed 
by a factor of more than 20. This is a strong indicator of model 
degeneracy. If you are reasonably certain that this is not the case, 
increase the MCMLE.density.guard control.ergm() parameter.

This means that you get a very quick indication that there is almost 
certainly a problem, but also have a means of overriding it and 
continuing the fit if you so desire.

Alas, with the software always evolving and improving, the old versions 
of tutorials will get out of date in their behavior. More good news: 
each year we upgrade a set of core tutorial materials for the INSNA 
Sunbelt Conference to work with the latest versions of the packages.  
These will available on the statnet website each year shortly after the 
conference (ie some time in late spring).

Cheers,
Steve

On Thu, Feb 14, 2013 at 3:05 PM, Juan Pablo Alperin <alperin@stanford.edu>wrote:

>  Pavel,
>
> Thanks for the response!
>
> For other's benefit, I wanted to point out that I did eventually manage to
> run that particular model by increasing the memory/swap space on the
> machine I was running it on. I actually just added 64Gb of Swap space and
> it got around the problem. This resource was useful in adding in swap on
> the fly, at least for those using Ubuntu (and possibly other UNIX
> flavours):
> http://askubuntu.com/questions/178712/how-to-increase-swap-space-in-ubuntu
>
> But you're right, I did realize it wasn't the right way to model the
> degree distribution.
>
> So, let me ask: what is the right way to model a network that has a
> power-law degree distribution? Is gwidegree the only type of preferential
> attachment model currently possible?
>
>  I will follow-up on the other issue in the other thread. Thanks.
>
> Juan
>
> On Thursday, 14 February, 2013 at 12:13 AM, Pavel N. Krivitsky wrote:
>
> Hi, Juan,
>
> The problem here is that you are using the receiver term, which adds a
> parameter for every node (but one), so you are trying to fit a model
> with ~9000 parameters. The MPLE procedure tries to allocate a vector to
> store all of them --- which is 9000*MPLE.max.dyad.types, which, by
> default, asks for a vector about 9e+9*8 = 72 gigabytes in length.
>
> Setting MPLE.max.dyad.types to too small a value means that the MPLE
> procedure cannot run, resulting in the "Too many unique dyad values"
> error.
>
> In other words, the problem is not so much that the network is too big,
> but that the model calls for too many parameters. My recommendation is
> to try modeling degree heterogeneity in some other way (e.g., using
> gwidegree).
>
> I hope this helps,
>  Pavel
>
> On Fri, 2013-02-08 at 21:26 -0800, Juan Pablo Alperin wrote:
>
> Hello all,
>
> I am a newcomer to statnet and ergms and struggling to run my first
> models. I have a network with ~9000 nodes, but even when I try to run

>

>
> A follow-up question: I've read of difficulties fitting ergm's to

>
> Really hope someone can help. Thanks!

messages.subject: [statnet_help] MCMC standard errors
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Kevin,

> 1. The ergm command currently provides as part of the output ?MCMC %.?
> Can someone explain precisely what this means? (i.e. I understand that
> there are two components to the standard error when using MCMC- so does
> the percentage refer to the proportion of the reported SE that is due to
> the MCMC process- and therefore the reported SE?s and p-values already
> reflect both types of SE?s- or is it an extra percentage that should
> somehow be ?added on??)

The SE reported includes the MCMC error, and the percentage is the 
percentage of the *variance* due to MCMC: SEmcmc^2 / (SEmcmc^2 + 
SEmodel^2) * 100%.

> Additionally, is there any guidance for how big
> we should usually expect these %?s to be, or techniques to minimize
> them? (Other than the standard recommendations in the documentation for
> improving convergence.)

Other than the standard recommendations --- increase MCMC sample size 
and/or interval, write a better MCMC sampler, etc. --- I don't have any.

> 2. For some reason, whenever I run a model that includes a coefficient
> that cannot be estimated (for instance, let?s say I am modeling an
> academic network and I include a nodematch term for sociologists, but
> there are no ties between sociologists so the parameter is fixed at
> ?-Inf?), all of my MCMC %?s appear as ?NA? instead of an actual number.
> Is there a reason for this; and should I be concerned about it? E.g.
> does this mean that the reported SE?s are not conservative enough
> because they don?t incorporate the extra MCMC SE?

No, this is a long-standing bug in a rather involved part of ergm, where 
models with any offset terms (not just the +-Inf ones from dropping) 
broke the MCMC SE calculation. Having taken another look, I think I know 
how to fix it, though, so we'll probably have it working in the next 
release.

                   I hope this helps,
                   Pavel

messages.body_plain:
Hello Narciso,

The error is strange, and not one I've seen before.  Can you let us know 
which version of the ergm package you are using?  We just uploaded a new 
one to CRAN a week ago.  If you are using an old one, you should try the 
newest first: upgrade to R 3.0.0 as well, and then all your packages 
with either update.packages() or with update.packages("name.of.package") 
for each of the statnet packages.  Let us know if the error is still there.

That said, from the evidence I am seeing, it would appear that your 
particular model is likely to be degenerate.  I can tell this by the 
fact that the log-likelihood improvements keep going back up to the 
maximum cap (around 20). That may not be the result you want, but it is 
still an informative about the fact that this model is not the right 
generative model for your data.  It doesn't explain the error though.

Cheers,
Steve

messages.body_plain:
For what it's worth, I'd love to add my own curiosity to Philip's. While I haven't yet been so courageous as to try to replicate published results with newer versions of ergm, I have been working on some other models for a year or two- and, in some cases, the results I am getting today are very different from those I obtained two years ago (although in the specific case I am thinking of, parameter estimates that were previously very unstable are now behaving much more stably). If possible, it would be great to hear about how statnet (and specifically, estimation using ergm) has changed/improved over time- I am not aware that a "version history" currently exists.

Many thanks in advance!

-Kevin

-----Original Message-----
From: statnet_help-bounces@mailman2.u.washington.edu [mailto:statnet_help-bounces@mailman2.u.washington.edu] On Behalf Of Philip Leifeld
Sent: Wednesday, July 10, 2013 3:04 AM
To: statnet_help mailing list
Subject: [statnet_help] Replication of old ergm analysis fails with new package versions but same seed, code, and data

Dear statnet developers and community,

I published an ERGM analysis in the American Journal of Political Science last year:

Leifeld, Philip and Volker Schneider (2012): Information Exchange in Policy Networks. American Journal of Political Science 53(3): 731-744. 
http://dx.doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5907.2011.00580.x

Replication data and code: http://hdl.handle.net/1902.1/17004

I was using the following package versions:

sna 2.1-0 (2010-04-15)
network 1.6 (2011-01-28)
ergm 2.4 (2011-05-24)

I am now trying to replicate my own results using the current versions of these packages:

sna 2.3-1 (2013-02-28)
network 1.7.2 (2013-03-15)
ergm 3.1-0 (2013-04-17)

However, although I am using exactly the same code and data including the same random seed in the ergm command, the results are very different.

The estimation in the new version takes much longer and shows signs of degeneracy (20 iterations between which the log-likelihood increases by more than 10, sometimes almost 20, each time). The diagnostics look quite OK though.

I installed the old package versions on another machine and there I can in fact replicate my old results. So why am I having degeneracy problems in the new version despite using the same data, commands, seed etc.? I have tried to increase the MCMC sample size to 50k, and I set MCMC.interval = 1000, but this does not help.

Any help would be appreciated. Thanks!

Philip

messages.subject: [statnet_help] MCMC standard errors
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

(Happy summer!)

I have a couple quick questions I'm hoping one of the developers can answer- the first of which I believe was posted a couple times last year, but I couldn't find a response in the archives or a clear answer in the documentation (apologies if I missed it!).

1. The ergm command currently provides as part of the output "MCMC %." Can someone explain precisely what this means? (i.e. I understand that there are two components to the standard error when using MCMC- so does the percentage refer to the proportion of the reported SE that is due to the MCMC process- and therefore the reported SE's and p-values already reflect both types of SE's- or is it an extra percentage that should somehow be "added on"?) Additionally, is there any guidance for how big we should usually expect these %'s to be, or techniques to minimize them? (Other than the standard recommendations in the documentation for improving convergence.)

2. For some reason, whenever I run a model that includes a coefficient that cannot be estimated (for instance, let's say I am modeling an academic network and I include a nodematch term for sociologists, but there are no ties between sociologists so the parameter is fixed at "-Inf"), all of my MCMC %'s appear as "NA" instead of an actual number. Is there a reason for this; and should I be concerned about it? E.g. does this mean that the reported SE's are not conservative enough because they don't incorporate the extra MCMC SE?

Thanks in advance for any guidance!

-Kevin

Kevin Lewis
Assistant Professor of Sociology
University of California, San Diego

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Network Layout For Valued Networks
messages.body_plain:
Is there a mistake in the code for the layout of valued networks?  If there
isn't then I'm making a mistake somewhere.  I have valued networks and the
layout algorithms passed through plot.network do not seem to be handling
edge values.  I've attached a simple example below.

set.seed(11)
X = matrix(floor(runif(25,0,5)),nrow=5,byrow=T)
Xnet = network(X,matrix.type='adjacency')
set.edge.value(Xnet,'value',X)
#these two lines demonstrate that the edgevalues seem to be set correctly
as.matrix(Xnet)
as.matrix(Xnet,attrname='value')
set.seed(11)
par(mfrow=c(2,2),mar=c(1,1,1,1))
plot.network(Xnet,main='Simple Layout')
set.seed(11)
plot.network(Xnet,attrname='value',main='Setting attrname (has no effect)')
set.seed(11)
x=gplot.layout.fruchtermanreingold(X,layout.par=NULL)
plot.network(Xnet,coord=x,main='Using gplot.layout with valued network')
set.seed(11)
x=gplot.layout.fruchtermanreingold(X>0,layout.par=NULL)
plot.network(Xnet,coord=x,main='Using gplot.layout with binary network')


I believe that the problem is that the network.layout.* functions don't
accept edge-values as arguments.  Both functions have the following in
their second line

d <- as.matrix.network(nw, matrix.type = "edgelist")[, 1:2, drop = FALSE]

Which returns a binary matrix even if an edge-attribute was passed.

I've figured out a way around it, but I'm wondering if I'm making a mistake
somewhere, and if there is a way to get valued layout without going through
gplot.layout.*

Thanks,
Sam
-- 
Sam Stewart, MMath, A.Stat
IDPhD Candidate (Health Informatics)
Faculty of Computer Science, Dalhousie University
6050 University Ave.
Halifax, NS, Canada, B3H 1W5

messages.subject: [statnet_help] missing data on node attributes
messages.body_plain:
Dear statnet folks,

I seem to be having more trouble with missing data.  I'm trying to estimate a model with missing data on a continuous vertex attribute and I receive the following error message:
Error in ergm.getglobalstats(nw, model, response = response) : 
  NA/NaN/Inf in foreign function call (arg 13)

Here is some example code that produces the error.

net <- as.network(matrix(rep(c(0,1),18),nrow=6))
attr <- c(rep(0,20),rep(1,16))
attr[3] <- NA
set.vertex.attribute(net, "attr", attr)
temp <- ergm(net ~ edges + absdiff("attr") )

The email below alludes to the same issue and I haven't been able to track down a resolution.  I've previously been able to estimate models with missing data like this, so I'm really stumped.  I'm using R 3.0.1 and statnet 1.7.2.  

Thanks,
David

-----Original Message-----
From: statnet_help-bounces@mailman2.u.washington.edu [mailto:statnet_help-bounces@mailman2.u.washington.edu] On Behalf Of Kevin Lewis
Sent: Wednesday, March 16, 2011 12:05 PM
To: statnet_help list
Subject: [statnet_help] missing data on node attributes

greetings,

please forgive me for what i fear is an extremely basic question- but is there any documentation on how to deal with missing data in node attributes using ergm? i.e. first, how such data should be entered, and second, how it is dealt with in the model itself. in the past i have used primarily categorical attributes, and so i just dealt with this by including the missing data code as part of the "base" for nodefactor terms and omitting the missing data code using the "keep" function for nodematch terms, but currently i have missing data on some continuous attributes and am not sure how i should deal with this (or if this is even possible). thanks very much!

-kevin

p.s. please forgive me if i've missed a prior message on this topic- the most recent post i can find in the archive is a note from mark handcock back in 2009:

"statnet does recognize missing data on vertex attributes...
However this version of the ergm() function does not adjust for missing data on vertex attributes - it only adjusts for missing values on the tie values. It is possible to do and we have worked out the statistical theory to do it, but have not implemented it in the public version. I expect it will appear in a major future release and we will communicate it to this forum."

--
Kevin Lewis
Ph.D. Candidate in Sociology
Harvard University
33 Kirkland Street
Cambridge, MA 02138

Hi, Philip et al.  

Several people have been looking into this question.  There are several models in the Leifeld and Schneider paper, but I've been focusing on the one called model 2 both in the paper and in the code (thanks for providing code that makes it so easy to test!), since it exhibits the behavior that Philip describes in his email.

We think we're closing in on understanding what's going on here, but the bottom line is, this seems like an intrinsically difficult model to fit!  In particular, we are not finding any bugs in the main fitting algorithm of either version of ergm.

More to follow as we figure things out.

Best,
Dave

Fruchterman-Reingold algorithm (the weight is basically a multiplier
for the attraction force between the linked pair of vertexes). To
achieve that with Kamada-Kawai you could go without a call to

geodesics. Not sure which variant would produce nicer layouts though.

From: statnet_help-bounces@mailman2.u.washington.edu [mailto:statnet_help-bounces@mailman2.u.washington.edu] On Behalf Of Carter T. Butts
Sent: Friday, July 12, 2013 4:31 PM
To: statnet_help@u.washington.edu
Subject: Re: [statnet_help] missing data on node attributes

Hi, David.  Missing data on attributes makes certain kinds of changescores indeterminate; there are ways to deal with that, but IIRC they're not currently built into ergm.  (The main exceptions are some categorical terms that by default treat NA as if it were a distinct
category.)  I was actually under the impression that ergm _always_ produced an error when the changescore was poorly defined, so if you were able to fit those models before, that might have been due to a bug that was fixed.  :-)

Mark and Ian have been thinking about this problem more than I have, and so may have a grander suggestion than my pragmatic one. My short-term suggestion would be to estimate your model via a two-stage procedure: 
first, impute your missing attribute data using a standard imputation method; and second, fit the ergm given the imputed data.  (It would probably be wise to create multiple imputed data sets in this manner, and examine the distribution of estimates across imputed values.)  This is not 100% ideal, but will probably work well so long as the results are not very sensitive to the missing values.  If the results _are_ sensitive to the missing values (something you can determine by looking at the distribution of estimates across imputed data sets), then you are likely in a bad spot regardless, and no method is going to be entirely trustworthy.  (See also, "you can only get a loan when you don't need it.")

By contrast, if you have missing data in the edges, ergm will indeed handle that.  (Or, at least, it will try.  You may still lack the power needed to answer your question of interest!)  The approach employed is the latent missing data technique developed by Gile and Handcock.

Hope that helps!

-Carter

Hi Skye?

Thank you very much for the suggestion.

I have figured out that I actually do not need to covert the categorical variables to factors because my goal was to fit a ERGM model. When fitting this model, the ergm-terms provide function for recognizing if a variable is categorical or continuous. For instance, if I include a gender predictor, then I can treat gender as continous and put it into the network object, then I fit the ERGM in which the gender is used with "nodefactor" like this: nodefactor(gender). messages.subject: [statnet_help] Replication of old ergm analysis fails with new package versions but same seed, code, and data (fwd)
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Replication of old ergm analysis fails with new package versions but same seed, code, and data (fwd)
messages.body_plain:
Dear statnet community --

We've tracked down what led to the issues that Philip raised in his email. 
Please see below for a summary.  The bottom line is good, in his case. If 
anyone else finds that results are not replicated by new releases of the 
software, it's really helpful for us to know about it, so please shoot
us an email.

best,
Martina (for the statnet dev team)

---------- Forwarded message ----------
Date: Fri, 2 Aug 2013 10:23:05 -0700 (Pacific Daylight Time)
From: martina morris <morrism@u.washington.edu>
To: Philip Leifeld <philip.leifeld@uni-konstanz.de>
Cc: dave hunter <dhunter@stat.psu.edu>,
     Steven M. Goodreau <goodreau@u.washington.edu>, 
statnet_dev@u.washington.edu
Subject: Re: [statnet_help] Replication of old ergm analysis fails with new
     package versions but same seed, code, and data

Hi Philip,

First, thanks for your patience.  This turned out to be a problem with many 
moving pieces, so it took a while to pin down each part.  And thanks for 
reporting this in the first place.

Second, I think we have basically good news to report:  your example revealed a 
couple of bugs (in both ergm 2.4 and 3.1), and a problem in your model, but the 
results you published were essentially correct.

In tracking down why your model didn't converge in 3.1, we ended up finding 4 
issues that contributed in different ways.  i'll list them in order of 
severity.

1. the unique naming problem

This was what prevented 3.1 from being able to fit your model at all (as Pavel 
correctly noted).  It's due to a change from 2.4 to 3.1 in the way variable 
names are used.  And while it's not clear that we want to encourage users to 
use the same name for two variables (in your case "weight"), ergm should detect 
and provide a warning rather than fail completely.  So this will be fixed.

As you and Pavel both noted, once you rename one of the offending variables, 
your model fits successfully and quickly in 3.1.  But, you don't get exactly 
the same results...

2. compression algorithm

There is an algorithm deep in ergm ("ergm.sufftoprob") that is intended to 
speed up computations, but was not written well.  It was called by default in 
2.4 (control=control.ergm(compress=T)), and is not called by default in 3.1 
(control=control.ergm(MCMC.compress=F)).  When it fails (as it did in your 
model), the result is that the SEs are often biased downward (as it was in your 
case).

Removing compression increases the size of the SEs.  Not enough to change the 
nominal significance levels for any of the coef you reported as significant, 
but enough to notice.


3. default fitting iterations

In 2.4, the default was 3 iterations, in 3.1 it has been raised to 20. If your 
model is difficult to fit or converges slowly (as it does in your case) more 
iterations can lead to different point estimates.

This is part of why the point estimates for your model are different in 3.1.


4. model issues:  colinearity

It turns out your model had a hidden colinearity problem.  The edges and gwesp 
statistic were nearly colinear (correlation above 0.99).  The reason is because 
you have a relatively dense network, so almost every edge is involved in at 
least one triangle.  Using a low alpha for gwesp (as you did) leads that 
statistic towards measuring how many edges are involved in at least one 
triangle (it is exactly that when alpha=0).  So each edge contributed the same 
amount to the change statistics for these two terms.

ergm 3.1 handles that colinearity better both because it has more fitting 
iterations, and because it doesn't use compression by default so the SEs are 
accurate.  so a default fit (with unique names) will show that edges and gwesp 
are highly correlated and the coef are not signficant.

But if you increase alpha (to, say, 1), you'll find that the colinearity is 
sufficiently reduced that the gwesp term becomes significant.  At this point, 
the gwDsp term is no longer significant.  You may find that changing the alpha 
for that term helps -- we left off here.


I've attached a spreadsheet that documents all of the models we fit to track 
down these different problems and verify what was causing what. There's a 
summary sheet up front that shows what matters substantively for your paper, 
and lots of stuff on the other two sheets to see the details.

I hope this helps -- let us know if you have any other questions.

best,
Martina, Dave and Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Statistical methods for a sample of networks
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Statistical methods for a sample of networks
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Patrick.  Just to add to what folks have already said, you might 
also find the following paper useful:

Butts, Carter T.  2011.  Bayesian meta-analysis of social network data 
via conditional uniform graph quantiles.  Sociological Methodology, 
41(1): 257-298. 
http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1467-9531.2011.01240.x/abstract

The approach described in that paper can be used to e.g. test hypotheses 
regarding structural biases across treatments, among other things.

Note that, if your data and hypotheses are group-level, they can be 
tested without any particularly network-specific techniques; for 
instance, a standard permutation test (or, for that matter, any of a 
range of similar procedures) can be used to test hypotheses regarding 
the association between a treatment and a graph-level index (e.g., 
degree centralization).  Just because your data involve networks does 
not per se mean that you need to use special procedures.  (It all 
depends on the details of your analysis.)  For some examples, you might 
want to look at the materials from our "Beyond Descriptives" statnet 
workshop (archived at www.statnet.org).

As far as pooled analysis of ERGMs, you can see some of our 
work-in-progress on this front at Sunbelt in February!  It's certainly 
doable (although, with only four nodes in each network, you will have 
little power to distinguish among competing structural mechanisms) - but 
for at least some of your questions, it may not be the tool you need.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

On 12/18/2013 11:23 AM, Patrick S Forscher wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> /Warning: This email is a little long/
>
> I am a social psychologist by training and am new to social network 
> analysis.  I am planning a series of studies that involve small groups 
> of people.  In a typical study, the participants will meet in groups 
> of 4 to have a discussion about a particular topic.  As a group, the 
> participants will reach a decision about the topic (e.g., whether to 
> support or oppose a proposed change in university policy).  The 
> discussion will be videotaped, and we will use transcripts of the 
> discussion to obtain information about who is talking to whom about 
> what topics.  In addition, the participants will complete ratings of 
> themselves and each other (e.g., What is your opinion about the 
> proposed change?  What do you think is this person's opinion of the 
> proposed change?).  I will also have a variety of data about the 
> individual characteristics of all the participants.  Thus, each group 
> from each study will give me a 4-node network with directed, valued 
> edges and a variety of attributes about each node.
>
> In all the studies, I will be interested in group-level, 
> relationship-level, and individual-level outcomes.  I have provided 
> below a sampling of the kinds of questions I would want to ask from 
> these data:
>
> (1) Which groups express the most agreement in their discussions? 
>  Which groups express the most disagreement?  Is group composition 
> related to agreement / disagreement and to the final decision outcome?
> (2) Which pairs of people like each other during the discussion? 
>  Which pairs of people dislike each other?  How are the pairwise 
> patterns of liking related to the final decision outcome?
> (3) Who has the most influence on the course of the discussion?  Who 
> has influence over the final decision of each group?  Are there any 
> individual difference characteristics that are related to influence 
> over the discussion and / or final decision?
>
> And so on.  What I am looking for from the mailing list is the proper 
> statistical model to use to investigate /samples/ of networks, rather 
> than individual networks.  I have read a bit about single-network 
> methods, like ERGM models, but these methods do not seem appropriate, 
> since I am dealing with a set of independent networks, rather than a 
> single network.  In addition, a plain linear mixed model does not seem 
> appropriate because I am collecting relational data.  Finally, 
> although a method like the social relations model seems appropriate 
> for this situation at first blush, the social relations model seems to 
> only partition the variance in round-robin ratings into perceiver, 
> target, and relationship sources rather than allowing me to, for 
> example, relate the patterns within a set of networks to overall 
> network outcomes.
>
> Perhaps I'm over-thinking this problem, and perhaps the choice of the 
> appropriate statistical model is obvious.  However, as I mentioned 
> earlier in the email, I am new to this stuff.  Could anyone offer some 
> advice about which statistical model might be appropriate for my 
> situation?  Also, is the proper analytic method possible in statnet?
>
> -- 
> Patrick S Forscher
> PhD Candidate
> University of Wisconsin-Madison
>
>

> statnet_help@u.washington.edu
> http://mailman2.u.washington.edu/mailman/listinfo/statnet_help

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] different types of triadic-based parameters (activity closure, popularity closure)
messages.body_plain:
Dear all researchers,

I have some questions about ERGM terms.

1. I wonder if statnet package has different terms for testing different
types of triadic-based parameters mentioned in Robins, Pattison, & Wang
(2009; attached), such as activity closure, popularity closure and cyclic
closure. Looks like that these authors use pnet software, and I am not sure
which ERGM terms in statnet package correspond to such different types of
transitive parameters.

I looked at Morris, Handcock, and Hunter (2008) paper about ERGM
specification,and there are terms like ctriple or ttriple, but I somehow
couldn't find "new specifications" (for non-degenerate models)
corresponding to those types like activity closure or popularity closure
except gwesp (transitive closure) and gwdsp terms.

2. According to the suggestions made in the same paper above, I am trying
to control a multiple 2-path while I model transitivity using 'gwesp' term,
and in statnet package, I see that there are three terms that look relevant
: 'm2star' or 'twopath' and 'gwdsp' in statnet. Which term is a correct one?

Thank you very much!

Sincerely,
Rose

-- 
Ji Youn (Rose) Kim
Doctoral Candidate
Department of Management & Organization
Michael G. Foster School of Business
University of Washington
rosejyk@uw.edu

messages.body_plain:
Hi Vicki.

I think you should try including an "edges" term before altering software
parameters. The edges term controls for the observed number of edges. It's
much like an intercept term, except it isn't included by default. There
could be more to that story...

messages.body_plain:
Martina, thanks for the clarification and sorry for the misunderstanding!

Karen, the only other suggestion I might have is hiking up the MCMC sample size and/or interval still further. In what limited experience I have with models for large networks, this has sometimes made a dramatic difference- taking me from a model that wanders around and gets nowhere for weeks, to one that "quickly" converges (i.e. with relatively few iterations... though recognizing that each iteration may take an agonizingly long time). You might also try the "stepping" method described in Hummel et al. 2012, something I have been playing around with a bit lately.

(This of course assumes that there is not some other technical problem going on that would be over my head.)

-Kevin

P.S. Feel free to correspond with me privately if you want more specifics!

messages.subject: [statnet_help] re: gwb1degree, gwb2degree, gwdsp, when alpha=0 or 1
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] re: gwb1degree, gwb2degree, gwdsp, when alpha=0 or 1
messages.body_plain:
Megumi,

These value of alpha are not inherently problematic.  But you should be 
aware of the impact on the interpretation of the gwdsp term, and pay 
attention to the impact on the correlation between the gwdsp term and the 
edges term.  For very dense networks, setting alpha=0 can result in very 
high correlations (.99+) between edges and gwEsp terms.  I'm not sure 
whether the same holds for gwDsp terms, but you should keep an eye on it. 
If that problem does occur, increasing alpha may help.

best,
Martina

On Sun, 11 Aug 2013, megumi nishimura wrote:

> Dear statnet community,
>
> Relating the below communications, I have slightly different questions.
>
> I run bipartite network models which include gwb1degree, gwb2degree, gwdsp.  I set my alphas for these parameter as gwb1degree(alpha=1), gwb2degree(alpha=1), gwdsp(alpha=0).  I could NON-degenerating models, and produced some estimations.
>
> I set these alpha parameters, because they recover my geodesic distance best in gof simulations from the various combinations of parameters.
>
> Is alpha=1 or 0 problematic?  Can someone explain qualitatively on how alpha=0 and alpha=1 differ substantially? Or, in other words, how lower values of alpha and higher value of alpha differ substantially?
>
> I look forward your reply.
>
> Sincerely,
>
> Megumi Nishimura
> Ritsumeikan University
>
>
>
>
> [statnet_help] interpreting GWDSP?
> Steven Goodreau goodreau at u.washington.edu
> Tue Aug 18 08:22:03 PDT 2009
> •Previous message: [statnet_help] interpreting GWDSP?
> •Next message: [statnet_help] interpreting GWDSP?
> •Messages sorted by: [ date ] [ thread ] [ subject ] [ author ]
>
> --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
>
> On Thu, 6 Aug 2009, Jenine Harris wrote:
>
>
>> I was wondering if anyone has an example of how a GWDSP term would be
>
>> interpreted in somewhat lay terms. From my understanding GWDSP accounts for
>
>> the distribution of shared partnership for each dyad in a network, but I'm
>
>> not sure how to go about interpreting a negative signficant GWDSP
>
>> coefficient of -0.25 in an actual ERGM model. What does this say about the
>
>> distribution and how does it influence the likelihood of a tie?
>
>
>
> Hi Jenine,
>
> A great question. Yes, I do think GWDSP is a bit trickier than interpret
> than any of the other terms we commonly work with. I can give you my own
> idiosyncratic approach.
>
> First, as technical background: As you probably know, GWDSP is a
> parametric summary measure of the tendency for two actors to have x
> partners in common, regardless of whether the two actors themselves are
> tied. GWESP is the same measure, but only counted across two actors who
> are tied. The two are comparable to the "alternating 2-paths" and
> "alternating k-triangles" that Snijders et al discuss in a series of
> papers. The two measures, combined with a third (GW degree, or the
> comparable alternating k-stars) are derived in those papers by placing a
> parametric constraint on three sets of statistics that emerge when making
> a very sociologically reasonable set of assumptions about relational
> dependence. The three parametric stats are also seen to work well in
> practice at modeling real-world social networks and avoiding degeneracy
> when doing so.
>
> So, on to interpretation. As I said, I agree that GWDSP is the hardest to
> interpret. In fact, I personally never use a GWDSP term without also
> using a GWESP term. And once I combined the two, I always find that the
> GWDSP coefficient is close to zero, and non-significant. Let me see if I
> can give good intuition as to why.
>
> GWESP has some relatively clear interpetations (which I discuss in a few
> of my papers). In real-world data of friendship or collaboration or
> similar kinds of networks, it is generally significantly positive. This
> means that those who are tied are more likely than chance to have multiple
> shared partners.
>
> GWDSP tells whether shared partners tend to clump together, regardless of
> whether two people are tied or not. For example, whether or not you and I
> are friends, if we have one friend in common, are we more likely than
> expected by chance to have a second friend in common? And so on. If yes,
> the GWDSP coefficient will be positive. If it is zero, then we are as
> likely as chance to have one in common; if negative, then less.
>
> If one only uses GWDSP and not GWESP, then it's hard to know whether an
> observed non-random shared partner distribution is driven by pairs who are
> themselves tied, pairs who are not tied, or both. If you include both
> GWESP and GWDSP, then it becomes clear - GWDSP is the base effect (which
> now isolates the effect for those not tied only); GWESP occurs on top of
> this base, and isolates the effect for those who are tied. And what I
> have always found is that the GWESP effect is then strong and significant,
> and the GWDSP is tiny and insignificant. It may be that in different
> kinds of data GWDSP would be significant itself, though.
>
> My questions for you are: is your GWDSP term significant? Does it remain
> so when GWESP is added? If the answer to both questions is yes, then you
> have something particuarly interesting (and unprecendented, at least for
> me) on your hands. If it remains negative and significant, then that says
> that people who are not tied tend not to have multiple shared partners.
> Once two unconnected people have one shared partner, they're less likely
> than chance to have a second; if they do have a second, they're less
> likely than chance to have a third, and so on. I can't think of a type of
> social relationship I would anticipate this pattern for, but it could just
> be that I've never thought about the kind of relaitonship that you're
> studying, and it makes perfect sense to you.
>
> My other quesiton would be what your alpha is; that changes the fine
> quantitative details of the interpretation, but not the general
> qualitative interpretation. Unless your alpha is either essentially 0 or
> very very high, in which case it would change the latter as well. If it's
> in the 0.1 - 2.0 range, I don't think it would.
>
> I hope that helps!
> Steve
>

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGM error
messages.body_plain:
Ian,

You are right. Having 'ergm' specify 'network' as both "Depends" and
"Imports" would do the job.

~michal

On Thu, Aug 1, 2013 at 2:25 AM, Ian Fellows <ian.fellows@stat.ucla.edu> wrote:
> Hi Michal,
>
> I would argue that in this case ergm is doing the right thing to depend on network not just import. The Depends field is reserved for dependancies which, if not loaded by the user, renders the package virtually unusable. This is the case with the network package as it provides the fundamental data structure upon which all ergm functions operate. ergm does have a number of pacakges which should be imported rather than depended upon. The trust package are the most obvious of these as the user will never call trust directly.
>
> That said, ergm should probably also import network to prevent internal functions from calling into igraph. This way the user can have both loaded, and distinguish between the two with network::is.directed and igraph::is.directed in their own code.
>
>
> Ian
>
>
> On Jul 31, 2013, at 4:58 PM, Micha? Bojanowski <michal2992@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>> Ngoni and others,
>>
>> Two points:
>>
>> First, Steve is very much correct that the error you are getting is
>> because you have loaded and attached network package first and then
>> igraph. To dodge the problem you have to detach igraph package before
>> running ergm by calling 'detach(package:igraph)'. If you are
>> interested in more details see my blog post here:
>> http://bc.bojanorama.pl/2010/08/namespaces-and-name-conflicts/
>>
>> Second point is more of a suggestion to statnet developers. The
>> problem is indirectly caused by the fact that package 'ergm' specifies
>> the 'network' package as a dependency through the "Depends" field in
>> its DESCRIPTION file. This mechanism is very fragile to the presence
>> of other packages the user may have loaded and attached (like 'igraph'
>> in Ngoni's case). The preferred mechanism would be for 'ergm' to
>> import 'network' package (just like 'network' package imports 'utils'
>> package). Without going into even more technical details (which are
>> available upon request :) ), the difference is that 'ergm's internal
>> code will be guaranteed to always try to use 'network's functions
>> first, and only later look in the global environment (workspace).
>>
>> You can try it yourself by modifying the source of 'ergm' by
>> 1. Modifying DESCRIPTION by moving 'network' from "Depends:" to "Imports:"
>> 2. Adding 'import(network)' to NAMESPACE file.
>>
>> The only side effect would be that if you load 'ergm' by using
>> 'library(ergm)' the network package will be loaded, but *not*
>> attached. The user would have to do that himself. If auto-attaching
>> 'network' when attaching 'ergm' is so desired, that could be done by
>> adding the '.onAttach' hook to 'ergm' that would also load and attach
>> 'network'.
>>
>> Best,
>> Michal
>>
>>
>>
>>
>> On Wed, Jul 31, 2013 at 11:45 PM, Steven Goodreau <goodreau@uw.edu> wrote:
>>> Hello Ngoni,
>>>
>>> My guess is that you attached the igraph package to your session after you
>>> attached statnet.  Unfortunately, when igraph was developed in 2006, the
>>> author used some function names that were already in use in the network
>>> package (the latter on CRAN at the time as an independent package, and then
>>> subsequently part of the statnet suite).  That means that now, if one
>>> attaches both, then whichever one gets attached later will be the source of
>>> the functions drawn when they are shared. If you're trying to use statnet
>>> functionality, this can cause problems, as it is expecting the network
>>> functionality, but if you attach igraph later it uses igraph functionality.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Basic modeling of medical facts
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am new to network modeling and am trying to figure out if the data I have is suitable for use in ERGM, or if some transformation of it would be.

I have medical history data on millions of people.  From this data, I computed a network where nodes are conditions and a link (i,j) indicates the number of people who had condition i prior to condition j. The conditions are summarized into roughly 500 conditions.  For each link I can define the probability of of the link (i,j) from the observed data (number of people who have j after i / number with i ), or a suitable weight for the strength of the association.

I can analyse this network assuming the edge weights are deterministic but that hasn't been very fruitful so far. I am not sure ERGM applies because all the examples I see involve unweighted edges.

I think I need to look into bnlearn or other Bayesian networks, but wanted to check here to see if there are any ideas on how to apply ERGM to this type of data.

Thanks,
Chris

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Statistical methods for a sample of networks
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Statistical methods for a sample of networks
messages.body_plain:
Hi Patrick,

If you can reasonably assume that the data-generating process is the 
same for all networks, you can combine them in a single matrix and use 
structural zeros for the between-network dyads which cannot have any 
connection. The problem is rather that there are not a lot of ways to 
model weighted network data. There are simply no model terms available 
for generalized ERGMs or count ERGMs (unless somebody from the statnet 
team has recently implemented some model terms for valued networks, 
which I don't know). See here: help("ergm-terms", package = 
"ergm.count"). If the timing of the edges matters, relational event 
models may be an alternative (look at the articles of Carter Butts and 
Brandes/Lerner/Snijders and at the relevent package). On the other hand, 
the questions you are asking are more related to explaining outcomes per 
network and describing the networks in terms of centrality. So I am not 
sure if you need a model which explains network formation at all. It may 
be more interesting for you to describe the network in terms of who is 
central (or any other interesting graph statistics) and use them as 
covariates when you model the outcomes of your networks (since they are 
independent by design).

As for the conversion of your transcripts into network matrices, this is 
not a trivial task. I wrote a Java software package for this purpose. 
It's called Discourse Network Analyzer (see www.github.com/leifeld/dna). 
Right now, however, you can only annotate what each person says (and 
whether the person agrees or disagrees with the concept). You can then 
produce two-mode network matrices of actors and concepts, or one-mode 
network matrices where two actors are connected if they have claims in 
common (both agreeing to the same concepts or both disagreeing to the 
same concepts). It is not possible right now to annotate direct 
connections between actors (at least not with additional qualifiers 
other than positive and negative). But I am working on a new version 
with more flexible ways of annotating text data and extracting networks 
from them.

Best,
Philip

> I am a social psychologist by training and am new to social network

> 4 to have a discussion about a particular topic.  As a group, the
> participants will reach a decision about the topic (e.g., whether to
> support or oppose a proposed change in university policy).  The
> discussion will be videotaped, and we will use transcripts of the
> discussion to obtain information about who is talking to whom about what
> topics.  In addition, the participants will complete ratings of
> themselves and each other (e.g., What is your opinion about the proposed
> change?  What do you think is this person's opinion of the proposed
> change?).  I will also have a variety of data about the individual
> characteristics of all the participants.  Thus, each group from each
> study will give me a 4-node network with directed, valued edges and a
> variety of attributes about each node.
>
> In all the studies, I will be interested in group-level,
> relationship-level, and individual-level outcomes.  I have provided
> below a sampling of the kinds of questions I would want to ask from
> these data:
>
> (1) Which groups express the most agreement in their discussions?  Which
> groups express the most disagreement?  Is group composition related to
> agreement / disagreement and to the final decision outcome?
> (2) Which pairs of people like each other during the discussion?  Which
> pairs of people dislike each other?  How are the pairwise patterns of

> influence over the final decision of each group?  Are there any
> individual difference characteristics that are related to influence over
> the discussion and / or final decision?
>
> And so on.  What I am looking for from the mailing list is the proper
> statistical model to use to investigate /samples/ of networks, rather
> than individual networks.  I have read a bit about single-network
> methods, like ERGM models, but these methods do not seem appropriate,
> since I am dealing with a set of independent networks, rather than a
> single network.  In addition, a plain linear mixed model does not seem

This is a statistical rather than a software question, but you are the best
audience to help me with this. I have a bipartite network where one set of

members of categories. I need to determine if there is a significant

messages.subject: [statnet_help] GOF with missing edges
messages.body_plain:
Hi Julija,

On 1/27/2014 2:31 AM, Julija Mell wrote:
>
> Hi all,
>
> I have a question about evaluating goodness of fit with missing data:
>
> I have a network with missing edges on which I fit an ergm model. When 
> I then proceed to gof -- how does gof treat the NAs in my network? 
> When I run gof(model) it seems that NAs are interpreted as 0s -- e.g. 
> non-respondents seem to be considered as isolates: the "observed" 
> statistics have a lot of degree-0's and infinite geodesic distances. 
> This doesn't seem to be right.
>
Indeed, this is the case: calculation for many of the summary statistics 
entails NAs being interpreted as 0s.  The documentation for the sna 
package (whose routines often lie behind other functions) provides some 
guidance about this.  There is some discussion about whether we ought to 
be returning NAs when someone attempts to calculate a statistic on a 
network when that network contains NAs instead of treating them as 0s.  
Thoughts form users welcome here.

In general, the missing data capabilities are not fully developed, and 
even knowing what it would mean to handle missing data is hard to define 
in some cases.  In the case of gof, for instance, we typically want to 
compare networks simulated from a model to the observed network on a 
number of network statistics.  If there's missing data in the observed 
network, then probably the fairest comparison for the simulated networks 
is to the observed network with its missing values imputed from the 
model.  Note that while this is not currently built into gof, it's 
something you can try to do on your own, and I think were headed in that 
direction with your subsequent code:
>
> I have also tried running gof(model,constraints=~observed) but then I 
> consistently receive the following error:
>
> > test2<-gof(mfit,verbose=T,constraints=~observed)
>
> Starting GOF for the given ERGM formula.
>
> Calculating observed network statistics.
>
> Starting simulations.
>
> Sim 1 of 100 : Starting MCMC iterations to generate 1 network
>
> Sampler accepted  46.970% of 10000 proposed steps.
>
> Finished simulation 1 of 1.
>
> Sim 2 of 100 :
>
> Error in InitMHP.randomtoggleNonObserved(list(constraints = 
> list(observed = list( :
>
>   The passed network does not have any non-observed dyads.
>
> Hence constraining to the observed will hold the network fixed at this 
> network.
>
> Either the network or the constraint need to be altered.
>
Yes, this constraint won't work with the gof command.  Note that it 
worked on the first simulation, because that one was simulated from the 
observed network, which contains missing data.  But then the second 
simulated network is simulated off the first simulated network, which 
doesn't contain missing data.  Instead, try using this same constraint 
with the simulate command instead of gof. Make sure to set the argument 
sequential=FALSE, so that each network will be simulated off the base.  
This will give you a bunch of networks in which the missing data are 
imputed.You can then do simulate without the constraint to simulate a 
bunch of new networks from the underlying model.  Then, you can write 
your own code to calculate the statistics you want to compare on the two 
sets, and then compare them numerically or graphically.  These last 
steps are what gof does automatically, but here you'll have to do it by 
hand because of having a set of imputed "observed" networks instead of 
just a single observed network.

Making some wrapper functions to make all this happen behind the scenes 
is something we can consider doing, but in the meantime, you should be 
able to make progress on your work this way.

There might also be other similar comparisons of interest here that I 
haven't thought of.  If others have ideas, please chime in!

HTH,
Steve

Vicki,

You are trying to fit a model that is the cannonical example of a model 
that is almost always degenerate.  There is a great deal written on the 
problem of degeneracy when using this kind of homogenous reduced Markov 
model.  There's some discussion of it in the ERGM tutorial on the statnet 
wiki:

https://statnet.csde.washington.edu/trac/wiki/Sunbelt2013#WorkshopMaterials

A more thorough discussion here:

NEW SPECIFICATIONS FOR EXPONENTIAL RANDOM GRAPH MODELS
Tom A. B. Snijders1, Philippa E. Pattison2, Garry L. Robins2, Mark S. 
Handcock3
http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1467-9531.2006.00176.x/abstract

And a good technical discussion is found here:

Mark S Handcock
?Assessing Degeneracy in Statistical Models of Social Networks?
http://www.csss.washington.edu/Papers/wp39.ps

The alternative is to use the gwesp term to capture triad closure instead. 
You can read about that in this paper:

Goodreau S, Kitts J, Morris M: Birds of a Feather, or Friend of a 
Friend? Using Statistical Network Analysis to Investigate Adolescent 
Social Networks. Demography 2009, 46(1):103?125.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Error when running ergm
messages.body_plain:
Hi Thomas,

Once you have sampled the network, you need to let ergm know what has been 
observed, and what is known to be missing by design.  Othewise, ergm is 
expecting a completely observed network, and any unobserved ties are 
assumed to be "0".  Among other things, this will influence how you 
specify the GD edgecov matrix, since edgecov expects a square matrix.

The ergm and tergm tutorials have writeups of how to use egocentrically 
sampled data properly.  For adaptively sampled data, your best bet is this 
post from Mark Handcock to the statnet help list:

http://mailman2.u.washington.edu/pipermail/statnet_help/2009/000524.html

HTH,
Martina

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Statistical methods for a sample of networks
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Statistical methods for a sample of networks
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

*Warning: This email is a little long*

I am a social psychologist by training and am new to social network
analysis.  I am planning a series of studies that involve small groups of
people.  In a typical study, the participants will meet in groups of 4 to
have a discussion about a particular topic.  As a group, the participants
will reach a decision about the topic (e.g., whether to support or oppose a
proposed change in university policy).  The discussion will be videotaped,
and we will use transcripts of the discussion to obtain information about
who is talking to whom about what topics.  In addition, the participants
will complete ratings of themselves and each other (e.g., What is your
opinion about the proposed change?  What do you think is this person's
opinion of the proposed change?).  I will also have a variety of data about
the individual characteristics of all the participants.  Thus, each group
from each study will give me a 4-node network with directed, valued edges
and a variety of attributes about each node.

In all the studies, I will be interested in group-level,
relationship-level, and individual-level outcomes.  I have provided below a
sampling of the kinds of questions I would want to ask from these data:

(1) Which groups express the most agreement in their discussions?  Which
groups express the most disagreement?  Is group composition related to
agreement / disagreement and to the final decision outcome?
(2) Which pairs of people like each other during the discussion?  Which
pairs of people dislike each other?  How are the pairwise patterns of
liking related to the final decision outcome?
(3) Who has the most influence on the course of the discussion?  Who has
influence over the final decision of each group?  Are there any individual
difference characteristics that are related to influence over the
discussion and / or final decision?

And so on.  What I am looking for from the mailing list is the proper
statistical model to use to investigate *samples* of networks, rather than
individual networks.  I have read a bit about single-network methods, like
ERGM models, but these methods do not seem appropriate, since I am dealing
with a set of independent networks, rather than a single network.  In
addition, a plain linear mixed model does not seem appropriate because I am
collecting relational data.  Finally, although a method like the social
relations model seems appropriate for this situation at first blush, the
social relations model seems to only partition the variance in round-robin
ratings into perceiver, target, and relationship sources rather than
allowing me to, for example, relate the patterns within a set of networks
to overall network outcomes.

Perhaps I'm over-thinking this problem, and perhaps the choice of the
appropriate statistical model is obvious.  However, as I mentioned earlier
in the email, I am new to this stuff.  Could anyone offer some advice about
which statistical model might be appropriate for my situation?  Also, is
the proper analytic method possible in statnet?

-- 
Patrick S Forscher
PhD Candidate
University of Wisconsin-Madison

It's not clear what your null hypothesis is here.  Do you think degree

mentioned in your paper to help fit the networks. I just updated to the
newest version of statnet.

jmodel.08 <-ergm(relations~nodematch('grade', diff=F)+nodematch('race',
diff=F)+gwesp(0.25, fixed=T)+nodematch('gender',
diff=F)+nodematch('educomb', diff=T), control = control.ergm(seed = 1,
MCMC.samplesize = 50000, MCMC.interval = 1000))

All of of the estimated model sample statistics are significantly different
(p<0.00) than the observed data, the autocorrelation statistics between
lags are very close to one, and the Geweke statistics are very close to
zero.

I just tweaked the terms to increase the intervals to 5000 and the burnin
for 5000, but that's running right now.

Thank you,
Karen

Thanks, I think you *may* be on the right track. If I rename the edge 
attributes as suggested, the estimation in the new statnet version runs 
considerably faster and shows much smaller log-likelihood improvements. 
The results are also closer to the original results. However, they are 
still not *very* close to the original results, with some of the 
estimates deviating significantly from the original estimates (in 
particular edges and gwesp but fortunately not the covariates).

I also re-ran the adjusted model 2 on the machine where the old package 
was installed, and the results didn't change compared to the published 
paper. I will paste the output of the estimation below. I don't remember 
exactly which version I was using in the paper (probably something close 
to 2.4 but not exactly 2.4), so the estimates below (produced using 
version 2.4) show some very small deviation from the AJPS version, but 
nothing to worry about. They are still different from the adjusted model 
2 estimates using the new ergm version though. You can also see that the 
names would *not* have ended up being identical in version 2.4, no 
matter if I renamed them or not.

The bottom line is that renaming doesn't change the results for version 
2.4, but it does change the results for version 3.1-0. In spite of the 
improvement, the adjusted model in the new ergm version still shows some 
deviations from the original results (but apparently much less severe 
than before).

Take care,

Philip

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Interpretation of curved model terms if MPLE is used
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Philip.  I'm not sure I fully understand:  I don't believe that an alpha value is reported by MLE when fixed=TRUE, only when fixed=FALSE.  But when MPLE is used, fixed=FALSE makes no sense.  In other words, for fixed=TRUE, both methods produce the same number of coefficients; whereas for fixed=FALSE, MPLE should not be used.

I think that maybe the confusion only arises when fixed=FALSE is used with MPLE.  I see your point that it might be helpful to have one additional coefficient output in that case, namely the (actually fixed!) value of alpha.  But it seems this might encourage the use of fixed=FALSE with MPLE, which is probably not good.

Sorry if I'm misunderstanding something!

Dave

PS.  I added alpha=0 to the documentation, so that should show up with the next release of ergm.



On Sep 14, 2013, at 8:20 AM, Philip Leifeld wrote:

> Great, this answers my question. Thanks very much. I think adding alpha = 0 to the documentation would be helpful. And it would be nice if MPLE and MCMC MLE reported the same coefficients (either with or without the fixed alpha value listed as a coefficient. In the current implementation, fixed alpha parameters are reported as coefficients by the MLE but not by the MPLE. This causes trouble in my case because I am using the simulate function to simulate new networks from an MPLE-based ERGM including a gwesp term. I think the problem is that coef.sublength.model() counts one more term than is actually present because it assumes that the alpha parameter is listed under coef, and thus the simulate function throws an error. Can you confirm this?
> 
> Philip
> 
> Am 14.09.2013 13:58, schrieb David Hunter:
>> Hi, Philip.  Just to add to what Martina said:  That will work for the MLE, but for the MPLE it's more subtle.  In fact, the value of alpha is zero--the default.  Observe:
>> 
>>> data(faux.mesa.high)
>>> ergm(faux.mesa.high~gwesp, estimate="MPLE")
>> 
>> MPLE Coefficients:
>>   gwesp
>> -0.4868
>>> ergm(faux.mesa.high~gwesp(alpha=0), estimate="MPLE")
>> 
>> MPLE Coefficients:
>>   gwesp
>> -0.4868
>> 
>> 
>> Bottom line, there is no implementation for a meaningful MPLE for alpha when fixed=FALSE is used.  Perhaps we could give a warning in this case, but trying to anticipate all possibilities where such a warning should be issued is probably too difficult.  Maybe the best thing for us to do is to add "alpha=0" to the documentation so it's clearer what the default is.
>> 
>> Best,
>> Dave
>> 
>>

messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,
I don't know if questions about this would be better posted elsewhere, but this seemed the logical list to me. I am having a minor issue getting colors to plot in the manner i'd expect within ndtv. I am specifying node color as a TEA based on vertex attributes on the network objects. Instead of using those values as the color vector, it appears to be using a "unique sort" on values and assigning colors to those sequentially. Is there a way to get it to do the former instead?
 
In other words (trivial example, code below), suppose the values in slice 1 of the color variable are 1, 2, 3, while in slice 2 they are 1, 2, 4. What I would expect is that slice 1 would have 3 colors, slice 2 would also have 3, but only 2 of them would be the same (i.e., those with label 4 in slice 2 should NOT be the same as those with label 3 in slice 1). However, what i'm getting is that each slice is using the same 3-color palette. Plotting the three initial network objects w/plot.network gives the result I was anticipating. Am i missing something obvious?

thanks!
jimi

Trivial example code:
t1 <- network.initialize(3)
add.edge(t1,1,2) 
add.edge(t1,2,3)
t1 <- set.vertex.attribute(t1, "col", c(1:3))
t2 <- t1
t2 <- set.vertex.attribute(t2, "col", c(1,2,4))
t3 <- t2
ex <- networkDynamic(network.list=list(t1, t2, t3), vertex.pid="vertex.names", create.TEAs=T)
compute.animation(ex, slice.par=list(start=1,end=3,interval=1, aggregate.dur=1,rule='all'))
render.animation(ex, vertex.col="col")

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] applying ERGM to a word co-occurrence network
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone!

As part of my master degree in statistics I'm writing a work on Network
Analysis and it requires a practical application of the analysis of a real
network.

The network in question is a co-occurrence network of words, obtained from
a collection of tweets regarding the food industry. The result is a
weighted undirected network of 346 nodes and 2123 edges where the weights
are the jaccard indexes (a standardized index of co-occurrence) between
words, but I used a cut-off to make it binary and keep things as simple as
possible. I also have some additional node attributes like word topic, word
type(noun, verb, etc) and word total frequency.

The objective of the analysis should be finding useful commercial insights
for a particular food brand.

As much as I searched I couldn't find much about this particular type of
network, except some articles about them used as visual rapresentation of
text, and the recognition of central concepts using betweenes centrality.

I'd like to put in the work an application of ERGM, but I have some doubts:

-First of all, I'm not really sure if ERGMs are useful or even viable for
this particular network type, this doubt coming from the fact that I
couldn't find anything about the modeling of such networks, and I can't
tell if it's because infeasibility, because no one ever tried or because
the natural language processing methods are much better for this
environment.

-If the application of ERGMs in this setting is viable, do you have any
suggestion regarding the terms to include? For a start I decided to include
the nodemix term for the topic (using only the interesting matches). I know
it's a decision that depends on the exact network arrangement, but any
generic advice is welcome.

I'm sorry in advance if this message is somewhat off-topic, not regarding
the statnet suite directly.

Goodbye and thanks for any advice,

Michael Rossero

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] ergm: calculate values of terms for given network
messages.body_plain:
Dear statnet users,

The ergm package supports a number of "terms" that can be used to construct ERG models.  Is there any functionality in statnet that will let me calculate the values of these "terms" for a given network?

For example, we have the terms 'edges', 'triangle', 'gwdsp'.  Are there corresponding functions for calculating the number of edges, triangles, GWDSP(?) for a given network object?

If I'm correct, the internally ergm package is only using changes of these quantities when a single edge is added or removed from the graph.  Are there any utility functions for the convenience of users that can calculate these quantities though, at least the ones that are supported out of the box?

Szabolcs

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Interpretation of curved model terms if MPLE is used
messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Philip, for the instructive example!  You're right that the first instance should not throw an error and should in fact behave like the second instance, since the default fixed=FALSE is implicitly being changed to fixed=TRUE because of the MPLE.

I'll see about trying to fix this for the next release.

Dave


On Sep 14, 2013, at 9:28 AM, Philip Leifeld wrote:

> Hi Dave,
> 
> You are right that MLE with fixed = TRUE produces only one coefficient. However, consider the following example:
> 
> library(ergm)
> data(faux.mesa.high)
> 
> test1 <- ergm(faux.mesa.high ~ gwesp(alpha = 0), estimate="MPLE")
> sim <- simulate(test1)  # throws an error
> 
> test2 <- ergm(faux.mesa.high ~ gwesp(alpha = 0, fixed = TRUE), estimate="MPLE")
> sim <- simulate(test2)  # works fine
> 
> The error message is:
> 
> coef has 1 elements, while the model requires 2 parameters.
> 
> Thanks,
> Philip
> 
> Am 14.09.2013 15:07, schrieb David Hunter:
>> Hi, Philip.  I'm not sure I fully understand:  I don't believe that an alpha value is reported by MLE when fixed=TRUE, only when fixed=FALSE.  But when MPLE is used, fixed=FALSE makes no sense.  In other words, for fixed=TRUE, both methods produce the same number of coefficients; whereas for fixed=FALSE, MPLE should not be used.
>> 
>> I think that maybe the confusion only arises when fixed=FALSE is used with MPLE.  I see your point that it might be helpful to have one additional coefficient output in that case, namely the (actually fixed!) value of alpha.  But it seems this might encourage the use of fixed=FALSE with MPLE, which is probably not good.
>> 
>> Sorry if I'm misunderstanding something!
>> 
>> Dave
>> 
>> PS.  I added alpha=0 to the documentation, so that should show up with the next release of ergm.
>> 
>> 
>> 
>> On Sep 14, 2013, at 8:20 AM, Philip Leifeld wrote:
>> 
>>> Great, this answers my question. Thanks very much. I think adding alpha = 0 to the documentation would be helpful. And it would be nice if MPLE and MCMC MLE reported the same coefficients (either with or without the fixed alpha value listed as a coefficient. In the current implementation, fixed alpha parameters are reported as coefficients by the MLE but not by the MPLE. This causes trouble in my case because I am using the simulate function to simulate new networks from an MPLE-based ERGM including a gwesp term. I think the problem is that coef.sublength.model() counts one more term than is actually present because it assumes that the alpha parameter is listed under coef, and thus the simulate function throws an error. Can you confirm this?
>>> 
>>> Philip
>>> 
>>> Am 14.09.2013 13:58, schrieb David Hunter:
>>>> Hi, Philip.  Just to add to what Martina said:  That will work for the MLE, but for the MPLE it's more subtle.  In fact, the value of alpha is zero--the default.  Observe:
>>>> 
>>>>> data(faux.mesa.high)
>>>>> ergm(faux.mesa.high~gwesp, estimate="MPLE")
>>>> 
>>>> MPLE Coefficients:
>>>>   gwesp
>>>> -0.4868
>>>>> ergm(faux.mesa.high~gwesp(alpha=0), estimate="MPLE")
>>>> 
>>>> MPLE Coefficients:
>>>>   gwesp
>>>> -0.4868
>>>> 
>>>> 
>>>> Bottom line, there is no implementation for a meaningful MPLE for alpha when fixed=FALSE is used.  Perhaps we could give a warning in this case, but trying to anticipate all possibilities where such a warning should be issued is probably too difficult.  Maybe the best thing for us to do is to add "alpha=0" to the documentation so it's clearer what the default is.
>>>> 
>>>> Best,
>>>> Dave
>>>> 
>>>> 
>>>> On Sep 13, 2013, at 1:58 PM, martina morris wrote:
>>>> 
>>>>> Hi Philip,
>>>>> 
>>>>> You can recover the alpha parameter with:  fit.mle$coef
>>>>> 
>>>>> fit.mle$coef
>>>>>      edges       gwesp gwesp.alpha
>>>>> -1.3518520   0.4408169  -0.9306589
>>>>> 
>>>>> best,
>>>>> mm
>>>>> 
>>>>> On Fri, 13 Sep 2013, Philip Leifeld wrote:
>>>>> 
>>>>>> Hi,
>>>>>> 
>>>>>> How can I interpret curved model terms like GWESP if I fit an ergm using MPLE and if the alpha value is not fixed? I noticed that no alpha value is reported. I guess the parameter is not estimated? If not, what fixed parameter is used? Here is a minimal example comparing MCMC and MPLE - MLE has 3 and MPLE has 2 parameters:

Rose,

When you say "control a multiple 2-path model", it's not clear exactly 
what you mean.

At this point the ergm term "gwesp", when used on a directed network, 
counts one possible configuration:  only partners on a directed two-path 
connecting the nodes in the dyad.

You might try looking at the terms "balance", "intransitive", 
"transitive", "transitiveties", "triadcensus", and "triangle"
to see if any of these do what you want.

Note that ergm is an open source package, and it is possible to code your 
own terms (see the  ergm.userterms package and paper for details).

best,
Martina
