messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Interpretation of curved model terms if MPLE is used
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Philip.  Just to add to what Martina said:  That will work for the MLE, but for the MPLE it's more subtle.  In fact, the value of alpha is zero--the default.  Observe:

> data(faux.mesa.high)
> ergm(faux.mesa.high~gwesp, estimate="MPLE")

MPLE Coefficients:
  gwesp  
-0.4868  
> ergm(faux.mesa.high~gwesp(alpha=0), estimate="MPLE")

MPLE Coefficients:
  gwesp  
-0.4868  


Bottom line, there is no implementation for a meaningful MPLE for alpha when fixed=FALSE is used.  Perhaps we could give a warning in this case, but trying to anticipate all possibilities where such a warning should be issued is probably too difficult.  Maybe the best thing for us to do is to add "alpha=0" to the documentation so it's clearer what the default is.

Best,
Dave

Hi Vicki.

I think you should try including an "edges" term before altering software parameters. The edges term controls for the observed number of edges. It's much like an intercept term, except it isn't included by default. There could be more to that story...

Nathan Doogan

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ADD Health Data - Fit ERGMS
messages.body_plain:
Karen, glad the comments were helpful.

Note also that there are a few settings you can fiddle with specific to stepping, in case that helps- specifically, "Step.MCMC.samplesize," "Step.maxit," and "Step.gridsize." Also, I believe that the TNT setting is the default for models (like yours) without any constraints, so this can probably be omitted if you like (others can correct me if I'm wrong).

For what it's worth, I would be curious also to hear if others have experience and/or practical advice for using the stepping technique. Based on the Hummel et al. article, it seems we should see dramatic improvements in the ability to fit SOME models to SOME networks (though hard to predict in advance which). I am also not sure if folks have experience/recommendations regarding the three specific settings I mention, above. All of my experience is limited to running these models on unusually large networks (i.e. a few thousand nodes), so it is always hard for me to tell if my experiences are generalizable... Ruth, David, and Mark are the experts here and as usual I am trying to do my best to drive the car while having only a general (though hopefully generally accurate) understanding of what goes on under the hood.

Best wishes,
Kevin

From: Karen Ertrachter [mailto:kae197@psu.edu]
Sent: Wednesday, February 05, 2014 1:20 PM
To: Lewis, Kevin
Cc: martina morris
Subject: Re: [statnet_help] ADD Health Data - Fit ERGMS

Thank you Martina and Kevin!

Sorry, I left the analyses to run overnight and I was stuck in meetings all day.  I just checked on my model and R-studio shut down at some point.

Based on your advice, I increased the sample size/interval even more.  I got the stepping technique to work and it seems to be working a lot faster.  Still don't have a result yet, but I appreciate the tip about stepping.  I read about it, but I hadn't tried it in the model since I was thinking that fixing the MCMC parameters were more important.

my new model:
jmodel.08 <-ergm(relations~edges+nodematch('grade', diff=F)+nodematch('race', diff=F)+gwesp(0.25, fixed=T)+nodematch('gender', diff=F)+nodematch('educomb', diff=T), control = control.ergm(main.method=c("Stepping"), MCMC.prop.weights="TNT", MCMC.samplesize = 50000, MCMC.burnin=5000, MCMC.interval = 5000))

Martina: The part about edges is really helpful to keep in mind.  I added it to my model.

Thank you both,
Karen

On Wed, Feb 5, 2014 at 2:41 PM, Lewis, Kevin <lewis@ucsd.edu<mailto:lewis@ucsd.edu>> wrote:
Martina, thanks for the clarification and sorry for the misunderstanding!

Karen, the only other suggestion I might have is hiking up the MCMC sample size and/or interval still further. In what limited experience I have with models for large networks, this has sometimes made a dramatic difference- taking me from a model that wanders around and gets nowhere for weeks, to one that "quickly" converges (i.e. with relatively few iterations... though recognizing that each iteration may take an agonizingly long time). You might also try the "stepping" method described in Hummel et al. 2012, something I have been playing around with a bit lately.

(This of course assumes that there is not some other technical problem going on that would be over my head.)

-Kevin

P.S. Feel free to correspond with me privately if you want more specifics!

messages.body_plain:
Hi Zane (and the statnet user group),
I've been corresponding with Martina Morris and I've been able to fix my
data, so the ergm works even with my missing attribute data (on average
20%).

There was something about the formatting of my missing data (imported from
STATA) that seemed to impact the statnet refusing to define my attribute
data. Hopefully my solution will help others who have had issues with
missing attribute data.  I did not need to impute!

Here's the code that I used
#make sure your variables are factored if they are factor variables
#I am using a dataset called JeffFactor where my categorical variables are
defined as factor variables in R
#Cutting down the number of variables used in the data
myvars <- c("biof", hispanic","race", "grade")
JeffDem <- JeffFactor[myvars]
attach(JeffDem)
#ensure missing has appropriate prefix
JeffDem$biof <- Recode(JeffDem$biof, 'NA=NA', as.factor.result=FALSE)
JeffDem$race <- Recode(JeffDem$race, 'NA=NA', as.factor.result=FALSE)
#mark as missing in R
JeffDem$biof[NA] <-NA
JeffDem$race <- Recode(JeffDem$race, 'NA=NA', as.factor.result=FALSE)
#define your adjacency matrix
relations <-net
relations %v% "race" <- JeffDem$race
relations %v% "gender" <-JeffDem$biof
#fit ergm
jmodel.01 <- ergm(relations~edges+nodematch('race', diff=T))

-Karen Ertrachter

[statnet_help] interpreting GWDSP?
 Steven Goodreau goodreau at u.washington.edu 
Tue Aug 18 08:22:03 PDT 2009 
•Previous message: [statnet_help] interpreting GWDSP? 
•Next message: [statnet_help] interpreting GWDSP? 
•Messages sorted by: [ date ] [ thread ] [ subject ] [ author ] 

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  
On Thu, 6 Aug 2009, Jenine Harris wrote: 


> I was wondering if anyone has an example of how a GWDSP term would be 

> interpreted in somewhat lay terms. From my understanding GWDSP accounts for 

> the distribution of shared partnership for each dyad in a network, but I'm 

> not sure how to go about interpreting a negative signficant GWDSP 

> coefficient of -0.25 in an actual ERGM model. What does this say about the 

> distribution and how does it influence the likelihood of a tie? 



Hi Jenine, 

A great question. Yes, I do think GWDSP is a bit trickier than interpret 
than any of the other terms we commonly work with. I can give you my own 
idiosyncratic approach. 

First, as technical background: As you probably know, GWDSP is a 
parametric summary measure of the tendency for two actors to have x 
partners in common, regardless of whether the two actors themselves are 
tied. GWESP is the same measure, but only counted across two actors who 
are tied. The two are comparable to the "alternating 2-paths" and 
"alternating k-triangles" that Snijders et al discuss in a series of 
papers. The two measures, combined with a third (GW degree, or the 
comparable alternating k-stars) are derived in those papers by placing a 
parametric constraint on three sets of statistics that emerge when making 
a very sociologically reasonable set of assumptions about relational 
dependence. The three parametric stats are also seen to work well in 
practice at modeling real-world social networks and avoiding degeneracy 
when doing so. 

So, on to interpretation. As I said, I agree that GWDSP is the hardest to 
interpret. In fact, I personally never use a GWDSP term without also 
using a GWESP term. And once I combined the two, I always find that the 
GWDSP coefficient is close to zero, and non-significant. Let me see if I 
can give good intuition as to why. 

GWESP has some relatively clear interpetations (which I discuss in a few 
of my papers). In real-world data of friendship or collaboration or 
similar kinds of networks, it is generally significantly positive. This 
means that those who are tied are more likely than chance to have multiple 
shared partners. 

GWDSP tells whether shared partners tend to clump together, regardless of 
whether two people are tied or not. For example, whether or not you and I 
are friends, if we have one friend in common, are we more likely than 
expected by chance to have a second friend in common? And so on. If yes, 
the GWDSP coefficient will be positive. If it is zero, then we are as 
likely as chance to have one in common; if negative, then less. 

If one only uses GWDSP and not GWESP, then it's hard to know whether an 
observed non-random shared partner distribution is driven by pairs who are 
themselves tied, pairs who are not tied, or both. If you include both 
GWESP and GWDSP, then it becomes clear - GWDSP is the base effect (which 
now isolates the effect for those not tied only); GWESP occurs on top of 
this base, and isolates the effect for those who are tied. And what I 
have always found is that the GWESP effect is then strong and significant, 
and the GWDSP is tiny and insignificant. It may be that in different 
kinds of data GWDSP would be significant itself, though. 

My questions for you are: is your GWDSP term significant? Does it remain 
so when GWESP is added? If the answer to both questions is yes, then you 
have something particuarly interesting (and unprecendented, at least for 
me) on your hands. If it remains negative and significant, then that says 
that people who are not tied tend not to have multiple shared partners. 
Once two unconnected people have one shared partner, they're less likely 
than chance to have a second; if they do have a second, they're less 
likely than chance to have a third, and so on. I can't think of a type of 
social relationship I would anticipate this pattern for, but it could just 
be that I've never thought about the kind of relaitonship that you're 
studying, and it makes perfect sense to you. 

My other quesiton would be what your alpha is; that changes the fine 
quantitative details of the interpretation, but not the general 
qualitative interpretation. Unless your alpha is either essentially 0 or 
very very high, in which case it would change the latter as well. If it's 
in the 0.1 - 2.0 range, I don't think it would. 

I hope that helps! 
Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] colors in ndtv
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jimi, great to see you are trying out the ndtv package!

On 02/04/2014 11:09 AM, jimi adams wrote:
> Hi folks,
> I don't know if questions about this would be better posted elsewhere, but this seemed the logical list to me.

This is definitely the right place to ask ndtv questions :-)

I am having a minor issue getting colors to plot in the manner i'd 
expect within ndtv. I am specifying node color as a TEA based on vertex 
attributes on the network objects. Instead of using those values as the 
color vector, it appears to be using a "unique sort" on values and 
assigning colors to those sequentially. Is there a way to get it to do 
the former instead?
>
> In other words (trivial example, code below), suppose the values in slice 1 of the color variable are 1, 2, 3, while in slice 2 they are 1, 2, 4. What I would expect is that slice 1 would have 3 colors, slice 2 would also have 3, but only 2 of them would be the same (i.e., those with label 4 in slice 2 should NOT be the same as those with label 3 in slice 1). However, what i'm getting is that each slice is using the same 3-color palette. Plotting the three initial network objects w/plot.network gives the result I was anticipating. Am i missing something obvious?

I think the issue is that you are plotting the wrong time range for the 
example network. I'll expand on your example below.

>
> thanks!
> jimi
>
> Trivial example code:
> t1 <- network.initialize(3)
> add.edge(t1,1,2)
> add.edge(t1,2,3)
> t1 <- set.vertex.attribute(t1, "col", c(1:3))
> t2 <- t1
> t2 <- set.vertex.attribute(t2, "col", c(1,2,4))
> t3 <- t2
> ex <- networkDynamic(network.list=list(t1, t2, t3), vertex.pid="vertex.names", create.TEAs=T)
> compute.animation(ex, slice.par=list(start=1,end=3,interval=1, aggregate.dur=1,rule='all'))
> render.animation(ex, vertex.col="col")

Note that when you called networkDynamic(), it reported that it was 
making some default assumptions:

"Neither start or onsets specified, assuming start=0
Onsets and termini not specified, assuming each network in network.list 
should have a discrete spell of length 1"

This may be confusing, but what it means is that the first network on 
the list will be start at 0 and extend until 1, the 2nd will start at 1 
and extend until 2, etc.

For this example you computed a movie for the range 1 to 3, so you were 
only viewing the values from the t2 network onward

If I directly query the values of the attributes at each time I see

 > get.vertex.attribute.active(ex,'col',at=0)
[1] 1 2 3
 > get.vertex.attribute.active(ex,'col',at=1)
[1] 1 2 4
 > get.vertex.attribute.active(ex,'col',at=2)
[1] 1 2 4

I re-ran the movie, shifting slice.par one unit earlier:

compute.animation(ex,slice.par=list(start=0,end=2,interval=1,aggregate.dur=1,rule='all'))
render.animation(ex, vertex.col="col")

I see the color of vertex '3' change from green to blue, which seems 
like what you were expecting, right?

Alternatively, if you want the "ex" network to actually start at time 1 
instead of 0, you can explicitly tell the networkDynamic() converter 
function when the first start time should be using the "start" parameter:

ex <- networkDynamic(network.list=list(t1, t2, 
t3),vertex.pid="vertex.names", create.TEAs=T,start=1)

or even give it the onset and terminus of each panel if they have 
different durations or you want to use different time units...

ex <- networkDynamic(network.list=list(t1, t2, t3), 
vertex.pid="vertex.names", create.TEAs=T,onsets=1:3,termini=2:4)


Please let me know if this resolves the issue.

best,
  -skye

p.s:  A Shameless Plug:  We will be running a pre-Sunbelt Networks 
conference workshop on plotting dynamic networks with the ndtv package 
on Tueseday Feb 18. I think there are still a few slots left...

messages.subject: [statnet_help] applying ERGM to a word co-occurrence network
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] applying ERGM to a word co-occurrence network
messages.body_plain:
Hi Michael,

The short answer is that ERGMs may be relevant, but it depends on your 
research question.

One of Mark Handcock's students used ERGMs for language analysis -- Danny 
Wyatt.  You can find some of his work from google scholar: 
http://scholar.google.com/citations?user=q9UyGCIAAAAJ&hl=en

The new weighted versions of ERGMs could be used for the original weighted 
networks, but weighted networks require (quite) a bit more thought than 
binary.  We have a tutorial up on the statnet website:

https://statnet.csde.washington.edu/trac/attachment/wiki/Sunbelt2013/Valued.pdf

For the binary network you describe, you can put in a nodemix term, but 
the question is what attributes should govern the mixing.  I'm assuming 
it's not just nouns vs. verbs.  If you were really interested in 
co-occurrence of specific words, then the attribute to mix on is node ID, 
but that would require 346x345/2 = 59K+ parameters, so I don't think you 
want to do that.

In short, ERGMs are potentially useful here, but you would need to specify 
a theoretical model first, and then assess the feasibility.

You might also consider an MDS approach on the original weighted network 
if you want to identify word "neighborhoods".  The "latentnet" package in 
statnet provides an alternative approach to this kind of latent space 
modeling.  Pavel will be teaching a workshop on latentnet at the Sunbelt 
this year.

HTH,
Martina

messages.subject: [statnet_help] modeling asymmetric ties in statnet
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I would like to hear your advice on a problem I am encountering.

My research question is whether the ties boys (coded as 1) send to girls
(coded as 0) are more likely to be un-reciprocated than those girls send to
boys. I am taking three approaches.

1. Keep the full network and use nodemix. I think nodemix will count both
the number of un-reciprocated ties from boys to girls and mutual ties
between girls and boys to calculate (1, 0) ties. Similarly, it will count
both the number of un-reciprocated ties from girls to boys and mutual ties
between them to calculate (0, 1) ties. If we use the former as the
reference group, the number of mutual ties cancel out so that we can
interpret the coefficient for the latter as a relative tendency. Does this
make sense?

2. Keep only un-reciprocated ties in the network since we are interested in
only un-reciprocated ties. Still use nodemix. But I think statnet is not
built to model this type of network yet because there are no built-in
constrains controlling the uniform asymmetry yet.

3. I am not familiar with the term asymmetric. Suppose I estimate a model
like

model <- ergm ( SNet~ edges + asymmetric("boy", diff = TRUE) )

                   Estimate Std. Error MCMC %       p-value
edges            -4.2698526 0.02007895      0  0.000000e+00
asymmetric.boy.0 -1.3784407 0.04340871      0 4.499525e-221
asymmetric.boy.1 -0.9322624 0.05927340      0  9.998334e-56

How do I interpret asymmetric.boy.0 and asymmetric.boy.1?

One last question, is it possible to let nodemix vary by the types of ties
(symmetric vs. asymmetric)? It seems that some new terms need to be made to
address that.

Any help will be greatly appreciated. Many thanks!

best,

Weihua

-- 
Weihua (Edward) An

Assistant Professor of Sociology and Statistics
Indiana University Bloomington
752 Ballantine Hall
1020 East Kirkwood Avenue
Bloomington, IN 47405-7103
http://mypage.iu.edu/~weihuaan/

messages.subject: [statnet_help] fitting ergms to data from link-tracing designs
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] fitting ergms to data from link-tracing designs
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Michal. The current version of ergm() will, when given a network 
with missing edges, find the observed-data MLE under the assumption that 
the observed data is ignorably sampled from the graph being modeled. H+G 
discuss the conditions under which that is a reasonable assumption...but 
where it is, ergm() should work out of the box.

An alternative approach (closer to what is in the tutorial you mention) 
is to obtain an approximate MLE by (1) using design-based estimation to 
obtain (approximate) sufficient statistics, and (2) fitting to those 
target stats (using the functionality currently in ERGM). Note that to 
do this in a valid manner, the graph used for simulation in ERGM must be 
of the same size as the graph from which your data was sampled -- this 
means that the method does not scale so well if one has a really large 
system (e.g., an OSN). One advantage of this approach is that it makes 
it easier to relax the assumption that the seed nodes for the link-trace 
were drawn from a probability sample (by using Markov chain-based 
sampling methods - see, e.g., Gjoka et al., IEEE JSAC, 2011). (Of 
course, that only helps you if you are in a position to choose your data 
collection design!) If your design-based estimators are consistent, then 
the associated approximate MLE should be consistent as well, but your 
measures of standard error will in general be underestimated (because 
they neglect the sampling variability in your estimates of the 
sufficient statistics). My impression is that Pavel is currently working 
on this (or, if not, a closely related problem!).

Mark or others may want to chime in on this, but that should at least 
give you the basic rundown....

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Basic modeling of medical facts
messages.body_plain:
On Wed, 9 Oct 2013, Hane, Christopher A wrote:

Hi Chris,

> I have medical history data on millions of people.? From this data, I computed a network where nodes are conditions
> and a link (i,j) indicates the number of people who had condition i prior to condition j. The conditions are
> summarized into roughly 500 conditions.? For each link I can define the probability of of the link (i,j) from the
> observed data (number of people who have j after i / number with i ), or a suitable weight for the strength of the
> association.

This is a fascinating use of network analysis -- it reminds me of a 
similar approach to modeling the occupational structure, using job titles 
as nodes, and people's job changes as links or link weights.

Note that you could also treat this as a 2 mode network: persons and 
conditions.  That would remove the temporal ordering, but would pick up 
clustering.

> I can analyse this network assuming the edge weights are deterministic but that hasn?t been very fruitful so far. I am
> not sure ERGM applies because all the examples I see involve unweighted edges.

You're in luck, if you call being first in line lucky.  Pavel Krivitsky 
has developed the theory, methods and code for analyzing networks with 
valued/weighted edges.  He taught a workshop on this at the Sunbelt 
meetings last May in Hamburg, and the materials from that tutorial are 
here:

https://statnet.csde.washington.edu/trac/attachment/wiki/Sunbelt2013/Valued.pdf
(all the tutorial materials are on the Sunbelt2013 page)

and the paper is here:

Pavel~N. Krivitsky. Exponential-family random graph models for valued 
networks. Electronic Journal of Statistics, 6:1100{1128, 2012. doi: 
10.1214/12-EJS696.

The key issue in valued ties is how to aggregate the values into the 
statistics that will be used in the model to represent processes of 
interest.  For binary ties, we typically use sums and sums of products, 
which is pretty simple.  With valued ties there is both the question of 
what summary (mean, max, min, sum, etc.) and what distributional 
assumptions to make for inference.

Take a look at the tutorial materials and let us know what you think.

best,
Martina

messages.body_plain:
Karen,

One last point -- it's not a good idea to use nodematch terms without also 
using the associated nodefactor.  nodematch is a bit like an interaction 
effect in a glm, the interaction of attr(node 1) x attr(node 2).  As in 
most modeling, if you include an interaction of two variables, you 
probably want to include the main effects for them also.

So, bottom line for this model, I would suggest:

1. use a nodefactor term for every attribute you're also nodematching on

2. if you want to exclude the intercept, make sure you use 
nodefactor('attrname', base=0) (thanks to Steve for reminding me of this)

3. see if this works before getting fancy with ergm controls of various 
kinds

best,
Martina

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Statistical methods for a sample of networks
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Statistical methods for a sample of networks
messages.body_plain:
Hi Philip, thanks very much for your reply!  From your description, it
sounds like, for any models that relate to group-level outcomes (e.g., the
decisions made by each group), it might be reasonable to extract the
relevant network statistics from each network and fit a regular logistic
regression -- is that correct?

However, some of the questions that I'm interested in relate to
individual-level outcomes.  For example, if I were interested in predicting
who has the most influence on the conversation (i.e., who is most central),
it seems to me that any statistical model that I fit to answer this
question should take into account the explicitly relational nature of the
study design.  In most of these cases, the outcome variable will be
measured on either an interval scale, and could either be a derived measure
(i.e., network centrality, in-degree / in-strength) or a raw measure (i.e.,
time spent speaking, participant self-ratings of how much they enjoyed the
discussion, etc).  In these cases, what options do I have given the design
of these studies?


On Wed, Dec 18, 2013 at 4:01 PM, Philip Leifeld <
philip.leifeld@uni-konstanz.de> wrote:

> Hi Patrick,
>
> If you can reasonably assume that the data-generating process is the same
> for all networks, you can combine them in a single matrix and use
> structural zeros for the between-network dyads which cannot have any
> connection. The problem is rather that there are not a lot of ways to model
> weighted network data. There are simply no model terms available for
> generalized ERGMs or count ERGMs (unless somebody from the statnet team has
> recently implemented some model terms for valued networks, which I don't
> know). See here: help("ergm-terms", package = "ergm.count"). If the timing
> of the edges matters, relational event models may be an alternative (look
> at the articles of Carter Butts and Brandes/Lerner/Snijders and at the
> relevent package). On the other hand, the questions you are asking are more
> related to explaining outcomes per network and describing the networks in
> terms of centrality. So I am not sure if you need a model which explains
> network formation at all. It may be more interesting for you to describe
> the network in terms of who is central (or any other interesting graph
> statistics) and use them as covariates when you model the outcomes of your
> networks (since they are independent by design).
>
> As for the conversion of your transcripts into network matrices, this is
> not a trivial task. I wrote a Java software package for this purpose. It's
> called Discourse Network Analyzer (see www.github.com/leifeld/dna). Right
> now, however, you can only annotate what each person says (and whether the
> person agrees or disagrees with the concept). You can then produce two-mode
> network matrices of actors and concepts, or one-mode network matrices where
> two actors are connected if they have claims in common (both agreeing to
> the same concepts or both disagreeing to the same concepts). It is not
> possible right now to annotate direct connections between actors (at least
> not with additional qualifiers other than positive and negative). But I am
> working on a new version with more flexible ways of annotating text data
> and extracting networks from them.
>
> Best,
> Philip
>
> Am 18.12.2013 20:23, schrieb Patrick S Forscher:
>
>> Hi all,
>>
>> /Warning: This email is a little long/
>>
>>
>> I am a social psychologist by training and am new to social network
>> analysis.  I am planning a series of studies that involve small groups
>> of people.  In a typical study, the participants will meet in groups of
>> 4 to have a discussion about a particular topic.  As a group, the
>> participants will reach a decision about the topic (e.g., whether to
>> support or oppose a proposed change in university policy).  The
>> discussion will be videotaped, and we will use transcripts of the
>> discussion to obtain information about who is talking to whom about what
>> topics.  In addition, the participants will complete ratings of
>> themselves and each other (e.g., What is your opinion about the proposed
>> change?  What do you think is this person's opinion of the proposed
>> change?).  I will also have a variety of data about the individual
>> characteristics of all the participants.  Thus, each group from each
>> study will give me a 4-node network with directed, valued edges and a
>> variety of attributes about each node.
>>
>> In all the studies, I will be interested in group-level,
>> relationship-level, and individual-level outcomes.  I have provided
>> below a sampling of the kinds of questions I would want to ask from
>> these data:
>>
>> (1) Which groups express the most agreement in their discussions?  Which
>> groups express the most disagreement?  Is group composition related to
>> agreement / disagreement and to the final decision outcome?
>> (2) Which pairs of people like each other during the discussion?  Which
>> pairs of people dislike each other?  How are the pairwise patterns of
>> liking related to the final decision outcome?
>> (3) Who has the most influence on the course of the discussion?  Who has
>> influence over the final decision of each group?  Are there any
>> individual difference characteristics that are related to influence over
>> the discussion and / or final decision?
>>
>> And so on.  What I am looking for from the mailing list is the proper
>> statistical model to use to investigate /samples/ of networks, rather
>>
>> than individual networks.  I have read a bit about single-network
>> methods, like ERGM models, but these methods do not seem appropriate,
>> since I am dealing with a set of independent networks, rather than a
>> single network.  In addition, a plain linear mixed model does not seem
>> appropriate because I am collecting relational data.  Finally, although
>> a method like the social relations model seems appropriate for this
>> situation at first blush, the social relations model seems to only
>> partition the variance in round-robin ratings into perceiver, target,
>> and relationship sources rather than allowing me to, for example, relate
>> the patterns within a set of networks to overall network outcomes.
>>
>> Perhaps I'm over-thinking this problem, and perhaps the choice of the
>> appropriate statistical model is obvious.  However, as I mentioned
>> earlier in the email, I am new to this stuff.  Could anyone offer some
>> advice about which statistical model might be appropriate for my
>> situation?  Also, is the proper analytic method possible in statnet?
>>
>> --
>> Patrick S Forscher
>> PhD Candidate
>> University of Wisconsin-Madison
>>
>>
>> _______________________________________________
>> statnet_help mailing list
>> statnet_help@u.washington.edu
>> http://mailman2.u.washington.edu/mailman/listinfo/statnet_help
>>
>>


-- 
Patrick S Forscher
PhD Candidate
University of Wisconsin-Madison

On Wed, Jan 29, 2014 at 8:58 PM, Carter T. Butts <buttsc@uci.edu> wrote:
> Hi, Michal. The current version of ergm() will, when given a network with
> missing edges, find the observed-data MLE under the assumption that the
> observed data is ignorably sampled from the graph being modeled. H+G discuss
> the conditions under which that is a reasonable assumption...but where it
> is, ergm() should work out of the box.
>
> An alternative approach (closer to what is in the tutorial you mention) is
> to obtain an approximate MLE by (1) using design-based estimation to obtain
> (approximate) sufficient statistics, and (2) fitting to those target stats
> (using the functionality currently in ERGM). Note that to do this in a valid
> manner, the graph used for simulation in ERGM must be of the same size as
> the graph from which your data was sampled -- this means that the method
> does not scale so well if one has a really large system (e.g., an OSN). One
> advantage of this approach is that it makes it easier to relax the
> assumption that the seed nodes for the link-trace were drawn from a
> probability sample (by using Markov chain-based sampling methods - see,
> e.g., Gjoka et al., IEEE JSAC, 2011). (Of course, that only helps you if you
> are in a position to choose your data collection design!) If your
> design-based estimators are consistent, then the associated approximate MLE
> should be consistent as well, but your measures of standard error will in
> general be underestimated (because they neglect the sampling variability in
> your estimates of the sufficient statistics). My impression is that Pavel is
> currently working on this (or, if not, a closely related problem!).
>
> Mark or others may want to chime in on this, but that should at least give
> you the basic rundown....

messages.subject: [statnet_help] mapply() and dyadcov term
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have 31 networks with which I am working (playmate ties of children in
villages; no cross-village ties) in a list object (i.e., each network is an
object in the list). Because I have these 31 networks in a list and I'm
fitting the same model, I have been using lapply() for ease of coding and
efficiency. I've fit a variety of ERGMs on these networks with no problems.
I'm now trying to fit one with a dyadic covariates (matrices of geographic
distance from child-to-child in each of the village networks) using the
mapply() function with the list of 31 networks and a corresponding list of
31 matrices.

When I add in the "dyadcov" term to the ERGM and use the mapply() function,
I get the following error: *Error in check.ErgmTerm(nw, arglist, varnames =
c("x", "attrname"), vartypes = c("matrix,network",  : object 'y' not found*,
where 'y' is parameter name (in the mapply() function) for the matrix in
the "dyadcov" term.

However, if I specify the ERGM with a particular network from the list
object and a particular matrix from the list object, the ERGM estimation
works just fine. Does anyone have thoughts as to what's going on? I'm at a
loss as to why the mapply() approach doesn't work and the other does.

I've included reproducible code below and I'm using R 3.0.0 and statnet
3.1-0 (ergm 3.1-0) on a MacBook Pro.

Thanks for listening!

Matt

# libraries
library(statnet)

# create network object
set.seed(02122013)
net <- network(rgraph(55, tprob = .1))

# create symmetric matrix (representing distances (say, in kilometers)
between nodes)
set.seed(02122013)
dist.mtx <- matrix(rnorm(3025), nr = 55, nc = 55)
diag(dist.mtx) <- 0
dist.mtx <- symmetrize(dist.mtx, rule = "upper")
dist.mtx[dist.mtx < 0] <- 0

# create list objects
net <- list(net)
dist.mtx <- list(dist.mtx)

# specifying objects directly (no issues in estimating)
mod1 <- ergm(net[[1]] ~ edges + mutual + twopath + gwidegree(2) +
gwodegree(2) + gwesp(log(2)) + ctriple + dyadcov(dist.mtx[[1]]), control =
control.ergm(MCMLE.maxit = 8))
params <- enformulate.curved(mod1)
mod2 <- ergm(params$formula, control = control.ergm(init = params$theta,
MCMLE.maxit = 20, MCMC.burnin = 100000, MCMC.interval = 1000,
MCMC.samplesize = 15000))

# using mapply function (problem after the 'mod1' code)
model <- mapply(function(x, y) {
mod1 <- ergm(x ~ edges + mutual + twopath + gwidegree(2) +
gwodegree(2) + gwesp(log(2)) + ctriple + dyadcov(y), control =
control.ergm(MCMLE.maxit = 8))
params <- enformulate.curved(mod1)
mod2 <- ergm(params$formula, control = control.ergm(init = params$theta,
MCMLE.maxit = 20, MCMC.burnin = 100000, MCMC.interval = 1000,
MCMC.samplesize = 15000))
return(list(mod2))
}, net, dist.mtx)

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Feature request: edge operator
messages.body_plain:
I would like to see the network package API evolve towards more consistent treatment of the %e% operator.

The usage of the %e% operator is confusing because as a setter it takes one type of object (a matrix) and as a getter it returns a different one (a list). My students have a lot of trouble with this. I can't think of another programming language where the result of a 'get' operation is not a valid argument to the 'set' operation.

Example:

# create simple network
n <- network.initialize(5)
n[1,] <- 1
n[2,3] <- 1
n[,5] <- 1

# set the bar attribute
set.edge.attribute(n, "bar", 1:8)
set.vertex.attribute(n, "baz", 1:5)

# naively set the foo attribute to be the "same" as the bar attribute
n %e% "foo" <- n %e% "bar"

# different assignment of attributes
as.sociomatrix(n, attrname="bar")
as.sociomatrix(n, attrname="foo")

I know this is "just how it works" and probably there is a lot of legacy code that depends on this idiosyncratic behavior. Still, I would suggest that the developers consider changing %e% (and I guess get.edge.value as well) to return a matrix value, so that the API is consistent. get.edge.attribute would still be there as the way to get a list of the attribute values.

__________________________________________________________
Robin Burke, Professor
College of Computing and Digital Media, DePaul University
rburke@cdm.depaul.edu

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Independence of centrality measures ?
messages.body_plain:
So long as (1) you are using node-level indices (NLIs) as fixed 
covariates, and (2) the realizations of your dependent variable are 
independent conditional on the covariates (including any NLIs), then 
there is no particular reason that you cannot use the NLIs as predictors 
in a typical regression setting.  (The idea that this is inherently 
problematic is a very common but incorrect belief.)  However, there 
_are_ various "gotchas" that can arise - these are not really unique to 
the network case, but most network analytic settings raise the risk 
level appreciably.  Among them are the following:

1. The realizations of your dependent variable might not actually be 
independent given your model.  (The most obvious way to get this is for 
your dependent variable to arise via an influence process.)

2. Your N may be too small to give you adequate power for a reasonable 
analysis.

3. If using multiple NLIs, they may be too strongly correlated to permit 
reliable estimation of coefficients.

The bottom line is that there are many settings in which such analyses 
are appropriate and useful, but one must be careful. Some discussion of 
the analysis of nodal covariates as dependent variables is included in 
one of my review papers; you might find it helpful:

Butts, Carter T.  2008.  "Social Networks: A Methodological 
Introduction."  Asian Journal of Social Psychology, 11(1): 13-41.

See also the statnet tutorial, "Beyond Descriptives," on the statnet web 
site.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
Hi Shane,

On 03/19/2014 12:25 PM, Shane Gleason wrote:
> Hello everyone,
>
> I have a bipartite network which is presently formated as such:
>
> Sender       Receiver     Value
>
>     21           33          1
>
>     22           33          4
>
>     23           32          8
>
>
> Presently, I am having a difficult time figuring out how to  assign
> attributes and labels.

If your data above is in a data.frame named theDataFrame, you should be 
able create a network with "Value" as an edge attribute with this command:

net<-as.network(theDataFrame,ignore.eval=FALSE,names.eval='Value',bipartite=30)

This is assuming that vertices with ids 30 and below are in the first 
mode of the bipartite network, and those with ids above 30 are in the other.

> I've googled high and low and searched the
> statnet archeives, but I can't seem to find anything about how to assign
> vertex labels for plotting purposes or attributes for ERGM purposes.

The network help page ?loading.attributes  may have some examples that 
might help.

>
> I presently have attributes (labels/values) etc. in a separate csv
> file.  I'd like to do all the things I have done with single mode
> networks (ie: nodematch, absolute difference etc).  Presently the file
> is composed as such:
>
> ID    Name     Attribute1
>
> 21     Bob         .35
>
> 22     Steve       .31
>
> 23     Sue         .55
> Is there an equivilent to rownames(attributes$names) for bipartite
> networks?  Likewise, is there an equivalent fornet %v%"attributeone" <- attribute$V1?

Bipartite networks use the same attribute assignments as single-mode 
networks, you just need to be careful with the ids as you assign 
attributes, perhaps using the "v" argument to only assign to one mode at 
a time.

Assuming your example above is a data.frame, have you tried:

net%v%"attributeone" <- attribute$Attribute1

This should assign the value of attribute$Attribute1  to an attribute 
named "attributeone" on ALL the vertices of "net"  HOWEVER, the 
correspondence of elements in "attribute" to vertices is by the row id, 
NOT by the ID column.  In other words, if the rows in the attributes 
file are not in the same order as your vertices, the wrong values may 
get assigned.

If you want to use the value of the ID column to determine which vertex 
the attribute gets assigned to, this should work:

net<-set.vertex.attribute(net,attrname='attributeone',value=attribute$Attribute1,v=attribute$ID)

If you have separate tables of attributes  for the vertices in each mode 
of the network, you can use the "v" argument to specifiy which vertices 
get assigned. Note that vertices do not all need to have attributes with 
the same name.

Please let me know if this solves your problem.

best,
  -skye

messages.subject: [statnet_help] how to preserve node attributes when converting a matrix to an edglist using as.matrix
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] how to preserve node attributes when converting a matrix to an edglist using as.matrix
messages.body_plain:
Hi Statnet users,

Does anyone know how to preserve node attributes when converting a matrix
to an edglist using as.matrix(x, matrix.type = "edgelist",
as.sna.edgelist=FALSE) ?

Here is an example that illustrates my problem. I did a work around using
"recode" from the car package, but this will get burdensome for a large
network.

#lode libraries
library(statnet)
library(car)

#Create a sample network and rename row and column numbers.
myNet <- matrix(1,5,5)
colnames(myNet)<- c(c(6:10)); rownames(myNet)<-colnames(myNet)
myNet0 <- diag.remove(myNet, remove.val=0) ;myNet0

#now convert the network to an edgelist
test <- as.matrix(as.network(myNet0), matrix.type = "edgelist",
as.sna.edgelist=FALSE) ;test

#Problem is that as.matrix replaces node IDs with row/col count. That is  6
goes back to 1, 7 to 2, etc. So I have to recode them back to the original
values.
test2<-recode(test, "1=6;2=7;3=8;4=9;5=10") ;test2

# Is there an easier way to preserve my original node ID values, perhaps
within the as.matrix command? While recode is no problem with 5 nodes, it
would be very burdensome for say 50 nodes.

Thanks and best wishes
Jesse


--

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Differences between simulate.formula and simulate.ergm?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Philip -

Thanks for your detailed example - it makes recreating straightforward, 
and helped me dramatically with the diagnosing.

It seems to be an issue of different default values for one of the 
control parameters between the two routines.  Specifically, 
simulate.formula invokes control.simulate.formula, which defaults to an 
interval of 1000 MCMC steps between draws in the simulation (via the 
argument MCMC.interval).  For simulate.ergm, it's only 100.  That means 
that by default simulate.ergm won't move as far away on average in 
consecutive draws, and there will be more auto-correlation between two 
consecutive draws for larger networks, as you saw in your plots.

Of course, the user always has the option to change these control 
parameters instead of accepting the default, but we recognize there are 
many such parameters and it's not practical to assume that every user 
will explore all of these all of the time.  I'll add a ticket now to 
standardize these for the next release.

Yours,
Steve

> they work:

> nw <- network(matrix(rbinom(10000, 1, 0.01), nrow = 100))
> fit <- ergm(nw ~ edges)
>
> # experiment 1:
> sim1 <- simulate.formula(nw ~ edges, nsim = 500, coef = coef(fit))
> mat1 <- as.matrix(sim1[[1]])
> for (i in 2:500) {

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Differences between simulate.formula and simulate.ergm?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Philip.  In response to your three questions, 

(1) Autocorrelation is not a bad thing per se.  There is a tradeoff in MCMC between storage and information:  Ideally, one should keep every single iteration because even highly correlated values provide some additional information about parameters.  However, in the ERGM context we don?t do this because the storage-cost-to-information ratio is too high.  This is not to say, though, that autocorrelation should be eliminated entirely, as the resulting loss of information and therefore efficiency might be too great?plus, it?s generally impossible to eliminate autocorrelation entirely and so one would have to implement some kind of (necessarily ad hoc) scheme to try to check for autocorrelation.  Bottom line, it?s not an exact science and ?accidental misinterpretation? is not necessarily caused by autocorrelation.

(2) In light of (1), I don?t think ?required MCMC interval? has any meaning.  That said, trying to find good (i.e., effective) default values is an interesting theoretical question, though from a practical point of view it may not be worth a great deal of effort to try to solve.  Also note that there is a huge literature on MCMC routines that attempts to answer roughly this same question, and for every effective-looking rule of thumb, there?s always a pathological counterexample on which it fails utterly.

(3) Good point.  Perhaps we should point out that when these control values are null, the value that?s used is the one contained in the ergm object itself (in object$control).  As this value comes from the control.ergm function by default, you?ll find this value in the help for control.ergm.

Hope this is helpful (and that my answers to (1) and (2) don?t sound flippant; they?re not intended to be!)
Dave

messages.subject: [statnet_help] trouble working with valued data for network objects
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] trouble working with valued data for network objects
messages.body_plain:
Hi Micheal,

Sorry it has taken me a few days to reply. I have been hard at work on
various things. Thank you for showing me how to preserve the valued data
with network objects. Your code fixes work fine, but I then seem to be
running into an odd behavior with the matrix data that only occurs when
converting it to a network object and back to a matrix. When I use the
output matrix format with other code I have written, it does not work
properly. But the same code works fine with matrix data that has not been
converted to network object and back to matrix. Here are both the
problematic code, functioning code, and full explanations. Any thoughts?

#(19 June 2014) this code takes a matrix, converts to network, removes
isolates (as it uses random data, there may be none to remove), and
converts back to matrix so that the valued data can be weak symmetrized by
max or min of ij-ji as described below. BUT -- the symmetrization code does
not work right when the data are converted from matrix to network and back
to matrix. It does work when the data input is just as a matrix.

library(statnet)

#make a sample matrix that includes NAs and set diag to 0.
test<-matrix(ncol=10, nrow=10, sample(c(NA, 1:5), 100, replace=TRUE,
c(.75,rep(.1,5)))) #NA has high prob
test0<-diag.remove(test, remove.val=0) ;test0

#make as network object and keep valued data (ignore.eval=FALSE,
names.eval="value")
testMeNet<-as.network.matrix(test0, ignore.eval=FALSE, names.eval="value",
na.rm=TRUE) ;testMeNet

#ID isoslets
isos <- isolates(testMeNet, diag=FALSE) ;length(isos)

#remove isolets
testMeCut<-delete.vertices(testMeNet,(isolates(testMeNet, diag=FALSE)))
;testMeCut

#convert back to matrix. #I have tried using
as.sociomatrix(testMeCut,"value") and get the same result
testMeOut <- as.matrix(testMeCut, "value", matrix.type='adjacency')
;testMeOut
class(testMeOut);class(test)

##now symmetrize network based on max or min
##This code symmetrizes a valued matrix by max or min values of ij-ji. For
max, steps 1 & 5 should use "-999" & step 3 must use ">" and ">=". For min,
use "999", "<", & "<=" respectively. The input data must use NA rather than
0 for non-ties. The code uses weak symmetrization, so an NA in ij or ji
will be replaced with valued data of ji or ij respectively.

#Step 1: convert NA to "999" for use with "<" and "-999" for use with ">"
so NA gets replaced with desired tie value (i.e., weak symmetrization)
testMeOut[is.na(testMeOut)]<- (-999) ;testMeOut

#Step 2: separate lower and upper tri
low<-upper.tri.remove(test0, remove.val=NA) ;low
upp<-lower.tri.remove(test0, remove.val=NA) ;upp

#Step 3: get min (<) or max (>) based on True/False, convert to 1/0, and
combine lower and upper. To deal with ij=ji, upp2 uses <= or >=, step2 uses
NA, and NAs are converted to 0 in step3. This avoids "full = 1+1"
low2 <- (ifelse((low > t(upp))==TRUE, 1, 0));low2[is.na(low2)]<- 0 ;low2
upp2 <- (ifelse((upp >= t(low))==TRUE, 1, 0));upp2[is.na(upp2)]<- 0 ;upp2
full <- (upp2 + low2) ;full

#Step 4: extract from original data using full binary mat (selects min/max
based on above choice (< or >))
tempNet <- testMeOut*full ;tempNet

#Step 5: final symmetrized mat based on min or max as specified above.
Then, just in case there were any NA-NA ij-ji pairs, convert those to 0
final <- tempNet + t(tempNet);final
final[final == -999] <- 0 ;final

#compare final, testMeOut, and test0. Not all NAs have been treated
properly. Rather than weak symmetrization, "final" has 0 where ij-ji had an
NA and value combo.
final
testMeOut
test0


# Now run symm with matrix data that does not get passed through network
object. It works fine.

newtest<-matrix(ncol=10, nrow=10, sample(c(NA, 1:5), 100, replace=TRUE,
c(.75,rep(.1,5)))) #NA has high prob
newtest0<-diag.remove(test, remove.val=0) ;newtest0

#Step 1: convert NA to "999" for use with "<" and "-999" for use with ">"
so NA gets replaced with desired tie value (i.e., weak symmetrization)
newtest0[is.na(newtest0)]<- (-999) ;newtest0

#Step 2: separate lower and upper tri
low<-upper.tri.remove(newtest0, remove.val=NA) ;low
upp<-lower.tri.remove(newtest0, remove.val=NA) ;upp

#Step 3: get min (<) or max (>) based on True/False, convert to 1/0, and
combine lower and upper. To deal with ij=ji, upp2 uses <= or >=, step2 uses
NA, and NAs are converted to 0 in step3. This avoids "full = 1+1"
low2 <- (ifelse((low > t(upp))==TRUE, 1, 0));low2[is.na(low2)]<- 0 ;low2
upp2 <- (ifelse((upp >= t(low))==TRUE, 1, 0));upp2[is.na(upp2)]<- 0 ;upp2
full <- (upp2 + low2) ;full

#Step 4: extract from original data using full binary mat (selects min/max
based on above choice (< or >))
tempNet <- testMeOut*full ;tempNet

#Step 5: final symmetrized mat based on min or max as specified above.
Then, just in case there were any NA-NA ij-ji pairs, convert those to 0
final <- tempNet + t(tempNet);final
final[final == -999] <- 0 ;final

#compare final and newtest0. Weak symm works. There are values where ij-ji
had one value and one NA.
final
newtest0

# So why does the symmetrization code work when input is an unmodified
matrix, but not when the input is a matrix that has been passed to a
network object and back to a matrix?

On Fri, 11 Apr 2014, Burke, Robin wrote:

> 
> I would like to see the network package API evolve towards more consistent treatment of the %e% operator.
>
> 
> 
> The usage of the %e% operator is confusing because as a setter it takes one type of object (a matrix) and as
> a getter it returns a different one (a list). My students have a lot of trouble with this. I can?t think of
> another programming language where the result of a ?get? operation is not a valid argument to the ?set?
> operation.
>
> 
> 
> Example:
>
> 
> 
> # create simple network
> 
> n <- network.initialize(5)
> 
> n[1,] <- 1
> 
> n[2,3] <- 1
> 
> n[,5] <- 1
>
> 
> 
> # set the bar attribute
> 
> set.edge.attribute(n, "bar", 1:8)
> 
> set.vertex.attribute(n, ?baz?, 1:5)
>
> 
> 
> # naively set the foo attribute to be the ?same? as the bar attribute
> 
> n %e% "foo" <- n %e% "bar"
>
> 
> 
> # different assignment of attributes

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Working with multiplex networks
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jacques,
  Although the network data structure facilitates multiplex ties, there 
is very little network or statnet functionality that is directly aware 
of them.   I'm including some example operations below, including 
tracking tie types with an attached attribute.  We should probably have 
some more specific multiplex functions in the network package 
(suggestions welcome).

best,
  -skye


## some toy example operations on a multiplex network ##

multi<-network.initialize(5,multiple=TRUE)

is.multiplex(multi)

# add parallel edges between v1 and v2
# also add an attribute names 'type' to each tie
multi<-add.edges(multi,tail=c(1,1,1,1),head=c(2,2,3,4),names.eval='type',vals.eval=c("A","B","A","B"))

# get ids of edges linking v1 and v2
get.edgeIDs(multi,v=1,alter=2)


# plot the types in different colors with some transparency to show overlap
plot(multi,edge.col=ifelse(multi%e%'type'=='A','#00FF0055','#0000FF55'),edge.lwd=10)

# get the ids of all edges with type B
which(get.edge.attribute(multi,'type')=='B')

# create a new network with only type B edges

multiB<-multi
multiB<-delete.edges(multiB,eid=which(get.edge.attribute(multi,'type')!='B'))
multiB%e%'type'

messages.body_plain:
I am trying to import a BioPAX format<http://biopax.org/> biological metabolism network (generated by BioCyc<http://biocyc.org/>'s Pathway Tools program<http://bioinformatics.ai.sri.com/ptools/>) into Statnet. A small 50Kb example of a BioPAX file is here<http://gis.tinyecology.com/biopax3RpomDmsp.owl> and the full 25 Mb BioPAX file is provided here<http://GIS.tinyecology.com/biopax-level3.owl>.


I have tied the following unsuccessful approaches:


1. Opening in Cytoscape then saving in the supported export file formats (SIF, Cytoscape.js json, nested network file .nnf, XGMML, PIS-MI level 1, and PIS-MI level 2.5). No formats are directly compatible with Statnet.


2. Saving the file BioPAX file as SIF in Cytoscape then converting it to Pajek format using pyNetConv<http://pynetconv.sourceforge.net/>. The resulting Pajek file can be opened in statnet but most of the nodes and edges are lost. The loss occurs when pyNetConv opens the SIF file.


3. Using the program Paxtools<http://www.biopax.org/paxtools.php> I can export BioPAX into SIF, SIFNX, PSI-MI, Systems Biology Graph Notation - Process Description(SBGN-PD) and Gene Set Enrichment Analysis format (GSEA) . No formats are directly compatible with Statnet.


I suspect the answer may lie in modifying the SIF format file (which contains the columns: 1. source, 2. relationship, 3. type, and 4. target) and importing it as an edge list. However, I wanted to see if anyone had a better suggestion for this type of conversion.


Thanks,


Adam Rivers

Postdoctoral Research Associate

Department of Marine Sciences

University of Georgia

Hi Jacques,

You might try using arrowhead.cex to control the size of the arrows at the end of the edges if they are directed. You could also try using a combination of line width and dashes. Finally, you might try using some more extreme values of edge.lwd so the differences are more obvious.

The first of the two graphs you included might benefit from straight edges, since the curves are causing edge overlaps.

A former student of mine, Melissa Clarkson, drafted a guide for gplot that you may find useful. It was not finalized but still may come in handy:  http://students.washington.edu/mclarkso/documents/gplot%20Ver2.pdf

As a last suggestion, you may consider separating the information into more than one graph.  I find that it's easy to overwhelm the reader by packing too much information into every graph attribute possible (Node color, node shape, edge color, multiple edges, edge width, etc).

Regards,

Neil Abernethy, Ph.D.

University of Washington

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Handling of matrices for undirected networks
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Handling of matrices for undirected networks
messages.body_plain:
Converting an undirected network to an adjacency matrix does not produce the expected result. An undirected network should have a symmetric adjacency matrix, but that is not what is returned by as.matrix (or as.sociomatrix.) Interestingly, a round trip through igraph returns the right result.

This problem showed up when my students were attempting to compute Bonacich centrality on a network converted from directed.

See the code below:

library(igraph)
library(network)
library(intergraph)
library(sna)

net <- network.initialize(5)

net[1,2] <- 1
net[2,3] <- 1
net[2,4] <- 1
net[2,5] <- 1
net[5,1] <- 1

undir <- as.network(net, directed=FALSE)
undir2 <- asNetwork(as.undirected(asIgraph(net)))

as.matrix(net)
as.matrix(undir)
as.matrix(undir2)

bonpow(undir) # Generates an error
bonpow(undir2) # Computes correct result

I realize that you can guarantee this via symmetrize but it seems to me that as.matrix should return a symmetric matrix when the network is undirected. Is there an option I?m missing (either to as.network or as.matrix) to guarantee this?

__________________________________________________________
Robin Burke, Professor
College of Computing and Digital Media, DePaul University rburke@cdm.depaul.edu<mailto:rburke@cdm.depaul.edu>

Here are a couple published examples, but they focus on the application, 
not the ergms:

2009.  "Concurrent partnerships and HIV prevalence disparities by race: 
Linking science and public health practice."  M. Morris, A. Kurth, D. T.

> 2)????? I get the impression that estimating triadic parameters is difficult or impossible with egocentric data.
> Can anyone clarify my impression? Or point me to existing clarifying discussion?
>

It all depends on what type of egocentric data you've collected, because 
that determines what kinds of statistics you can observe empirically.  If 
you have the alter-alter matrix, then you have some estimates of 
triangles, and, in theory, could use this to estimate a model with triadic 
terms.  However, our team hasn't developed this or worked through an 
example yet, and it may be that you would need to write a custom ergm term 
(something other than triangles or gwesp) to estimate this properly.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Stacking Networks
messages.body_plain:
I believe that the make.stochastic command refers to creating a 'stack' 
of graphs but from my experience there's no reason you can't perform the 
same operations on graphs stored in a normal r style list. I just tested 
this with some data of my own and the operations work fine.

More to the point, the Coleman data actually looks like a 2 x 73 x 73 
array, not a list. It should be easy to put your data into array format 
using the syntax:


"array(data = NA, dim = length(data), dimnames = NULL)"


Actually, if a graphstack is somehow distinct from a list (or an array) 
I'd be curious to know how.


Best,

Zane

> Dear Carter and others,
>
> I think I have discovered a bug in the constructor for network objects. 
> Two-mode (= non-square) matrices with NA values cause an error message when 
> they are converted into bipartite network objects.
>
> The reason seems to be that you are using the 'min' and 'max' functions 
> without specifying 'na.rm = TRUE' several times in the 'which.matrix.type' 
> function. I will provide a minimal self-contained example as well as a 
> proposed bugfix below.
>
> It would be helpful if the SVN or Git repository was publicly accessible. 
> Then users like me could propose bugfixes as pull requests.
>
> Best,
> Philip
>
>
> Reproducible example:
>
> ##########
> # one-mode network with NAs --> works fine!
> mat <- matrix(rbinom(400, 1, 0.2), nrow = 20)
> naIndices <- sample(1:400, 20)
> mat[naIndices] <- NA
> nw <- network(mat)
>
> # two-mode network with NAs --> error!
> mat <- matrix(rbinom(200, 1, 0.2), nrow = 20)
> naIndices <- sample(1:200, 20)
> mat[naIndices] <- NA
> nw <- network(mat)
> ##########
>
>

>
> 1) Line 215 of file 'R/misc.R':
>
> Change the following line:
>
> else if (max(abs(x))==1 && max(abs(x-as.integer(x)))==0)

>

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Error with ergm with weighted networks: could not find function "InitWtMHP.TNT"
messages.body_plain:
Dear statnet users & developers,

I?m trying to fit an ergm to a weighted network, a one-mode projection from a bipartite network where links represent the number of events where two actors co-occur.  When I create the one-mode network I also declare the attribute ?paths? which stores the weight of the links. 

I?ve been encountering errors when fitting the ergm and struggle to find where is the mistake. The ergm-terms says:

?ergm functions such as ergm and simulate (for ERGMs) may operate in two modes: binary and weighted/valued, with the latter activated by passing a non-NULL value as the response argument, giving the edge attribute name to be modelled/simulated?

At first ergm didn?t recognise the argument ?response?. I try to update my ?ergm? version and downloading the complementary package ?ergm.count? but couldn?t do it from CRAN. Then I upgraded my R version (now 3.1.0) and download the latest ?ergm?, ?ergm.count?, and ?network? packages from the statnet preview repository   But I still encounter an error. Here is a reproducible example:

mat <- matrix(rbinom(25,10,0.05),5,5) 	# create a matrix with values
net <- network(mat) 			# create the network
net %e% 'paths' <- mat			# declare the edge values as attribute	

mod0 <- ergm(net~edges, response='paths?)

Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : 
  could not find function "InitWtMHP.TNT"

And when I google it, this is what I found from the statnet_help, it seems that the function is missing from the the ergm_x.taz.gz files. Any advise on how to solve the problem?

I?m working on R 3.1.0
ergm: version 3.1.2 (from statnet preview repository, otherwise 3.1.0)
ergm.count: version 3.1.1 (from statnet preview repository, otherwise 3.1.0)

Thanks in advance for your advise and for putting together such a nice software!
Cheers,

	Juan

On Mon, Apr 28, 2014 at 4:06 PM, Skye Bender-deMoll <skyebend@skyeome.net>wrote:

> Hi Jacques,
>
> Here are a few suggestions for visualizing multiplex ego nets:
>
> # construct a toy ego net
> curvy<-network.initialize(4,multiple=TRUE)
> add.edges(curvy,c(1,1,1,1,1,1),c(2,2,2,3,3,4))
> set.edge.attribute(curvy,'weight',c(1,2,3,1,3,2))
>
> # use weight to control curviness and width of edge
> # scale the weights to better curve values
> # scale the weights to make them more obvious
> plot(curvy,
>      usecurve=TRUE,
>      edge.curv=(curvy%e%'weight'/10),
>      edge.lwd=curvy%e%'weight'*5-4
>      )
>
>
> In the plot above, the "heavier" edges will be drawn 'more curvy', and
> with a thicker line.  I find that I usually need to provide some sort of
> scaling to the edge.lwd values to be able to visually distinguish them.
>  Above, curvy%e%'weight'*5-4  produces values between 1 and 11
>
>
> use weight for curvy, and map values to colors
> # scale the weights to better curve values
> # map values to 3-color rainbow palette
> plot(curvy,
>      usecurve=TRUE,
>      edge.curv=(curvy%e%'weight'/10),
>      edge.col=rainbow(3)[curvy%e%'weight']
> )
>
> Looks like you already did this, so would just need to add a key showing
> which color corresponds to each value.
>
>
> # don't use curves, but use partial transparency to see color overlaps
> # scale the weights to make them more obvious
> plot(curvy,
>      edge.lwd=15,
>      edge.col=rainbow(3,alpha=0.2)[curvy%e%'weight']
> )
>
> This version abandons curves, but uses partial transparency so that the
> multiple colors can overlay.  So red+blue = a purple edge.   Not as useful
> in this case with ego nets, but can help when the overall graph is too
> crowded to draw lots of curvy edges.
>
>
>

>
> Yes, I've put it on the list of things we should implement

>
> hope that helps!

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have previously been able to successfully fix ergm terms at -Inf to
forbid ties between certain groups of nodes. However, I am running into a
problem when I try to offset two different terms (I would like also like to
offset a mutual term to forbid reciprocal ties). The problem seems to be
when specifying the offset.coef parameter, as I cannot seem to feed it the
right length vector. In the example below I get both the error "expected 2
got 3" and "expected 3 got 2", when I feed it vectors of length 3 and 2
respectively.

Here is an example:

##Create directed binary network of dominants (1) and subordinates (0), and
restrict ties to within each group
m<-matrix(rmultinom(1,500,rep(1/100, 100)),10,10)
m[1:5,6:10]<-0
m[6:10,1:5]<-0
winlos<-m/(m+t(m))
winlos[winlos>0.5]=1
winlos[winlos<0.5]=0
winlos[is.na(winlos)]=0
winlos[winlos==0.5]=0
winlos
g<-network(winlos, matrix.type= "adjacency", directed=TRUE)

set.vertex.attribute(g, "Group", c(rep("G1",5), rep("G2",5)))

####This seems to work
M<-ergm(g~edges
        +offset(nodemix("Group", base=c(1,4))), offset.coef=c(rep(-Inf, 2)))

###This also seems to work
M<-ergm(g~edges
        +offset(mutual),
        offset.coef=-Inf)

###Doesn't work (expected 2 got 3)
M<-ergm(g~edges
        +offset(mutual)
        +offset(nodemix("Group", base=c(1,4))), offset.coef=c(rep(-Inf, 3)))

##Doesn't work (expected 3 got 2)
M<-ergm(g~edges
        +offset(mutual)
        +offset(nodemix("Group", base=c(1,4))), offset.coef=c(rep(-Inf, 2)))

Thanks for your help in advance

Here are a couple published examples, but they focus on the application, not the ergms:

2009.  "Concurrent partnerships and HIV prevalence disparities by race: 
Linking science and public health practice."  M. Morris, A. Kurth, D. T. 
Hamilton, J. Moody, S. Wakefield and for The Network Modeling Group.  Amer J Pub Health  99 (6):  1023 - 1031

10.1007/s10461-010-9858-x:   (PMCID:  3394592).

> 2)????? I get the impression that estimating triadic parameters is difficult or impossible with egocentric data.
> Can anyone clarify my impression? Or point me to existing clarifying discussion?

It all depends on what type of egocentric data you've collected, because that determines what kinds of statistics you can observe empirically.  If you have the alter-alter matrix, then you have some estimates of triangles, and, in theory, could use this to estimate a model with triadic terms.  However, our team hasn't developed this or worked through an example yet, and it may be that you would need to write a custom ergm term (something other than triangles or gwesp) to estimate this properly.

It depends on what kind of data you have.  If you have a single 
cross-sectional snapshot of a network, Ian Fellows (fellstat.com) has a

If you have longitudinal panel data on the networks, we don't (yet) have 
that functionality built.  But we do have a student working on this for 
his dissertation project, so it's in the works.

Martina

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Can EpiModel cover what I need? (Duncan McPherson)
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Can EpiModel cover what I need? (Duncan McPherson)
messages.body_plain:
Duncan,

EpiModel may help depending on your question of interest and the structure
of your data. To address your specific questions:

1. Using the epiDCM or epiICM (note: the latest release v0.95 -- available
on CRAN -- has changed the terminology of these non-network stochastic
microsimulation models from SPM to ICM for "individual contact models"
although the core internals remain the same), it is  possible to input a
range of parameters and evaluate which set most closely fits to empirical
disease incidence or prevalence data (I assume you mean this sort of
fitting). The qualitative way of doing this is to choose a combination of
parameters for counterfactual models and see what set best minimizes the
distance to the data. If the deterministic compartmental modeling suits
your research question (which seems unlikely since you want to use network
models, but DCMs are an easy place to start), then this may be performed
with the sensitivity analysis framework of epiDCM (see Section 2.3 of our
Tutorial: statnet.org/EpiModel/vignette/Tutorial.pdf). More complex model
fitting procedures, such as Bayesian melding, are certainly possible with
DCMs, but not currently integrated into EpiModel; it is a potential area of
future software development. I'm not aware of any R package that does
automated melding for epidemic models (because epidemic software itself is
limited in R), although the method could be programmed for your specific
research questions.

2. Our guiding framework for network modeling is to use egocentric data on
contacts (or edges or partnerships) with estimates of the average duration
of those contacts. We rarely have a longitudinal census of a disease-risk
network, and even if we did have such data, we would need a statistical
model to estimate the properties of the data generating process and
simulate that process forward. There are a number of ways to estimate such
a model (see, for example:
http://statnet.org/workshops/SUNBELT/current/tergm/tergm_tutorial.pdf). But
to use a non-egocentric approach in EpiModel, currently it would be
necessary to: 1) use a STERGM to estimate the parameters given your
observed network data; 2) simulate a complete network dynamically to
calculate summary target statistics of interest; then 3) plug those target
statistics into EpiModel with the framework outlined in our EpiModel
tutorial (linked above). One area of future EpiModel development may be
integration of complete network data, but it is not our highest priority
because the data are so rare within epidemiology.

One additional note is that you will likely need to extend the code within
EpiModel to suit your specific research questions, as the built-in models
are relatively simplistic SI-SIS-SIR disease models. The framework for
extension has been outlined for DCMs (see
http://statnet.org/EpiModel/vignette/ExtendepiDCM.html). We will be
focusing our much of our development efforts over the next year to help
facilitate this process of extension for network models.

Finally, just to note that we have established an EpiModel-specific mailing
list, which you are encouraged to subscribe and pose future EpiModel
questions there (although we'll still respond on the statnet list too!).
http://mailman11.u.washington.edu/mailman/listinfo/epimodel

Best,
Sam Jenness

Fellow, Center for Studies in Demography & Ecology
University of Washington

messages.subject: [statnet_help] symmetrize valued data for max min and avg
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] symmetrize valued data for max min and avg
messages.body_plain:
Hi James, Thomas, and others who are interested.

First, thanks for you help. I guess my case was a little different than how
you guys did it, so I built off of your advice and came up with the
following.

#This code symmetrizes a valued matrix by max or min values of ij-ji. For
max, steps 1 & 5 should use "-999" & step 3 must use ">" and ">=". For min,
use "999", "<", & "<=" respectively. The input data must use NA rather than
0 for non-ties. The code uses weak symmetrization, so an NA in ij or ji
will be replaced with valued data of ji or ij respectively.

#make a sample matrix that includes NAs and set diag to 0.
test<-matrix(ncol=10, nrow=10, sample(c(NA, 1:5), 100, replace=TRUE,
c(.5,rep(.1,5)))) #NA has high prob
#test<-matrix(ncol=10, nrow=10, 5, 100) #to test with full mat of single
values if desired
test0<-diag.remove(test, remove.val=0) ;test0

#Step 1: convert NA to "999" for use with "<" and "-999" for use with ">"
so NA gets replaced with desired tie value (i.e., weak symmetrization)
test0[is.na(test0)]<- (-999) ;test0

#Step 2: separate lower and upper tri
low<-upper.tri.remove(test0, remove.val=NA) ;low
upp<-lower.tri.remove(test0, remove.val=NA) ;upp

#Step 3: get min (<) or max (>) based on True/False, convert to 1/0, and
combine lower and upper. To deal with ij=ji, upp2 uses <= or >=, step2 uses
NA, and NAs are converted to 0 in step3. This avoids "full = 1+1"
low2 <- (ifelse((low > t(upp))==TRUE, 1, 0));low2[is.na(low2)]<- 0 ;low2
upp2 <- (ifelse((upp >= t(low))==TRUE, 1, 0));upp2[is.na(upp2)]<- 0 ;upp2
full <- (upp2 + low2) ;full

#Step 4: extract from original data using full binary mat (selects min/max
based on above choice (< or >))
tempNet <- test0*full ;tempNet

#Step 5: final symmetrized mat based on min or max as specified above.
Then, just in case there were any NA-NA ij-ji pairs, convert those to 0
final <- tempNet + t(tempNet)
final[final == -999] <- 0 ;final

messages.body_plain:
Michal, thanks so much for the response! Really appreciate it.

Best wishes,
Kevin

-----Original Message-----
From: Micha? Bojanowski [mailto:michal2992@gmail.com] 
Sent: Thursday, July 17, 2014 9:10 AM
To: Lewis, Kevin
Cc: statnet_help@u.washington.edu
Subject: Re: [statnet_help] large ERGMs and sampling

Kevin,

As far as I know, if you are only
interested in dyad-independent ERGM. The model simplifies to a GLM on data, where each case is a (possibly directed) pair of nodes and dependent variable is binary (tie/notie). You could in principle estimate such model on very large data by e.g. one of

1. Using an estimation algorithm that can be supplied with data in chunks (e.g. R packages 'biglm').

2.  sampling/bootstrapping: take multiple samples, fit the model to each, and then analyse the distribution of model parameters across samples (possibly summarizing them with some sort of a random effect model like in meta-analysis).

In both cases the difficulty might be to correctly construct the model matrix, i.e. construct the independent variables so that they represent the ERGM terms correctly.

Going beyond dyad-independent ERGMs becomes tricky as GLM approximation (MPLE) is not good anymore.


Best wishes,
~michal

Hi Jesse,

You just need to make two minor adjustments to your code. 


1. Add names.eval="value" to the line where you create the network object.? This assigns the name for the attribute to store the edge values.

2. When converting back to the matrix use the function as.sociomatrix with the argument "value".


Here is your code with the changes added in. Best,

Michael Siciliano

#make a sample matrix that includes NAs and set diag to 0. 
test<-matrix(ncol=10, nrow=10, sample(c(NA, 1:5), 100, replace=TRUE, c(.5,rep(.1,5)))) #NA has high prob
test0<-diag.remove(test, remove.val=0) ;test0

#make as network object and try to keep valued data using ignore.eval
testMeNet<-as.network.matrix(test0, ignore.eval=FALSE, na.rm=TRUE, names.eval="value") ;testMeNet

#find isolates
isos <- isolates(testMeNet, diag=FALSE)
length(isos)

#remove isolates
testMeCut<-delete.vertices(testMeNet, (isolates(testMeNet, diag=FALSE))) ;testMeCut

#convert back to matrix. Problem is, valued ties are lost. They are now 1s
testMeOut <- as.sociomatrix(testMeCut, "value") ;testMeOut

messages.body_plain:
On 04/05/2014 05:15 PM, Jesse Sayles wrote:
> Does anyone know how I can print the name of a given node / vertex using
> the network or sna package?

Assuming you have previously set the vertex names, you can get them with

network.vertex.names(myNetwork)

you can also set them with

network.vertex.names(myNetwork)<-myVectorOfNames

since vertex names are essentially an ordinary attribute you can also 
get and set them with the regular attribute tools.

get.vertex.attribute(myNetwork,'vertex.names')


If you are working in a dynamic case, and are using the names as unique 
identifiers for the vertices, you may want to check out the Persistent 
IDs functionality in the networkDynamic package for translating between 
the ids and network ids

?persistent.ids

best,

messages.body_plain:
Hi Robin,

On 04/27/2014 01:33 PM, Burke, Robin wrote:
> This is very helpful, thanks. Just to make this point clear, maybe the documentation for as.network could be amended as follows:
>
> "as.network tries to coerce its argument to a network, using the network function if necessary. If the argument is already a network object, it is returned as-is and all other arguments are ignored."

Thanks for the addition, I've added it to the docs for next release

> I guess my next question is what to use for this conversion.
I don't think conversion necessary if you initialize the network as 
undirected or set the network property of "directed" to FALSE?

# create an undirected network and then load edges
net <- network.initialize(5,directed=FALSE)

# initialize edges
net[1,2] <- 1
net[2,3] <- 1
net[2,4] <- 1
net[2,5] <- 1
net[5,1] <- 1

# edges can be addressed by either vertex
net[1,2]
[1] 1
net[2,1]
[1] 1

# output matrix is symmetrical.
as.matrix(net)
   1 2 3 4 5
1 0 1 0 0 1
2 1 0 1 1 1
3 0 1 0 0 0
4 0 1 0 0 0
5 1 1 0 0 0


You can also set the directed property of the network after it has been 
created using set.network.attribute.

# create an directed network
net <- network.initialize(5)

# initialize edges
net[1,2] <- 1
net[2,3] <- 1
net[2,4] <- 1
net[2,5] <- 1
net[5,1] <- 1

is.directed(net)
[1] TRUE

# now redefine the network attribute to make it undirected

net<-set.network.attribute(net,'directed',FALSE)
is.directed(net)
[1] FALSE
as.matrix(net)
   1 2 3 4 5
1 0 1 0 0 1
2 1 0 1 1 1
3 0 1 0 0 0
4 0 1 0 0 0
5 1 1 0 0 0


Seems like this already gives functionality you want-- as long as the 
undirected network is full unsymmetrical to start with.  If 'net' does 
contain some reciprocated ties where i,j and j,i are both defined before 
you set directed=FALSE, you will be implicitly creating a multiplex 
network in the conversion as there will be two edge objects defining the 
relationship i,j

best,
  -skye

From: Carter T. Butts [mailto:buttsc@uci.edu] 
Sent: Wednesday, March 26, 2014 2:34 PM
To: Tom Valente; statnet_help@u.washington.edu
Subject: Re: [statnet_help] help with components command

 

Hi, Tom.  Your example has a spanning cycle - thus, for every pair of nodes
(i,j), one can get from i to j or from j to i.  Specifically, let's number
the nodes in your case as 1,2,3, with 1->2, 2->3, and 3->1.  Then e.g., we
can get from 1 to 2 by the 1->2 edge, and from 2 to 1 via the path 2->3->1.
(The same holds, mutatis mutandis, for all other pairs.)  This highlights a
potentially counterintuitive aspect of strong connectivity: it requires no
mutuality at all, and the two connecting paths for a given vertex pair can
be entirely disjoint (excepting their endpoints)!  But if one is interested
in flows that need not traverse any particular path, strong connectivity can
be a useful concept.

Hope that helps!

-Carter

On 03/26/2014 11:28 AM, Tom Valente wrote:

Carter

Thanks, I understand the recursive bit now, the indirect paths need to be
symmetric; but I still don't understand the strong condition because in this
test case I have only (i,j) paths and no (j,i) ones.

-Tom

 

From: statnet_help [mailto:statnet_help-bounces@mailman13.u.washington.edu]
On Behalf Of Carter T. Butts
Sent: Wednesday, March 26, 2014 11:19 AM
To: statnet_help@u.washington.edu
Subject: Re: [statnet_help] help with components command

 

Hi, Tom.  Two vertices, i and j, are said to be strongly connected in graph
G if there exists an (i,j) path in G and a (j,i) path in G.  i and j are
said to be recursively connected if there exists an (i,j) path in G with
vertices (i,a,b,...,j) such that its reversal (j,...,b,a,i) is also a path
in G.  Strong and recursive components, then, are maximal sets of vertices
that are respectively strongly and recursively connected.    (See also
?component.dist.)  Your test case is weakly and strongly connected, and
hence has one component under these notions of connectedness.  It has no
recursively connected paths, however, and hence the maximum component size
is 1 (yielding three components).

Hope that helps!

-Carter
