messages.subject: [statnet_help] Comparing Parameter Estimates Across Models - Progress since 2007?
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Comparing Parameter Estimates Across Models - Progress since 2007?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Louis,

Just a few additional comments.

Since your networks are all the same size and composition, the question of 
comparability could be addressed in a more traditional fashion.  You could 
fit the same model to each network, and compare the transitivity 
coefficients by testing whether the differences between them are 
statistically significant, based on a t-test for differences, using the 
estimated SEs of each coefficient, and adjusting for multiple comparisons 
(presumably 5 choose 2 = 10 comparisons).

This doesn't incorporate the repeated measure design of your data (i.e., 
the consistent labeling of the nodes), but it would provide a network wide 
assessment of differences in transitivity.

As Carter noted, we have a number of projects in the pipeline that will 
extend ergm for multiple/multi-level networks.

best,
Martina

On Wed, 10 Sep 2014, Carter T. Butts wrote:

> Hi, Louis.  What you are describing would be a pooled ERGM.  It can certainly 
> be done, and papers on multiple-network ERGMs are starting to appear. 
> Software development has lagged somewhat, both because (1) there are so many 
> things that need to be done on single-network ERGMs (and limited time to do 
> it), and (2) there have been fewer available data sets to support model 
> development than would be ideal.  This is something that some of us are 
> actively working on, however, so the situation should be starting to change.
>
> I have a prototype implementation of an ergm extension package that supports 
> pooled ergms (and another for multiplex ergms, which is a special case that 
> has somewhat different requirements). Right now, they are held together with 
> twine and might set your hair on fire.  However, if you are potentially 
> interested in being a beta tester for them when they are in a fit state for 
> such, then send me a note off-list.
>
> Hope that helps,
>
> -Carter
>
> On 09/10/2014 01:15 PM, Boguchwal, Louis CTR USA USMA wrote:
>> Hi Statnet Users,
>> 
>> Admittedly, this question is a rehash of one asked by Brian Rubineau in 
>> 2007.  But when asked, David Hunter answered that it was unresolved (see 
>> https://mailman13.u.washington.edu/mailman/htdig/statnet_help/2007/000119.html). 
>> This question has come up in my own research, and I was wondering if it had 
>> been resolved at this point in time.
>> 
>> Somewhat similar questions were asked in 
>> https://mailman13.u.washington.edu/mailman/htdig/statnet_help/2013/001493.html 
>> and 
>> https://mailman13.u.washington.edu/mailman/htdig/statnet_help/2010/000804.html. 
>> The former received no answer and the latter requires a strong assumption 
>> (edge independence) and a quantitative (rather than categorical) variable.
>> 
>> I apologize for the lengthy documentation, though I wanted to demonstrate 
>> that I attempted to resolve this myself before turning to the statnet 
>> group.
>> 
>> I have data with one set of nodes and several sets of edges (5 to be exact 
>> - different areas of collaboration amongst entrepreneurs in developing 
>> countries).  I would like to compare the forces governing link formation in 
>> each network.  I have combined all my adjacency matrices into one big 
>> adjacency matrix (node names were adjusted to be unique; names are the 
>> original name + the network name).  This matrix is defined such that edges 
>> only exist between nodes from the same original network.
>> 
>> Ideally, this would mean constructing an ERGM with the same right-hand side 
>> (explanatory variables) for each network (different dependent variables, 
>> corresponding to each network), with the goal of comparing parameter 
>> estimates.  Comparing these parameter estimates would allow me to answer 
>> questions of the following form: Is transitivity stronger in one 
>> collaboration area versus another?
>> 
>> I'd like to adapt classical regression techniques by introducing dummy 
>> variables and interaction terms to statistically discern the differences in 
>> effects amongst the networks.  I've tried constructing a dummy variable off 
>> of my attribute list manually, and then including it in my ERGM, though I 
>> get an error and my code is not accepted by R.  I am also unable to 
>> multiply variables (as one must to construct an interaction term) in the 
>> ERGM function.
>> 
>> Thoughts?  Thank you for your time and consideration.
>> 
>> Cheers,
>> Louis

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Nodemix interpretation
messages.body_plain:
Good afternoon,

I have a question about the interpretation of nodemix coefficients. Let's say I have a simple model looking at associations among sexes and I use the default of 0 for the base option [edges +nodemix("sex")] .

If the coefficient for male-male associations was significant and positive, would it be correct to interpret this as
male-male associations positively affect (i.e., increase) the likelihood of edges occurring in the network? Would it also be accurate to say that male-male associations are more likely to occur than expected by chance given the density of the network?

If a base was specified (say it was set to female-female associations) and the male-male coefficient was still significant and positive, would the interpretation change to edges are more likely occur between males than between females? Or does the base option just specify terms that are not of interest and should be left out of the model?

Thank you for your time,
Jason Fischer

messages.subject: [statnet_help] STERGM: stable/changing dyadic covariates—is it possible and how?
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] STERGM: stable/changing dyadic covariates—is it possible and how?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Achim,

On Tue, 2014-08-26 at 08:07 +1000, Achim Edelmann, Ph.D. wrote:
> Dear Statnet group, 
> 
> this is a question about the STERGM.  I would like to know if and how
> it is possible to include stable and, eventually, even (externally)
> changing dyad covariates.  Say, for example, I would like to model the
> formation/dissolution of relationships among a small group of
> neighbors over several waves.  How could I include a term for whether
> people had known each other before the first wave?  

You can do it by using an edgecov term. Generally, almost all ergm terms
still work.

> And, ideally, how
> could I include a term for the (exogenously) changing distances
> between their work places?  Can STERGM handle any of this and, if so,
> how to best feed the model with the stable/changing matrices in R?

For setting edge covariates, I would suggest taking a look at ergm
tutorials. You will need to construct a network with the attributes and
covariates you are looking for, then give the stergm() call a list of
the networks in the series.

                                  I hope this helps,
                                  Pavel

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris and Nate,

I think there are two important things here: modeling the distribution 
of the relation(s) adequately, and deciding whether it's necessary and 
useful to model them jointly in one dependent variable. The alternative 
would be to model them separately and include each relation or a 
transformation thereof as a covariate (which would make it easier to 
think of endogenous network statistics), but I assume you have already 
tried that. Given that you are quite sure that both should be modeled 
jointly, you could accommodate both relations/networks in a single 
matrix (with each node being duplicated, e.g., in a block-diagonal 
matrix) and set the type of nodes (i.e., which original network relation 
is this node from?) as a nodal covariate. Then you would have to come up 
with statistics that describe the features of the joint network, for 
example a statistic counting how often x_ij from relation 1 and x_ij 
from relation 2 are both tied (= cross-relation reciprocity), or how 
often x_ij and x_jk form a two-path in relation 1 AND x_ik are tied in 
relation 2 or vice-versa (= cross-relation triadic closure), and so on. 
This is kind of the bottleneck because you would presumably have to 
implement some of these statistics on your own while others can probably 
be implemented using covariates (as suggested by Nate in his example). 
For example, if you want to model interdependent triadic closure as in a 
collaboration and conflict setting (where A and C are likely to have a 
positive tie when A and B as well as B and C have negative ties, due to 
social balance), you can most likely do that by creating a covariate 
matrix which contains the two-paths of relation 1 as direct ties in the 
block of relation 2 and possibly vice-versa. That might work, but I am 
still a bit hesitant because simple triadic closure and other simpler 
network statistics might actually look very different across the two 
relations, and modeling these different distributions through one joint 
model term at a time may not necessarily capture their joint 
distribution very well. It may also be problematic because things like 
social balance may not necessarily work in the same way for both 
relations or directions (--+ is social balance, but ++- would not be 
balanced), so you really have to think about theory and about how to 
accommodate this in covariate matrices. So I would say it's possible in 
principle but use it cautiously.

Funny coincidence: the two of you are located at Columbus and Amherst, 
and I am currently a visiting scholar at OSU in Columbus and will then 
move on to Amherst for a couple of days in mid-November.

I hope that's helpful.

Best,
Philip

messages.body_plain:
Hi Sebastian,

The network() conversion function is expecting that your ids are 
integers from 1 to the size of the network. Since your ids are very big, 
it creates a very big network.  However, if you trick it into seeing the 
ids as labels, it will probably do what you want.  You can do this by 
converting the unitid and punit ids into characters instead of numeric 
values

Then you should be able to create the network with using the two 
character columns

 > net<-network(rawData[,1:2])


# load in the distance edge attribute
 > set.edge.attribute(net,'distance',rawData[,3])
 > net
  Network attributes:
   vertices = 15
   directed = TRUE
   hyper = FALSE
   loops = FALSE
   multiple = FALSE
   bipartite = FALSE
   total edges= 15
     missing edges= 0
     non-missing edges= 15

  Vertex attribute names:
     vertex.names

  Edge attribute names:
     distance

# check that they were loaded in as names correctly
 > network.vertex.names(net)
  [1] "100636" "100654" "100663" "100690" "100706" "100724" "100733" 
"100751" "100760" "100812" "100830" "100858"
[13] "100937" "101028" "101073"


The challenge of course is that you can't use your big ids directly in 
queries, you have to match them back to your vertex.names attribute like

 > get.edgeIDs(net,v=match("100654",network.vertex.names(net)),
             alter=match("100636",network.vertex.names(net)))
[1] 2



If you need to do a bunch of work tracking these external ids, you may 
want to use the 'persistent id' functionality in the networkDynamic package

best,
  -skye

From: statnet_help [mailto:statnet_help-bounces@mailman13.u.washington.edu] On Behalf Of Steven Goodreau
Sent: Tuesday, August 05, 2014 5:06 PM
To: statnet_help@u.washington.edu
Subject: Re: [statnet_help] MPLE with offset terms

Hi Kevin -

I'm still looking into your issues - it seems to be something deep.  In the meanwhile, I will mention that there is a workaround that seems to work just fine.  Try representing your network as an undirected bipartite network.  Bipartite makes the M-M and F-F ties into structural zeros.  And undirected, because there really is only possible relationship of interest for you within each dyad, given your focus on F->M ties; this means that the M->F ties are not being modeled.  I tested this, and it works fine, giving you the expected log-odds for the simple edges only models.  Hopefully, all of the other terms you are interested in can be represented in this format, using the various b1... and b2... parameters.

This is probably the way I would have gone about it in the first place - it seems a bit neater to remove the structural zeros by force in advance when possible.  But you're absolutely right that your method should still work fine, and doesn't seem to be.

Yours,
Steve

Hi everyone (especially developers),

I worry these issues might be a bit specific, but I believe I have found a few calculations misbehaving that could reflect something going wrong beneath the hood (or perhaps more likely, something wrong with the driver...). The issues are specific because they all have to with dyad-independent models (i.e. what should be straightforward logistic regression), and in particular applied to a large social network (thousands of nodes) and using models that include offset terms- i.e. where the observed count of a statistic is zero and so the coefficients are automatically fixed at negative infinity. My specific application is that I want to estimate some models of what influences a female to look at a male's profile on an online dating site; so, if we consider the gender binary mixing matrix, I am interested ONLY in female/male ties and need to set female/female ties, male/male ties, and male/female ties all to negative infinity. I am using statnet version 2014.2.0, running on 64-bit R version 3.1.1.

There are three different issues I've come across- not sure if they are related:

1. First, I start with a basic model- *only* the edges term- with the restriction that only female/male ties are permitted. Interestingly, it seems to matter *how* I prohibit all other types of ties for whether the results are reasonable. In the first instance, I block all male/female ties using nodemix, and (separately) I block male/male ties and female/female ties using nodematch(diff=TRUE). Results are bizarre. In the second instance, I do the exact same thing except this time I block both kinds of same-gender ties at the same time using nodematch(diff=FALSE)- and this time, results *seem* much more reasonable.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Prof. Morris,

Thank you very much for the response.

So when we talk about homophily, it is usually the situation with only one nodal attribute (e.g., gender)? The interaction effect means that for the tie between a pair of nodes, the gender effect on one node is significantly different from the gender effect on the other node, right?

In this case, for the gender (boys vs. girls)*school (public vs. private) design, I should combine the categories of the two nodal attributes, and get a new nodal attribute with 4 categories: public boys, public girls, private boys, and private girls. Then use this new 4-category nodal attribute to represent the homophily and test its significance for the interaction between gender and school type. Do I understand it correct?

Best regards,




ya





From: martina morris
Date: 2014-09-16 23:02
To: xinxi813@126.com
CC: statnet_help@u.washington.edu
Subject: Re: [statnet_help] interaction effect for nodal attributes
On Sat, 13 Sep 2014, xinxi813@126.com wrote:

> 2. Does the above logic apply to the interaction effect in the social network context? With
> the same gender and school variables as nodal predictors, for an observed friendship
> network, if there is a significant interaction effect, does it mean that the gender effect
> for forming a new tie in public school is significantly different from forming a new tie in
> private school? For example, boys are more likely to form a new tie than girls in public
> school, but less likely to form a new tie in private school?

Yes, it would.  But note that we do not currently support interaction 
effects in statnet using the formula syntax covar1*covar2.

> 3. I noticed that in the three references I mentioned, the interaction effect between nodal
> predictors are usually examined by testing homophily (using nodematch() in statnet). If my
> understanding about interaction effect between nodal predictors in the network context in
> point 2 is correct, why the homophily is used to test interaction effect? How to understand
> this?

Homophily is an interaction between the attribute of node1 and the 
attribute of node1.  That is, given main effects for node1 attribute 
(attr(i)) and node 2 attribute (attr(j)) -- e.g., relatively higher 
degree for attr(i) than attr(j) -- is there an *additional* propensity for 
nodes to form ties within attribute levels.  Think about it as a mixing 
matrix, where the main effects represent the variation in the marginal 
distributions, and the interactions represent deviation of the cell counts 
from the expected value given the margins.

So, homophily is not the interaction term that you seem to be interested 
in -- you're looking for an interaction between homophily and school type. 
For that, you would need to calculate a new nodal attribute to represent 
the homophily attribute x school type classification, and test whether it 
is significant.

hth,
mm

Sorry again for these questions ...

Vanesse

messages.body_plain:
Hi again,

I am really sorry, but I'm still struggling with ergm fitting...

Following the previous advice, I increased the MCMC samplesize, interval
and MCMLE.maxit.

Here is the model I tried to fit:

ergm(net~edges+gwdegree(1.35,fixed=F)+gwdsp(0.1,fixed=T) +
gwesp(0.1,fixed=T),control=control.ergm(MCMC.burnin=100000,
MCMC.samplesize=50000, MCMC.interval=1000,seed=55,MCMLE.maxit=200) )

but after 200 iterations, it still not appear to converge (the iterations
stopped at 200 [ "*Iteration 200 of at most 200: Convergence test P-value:
0e+00 The log-likelihood improved by < 0.0001*"] ) ...

Computation time was already very long, shall I continue to increase the
MCMC parameters or shall I conclude that convergence can't be reached ?

I launched the same analysis on PNet and can't reach convergence too ...

I found the following statement in a paper of Harris : "*When models with
all three geometric terms did not converge, we followed a strategy
demonstrated by Hunter et al. using bivariate analyses to determine which
of the geometric terms may be helpful in explaining existing global network
structures [22,23]. The full model was then re-estimated retaining only
those global terms that demonstrated a significant relationship with the
outcome in this bivariate testing*."

Is it the right way to do ? I looked in the references cited but I didn't
found any mention of this procedure in them ...

Many thanks for your help

Vanesse

-Kevin

Hi Kevin -

I started looking at this, and one quick question to  clarify.  How is your network object "female_views" set up?  I think from reading through your code that it is not bipartite, it has 0s for all the M->M, M->F and F->F ties, and for the attribute "female", 1=female and 0 = male, yes?  Just double-checking that I have the network 100% right before I delve into recreating things.

Steve

On 8/4/2014 3:52 PM, Lewis, Kevin wrote:
Hi everyone (especially developers),

I worry these issues might be a bit specific, but I believe I have found a few calculations misbehaving that could reflect something going wrong beneath the hood (or perhaps more likely, something wrong with the driver...). The issues are specific because they all have to with dyad-independent models (i.e. what should be straightforward logistic regression), and in particular applied to a large social network (thousands of nodes) and using models that include offset terms- i.e. where the observed count of a statistic is zero and so the coefficients are automatically fixed at negative infinity. My specific application is that I want to estimate some models of what influences a female to look at a male's profile on an online dating site; so, if we consider the gender binary mixing matrix, I am interested ONLY in female/male ties and need to set female/female ties, male/male ties, and male/female ties all to negative infinity. I am using statnet version 2014.2.0, running on 64-bit R version 3.1.1.

There are three different issues I've come across- not sure if they are related:

1. First, I start with a basic model- *only* the edges term- with the restriction that only female/male ties are permitted. Interestingly, it seems to matter *how* I prohibit all other types of ties for whether the results are reasonable. In the first instance, I block all male/female ties using nodemix, and (separately) I block male/male ties and female/female ties using nodematch(diff=TRUE). Results are bizarre. In the second instance, I do the exact same thing except this time I block both kinds of same-gender ties at the same time using nodematch(diff=FALSE)- and this time, results *seem* much more reasonable.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Error in solve.default(H)
messages.body_plain:
Hello Narges,

I just took a look at your degree distributions to make sure that they 
were in balance (female total degree = male total degree) and indeed 
they are, so that's good.

Looking at the actual distributions, my suspicion is that the issue is 
just with the females (of whom very few are above degree 1; 20 with 
degree 2 and 3 with degree 3) but not with the men (where the 
corresponding figures are 136 and 36).  You tried reducing the terms for 
both females and males, and that prevented the eror but provided poor 
fit.  I would try just reducing the females down to a single degree 
term, but leaving the males at both.

Also, I notice that you don't have a maximum degree constraint in the 
model.  Did you intend to?  If so, the argument would be 
constraints=~bd(maxout=3).  That might add to your problems with 
computational singularity, or it might actually be the trick you need.  
Perhaps that in combination with one of the reduced models will be the 
combo you need.

Yours,
Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] interaction effect for nodal attributes
messages.body_plain:
On Sat, 13 Sep 2014, xinxi813@126.com wrote:

> 2. Does the above logic apply to the interaction effect in the social network context? With
> the same gender and school variables as nodal predictors, for an observed friendship
> network, if there is a significant interaction effect, does it mean that the gender effect
> for forming a new tie in public school is significantly different from forming a new tie in
> private school? For example, boys are more likely to form a new tie than girls in public
> school, but less likely to form a new tie in private school?

Yes, it would.  But note that we do not currently support interaction 
effects in statnet using the formula syntax covar1*covar2.

> 3. I noticed that in the three references I mentioned, the interaction effect between nodal
> predictors are usually examined by testing homophily (using nodematch() in statnet). If my
> understanding about interaction effect between nodal predictors in the network context in
> point 2 is correct, why the homophily is used to test interaction effect? How to understand
> this?

Homophily is an interaction between the attribute of node1 and the 
attribute of node1.  That is, given main effects for node1 attribute 
(attr(i)) and node 2 attribute (attr(j)) -- e.g., relatively higher 
degree for attr(i) than attr(j) -- is there an *additional* propensity for 
nodes to form ties within attribute levels.  Think about it as a mixing 
matrix, where the main effects represent the variation in the marginal 
distributions, and the interactions represent deviation of the cell counts 
from the expected value given the margins.

So, homophily is not the interaction term that you seem to be interested 
in -- you're looking for an interaction between homophily and school type. 
For that, you would need to calculate a new nodal attribute to represent 
the homophily attribute x school type classification, and test whether it 
is significant.

hth,

messages.subject: [statnet_help] tips to speed up ergm
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sebasti?n,

It usually takes longer if the theoretical model doesn't fit the data 
very well. This seems to be the case here because it takes long and the 
observed and simulated statistics are different (looks like a 
close-to-degenerate solution?). I would try to get the theory part 
right, then the computation time should significantly go down.

Second, to get an idea which of the model terms roughly look good or 
bad, you may want to try MPLE first. This gives you potentially biased 
standard errors, but it is faster and may at least help you to find out 
roughly where things are going terribly wrong. Later on, you can still 
switch back to MCMC MLE once you have replaced the problematic model terms.

Third, I think the parallelization code has been rewritten (I made a 
couple of suggestions about this, and I think they have been 
implemented). It may or may not be faster in the new release, which will 
be available soon (that's at least what I read).

Take care

Philip

On 8/4/2014 3:52 PM, Lewis, Kevin wrote:
Hi everyone (especially developers),

I worry these issues might be a bit specific, but I believe I have found a few calculations misbehaving that could reflect something going wrong beneath the hood (or perhaps more likely, something wrong with the driver?). The issues are specific because they all have to with dyad-independent models (i.e. what should be straightforward logistic regression), and in particular applied to a large social network (thousands of nodes) and using models that include offset terms- i.e. where the observed count of a statistic is zero and so the coefficients are automatically fixed at negative infinity. My specific application is that I want to estimate some models of what influences a female to look at a male?s profile on an online dating site; so, if we consider the gender binary mixing matrix, I am interested ONLY in female/male ties and need to set female/female ties, male/male ties, and male/female ties all to negative infinity. I am using statnet version 2014.2.0, running on 64-bit R version 3.1.1.

There are three different issues I?ve come across- not sure if they are related:

1. First, I start with a basic model- *only* the edges term- with the restriction that only female/male ties are permitted. Interestingly, it seems to matter *how* I prohibit all other types of ties for whether the results are reasonable. In the first instance, I block all male/female ties using nodemix, and (separately) I block male/male ties and female/female ties using nodematch(diff=TRUE). Results are bizarre. In the second instance, I do the exact same thing except this time I block both kinds of same-gender ties at the same time using nodematch(diff=FALSE)- and this time, results *seem* much more reasonable.

2. Second- while the second set of results above seem reasonable- they?re not exactly accurate. Specifically, this network has 13,476 men, 11,524 women, and 17,971 female/male ties. So by my calculation- if we impose the above restrictions (i.e. assume only female/male ties are possible)- the edges coefficient should be -9.064, not -10.457. Finally, something weird appears to be happening the larger the model gets (and in fact, particularly when the model gets right up against the limit I set in MPLE.max.dyad.types, which I believe here I increased to 1e+7). In the first model, everything seems to be running normally. In the second model, I add an additional set of terms (namely, nodefactor terms related to income); and while the parameter estimates still seem reasonable, all of a sudden the standard errors increase tenfold, almost nothing is significant, and the AIC and BIC skyrocket. messages.subject: [statnet_help] interaction effect for nodal attributes
messages.body_plain:
On Wed, 17 Sep 2014, ya wrote:

> Dear Prof. Morris,
> 
> Thank you very much for the response.
> 
> So when we talk about homophily, it is usually the situation with only one?nodal?attribute?(e.g., gender)? The
> interaction effect means that for the tie between a pair of nodes, the gender effect on one node is significantly
> different from the gender effect on the other node, right?

Not quite.  It means the effect of gender (for ego) depends on the 
gender of the alter.  Say there is a main effect of sex on the 
probability of a tie (for example, boys nominate more alters than 
girls), and positive homophily on sex.  That would mean the effect of 
ego's sex on the probability of a tie depends on alter's sex.

Depending on the size of the coefficients, a girl-girl tie may have higher 
probability than a boy-girl tie, even though boys have higher overall 
probability of making a tie, because the positive homophily on sex is 
stronger than the main effect.

> In this case, for the gender (boys vs. girls)*school (public vs. 
> private) design, I should?combine the?categories of the two 
> nodal?attributes, and get a new nodal attribute with 4 
> categories:?public boys, public girls, private boys, and private 
> girls.?Then use this new 4-category nodal attribute to represent the 
> homophily and test its significance for the interaction between 
gender > and school type. Do I understand it correct?

Yes, though the additional issue here is the structural zeros induced by 
the multilevel nature of this model: at the school level, there are no 
ties between public and private students, so your 4x4 matrix will have a 
block diagonal structure.

We're currently developing the methods for fitting multilevel models in 
statnet.  In the meantime, let me poll the rest of the crew here to see 
what your options are now.

best,
mm

> >?network,?if?there?is?a?significant?interaction?effect,?does?it?mean?that?the?gender?effect

> >?school,?but?less?likely?to?form?a?new?tie?in?private?school?
> 
> Yes,?it?would.??But?note?that?we?do?not?currently?support?interaction 
> effects?in?statnet?using?the?formula?syntax?covar1*covar2.
> 
> >?3.?I?noticed?that?in?the?three?references?I?mentioned,?the?interaction?effect?between?nodal
> >?predictors?are?usually?examined?by?testing?homophily?(using?nodematch()?in?statnet).?If?my
> >?understanding?about?interaction?effect?between?nodal?predictors?in?the?network?context?in
> >?point?2?is?correct,?why?the?homophily?is?used?to?test?interaction?effect??How?to?understand
> >?this?
> 
> Homophily?is?an?interaction?between?the?attribute?of?node1?and?the 
> attribute?of?node1.??That?is,?given?main?effects?for?node1?attribute 
> (attr(i))?and?node?2?attribute?(attr(j))?--?e.g.,?relatively?higher 
> degree?for?attr(i)?than?attr(j)?--?is?there?an?*additional*?propensity?for 
> nodes?to?form?ties?within?attribute?levels.??Think?about?it?as?a?mixing 
> matrix,?where?the?main?effects?represent?the?variation?in?the?marginal 
> distributions,?and?the?interactions?represent?deviation?of?the?cell?counts 
> from?the?expected?value?given?the?margins.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] 4-cycles
messages.body_plain:
Hi jimi,

gwnsp actually measures 4 cycles, but not as a cycle census.  I'm guessing 
a 4-cycle term would have the same unfortunate properties that we've come 
to know and love about the triangle term.  So it may be that gwnsp is a 
good first cut.  And if you set gwnsp(alpha=0, fixed=TRUE), the term 
measures how many dyads (without a tie) are in at least one 4-cycle.

best,
mm

messages.subject: [statnet_help] sampling in ergm()
messages.body_plain:
Junchi,

The simulate() function is not what generates the samples, both 
estimation and simulation depend on the underlying MH algorithm (unless 
the model can be fit using glm).

There is information on the design and use of the algorithms in the JoSS 
papers "ergm" and "Using ergm", linked on the statnet wiki here:

https://statnet.csde.washington.edu/trac/wiki/Resources

And, of course, the code is publicly available on CRAN if you want to see 
exactly how this algorithm is implemented.

best,
Martina

messages.subject: [statnet_help] sampling in ergm()
messages.body_plain:
Junchi,

Simulate(), like ergm() and gof() all rely on the MH algorithm.  if you 
take a look at the ergm help page, you'll see you can modify many of the 
MH parameters there too.

best,
mm

On Wed, 10 Sep 2014, Junchi Guo wrote:

> Hi Martina,
> I think the MH algorithm is built in simulate()? I think the the following example is how to
> simulate samples from a given ergm, where one can modify many criterions. (2008, Volume 24, Issue
> 9.)
>
> ?simulate(model, burnin = 1e+5, interval = 1e+5, nsim = 1, verbose = TRUE, seed = 321)
> 
> Best,
> Junchi
> 
> On Wed, Sep 10, 2014 at 4:43 PM, martina morris <morrism@u.washington.edu> wrote:
>       Junchi,
>
>       The simulate() function is not what generates the samples, both estimation and
>       simulation depend on the underlying MH algorithm (unless the model can be fit using
>       glm).
>
>       There is information on the design and use of the algorithms in the JoSS papers "ergm"
>       and "Using ergm", linked on the statnet wiki here:
>
>       https://statnet.csde.washington.edu/trac/wiki/Resources
>
>       And, of course, the code is publicly available on CRAN if you want to see exactly how
>       this algorithm is implemented.
>
>       best,
>       Martina
>

messages.subject: [statnet_help] do you use statnet's parallel functionality on non-unix MPI clusters?
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] do you use statnet's parallel functionality on non-unix MPI clusters?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Statnet Users,

Do you run statnet on windows- or mac-based MPI parallel computing
clusters?  Are you aware of any statnet users or colleagues who use a
non-unix cluster? If so, please let me know.

The statnet team is in the process of overhauling and improving the 
parallelization functionality in ergm, and we are trying to determine if 
non-unix clusters are something we need to actively support for statnet 
-- which would require that we devote additional time to testing and 
maintaining the functionality on other platforms.

If we do de-prioritize testing on non-unix MPI clusters, we would of

As an interested third party, I am going to expand a bit, or possibly take this in a different direction (since I'm not sure I understand Philip's suggestion entirely). Say the two relations on the same set of nodes are represented in matrices A and B. Then the network to model is 

A 0
0 B

Where a 0 represents structural zeros. If cross network reciprocity is a desired model term, then the covariate matrix would look something like 

B' 0
0  A'

Hi Chris,

I think one potential solution would be to include both networks in a single block-diagonal matrix and use structural zeros for the off-diagonal blocks. You can code independent variables as matrices which are conformable to the block-diagonal dependent matrix. I did something like this for my MCMC MLE implementation of TERGMs in the xergm package (the mtergm function). But to see whether this actually works in your case, it would be helpful to see the model terms you want to include. Philip

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Node match v. node factor in papers
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Node match v. node factor in papers
messages.body_plain:
Nodefactor is a term that will capture only Marginal effects by factor 
level

* e.g., heterogeneity in mean degree by factor level

nodematch is different -- it captures homophily effects.

* e.g., heterogeneity in the probability of a tie as a function of 
matching nodal attributes (homophily)

and in general, if you want to test for homophily effects, you should 
have both nodefactor and nodematch terms in your model.

in addition, if you think there are differential rates of homophily by 
node factor level, you can test for this using nodematch("attr", diff=T). 
this again is a mode specification.

* it allow for different levels of homophily by nodefactor level.

these are three separate specifications; the idea is to test which one 
fits the data best.

hth,
mm

messages.body_plain:
Dear Statnet,

I have a problem that I believe can be resolved with a QAP procedure, but I need advice on whether the approach I propose is appropriate and then how to get the QAP estimates necessary to implement the approach.

I have a mixed effects model where I predict certain attitudes of organizational members within a collaborative system. The model estimates attitudes based on individual and group-level attributes.  Most of the group-level attributes are ego-network measures connecting the organization to others outside the collaborative.  Those should not pose a problem with autocorrelation.  On the other hand, I also include Burt's measure of network constraint for each organization within the collaborative.  Obviously, this independent variable introduces autocorrelation.

So I have three questions:


1.      Does the autocorrelation introduced by this independent variable affect the standard errors for all of the estimated standard errors of the coefficients.  Or do I only need to worry about an inflated standard error for the coefficient for the constraint measure?

2.      It would appear that I could estimate the distribution of the coefficient for the constraint measure under the null hypothesis, by doing a QAP on the matrix, recalculating the constraint measure, and then re-estimating mixed effects model.  Is that an appropriate remedy for this problem?

3.      Where can I find a procedure to produce 500-1000 iterations of the constraint scores using a QAP.  The QAP procedures that I see in sna, UCINET, and a procedure written by Simpson for STATA, all produce summary statistics for a particular estimate based on the QAP'd matrix, but they do not provide intermediate estimates.  Any idea how to calculate constraint on 1000 permuted matrices.


Thanks in advance

messages.subject: [statnet_help] calculating Moran’s I and Geary’s C statistics using nacf
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] calculating Moran’s I and Geary’s C statistics using nacf
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jesse,

maybe I am wrong, but as far as I know, the nacf-function in sna only 
calculates the coefficient, not its standard error nor the test result 
for departure from randomness. Syntax:

    nacf(network,attribute,type='moran',neighborhood.type='out')[2]

Index [2] is needed for extracting the direct (at geodesic outgoing 
distance 1) neighbours' autocorrelation (index [1] stands for 
autocorrelation at distance zero, i.e., self-correlation=value one; 
higher indices stand for correlations larger geodesic outgoing distances).

For the testing, I guess you could use the sna-function cugtest, but 
that might give a different type of null hypothesis tested than what 
Moran envisioned.

There also is a pre-programmed Moran's I in the package 'ape' (called 
Moran.I) which does give the st.error and significance test according to 
Moran. Funny thing is, last time I tried, the Moran calculations by 
UCINET, sna and ape tended to give slightly different results, for 
reasons I didn't understand at the time - probably related to 
directedness of the network or missing data entries. I ended up 
programming my own, to be sure what happens.

Best,
Christian

messages.body_plain:
Hi Vanesse and all,

I recently did something similar to what you're proposing using BIC. It
seems to have worked for me, so I thought I'd throw it out here in case
it's useful to you or anyone thinks it was a bad idea (which I would
definitely like to hear about!).

I was only using two of those three parameters, but I fit ERGMs to my
networks using a full factorial crossing of potential decay parameter
values (along with other terms of interest). I took the combination of
decay parameter values that minimized BIC to be the best model. This was
computationally demanding even with just two GW-parameters, but if your
networks are smaller (mine were near 1000 nodes each times three networks),
it might not take too long.

Hope that helps,

Michael

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Sample Space is not dyad-independent
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am trying to use ERGM for analyzing the cooperation behavior of Parliamentarians in Ghana. I have binary directed network data for all 237 Parliamentarians. Our network question was ?If you need political advice, whom of the other Parliamentarians do you ask??. 

The printed version of our survey had 5 lines under the question, so most of the respondents gave their top 5 contacts. No actor in the network has an outdegree greater than 5, whereas some named less than 5 contacts. 

As soon as I try to account for that problem with the constrain-commend as for example here,

model.ghana_dich <- ergm(ghana_dich.nw ~ edges, constraints=~bd(maxout=5)) 

I receive the results with the following warning message:

"In logLikNull.ergm(object, ...) :
  The constraint on the sample space is not dyad-independent. Null model likelihood is only implemented for dyad-independent constraints at this time. Number of observations is similarly ill-defined."

I am not sure what this warning means and how I could fix it? 

I appreciate very much if someone can point out the direction, thank you very much for your time.

Thank you very much-

Thomas Malang
University of Konstanz

correct

not directly, since this is an endogenous property.  however, if

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Coercing Network Object From List
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sean

On 09/23/2014 03:17 PM, Gmail wrote:
> Hello:
>
> I was wondering how to coerce a network object from a list. In particular, I am working with Butts et al Katrina data, which are stored as a list, and I would like to extract each of the 13 time periods and convert them to a network object.

I assume you are refering to this dataset?:
http://www.cmu.edu/joss/content/articles/volume13/katrina_1.0.tar.gz

It seems like this is an old package so I get NAMESPACE errors when 
trying to load it.  I was able to access the data by unzipping the 
package, and loading in the data object in the data directory.  For example

 > load("~/data/katrina.bydate.rda")

I was then able to access the network by explicitly loading the network 
library.

 > library(network)

and then the individual networks can be acessed with normal list operations:

 > katrina.bydate[[1]]
  Network attributes:
   vertices = 13
   directed = FALSE
   hyper = FALSE
   loops = FALSE
   multiple = FALSE
   bipartite = FALSE
   Date = 082405
   Doc.ID = 19005510 19455500 19455501 53005501 53005502 53005503
   Source.ID = 1900 1945 5300
   Source.Name = fldem flpalmbe txdem
   Start.Date = 82305
   End.Date = 82505
   total edges= 1
     missing edges= 0
     non-missing edges= 1

  Vertex attribute names:
     combined.id fema.region first.appearance group hq.city hq.state 
scale source.org.status type vertex.names

  Edge attribute names:
     Count


Is that what you meant? I'm not sure exactly which networks you are 
trying to do with them.  If you wanted to convert to a dynamic network:

 > library(networkDynamic)

 > katrinaDyn<-networkDynamic(network.list=katrina.bydate,vertex.pid = 
'vertex.names')

Neither start or onsets specified, assuming start=0
Onsets and termini not specified, assuming each network in network.list 
should have a discrete spell of length 1
Argument base.net not specified, using first element of network.list instead
Initialized network of size 1577 inferred from number of unique vertex.pids
Created net.obs.period to describe network
  Network observation period info:
   Number of observation spells: 1
   Maximal range of observations: 0 to 13
   Temporal mode: discrete
   Time unit: step
   Suggested time increment: 1

If you want to use the timing information included as network 
attributes, perhaps this would work:

katrinaDyn<-networkDynamic(network.list=katrina.bydate,
                       vertex.pid = 'vertex.names',
onsets = as.numeric(sapply(katrina.bydate,'%n%', 'Start.Date')), 
termini=as.numeric(sapply(katrina.bydate,'%n%', 'End.Date')))

Argument base.net not specified, using first element of network.list instead
Initialized network of size 1577 inferred from number of unique vertex.pids
Created net.obs.period to describe network
  Network observation period info:
   Number of observation spells: 13
   Maximal range of observations: 82305 to 90605
   Temporal mode: continuous
   Time unit: unknown
   Suggested time increment: NA

best,
  -skye

to existing clarifying references that can help me in writing the correct
script on Statnet.



Thank you in advance,

messages.body_plain:
Ok, many thanks to Steve and Martina for their help.

 I share my experience as it might interest other users,

The model I tried to fit was not able to converge when the decay parameter
of gwdegree was not fixed (CEF model),
so I adopted the method proposed by Hunter et al. 2008 and increased
progressively alpha (fixed =T), but for alpha > 0.1 for the three geometric
terms, the models were degenerate.
The problem came mainly from the gwdsp term, in my case the alpha parameter
for gwdsp shall not exceed 0.1.

So after fixing the gwdsp's alpha to 0.1, I tried several values of alpha
for the other geometric terms and the model with the best GOF in my case
was the one with alpha =0.1 for gwdegree and gwdsp and alpha=0.5 for gwesp.

GOF appears good visually for gwdegree gwesp and geodesic distance.

Is it the right way to proceed ?

Thanks

Vanesse





2014-09-09 17:32 GMT+02:00 martina morris <morrism@u.washington.edu>:

> Vanesse -- Yes, it would be useful to try all single terms first, then all
> 3 possible pairs, to see if you can isolate the problem term.  If you can
> get the pairs models to fit, you should also check for colinearity (the
> "covar" element of the ergm fit object).
>
> best,
> Martina
>
>
> On Tue, 9 Sep 2014, vanesse labeyrie wrote:
>
>  Hi again,
>>
>> I am really sorry, but I'm still struggling with ergm fitting...
>>
>> Following the previous advice, I increased the MCMC samplesize, interval
>> and MCMLE.maxit.
>>
>> Here is the model I tried to fit:
>>
>> ergm(net~edges+gwdegree(1.35,fixed=F)+gwdsp(0.1,fixed=T) +
>> gwesp(0.1,fixed=T),control=control.ergm(MCMC.burnin=100000, MC
>> MC.samplesize=50000, MCMC.interval=1000,seed=55,MCMLE.maxit=200) )
>> but after 200 iterations, it still not appear to converge (the iterations
>> stopped at 200 [ "Iteration 200 of at most 200:
>> Convergence test P-value: 0e+00 The log-likelihood improved by < 0.0001"]
>> ) ...
>>
>> Computation time was already very long, shall I continue to increase the
>> MCMC parameters or shall I conclude that
>> convergence can't be reached ?
>>
>> I launched the same analysis on PNet and can't reach convergence too ...
>>
>> I found the following statement in a paper of Harris : "When models with
>> all three geometric terms did not converge, we
>> followed a strategy demonstrated by Hunter et al. using bivariate
>> analyses to determine which of the geometric terms may
>> be helpful in explaining existing global network structures [22,23]. The
>> full model was then re-estimated retaining only
>> those global terms that demonstrated a significant relationship with the
>> outcome in this bivariate testing."
>>
>> Is it the right way to do ? I looked in the references cited but I didn't
>> found any mention of this procedure in them ...
>>
>> Many thanks for your help
>>
>> Vanesse
>>
>> 2014-09-08 18:05 GMT+02:00 Steven Goodreau <goodreau@uw.edu>:
>>       Hi Vanessa -
>>
>>       Yes, in that case increasing the MCMC is a good idea, since it
>> sounds as if the model has not yet converged.
>>       Key parameters to tr increasing are
>>       to start with are MCMLE.maxit, MCMC.interval, and MCMCsamplesize.
>>
>>       Steve
>>
>>
>>       On 9/7/2014 11:35 PM, vanesse labeyrie wrote:
>>             Many thanks for you answer, Steve.
>>
>>             My data are very sparse too, the density is 0.01. I tried to
>> let the alpha for gwdegree vary
>>             (with fixed=F), but the problem is that results strongly

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Comparing Parameter Estimates Across Models - Progress since 2007?
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Comparing Parameter Estimates Across Models - Progress since 2007?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Statnet Users,

Admittedly, this question is a rehash of one asked by Brian Rubineau in 2007.  But when asked, David Hunter answered that it was unresolved (see https://mailman13.u.washington.edu/mailman/htdig/statnet_help/2007/000119.html).  This question has come up in my own research, and I was wondering if it had been resolved at this point in time.

Somewhat similar questions were asked in https://mailman13.u.washington.edu/mailman/htdig/statnet_help/2013/001493.html and https://mailman13.u.washington.edu/mailman/htdig/statnet_help/2010/000804.html.  The former received no answer and the latter requires a strong assumption (edge independence) and a quantitative (rather than categorical) variable.

I apologize for the lengthy documentation, though I wanted to demonstrate that I attempted to resolve this myself before turning to the statnet group.

I have data with one set of nodes and several sets of edges (5 to be exact - different areas of collaboration amongst entrepreneurs in developing countries).  I would like to compare the forces governing link formation in each network.  I have combined all my adjacency matrices into one big adjacency matrix (node names were adjusted to be unique; names are the original name + the network name).  This matrix is defined such that edges only exist between nodes from the same original network.

Ideally, this would mean constructing an ERGM with the same right-hand side (explanatory variables) for each network (different dependent variables, corresponding to each network), with the goal of comparing parameter estimates.  Comparing these parameter estimates would allow me to answer questions of the following form: Is transitivity stronger in one collaboration area versus another?

I'd like to adapt classical regression techniques by introducing dummy variables and interaction terms to statistically discern the differences in effects amongst the networks.  I've tried constructing a dummy variable off of my attribute list manually, and then including it in my ERGM, though I get an error and my code is not accepted by R.  I am also unable to multiply variables (as one must to construct an interaction term) in the ERGM function.

Thoughts?  Thank you for your time and consideration.

Cheers,
Louis


Louis Boguchwal
Louis.Boguchwal@usma.edu<mailto:Louis.Boguchwal@usma.edu>
Research Mathematician
Network Science Center at West Point, US Military Academy

messages.body_plain:
Hello Kevin--

It turns out that you did indeed uncover a bug.  And it's something that 
only arose when one had a dyadic independent model and multiple offset 
terms - a sufficiently unique experience that we hadn't caught it 
before, but our students Kirk and Li were able to track it down.  It 
will be fixed in the next release, which we anticipate should be in the 
next month or so.

Thanks again for bringing this up - we rely on folks doing this to make 
the software better for everyone.

Yours,
Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] decay parameter for gwdegree term
messages.body_plain:
Many thanks for you answer, Steve.

My data are very sparse too, the density is 0.01. I tried to let the alpha
for gwdegree vary (with fixed=F), but the problem is that results strongly
differ depending on the alpha I specify as an a priori. It suggest that the
algorithm was not able to find the MLE ?
I'm going to try while increasing the MCMC.

Thanks

Vanesse




2014-09-05 19:22 GMT+02:00 Steven Goodreau <goodreau@uw.edu>:

>  Hi Vanessa,
>
> I have not spent much time working with gwdegree myself.  But I can share
> an experience with gwesp that may be of use.  The more I have worked with
> users troubleshooting their data, the more I have found that a higher alpha
> is often useful for gwesp when the data are more dense.  In my own domain I
> mostly work with sparse data, and that is also the case in the Goodreau et
> al. 2008 paper.  Since then I have come to realize how things can be more
> complicated than that, and at least for gwesp, for dense data the lowest
> alphas can indeed cause problems.
>
> You might try fixing the gwesp and gwdsp alphas, given your previous
> findings, but let the gwdegree one vary (with fixed=F) and see if the
> algorithm is able to find the MLE.  Given that there seems to be more
> impact for this value in your data than the others, there may well be
> plenty of information there for it to do the joint estimation easily.
>
> I hope that helps a little,
> Steve
>
>
> On 9/5/2014 4:55 AM, vanesse labeyrie wrote:
>
>     Dear all,
>
>  many thanks for your help on my previous questions,
>
> I have one more question concerning the definition of the "decay" in the
> gwdegree term.
>
>  I wish to run a model including gwdegree, gwdsp and gwesp. I have no
> problem for gwdsp and gwesp terms, and the value of alpha does not have a
> strong influence on the results as it was underlined previously in this
> forum.
>
>  However, the decay parameter for the gwdegree has a strong influence on
> the results.
>
>  I tried the procedure recommended by Goodreau et al. 2008 and detailed in
> the book of Harris, chap.3, by increasing progressively the decay and alpha
> parameters as follow:
>
> M.1 <- ergm(net~edges+gwdegree (0,fixed=T) + gwdsp
> (0,fixed=T)+gwesp(0,fixed=T))
> M.2 <- ergm(net~edges+gwdegree (0.1,fixed=T) + gwdsp
> (0.1,fixed=T)+gwesp(0.1,fixed=T))
> M.3 <- ergm(net~edges+gwdegree (0.2,fixed=T) + gwdsp
> (0.2,fixed=T)+gwesp(0.2,fixed=T))
>  etc.. up to decay and alpha =1.1
>
>  My first question is whether I am right to use this procedure,
> considering the three terms together ?
>
> Models start to show signs of degeneracy for very low values of alpha and
> decay (0.2), so in fact, the only models which are not degenerated are for
> alpha/decay = 0.1 or 0 ...
>
>  I tried CEF models, but they showed signs of degeneracy.
>
>  Can anybody help me on this topic and share experience concerning the
> model specification with these terms ?
>
>  Many thanks
>
>
>  Vanesse Labeyrie
>  post-doctoral fellow at UMR AGAP, CIRAD, France
>

messages.subject: [statnet_help] MPLE with offset terms
messages.body_plain:
Dear Steve (and Kirk and Li),

Thank you so much for your help!!! I only hope I can continue doing things that are sufficiently odd that I stumble across bugs that otherwise escaped detection :).

Best wishes,
Kevin

From: statnet_help [mailto:statnet_help-bounces@mailman13.u.washington.edu] On Behalf Of Steven Goodreau
Sent: Thursday, August 28, 2014 9:23 AM
To: statnet_help@u.washington.edu
Subject: Re: [statnet_help] MPLE with offset terms

Hello Kevin--

It turns out that you did indeed uncover a bug.  And it's something that only arose when one had a dyadic independent model and multiple offset terms - a sufficiently unique experience that we hadn't caught it before, but our students Kirk and Li were able to track it down.  It will be fixed in the next release, which we anticipate should be in the next month or so.

Thanks again for bringing this up - we rely on folks doing this to make the software better for everyone.

Yours,
Steve



On 8/4/2014 3:52 PM, Lewis, Kevin wrote:
Hi everyone (especially developers),

I worry these issues might be a bit specific, but I believe I have found a few calculations misbehaving that could reflect something going wrong beneath the hood (or perhaps more likely, something wrong with the driver...). The issues are specific because they all have to with dyad-independent models (i.e. what should be straightforward logistic regression), and in particular applied to a large social network (thousands of nodes) and using models that include offset terms- i.e. where the observed count of a statistic is zero and so the coefficients are automatically fixed at negative infinity. My specific application is that I want to estimate some models of what influences a female to look at a male's profile on an online dating site; so, if we consider the gender binary mixing matrix, I am interested ONLY in female/male ties and need to set female/female ties, male/male ties, and male/female ties all to negative infinity. I am using statnet version 2014.2.0, running on 64-bit R version 3.1.1.

There are three different issues I've come across- not sure if they are related:

1. First, I start with a basic model- *only* the edges term- with the restriction that only female/male ties are permitted. Interestingly, it seems to matter *how* I prohibit all other types of ties for whether the results are reasonable. In the first instance, I block all male/female ties using nodemix, and (separately) I block male/male ties and female/female ties using nodematch(diff=TRUE). Results are bizarre. In the second instance, I do the exact same thing except this time I block both kinds of same-gender ties at the same time using nodematch(diff=FALSE)- and this time, results *seem* much more reasonable.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Possible network.arrow() bug
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I ran into a possible bug with network.arrow(). Basically, when you specify
the "curve" option, the arrows look strange. I have documented this
phenomenon on stackoverflow at:

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/25777757/r-network-arrow-looks-strange-when-curved

Alternately, you can simply run the following code to generate an example:

library(maps)
library(network)
map("usa")
network.arrow(-110,37,-85,40,length=5,width=1,angle=20,curve=2)

To whom it may concern, I am running Mac OSX 10.9.5 with R version 3.02. My
network package is version 1.10.2.

Sincerely,

Warren Ronsiek

messages.body_plain:
Zachary
One solution would be to generate a reflexive tie for everyone in each relation and then zero out the diagonal at a later step.
-Tom

From: statnet_help [mailto:statnet_help-bounces@mailman13.u.washington.edu] On Behalf Of Atropos Xanthus
Sent: Thursday, August 21, 2014 4:37 PM
To: statnet_help@u.washington.edu
Subject: [statnet_help] Splitting a network based on edge attributes

I need to split a network by edge attributes into subgraphs.  My preference is for the resulting networks to retain all vertices of the original network.

Here's an example where edges represent ties associated with breakfast and supper:

ego, alter, meal
1, 2, "breakfast"
1, 3, "breakfast"
1, 4, "breakfast"
1, 4, "supper"
1, 2, "supper"
3, 4, "breakfast"

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the followup Vanesse --

Glad to hear you got the models to behave :)

Just out of curiousity, did you ever try fixing the alphas (for all the gw 
terms) to 0?  I ask because with this value of alpha, the terms all have 
very simple interpretations:  the number of dyads/edges (gwdsp/gwesp) with 
at least one shared partner.  If you can get these to converge, the 
deviations in the GOF plots from these models, relative to your best 
fitting models, can help you to interpret the value of the best fitting 
alpha in terms of what patterns in the observed network are captured by 
allowing alpha to vary.

I'd also suggest looking at all the GOF terms available to get the most 
complete picture (see the documentation).

best,
Martina

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

I think one potential solution would be to include both networks in a 
single block-diagonal matrix and use structural zeros for the 
off-diagonal blocks. You can code independent variables as matrices 
which are conformable to the block-diagonal dependent matrix. I did 
something like this for my MCMC MLE implementation of TERGMs in the 
xergm package (the mtergm function). But to see whether this actually 
works in your case, it would be helpful to see the model terms you want 
to include. (Note that I will be traveling for the next couple of days 
and might not be able to reply immediately.)

Best,
Philip

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Significant memory use for gof.ergmm
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'm trying to use the gof.ergmm function from the latentnet package, and it
seems to be creating unexpectedly large gofobject objects, which is causing
problems when I'm trying to save a goodness of fit object from several
networks.  Does anyone know why, or how to fix it?  I've included more
detail, and a possible partial solution below.

Here's an example:

> rm(list = ls())> library(statnet)> > # Library for memory use; see http://adv-r.had.co.nz/memory.html> library(pryr)> > data(sampson)> samp.fit <- ergmm(samplike ~ euclidean(d = 2))> > samp.gof <- gof(samp.fit)> object_size(samp.gof)6.98 MB

Running gof.ergmm on the example from the documentation gives a 7MB file.
For a single network, this isn't a huge problem -- my computer isn't
choking on 7MB -- but it becomes a problem when you try to loop over many
model fits, for many networks.

My best guess is that R is doing a poor job of garbage collection at the
end of the gof.ergmm function.  The gof.ergmm function simulates several
networks from the model fit, and then calculates statistics using those.
When it's done, it doesn't seem to return the memory used by the
simulations.  Adding a rm(SimNetworkSeriesObj) statement in the function
seems to produce much smaller gofobject objects, presumably because then R
returns the memory used by the simulations.  Code for this is below
(apologies for the length -- I copied and pasted the gof.ergmm function).

nsim = 100, GOF = ~idegree + odegree + +                            distance, verbose = FALSE) + {+   formula <- object[["model"]][["formula"]]+   trms <- ergm.getterms(formula)+   if (length(trms) > 2) {+     nw <- eval(trms[[2]], sys.parent())+   }+   else {+     stop("A network object on the RHS of the formula argument must be given")+   }+   nsim <- max(nsim, dim(object[["Z"]])[3])+ pval.odeg <- NULL+   n <- network.size(nw)+   if ("model" %in% all.gof.vars) {+     obs.model <- summary(formula)+     sim.model <- array(0, dim = c(nsim, length(obs.model)))+     dimnames(sim.model) messages.subject: [statnet_help] Sample Space is not dyad-independent
messages.body_plain:
Hi Thomas,

Thanks for asking. This is actually an example of a "good"warning that 
we put in there to be informative; it doesn't need to be fixed.  Some 
models are dyadic-independent, and others dyadic dependent, and this 
distinction leads to a number of important implications (e.g. whether 
MCMC is needed to fit the model).  This is a case where the model would 
be dyadic independent based on the terms in the formula, but because of 
the constraint it gets kicked into the category of dyadic dependent.  So 
we are pointing that out to people in case they have the wrong 
expectation based on the terms alone. There are also aspects of the 
statistical theory behind the models that works differently for models 
with dyadic dependent constraints. But again, you don't necessarily have 
to do anything about the warning.

I've seen other confusion around this as well, so I think we should 
probably change the warning to make it more clear, or perhaps remove it 
altogether.  I'll add it to our development team's decision list.

Thanks,
Steve

messages.body_plain:
Hi Zachary,

The easiest way I can think of doing this is to copy the network and 
delete all the edges of the type you don't want.

Assuming you've got a network named mealNet with your data below and an 
edge attribute meal

# peek at the attribute
 > mealNet%e%'meal'
[1] "supper"    "breakfast" "breakfast" "breakfast" "supper"    "breakfast"

# make a copy of the network that we want to have only the 'breakfast' edges
 > breakfast<-network.copy(mealNet)

# get the ids of all the non-breakfast edges
 > which(breakfast%e%'meal'!='breakfast')
[1] 1 5

# delete those edges from the network
 > delete.edges(breakfast,eid = which(breakfast%e%'meal'!='breakfast'))

# check the results
 > breakfast%e%'meal'
[1] "breakfast" "breakfast" "breakfast" "breakfast


can generalize this into a splitNetworks function which would give you a 
list of networks with each having only the appropriate edges:

splitNetworks<-function(net,attrname){
   # find the unique values
   vals<-get.edge.attribute(net,attrname)
   uniqueVals<-unique(vals)
   nets<-list()
   # for each value of attrname, create a network
   # containing only edges that have that value
   for (val in uniqueVals){
     subNet<-net
     delete.edges(subNet,eid=which(vals!=val))
     nets<-c(nets,list(subNet))
   }
   # name the elements of the list according to values
   names(nets)<-uniqueVals
   return(nets)
}





hopefully this works for your data,
  best,
  -skye

a higher alpha is often useful for gwesp when the data are more dense.  
In my own domain I mostly work with sparse data, and that is also the 
case in the Goodreau et al. 2008 paper.  Since then I have come to 
realize how things can be more complicated than that, and at least for 
gwesp, for dense data the lowest alphas can indeed cause problems.

You might try fixing the gwesp and gwdsp alphas, given your previous 
findings, but let the gwdegree one vary (with fixed=F) and see if the 
algorithm is able to find the MLE.  Given that there seems to be more 
impact for this value in your data than the others, there may well be 
plenty of information there for it to do the joint estimation easily.

I hope that helps a little,
Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] tips to speed up ergm
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I am trying to run some ERG models using a network with 1172 vertices
and 14757 edges. After running some models with the  default MCMC
specifications and exploring MCMC diagnostics, I decided to increase
the samplesize, interval, and burnin. The problem is that it takes so
long (more than 15 hours). Using parallel (16 cores) does not improve
much. In addition, increasing the MCMC specifications doesn't solve
most of the problems with the simulations (significant differences
between observed and simulated terms and autocorrelation).

Any suggestions about how to face these problems? Probably the network
is too big and I should identify smaller communities, and then run
separate ERG models with them. I don?t know if there are other
strategies.

Thanks,
Sebastian

Example:

dyadcount <-1.883515e+12

control04 <- control.ergm(MCMC.samplesize=50000, MCMC.interval=5000,
MCMC.burnin=50000, MCMLE.maxit=20, MPLE.max.dyad.types=dyadcount)

m02 <- ergm(n ~ edges + mutual + gwdsp(1, fixed=FALSE) + gwesp(1,
fixed=FALSE), control=control04, eval.loglik=FALSE, verbose=FALSE)

messages.subject: [statnet_help] MPLE with offset terms
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone (especially developers),

I worry these issues might be a bit specific, but I believe I have found a few calculations misbehaving that could reflect something going wrong beneath the hood (or perhaps more likely, something wrong with the driver...). The issues are specific because they all have to with dyad-independent models (i.e. what should be straightforward logistic regression), and in particular applied to a large social network (thousands of nodes) and using models that include offset terms- i.e. where the observed count of a statistic is zero and so the coefficients are automatically fixed at negative infinity. My specific application is that I want to estimate some models of what influences a female to look at a male's profile on an online dating site; so, if we consider the gender binary mixing matrix, I am interested ONLY in female/male ties and need to set female/female ties, male/male ties, and male/female ties all to negative infinity. I am using statnet version 2014.2.0, running on 64-bit R version 3.1.1.

There are three different issues I've come across- not sure if they are related:

1. First, I start with a basic model- *only* the edges term- with the restriction that only female/male ties are permitted. Interestingly, it seems to matter *how* I prohibit all other types of ties for whether the results are reasonable. In the first instance, I block all male/female ties using nodemix, and (separately) I block male/male ties and female/female ties using nodematch(diff=TRUE). Results are bizarre. In the second instance, I do the exact same thing except this time I block both kinds of same-gender ties at the same time using nodematch(diff=FALSE)- and this time, results *seem* much more reasonable.

Pajek makes this very simple.

1. Assign a numeric code to identify the edge in question, e.g.,

wrote:

> Hi Zachary,
>
> The easiest way I can think of doing this is to copy the network and
> delete all the edges of the type you don't want.
>
> Assuming you've got a network named mealNet with your data below and an
> edge attribute meal
>
> # peek at the attribute
> > mealNet%e%'meal'
> [1] "supper"    "breakfast" "breakfast" "breakfast" "supper"    "breakfast"
>
> # make a copy of the network that we want to have only the 'breakfast'
> edges
> > breakfast<-network.copy(mealNet)
>
> # get the ids of all the non-breakfast edges
> > which(breakfast%e%'meal'!='breakfast')
> [1] 1 5
>
> # delete those edges from the network
> > delete.edges(breakfast,eid = which(breakfast%e%'meal'!='breakfast'))
>
> # check the results
> > breakfast%e%'meal'
> [1] "breakfast" "breakfast" "breakfast" "breakfast
>
>
> can generalize this into a splitNetworks function which would give you a
> list of networks with each having only the appropriate edges:
>
> splitNetworks<-function(net,attrname){
>   # find the unique values
>   vals<-get.edge.attribute(net,attrname)
>   uniqueVals<-unique(vals)
>   nets<-list()
>   # for each value of attrname, create a network
>   # containing only edges that have that value
>   for (val in uniqueVals){
>     subNet<-net
>     delete.edges(subNet,eid=which(vals!=val))
>     nets<-c(nets,list(subNet))
>   }
>   # name the elements of the list according to values
>   names(nets)<-uniqueVals
>   return(nets)
> }
>
>
>
>
>
> hopefully this works for your data,

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

If I understand it correctly, then we might get biased estimates on the
homophily parameters (the nodematch term) if some groups are just much more
"sociable" than others, and therefore I should also always add a nodefactor
term, correct?

However, what if I suspect that the network of interest is determined not
simply by belonging to one or another group, but by the underlying social
structure within the groups and therefore instead include an edgecov term
(and enter the network that represents this underlying social structure, in
my case a complex star network with quite a few isolates).

Is there an equivalent to the nodefactor term that I should add to avoid
bias (e.g. a nodefactor term for "part of underlying network vs. isolate")?

Thanks in advance for any suggestions,

Franziska

messages.subject: [statnet_help] 4-cycles
messages.body_plain:
Just to comment further on this, the dyadwise shared partner (DSP) terms 
of order >=2 will measure the concentration of 4-cycles on arbitrary 
dyads; if you want 4-cycles _with at most one chord_, then the nullwise 
shared partners  (NSPs) of order >=2 will pick this up.  (ESPs >=2 will 
correspondingly capture 4-cycles with at _least_ one chord.) As Martina 
noted, none of these are directly counting the 4-cycles per se, so one 
would need to be careful in their interpretation vis a vis 
cycle-specific mechanisms.  Also, gwdsp/gwnsp/gwesp will put weight on 
DSP/NSP/ESP terms of order 0 and 1 (which do not contain 4-cycles), so 
this may require correction.

While it is true that the k-cycles for k>3 are not provably safe 
statistics, in my experience they are often better behaved than the 
triangle term.  "Often" does not mean "always."  They can certainly 
produce poor results...on the other hand, I'm currently fitting models 
with cycle lengths as large as 10 to networks with >250 nodes.  Much 
depends on the details of the network, the other terms in the model, 
constraints, etc.

One additional point that bears note is that a 4-cycle term with a 
negative parameter (as proposed here) will not lead e.g. to the density 
explosion route to degeneracy.  That does not in and of itself guarantee 
good behavior, but as a practical matter it is usually the positive 
terms that cause problems.  (An easy way to probe the impact of such a 
term is to refit the model with the cycle term as an offset, and examine 
the behavior of simulated networks under the refitted model as a 
function of the offset parameter.  This can be useful in identifying 
whether e.g. models in the portion of the parameter space that is of 
interest are well-behaved, one is close to a phase transition, etc.)

Cycles are a rich source of interesting problems, of both the good kind 
and the bad kind.  Hopefully, the above observations will prove useful 
to those seeking to employ cycle terms in their models!

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] QAP for a single regression independent variable
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] QAP for a single regression independent variable
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

Let me summarize your situation: You've got (a) an outcome variable on 
the nodes, (b) a network matrix that shows the dependencies between your 
units of observation, (c) an independent variable which is derived from 
this matrix, and (d) a bunch of other independent variables at the node 
level. Correct?

In that case, it is not the variable in (c) which introduces the bias 
into the model. It is rather the matrix in (b) which causes your trouble 
because your observations are not independent. (c) is rather a partial 
remedy for the problem because you are modeling parts of the 
dependencies as part of the data-generating process.

It would be ideal if you could also incorporate other types of 
dependencies which explain your outcome variable in order to reduce the 
bias, which may be framed as a special kind of omitted variable bias.

For example, it may be the average outcome of actor i's contacts j that 
influences i's outcome. Or it may be i's total exposure to the sum of 
all of i's contacts j's outcomes. Or maybe i's outcome is affected by 
the friends k of his friends j (i.e., indirect friends). Or maybe i 
compares his or her potential outcome to that of other nodes j which are 
connected to the same other nodes k, which is essentially structural 
similarity. Or maybe i's cliques' outcomes influence i's outcomes (to a 
greater extent than bilateral influence). Or perhaps isolates have 
different outcomes than connected nodes etc.

The basic version of this is called the linear network autocorrelation 
model, and it was implemented in the lnam function in the sna package. 
But this function can only control for the first of the dependencies 
outlined above. A more comprehensive solution would be the tnam function 
("temporal network autocorrelation model") in the xergm package. It 
includes all of the above-mentioned dependencies and some others for any 
kind of dependent variable (not just a linear model) and possibly 
including random effects and possibly modeling multiple time steps 
(which would enable you to assess diffusion of behavior over time).

The caveat is that this kind of model does not tell you which 
dependencies you have to model. This is part of the modeling process, 
just like the way you model dependencies in an ERGM by adding some more 
model terms and checking if this improves the model fit. But you can 
never know if you have captured all of the dependencies (but I guess you 
have to live with this in the ERGM world, too).

It should be obvious now that a QAP approach does not really help you 
out because it is not your independent variable that is causing the bias 
but rather your network dependencies and the omitted variable bias 
resulting from the unmodeled dependencies.

So my answers to your three questions would be:

1. It affects all parameters, but the reason is not the independent 
variable.

2. I think this would not work because the dependent variable would 
still be contaminated by autocorrelation because your observations are 
nested in the network.

3. I don't know, but I think the question got obsolete now.

Does anybody have a better solution for this kind of problem? I'd be 
curious to hear about it because I am relatively new to the world of 
autocorrelation models; I just implemented the tnam stuff this month.

Best,
Philip
