On 03/27/2015 11:31 PM, Fabiola martinoli wrote:
> Dear Statnet's users and developers,
> i'm very new in ERGMs and i'm studying a network of 200 nodes for my 
> master's degree thesis. I have two questions for you:
>
> 1. How can i assess that my model converges properly? I mean, after i 
> receive my coefficients from the ergm() function, i check it with 
> mcmc.diagnostics(): the only important thing is that the MCMC sample 
> statistic are varying randomly around the observed values at each step 
> and that the difference between the observed and simulated values have 
> a roughly bell-shaped distribution centered in 0? Or should i also 
> check the individual p-values given at the end of the diagnostics?
> If so, what is the lower bound tha makes my p-value acceptable?
> I read a lot of papers and tutorial but i haven't found a clear answer 
> to my doubt.
>
As a practical matter, you want to verify that (1) the Markov chain is 
mixing well (e.g., you are covering the region of high probability with 
respect to each model statistic, the chain is not strongly 
autocorrelated, and the chain shows no signs of being "stuck" for long 
periods in a single state); (2) the mean of the sufficient statistics 
for the retained draws is close to their observed values; and 
(relatedly) (3) the Markov chain appears to be stationary (e.g., the 
first and second moments show no signs of "wandering").  The various 
diagnostics can assist with this process, although they can be 
over-interpreted.  (For instance, it is possible to obtain a perfectly 
reasonable parameter estimate from a sample that shows a significant 
departure of the simulated mean from (say) one of the observed 
statistics, and one can likewise obtain good results from a chain that 
is reasonably autocorrelated.  These are not good signs, however, and in 
practice one should work to minimize them.)

My own _practical_ advice for a typical case would be as follows:
   1. Verify that the first moment of the Markov chain has converged - 
the running mean line should be flat.  If there is evidence of a trend, 
either (1) the model is degenerate, and trying to head off to la-la 
land, or (2) you need to increase your burn-in time.
   2. Verify that the chain is mixing well.  You should see relatively 
smooth marginal distributions, there should be little visual evidence of 
strong autocorrelation in the trace plot, and autocorrelation 
diagnostics should show reasonably small correlations at reasonable 
lags.  If the chain isn't mixing well, either (1) your model is showing 
signs of being poorly behaved, or (2) you need to increase the thinning 
interval.
   3. Verify that the mean values of the sufficient statistics are 
reasonably close to the target values.  (Note that they may be a bit 
off, because if how the fitting algorithm works - we will provide a 
better test below.)  Ideally, the means will be within a standard 
deviation or so of the observed or target values.  If the means seem to 
be way off, this usually indicates insufficient burn-in and/or thinning 
length, but it can also result from a highly recalcitrant model with 
which the estimation algorithm cannot easily deal.
   4. Having done all of the above, produce a new, high-quality 
simulation from the fitted model (using simulate() or gof()). Verify 
(1)-(3) on the new sample; but this time, pay closer attention to (3).  
For a reasonable sample size (say, 250), I would usually be concerned if 
my mean statistics were significantly different from their target values 
(with the usual caveats about multiple testing and such).
   5. If your model clears all of the above, the fitting process itself 
has probably been successful.  You will still want to perform model 
adequacy checking and such, as described in the various available tutorials.

Again, these are heuristics, and one can identify exceptions and/or more 
specific directives for special cases.  But they should provide you with 
a good place to start.

> 2. I'm interested in studying a brokerage effect due to a nodal 
> attribute, is there any effect able to test it? I looked for it but i 
> can't find nothing.
>

This (and related!) problems are addressed in a forthcoming JSS paper:

Yaveroglu, Omer Nebil; Fitzhugh, Sean M.; Kurant, Maciej; Markopoulou, 
Athina; Butts, Carter T.; and Przulj, Natasa. (2015). ``ergm.graphlets: 
A Package for ERG Modeling Based on Graphlet Statistics.''  Journal of 
Statistical Software, forthcoming.

Unfortunately, it's been held up in the JSS editorial queue for months 
and months.  However, you can find a pre-print on arXiv: 
http://arxiv.org/abs/1405.7348.  Likewise, the package needed to add the 
associated statistics to ergm is on CRAN: 
http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ergm.graphlets/index.html. Once 
you load the ergm.graphlets package, you can use the associated terms 
within ergm just as you would any other model terms.  (See the paper for 
examples.)

Hope that helps,

-Carter

> Thank you very much for your precious help.
> Fabiola Martinoli.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Simulating for ERGMs
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Justin -

Have you tried ensuring that your burn-in and thinning intervals are 
both substantially larger than N^2 (where N is the number of vertices)?  
The intervals you include below may prove insufficient once N approaches 
100 or so (though this depends).  Without having the chance to check 
over your code in detail, this immediately occurs to me as one factor 
that can lead to the effect you describe.  (FWIW, I recently did a 
simulation study using MCMC on the edge/mutual model for a different 
purpose, and I found that I needed about N^3 iterations to guarantee 
high quality draws.  For an N of 100, that means you ought be looking at 
about a million iterations, if you want to be extra safe.)  Try running 
the MCMC longer, and see if that works.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

On 11/25/2014 07:39 PM, Kirkland, Justin H wrote:
> Dear StatNet Listserv,
>
> As both an exercise for my students, and for my own education, I've 
> been conducting some Monte Carlo experiments/simulations on the ERGM 
> in order to ascertain how robust inferences from the ERGM are to a 
> variety of simple specification and measurement issues. For example, 
> one example might be trying to discover how severe coefficient biases 
> are in the face of mounting data missingness. Such a simulation 
> exercise requires that 1) I be able to replicate the data-generating 
> process implied by ERGMs to create a network in which I know the 
> relevant relationships perfectly, 2) be able to create some set of 
> problems in said network, and then 3) estimate coefficients from an 
> ERGM both on a true network and a network with some sort of problem to 
> gauge the difference between those estimates.
>
> Thus far, I have been using the "simulate.ergm" command from statnet 
> to create networks in which I can control coefficients perfectly. The 
> simulate.ergm help file suggests that the command is used to "draw 
> from exponential family random network models," and allows a user to 
> set coefficient values using a "coef" vector. So if I create a network 
> with high levels of reciprocity using the simulate command by setting 
> the "mutual" coefficient for simulate to a value of 2, and then run an 
> ERGM on the created network with a mutual term as a covariate, the 
> coefficient on the mutual term /should/ return a value of 2 (in 
> expectation).
>
> What I and my team are finding is that when networks are small (25 
> actors) this process works exactly as we thought, but as the network 
> size increases (to say 75 or 100 actors), the simulate command no 
> longer produces networks whose ERGM coefficients match what we think 
> they should. In the above example, if we use simulate to create a 
> network and set the mutual coefficient to 2 in the simulate command, 
> then run an ERGM on that network, the estimated ERGM will report a 
> mutual coefficient of 2 when the network is small, but as the network 
> size increases, the estimated ERGM will report increasingly small 
> coefficients even before we've introduced any sort of problems.
>
> Since our ability to control the data generating process of the ERGM 
> is central to our statistical experiments, we were hoping someone 
> might be able to shed light on why the simulate.ergm command isn't 
> consistently producing networks in which the ERGM coefficients are 
> what we would expect, particularly as our network sizes get larger. 
> Below I've posted some sample R-code for how we've been running things 
> along with some heavy commenting to illustrate what we're trying to 
> do, and I'm happy to chat off list if that's easier for folks. Thanks 
> in advance for any help anyone can provide.
>
> -----------------------------------------------------------
> *_EXAMPLE CODE:_*
>
> #Clear Memory
> rm(list=ls())
>
> #load libraries
> library(statnet)
>
> #set seed
> set.seed(1234)
>
> #set parameters
> initial.density<-0.2
>
> #This sets the actor size of the network; increase this number and bad 
> things happen
> actors<-50
>
> #Number of simulations
> sims<-100
>
> #These are our model parameters that we hope ERGM will recover; as our 
> sample size gets larger, the ERGM coefficients are further
> #and further from these parameters, even across thousands of simulations
> update.density<-0.1
> update.mutual<-2
>
> #Create a place to store things
> TrueCoefsE<-numeric(sims) #Store edges coefficients
> TrueCoefsM<-numeric(sims) #Store mutual coefficients
>
> for(k in 1:sims){
>
>   #Draw a blank matrix
>   Net<-matrix(0, actors, actors)
>
>   #Fill in a blank adjacency matrix using the initial density 
> parameter; this is largely just a set up to the actual network development
>   for(i in 1:nrow(Net)){
>     for(j in 1:nrow(Net)){
> Net[i,j]<-rbinom(1,1,initial.density)
>     }
>   }
>   diag(Net)<-0
>
>   #Turn into network object
>   Net2<-network(Net, directed=TRUE)
>
>   #Simulate intial ergm to get manipulable object; we're going to use 
> this model to control the DGP of the ERGM (hopefully)
> summary(mod.ini<-ergm(Net2~edges+mutual, 
> control=control.ergm(MCMC.samplesize=5000, MCMLE.maxit=100, 
> MCMC.burnin=10000, MCMC.interval=1000, drop=TRUE)))
>
>   #Alter to coefficients to make into values you control; this is 
> where we specify exactly what we want the coefficients from the ERGM to be
>   coefs.ini<-coef(mod.ini)
>   coefs.new<-coefs.ini
>   coefs.new[1]<-update.density
>   coefs.new[2]<-update.mutual
>
>   #simulate new network with known coefficients; this SHOULD create a 
> network in which the ERGM would report a mutual coefficient of 2/
>   sim.new<-network(simulate(mod.ini, coef=coefs.new))
>
>   #estimate ergm on new network with known coefficients
> summary(mod.new<-ergm(sim.new~edges+mutual, 
> control=control.ergm(MCMC.samplesize=5000, MCMLE.maxit=100, 
> MCMC.burnin=10000, MCMC.interval=1000, drop=TRUE)))
>
>   #Store Coefficients
>   TrueCoefsE[k]<-coef(mod.new)[1]
>   TrueCoefsM[k]<-coef(mod.new)[2]
>   print(k) #for tracking
> }
>
>
> #Plot the results
> plot(density(TrueCoefsM), lwd=3, col="red", xlim=c(0, 3.5), ylim=c(0, 
> 4), main="Distribution of Mutual Coefficients from ERGM")
> abline(v=2, lwd=3, lty=2, col="black")
> grid()
> legend("topleft", c("Estimated Coefficients", "Truth"), lwd=c(3,3), 
> lty=c(1,2), col=c("red", "black"))
>
>
> *_End of Code_*
> --------------------------------------------------------------------------
>
>
> In the above code, we simulate a network with a clearly defined 
> reciprocity coefficient, and then run an ERGM on that network that 
> ought to return the coefficient value of 2 (or some number close to 
> 2). We can increase the network's size by changing the "actors" 
> parameter. As the number of actors in the network increases, the 
> difference between the distribution of coefficients and the "truth" 
> grows, even though absolutely nothing else about the simulation is 
> changing. We don't understand why this is happening. I'm sure I'm 
> missing something self-evident, but I've been wracking my brain about 
> why the ERGMs coefficients would decline as the networks size grows, 
> though nothing else in the network DGP is changing. Any clarity would 
> be really helpful.
>
>
> Thanks in advance. Best,
> Justin

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGM unbalanced group size
messages.body_plain:
Hi Vanesse,

Short answer: yes, it is already controlling for group *sizes*.  But it 
is not controlling for possible differences in group *sociality*, which 
one typically wants to do as well.

Long answer: because ERGMs are based on log odds, the group sizes 
implicitly end up in both the numerator and the denominator of all 
terms, and in that sense are controlled for.  So, if you have just a 
nodematch term, the null hypothesis against which the term is comparing 
is *not* that each group receives an equal absolute number of ties from 
each group; rather, each group receives ties in proportion to its group 
size from each group. In that sense, group size is controlled for.  But, 
often, different groups have overall different propensities for ties (in 
directed networks, this can break down into differences in sending 
and/or differences in receiving ties), regardless of who they are 
connecting to.  This is what nodefactor measures.  If you don't include 
nodefactor in your model, then different groups' propensities to have 
different amounts of ties overall will change the number of within-group 
ties away form the null described above, and appear as homophily when it 
really isn't.  So it is generally good to have a nodefactor term in 
there as well to disentangle this possible first-order (node-level) 
effect from the second-order (dyad-level) effect of homophily.

Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Nonedgewise Shared Partners
messages.body_plain:
Hi Zachary-

It's perhaps clearest if you think of the first term (edgewise, 
dyadwise, non-edgewise) in the context of the base unit the distribution 
is summed on.  I.e.

ESP distribution: for each pair of actors who are directly linked, how 
many shared partners do they have?
DSP distribution: for each pair of actors --regardless of whether they 
are linked or not--how many shared partners do they have?
NSP distribution: for each pair of actors who are *not* directly linked, 
how many shared partners do they have?

Thus the NSP distribution must equal the DSP distribution minus the ESP 
distribution.

You might wonder why one would ever use this?  Its uses are indeed rare 
and less easily interpreted relative to the ESP distribution, but it can 
be interesting as a point of comparison to have either the DSP or NSP in 
a model as well.

Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Rglpk package problem
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jacob,

For now the direct solution is to install GLPK, which Rglpk on the Mac 
requires. This is not necessary on Windows. You will need administrator 
privileges on the Mac to do this.

1) Download the latest version of GLPK by pointer your browser to:

ftp://mirrors.kernel.org/gnu/glpk/glpk-4.55.tar.gz

2) Assuming it is downloaded to your "~/Downloads" directory, go there 
and execute the following commands (using the terminal)

cd ~/Downloads
tar -xzf glpk-4.55.tar.gz
cd glpk-4.55
./configure --prefix=/usr/local
make
sudo make install

3) Try to reinstall Rglpk in R.

Good luck!

Mark

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Plotting valued dynamic network?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jeff,

 >
 > This prints all “weight” values on 1->2 in period 1, creating
 > overlapping labels. So how do I show only the highest weight from each
 > period?


First,  in your example, by repeatedly added edges between the same 
tail,head pair of vertices, you are actually creating a multiplex 
network.  I'm not sure if this was your intention, but I don't see an 
easy way to collapse the labels for this case, since you would need to 
look up the 'edge' objects by their endpoints.  If that is what you need 
to do, let me know I'll figure out a way..

But assuming that this was not intended to be a multiplex network, you 
should use 'activate.edges' to add additional activity spells after the 
edge is created (either with add.edge or add.edges.active).

re-writing your example

net<-network.initialize(5)
add.edges.active(net, tail=1, head=2, onset=1, terminus=1.5)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',1,onset=1, terminus=1.5, e=1)
activate.edges(net, e=1, onset=1.5, terminus=1.7)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',2,onset=1.5, terminus=1.7, e=1)
activate.edges(net, e=1, onset=1.7, terminus=4)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',4,onset=1.7, terminus=4, e=1)
activate.edges(net, e=1, onset=4, terminus=5)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',3,onset=4, terminus=5, e=1)
add.edges.active(net, tail=1, head=3, onset=2.1, terminus=2.2)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',1,onset=2.1,terminus=2.2, e=2)
add.edges.active(net, tail=3, head=4, onset=2, terminus=3)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',1,onset=2,terminus=3, e=3)
activate.edges(net, e=3, onset=3, terminus=4)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',2,onset=3,terminus=4, e=3)
add.edges.active(net, tail=5, head=4, onset=3, terminus=5)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',4,onset=3,terminus=5, e=3)

or in a slightly condensed form, do all the edge activation at the same time

net<-network.initialize(5)
add.edges.active(net, tail=1, head=2, onset=c(1,1.5,1.7,4), 
terminus=c(1.5,1.7,4,5))
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',1,onset=1, terminus=1.5, e=1)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',2,onset=1.5, terminus=1.7, e=1)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',4,onset=1.7, terminus=4, e=1)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',3,onset=4, terminus=5, e=1)
add.edges.active(net, tail=1, head=3, onset=2.1, terminus=2.2)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',1,onset=2.1,terminus=2.2, e=2)
add.edges.active(net, tail=3, head=4, onset=c(2,3), terminus=c(3,4))
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',1,onset=2,terminus=3, e=3)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',2,onset=3,terminus=4, e=3)
add.edges.active(net, tail=5, head=4, onset=3, terminus=5)
activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',4,onset=3,terminus=5, e=4)

when set up this way, your plot command will give you a warning 
indicating that it couldn't figure out which value to use

 > plot(network.extract(net,onset=1,terminus=2, 
trim.spells=TRUE),main='at time 1',arrowhead.cex=2, displaylabels=TRUE, 
boxed.labels=TRUE, label.pos=5, 
edge.label=na.omit(get.edge.value.active(net, "weight", 
onset=1,terminus=2)))

Warning message:
In get.edge.value.active(net, "weight", onset = 1, terminus = 2) :
   Multiple attribute values matched query spell for attribute 
weight.active on some edges. Only earliest value used


if you just wanted the earliest or latest value you could avoid the 
warning by specifying a rule:

 > get.edge.value.active(net, "weight", onset=1,terminus=2,rule='latest')
[1]  4 NA NA NA

 > get.edge.value.active(net, "weight"onset=1,terminus=2,rule='earliest')
[1]  1 NA NA NA

you could also do this by using network.collapse instead of network.extract


However, since you want the label with the maximum value, you will have 
to process the TEA attribute directly yourself

get.edge.value.active(net, "weight",onset=1,terminus=2,return.tea = TRUE)

The first element of each TEA attribute is the list of values 
appropriate for the time range (second is spell matrix) so should work 
to set your edge.label equal to

sapply( 
get.edge.value.active(net,"weight",onset=1,terminus=2,return.tea = TRUE),
    function(e){
       max(unlist(e[[1]]))
})

[1]  4 NA NA NA


If you were doing this as part of ndtv animation, you would probably 
want to make use of 'functional' attribute forms so that the values 
would be recalculate for each slice

library(ndtv)

render.animation(net,
           main=function(onset,terminus){paste('at 
time',onset,'-',terminus)},
           arrowhead.cex=2,
           displaylabels=TRUE,
           boxed.labels=FALSE,
           label.pos=5,
           edge.label=function(net,onset,terminus){
 
sapply(get.edge.value.active(net,"weight",onset=onset,terminus=terminus,return.tea 
= TRUE),
                     function(e){
                        max(unlist(e[[1]]))
                     }
             )
           }
)
ani.replay()


let me know if that works!

best,
  -skye

messages.subject: [statnet_help] issues with representing edges weight
messages.body_plain:
Hi Margaux,

It can't cope with NA values. There is a missing value for the dyad 
{B,C}. If you replace it with a non-negative real value, it works fine.

You may also want to use plot instead of gplot when you deal with 
network objects because it makes use of additional information like 
whether the network is directed (and thus omit the arrow heads 
automatically) etc.

Best,
Philip

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Multilevel ergm in Statnet?
messages.body_plain:
This is only possible if PNet has a publicly documented API. At the very 
least, they must declare their classes as public in order for you to use 
them with rJava. PNet, however, does not seem to have classes declared 
as public, at least I can't see any because the source code is not 
available (at least not on http://sna.unimelb.edu.au/PNet). What is 
more, the version needed for fitting multilevel ERGMs, MPNet, is only 
available as an EXE file, and rJava requires a .jar or .class file.

Unless they make their source code available or provide an API, the more 
promising avenue is to write a wrapper for the functions contained in 
the ergm package (e.g., ergm.Cprepare, ergm.design etc., or just ergm) 
that takes multiple dependent networks, combines them in a 
block-diagonal matrix using the bdiag function in the Matrix package (I 
think there are even facilities for fitting block-diagonal models in the 
ergm package), creates a matrix that specifies which dyad belongs to 
which network (as input information for the multi-level model terms) and 
fits an ergm with some new user terms where the user can specify the 
interactions between the "dependent" networks (e.g., a triadic closure 
term with a twopath ijk in one network and the closure ik of that triad 
in the other network; or a GWESP term that returns different counts for 
the different blocks of the matrix). I *think* something like this could 
fully rely on the MCMC code and package infrastructure that is already 
there, so it shouldn't be too big of a project (except for coding the 
statistics). I would do it if I had time.

Another helpful thing would be a dictionary that translates terms 
between statnet, PNet, and SIENA. I hope others will feel encouraged to 
come up with something like this at some point.

Take care,

Philip

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGMs
messages.body_plain:
Assuming the media are a passive node class (they don't create ties, only 
people can do that), this is neither a simple nor a bipartite network. 
Media are one mode with ties only to the other mode, while {students & 
teachers} are the other mode, for which all forms of within mode and 
between mode ties are allowed.  Courses form another "layer".  All in a 
dynamic setting where the evolution of different types of ties give rise 
to emergent positions.

That's a complicated process to model.

Since your events are instantaneous in continous time, you might want to 
look into Carter's relevent package.  ERGMs are designed for 
cross-sectional network analysis, and TERGMs are better suited to 
partnerships that have some kind of duration.

best,
Martina

messages.body_plain:
Dear statnet users,

The statnet team has been working on a web application to serve as a GUI for some of the
functionality?of the statnet packages. We envision that this web app - called statnetWeb -
will be an accessible?introduction to statnet for researchers without experience working in R
and a useful tool for teaching?statistical network analysis.

statnetWeb is written in R-Shiny (http://shiny.rstudio.com/) and the code is hosted on GitHub
(https://github.com/statnet/statnetWeb). We currently incorporate functionality from the
network, sna?and ergm packages so that users can upload network data, look at network plots
and summary statistics,?fit an ergm, assess the fit and simulate from the model.

The app is still in a prototype stage, but it's at a point where we would like feedback from
the community of existing statnet users.

You can run statnetWeb in two ways:
 ?*? Through the shinyapps server, by clicking this link:?https://ebey.shinyapps.io/statnetWeb/
 ?*? On your own machine through RStudio
 ? ? ?+? > install.packages(c("shiny", "shinyBS", "RColorBrewer", "statnet", "lattice",
"latticeExtra"))
 ? ? ?+? > library(shiny)
 ? ? ?+? > runGitHub("statnetWeb", "statnet")


Comments, questions, complaints and suggestions are all welcome. You can submit these through
the?Issues link on our GitHub page (https://github.com/statnet/statnetWeb) or via email.

Best,
Emily Beylerian and Martina Morris
for the statnet development team

Hi Tom,

Here is some code to do it.  Notice that I altered your example so that 
there are only "" (zero length string) not also " " (a single space).


data<-matrix(c("a", "b", "a", "c", "a", "d", "b", "a", "b" , "c", "b", 
"b", "d", "e", "c", "", "d", "a","d", "b", "d", "e", "f", "", "g", 
""),13,2,byrow=TRUE)


Here is a quick and dirty way via a vertex deletion:

data_net2<-as.network(data,directed=FALSE)
data_net2<-delete.vertices(data_net2,which(network.vertex.names(data_net2)==''))
plot(data2_net,displaylabels=TRUE)



Here is a much longer (and perhaps more flexible?) way to do it 
step-by-step with no deletion


#figure unique labels/non-numeric ids for vertices
ids<-unique(as.vector(data))

# remove the blank id and sort
ids<-sort(ids[ids!=''])

# remove the rows in the matrix that have ""
data<-data[data[,2]!="",]

# replace the labels with numeric indices
data[,1]<-match(data[,1],ids)
data[,2]<-match(data[,2],ids)

# initialize the network with the right number of vertices
data_net<-network.initialize(length(ids),directed=FALSE)

# set the vertex names
network.vertex.names(data_net)<-ids

# use the edgelist constructor load edges into the network
data_net<-network.edgelist(data,data_net)

plot(data_net,displaylabels=TRUE)


In your example, "c" wasn't actually an isolate, but id was missing the 
other half of its dyad

best,
  -skye

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ergm: non-integer "receiver" target.stats
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Carlo,

I am not 100% certain whether this is what you want, but it's perfectly
legal to set target.stats to a fractional value, even if it's for
something like edge count or in-tie count. This is because the model is
not about a specific graph but about a *distribution* of graphs, and
specifying that the expected number of in-ties of the node in question
is to be 0.2 is perfectly sensible. Most graphs in that distribution
will give that node 0 in-ties; some will give 1; and a few will give 2
or more, but on average, it will be 0.2.

                        I hope this helps,
                        Pavel

P.S. Depending on your specific model, you might be able to make this
more explicit using the valued ERGM framework. There, you can, in fact,
say that the ties are binomial(n=100), and that the target.stat is 20.
One can also specify a continuous uniform reference measure between 0
and 1, and use a beta-distribution-like model to the same effect.
However, these approaches are not as well understood as binary ERGMs.

On Thu, 2015-04-30 at 10:33 +1000, martina morris wrote:
> Hi Carlo,
> 
> Unfortunately, receiver stats are not "ensembles" -- they are node 
> specific integer counts of ties.  If you combine other nodes into the 
> base, it can function as an ensemble for a target count.  So, if you put 5 
> nodes into the base, and have a target of 1 tie, each node would get your 
> 0.2 ties in expectation.  Alternatively, you might be able to set the coef 
> for this receiver node using an offset to achieve the desired tie 
> probability, but the value may be difficult to find given the correlation 
> with other terms in the model.
> 
> I'm replying to the list here in case someone else has a better idea.
> 
> best,
> mm
>

> 
> > 
> > It would imply that say on 100 sampled graphs from the resulting distribution, roughly 20
> > would have receiver=1 for that node and the remaining would have 0. In principle target.stats
> > should fix the ensemble averages, so even an integer-valued quantity might have non-integer
> > mean value.
> >

messages.subject: [statnet_help] missing value in statnet
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

I have a question about how the missing values were handled in statnet.

I am following this tutorial for modeling ERGM with missing values: 
https://statnet.csde.washington.edu/trac/raw-attachment/wiki/Resources/statnet_polnet2011_modeling_missingness.pdf

The working RData file can be found here:
https://statnet.csde.washington.edu/trac/attachment/wiki/Resources/polnet2011.Rdata 

On page 14 of the above tutorial, the adjacency matrix with three non-responding individuals (outgoing ties are "NA") were modeled. The modeling results are different from those when the "NA"s were set as 0, or the correponding vertices were excluded from the model.

My questions:

In the second paragraph on page 15, it says "By contrast, modeling the missing data allows us to get some sense of the unobserved edges via multiple imputation. We can 
easily accomplish this via simulate, using the constraints=~observedsetting (which forces the underlying MCMC algorithm to simulate only networks for which the non-missing edge variables match their observed values)." Does it mean the multiple imputation is used for handling missing data when running ergm() command? If so, why we "easily accomplish this via simulate"? I mean, what is the relationship between this two moves?

I ran the following code:

ssad.sim<-simulate(ssad.fit,constraints=~observed,nsim=100) # Simulate | observed edges

it shows the same parameter estimates as the following code:

ssad.fit<-ergm(ssad~edges+mutual+nodeicov("Charisma")+nodeicov("Rank")+ 
+ nodeicov("Potency")+nodeocov("Charisma")+nodeocov("Rank")+nodeocov("Potency")+ 
+ nodematch("Bargaining.Unit",diff=TRUE))

Please give me some advice. Thank you very much.

Best regards,



ya

messages.subject: [statnet_help] trouble working with set.edge.attribute()
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jesse,


I believe that the problem in your example is that you are trying to set 
the edge values using the wrong function for the shape of your input 
data.  There are two functions for setting the values edge attributes of 
a network:

set.edge.value()  sets the values from a matrix input , and maps the 
elements of the matrix to the corresponding edges (if they exist)

set.edge.attribute() sets the values from a vector input, where each 
element of the vector is mapped to the edge with the corresponding edge id.

It warned you that something was wrong with the "Inappropriate edge 
value" error.  Looks like you 'fixed' it by c(pp), which effectively 
unwrapped the pp matrix into a long vector to avoid the error ... but 
then the elements no longer match up to the correct edges.

I expect that your code will work if you change to set.edge.value(), but
bellow may be a more efficient way to set up your networks:

# create the valued matrix
mat<-matrix(c(0,5,0,3,0,
               5,0,2,1,0,
               0,2,0,3,3,
               3,1,3,0,4,
               0,0,3,4,0),nrow=5,ncol=5,byrow=TRUE)

# directly create a network from valued matrix,
# storing values as attribute named 'pp'
net<-as.network(mat,ignore.eval = FALSE,names.eval = 'pp')

# check that it worked
as.matrix(net,attrname='pp')
   1 2 3 4 5
1 0 5 0 3 0
2 5 0 2 1 0
3 0 2 0 3 3
4 3 1 3 0 4
5 0 0 3 4 0

# extract subgraph
test <- get.inducedSubgraph(net,v=(get.neighborhood(net,v=2)))

# print valued matrix for subgraph
as.matrix(test,attrname='pp')
   1 3 4
1 0 0 3
3 0 0 3
4 3 3 0

get.edge.attribute(test,"pp")
[1] 3 3 3 3


hope that works!

best,
  -skye

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Multilevel ergm in Statnet?
messages.body_plain:
Michal & Philip - thank you both for the input. My impression was 
similarly that building on existing statnet ergm infrastructure may be 
more promising than a wrapper for MPNet. I was hoping someone might have 
looked into multilevel ergm with statnet -- but perhaps not. I'd take a 
stab at it, but I haven't looked under the hood of the ergm functions 
enough to be confident that I can get this done fast or well.
I also have a vague recollection that someone talked about work in that 
area at the last Sunbelt conference. I may be mistaken though: it might 
have been only about multilevel models in RSiena, and that doesn't help 
with cross-sectional data.

Philip, +1 vote for a term dictionary - the only attempt along those 
lines I've seen was in the Lusher, Koskinen & Robins ERGM book, and I 
don't think it included RSiena.

Best,
Katya

On 4/15/2015 1:46 PM, Philip Leifeld wrote:
> This is only possible if PNet has a publicly documented API. At the very
> least, they must declare their classes as public in order for you to use
> them with rJava. PNet, however, does not seem to have classes declared
> as public, at least I can't see any because the source code is not
> available (at least not on http://sna.unimelb.edu.au/PNet). What is
> more, the version needed for fitting multilevel ERGMs, MPNet, is only
> available as an EXE file, and rJava requires a .jar or .class file.
>
> Unless they make their source code available or provide an API, the more
> promising avenue is to write a wrapper for the functions contained in
> the ergm package (e.g., ergm.Cprepare, ergm.design etc., or just ergm)
> that takes multiple dependent networks, combines them in a
> block-diagonal matrix using the bdiag function in the Matrix package (I
> think there are even facilities for fitting block-diagonal models in the
> ergm package), creates a matrix that specifies which dyad belongs to
> which network (as input information for the multi-level model terms) and
> fits an ergm with some new user terms where the user can specify the
> interactions between the "dependent" networks (e.g., a triadic closure
> term with a twopath ijk in one network and the closure ik of that triad
> in the other network; or a GWESP term that returns different counts for
> the different blocks of the matrix). I *think* something like this could
> fully rely on the MCMC code and package infrastructure that is already
> there, so it shouldn't be too big of a project (except for coding the
> statistics). I would do it if I had time.
>
> Another helpful thing would be a dictionary that translates terms
> between statnet, PNet, and SIENA. I hope others will feel encouraged to
> come up with something like this at some point.
>
> Take care,
>
> Philip
>

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Example of STERGM with edgecov
messages.body_plain:
Dear Jeff,

On Fri, 2015-04-17 at 01:59 +1000, Jeffrey Alan Carnegie wrote: 

> I need to get an example of STREGM using edgecov or dyadcov as terms
> for a directed network outcome. When I run the code below, I am
> getting an error, which Nicole says has to do with NAs in a matrix
> which gets blown up to 36x36 instead of 18x18. She can get it to work
> by increasing the size of the matrix attribute, but I am not sure what
> the other 18 rows and columns mean.


This is a bug in tergm. The "blown up" thing is supposed to happen, as
the current implementation of stergm CMLE works by constructing a pair
of block-diagonal networks with the following sociomatrices:


[y0  0]
[ 0 y1]

[y1  0]
[ 0 y2]


and fitting the transition from the first block-diagonal network to the
second (and thus from y0 to y1 and from y1 to y2). When it combines the
networks in this way, it tries to guess when you have a dyadic
covariate, by looking to see if there are any network attributes that
are matrices of appropriate dimension, and, if so, constructing a
block-diagonal matrix out of them. Unfortunately, I I've put NAs in
place of the structural zeros, forgetting that R's C calling routines
are allergic to those.

We'll fix it in the next release, but, for now, if you can rebuild tergm
from source, you can fix it as follows:

     1. In tergm source's R directory, open combine.networks.R.
     2. Find the line containing "m <- matrix(NA, sum(ns), sum(ns))". It
        should be Line 42, or close.
     3. In that line, replace "NA" with "0", save, rebuild, and
        reinstall.


Note that this workaround may fail if you have a non-numeric covariate
matrix. If you can't rebuild, I can try to send a patched build to you
in the next day or two.

                            Best,
                            Pavel

P.S. The reason Nicole's trick works is that if the attribute matrix is
no longer n*n, the code that tries to detect dyadic covariates no longer
treats it as such and leaves it alone.

--

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Comparing coefficients in same model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Julija,

I don't know if such a comprehensive approach is actually needed in your 
case, but Desmarais and Cranmer proposed a unified approach to the 
micro-level interpretation of ERGMs at the tie-, dyad- and block level:

Desmarais, Bruce A. and Skyler J. Cranmer (2012): Micro-Level 
Interpretation of Exponential Random Graph Models with Application to 
Estuary Networks. The Policy Studies Journal 40(3): 402-434.

With this approach, you can also answer more complicated questions, such as:
- What is the probability of a tie between nodes i and j if j has three 
other incoming ties (given the rest of the network and the model)?
- How much more (or less) likely is a tie in a dyad when a specific 
coefficient is set to zero?
- How likely is an edge from i to j if the reciprocal edge (ji) exists 
(vs. does not exist)?
- What is the probability that i is tied to j but not to k and l?
etc.

These questions can be answered for specific nodes or dyads (using the 
node index or the vertex name), but one can also use sampling to 
generalize this to all nodes or dyads or specific subsets of them.

If you have dichotomous covariates, you could, for example, sample among 
dyads where one covariate exclusively holds, then sample again from 
dyads where the other covariate exclusively holds, then do the same 
thing again for dyads where both covariates hold, and compare the tie 
probabilities of those groups and compute confidence intervals for each 
of them. Or you could compute the tie probabilities for each level of an 
ordinal covariate and look at the shape of the association, and compare 
this for several covariates.

While their paper comes with some companion R code, the code is a little 
buggy and outdated. Meanwhile, I have rewritten their original code and 
included it in the xergm package as a function called "interpret". The 
help page for that function contains some examples on micro-level 
interpretation. Note that the xergm package is not part of the statnet 
suite of packages; it just provides some support functions for the ergm 
package and other extensions.

Best,
Philip

> Short answer: yes, it is already controlling for group *sizes*.  But it is
> not controlling for possible differences in group *sociality*, which one
> typically wants to do as well.
>
> Long answer: because ERGMs are based on log odds, the group sizes
> implicitly end up in both the numerator and the denominator of all terms,
> and in that sense are controlled for.  So, if you have just a nodematch
> term, the null hypothesis against which the term is comparing is *not* that
> each group receives an equal absolute number of ties from each group;
> rather, each group receives ties in proportion to its group size from each
> group. In that sense, group size is controlled for.  But, often, different
> groups have overall different propensities for ties (in directed networks,
> this can break down into differences in sending and/or differences in
> receiving ties), regardless of who they are connecting to.  This is what
> nodefactor measures.  If you don't include nodefactor in your model, then
> different groups' propensities to have different amounts of ties overall
> will change the number of within-group ties away form the null described
> above, and appear as homophily when it really isn't.  So it is generally
> good to have a nodefactor term in there as well to disentangle this
> possible first-order (node-level) effect from the second-order (dyad-level)
> effect of homophily.
>
> Steve
>
>
>
>
> On 3/4/2015 12:17 AM, vanesse labeyrie wrote:
>
>    Hi all,
>
>  I am testing the homophily effect using ERGM (plus other structural
> effects) but the groups present unbalanced sizes.
>
>  I thought that specifying my model as following, with only the
> nodematch  term, accounted for unbalanced group size:
>
> ergm(net.E.G.undir~edges+ nodematch("dialect",diff=F) + gwdegree
> (0.1,fixed=T) + gwdsp (0.1,fixed=T)+gwesp(0.1,fixed=T))
>
>
>  But a previous message on statnet help raised this issue, suggesting that
> we shall add a nodefactor term to control for unbalanced group sizes.
>
>  So is it necessary to add a nodefactor term to control fro different
> group sizes or is nodematch already controlling for this effect ?
>
> ergm(net.E.G.undir~edges+ nodematch("dialect",diff=F) +
> nodefactor("dialect")+
>  gwdegree (0.1,fixed=T) + gwdsp (0.1,fixed=T)+gwesp(0.1,fixed=T))
>
>
>  Many thanks for you answer
>
>  Sincerly,
>
>  Vanesse Labeyrie
>  post-doctoral fellow at CIRAD, France

messages.subject: [statnet_help] visualization assistance
messages.body_plain:
Hi jimi,

On 05/28/2015 10:34 AM, jimi adams wrote:
> Hi all,
> I have a data set I???ve been working with that was from a teaching
> example, and I???m trying to get a dynamic visualization of it
> configured. The basics are working, but I am trying to figure out if a
> few tweaks are possible, and I haven???t come up with anything yet, so
> any help on these would be much appreciated.
>
> 1 - As far as I can tell, tie directionality is fixed across the entire
> visualization. Is that so? I have 5 tie types (encoded as weights) some
> of which are directed, some of which are not. I???d like to allow the
> directionality to vary according to the type being visualized.

Yes, tie directionality is fixed.  However, for the purposes of 
rendering you can turn on and off the arrow based on edge type.  You 
could do this with some logic in the plot command

test<-network.initialize(3)
test[1,2]<-1
test[1,3]<-1
set.edge.attribute(test,'type',c('A','B'))
plot(test, arrowhead.cex = ifelse(test%e%'type'=='A',0,1),)

or perhaps by pre-caching an attribute for each edge to indicate if it 
should be drawn.

> 2 - I???m not figuring out how to change node color based on edge
> patterns (e.g., can someone pass something to / contract something from
> others dynamically, or should I code that outside of the visualization)?

You could probably encode some sort of edge pattern logic into plot 
commands (i.e. show vertices with degree > 2 in red) but if you have 
some sort of transmission process in mind, you will probably need to run 
a simulation ahead of time, cache a status variable on the vertices, and 
then plot that.  Have you seen the EpiModel package?  It may have a 
model that does what you want right out of the box.

best,
  -skye

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGMs
messages.body_plain:
That would be a standard ERGM.

ERGMs are generally used to represent the patterns of tie prevalence. 
TERGMS explicitly represent the process of tie formation and dissolution 
-- and the type of TERGM we have in statnet is a "separable" TERGM that 
uses an ERGM for each component.

Search for Pavel Krivitsky's papers -- they present the theory and 
methods.

hth,
mm

messages.body_plain:
Network Modeling for Epidemics
Summer short course at the University of Washington Aug 24-28, 2015

Network Modeling for Epidemics (NME) is a 5-day short course at the
University of Washington that provides an introduction to stochastic
network models for infectious disease transmission dynamics, with a focus
on empirically based modeling of HIV transmission.  It is a ?hands-on?
course, with the EpiModel software package (www.epimodel.org) that uses the
Statnet software suite in R, providing a unified framework for modeling
networks and epidemics.  Epimodel has a flexible open-source platform for
learning and building models. Resources include web-based tools, built-in
generic models that provide basic control over networks, pathogen
properties and demographics, and templates for user-programmed modules that
allow EpiModel to be extended to the full range of pathogens, hosts, and
disease dynamics.

The course uses mornings for lectures, and afternoons for labs with
students working in small groups.  On the final day, students have the
option of developing an EpiModel prototype for their own research projects,
with input from the instructors, which includes the lead EpiModel software
developer, Dr. Samuel Jenness.

Dates and location:
The course will be taught August 24-28 on the University of Washington
campus in Seattle.
Application dates and decision dates:
? April 15: Fellowship application deadline. Decisions will be made by
April 30.
? June 1:  General application deadline.  Applications will continue to be
accepted on a rolling basis until this date.  Decisions will be made by June
15.

Costs:
Course fee is $250. Travel and accommodation are the responsibility of the
participant, although discounted hotel rates are available, as are a
limited number of fellowships for pre-doctoral students or for attendees
from outside the US/Canada.

Application:
Apply online at https://catalyst.uw.edu/webq/survey/morrism/261658

Course website and more information:
http://bit.ly/NetworkEpi
http://epimodel.org

Returning students: For the first time this year, we encourage previous
attendees with active modeling projects to apply to return for a refresher
course. The EpiModel package has been significantly enhanced over the last
two years. Returning students with active projects will have the
opportunity to work closely with course instructors to address key
challenges in the design of their network model code.

Please free to share widely!

Yours,
Martina Morris, Steve Goodreau and Samuel Jenness

*--*
*Samuel M. Jenness, PhD MPH*
Postdoctoral Research Associate
Center for Studies in Demography & Ecology
University of Washington
917-414-6566 / sjenness@uw.edu

messages.body_plain:
Shupin,

I'm not sure that has been established for ergms yet.

In this case I would recommend using something like the rule of thumb for 
loglinear models, since you are fitting something similar to a multi-way 
table (at least 5 observations per cell) or the rule of thumb for logistic 
regressions (at least 10 "events" per predictor).  There's a good paper 
by Vittinghoff and McCullough on the latter here:
http://aje.oxfordjournals.org/content/165/6/710.full

The dependence across observations in network data make these rules of 
thumb for GLMs not directly comparable.

Perhaps someone else on the list has a better suggestion?

best,
mm

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Doubt with MCMC.diagnostics()
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Vanesse -

On 03/29/2015 08:03 AM, vanesse labeyrie wrote:
> Following these interesting precision, I have some additionnal questions concerning mcmc.diagnostics as I am concerned by the fairly subjective assessment of what is "reasonable"

Like virtually any statistical analysis conducted in a real world 
setting, expert judgment is an inescapable part of the ERGM model 
building, assessment, and interpretation process; anyone who tells you 
otherwise is trying to sell you something.  Just as there is no 
universally applicable rule for determining when the residuals in a 
regression are sufficiently well-behaved to permit the model to be 
trusted,* there is no simple and universal criterion for determining 
whether an ERGM MCMC is good enough for the model to be used - too much 
depends on the details of the situation, and the use to which the model 
will be put.  There are, however, a number of very effective heuristics 
that can and generally should be employed to assess convergence, fit, 
and adequacy.  As with other forms of statistical modeling, learning to 
use these heuristics effectively requires practice, and the component of 
expert judgment cannot be eliminated.

(*And, in any event, the residuals alone do not guarantee that the model 
has the properties that you want.)

> 1.could you precise what du you mean by "*autocorrelation diagnostics should show reasonably small correlations at reasonable lags*" ? what is a typical "small correlation" value ? (1 is not and 0 is, but in between ?)  and a reasonable lag ?
> as a non-expert it is difficult to know what is reasonable and what is not. I put one of my mcmc.diagnostics outputs at the end of the post as an example
>

The generality of my statement was not accidental: to determine whether 
your level of autocorrelation is problematic, you need to know something 
about the nature of the model, the sample size, etc. To learn more, I 
suggest taking a look at a good text on MCMC (I like the now old volume 
_Markov Chain Monte Carlo in Practice_, although there are many others) 
and looking at some of the results relating to autocorrelation, 
convergence, and effective sample size.  In the diagnostics returned by 
ergm(), you are going to want to assess whether your Markov chain's 
autocorrelation is reducing the effective sample size to the point where 
problems are arising. (This should happen less and less, because more 
and more automated checks for these sorts of issues are being 
implemented in ergm().) If you examine the detailed diagnostics, you 
should see for each statistic a "naive standard error" estimate and a 
"time series standard error" estimate - the former is based on an 
independent sample approximation, and the latter is corrected for serial 
autocorrelation.  To the extent that the latter is larger than the 
former, then serial autocorrelation in your sample (associated with e.g. 
slow mixing) is reducing the precision of calculations based on it.  (Of 
course, if both SEs are tiny, then this may be of no consequence: you 
need to compare them to the scale of reasonable variation in the 
associated statistic!  This is something that requires substantive 
knowledge, although the simulated standard deviation and the magnitude 
of the mean itself also provide useful clues.)   As far as the magnitude 
of the autocorrelation itself, you want it to be close to zero within a 
number of iterations that is small compared to your sample size.  There 
is no fixed value that is universally "small enough," but you can get a 
good sense of the impact of the degree of autocorrelation by studying 
the widely used "effective sample size" estimate of Neal: M = 
n/(1+2*sum_{k=1}^\infty rho_k), where M is the ESS, n is the total 
number of draws, and rho_k is the autocorrelation function at lag k.  If 
rho_k<<1 for k greater than some k', then M is going to be reduced (from 
n) by a factor of at most approximately 1+2*k'.  If n is big enough, you 
can tolerate a _lot_ of autocorrelation - but you are going to pay for 
it by having to run a very long Markov chain.  Likewise, the extent that 
you need a large ESS depends on how hard your model is to fit (which 
depends, among other things, on the roughness of exp(theta t(Y)) and the 
sharpness of the derivatives of the log normalizing factor in theta), 
and on how precise you need your estimates to be (which can depend e.g. 
on whether you are just trying to infer the signs of the elements of 
theta versus trying to simulate draws from a fitted model).  These 
tradeoffs are application-specific, and can in some cases require one to 
study one's problem at considerable length.

To turn to the case you showed, it looks to me like you have enough 
autocorrelation that its effects are noticeable (e.g., in the corrected 
SEs of the mean stats).  OTOH, the time series SEs are still a few 
orders of magnitude smaller than the variation around the mean stats, so 
this may not be a problem; given that your trace plots are OK in that 
specific respect, I wouldn't worry about it. I'm more concerned about 
the fact that the trace plots suggest that your mean stats 
systematically depart from the observed values. That and the Geweke 
diagnostic suggest that you haven't burned the model in sufficiently - 
given how slowly it's mixing, you might need a lot more iterations, or 
else you might need to inspect the model and see if one of the terms 
(e.g., one of the curved terms) is poorly calibrated.  (Using gwesp and 
gdsp in the same model can also cause problems.)  However, a better way 
to assess whether the mean stats have really converged is to simulate 
draws from the fitted model, and examine them in that context.  (You are 
really looking at the model that was one iteration removed from the 
final fitted model.)  If the mean model statistics from the fitted model 
closely match the target statistics, then absent other problems I would 
not be inclined to worry overmuch about the above.  If, OTOH, you see 
the same problems in the new simulation, then you probably need to 
return to the fitting process.

> 2.  when saying that "t*he mean values of the sufficient statistics are reasonably close to the target values*" this is also fairly subjective - For instance, what shall I conclude from my example mcmcm.diagnostics output plots attached to this post ?
> For instance, the gwdegree is the term which shows the most important departure from observed, but when assessing GOF, the plots and p-values are not bad (see attached file gof).
> Tutorial moslty provide fairly extreme examples of non-convergence, but I find it difficult to asses convergence quality when situations are less contrasted.
>

See above.  What constitutes "close enough" in an ambiguous case is 
going to depend on how bad the model's problems seem to be, whether 
those problems seem to impact the features about which you care, and the 
level of precision you need in your answer.  While there are cases that 
are obviously and pretty universally pathological, and cases that are 
obviously and near-universally well-behaved, many real-world models lie 
somewhere between.  In those cases, there is no escaping the exercise of 
judgment, informed by knowledge of the system under study and the 
problem one is trying to solve.  That doesn't mean that "anything goes" 
- decisions made during the modeling process should be defensible, and 
guided by principle - but there is unlikely to be a single, uniform 
protocol that one can automatically follow and that solves all problems.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

>     Hi, Fabiola -
>
>     On 03/27/2015 11:31 PM, Fabiola martinoli wrote:
>>     Dear Statnet's users and developers,
>>     i'm very new in ERGMs and i'm studying a network of 200 nodes for
>>     my master's degree thesis. I have two questions for you:
>>
>>     1. How can i assess that my model converges properly? I mean,
>>     after i receive my coefficients from the ergm() function, i check
>>     it with mcmc.diagnostics(): the only important thing is that the
>>     MCMC sample statistic are varying randomly around the observed
>>     values at each step and that the difference between the observed
>>     and simulated values have a roughly bell-shaped distribution
>>     centered in 0? Or should i also check the individual p-values
>>     given at the end of the diagnostics?
>>     If so, what is the lower bound tha makes my p-value acceptable?
>>     I read a lot of papers and tutorial but i haven't found a clear
>>     answer to my doubt.
>>
>     As a practical matter, you want to verify that (1) the Markov
>     chain is mixing well (e.g., you are covering the region of high
>     probability with respect to each model statistic, the chain is not
>     strongly autocorrelated, and the chain shows no signs of being
>     "stuck" for long periods in a single state); (2) the mean of the
>     sufficient statistics for the retained draws is close to their
>     observed values; and (relatedly) (3) the Markov chain appears to
>     be stationary (e.g., the first and second moments show no signs of
>     "wandering"). The various diagnostics can assist with this
>     process, although they can be over-interpreted.  (For instance, it
>     is possible to obtain a perfectly reasonable parameter estimate
>     from a sample that shows a significant departure of the simulated
>     mean from (say) one of the observed statistics, and one can
>     likewise obtain good results from a chain that is reasonably
>     autocorrelated.  These are not good signs, however, and in
>     practice one should work to minimize them.)
>
>     My own _practical_ advice for a typical case would be as follows:
>       1. Verify that the first moment of the Markov chain has
>     converged - the running mean line should be flat. If there is
>     evidence of a trend, either (1) the model is degenerate, and
>     trying to head off to la-la land, or (2) you need to increase your
>     burn-in time.
>       2. Verify that the chain is mixing well.  You should see
>     relatively smooth marginal distributions, there should be little
>     visual evidence of strong autocorrelation in the trace plot, and
>     autocorrelation diagnostics should show reasonably small
>     correlations at reasonable lags.  If the chain isn't mixing well,
>     either (1) your model is showing signs of being poorly behaved, or
>     (2) you need to increase the thinning interval.
>       3. Verify that the mean values of the sufficient statistics are
>     reasonably close to the target values. (Note that they may be a
>     bit off, because if how the fitting algorithm works - we will
>     provide a better test below.)  Ideally, the means will be within a
>     standard deviation or so of the observed or target values.  If the
>     means seem to be way off, this usually indicates insufficient
>     burn-in and/or thinning length, but it can also result from a
>     highly recalcitrant model with which the estimation algorithm
>     cannot easily deal.
>       4. Having done all of the above, produce a new, high-quality
>     simulation from the fitted model (using simulate() or gof()). 
>     Verify (1)-(3) on the new sample; but this time, pay closer
>     attention to (3).  For a reasonable sample size (say, 250), I
>     would usually be concerned if my mean statistics were
>     significantly different from their target values (with the usual
>     caveats about multiple testing and such).
>       5. If your model clears all of the above, the fitting process
>     itself has probably been successful.  You will still want to
>     perform model adequacy checking and such, as described in the
>     various available tutorials.
>
>     Again, these are heuristics, and one can identify exceptions
>     and/or more specific directives for special cases.  But they
>     should provide you with a good place to start.
>
>>     2. I'm interested in studying a brokerage effect due to a nodal
>>     attribute, is there any effect able to test it? I looked for it
>>     but i can't find nothing.
>>
>
>     This (and related!) problems are addressed in a forthcoming JSS paper:
>
>     Yaveroglu, Omer Nebil; Fitzhugh, Sean M.; Kurant, Maciej;
>     Markopoulou, Athina; Butts, Carter T.; and Przulj, Natasa.
>     (2015).  ``ergm.graphlets: A Package for ERG Modeling Based on
>     Graphlet Statistics.''  Journal of Statistical Software, forthcoming.
>
>     Unfortunately, it's been held up in the JSS editorial queue for
>     months and months.  However, you can find a pre-print on arXiv:
>     http://arxiv.org/abs/1405.7348. Likewise, the package needed to
>     add the associated statistics to ergm is on CRAN:
>     http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ergm.graphlets/index.html.
>     Once you load the ergm.graphlets package, you can use the
>     associated terms within ergm just as you would any other model
>     terms.  (See the paper for examples.)
>
>     Hope that helps,
>
>     -Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] degrees of separation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Vicki,

I think you are talking about two-paths, three-paths, and four-paths, 
right? Just to make sure we are talking about the same thing because a 
dyad and triad can usually be any permutation of edge configurations 
including two or three nodes, respectively.

In that case, you could apply a threshold value to the reachability 
matrix to retain only indirect paths of a certain length, sample dyads 
from the non-null entries of this matrix, and compute your test based on 
the two nodes' attributes.

You can compute the reachability matrix by using the "reachability" 
function from the sna package.

Best,
Philip

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ergm: non-integer "receiver" target.stats
messages.body_plain:
Hi Carlo,

Unfortunately, receiver stats are not "ensembles" -- they are node 
specific integer counts of ties.  If you combine other nodes into the 
base, it can function as an ensemble for a target count.  So, if you put 5 
nodes into the base, and have a target of 1 tie, each node would get your 
0.2 ties in expectation.  Alternatively, you might be able to set the coef 
for this receiver node using an offset to achieve the desired tie 
probability, but the value may be difficult to find given the correlation 
with other terms in the model.

I'm replying to the list here in case someone else has a better idea.

best,
mm

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ergm for weighted graphs
messages.body_plain:
Dear Giulia,

> I have a weighted network which is made of countries and the drug
> exchanges (estimated quantity) among them, and I would like to use an
> ergm to analyse it. I see from the workshop materials of the 2014
> Sunbelt that ergms for valued ties has been added in the list of
> additional functionalities. I have two questions about this:
> - Is there an updated tutorial on ergms for weighted graphs? (Or
> should I refer to the 2013 Sunbelt tutorial on valued networks? And,
> if so, is there any update since then?)

There is no updated tutorial, though we are planning to update it for
the 2016 Sunbelt. The 2013 tutorial is still valid, I think.

> - Do I need discrete data in my weighted network to run the ergm?

The ERGM terms designed for counts should also work reasonably well for
positive continuous measurements like what you have.

You can specify a continuous reference distribution by setting
reference=~Unif(a,b) where a and b are the minimum and the maximum
values or using reference=~StdNorm (with terms to model mean and
standard deviation --- let me know if you want more details), but
formulation and interpretation of these models has not yet been
explored.

In particular, if, in your data, there are 0s that are not just there
because the data are not available (missing), then the two references
above might not be appropriate. This is subject for ongoing work, but as
a stopgap, it might be appropriate to model such data conditionally: set
0s to NAs and fit a valued model using Unif or StdNorm, then fit a
binary ERGM for whether the value is 0 vs. nonzero (coded as 1).

I can't be more helpful,

data<-matrix(c("a", "b", "a", "c", "a", "d", "b", "a", "b" , "c", "b",

data_net2<-as.network(data,directed=FALSE)

plot(data2_net,displaylabels=TRUE)



Here is a much longer (and perhaps more flexible?) way to do it 
step-by-step with no deletion


#figure unique labels/non-numeric ids for vertices
ids<-unique(as.vector(data))

# remove the blank id and sort
ids<-sort(ids[ids!=''])

# remove the rows in the matrix that have ""
data<-data[data[,2]!="",]

# replace the labels with numeric indices
data[,1]<-match(data[,1],ids)
data[,2]<-match(data[,2],ids)

# initialize the network with the right number of vertices
data_net<-network.initialize(length(ids),directed=FALSE)

# set the vertex names
network.vertex.names(data_net)<-ids

# use the edgelist constructor load edges into the network
data_net<-network.edgelist(data,data_net)

plot(data_net,displaylabels=TRUE)


In your example, "c" wasn't actually an isolate, but id was missing the 
other half of its dyad

best,

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Simulating for ERGMs (fwd)
messages.body_plain:
>From Li Wang:

Carter is right about the burn-in not being enough. Simply upping the
MCMC.burnin of simulate to 100000 solves the problem.

But, it's also worth noting the relationship between network density and 
the edge coefficient. By using an edge coefficient of 0.1, you are trying 
to simulate networks that are over 50% full from the edges term alone, and 
around 80% full after adding the mutual coef of 2. The initial network 
you use has density of 0.2; that's why such a long burn-in is necessary 
(to get to density 0.8).  So, this suggests other changes.

I've simplified and recoded your example to target a network with
density 0.1 (edge coef = -2.197) instead. The estimates match the true
value well.


#load libraries
library(statnet)

#set seed
set.seed(1234)

#set parameters
initial.density<-0.2

#This sets the actor size of the network
actors<-50

#Number of simulations
sims<-100

#These are our model parameters that we hope ERGM will recover; a
# note that the first one is a density, not an ERGM coefficient
update.density<-0.1
update.mutual<-2

#Create a place to store things
TrueCoefsE<-numeric(sims) #Store edges coefficients
TrueCoefsM<-numeric(sims) #Store mutual coefficients

for(k in 1:sims){
   #Initialize network with the right density
   Net <- network.initialize(actors, directed=T)
   Net <- san(Net ~ edges, target.stats=(actors^2-actors)*initial.density)

   # the edge coefficient is logit of density, if there are no other
terms involved
   edge.coef <- log(update.density/(1-update.density))
   coefs.new<-c(edge.coef, update.mutual)

   #simulate new network with known coefficients; this SHOULD create a
network in which the ERGM would report a mutual coefficient of 2/
   sim.new<-simulate(Net~edges+mutual, coef=coefs.new,
control=control.simulate(MCMC.burnin=100000))

   #estimate ergm on new network with known coefficients
   summary(mod.new<-ergm(sim.new~edges+mutual,
control=control.ergm(MCMC.samplesize=2^11, MCMLE.maxit=100,
MCMC.burnin=50000, MCMC.interval=2^11, drop=TRUE)))

   #Store Coefficients
   TrueCoefsE[k]<-coef(mod.new)[1]
   TrueCoefsM[k]<-coef(mod.new)[2]
   print(k) #for tracking
}

#Plot the results
plot(density(TrueCoefsM), lwd=3, col="red", xlim=c(0, 3.5), ylim=c(0,
4), main="Distribution of Mutual Coefficients from ERGM")
abline(v=2, lwd=3, lty=2, col="black")
grid()
legend("topleft", c("Estimated Coefficients", "Truth"), lwd=c(3,3),
lty=c(1,2), col=c("red", "black"))

>
> Thus far, I have been using the ???simulate.ergm??  command from statnet to

> simulate.ergm help file suggests that the command is used to ???draw from
> exponential family random network models,??  and allows a user to set
> coefficient values using a ???coef??  vector. So if I create a network with

> ???mutual??  coefficient for simulate to a value of 2, and then run an ERGM

> this process works exactly as we thought, but as the network size increases
> (to say 75 or 100 actors), the simulate command no longer produces networks

> central to our statistical experiments, we were hoping someone might be able

> producing networks in which the ERGM coefficients are what we would expect,
> particularly as our network sizes get larger. Below I???ve posted some

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Network size limitations of ntelm and netlogit
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Network size limitations of ntelm and netlogit
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Mahmood -

At present, those functions make heavy use of adjacency representations 
for the underlying data, and hence do not scale to graphs with more than 
~40,000 or so nodes (give or take) - getting around this limit would 
require a very different implementation. (Generating sufficiently high 
quality random permutation vectors might also become a problem as N 
becomes large, since this is a known challenge for pseudorandom number 
generators.  However, I am not aware of anyone who has closely examined 
the issue in this context, so the impact on real-world performance is 
hard to assess.)  A sparse-data MRQAP implementation for very large 
graphs could certainly be written, but to make it practical one would 
need to use an ergm-like term system to calculate covariate values on 
the fly (since you don't want to store all N^2 values) and whatnot.  
Doable, but I don't know if anyone has done it.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

A couple weeks back there was some discussion on the list about how to 
interpret gw term components.  I mentioned I had a worksheet that I'd used 
to get some intuition about the function of the decay parameter (called 
"decay" for gwdegree and "alpha" for gw*sp), and some of you indicated an 
interest in seeing it.

So I've placed it up on the statnet wiki, on the Resources page:

https://statnet.csde.washington.edu/trac/attachment/wiki/Resources/GWDegree.xlsx

It works through how the decay influences the change statistic for the 
gwdegree term.  The gw*sp terms have similar responses to their decay 
parameter, but are a bit harder to explore in a simple sheet like this.

best,
Martina

messages.subject: [statnet_help] uniform homophily?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ya,

Yes, the statistic that one is examining with nodematch(attrname, 
diff=F) is indeed uniform homophily.  We will make sure to make the 
documentation more explicit on this point.

Yours,
Steve

> analyses interpreted sometimes as "homophily", sometime as "uniform 
> homophily" or "differential homophily". I know that when diff=T, it is 
> testing differential homophily; but when diff=F, is it testing uniform 
> homophily or some other kind of homophily?

> keep=NULL)|(binary), |nodematch(attrname, diff=FALSE, keep=NULL,

> network statistic to the model, which counts the number of edges 
> /(i,j)/for which |attrname(i)==attrname(j)|."

(0.1,fixed=T) + gwdsp (0.1,fixed=T)+gwesp(0.1,fixed=T))

we shall add a nodefactor term to control for unbalanced group sizes.

So is it necessary to add a nodefactor term to control fro different group
sizes or is nodematch already controlling for this effect ?

ergm(net.E.G.undir~edges+ nodematch("dialect",diff=F) +
nodefactor("dialect")+
 gwdegree (0.1,fixed=T) + gwdsp (0.1,fixed=T)+gwesp(0.1,fixed=T))

Sincerly,

Vanesse Labeyrie

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Degree assortativity parameter
messages.body_plain:
Hi Alex,
I think the ergm term "degcor" may be what you're looking for.  So if 
you just want to calculate it for an observed network (not conduct 
inference about it), the syntax would be:

summary(mynetwork~degcor)

You can see more info at help("ergm-terms") and scrolling down to degcor.

HTH,
Steve

From: Carter T. Butts
Date: 2014-11-27 23:13
To: statnet_help
Subject: Re: [statnet_help] missing value in statnet
Hi, Ya -

There is no uniform default way of handling missing data in networks - the applicable methods are necessarily technique and situation specific.  In the context of the ergm() function per se, the default is to use the latent missing data approach of Gile and Handcock; this marginalizes across the possible values of the missing edge variables, under the assumption that they and the observed edge variables were drawn from the same model (and that the pattern of missingness is ignorable).  Performing simulation from a model fit using this strategy, conditional on the observed data, can be used as a multiple imputation technique (e.g., for subsequent exploratory data analysis) and/or to get a sense of how well the model and observed data constrain the edge variables that were not observed.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Simulating for ERGMs
messages.body_plain:
Dear StatNet Listserv,

As both an exercise for my students, and for my own education, I?ve been conducting some Monte Carlo experiments/simulations on the ERGM in order to ascertain how robust inferences from the ERGM are to a variety of simple specification and measurement issues. For example, one example might be trying to discover how severe coefficient biases are in the face of mounting data missingness. Such a simulation exercise requires that 1) I be able to replicate the data-generating process implied by ERGMs to create a network in which I know the relevant relationships perfectly, 2) be able to create some set of problems in said network, and then 3) estimate coefficients from an ERGM both on a true network and a network with some sort of problem to gauge the difference between those estimates.

Thus far, I have been using the ?simulate.ergm? command from statnet to create networks in which I can control coefficients perfectly. The simulate.ergm help file suggests that the command is used to ?draw from exponential family random network models,? and allows a user to set coefficient values using a ?coef? vector. So if I create a network with high levels of reciprocity using the simulate command by setting the ?mutual? coefficient for simulate to a value of 2, and then run an ERGM on the created network with a mutual term as a covariate, the coefficient on the mutual term should return a value of 2 (in expectation).

What I and my team are finding is that when networks are small (25 actors) this process works exactly as we thought, but as the network size increases (to say 75 or 100 actors), the simulate command no longer produces networks whose ERGM coefficients match what we think they should. In the above example, if we use simulate to create a network and set the mutual coefficient to 2 in the simulate command, then run an ERGM on that network, the estimated ERGM will report a mutual coefficient of 2 when the network is small, but as the network size increases, the estimated ERGM will report increasingly small coefficients even before we?ve introduced any sort of problems.

Since our ability to control the data generating process of the ERGM is central to our statistical experiments, we were hoping someone might be able to shed light on why the simulate.ergm command isn?t consistently producing networks in which the ERGM coefficients are what we would expect, particularly as our network sizes get larger. Below I?ve posted some sample R-code for how we?ve been running things along with some heavy commenting to illustrate what we?re trying to do, and I?m happy to chat off list if that?s easier for folks. Thanks in advance for any help anyone can provide.

-----------------------------------------------------------
EXAMPLE CODE:

#Clear Memory
rm(list=ls())

#load libraries
library(statnet)

#set seed
set.seed(1234)

#set parameters
initial.density<-0.2

#This sets the actor size of the network; increase this number and bad things happen
actors<-50

#Number of simulations
sims<-100

#These are our model parameters that we hope ERGM will recover; as our sample size gets larger, the ERGM coefficients are further
#and further from these parameters, even across thousands of simulations
update.density<-0.1
update.mutual<-2

#Create a place to store things
TrueCoefsE<-numeric(sims) #Store edges coefficients
TrueCoefsM<-numeric(sims) #Store mutual coefficients

for(k in 1:sims){

  #Draw a blank matrix
  Net<-matrix(0, actors, actors)

  #Fill in a blank adjacency matrix using the initial density parameter; this is largely just a set up to the actual network development
  for(i in 1:nrow(Net)){
    for(j in 1:nrow(Net)){
      Net[i,j]<-rbinom(1,1,initial.density)
    }
  }
  diag(Net)<-0

  #Turn into network object
  Net2<-network(Net, directed=TRUE)

  #Simulate intial ergm to get manipulable object; we?re going to use this model to control the DGP of the ERGM (hopefully)
  summary(mod.ini<-ergm(Net2~edges+mutual, control=control.ergm(MCMC.samplesize=5000, MCMLE.maxit=100, MCMC.burnin=10000, MCMC.interval=1000, drop=TRUE)))

  #Alter to coefficients to make into values you control; this is where we specify exactly what we want the coefficients from the ERGM to be
  coefs.ini<-coef(mod.ini)
  coefs.new<-coefs.ini
  coefs.new[1]<-update.density
  coefs.new[2]<-update.mutual

  #simulate new network with known coefficients; this SHOULD create a network in which the ERGM would report a mutual coefficient of 2/
  sim.new<-network(simulate(mod.ini, coef=coefs.new))

  #estimate ergm on new network with known coefficients
  summary(mod.new<-ergm(sim.new~edges+mutual, control=control.ergm(MCMC.samplesize=5000, MCMLE.maxit=100, MCMC.burnin=10000, MCMC.interval=1000, drop=TRUE)))

  #Store Coefficients
  TrueCoefsE[k]<-coef(mod.new)[1]
  TrueCoefsM[k]<-coef(mod.new)[2]
  print(k) #for tracking
}


#Plot the results
plot(density(TrueCoefsM), lwd=3, col="red", xlim=c(0, 3.5), ylim=c(0, 4), main="Distribution of Mutual Coefficients from ERGM")
abline(v=2, lwd=3, lty=2, col="black")
grid()
legend("topleft", c("Estimated Coefficients", "Truth"), lwd=c(3,3), lty=c(1,2), col=c("red", "black"))


End of Code
--------------------------------------------------------------------------


In the above code, we simulate a network with a clearly defined reciprocity coefficient, and then run an ERGM on that network that ought to return the coefficient value of 2 (or some number close to 2). We can increase the network?s size by changing the ?actors? parameter. As the number of actors in the network increases, the difference between the distribution of coefficients and the "truth? grows, even though absolutely nothing else about the simulation is changing. We don?t understand why this is happening. I?m sure I?m missing something self-evident, but I?ve been wracking my brain about why the ERGMs coefficients would decline as the networks size grows, though nothing else in the network DGP is changing. Any clarity would be really helpful.


Thanks in advance. Best,
Justin

Justin H. Kirkland
Assistant Professor
Department of Political Science
University of Houston
www.jhkirkla.wordpress.com<http://www.jhkirkla.wordpress.com>
