messages.subject: [statnet_help] Example of STERGM with edgecov
messages.body_plain:
I need to get an example of STREGM using edgecov or dyadcov as terms for a
directed network outcome. When I run the code below, I am getting an error,
which Nicole says has to do with NAs in a matrix which gets blown up to
36x36 instead of 18x18. She can get it to work by increasing the size of
the matrix attribute, but I am not sure what the other 18 rows and columns
mean.

# example
library(ergm)
library(statnet)
library(tergm)
data(samplk)
samp <- list()
samp[[1]] <- samplk1
samp[[2]] <- samplk2
samp[[3]] <- samplk3
samp[[1]] %v% "charm" <- runif(18)
samp[[2]] %v% "charm" <- runif(18)
samp[[3]] %v% "charm" <- runif(18)
samp[[1]] %n% "closeness" <- matrix(runif(18*18),ncol=18,nrow=18)
samp[[2]] %n% "closeness" <- matrix(runif(18*18),ncol=18,nrow=18)
samp[[3]] %n% "closeness" <- matrix(runif(18*18),ncol=18,nrow=18)
fit1 <- ergm(samp[[1]] ~ edges +nodecov("charm") +edgecov("closeness") )
samp.fit <- stergm(samp,
formation = ~edges +nodecov("charm") +edgecov("closeness"),
dissolution = ~edges +mutual,
estimate = "CMLE", times = 1:3)

Any help on syntax would be appreciated.

Thanks
Jeff Carnegie

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am trying to model a series of directed, valued, one-mode networks.
The nodes are members of European parliaments, and edges are bill
cosponsorships.

All nodes carry the following attributes:

- a leftwing/rightwing score (0-10)
- a government/opposition dummy (0/1)

Using the `ergm` package, I am interested in modelling the effect of
leftwing/rightwing ideology within each possible type of dyads, in
order to ask:

  Is the absolute difference in leftwing/rightwing ideology
significant to predict edge formation when ...

  - ... both nodes are from the government majority?
  - ... both nodes are from opposition parties?
  - ... the nodes are asymmetric (gov/opp or opp/gov)?

Unfortunately, I could not figure out a way to code this into a proper
ERGM equation so far. As far as I understand, the net effects are:

  - `absdiff("score")` for the absolute difference in leftwing/rightwing
  - `nodematch("dummy", diff = TRUE)` for the differential homophily term

... but how do I code the interaction?

Any help would be very appreciated.

Best regards,

Fran?ois

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Notice: Bug in latentnet's BIC calculation.
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Notice: Bug in latentnet's BIC calculation.
messages.body_plain:
Dear Users,

A bug has been discovered in latentnet versions prior to 2.7.0, in the
calculation of the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC). p + n(d+r+s)
was used as the number of parameters in the likelihood (where p is the
number of fixed effects, n the number of actors, d, the latent space
dimension, and r and s indicators of presence of sender and receiver (or
sociality) effects). This value should have been just p.

The following applications could have produced different results:
      * Using the BIC to select latent space dimension.
      * Using the BIC to decide whether or not to include random
        effects.

The following applications could not (i.e., would only be off by a
constant):
      * Using the BIC to select the number of clusters.
      * Using the BIC to select the fixed effects to be used.

We apologize for this error.

                                             Best Regards,
                                             Pavel Krivitsky

--

National Institute of Applied Statistics Research Australia (NIASRA)
School of Mathematics and Applied Statistics

University of Wollongong NSW 2522

messages.body_plain:
Dear Statnet Users,

I am trying to analyze the impact of space on a network. My idea is to see
if distances (log kilometers) among nodes has an impact on the network
formation process.

In order to implement this analysis, I am using the distance matrix as a
dyadcov term. Since I have panel data, I am using this specification both
for erg and sterg models. But I am experiencing several problems:


   1. A warning is always reported by R both for erg and sterg models.
      - The warning concerning the ergm is:
      "Warning messages: 1: In ergm.mple(Clist, Clist.miss, m, MPLEtype =
      MPLEtype, init = init,  :  glm.fit: fitted probabilities
numerically 0 or 1
      occurred".
      - The warning concerning the stergm is:
      "In .ergm.mvar.spec0(z) :  Excessive correlation among the
      statistics. Using a no-crosscorrelation approximation.".

      2. R can't compute the pvalue of one or more dyadcov coefficients and
   returns NA (most of the problems are with the dyadcov....ltri coefficient).
   Nonetheless, I get very good fits for the erg model.

   3. In relation to the stergm application, when adding one or more
   structural terms (e.g. mutual, asymmetric, simmelian, gwesp, gwdsp,
   ttriple, ctriple, istar(2), ostar (2)) in addition to the dyadcov
   parameter, R returns NA for all coefficients and pvalue. While if I use
   only structural parameters, without the dyadcov term, I get all the results
   without problems and a better AIC.

My idea is that all these problems are generated by the same issue. The
point is that I don't know how to interpret R results and fix these
problems (I have also tried to raise the control parameters, but it was
useless).


As for the sterg model, I am experiencing also a technical issue:

My network describes people exchanging a number of information in four
different periods. Therefore I have 4 valued adjacency matrix. To implement
all my models, I have transformed these matrices in a binary form. But in
this way I am loosing important features of my network. My idea is that
these exchanges has a "memory", saying that the more I wrote you in the
past, the more I will write you in the future. My idea was to use the
differences in the number of information exchanged between two periods as a
edgecov term. But since I have for periods, this means to use three
different edgecov term and I have no idea about the way in which should I
pass this formulation to the STERG function.


Does anyone of you has some hints to solve these issues?

Any help will be much appreciated,

Paul

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Multilevel ergm in Statnet?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Katherine.  Such models should probably be viewed as "multi-mode" 
networks, rather than "multi-level" networks, but the terminology in the 
field is hopelessly muddled at this point.  These can be fit within 
ergm(), but you will need:

1. To ensure that you have set any constraints necessary to prevent ties 
among entities that cannot in theory be tied; and

2. To employ a set of statistics that implement the inhomogeneities 
inherent in the model class you seek.  As others have noted, this may 
require you to implement your own statistics using the ergm userterms 
package, but it can be done (and once those terms are implemented, they 
will interoperate with the rest of the statnet suite).

Hope that helps,

-Carter

 Hi, Fabiola -
>
> On 03/27/2015 11:31 PM, Fabiola martinoli wrote:
>
>  Dear Statnet's users and developers,
> i'm very new in ERGMs and i'm studying a network of 200 nodes for my
> master's degree thesis. I have two questions for you:
>
>  1. How can i assess that my model converges properly? I mean, after i
> receive my coefficients from the ergm() function, i check it with
> mcmc.diagnostics(): the only important thing is that the MCMC sample
> statistic are varying randomly around the observed values at each step and
> that the difference between the observed and simulated values have a
> roughly bell-shaped distribution centered in 0? Or should i also check the
> individual p-values given at the end of the diagnostics?
> If so, what is the lower bound tha makes my p-value acceptable?
> I read a lot of papers and tutorial but i haven't found a clear answer to
> my doubt.
>
>   As a practical matter, you want to verify that (1) the Markov chain is
> mixing well (e.g., you are covering the region of high probability with
> respect to each model statistic, the chain is not strongly autocorrelated,
> and the chain shows no signs of being "stuck" for long periods in a single
> state); (2) the mean of the sufficient statistics for the retained draws is
> close to their observed values; and (relatedly) (3) the Markov chain
> appears to be stationary (e.g., the first and second moments show no signs
> of "wandering").  The various diagnostics can assist with this process,
> although they can be over-interpreted.  (For instance, it is possible to
> obtain a perfectly reasonable parameter estimate from a sample that shows a
> significant departure of the simulated mean from (say) one of the observed
> statistics, and one can likewise obtain good results from a chain that is
> reasonably autocorrelated.  These are not good signs, however, and in
> practice one should work to minimize them.)
>
> My own _practical_ advice for a typical case would be as follows:
>   1. Verify that the first moment of the Markov chain has converged - the
> running mean line should be flat.  If there is evidence of a trend, either
> (1) the model is degenerate, and trying to head off to la-la land, or (2)
> you need to increase your burn-in time.
>   2. Verify that the chain is mixing well.  You should see relatively
> smooth marginal distributions, there should be little visual evidence of
> strong autocorrelation in the trace plot, and autocorrelation diagnostics
> should show reasonably small correlations at reasonable lags.  If the chain
> isn't mixing well, either (1) your model is showing signs of being poorly
> behaved, or (2) you need to increase the thinning interval.
>   3. Verify that the mean values of the sufficient statistics are
> reasonably close to the target values.  (Note that they may be a bit off,
> because if how the fitting algorithm works - we will provide a better test
> below.)  Ideally, the means will be within a standard deviation or so of
> the observed or target values.  If the means seem to be way off, this
> usually indicates insufficient burn-in and/or thinning length, but it can
> also result from a highly recalcitrant model with which the estimation
> algorithm cannot easily deal.
>   4. Having done all of the above, produce a new, high-quality simulation
> from the fitted model (using simulate() or gof()).  Verify (1)-(3) on the
> new sample; but this time, pay closer attention to (3).  For a reasonable
> sample size (say, 250), I would usually be concerned if my mean statistics
> were significantly different from their target values (with the usual
> caveats about multiple testing and such).
>   5. If your model clears all of the above, the fitting process itself has
> probably been successful.  You will still want to perform model adequacy
> checking and such, as described in the various available tutorials.
>
> Again, these are heuristics, and one can identify exceptions and/or more
> specific directives for special cases.  But they should provide you with a
> good place to start.
>
>   2. I'm interested in studying a brokerage effect due to a nodal
> attribute, is there any effect able to test it? I looked for it but i can't
> find nothing.
>
>
> This (and related!) problems are addressed in a forthcoming JSS paper:
>
> Yaveroglu, Omer Nebil; Fitzhugh, Sean M.; Kurant, Maciej; Markopoulou,
> Athina; Butts, Carter T.; and Przulj, Natasa. (2015).  ``ergm.graphlets: A
> Package for ERG Modeling Based on Graphlet Statistics.''  Journal of
> Statistical Software, forthcoming.
>
> Unfortunately, it's been held up in the JSS editorial queue for months and
> months.  However, you can find a pre-print on arXiv:
> http://arxiv.org/abs/1405.7348.  Likewise, the package needed to add the
> associated statistics to ergm is on CRAN:
> http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ergm.graphlets/index.html.  Once
> you load the ergm.graphlets package, you can use the associated terms
> within ergm just as you would any other model terms.  (See the paper for
> examples.)
>
> Hope that helps,
>
> -Carter
>
>   Thank you very much for your precious help.
> Fabiola Martinoli.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] help with ergm.count
messages.body_plain:
Hello, Iris,

> I am working with weighted network data and would very much like to
> use ergm.count in my analyses. I am not sure how to use the form
> object properly, and I am getting an error: 'Error: The term sum does
> not exist for this type of ERGM. Are you sure you have the right
> name??.  I get the same error for the nonzero value. I am able to run
> ergm without weights (or at least I think it ignores weights without
> specifying the form object!) using:
> 
> > dat=read.csv(file.choose(),header=TRUE,row.names=1,check.names=FALSE)
> > m=as.matrix(dat)
> >net=network(m,matrix.type="adjacency",directed=FALSE,ignore.eval=FALSE,names.eval="value") 
> >nodeInfo<-read.csv(?Attribute.csv", header=TRUE, stringsAsFactors=FALSE, row.names=1)
> >dat2=as.network(net, vertex.attr=nodeInfo, directed=FALSE, edge.lwd=net%e%'value')

Take a look at the first section of this tutorial for how to set edge
values in network:
https://statnet.csde.washington.edu/trac/attachment/wiki/Sunbelt2013/Valued.pdf .

> >dat2 %v% "Sex"<-nodeInfo$Sex #Similar thing done for all attributes I am interested in using in my model
> >model<-ergm(dat2~edges+nodematch('Sex', diff=FALSE)+nodecov(?Color?))

You need to specify a response= argument and a reference= argument. In
particular, a response= argument shifts ergm() into the valued mode,
enabling statistics like sum() and nonzero(). Take a look at
example(zach) in the ergm.count package and the tutorial linked above.

> Also, the only paper in my field to utilize ergm.count lists that both
> ?sum? and ?nonzero? were used in the same model. However, in the help
> file, it appears these are two different options for the form object -
> can someone please clarify this?

Sum models the overall average count, while nonzero models tendency to
have too many or too few zeros. They can both be in the model at the
same time. In particular, if you have a Poisson-reference ERGM with both
nonzero and sum terms in it, you get a form of the zero-modified
Poisson.

              I hope this helps,
              Pavel

--

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Unable to install statnet
messages.body_plain:
Hi Joe -

R 3.2.0 was released just last week.  Any time a new major R release 
happens, all of the contributed packages need to be rebuilt by the CRAN 
team for it.  My understanding is that this is all done by volunteers, 
and there is a larger pool of volunteers for the Windows builds than for 
the MacOS builds.  Consequently, it can take some time (up to a week or 
so?) after a major R release for all of the packages to be available 
again in pre-built forms for Mac.  (I may have some of the details 
wrong, but I think I'm capturing the big picture).

This means your options are:

(1) Wait a few days
(2) Build the packages you want from source - instructions abound online
(3) Switch to a Windows machine for the time being
(4) Revert to R 3.1.X

HTH,
Steve

As far as I now, we don't have a directed version of it available. I think this is in part because we haven't seen demand for it before, and because 
there are multiple different ways to consider measures like this for directed networks (correlation in in-degree, out-degree, total degree, head's 
in-degree with tail's out-degree, etc.) So your quickest optionis to use igraph or another program, if it has the statistic you want. Alternately, if 
you wish to be able to conduct statistical inference on your model with the ergm framework, then you can code up the statistic yourself with help from 
the ergm.userterms package and instructions here: http://www.jstatsoft.org/v52/i02

Yours,
Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Imputate missing edges with ERGM using an EM approach
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Imputate missing edges with ERGM using an EM approach
messages.body_plain:
Hi statnet users,

As part of my PhD, I'm working with a huge dynamical contact network 
(30s granularity, 600 nodes, ~6 months of data collection, roughly 3M 
edges in an undirected network). Ultimately, the idea is to study how 
dynamical processes influence the spread of nosocomial pathogens. The 
contact network was measured in a hospital and there is a clear 
clustering according to medical wards (5 in the dataset). Before doing 
anything about a spreading process, I'm trying to deal with missing 
data. I'm working with daily-aggregated networks for now, i.e. a set of 
daily edges between each pair of nodes. Although I could weight edges 
with daily-cumulative contact time, it's not really important right now.

All records were captured with individual sensors (meaning all 
participants wore a small wireless sensor at all time) that recorded the 
ID of other sensors in close proximity. Obviously some sensor batteries 
failed before others, and were not replaced until sheduled (there were 3 
interruptions in data collection on fixed date). Plotting the number of 
daily edges shows a tendency to decrease after batteries are replaced, 
which makes sense: therefore, the dataset is incomplete, with missing 
vertices (and edges going from/to them)... up until the next battery change.

i'm trying to implement an EM-like algorithm to impute missing edges, 
but so far it leads to degeneracy by leading to a graph with way more 
edges than I should expect (initially 1900 edges, 10% density ; ends at 
16000 edges ; 40% density). Here is the idea:
1) Initialize the network (let's call it nw) with all observed vertices 
and edges on day T.
2) From sensor attribution record, identify missing vertices from the 
network and add them (with add.vertices) along with a nodal attribute 
that keeps trace of them.
3) Fit an ERGM to nw, e.g.:
ergm.fit <- ergm(nw ~ edges + nodematch("affectation", diff=TRUE, 
keep=4:8) + nodematch("building", diff=T, keep=c(1,3)) + 
nodefactor("service") + nodecov("mif"))

NB: I have tried many of the higher-order structure ERGM termes (gwesp, 
gwdsp, altkstar) but couldn't really reproduce my observed graphs using 
them. However the ERGM I quote here is able to reproduce graphs that 
look a lot like the one I have observed in my dataset.

4) Simulate a new graph from the fit (call it nw.sim)
5) Extract the neighborhood of all vertices that have the "missing" 
attribute, and add these edges to the observed network nw
6) Repeat steps 4 and 5 until Beta estimates are stable enough between 
two iterations.


Here is the code I'm using:

nw.orig <- nw
converge <- FALSE
iter <- 1
trace <- list()
trace[[iter]] <- list(nw=nw.orig, ergm=ergm.fit)

while(!converge) {

   #Simulate from previous ERGM fit
   my.sim <- simulate(ergm.fit)

   #Extract new edges from missing vertices
   for (v in which(nw.orig %v% "missing")) {
     #cat(match(v, which(nw.orig %v% "missing")), "/", 
length(which(nw.orig %v% "missing")), "\n", sep="")
     v.neighbors <- get.neighborhood(my.sim, v=v)
     if (iter > 1) v.neighbors <- setdiff(v.neighbors, 
get.neighborhood(trace[[iter-1]]$nw, v=v))

     #Add them to the original network
     add.edges(nw, head=rep(v, length(v.neighbors)), tail=v.neighbors)
   }
   ergm.fit <- ergm(nw ~ edges + nodematch("affectation", diff=TRUE, 
keep=4:8) + nodematch("building", diff=T, keep=c(1,3)) + 
nodefactor("service") + nodecov("mif"))
   trace[[iter+1]] <- list(nw=nw, ergm=ergm.fit)
   plot(trace[[iter]]$ergm$coef - ergm.fit$coef, main=paste0("Iteration 
", iter))

   #Is convergency reached ? Obviously the threshold is too high, but 
for testing purposes ATM
   conv <- trace[[iter]]$ergm$coef - ergm.fit$coef
   if (!(any(conv > 0.1))) converge <- TRUE

   #Failsafe...
   if (iter > 100) break
   iter <- iter+1
}



I am wondering if this approach is correct. Maybe I should constrain 
fits to graphs that have the same density as the observed ones ? Offset 
the edges term ? I think degeneracy has to do with the terms in the ERGM 
being dependant on the number of edges, which is increasing from an 
iteration to the next.

I have another unrelated question, about ST-ERGMs. Are they in any way 
suitable to use with this kind of data (see first paragraph with a quick 
description of the dynamical network), to simulate formation and 
dissolution of edges ? Daily-aggregated networks are already a 
compressed version of the network, with time consistency not being kept, 
and I'm wondering how discretization might affect a spreading process. 
But fitting an ST-ERGM to such a big dataset... maybe not a good idea ?

Any help will be appreciated, and I hope I was clear enough!
Regards,
Thomas

--

messages.subject: [statnet_help] missing value in statnet
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Ya -

There is no uniform default way of handling missing data in networks - 
the applicable methods are necessarily technique and situation 
specific.  In the context of the ergm() function per se, the default is 
to use the latent missing data approach of Gile and Handcock; this 
marginalizes across the possible values of the missing edge variables, 
under the assumption that they and the observed edge variables were 
drawn from the same model (and that the pattern of missingness is 
ignorable).  Performing simulation from a model fit using this strategy, 
conditional on the observed data, can be used as a multiple imputation 
technique (e.g., for subsequent exploratory data analysis) and/or to get 
a sense of how well the model and observed data constrain the edge 
variables that were not observed.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

net_summary <- function(net){

        size <- network.size(net)
        net_density <- gden(net)
        dyad_recip <- grecip(net)
        edge_recip <- grecip(net, measure="edgewise")
        trans <- gtrans(net)

             "Max betweenness" = max_bet,
             "Dyadic reciprocity" = dyad_recip,

}

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Nodemix interpretation
messages.body_plain:
On 10/26/2014 11:41 AM, Fischer, Jason Donald wrote:
> I have a question about the interpretation of nodemix coefficients. 
> Let's say I have a simple model looking at associations among sexes 
> and I use the default of 0 for the base option [edges +nodemix("sex")] .
>
> If the coefficient for male-male associations was significant and 
> positive, would it be correct to interpret this as
> male-male associations positively affect (i.e., increase) the 
> likelihood of edges occurring in the network? Would it also be 
> accurate to say that male-male associations are more likely to occur 
> than expected by chance given the density of the network?
>
> If a base was specified (say it was set to female-female associations) 
> and the male-male coefficient was still significant and positive, 
> would the interpretation change to edges are more likely occur between 
> males than between females? Or does the base option just specify terms 
> that are not of interest and should be left out of the model?
Hi Jason,

I think it'll be most clear if I walk through three models in turn. Let 
me create a network with a single attribute, and then purely random ties 
unrelated to that attribute. Because this is undirected, there are only 
a total of three kinds of attribute combos, not four:

 > library(ergm)
 > aaa <- network.initialize(100, directed=F)
 > aaa %v% 'sex' <- sample(c('F','M'),100, replace=T)
 > aaa <- simulate(ergm(aaa~edges,target.stats=200))

First, if you have a nodemix term with a base of 0 and you *don't* have 
an edges term, then you can interpret each coefficient in there as an 
effect for that type of tie.  But note that you are *not* conditioning 
on the density of the network in this case, because there is no edges 
term.  If nodemix were the only term in your model, then the 
coefficients would all be defined as the propensity for that type of 
tie, relative to a density of 0.5.  Note how the coefficients are all 
roughly equal to each other; each is defined relative to a density of 0.5:

 > (ccc <- ergm(aaa~nodemix('sex')))

MLE Coefficients:
mix.sex.F.F  mix.sex.F.M  mix.sex.M.M
      -3.185       -3.211       -3.104

Second, if you have an edges and nodemix term, and you leave one 
category out as a base, then the edges term can be interpreted in terms 
of the propensity for ties of the omitted category, and the others can 
be interpreted as the propensity for the various groups, relative to the 
omitted category:

 > (ddd <- ergm(aaa~edges+nodemix('sex',base=1)))

MLE Coefficients:
       edges  mix.sex.F.M  mix.sex.M.M
    -3.18475     -0.02635      0.08064

Note how here the edges coefficient is equal to the nodemix.FF 
coefficient in the previous model; and the other two represent the 
difference between that value and the other values in the previous model.

Finally, if you have a nodemix with a base of 0 in combination with an 
edges term, then you will end up with collinearity: one of your terms 
will be dropped out.  E.g.:

 > (bbb <- ergm(aaa~edges+nodemix('sex')))

MLE Coefficients:
       edges  mix.sex.F.F  mix.sex.F.M  mix.sex.M.M
    -3.10411     -0.08064     -0.10699           NA

HTH,
Steve

Hi Matt,

These are not errors, they are diagnostic warnings that provide additional 
information on the performance of the MCMC estimation algorithm.  You 
should still be getting results -- let me know if that's not the case.

When you see this kind of error, it suggests you might want to increase 
your MCMC.interval to reduce the correlation between draws from the chain 
(see the documentation for control.ergm).

best,
Martina

Old versions of R packages are archived on CRAN. For example for
package 'ergm' they are here
http://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/ergm/

In principle, when you open package page on CRAN (like this for ergm
http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ergm/index.html) there should
be a link "old sources" that should direct to a page with older
versions of that particular package.

Do mind that these are package sources. If you work on Windows you
will have to install additional software to install these old package
versions. For more info see e.g. here:
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/4739837/how-do-i-install-an-r-package-from-the-source-tarball-on-windows

Michal

ii) Exponential Random Graph Modelling.



So far, in my understanding (which I?m not sure is true or not), We can

like the factors (such as power, education, and gender) could affect the

Thanks Skye, that is brilliant. I would never have figured that out on my
own.

I do intend to use ndtv and animate it, but I will want to color the edges
by the weight (1 gold, 2 orange, 3 red, 4 violet, 5 black). Since I am
entering the spells in continuous time, I don't know if the animation will
show all spells or if I need to specify the highest value in each time
increment.

That is, my time increments are in years, and the weight is the level of
conflict. Suppose I have the following values for and edge A->B:
1990.3 to 1990.5: 1
1990.5 to 1990.8: 3
1990.5 to 1990.8: 2

I assume that for the animation to cover every transition would be too
much, so that it would use snapshots every year (I will have about 240
edges over 195 years). If that is the case, I would prefer to color each

On Fri, May 8, 2015 at 3:25 PM, Skye Bender-deMoll <skyebend@skyeome.net>
wrote:

> Hi Jeff,
>
> >
> > This prints all ???weight??  values on 1->2 in period 1, creating
> > overlapping labels. So how do I show only the highest weight from each
> > period?
>
>
> First,  in your example, by repeatedly added edges between the same
> tail,head pair of vertices, you are actually creating a multiplex network.
> I'm not sure if this was your intention, but I don't see an easy way to
> collapse the labels for this case, since you would need to look up the
> 'edge' objects by their endpoints.  If that is what you need to do, let me
> know I'll figure out a way..
>
> But assuming that this was not intended to be a multiplex network, you
> should use 'activate.edges' to add additional activity spells after the
> edge is created (either with add.edge or add.edges.active).
>
> re-writing your example
>
> net<-network.initialize(5)
> add.edges.active(net, tail=1, head=2, onset=1, terminus=1.5)
> activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',1,onset=1, terminus=1.5, e=1)
> activate.edges(net, e=1, onset=1.5, terminus=1.7)
> activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',2,onset=1.5, terminus=1.7, e=1)
> activate.edges(net, e=1, onset=1.7, terminus=4)
> activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',4,onset=1.7, terminus=4, e=1)
> activate.edges(net, e=1, onset=4, terminus=5)
> activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',3,onset=4, terminus=5, e=1)
> add.edges.active(net, tail=1, head=3, onset=2.1, terminus=2.2)
> activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',1,onset=2.1,terminus=2.2, e=2)
> add.edges.active(net, tail=3, head=4, onset=2, terminus=3)
> activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',1,onset=2,terminus=3, e=3)
> activate.edges(net, e=3, onset=3, terminus=4)
> activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',2,onset=3,terminus=4, e=3)
> add.edges.active(net, tail=5, head=4, onset=3, terminus=5)
> activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',4,onset=3,terminus=5, e=3)
>
> or in a slightly condensed form, do all the edge activation at the same
> time
>
> net<-network.initialize(5)
> add.edges.active(net, tail=1, head=2, onset=c(1,1.5,1.7,4),
> terminus=c(1.5,1.7,4,5))
> activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',1,onset=1, terminus=1.5, e=1)
> activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',2,onset=1.5, terminus=1.7, e=1)
> activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',4,onset=1.7, terminus=4, e=1)
> activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',3,onset=4, terminus=5, e=1)
> add.edges.active(net, tail=1, head=3, onset=2.1, terminus=2.2)
> activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',1,onset=2.1,terminus=2.2, e=2)
> add.edges.active(net, tail=3, head=4, onset=c(2,3), terminus=c(3,4))
> activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',1,onset=2,terminus=3, e=3)
> activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',2,onset=3,terminus=4, e=3)
> add.edges.active(net, tail=5, head=4, onset=3, terminus=5)
> activate.edge.attribute(net,'weight',4,onset=3,terminus=5, e=4)
>
> when set up this way, your plot command will give you a warning indicating
> that it couldn't figure out which value to use
>
> > plot(network.extract(net,onset=1,terminus=2, trim.spells=TRUE),main='at
> time 1',arrowhead.cex=2, displaylabels=TRUE, boxed.labels=TRUE,
> label.pos=5, edge.label=na.omit(get.edge.value.active(net, "weight",
> onset=1,terminus=2)))
>
> Warning message:
> In get.edge.value.active(net, "weight", onset = 1, terminus = 2) :
>   Multiple attribute values matched query spell for attribute
> weight.active on some edges. Only earliest value used
>
>
> if you just wanted the earliest or latest value you could avoid the
> warning by specifying a rule:
>
> > get.edge.value.active(net, "weight", onset=1,terminus=2,rule='latest')
> [1]  4 NA NA NA
>
> > get.edge.value.active(net, "weight"onset=1,terminus=2,rule='earliest')
> [1]  1 NA NA NA
>
> you could also do this by using network.collapse instead of network.extract
>
>
> However, since you want the label with the maximum value, you will have to
> process the TEA attribute directly yourself
>
> get.edge.value.active(net, "weight",onset=1,terminus=2,return.tea = TRUE)
>
> The first element of each TEA attribute is the list of values appropriate
> for the time range (second is spell matrix) so should work to set your
> edge.label equal to
>
> sapply( get.edge.value.active(net,"weight",onset=1,terminus=2,return.tea =
> TRUE),
>    function(e){
>       max(unlist(e[[1]]))
> })
>
> [1]  4 NA NA NA
>
>
> If you were doing this as part of ndtv animation, you would probably want
> to make use of 'functional' attribute forms so that the values would be
> recalculate for each slice
>
> library(ndtv)
>
> render.animation(net,
>           main=function(onset,terminus){paste('at
> time',onset,'-',terminus)},
>           arrowhead.cex=2,
>           displaylabels=TRUE,
>           boxed.labels=FALSE,
>           label.pos=5,
>           edge.label=function(net,onset,terminus){
>
> sapply(get.edge.value.active(net,"weight",onset=onset,terminus=terminus,return.tea
> = TRUE),
>                     function(e){
>                        max(unlist(e[[1]]))
>                     }
>             )
>           }
> )
> ani.replay()
>
>
> let me know if that works!
>
> best,
>  -skye
>
>
>
>

messages.subject: [statnet_help] STERGM and bipartite networks
messages.body_plain:
Hi all -

The issue seems to be that both networksis and tergm contain a function 
named simulate.network.  This is an unfortunate choice on our part.  
We'll be revisiting the packages sometime soon, and we will decide on 
the best path forward.  In the meanwhile, a workaround is to use 
namespace notation to call the function you want, like so:

tergm:::simulate.network
networksis:::simulate.network

Note that because of R's dispatching rules, if you make a call to 
simulate with a network object as the first argument, it will then 
dispatch to simulate.network.  So if you need control over which version 
of simulate.network is being invoked there, don't call simulate; call 
simulate.network directly, with the above package name and triple colon.

I hope that helps,
Steve

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

My coauthor and I are interested in assessing how individuals belonging to
different groups vary in their tendency to form network ties following a
triadic closure logic. In other words, we are interested in answering the
following question: are individuals belonging to one group more likely to
close triads than individuals belonging to the other group? Here is a
simple example: assume we have three age groups and we have reason to
believe that individuals in the youngest age group are more likely to close
triads than those in the two other age groups.

Two questions:

1. Any references to papers implementing such a hypothesis test using an
ERGM?
2. Any suggestions on how to implement a test of this hypothesis in
Statnet's ergm function? Intuitively, one would include an interaction
effect of the nodefactor variable and the network statistic.

Thanks for your help!

--
Mathijs de Vaan

messages.subject: [statnet_help] how to combine several networks
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Andreas -

If the alters are labeled, and if individuals can appear more than once 
across the ego nets, then these are not independent networks.  There is 
no single command to combine these into one aggregate network, but one 
reasonable strategy would be as follows:

1. Use network.initialize to create an empty graph of the appropriate 
size, with such vertex attributes as are appropriate. (These can also be 
added later.)

2. Use a for loop to walk through your list of individual networks, 
extracting and adding the edges from each one to their appropriate 
places in the master network using e.g. add.edges or the assignment 
operator.  (If you have edge attributes, these may be added at this time 
via the additional arguments to add.edges.)

Note that, depending on your design, some edge variables may have been 
unobserved; these should be set to NA, assuming that you intend to model 
the resulting graph using e.g. ergm().  (You will also want to take care 
that any subsequent analysis accounts for your measurement design, to 
the extent possible.)

Hope that helps,

-Carter

>
> nodemix(attrname, base <http://inside-r.org/r-doc/base>=NULL) (binary),
> nodemix(attrname, base <http://inside-r.org/r-doc/base>=NULL, form="sum")
> (valued)
> *Nodal attribute mixing:* The attrname argument is a character vector
> giving the names of categorical attributes in the network's vertex
> attribute list. By default, this term adds one network statistic to the
> model for each possible pairing of attribute values. The statistic equals
> the number of edges in the network in which the nodes have that pairing of

> combination of attribute values for those names.) In other words, this term
> produces one statistic for every entry in the mixing matrix for the
> attribute(s). The ordering of the attribute values is alphabetical (for
> nominal categories) or numerical (for ordered categories). The optional

> <http://inside-r.org/r-doc/base> contains only negative integers, then

>

> reference that you sent to be very useful.
>
> I do notice that I receive the following error when I attempt to run "m1
> <- mtergm(l ~ edges + mutual)" as you described: Error in
> match.arg(estimate) : 'arg' must be of length 1
>
> It seems like there is an obvious reason for this, but I don't quite
> understand at this point. Thanks again,
>

>
>
>
> On Wed, Aug 5, 2015 at 10:55 AM, Philip Leifeld
> <philip.leifeld@uni-konstanz.de <mailto:philip.leifeld@uni-konstanz.de>>
> wrote:
>
>     Hi Tom,
>
>     What you are describing is essentially the same data structure as in a
>     TERGM (*not* STERGM) without temporal dependencies, a.k.a. pooled ERGM.
>     See here for details:
>     http://people.reed.edu/~ahm//polnet2015/TERGM%20Workshop%20Leifeld%202015-06-17/btergm-paper.pdf
>
>     This can be conveniently estimated using the xergm package, more
>     specifically the btergm function (for pseudolikelihood estimation with
>     bias correction via bootstrapping) and the mtergm function (for MCMC
>     MLE). Both have the same syntax and model terms as the ergm function
>     because ergm's model specification is used internally (i.e., you can
>     integrate it in your statnet workflow). Multiple networks are handed
>     over to the formula by wrapping them in a list. No need to use
>     structural zeros with this approach.
>
>     Your example can be respecified as follows:
>
>     library("statnet")
>     net1 <- network(10, directed=T, density=.2)
>     net2 <- network(8, directed=T, density=.2)
>     library("xergm")
>     l <- list(net1, net2)
>     m1 <- btergm(l ~ edges + mutual)  # or m1 <- mtergm(l ~ edges + mutual)
>
>     If you need to control for differential tie probability of nodes across
>     networks, this is essentially a dependency across networks that can be
>     implemented via edgecov terms (like a fixed effect). Temporal
>     dependencies are described in the paper referenced above. E.g., you can
>     provide a list of matrices where 1 indicates a specific actor (in all

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Geographic distance in ergm
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Francesco.  This is because you are only considering the distance 
between nodes that have ties - non-adjacent dyads are being treated as 
co-located (i.e., distance 0).  That will indeed produce a positive 
"effect" of distance under propinquity.  Instead, what you want to do is 
produce an n x n distance matrix and pass that to edgecov; in typical 
use cases I would suggest using the log distance, as this approximates a 
power law SIF (see e.g. Butts and Acton (2011) for a description of SIFs 
and the difference they make for network structure).

Hope that helps!

-Carter

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] single ergm for multiple networks follow-up
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I would like to ask a follow-up question to a discussion that has popped up
in this forum several times before regarding the use of a single ERG model
to describe multiple networks. In my situation I have multiple
cross-sectional observations of a network through time, but I am not
interested in formation/dissolution of ties (as in the tergm case).
Instead, I would like to use information from all the networks to build a
single ergm while acknowledging that ties cannot be formed between nodes
across networks. Many of the nodes are the same across networks, but not
all of them, so the total number of nodes in each network fluctuates
slightly. My network is also directed.

I understand that this problem can perhaps be addressed using "structural
zeros" to prohibit ties across networks. I am also aware that this issue
has been discussed in some detail already in this previous post (
http://mailman13.u.washington.edu/pipermail/statnet_help/2012/001214.html).

My question is specifically about the implementation discussed in the
previous post -- I am not certain that I fully understand the given
description and would like to make sure that I get it right. Below is some
simulated data and example code that I am hoping someone here might be able
to confirm whether it implements the previous solution properly:

#simulate networks
> net1 <- network(10, directed=T, density=.2)
> net2 <- network(8, directed=T, density=.2)

#create a joint adjacency matrix
> combined <- as.network(bdiag(as.matrix.network(net1),
as.matrix.network(net2)), directed=T, matrix.type="adjacency") #create a
joint adjacency matrix and

# set attributes: unique group for each network and names that reflect some
of the same nodes in each graph

> set.vertex.attribute(combined, "vertex.names", c(1:10, 1:8))
> set.vertex.attribute(combined, "group",
c(rep("A",length(network.vertex.names(net1))), rep("B",
length(network.vertex.names(net2)))))


> (m1 <- ergm(combined ~ edges + nodemix("group")))  # should there be a
"base=" argument within nodemix?

Observed statistic(s) mix.group.B.A and mix.group.A.B are at their smallest
attainable values. Their coefficients will be fixed at -Inf.

MLE Coefficients:
        edges  mix.group.A.A  mix.group.B.A  mix.group.A.B  mix.group.B.B
      -1.1963         0.1271           -Inf           -Inf             NA

#alternatively should I set categories 1 and 4 (categories within networks)
to base to get rid of them?

> summary(combined~nodemix("group"))

mix.group.A.A mix.group.B.A mix.group.A.B mix.group.B.B
           23             0             0            13

> (m2<- ergm(combined ~ edges + nodemix("group", base=c(1,4))))

Observed statistic(s) mix.group.B.A and mix.group.A.B are at their smallest
attainable values. Their coefficients will be fixed at -Inf.

MLE Coefficients:
        edges  mix.group.B.A  mix.group.A.B
       -1.117           -Inf           -Inf

###

In particular, if someone could help me understand whether "m1" or "m2"
above achieves the described goal I would be very grateful. Finally, if one
of the above approaches is appropriate, I am also curious if it is possible
to model the non-independence of the same nodes occurring in multiple
networks (similar to a random intercept term in a GLMM for nodeID in this
case). It seems like "hergm" might be used for this purpose but I am having
trouble finding resources.

Thank you very much in advance for the help and your continued work on
these resources,

Tom

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Fitting a model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Srecko,
I think what you are looking for is nodemix.? Below is from the ergm-terms help file:
   
   - nodemix(attrname, base=NULL) (binary), nodemix(attrname, base=NULL, form="sum") (valued)
      - Nodal attribute mixing: The attrname argument is a character vector giving the names of categorical attributes in the network's vertex attribute list. By default, this term adds one network statistic to  the model for each possible pairing of attribute values. The statistic equals the number of edges in the network in which the nodes have that pairing of values. (When multiple names are given, a statistic is added for each combination of attribute values for those names.) In other words, this term produces one statistic for every entry in the mixing matrix for the attribute(s). The ordering of the attribute values is alphabetical (for nominal categories) or numerical (for ordered categories). The optional base argument is a vector of integers corresponding to the pairings that should not be included. If base contains only negative integers, then these integers correspond to the only pairings that should be included. By default (i.e., with base=NULL or base=0), all pairings are included.
   -    

Also, given that you see "fails" as a factor, you likely don't want to use nodecov as it is for numeric variables. 

Best,
Michael
-- 
Michael D. Siciliano, PhD
Assistant Professor
Department of Public Administration
University of Illinois at Chicago

When I run an ERGM with nodemix, excluding one of the pairwise relationships as the reference group, the model does not converge. I've included six other node level continuous variables and a 'mutual' term for reciprocity in the specification. Does anyone have any ideas on how to get the model to converge using all actor mixing combinations minus one reference group? I've tried all possible relationships as the reference group, to no avail. 




When I exclude a few other relationships from the nodemix argument, my model does converge. 


Typically when using a categorical variable in regression we need one reference group against which to compare the other coefficients. In this case, it doesn't seem possible to isolate the ref erence group using a single mixing relationship . That said, I've excluded additional mixing relationships to expand the reference group based on theory. Have people encountered this same issue, and have folks been able to "explain away" this problem as a peculiarity of ERGMs? 


Many thanks, 



Sanjay K. Arora 
Doctoral Candidate, School of Public Policy 
Georgia Institute of Technology 
sanjayk.arora@gatech.edu

messages.subject: [statnet_help] STERGM errors
messages.body_plain:
Dear Jeff,

This did expose a bug in tergm, which will be fixed in the next release.
Other than that,

> 
> for (i in 1:10) {
> activate.network.attribute(net, "dyadic", x[i], onset=i, length=1)
> }


x is a 3D array, so x[i] will extract its i'th element. I think you're
looking for x[,,i]. Also, NAs for covariates are not allowed.

> net.fit <- stergm(net, formation= ~edges + mutual + dyadcov(net,
> "dyadic") , dissolution= ~edges + mutual  + dyadcov(net, "dyadic"),
> estimate = "CMLE", times = c(1:11))


Also, unfortunately, tergm doesn't support a series of networks with
heterogeneous sizes at this time, though it isn't explicit about it. A
full support is a complicated question, but it'll handle it more
gracefully in the next release (hopefully, next week).

                                    Pavel

Dear statnet developers,

I have a problem regarding a statistical interaction effect which I
would like to model using an ERGM. My network contains the interactions
of politicians on an online discussion website. I have both the
politicians' party affiliation, and their position in an "ideological
space", i.e. a 2D-space spanned by left-right and liberal-conservative
political attitude. From the latter, I can compute a n x n matrix of
ideological distance between politicians. I suspected that there is a
homophily effect both for party affiliation and political distance, and
modelled this thusly:

Network ~ edges + nodematch("party") + edgecov(IdeologicalDistanceMatrix)

However, I also suspect that the effect of ideological distance is
different for dyads where both politicians belong to the same party than
for politicians of different parties (I think that ideological distance
matters more with regard to party outsiders than fellow members). I
thought that I could model this with an interaction term between
nodematch("party") and  edgecov(IdeologicalDistanceMatrix). However,
this doesn't seem to be possible with statnet ergm. Is there a workaround?

Thank you very much in advance!

Simon Schweighofer

PhD Student in Systems Design at ETH Zurich

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Memory-related question
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Aditya -

Your second method of network creation can indeed omit isolates 
(specifically, it uses the maximum observed vertex ID as the number of 
vertices unless an "n" attribute is present), so the first method might 
result in a larger object.  Also, you did not in the second case 
indicate that the graph should be undirected (so the two objects will 
not be equivalent).  However, neither approach should produce memory 
errors if the data is well-formed. My guess is that there is something 
glitchy in the edgelist; add.edges will try to catch things that would 
produce issues, but some things can get past the default checks.  Can 
you verify that the values of fb.edge.list are integers denoting vertex 
IDs, that these IDs are all within the range 
1,...,length(full.node.list)? Since this is a simple graph, you will 
want to also verify that each unordered pair appears only once and that 
there are no loops.  You can also check the resulting object by coercing 
it back to an edgelist and verifying that it matches your data.  (The 
summary command should likewise show the correct number of vertices and 
edges.)

The other possibility is that your network objects are fine, and that 
your errors have to do with what you are doing downstream. But I would 
verify the objects first.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Model not converging with single reference group
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sanjay,

One possibility is that there are one or more cells with few observations. 
Have you run a summary command to see what the nodemix matrix looks like? 
ERGM should just return an "-inf" estimate for these cells, but if there 
are too many -- or you use one of them for the reference group -- that 
could cause problems.

Also, with 6 other continuous nodal attributes, I'd check to see what the 
correlation is among them.

I'd recommend looking at the covariates one at a time, first in an 
exploratory way, then by putting them the ERGM, to see if you can find out 
which one(s) are causing the problem.

hth,
Martina

Subject: [statnet_help] Interaction between a nodefactor variable and a network statistic?

Hi all,

My coauthor and I are interested in assessing how individuals belonging to different groups vary in their tendency to form network ties following a triadic closure logic. In other words, we are interested in answering the following question: are individuals belonging to one group more likely to close triads than individuals belonging to the other group? Here is a simple example: assume we have three age groups and we have reason to believe that individuals in the youngest age group are more likely to close triads than those in the two other age groups.

Two questions:

1. Any references to papers implementing such a hypothesis test using an ERGM?
2. Any suggestions on how to implement a test of this hypothesis in Statnet's ergm function? Intuitively, one would include an interaction effect of the nodefactor variable and the network statistic.

Thanks for your help!

--
Mathijs de Vaan

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Questions on 'cug.test' with FUN=centralization
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

Thank you in advance for your help with a first-time poster's questions!

I recently ran some 'cug.test's with 'FUN=centralization', and I had
questions about the output p-values not adding up to 1 and the
'ignore.eval' argument possibly being reversed (in the sense of what it
does when given 'TRUE' vs 'FALSE').

Pasted below are two runs on a dataset and the results from each, and the
network (n2014) is attached. Please let me know if the attachment doesn't
work.

First, you can see clearly that  Pr(X>=Obs) +  Pr(X<=Obs) is much larger
than 1 (0.30985 + 0.8965 = 1.20635). This seems like a bigger difference
than should happen due to rounding or very small numbers. The numbers were
even larger for some other datasets I tested.

Second, I did several analyses with both 'ignore.eval=FALSE' and
'ignore.eval=TRUE', and after much checking and head-scratching, I have to
ask if these are logicals are actually reversed? If I understand correctly,
'ignore.eval=TRUE', the default, should run the analysis on a binary
version of the network. Yet setting 'ignore.eval=FALSE' (supposed to turn
on edge weights) gives the same output as running the analysis on the
actual binary version of the network.

Any insight you all have would be much appreciated. Thank you!

Cheers,
Tina


c2014.out <- cug.test (dat = n2014   # input graph(s)
                       , FUN = centralization
                       , mode = c("digraph")
                       , cmode = c("edges")
                       , reps = 20000
                       , ignore.eval = FALSE  ## IS THIS REVERSEd?
                                          , FUN.args = list(degree,
cmode="outdegree")
)
c2014.out
# Conditioning Method: edges
# Graph Type: digraph
# Diagonal Used: FALSE
# Replications: 20000
#
# Observed Value: 0.1574074

c2014.out2 <- cug.test (dat = n2014   # input graph(s)
                        , FUN = centralization
                        , mode = c("digraph")
                        , cmode = c("edges")
                        , reps = 20000   # number of Monte Carlo reps to use
                        , ignore.eval = TRUE    ## IS THIS REVERSEd?

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Questions on 'cug.test' with FUN=centralization
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Tina -

The sum of Pr(X>=Obs) and Pr(X<=Obs) can certainly be greater than 1; 
indeed, Pr(X==Obs)=Pr(X>=Obs)+Pr(X<=Obs)-1. Depending on your network, 
the properties of the measure you are using, etc., you may find the 
probability of observing your exact GLI value under your chosen null 
model to be quite large.  (It can be important to take this into account 
when comparing results across graphs; see Butts (2011, "Bayesian 
Meta-Analysis of Social Network Data via Conditional Uniform Graph 
Quantiles" for one approach to dealing with the issue.)  If you want to 
examine the discreteness of the distribution, examining the replicate 
statistics (stored in the $rep.stat element of the list returned by 
cug.test) can prove useful.

As far as ignore.eval, note that you need to pass this to the degree and 
centralization routines as well.  Adding it to FUN.args is necessary to 
avoid getting the default behavior from centralization() (and the 
centrality function it calls).  Note that whatever function you call in 
FUN may or may not respect edge values, so this is something you will 
want to check.  At any rate, I just ran a test and the argument seems to 
be working fine - just remember that ignore.eval has to be manually 
passed to the downstream function with FUN.args.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

Hello Oliver,

I don?t have your data, but when I run a stripped-down version of the 
code with made-up data in the same structure as yours, the term appears 
works fine.  Since it?s a relatively new addition to our toolkit, I 
think the most likely explanation is that you have an old version of 
ergm loaded? You can find out which with sessionInfo().    I have ergm 
3.2.4 and the following code works just fine:

library(ergm)
mat <- matrix(0,952,952)
net<-network(mat, bipartite=545, directed=F)
net<- san(net~edges,target.stats=2137)
net
district1 <- sample(2:8, 952, replace=T)
set.vertex.attribute(net, "district1", district1)
myergm <- ergm(net ~ edges + b1nodematch("district1"))

My other guess was that maybe you had missing values in your district1 
attribute, and the error message was triggered by that, even if it 
pointed to a different problem.  But it appears that the attribute works 
just fine with missing data as well:

set.vertex.attribute(net, "district1", district1, v=c(1:20))
myergm <- ergm(net ~ edges + b1nodematch("district1"))

If it does turn out to be an old version, then either of the following 
should help:

update.packages(?statnet?)
update.packages(?ergm?)

Let us know if that solves the problem.

Yours,
Steve

Greetings everyone,

I am working with a bipartite network (545 Actors X 407 Events). At present, I am having trouble getting ergm to recognize the network as bipartite. When I attempt to model using ergm, I receive the following error message:

> ergm(net ~ edges + b1nodematch("district1?))

> net<-network(mat, bipartite=545)
>

 Network attributes:
  vertices = 952
  directed = FALSE
  hyper = FALSE
  loops = FALSE
  multiple = FALSE
  bipartite = 545
  total edges= 2137
    missing edges= 0
    non-missing edges= 2137

 Vertex attribute names:
    vertex.names


I am just getting started with the statnet suite so this is a true beginner?s mistake. More generally, is there a good guide or tutorial for dealing specifically with bipartite networks in statnet that anyone can recommend for a beginner?

Steve Oliver

messages.subject: [statnet_help] how to have both directed and undirected edges?
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] how to have both directed and undirected edges?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Andreas,

"directed-ness" is a network-level property.  So if your network 
contains directed edges, all of the edges must be directed, and you will 
have to represent mutual ties with one edge in each direction as you 
suggest.

You can set a network's 'directed' attribute to FALSE, which means that 
all edges will be considered undirected.

myNet%n%'directed'<-FALSE

If you are generating a 'multiplex' network, in which there is the 
possibility of having more than one edge (of different types) you will 
probably want to set the 'multiple' property to TRUE.


 > network.initialize(50,directed = TRUE,multiple = TRUE)
  Network attributes:
   vertices = 50
   directed = TRUE
   hyper = FALSE
   loops = FALSE
   multiple = TRUE
   bipartite = FALSE
   total edges= 0
     missing edges= 0
     non-missing edges= 0

  Vertex attribute names:
     vertex.names

No edge attributes


If you need to be able to distinguish the various types of edges you 
should set some sort of type attribute on the edges as well.

best,
  -skye

messages.subject: [statnet_help] how to combine several networks
messages.body_plain:
Hello Andreas,

I am a fellow statnet user, not a developer, but I have an idea that might be worth trying.

I'd start by combining the node lists 'nodes.N1' and 'nodes.N2':
nodes.N <- c(nodes.N1, nodes.N2)

N <- network.initialize(nodes.N)

Then combine the edgeliststs by 'edges.N1 <-network.edgelist(N1)', and 'edges.N2 <- network.edgelist(N2)'.
edges.N <- rbind(edges.N1, edges.N2)

Add these edges to the large network N
add.edges(N, edges.N)

I think the above code should merge the two small network datasets into one large one. I'd be curious to hear if the above works.

Aditya Khanna
University of Chicago

if person X and Y turn out to be the same, I combine them and their connections into 1 person).

N1+N2 vertices. It seems like it should be simple, but I just can't find

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] single ergm for multiple networks follow-up
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tom,

What you are describing is essentially the same data structure as in a 
TERGM (*not* STERGM) without temporal dependencies, a.k.a. pooled ERGM. 
See here for details: 
http://people.reed.edu/~ahm//polnet2015/TERGM%20Workshop%20Leifeld%202015-06-17/btergm-paper.pdf

This can be conveniently estimated using the xergm package, more 
specifically the btergm function (for pseudolikelihood estimation with 
bias correction via bootstrapping) and the mtergm function (for MCMC 
MLE). Both have the same syntax and model terms as the ergm function 
because ergm's model specification is used internally (i.e., you can 
integrate it in your statnet workflow). Multiple networks are handed 
over to the formula by wrapping them in a list. No need to use 
structural zeros with this approach.

Your example can be respecified as follows:

library("statnet")
net1 <- network(10, directed=T, density=.2)
net2 <- network(8, directed=T, density=.2)
library("xergm")
l <- list(net1, net2)
m1 <- btergm(l ~ edges + mutual)  # or m1 <- mtergm(l ~ edges + mutual)

If you need to control for differential tie probability of nodes across 
networks, this is essentially a dependency across networks that can be 
implemented via edgecov terms (like a fixed effect). Temporal 
dependencies are described in the paper referenced above. E.g., you can 
provide a list of matrices where 1 indicates a specific actor (in all 
matrices in the list). Note that this requires as many edgecov terms as 
there are unique nodes, but perhaps you don't need this for all actors. 
Random effects such as the ones you are describing are currently not 
implemented. I have never used hergm before, so I cannot comment on its 
ability to do this.

Best,
Philip

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGM Dyadic Covariate Issue
messages.body_plain:
Maureen,

Given the number of terms in your model, and esp. the number of 
dyadic-dependent terms, relative to the information in your data (11 
replicates of 81 tie variables), I'm guessing one problem is that you 
don't have enough data to fit all of these terms.  I'd be worried in 
particular about the combination of twopaths and 2star terms here, as 
these types of terms tend to be less stable in small nets.

But in the first example, the 1.0 correlation between the edges and 
dyadcov suggests you have a more basic problem. Since I can't see what is 
in Behaviors_matrix.csv file, I can't replicate what you have, but see if 
your dyadcov is identical (or nearly identical) to your outcome variable 
by running a correlation on them alone.

Have you tried to fit some smaller models, and then build up the 
additional terms to see when the problem arises?

best,
Martina

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Fitting a model
messages.body_plain:
Srecko, the syntax for nodemix is:

nodemix(attrname, base)

So, in your case it sounds like this should be

nodemix("fail_count_factor")

To get the default model, which omits the last category for the reference 
group.

In order to create a special reference category, I'd suggest you do a bit 
of exploratory work first:

mixingmatrix("fail_count_factor")

To look at the mixing pattern that nodemix will be representing

And then to see how nodemix works:

summary(gnsocial ~ nodemix("fail_count_factor"))
summary(gnsocial ~ nodemix("fail_count_factor", base=1))
summary(gnsocial ~ nodemix("fail_count_factor", base=c(0,1))

etc.

Note that once you put an edges term in, you've used a degree of freedom, 
so you'll have one less for the nodemix term

summary(gnsocial ~ edges + nodemix("fail_count_factor"))

Basically, learn to use the terms, and make sure you understand what they 
do.

hth,
Martina

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Visualizing a Changing Social Network
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

My name is Kate Chandler and I am a masters student at the University of British Columbia.  I would like to visualize a social network that changes over time, so that it looks something like this<http://www.archivalscience.ca/communities.gif> (you might need Chrome to view it, and the visualization starts after a couple of seconds.)

I am using a subset of the Enron Email Dataset, which includes only the top ten emailers.  You can see this dataset here<http://www.archivalscience.ca/enron_bigplayers.csv>.

My previous attempts to visualize this data has been confusing to the viewer, because the layout switches the position of the vertices from one time frame to another.  My previous attempts to visualize the network are visible here <http://www.archivalscience.ca/igraph.gif> (igraph static images of time-based subsets of the dataset shown one after the other) and here <http://www.archivalscience.ca/bigplayers_movie.gif> (ndtv animation).

To make clear the changing social network, I plan to create custom software.  So far, this is my general strategy:

First, run the igraph's fastgreedy algorithm on time-based subsets of the dataset, and for each subset run the igraph function "community(fg)" which creates a list of groups of vertices.  Then, get the program to randomly select a vertex within a group and assign it a set of coordinates.  The other vertices in this group would be given an offset of this original coordinate so that the entire group is positioned together on the graph.  This would be repeated for all groups of vertices.

In the next increment of the dataset, the program would again begin with the same first selected vertex of each group, and would again put vertices of the same group close to one another together.  Vertices which have left their original group to form new groups, should be shown as moving from their parent group toward their new group.

So I am trying to figure out several things: how to assign a coordinate to a vertex, how to assign an off-set coordinate to vertices in the same group, and how to animate the movement of vertices away from their parent group.

Any ideas or suggestions would be much appreciated.

Kate Chandler

Candidate, MAS/MLIS
School of Library, Archival, and Information Studies
University of British Columbia
Email: kate.chandler@ubc.ca<mailto:kate.chandler@ubc.ca>

Hi Martina,

I think I finally figured out most of the details. Already did a few
interesting analysis and starting to get much better understanding of
ERGMs. However, I was wondering about one general thing, that again could
be quite obvious. Let's say we have two factors - gender and the level of
education (graduate, undergraduate). If I was going to fit a generalized
linear mixed-model (for example), I would try to fit something like
outcome~gender+level+some_random_effect. Both, gender and the level would
be in the same model (if that model is a good fit, of course). But, what
would be the approach here if I want to examine whether there is a
homophily effect between males/females and, on the other hand, between
grads and undergrads?

That is, should I try to fit *graph~edges+nodematch("gender")* and
*graph~edges+nodematch("level"),* and perhaps explain these two effects
separately. Or, should I try fitting
*graph~edges+nodematch("gender")+nodematch("level")*, assess the goodness
of fit and try to interpret this model?

Again, apologize if this is too obvious.

Best,
Srecko

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ergm's that adjust for network size and composition effects
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] ergm's that adjust for network size and composition effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi Statnet community,

I have been working with some agent-based modelers, and I received a question from them that I didn't know the answer to. Can one of you please help out? The question pertains to Pavel and colleagues' 2011 paper, Adjusting for network size and composition effect, and is quoted below.


One of the points that the Krivitsky et al. - 2011 paper made was how the network statistics are derived from an egocentric census. E.g., network level properties calculated via f(x_i,x_j) are slightly modified when considering egos and alters (equation 4), whereas actor level statistics are unchanged (equation 5). So this got me thinking about the types of statistics that can be extracted from not just a single level egocentric sample, but what if you ask the alters who THEY talked to etc. (i.e., snowball or forest fire sampling) and if there were any assumptions that Krivitsky's paper makes that would need  to be adjusted to include those. Specifically, in their discussion section they state:
"We limit our statistics to first- and second-order effects - dyadic and degree distribution effects - and do not discuss third-order effects such as triad-closure bias, and while two of the notions of locality that we describe allow modeling of such effects, we do not examine the properties of these in the presence of an offset, because the egocentrically sampled data available do not contain information about such effects."
This is what prompted my question about any follow up work that they've done in this area, as they hinted at wanted to do something in the future (at that time, and maybe in the past now!).

Thanks,
Aditya Khanna
University of Chicago

> btergm.se function therefore generally prints a warning message). That said, 
> you can also use the mtergm function to compute estimates and uncertainty

messages.body_plain:
Hi

I noticed that vcov() doesn't return a variance/covariance matrix of a
model fit with btergm of the xergm package. I tried to write few lines of
code to compute it (based on the formula for the logistic regression). Can
anyone confirm that the code is correct? Is there any substantial reason
for not implementing vcov() for btergm objects?

require(xergm)

mod_xergm <- mod_xergm(...)

X <- as.matrix(mod_xergm@effects)
beta.hat <- as.matrix(coef(mod_xergm))

require(slam)

p <- 1/(1+exp(-X %*% beta.hat))
V <- simple_triplet_zero_matrix(dim(X)[1])
diag(V) <- p*(1-p)
IB <- matprod_simple_triplet_matrix(t(X), V) %*% X
varcov_mat <- solve(IB)

Thanks!

Francesco

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGM Dyadic Covariate Issue
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

My name is Maureen McCusker, and I?m a graduate student at Virginia Tech, earning my Ph.D. in I/O Psychology. First of all, thank you for making yourselves available. I am writing to you because I have been working on on a project running an ERGM model for several months and have been struggling with my dyadic covariate term. To give you a little background, I am analyzing some data on dyadic leadership perceptions within 11 teams of 9, where the outcome is a dichotomous rating. In addition to several other predictors in the model (icov, ocov, absdiff), my model includes 2 edcov terms: the structural zero matrix, reflecting the teams, and the directed dyadic covariate. I have seen the dyadic covariate matrix read into R using run using two different codes, and I am receiving error codes for both (please see below).  I am wondering if you might be able to tell me which is the correct R code for dyadic covariates, and for the correct one, what the error code means.

For the following code, Beh is the dyadic covariate term.  

1. The first code I?m using simply reads the data in as a CSV, converts it to a matrix, and then converts it to a network. In the ERGM code itself, I run the network in as an edcov term (see this below). When I run this method, the dyadic covariate term is HIGHLY unstable and changes values as signs with a slight change in the parameters, such MCMC sample size. I also receive a message stating that I likely have highly correlated terms, which is what I assume is driving the instability in the dyadic covariate term. When I check MCMC Diagnostics, I find that the dyadic covariate and the edges term are perfectly correlated at 1.0. I know there have been some recent findings that ERGM may have some issues with small groups and also that there are potentially some problems with highly correlated model terms. If this is the correct way to run the dyadic covariate term, do you have any ideas of how I can fix this issue?  R Code: 
#reading behavior file

Beh <- read.csv("Behaviors_Matrix.csv", header = FALSE)

Beh.mat1<-as.matrix(Beh)

Beh.mat2<-apply(Beh.mat1,1,as.numeric)

Beh.mat2[is.na(Beh.mat2)]<-0

Beh.mat2

Beh.net <-as.network.matrix(Beh.mat2,directed=T,matrix.type="adjacency?)

And then here is the ERGM: 

New_Model_2_beh_2<-ergm(DV.net ~edges+ostar(2)+ mutual + twopath + istar(2) + edgecov(Struc_Zero.net) + edgecov(tasks.net)+ nodeocov("Dom")+nodeocov("Self_Eff")+nodeicov("SAT_Tot") +nodeicov("Dom") +nodeicov("Self_Eff") +nodeicov("Self_Mon") + absdiff("Self_Mon")+absdiff("Dom") + dyadcov(Beh.net), eval.loglik=TRUE,  seed=20, burnin=2000, interval=50, MCMCsamplesize=100000, maxit=10, control=control.ergm(steplength=.25))

summary(New_Model_2_beh_2)

2. The second way I?m running the model is similar to the way that another researcher, who I know also posted on Statnet_help regarding a similar issue back in February, ran hers. When I do it this way, I receive the same error message she received (In m[tl[!nal] + (hl[!nal] - 1) * network.size(x)] <- val[!nal] : number of items to replace is not a multiple of replacement length). Using this strategy, I first create a megamatrix of all possible ties, then I run in a matrix of all the dyadic ?attributes? to assign to the ties, then I assign attributes to the ?all-possible ties" matrix. The edgecov term in the ERGM is also different. Please see below: 

#reading behavior file
Beh <- read.csv("Behaviors_Matrix.csv", header = FALSE)
Beh.mat1<-as.matrix(Beh)
Beh.mat2<-apply(Beh.mat1,1,as.numeric)
Beh.mat2[is.na(Beh.mat2)]<-0 
Beh.mat2
Beh.net <-as.network.matrix(Beh.mat2,directed=T,matrix.type="adjacency")
summary(Beh.net)

#making all possible ties matrix: 
Poss_ties<- read.csv("poss_ties_mat2.csv", header = FALSE) 
Poss_ties.mat1<-as.matrix(Poss_ties)
Poss_ties.mat2<-apply(Poss_ties.mat1, 1, as.numeric)
Poss_ties.net<-as.network.matrix(Poss_ties,directed=F,matrix.type="adjacency?)

#assigning behaviors to possible ties 
set.edge.attribute(Poss_ties.net,"Beh.net",Beh.net)

The ERGM for strategy 2 is then as follows: 
New_Model_2<-ergm(DV.net ~edges+ostar(2)+ mutual + twopath + istar(2) + edgecov(tasks.net) + edgecov(Poss_ties.net,attrname="Beh.net")+ edgecov(Struc_Zero.net) + nodeocov("Dom")+nodeocov("Self_Eff")+nodeicov("SAT_Tot") +nodeicov("Dom") +nodeicov("Self_Eff") +nodeicov("Self_Mon") + absdiff("Self_Mon")+absdiff("Dom"), eval.loglik=TRUE,  seed=20, burnin=3000, interval=50, MCMCsamplesize=50000, maxit=10, control=control.ergm(steplength=.25))

As you can see, for both of these strategies, I employ a structural zero matrix. The structural zero matrix has given me problems since i started because the output because the output produces a ?-INF? estimate and NA for standard errors. Perhaps this is part of the issue. 


Thank you in advance for your help.

Maureen

Hi Statnet community,

I have been working with some agent-based modelers, and I received a question from them that I didn?t know the answer to. Can one of you please help out? The question pertains to Pavel and colleagues? 2011 paper, Adjusting for network size and composition effect, and is quoted below.


One of the points that the Krivitsky et al. - 2011 paper made was how the network statistics are derived from an egocentric census. E.g., network level properties calculated via f(x_i,x_j) are slightly modified when considering egos and alters (equation 4), whereas actor level statistics are unchanged (equation 5). So this got me thinking about the types of statistics that can be extracted from not just a single level egocentric sample, but what if you ask the alters who THEY talked to etc. (i.e., snowball or forest fire sampling) and if there were any assumptions that Krivitsky?s paper makes that would need  to be adjusted to include those. Specifically, in their discussion section they state:
?We limit our statistics to first- and second-order effects ? dyadic and degree distribution effects ? and do not discuss third-order effects such as triad-closure bias, and while two of the notions of locality that we describe allow modeling of such effects, we do not examine the properties of these in the presence of an offset, because the egocentrically sampled data available do not contain information about such effects.?
This is what prompted my question about any follow up work that they?ve done in this area, as they hinted at wanted to do something in the future (at that time, and maybe in the past now!).

Thanks,

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Specifying missing/unobserved edges in a network object
messages.body_plain:
HI Pavel,

Thanks for your response. I paraphrase the problem in a hypothetical scenario below.

Consider 30 participants recruited for a public health study. We have information on their online Facebook network, say they are connected to a  total of 130 individuals. Thus, we have information on all ties for the first 30 individuals, but for the next 100, we only know of their tie(s) to the 30 participants. We have no information on the ties that might exist between these 100 individuals. 

I am interested in identifying sets of most "central" nodes (via different algorithms, eg. betweenness, bridging, key player, etc). But our assessment of such centralities will be incorrect because we don't have information on all edges in the network. Therefore, one possible approach is to use ergm's to model the unobserved edges, between the 100 Facebook friends of the study participants, to get a complete picture of the network, before applying graph centrality algorithms. 

I thought one way to mark edges as being unobserved is in the `network` package, by setting the value of an edge equal to NA, as opposed to 0 or 1. For a network object `net`, if I wanted to mark an edge between nodes i and j as NA, I could do the following:

net.edges[i,j, add.edges=TRUE] <- NA

If I iterate the above process between all nodes that have unobserved ties, the goal is accomplished, in theory at least. In practice, given the size of Facebook networks, the above process is simply too slow. I didn't see a need here to write a custom MH proposal, but maybe I am missing something?

Thanks,
Aditya

messages.body_plain:
Hi statnet list, Aditya,

As I've already run into this error and it took some reading to find out where it came from, I'll share this here. It could be useful to anyone running jobs on a cluster.
Note that it is not specific to ERGM libraries, but rather to the Rscript call.
See ?Rscript:
"--default-packages=list
where list is a comma-separated list of package names or NULL. Sets the environment variable R_DEFAULT_PACKAGES which determines the packages loaded on startup. The default for Rscript omits methods as it takes about 60% of the startup time."

The function being called during the summary ends up calling findFunction, which has not been loaded since the "methods" library hasn't been loaded.
Quick fix is to load it by hand at the beginning of your file.R with library(methods)

Hope that helps,
Thomas

messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

Just a quick update to say that the statnet team has released the alpha 
version of the 'tsna' (Temporal Social Network Analysis) pack to CRAN.
The new package has:

* Code for finding forward temporal paths through networks which will 
hopefully serve as the basis of lots of extensions of centrality measures.
* Tools for evaluating durations of ties, rates of change, etc
* Measures of sequence (Gibson?s p-shifts) from the relevent package
* Static projections of dynamic networks
* And of course it has wrappers for evaluating standard ?static? SNA 
metrics at multiple time points and returning a time series (using the 
ergm and sna packages).

A vignette for tsna is located here:
http://cran.fhcrc.org/web/packages/tsna/vignettes/tsna_vignette.html

please let me know if you have questions or see issues :-)


Yesterday we also released an update to the 'ndtv' package for 
visualizing temporal networks. It has some neat new features, including 
the ability to easily embed animations as widgets in Rmarkdown 
documents. I wrote a blog post with a quick overview here: 
http://skyeome.net/wordpress/?p=775

And a heads up, we've been previwing a new ergm release and hope to have 
it up to CRAN very soon.  In addition to bug fixes and features, this 
will get rid of the warnings like:

"Warning: replacing previous import by ?network::as.edgelist.network? 
when loading ?tergm?"

which you may have been seeing due to the migration of some functions 
from ergm to network in the last network release.

best,
  -skye
