messages.subject: [statnet_help] Complex ERG Model
messages.body_plain:
Dear statnet community,

I recently acquired data from an online political debate network, and I 
would like to analyze it with a somewhat complex erg model. The network 
comprises 3 different directed link types, which I want to analyze like 
separate networks. Furthermore, I want to distinguish between 3 
different political situations (before elections, before referenda, and 
other periods; each situation comprises several different time 
intervals). Basically, I am interested in comparing the strength of 
several homophily parameters a) across the 3 different linkstypes and b) 
across the 3 different situations. Basically, my hpothesis is that 
homophily will be strongest before elections and weakest before 
referenda, and that this effect in turn varies with link type. I already 
implemented this model as a logistic regression, by simply merging the 
dyad lists of all 9  combinations of the 3 link types and 3 situations, 
and including them as dummy variables. The outcomes supported my 
hypotheses, but now I would like to see if I can reproduce them in an 
ergm including parameters for reciprocity and triadic closure. At the 
moment, however, I am only able to do this by computing a separate ergm 
for each of the 9 combinations. This is of course also problematic since 
it ignores that a link formed in one period might form a triad with a 
two-path from a previous period. Additionally, while I can rertieve 
homophily parameters from every combination and compare them, I have no 
comprehensive test of whether they really vary in strength according to 
my hypotheses. I would be very glad for hints of how to combine this in 
one big model - Thanks!

Simon Schweighofer,
PhD candidate at Chair of Systems Design,
ETH Zurich

messages.subject: [statnet_help] STERGM and bipartite networks
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Richard,
> Specific to my case: I'm still trying to figure out how to implement
> an ergm for a bipartite network with continuous node covariates
> similar to the b1factor ergm term - something like b1nodecov or some
> such.
That looks like an omission that we probably should remedy in the next
release. For the moment, the following workaround should work. Let b1x
be a vector of actors' covariates, b2x be a vector of events'
covariates, and nw the response network. If you set it up as follows:
nw %v% "b1x" <- c(b1x, rep(0, network.size(nw)-(nw%n%"bipartite")))
nw %v% "b2x" <- c(rep(0, nw%n%"bipartite"), b2x)
then
ergm(nw ~ nodecov("b1x") + nodecov("b2x"))
should fit the model with b1 covariate and b2 covariate, because the
covariate for the b2s in b1x would be all 0s and vice versa. (Of
course, you don't have to put both terms in the model.)
				I hope this helps,
				Pavel


--

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Interaction between a nodefactor variable and a network statistic?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mathijs,

Some of the model terms have an "attrname" argument, e.g., 
transitiveties(attrname=NULL) or triangle(attrname=NULL). Have you 
checked if this can be used for your purposes?

If not, you may want to look up the concept of a change statistic (for 
example, in Snijders/Pattison/Robins/Handcock 2006; 
Anderson/Wasserman/Crouch 1999 and others).

In principle, it should be possible to compute the Hadamard product 
(i.e., element-wise product) of the covariate matrix and the matrix 
containing the change statistic and include that as an interaction term 
in your model. However, you may need to compute the change statistic 
manually or dig really deep into the code of the ergm package to compute 
the change statistic directly.

Best regards

Philip

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Variance/covariance matrix from btergm model of xergm package
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Variance/covariance matrix from btergm model of xergm package
messages.body_plain:
Hi Francesco,

Note that xergm is not part of statnet. We should probably continue to 
discuss this bilaterally as I don't want to hijack the statnet-help list 
for xergm-related questions.

btergm corrects the uncertainty measures of the MPLE estimates by means 
of bootstrapping because the standard errors are otherwise inherently 
biased. So it's probably a bad idea to compute anything related to 
uncertainty from mod_xergm@effects. The bootstrapping results are saved 
in mod_xergm@bootsamp, but I don't know if that's helpful: E.g., I wrote 
a btergm.se function a while ago, which computes standard errors from 
that, but they are only valid if the samples are normally distributed, 
which is not always the case (the btergm.se function therefore generally 
prints a warning message). That said, you can also use the mtergm 
function to compute estimates and uncertainty measures for TERGMs via 
MCMC MLE. It is just going to be prohibitively slow for anything larger 
than a few networks, which is why I wrote btergm in the first place. 
mtergm returns an ergm object, and I believe there is a vcov method 
available for ergm objects.

Best,
Philip

> Rscript call.
> See ?Rscript:
> "--default-packages=list
> where list is a comma-separated list of package names or NULL. Sets
> the environment variable R_DEFAULT_PACKAGES which determines the
> packages loaded on startup. The default for Rscript omits methods as

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] [Help] Interpret alpha and decay of GW-terms; how to improve GOF for in-degree
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

When fitting models that have gwesp, gwdsp, gwidegree, and gwodegree with
their alphas and decays not fixed (i.e. fixed=FALSE), I have the following
models and results:

Model 1: fixed alphas of shared partners terms

inflNet ~ edges +  gwdsp(0.2, fixed = TRUE) + gwesp(0.2, fixed = TRUE) +
gwidegree(1) +
    gwodegree(1)

gwdsp.fixed.0.2          -0.04752    0.02463      1  0.0536 .
gwesp.fixed.0.2           0.25211    0.10553      5  0.0169 *
gwidegree                -0.86060    0.34143      1  0.0117 *
gwidegree.decay           0.94548    0.50543      1  0.0614 .
gwodegree                -2.30413    0.40254      1  <1e-04 ***
gwodegree.decay           1.03374    0.16190      1  <1e-04 ***

Model 2: fixed decays of degree distributions terms (also increased the
decays from 1 to 2, and I found these increases do not produce much
difference)

inflNet ~ edges + gwdsp(0.2) + gwesp(0.2) + gwidegree(2, fixed = TRUE) +
gwodegree(2, fixed = TRUE)

gwdsp                    -0.06876    0.02298      0 0.00277 **
gwdsp.alpha              -1.04984    0.15941      1 < 1e-04 ***
gwesp                     0.22824    0.10061      0 0.02330 *
gwesp.alpha              -0.83378    0.35282      1 0.01812 *
gwidegree                -1.48455    0.36201      1 < 1e-04 ***
gwodegree                -2.70058    0.23600      0 < 1e-04 ***

I have four questions:
1) How should I interpret the alphas and decays if they are not fixed? If
the term's effect is significant but the decay is not (e.g. gwidegree in
Model 1), should I interpret that the term's effect is also not significant?

2) When gwdsp and gwesp in Model 1 have their alphas fixed, only
gwesp.fixed.0.2 is significant. But when the alphas are not fixed like in
Model 2, both gwdsp and gwesp and their alphas are significant. Could you
please explain why this happened?

3) Regarding calculating GOF, I found there are two functions gof() and
gof.ergm(), and most ERGM tutorials that I foud use gof(). Is there any
difference between these two functions?

4) Also regarding GOF, it appears that I have many issues with the GOF for
in-degree (the others are fine)

Goodness-of-fit for in-degree

   obs min   mean max MC p-value

8    0   0   2.91   8       0.08 (underestimate - borderline)
9    0   0   1.40   6       0.56 (underestimate - borderline)
10   0   0   0.51   3       1.00
11   0   0   0.33   3       1.00
12   0   0   0.20   2       1.00
13   0   0   0.14   1       1.00
14   0   0   0.02   1       1.00
16   0   0   0.01   1       1.00

What should I do to improve the GOF for in-degree? I read a tutorial that
suggests adding degree() term to control for the over- or underestimated
degrees, and I have tried adding istar(7) with the hopes to fix it but
failed.

Great thanks in advance.

All the best,
Duy

I asked a similar question couple of years ago:
http://mailman13.u.washington.edu/mailman/htdig/statnet_help/2010/000710.html

In general ERGMs are not GLMs: you can calculate tie probabilities
*conditional on the rest of the graph*. You can also simulate a bunch
of networks from the model and for each dyad calculate proportion of
realizations in which there was a tie in this dyad.

> On Apr 23, 2016, at 12:43 PM, Steven Goodreau <goodreau@uw.edu> wrote:
> 
> Hello Jesse-
> 
> Alas, it sounds like you have discovered the wonders of model degeneracy -- that is, you've specified a model where even the true maximum likelihood estimates for the model would be so unlikely to produce the observed network that the estimation algorithm is unable to converge. This is a challenge with network models, where the intuition we bring from simple linear models is often confounded by the complex dependence in our data and among our model terms. And unlike in linear world, where starting with a simple model and building complexity is generally guaranteed to work, here a simple model can often be the source of the problem, because it doesn't capture the real-world processes that offset one another to prevent our social worlds from going off in one direction or another.
> 
> You might find it useful to go through the ERGM tutorial if you haven't before, and see the advice we give for diagnosing degeneracy:
> 
> https://statnet.org/trac/wiki/Sunbelt2016#WorkshopMaterials <https://statnet.org/trac/wiki/Sunbelt2016#WorkshopMaterials>
> 
> You could also read up a lot more in depth on the statistical underpinnings of degeneracy if you wish, using resources pointed to on the statnet wiki.  I suspect your more immediate concern is finding a model that fits - and this group has a lot of built-up knowledge that they may offer. messages.subject: [statnet_help] Microstructure of brokerage
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Andrew -

It is not obvious how one would be able to infer matchmaking brokerage 
from cross-sectional data, since it cannot be distinguished from any 
other form of clustering (and, in some cases, eliminates the evidence of 
its own pre-condition - i.e., after i brokers the formation of the {j,k} 
edge, the {i,j} and {i,k} edges may break).  I can imagine some very 
clever tricks using supplemental data in special cases, but as a general 
matter I suspect that it is impossible.  If you are interested in 
detecting the evidence of processes like matchmaking, you are going to 
need dynamic data.  (See e.g. Spiro et al. (Social Networks, 2013) for a 
discussion of some of the issues involved in assessing dynamic versus 
static brokerage.)

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
Hi, John -

You asked for our opinions on the issue of degeneracy, and you obtained 
one: (1) building good models in any complex system is a challenging 
task that requires knowledge of how the model class operates; (2) ERGMs 
are no exception; and (3) if you put together a bad model (e.g. the 
example that was offered) you will get poor results.  My comments 
regarding the necessity of learning and practice were made in response 
to your own claims to be a newcomer, your evident concern at the 
behavior of a very well-studied model class (see, e.g. Snijders's 2002 
JoSS paper for details on the edge/k-star family), and your apparent 
concern that failure to obtain a good model on a first try implies that 
the whole approach is broken.  I would be inclined to take those 
comments positively - i.e., this _is_ a learnable task, and indeed there 
are many exciting and intriguing things to discover - but they are 
relating a basic fact that you can celebrate or decry as you choose.

Substantively, Steve and Martina have made some very excellent comments 
on the modeling issues, which underscore some of the things to which one 
needs to attend in building good models.  The many threads in the 
current literature regarding model parameterization are an outgrowth of 
these important and hard-won lessons, and to understand this new work it 
is likewise necessary to know something about the foundational 
challenges that all such modeling efforts face.  (This knowledge is also 
important for sorting out the sometimes dubious claims that are made 
regarding what constitutes an "extension" or a fundamentally alternative 
approach - caveat emptor.)  These are as much substantive theoretical 
challenges as they are technical ones, as Martina, Steve, and many 
others have frequently emphasized: "bad" models generate unrealistic 
behavior because they posit social mechanisms that are themselves 
unrealistic.  As with any complex system, determining what is 
unrealistic in a network model is not trivial, and indeed we are 
learning quite a lot about the social world by studying "bad' models and 
mechanisms!  (I cut my teeth as an agent-based modeler, and my view was 
always that one learned more from the models that failed than from the 
ones that succeeded: there are lots of "obvious" ways to construct a 
system with specified behavior that do not in fact behave as you expect, 
usually for reasons that are clear only after one has banged one's head 
against the proverbial or actual table many times.)  To take the example 
of the edge/k-star/triangle family (which you raised), there were many 
plausible a priori arguments that suggested that such families would 
provide a good characterization of many classes of social networks.  
(See, e.g., the classic dependence arguments of Frank and Strauss 
(1986), although the thread goes back farther than that.)  When it was 
discovered that these models tended to be ill-behaved (a phenomenon of 
which Strauss himself warned in his 1986 SIAM paper), this meant that 
the underlying theoretical rationale for those models - that is, the 
ideas about how, when, and how strongly one edge could affect another - 
had to be revisited.  This has led to a whole slew of interesting 
proposals for alternative specifications, each of which is based on a 
substantively different notion of the mechanisms behind triangulation.  
This represents theoretical progress: the early models helped us learn 
that the world didn't work as we naively expected, and we are now 
investigating other ways that the world might work (with those proposals 
being guided by what we learned from the initial effort).  As of right 
now, it appears that there are several classes of factors that act in 
the real world to inhibit phenomena such as the density explosion, 
including (1) decoupling of edges across social or physical barriers, 
(2) heterogeneity in opportunity structures, and (3) diminishing 
marginal effects of closure on edge formation.  The jury is still out on 
exactly where, when, and how much these factors are active, but I expect 
that we will know more in the coming years as more models get tried, 
more/better data is acquired, and the properties of different 
specifications become better understood.  It's an exciting time to be in 
the field.

Hopefully, the above provides further elaboration of why familiarizing 
oneself with some background information is important for making 
progress with ERGMs (or any other modeling approach), and why I and 
others typically give this advice to newcomers.  It's natural to wander 
into the field, throw together some models that seem intuitively 
sensible (or are mentioned in old papers or more recent papers studying 
pathological models), and accidentally rediscover degeneracy.  This can 
be a useful learning experience (I suggest that everyone play with such 
models!) but can be frustrating if your proximate objective is getting a 
good model for some substantive purpose.  There's nothing unique about 
ERGMs in this regard; for instance, when I first started dabbling in 
molecular dynamics (and I'm still a neophyte in that domain), it took me 
a while to figure out that my proteins kept unfolding because I hadn't 
properly specified the disulfide bonds that were stitching them together 
(oops).  The model wasn't wrong per se - it was predicting what would 
really happen if those bonds got reduced - but it certainly wasn't doing 
what I intended.  (Ditto for getting protonation states right, something 
which can require some significant homework.)  In my experience, most 
folks readily expect that they will need to learn about such things to 
model physical systems, but some are surprised that modeling social 
networks also requires one to develop a deeper understanding of the 
underlying technical and substantive issues.  Indeed, this is the case.  
The good news, however, is that there _is_ more to learn than there was 
say, 15 years ago.  The science continues to advance.

Ultimately, you should choose the right tool for your problem, and that 
tool might or might not be a stochastic network model in ERGM form.  If 
you elect to work with the latter, the discussion and references posted 
here will hopefully provide you with information that can help you get 
started in this rich and fascinating research area.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
Ah, OK now I understand. That's a cool idea!  As you point out, the time 
in the input file has nothing to do with the speed/duration of the movie 
that will be created (because what if the time units were years!).   The 
speed of the movie is controlled by three things:

1) how you set the slice.par paramters to chop up your movie (i.e. 1 
network = 1 second of time, vs 5 seconds, etc)

2) How many 'in between' animation frames you tell it to render

3) How long it tries to keep each frame on screen


Assuming that you are happy with the movie are getting with your 
settings for (1), the easiest way to make your animation output go 
faster (and jerkier) or slower (and smoother) is to adjust the number of 
'in between' animation frames it renders by setting a value for the 
'tween.frames' parameter (default is 10).

render.animation(myNetwork,render.par=list(tween.frames=1))

vs

render.animation(myNetwork,render.par=list(tween.frames=30))


There is also an option provided by the animation package to set the 
duration that each frame of the animation should remain on screen. By 
default it is set to 1/10th of a second.

ani.options=list(interval=0.1)

oddly, it seems that these default settings actually *should* produce 
movies in which one time unit ~ second on screen if you have your 
slice.par set to break the network into 1 sec bins.  So I think if it 
isn't quite lining up, you may have to do some trial and error 
adjustments until you get it to sync.


BTW, dear list members, if this doesn't scare you off, we will be giving 
a workshop on ndtv and statnet's dynamic network tools at the INSNA 
conference next Tuesday evening.  Perhaps we can convince Jimi to make a 
guest appearance with this video?

best,
  -skye

messages.body_plain:
And just in case Carter's answer isn't long enough for you :)

It's worth making a distinction between the general form of the Markov 
model, and the homogeneous reduced form that most folks are familiar with.

The general specification allows for each configuration (edge, k-star or 
triangle) to have it's own coefficient.  That model is not identifiable. 
In fact, you run out of degrees of freedom on the edges terms alone, since 
each edge would have its own coefficient.

Hence the "simpler" 3 parameter model we've come to know and hate:  the 
edges+2star+triangle model.  It imposes both homogeneity constraints (each 
configuration now has a single coefficent, node labels don't matter 
anymore) and a reduced form from k-stars to 2-stars.

This homogenous reduced form Markov is, we now know, just a bad model. 
It doesn't produce interesting graphs, and it wouldn't produce any of the 
networks we're likely to analyze. Frank and Strauss committed the original 
sin, but the entire field is still learning this lesson.

But I don't think that means the Markov class as a whole is bad.  The 
heterogeniety is there in the class to exploit.  But the way to do it is 
with other effects, like homophily, that introduce interpretable 
heterogeneity into the configurations, and declining marginal returns (as 
Carter notes).

best,
mm

On Sun, 24 Apr 2016, Carter T. Butts wrote:

> Hi, John -
> 
> You asked for our opinions on the issue of degeneracy, and you obtained one: (1) building good models
> in any complex system is a challenging task that requires knowledge of how the model class operates;
> (2) ERGMs are no exception; and (3) if you put together a bad model (e.g. the example that was offered)
> you will get poor results.? My comments regarding the necessity of learning and practice were made in
> response to your own claims to be a newcomer, your evident concern at the behavior of a very
> well-studied model class (see, e.g. Snijders's 2002 JoSS paper for details on the edge/k-star family),
> and your apparent concern that failure to obtain a good model on a first try implies that the whole
> approach is broken.? I would be inclined to take those comments positively - i.e., this _is_ a
> learnable task, and indeed there are many exciting and intriguing things to discover - but they are
> relating a basic fact that you can celebrate or decry as you choose.
> 
> Substantively, Steve and Martina have made some very excellent comments on the modeling issues, which
> underscore some of the things to which one needs to attend in building good models.? The many threads
> in the current literature regarding model parameterization are an outgrowth of these important and
> hard-won lessons, and to understand this new work it is likewise necessary to know something about the
> foundational challenges that all such modeling efforts face.? (This knowledge is also important for
> sorting out the sometimes dubious claims that are made regarding what constitutes an "extension" or a
> fundamentally alternative approach - caveat emptor.)? These are as much substantive theoretical
> challenges as they are technical ones, as Martina, Steve, and many others have frequently emphasized:
> "bad" models generate unrealistic behavior because they posit social mechanisms that are themselves
> unrealistic.? As with any complex system, determining what is unrealistic in a network model is not
> trivial, and indeed we are learning quite a lot about the social world by studying "bad' models and
> mechanisms!? (I cut my teeth as an agent-based modeler, and my view was always that one learned more
> from the models that failed than from the ones that succeeded: there are lots of "obvious" ways to
> construct a system with specified behavior that do not in fact behave as you expect, usually for
> reasons that are clear only after one has banged one's head against the proverbial or actual table many
> times.)? To take the example of the edge/k-star/triangle family (which you raised), there were many
> plausible a priori arguments that suggested that such families would provide a good characterization of
> many classes of social networks.? (See, e.g., the classic dependence arguments of Frank and Strauss
> (1986), although the thread goes back farther than that.)? When it was discovered that these models
> tended to be ill-behaved (a phenomenon of which Strauss himself warned in his 1986 SIAM paper), this
> meant that the underlying theoretical rationale for those models - that is, the ideas about how, when,
> and how strongly one edge could affect another - had to be revisited.? This has led to a whole slew of
> interesting proposals for alternative specifications, each of which is based on a substantively
> different notion of the mechanisms behind triangulation.? This represents theoretical progress: the
> early models helped us learn that the world didn't work as we naively expected, and we are now
> investigating other ways that the world might work (with those proposals being guided by what we
> learned from the initial effort).? As of right now, it appears that there are several classes of
> factors that act in the real world to inhibit phenomena such as the density explosion, including (1)
> decoupling of edges across social or physical barriers, (2) heterogeneity in opportunity structures,
> and (3) diminishing marginal effects of closure on edge formation.? The jury is still out on exactly
> where, when, and how much these factors are active, but I expect that we will know more in the coming
> years as more models get tried, more/better data is acquired, and the properties of different
> specifications become better understood.? It's an exciting time to be in the field.
> 
> Hopefully, the above provides further elaboration of why familiarizing oneself with some background
> information is important for making progress with ERGMs (or any other modeling approach), and why I and
> others typically give this advice to newcomers.? It's natural to wander into the field, throw together
> some models that seem intuitively sensible (or are mentioned in old papers or more recent papers
> studying pathological models), and accidentally rediscover degeneracy.? This can be a useful learning
> experience (I suggest that everyone play with such models!) but can be frustrating if your proximate
> objective is getting a good model for some substantive purpose.? There's nothing unique about ERGMs in
> this regard; for instance, when I first started dabbling in molecular dynamics (and I'm still a
> neophyte in that domain), it took me a while to figure out that my proteins kept unfolding because I
> hadn't properly specified the disulfide bonds that were stitching them together (oops).? The model
> wasn't wrong per se - it was predicting what would really happen if those bonds got reduced - but it
> certainly wasn't doing what I intended.? (Ditto for getting protonation states right, something which
> can require some significant homework.)? In my experience, most folks readily expect that they will
> need to learn about such things to model physical systems, but some are surprised that modeling social
> networks also requires one to develop a deeper understanding of the underlying technical and
> substantive issues.? Indeed, this is the case.? The good news, however, is that there _is_ more to
> learn than there was say, 15 years ago.? The science continues to advance.
> 
> Ultimately, you should choose the right tool for your problem, and that tool might or might not be a
> stochastic network model in ERGM form.? If you elect to work with the latter, the discussion and
> references posted here will hopefully provide you with information that can help you get started in
> this rich and fascinating research area.
> 
> Hope that helps,
> 
> -Carter
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Andreas,

Yes, via edgecov terms. Alternatively, you may theorize about how a 
closure of a tie in the respective network/setting is influenced by 
endogenous properties of the other settings. That is, you could include 
functions of the other network relations other than edgecov terms. For 
example, it may or may not make sense if A and B as well as B and C are 
connected in network relation 1 that this has an impact on A and C being 
connected in the other network relation. In this case, you would create 
a covariate matrix where a value of 1 between A and C indicates that 
there was a two-path between A and C in the other relation. Not sure how 
something like this would translate into a valued network context, but 
that is ultimately a matter of theory building. This is kind of the same 
logic as in a multilevel/multiplex/multirelational ERGM, except that you 
are going to estimate separate ERGMs for each relation because a 
combination of muliplex and valued ERGMs does not exist yet (which is to 
say that this would be more adequate, but it's not doable at this point, 
at least as far as I know). Not sure what your "meta analysis" 
suggestion is about.

Philip

>
>     It sounds like you are looking for a combination of a valued ERGM
>     (e.g., via ergm.count or GERGM) and a multiplex ERGM. As far as I
>     know, that combination does not exist yet. To explore how each of
>     the settings works (as a second-best solution), you can try to model
>     each of them separately for now and include (functions of) the other
>     settings as covariates.
>
>     Note: there is quite some confusion over terminology. Some people
>     call multiplex ERGMs multi-level ERGMs while others reserve that
>     term for things like social-ecological networks where you have
>     multiple node sets AND within- and between-set relations. In some

Dear Fabian,

Is the advice of a pupil to a pupil equivalent to the advice of a
professional to a professional? (Is Xij = 1 qualitatively the same
relationship as Xim = 1? With "i" and "j" being pupils and "m" being a
professional?)

If this is not the case, what you describe sounds to me like a multilevel
network. Here you have both, the unipartite structure of ties between nodes
of the same type (your pupil to pupil advice) and the bipartite structure
of ties between different types of nodes (often used to express affiliation
to organizations - but could also express advice from qualitatively
different types of nodes). It is possible but not necessary to allow links
between the other type of nodes.
It sounds to me that the relationships here are qualitatively different
between different types of nodes but if you simply code them in one matrix
the program cannot see that and they would contribute to the statistics in
the same way that pupil-pupil ties do.
Example: You observe  the following constellations pupil1 -> pupil2, pupil1
-> pupil3, pupil2 -> pupil3 and professional1 -> pupil1, professional1 ->
pupil2. These 5 ties look like 2 transitive triads, however, the triad with
the professional involved should probably not count to the same triad
statistics as the triads with only pupils involved.

Unfortunately I do not have hands on experience with multilevel networks in
statnet. The ERGM package is able to model bipartite networks (I did not
find anything about multilevel) and I assume there is a way to model
multilevel networks in the statnet packages (otherwise MPNet might be an
alternative).

Eventually, I recommend using a multiplex multilevel network. Statnet is
able to handle multiplex networks (multiplex means different types of edges
between nodes).
This, I think, would capture the data in the way you describe it.

For further reading on multilevel networks I recommend this book:

Multilevel Network Analysis for the Social Sciences.

Emmanuel Lazega and Tom A.B. Snijders (eds).

Cham: Springer, 2016. Methodos Series: Methodological Prospects in the
Social Sciences.

ISBN 978-3-319-24518-8

ISBN 978-3-319-24520-1 (eBook)

DOI: 10.1007/978-3-319-24520-1

Best Regards,

Robert Krause

ICS Sociology, PhD Student
University of Groningen
Grote Rozenstraat 31,
Room B119
9712 TG Groningen, The Netherlands

> Hi Fabian,
>
> A TERGM (not STERGM) without any temporal dependencies can be applied to
> multiple separate groups. This essentially reduces to a pooled ERGM.
> Estimation is possible using the xergm package, which builds on many
> statnet functions. There are two estimation strategies: structural zeros in
> an MCMC MLE framework (the mtergm function can do this) and MPLE with
> bootstrapped confidence intervals (use the btergm function to do this). The
> latter is faster but becomes more accurate and less biased with larger
> networks and more groups); the former is more accurate with smaller numbers
> of groups but also prohibitively slow for more than a couple of networks.
> Of course, you can also construct a block-diagonal matrix with off-diagonal
> structural zeros manually and then use the ergm package, which is basically
> what mtergm does for you.
>
> Note, however, that the ERGM or TERGM does not solve the problem with the
> violation of the i.i.d. assumption for you; you must explicitly control for
> network dependencies in your groups for an ERGM to yield results that are
> less biased than a GLM. In other words, just adding density and node
> attributes is likely not enough.
>
> Best,
> Philip

Hey,

I am sorry for reviving the thread, but I did see that Sebastian got any
reply.

The authors of the working paper in question made the claim that SAOMs are
a special case of TERGMs referring to Snijders 2001. And indeed Snijders
2001 (referring to Snijders & van Duijn 1997) shows that if you take a very
specific, unnatural, setting for the rate function you obtain Wassermann's
reciprocity model (1979) -  see:
https://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~snijders/sie_the.pdf page 22. This, however,
does not imply that any other (realistic) SAOM behaves like a (realistic)
ERGMs. Wassermann's reciprocity model is not a well fitting model for most
social networks either. It only shows that there is a mathematical
intersection of both model families.

Best Regards,

Robert Krause

ICS Sociology, PhD Student
University of Groningen
Grote Rozenstraat 31,
Room B119
9712 TG Groningen, The Netherlands

On Thu, Apr 21, 2016 at 12:07 PM, Micha? Bojanowski <michal2992@gmail.com>
wrote:

> This seems to be an old thread. I don't know if Sebastian already
> received some answer off the list... Nevertheless:
>
> @Sebastian, regarding the error messages. I presume the data is an
> undirected network. One thing I notice immediately is that you
> included Sex and Matrilines node-level variables in both nodefactor
> and nodecov terms. This is redundant as nodefactor and nodecov are
> analogous and the only difference is that nodefactor treats the node
> attribute as categorical while nodecov treats it as a continuous
> variable. The difference is analogous to representing an effect of
> some X in linear regression either (1) as is with beta*X or (2) as a
> set of dummy variables with own beta's. I think this is the reason for
> the "MCMLE estimation stuck. There may be excessive correlation
> between model terms" error as both terms are probably linear functions
> of each other. I am not sure about the origin of the first two errors,
> but it may very well be that they are a consequence of the first
> error.
>
> @Robert, thanks for a very interesting summary!! I will be very
> interested to read statnet-core members take on it. Meanwhile, can you
> point me to a paper/publication based on which you wrote your first
> comment about the ERGM vs SAOM and long-run equilibrium and rate
> specification assumptions? I would really like to educate myself in
> that respect.
>
> Best,
> Michal
>
>
>
>
>
>
> On Thu, Apr 21, 2016 at 11:12 AM, Krause, R.W. <r.w.krause@rug.nl> wrote:
> >
> > Dear Sebastian,
> >
> > I have not used TERGMs yet so I cannot help you with this explicit
> error. However, I have some serious concerns with this reasoning for using
> a TERGM instead of SIENA. The working paper (I do not think the paper is a
> published, peer reviewed article - please correct me if I am wrong), has
> some serious flaws.
> >
> > First: SAOMs are not a special case of a TERGM. Both are stochastic
> models of networks but the SAOM only behaves like an ERGM in is long-run
> equilibrium if a very, very unnatural and specific setting for the rate
> function is used. In virtually all real world applications, it does not.
> Also, unlike the ERGM, the SAOM is not typically used to analyse networks
> in equilibrium. The TERGM, however, is special case of an ERGM - an ERGM
> conditioned on another network.
> >
> > Second: Some (Most?) of the critique IN THE ARXIV PAPER against SAOMs is
> equally valid against (T)ERGMs:
> > a) It is absolutely true that SAOMs have problems capturing joint
> actions, as common in politics (i.e. formation of the European Union), but
> the same type of emergence is, as far as I know, hard to model in (T)ERGMs.
> It would require a clique effect, which I have not encountered and I think
> does not exists. SAOMs probably should not be used for joint action
> networks, but this does not apply for your data. (I assume that the
> primates you study behave somewhat like small human social networks.)
> > b) Of course it is unnatural to assume that every single actor has the
> exact same objective function. But the same is true for a (T)ERGM. In a
> SAOM we assume that our parameters model the average decision of the
> average person (given its network position and covariates), in an ERGM we
> assume our parameters capture the formation of an average tie (given its
> network position and covariates). If we do not specify a specific subgroup
> (i.e. by interacting a parameter with a co-variate like gender), both TERGM
> and SAOM assume that processes are similar for all members of the network
> (given their position in it). The (T)ERGM in fact makes stronger
> homogeneity assumptions because not only actors but even all tie variables
> follow the same probabilistic rules!
> > c) Another critique is that SAOMs assume that everyone is aware of the
> whole network state, when they make a decision. As before it is clear that
> this assumption is unnatural, especially in larger networks. But in a
> (T)ERGM the probability of a tie is also dependent on the existence of
> other ties in the network. In terms of information needed, the TERGM and
> the SAOM are no different - only most TERGM papers are silent about this
> complete information assumption, while SAOM papers are more often open
> about it.
> >
> > Third: The simulation part of the paper in section 5 uses quite "weird"
> parameters to compare the model families. Choosing random draws from a
> uniform distribution of -3 to +3 with steps of .001 does not lead to
> meaningful parameters for neither a TERGM nor SAOM. The resulting networks
> will be mostly degenerate or at least will not look like your average
> social network. A simulation should be based on target statistics of a
> network.
> >
> > What I wanted to say is, that the paper has flaws. I am not a
> mathematically trained statistician, like the inventors of ERGMs, TERGMs
> and SAOMs so I am sure that I have some inaccuracies in the way that I
> wrote things down here and I would love to hear what the statnet authors
> and other statisticians/mathematicians or more knowledgeable people have to
> say about this paper. But I am quite sure that SIENA is not a bad choice
> for the type of network you are dealing with. Additionally, if the results
> of TERGM and SAOM differ, I would not know what that meant.
> >
> >
> > A positive thing in SAOMs is that the parameters are time independent
> because it is a continuous time model (TERGM is discrete-time). If you
> observe the same network at  multiple points in time and the underlying
> process is constant, then the parameter estimates of the SAOMs should be
> the same for T1-T2-T3 compared to T1-T3. Or if the time intervals are of
> different length (e.g. First measurements apart by 2 months and later by 6
> months). If your model is well fitting and the process is stable, the
> parameters will be the same, because it is a model of individual decisions.
> The same does not hold TERGMs, as far as I know.
> >
> > I want to emphasize that I do not think that TERGMs are worse than SAOM.
> They are different mathematical models with different goals. One is
> modelling the state of a network given a previous time point and one models
> the process of change. If your interest is in how behavior and social
> relations of primates co-evolve, SAOMs should work fine. If you are
> interested in how the structure of your primate group is, conditioned on a
> previous observation, than TERGMs are the model for you.
> >
> > I am sorry that I cannot help you with your errors, but I wanted to
> re-assure you that your SIENA results could be sufficient after all.
> >
> >
> > Best Regards,
> >
> > Robert Krause
> >
> > ICS Sociology, PhD Student
> > University of Groningen
> > Grote Rozenstraat 31,
> > Room B119
> > 9712 TG Groningen, The Netherlands
> >

This seems to be an old thread. I don't know if Sebastian already
received some answer off the list... Nevertheless:

@Sebastian, regarding the error messages. I presume the data is an
undirected network. One thing I notice immediately is that you
included Sex and Matrilines node-level variables in both nodefactor
and nodecov terms. This is redundant as nodefactor and nodecov are
analogous and the only difference is that nodefactor treats the node
attribute as categorical while nodecov treats it as a continuous
variable. The difference is analogous to representing an effect of
some X in linear regression either (1) as is with beta*X or (2) as a
set of dummy variables with own beta's. I think this is the reason for
the "MCMLE estimation stuck. There may be excessive correlation
between model terms" error as both terms are probably linear functions
of each other. I am not sure about the origin of the first two errors,
but it may very well be that they are a consequence of the first
error.

@Robert, thanks for a very interesting summary!! I will be very
interested to read statnet-core members take on it. Meanwhile, can you
point me to a paper/publication based on which you wrote your first
comment about the ERGM vs SAOM and long-run equilibrium and rate
specification assumptions? I would really like to educate myself in
that respect.

Best,
Michal






On Thu, Apr 21, 2016 at 11:12 AM, Krause, R.W. <r.w.krause@rug.nl> wrote:
>
> Dear Sebastian,
>
> I have not used TERGMs yet so I cannot help you with this explicit error. However, I have some serious concerns with this reasoning for using a TERGM instead of SIENA. The working paper (I do not think the paper is a published, peer reviewed article - please correct me if I am wrong), has some serious flaws.
>
> First: SAOMs are not a special case of a TERGM. Both are stochastic models of networks but the SAOM only behaves like an ERGM in is long-run equilibrium if a very, very unnatural and specific setting for the rate function is used. In virtually all real world applications, it does not. Also, unlike the ERGM, the SAOM is not typically used to analyse networks in equilibrium. The TERGM, however, is special case of an ERGM - an ERGM conditioned on another network.
>
> Second: Some (Most?) of the critique IN THE ARXIV PAPER against SAOMs is equally valid against (T)ERGMs:
> a) It is absolutely true that SAOMs have problems capturing joint actions, as common in politics (i.e. formation of the European Union), but the same type of emergence is, as far as I know, hard to model in (T)ERGMs. It would require a clique effect, which I have not encountered and I think does not exists. SAOMs probably should not be used for joint action networks, but this does not apply for your data. (I assume that the primates you study behave somewhat like small human social networks.)
> b) Of course it is unnatural to assume that every single actor has the exact same objective function. But the same is true for a (T)ERGM. In a SAOM we assume that our parameters model the average decision of the average person (given its network position and covariates), in an ERGM we assume our parameters capture the formation of an average tie (given its network position and covariates). If we do not specify a specific subgroup (i.e. by interacting a parameter with a co-variate like gender), both TERGM and SAOM assume that processes are similar for all members of the network (given their position in it). The (T)ERGM in fact makes stronger homogeneity assumptions because not only actors but even all tie variables follow the same probabilistic rules!
> c) Another critique is that SAOMs assume that everyone is aware of the whole network state, when they make a decision. As before it is clear that this assumption is unnatural, especially in larger networks. But in a (T)ERGM the probability of a tie is also dependent on the existence of other ties in the network. In terms of information needed, the TERGM and the SAOM are no different - only most TERGM papers are silent about this complete information assumption, while SAOM papers are more often open about it.
>
> Third: The simulation part of the paper in section 5 uses quite "weird" parameters to compare the model families. Choosing random draws from a uniform distribution of -3 to +3 with steps of .001 does not lead to meaningful parameters for neither a TERGM nor SAOM. The resulting networks will be mostly degenerate or at least will not look like your average social network. A simulation should be based on target statistics of a network.
>
> What I wanted to say is, that the paper has flaws. I am not a mathematically trained statistician, like the inventors of ERGMs, TERGMs and SAOMs so I am sure that I have some inaccuracies in the way that I wrote things down here and I would love to hear what the statnet authors and other statisticians/mathematicians or more knowledgeable people have to say about this paper. But I am quite sure that SIENA is not a bad choice for the type of network you are dealing with. Additionally, if the results of TERGM and SAOM differ, I would not know what that meant.
>
>
> A positive thing in SAOMs is that the parameters are time independent because it is a continuous time model (TERGM is discrete-time). If you observe the same network at  multiple points in time and the underlying process is constant, then the parameter estimates of the SAOMs should be the same for T1-T2-T3 compared to T1-T3. Or if the time intervals are of different length (e.g. First measurements apart by 2 months and later by 6 months). If your model is well fitting and the process is stable, the parameters will be the same, because it is a model of individual decisions. The same does not hold TERGMs, as far as I know.
>
> I want to emphasize that I do not think that TERGMs are worse than SAOM. They are different mathematical models with different goals. One is modelling the state of a network given a previous time point and one models the process of change. If your interest is in how behavior and social relations of primates co-evolve, SAOMs should work fine. If you are interested in how the structure of your primate group is, conditioned on a previous observation, than TERGMs are the model for you.
>
> I am sorry that I cannot help you with your errors, but I wanted to re-assure you that your SIENA results could be sufficient after all.
>
>
> Best Regards,
>
> Robert Krause
>
> ICS Sociology, PhD Student

> Grote Rozenstraat 31,

(a second question for the day).

Let's consider the famous high school friendship network. Now assume that
student are taking extra-curricular activities such as clubs. Unlike the
"grade" covariate, assume that a student can be affiliated with more than
one club.
I would like to introduce a term (binary/weighted) that reflects the facts
that two students are members of the same club as I suspect that such a
nodematch increase the likelihood of an edge.

I could have a binary nodal attribute for each club then use nodematch for
each of these attributes but (a) I suspect it will be very inefficient and
(b) I don't care about the specific clubs - I only care about the mutual
membership (this can be viewed as another network N based on mutual
membership where N[i,j] = k where k is the number of clubs i and j share
membership to. In a more simplistic scenario k is a binary attribute
indicating if they share any club membership or not).

Is there a way to introduce such a term into an ERGM model (and represent
it as a node attribute of type list) or that I have to add a separate nodal
attribute for each club and introduce a nodematch("<club>") term for each
club?

An alternative way to think about it whether it is possible to have a term
representing *another network* N2, hypothesizing that a (weighted?) tie in
N2 increases the likelihood of observing a tie in the network in question.

Thanks again!

--
Oren Tsur
Network Science Institute, Northeastern University

messages.body_plain:
Hi Shupin,
  I can't speak well about the appropriateness of the model, but from a 
data handling perspective I think you would need to use a term like 
'edgecov' or 'dyadcov' that accepts a matrix of dyadic covariates.  This 
would allow you to have time1 values corresponding to both edges that 
exist and don't exist in time2.  However, you will need to make the 
networks comparable, either by sub-setting both networks to only include 
the vertices present in both (perhaps using get.inducedSubgraph) or 
using xergm's adjust() function as Phillip suggests to scale the t1 
matrix according to the matrix labels in t1 and t2 -- although this will 
require introducing missing data.

If you definitely want to apply the t1 edge attributes to t2 edges, you 
need to be very careful when mapping edge attributes from one network to 
another using %e% to ensure that you are using a matrix of edge values 
and not the vector of values ordered by an arbitrary edgeId. Otherwise 
there is no guarantee that they would get applied to the same dyads. 
You would still need to transform the t1 matrix to match the t2 network, 
but the t1 values corresponding to edges that don't exist in t2 would 
not get recorded since there is no edge to attach them to.

Here is a toy example:

library(network)
t1<-network.initialize(3)
# label the vertices
network.vertex.names(t1)<-c("a","b","c")
# add some edges
t1[1,2]<-1  # 'a-b edge'
t1[2,3]<-1  # 'b-c edge'
# add an attribute
t1%e%'value'<-7

# peek at the matrix
# need to tell it attrname to fill in
as.matrix(t1,attrname='value')

   a b c
a 0 7 0
b 0 0 7
c 0 0 0


t2<-network.initialize(4)
# vertex set will partially overlap with t1
network.vertex.names(t2)<-c("b","c","d","e")
# remember that vertex '1' in t1 is not the same as '1' in t2!
t2[1,2]<-1  # the 'b-c' edge still exists
t2[2,3]<-1  # there is a new 'c-d' edge
as.matrix(t2)

   b c d e
b 0 1 0 0
c 0 0 1 0
d 0 0 0 0
e 0 0 0 0

# do this:
library(xergm.common)
# construct the matrix of t1 values for vertices
# that appear in t2 and fill in NA for missing vertices
t1val<-adjust(as.matrix(t1,attrname = 'value'),t2)
t1val # peek at matrix, notice NAs

    b  c  d  e
b  0  7 NA NA
c  0  0 NA NA
d NA NA NA NA
e NA NA NA NA


# assign the matrix
t2%e%'value'<-t1val
as.matrix(t2,attrname='value')
# notice that the 'b-c' edge took the value 7,
# but the 'c-d' edge is now NA

   b c  d e
b 0 7  0 0
c 0 0 NA 0
d 0 0  0 0
e 0 0  0 0

# DON"T DO THIS:
# tries to break the network object up
# and attach parts of it to random edges (ouch!)
# and so gives error
t2%e%'value'<-t1

# DON'T DO THIS:
# gives error t1 matrix is not same size as t2
t2%e%'value'<-as.matrix(t1)

# THIS WILL SHOOT YOU IN THE FOOT:
# the two edge values from t2 will get applied to the
# two edges in t2, BUT TO THE WRONG EDGES
t2%e%'value'<-t1%e%'value'


If you were working with a longer network time series, I would recommend 
using the networkDynamic package and dynamic network attributes and 
persistent ids as a data model keep everything organized -- but it may 
not be worth the trouble for two time steps.

Hope I didn't just make things more confusing

best,
  -skye

Nope, the esp counts are like degree counts, not like star counts.  Just 
as there are not 2 degree1 nodes in a degree2 node, an esp of 2 means

messages.body_plain:
Duy,

Have you examined the idegree distribution to see if there are any strange 
patterns in it?  You can do that with the summary command.  For example:

summary(net ~ idegree(1:20))

Or you can use the graphics from the gof command for the idegree 
distribution.

In principle, you should conduct exploratory analysis on all of the terms 
in your model -- the same way you would look at the univariate (and 
possibly bivariate) distributions for the covariates in a non-network 
setting.  You want to make sure there are no strange artifacts, inadequate 
cell counts, or just plain errors in the data.  The only difference here 
is that your covariates have to be constructed before you can conduct EDA 
on them.

In your previous email, you sequentially fixed the decay parameters in the 
gw* terms, but the values you chose did not match the values that were 
estimated when they were not fixed.  How did you choose the fixed values?

Finally, if controlling for idegree(7) changes your gw*sp terms to 
insignificant, this means the two are correlated, just as in a standard 
regression context.  There is no single "correct" way to handle this. 
Some might argue that degree terms establish basic constraints for all the 
other terms, and that interpretation is therefore cleaner when you control 
properly for the degree distribution before testing for higher order 
effects (like shared partners).  But Granovetter's classic article on the 
"The Theory Gap in Social Network Analysis" (1979) argued that this may 
not be the right approach, if e.g., the propensity to close triads is 
driving the degree distribution.

hth,
mm

messages.body_plain:
Hi

I have been trying out the ergm package the past day or so. I am exploring knowledge sharing networks and how these relate to innovation.

I have the following complete directed networks (constructed from a binary adjacency matrix):

- knowledge.provider.net
- affect.based.trust.net
- cognition.based.trust
- idea.generation.net
- idea.realisation.net

I postulate that trust is key to knowledge sharing, idea generation and idea implementation. Furthermore, I believe idea generation and idea implementation require knowledge sharing. To test for this I run the following models:

model.01 <- ergm(knowledge.provider.net~edges+
                mutual+
                edgecov(affect.based.trust.net)+
                edgecov(cognition.based.trust.net))

model.02 <- ergm(idea.generation.net~edges+
                mutual+
                edgecov(knowledge.provider.net)+
                edgecov(affect.based.trust.net)+
                edgecov(cognition.based.trust.net))

model.03 <- ergm(idea.realisation.net~edges+
                mutual+
                edgecov(idea.generation.net)+
                edgecov(knowledge.provider.net)+
                edgecov(affect.based.trust.net)+
                edgecov(cognition.based.trust.net))

All three models converge and seem to confirm my postulated hypotheses. There are significant covariate effects (which one can sort of see by examining plotted network graphs).  However, when checking goodness of fit, things start to unravel:

model.01.gof <- gof(model.01~ idegree + odegree + espartners + distance, directed = TRUE)

Some of my p-values are pretty low. So my questions to the list are: did I specify my ergm correctly and what adjustments could I try to improve my goodness of fit?

Thanks.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Structural zeros between most classes of nodes?
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Structural zeros between most classes of nodes?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Fabian,

A TERGM (not STERGM) without any temporal dependencies can be applied to 
multiple separate groups. This essentially reduces to a pooled ERGM. 
Estimation is possible using the xergm package, which builds on many 
statnet functions. There are two estimation strategies: structural zeros 
in an MCMC MLE framework (the mtergm function can do this) and MPLE with 
bootstrapped confidence intervals (use the btergm function to do this). 
The latter is faster but becomes more accurate and less biased with 
larger networks and more groups); the former is more accurate with 
smaller numbers of groups but also prohibitively slow for more than a 
couple of networks. Of course, you can also construct a block-diagonal 
matrix with off-diagonal structural zeros manually and then use the ergm 
package, which is basically what mtergm does for you.

Note, however, that the ERGM or TERGM does not solve the problem with 
the violation of the i.i.d. assumption for you; you must explicitly 
control for network dependencies in your groups for an ERGM to yield 
results that are less biased than a GLM. In other words, just adding 
density and node attributes is likely not enough.

Best,
Philip

messages.body_plain:
Dear statnet users

I would like to determine if there is a difference in
contributions/importance of different classes of nodes between three
directed advice networks.

Basically the data contain three separate networks for different types of
advice. The nodes differ with regards to one categorical attribute (five
distinct classes) and we assume that only nodes in one of these classes
would want to receive advice (let's call these"pupils", while all the
others are professionals of some kind). Pupils can receive advice from each
other, or from any of the other categories. There are 8 pupils and 20 other
nodes.

I'm thinking of modelling this as an ERGM, with a parameter for density and
a node attribute effect on indegree (links pointing where the advice came
from). "Forbidden" relations could be represented with structural zeros,
but my concern is that there are quite many of them. Would this
configuration violate any model assumptions? Or is there a different
approach that you would recommend?

Thanks in advance
Fabian

> Hi Andreas,
>
> It sounds like you are looking for a combination of a valued ERGM (e.g.,
> via ergm.count or GERGM) and a multiplex ERGM. As far as I know, that

> for now and include (functions of) the other settings as covariates.
>
> Note: there is quite some confusion over terminology. Some people call
> multiplex ERGMs multi-level ERGMs while others reserve that term for things
> like social-ecological networks where you have multiple node sets AND
> within- and between-set relations. In some parts of the literature (mainly

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Steps to develop an ERG model
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Steps to develop an ERG model
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am confused about the steps to develop an ERG model.

I read the paper "An introduction to exponential random graph (p*) models
for social networks" by Robins et al. (2007), and they explained the five
steps to construct a model. It reads to me that one would start by
constructing a model with (possibly) many terms/configurations that reflect
the hypotheses (Step 3), and then reduce/constrain the parameters to
achieve a more parsimonious model (Step 4). By doing this way, I imagine
that only one final model should be reported in a study.

However, I found quite a number of ERGM studies which constructed multiple
models and compare them. Specifically, they constructed a baseline model
which only has the "edges" term, then a "Pure Attributes" model which
describes homophily effects, then a "Structural" model (which either adds
new structural terms to the previous model or serves a standalone model),
then finally a "Combined" model with all the terms. They seem to follow an
approach that builds up the model's complexity over time, rather than
reduce the model's complexity to the finest state.

I would like to understand more about the differences of these approaches
to construct an ERG model. Could you please advise and/or point me to the
main literature about constructing ERG models?

Thank you very much.

Best regards,
Duy

messages.subject: [statnet_help] version of 2016.4 of statnet released
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,
  Just wanted to let everyone know that the statnet team has released 
updates to most of the major statnet packages in the last week or so 
including some new features and a number of bug fixes.  You should be 
able to update everything to the most recent versions by installing the 
new "2016.4" version of the statnet package.

The ergm.ego and ergm.rank and statnetWeb packages have been released to 
CRAN as well.

best,
  -skye (for the statnet team)


Below are relevant excerpts from to the NEWS files for some of the packages:
----------------------------
ergm  version 3.6.0
NEW FEATURES

     A new suite of geometrically-weighted family of terms has been 
added that allow the user to specify what directions of shared 
partnerships are of interest. The new terms are,

         (Directed) geometrically weighted dyadwise shared partners (dgwdsp)

         (Directed) geometrically weighted edgewise shared partners (dgwesp)

         (Directed) geometrically weighted non-edgewise shared partners 
(dgwnsp)

     In addition, terms for specific shared partner counts (ddsp, desp, 
and dnsp) are also implemented. See ergm-terms for help.

     New terms (binary and valued) b1cov and b2cov have been 
implemented, analogous to nodecov, nodeicov, and nodeocov but for 
bipatite networks.

     New valued terms atleast, equalto, and smallerthan have been 
implemented. A number of terms that were binary-only before have been 
implemented for valued ERGMs.

     ergm package now works when loaded (e.g., using requireNamespace) 
but not attached (e.g., using library).

BUG FIXES

     A number of implementation bugs in the valued ERGM terms have been 
fixed.

     Parallel processing when using ergm.userterms and similar was 
accidentaly broken in the previous release.

     Calculation of Hummel et. al. (2010) steplength for missing data 
MLE was incorrect; a slower but more accurate algorithm is now used.

     Miscellaneous bugfixes and robustifications.

     gof.formula and others now work with missing data.

     Miscelaneous cleanups and bug fixes.

OTHER USER-VISIBLE CHANGES

     robust.inverse has been deprecated in favor of ginv.

     simulate.formula now does parallel processing more efficiently.

----------------------------

tergm  version 3.4.0
BUG FIXES

     Miscellaneous bugfixes.

     The list of functions exported is now explicitly defined.

     robust.inverse has been replaced by ginv.


-------------------

EpiModel Version 1.2.5

NEW FEATURES
* Added multicore functionality to simulating stochastic network models 
with `netsim`. This
   only supports single-node frameworks currently, using the 
`doParallel` package. Run models
   in parallel by using the `ncores` parameter in `control.net`.
* Modifications to the `as.phylo.transmat` function to construct the 
phylo tree with all
   network vertices as phylo-tips and all transmissions as phylo nodes.

OTHER
* General code cleanup and improvement of package tests to increase 
coverage about 90%.


---------------------------
ergm.count version 3.2.1
BUG FIXES

     Package now works when loaded but not attached.

     Test that was failing with ergm 3.6.0 has been fixed.

----------------------------
ndtv v0.9

  - added a jitter parameter to transmission timeline
  - fixed ndtv-d3 htmlwidget to correctly use a unique javascript id for 
the animation so that multiple animations can appear in the same 
Rmarkdown document
  - fixed warning and extra diagonal line drawn in timePrism plot when 
planes=TRUE and network had odd number of vertices.
  - updated MDSJ url to reflect changes at hosting server and correct 
CRAN error

----------------------------

tsna v 0.2
   - Added aggregate.dur parameters to the tErgmStats and tSnaStats 
wrapper functions so they can be used with networks having momentary ties
   - moved ergm package from Depends to Suggests now that ergm permits 
loading via requireNamespace

----------------------------

networkDynamic v0.9
   - vignette updates
   - fixed issue where network.collpase would incorrectly nest dynamic 
network-level attributes if there was only one of them
   - updated McFarland classroom networks to include TEA edge attributes
   - updated as.data.frame.networkDynamic() to mostly fix dramatic speed 
cost of filtering features from previous release, doc corrections
   - removed warning generated by as.data.frame.networkDynamic() when

messages.subject: [statnet_help] There may be excessive correlation between model terms
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] There may be excessive correlation between model terms
messages.body_plain:
Hello Andrew --

My guess is that your network is relatively dense, yes?  Our group has 
traditionally worked with relatively sparse networks, and our tutorials 
all reflected that.  Recently, as more folks have been modeling denser 
networks with ERGMs, we've come to see the same issue you are 
mentioning. The reason can be seen by thinking through the logic of what 
GWESP represents when alpha is 0: it simplifies to the number of edges 
in at least one triangle.  For sparse networks you would generally only 
expect a few edges to be in triangles, and then when you see a lot more 
then there is something special going on, and sufficient information to 
estimate what it is.  But for a dense network, you might expect nearly 
every edge to be in at least one triangle; effectively, the edges term 
and the GWESP(alpha=0) term are collinear. You are using a higher value 
for alpha -- 0.5 -- but it may still be sufficiently low that the terms 
are nearly collinear rather than exactly so.

My advice is to increase the starting alpha, perhaps into the range of 1 
to 2.  It may be easier to fix it in order to improve convergence, and 
then once you know you're in a realm that is successful, only then let 
it vary. Keep trying, and let us know what happens.

All of this has shown us that GWESP is even more subtle and complex than 
we had already appreciated.  There is a lot more theoretical work to be 
done around its interpretation in different settings, and its 
relationship to network concepts beyond just transitivity. Contributions 
to that literature, from you or anyone else reading this - are highly 
welcome!

Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ndtv slices by time
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jimi,
  Not sure I'm exactly understanding your question.  The timestamps can 
be any numeric value, they don't have to be integer steps. But I'm 
thinking you mean that when you watch the movie you want to see 
"3:24.05" instead of "204.05" seconds?

If so, you can do nice tricky things with the labelling by passing in an 
'xlab' (x-axis label) argument to overide the default time label created 
by render.animation().  This argument can be a special function so it 
will get updated as the movie progresses.

For example, assuming you coded the ties in seconds:

render.animation(yourMovieObject,
   xlab=function(onset){paste(onset%/%60,onset%%60,sep=":")})

should label each time slice with the minutes and seconds.  The render 
code is smart enough that if it sees that the argument is a function 
with an argument named 'onset' (or terminus, etc, see ?render.animation 
for details) it will call the function each time it plots the network, 
substituting in the current value of onset for each slice.

hope that is what you were asking :-)

best,
  -skye

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am seeking to calculate eigenvector centrality of all nodes for a
directed, weighted network. My empirical network also has some missing edge
data in which I do not know whether or not a tie was formed between nodes.

My understanding is that I can do this by using the evcent() function in
"sna" and specifying gmode="digraph. Although there is not an option in the
parameters of evcent(), I believe that this automatically calculates the
*out-*eigenvector centrality, whereas transposing the weighted adjacency
matrix and running the same function will calculate the *in-*eigenvector
centrality of nodes. The following code gives an example of this:

##
> library(statnet)
> g <- network(rgraph(20, tprob=.4), directed=T)   #generate sample network
> g %e% "weight" <- sample(1:10, network.edgecount(g), replace=T)   # add
edge weights
> g[c(sample(1:network.size(g), 5)), c(sample(1:network.size(g), 5))] <- NA
  #add some NAs randomly

> sna::evcent(as.sociomatrix(g, attr="weight"), rescale=F, gmode="digraph")
  # calculate out-eigenvector centrality?
> sna::evcent(t(as.sociomatrix(g, attr="weight")), rescale=F,
gmode="digraph") # calculate in-eigenvector centrality?
##

I have 3 main questions:

1) Could someone please help me verify whether my understanding of how to
calculate in vs. out-eigenvector centrality is correct and if the procedure
I am implementing above is valid?

2) In order to calculate a "total" eigenvector centrality for the directed
graph, would it be reasonable to sum the upper and lower triangles of the
directed adjacency matrix, create a symmetric (undirected) matrix from the
result and calculate eigenvector centrality as you would for an undirected
graph?

3) Finally, I have run some simple tests of missing values and it appears
as though they are being handled reasonably, although I lack a good
mechanistic understanding of how they are being treated. Thus, I would also
be very grateful is anyone here could provide a simplified description of
how missing values are handled in evcent() or point me to some material to
help me understand. Available literature (
http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378873305000353) seems
to suggest that centrality measures are relatively robust to a low
proportion of missing edge data.

My apologies for the long message and thank you in advance for the
continued help,

Tom

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGM - multiple different edge types - edges formed in different settings
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] ERGM - multiple different edge types - edges formed in different settings
messages.body_plain:
Hi Andreas,

It sounds like you are looking for a combination of a valued ERGM (e.g., 
via ergm.count or GERGM) and a multiplex ERGM. As far as I know, that 
combination does not exist yet. To explore how each of the settings 
works (as a second-best solution), you can try to model each of them 
separately for now and include (functions of) the other settings as 
covariates.

Note: there is quite some confusion over terminology. Some people call 
multiplex ERGMs multi-level ERGMs while others reserve that term for 
things like social-ecological networks where you have multiple node sets 
AND within- and between-set relations. In some parts of the literature 
(mainly the hard sciences), you can also find the term 'multilayer 
networks'.

Best,
Philip

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Comparing observed to simulated networks on arbitrary statistics
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Comparing observed to simulated networks on arbitrary statistics
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Michael -

There are many ways to make such comparisons, although the most direct 
is to examine the quantiles of the observed graph statistics in the 
distribution of simulated statistics under your proposed model.  Testing 
a joint hypothesis is more complex, and will depend on how the 
hypothesis is defined; a good example is the classic omnibus triad 
census test, of which you can find a discussion in Wasserman and Faust 
(1994).  (One need not use Gaussian approximations in a modern setting: 
one can just simulate the distribution of the test statistic under one's 
proposed model.)  If you want a more elaborate approach, you could also 
consider the quantile modeling methods in Butts (Sociological 
Methodology, 2011); see the comments in section 5.1 about using a 
general probability model (rather than a CUG model) to produce reference 
quantiles.  I would not recommend this for basic hypothesis testing, but 
the approach can be useful in meta-analytic settings where one has 
multiple networks from a possibly heterogeneous population.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
Hello


I am looking at absorptive capacity in open innovation collaborations. Essentially absorptive capacity is a form of organisational learning where knowledge acquired by individuals is transformed into new ideas/innovations at the group and organisational level.  I believe brokerage is a key social mechanism in absorptive capacity and I would like to analyse this in terms of the conduit, tertius gaudens and terius iungens processes as outlined by Obstfeld, Borgatti and Davis (2014).


I have directed knowledge provider networks from three open innovation case studies with codifiability, observability and complexity of knowledge provided rated on a scale of 1 to 10 (three measures of tacitness).  Using exponential random graph models, I want to see how patterns of brokerage differ with different levels of tacit knowledge sharing in an open innovation collaboration. My goal is to look at absorptive capacity at the level of the collaboration as well as at the firm level.


I am presented with a challenge of specifying network triadic microstructures of interest (namely the tertius gaudens/iungens orientations).


I reckon I can use two-paths (021C) to describe conduit processes and two paths (021D) with a tail  to describe tertius gaudens processes, and triads (120D) with a tail to describe tertius iungens processes.  I would like to examine these in purely structural terms or consider these microstructures with each node having an attribute = membership of a particular organisation. Dear Sebastian,

I have not used TERGMs yet so I cannot help you with this explicit error.
However, I have some serious concerns with this reasoning for using a TERGM
instead of SIENA. The working paper (I do not think the paper is a
published, peer reviewed article - please correct me if I am wrong), has
some serious flaws.

First: SAOMs are not a special case of a TERGM. Both are stochastic models
of networks but the SAOM only behaves like an ERGM in is long-run
equilibrium if a very, very unnatural and specific setting for the rate
function is used. In virtually all real world applications, it does
not. Also, unlike the ERGM, the SAOM is not typically used to analyse
networks in equilibrium. The TERGM, however, is special case of an ERGM -
an ERGM conditioned on another network.

Second: Some (Most?) of the critique IN THE ARXIV PAPER against SAOMs is
equally valid against (T)ERGMs:
a) It is absolutely true that SAOMs have problems capturing joint actions,
as common in politics (i.e. formation of the European Union), but the same
type of emergence is, as far as I know, hard to model in (T)ERGMs. It would
require a clique effect, which I have not encountered and I think does not
exists. SAOMs probably should not be used for joint action networks, but
this does not apply for your data. (I assume that the primates you study
behave somewhat like small human social networks.)
b) Of course it is unnatural to assume that every single actor has the
exact same objective function. But the same is true for a (T)ERGM. In a
SAOM we assume that our parameters model the average decision of the
average person (given its network position and covariates), in an ERGM we
assume our parameters capture the formation of an average tie (given its
network position and covariates). If we do not specify a specific subgroup
(i.e. by interacting a parameter with a co-variate like gender), both TERGM
and SAOM assume that processes are similar for all members of the network
(given their position in it). The (T)ERGM in fact makes stronger
homogeneity assumptions because not only actors but even all tie variables
follow the same probabilistic rules!
c) Another critique is that SAOMs assume that everyone is aware of the
whole network state, when they make a decision. As before it is clear that
this assumption is unnatural, especially in larger networks. But in a
(T)ERGM the probability of a tie is also dependent on the existence of
other ties in the network. In terms of information needed, the TERGM and
the SAOM are no different - only most TERGM papers are silent about this
complete information assumption, while SAOM papers are more often open
about it.

Third: The simulation part of the paper in section 5 uses quite "weird"
parameters to compare the model families. Choosing random draws from a
uniform distribution of -3 to +3 with steps of .001 does not lead to
meaningful parameters for neither a TERGM nor SAOM. The resulting networks
will be mostly degenerate or at least will not look like your average
social network. A simulation should be based on target statistics of a
network.

What I wanted to say is, that the paper has flaws. I am not a
mathematically trained statistician, like the inventors of ERGMs, TERGMs
and SAOMs so I am sure that I have some inaccuracies in the way that I
wrote things down here and I would love to hear what the statnet authors
and other statisticians/mathematicians or more knowledgeable people have to
say about this paper. But I am quite sure that SIENA is not a bad choice
for the type of network you are dealing with. Additionally, if the results
of TERGM and SAOM differ, I would not know what that meant.


A positive thing in SAOMs is that the parameters are time
independent because it is a continuous time model (TERGM is discrete-time).
If you observe the same network at  multiple points in time and the
underlying process is constant, then the parameter estimates of the SAOMs
should be the same for T1-T2-T3 compared to T1-T3. Or if the time intervals
are of different length (e.g. First measurements apart by 2 months and
later by 6 months). If your model is well fitting and the process is
stable, the parameters will be the same, because it is a model of
individual decisions. The same does not hold TERGMs, as far as I know.

I want to emphasize that I do not think that TERGMs are worse than SAOM.
They are different mathematical models with different goals. One is
modelling the state of a network given a previous time point and one models
the process of change. If your interest is in how behavior and social
relations of primates co-evolve, SAOMs should work fine. If you are
interested in how the structure of your primate group is, conditioned on a
previous observation, than TERGMs are the model for you.

I am sorry that I cannot help you with your errors, but I wanted to
re-assure you that your SIENA results could be sufficient after all.


Best Regards,

Robert Krause

ICS Sociology, PhD Student
University of Groningen
Grote Rozenstraat 31,
Room B119
9712 TG Groningen, The Netherlands
