>>>>> On 04/24/2016 05:31 AM, John Burrett wrote:
>>>>>      Wow, Carter, thanks for the pedantic and condescending answer. Fact is, researchers are
>>>>>      working on SUGMs and SERGMs because ERGMs fail to be useful so often, and generally work
>>>>>      for networks that are less than interesting in structure.   Moreover, if you can?t even
>>>>>      look for dyads and triangles/stars at the same time, including using GWESP, etc, then it?s
>>>>>      a method that is problematic, per se. All I wanted was some thoughts on the matter, and not your opinion of my assumed ignorance.
>>>>> John Burrett
>>>>> haikuanalytics inc
>>>>> clarity in data, power in presentation
>>>>> jburrett@haikuanalytics.com <mailto:jburrett@haikuanalytics.com>
>>>>> 613.818.2848
>>>>> 
>>>>>      On Apr 23, 2016, at 11:26 PM, Carter T. Butts <buttsc@uci.edu <mailto:buttsc@uci.edu>> wrote:
>>>>> The problem is not with ERGMs per se - the problem is that you chose a model that was
>>>>> ill-suited to your system.  Poor specification is a problem in any context; try e.g.
>>>>> putting multiple high-order polynomial terms in a typical OLS and see how that goes.  Of
>>>>> course, learning how to specify better models takes some reading, and some practice, so one
>>>>> should not be surprised if one's first efforts go poorly.  (And the field as a whole is
>>>>> continuing to learn about how to specify improved models for different applications...it's
>>>>> a very active area.)  But the bottom line is that parametric modeling of an entire social
>>>>> network is a challenging problem that requires some expertise (!), and software tools can't
>>>>> substitute for that.  Learning is required.
>>>>> Vis a vis permutation methods, there are many clever things that can be done with those
>>>>> approaches.  They do, however, have a lot of intrinsic limitations, and are never going to
>>>>> be a general-purpose substitute for full probability models.  (By turns, there are things
>>>>> that you can do very easily and robustly with permutation techniques that are very hard to
>>>>> do in other ways.  As always, one wants to pick the right tool for the job.) -Carter

>>>>> Hello Jesse-
>>>>> Alas, it sounds like you have discovered the wonders of model degeneracy --
>>>>> that is, you've specified a model where even the true maximum likelihood
>>>>> estimates for the model would be so unlikely to produce the observed network
>>>>> that the estimation algorithm is unable to converge. This is a challenge with
>>>>> network models, where the intuition we bring from simple linear models is often
>>>>> confounded by the complex dependence in our data and among our model terms. And
>>>>> unlike in linear world, where starting with a simple model and building
>>>>> complexity is generally guaranteed to work, here a simple model can often be
>>>>> the source of the problem, because it doesn't capture the real-world processes
>>>>> that offset one another to prevent our social worlds from going off in one
>>>>> direction or another.

Dear Statnet community,

I am trying to use multiple cores to simulate a network. I have had success with control.simulate.ergm (http://finzi.psych.upenn.edu/library/ergm/html/control.simulate.ergm.html), but it appears that the control.simulate.stergm does not include an implementation of the parallelization routines (see control.simulate.network: http://search.r-project.org/library/tergm/html/control.simulate.stergm.html).

I tried to specify the 'parallel' argument in control.simulate.network, and I got an 'unused arguments' error, which would indicate that the parallel argument does not exist for this function.

Is it true that control.simulate.network does not contain parallel routines?

Thanks,
Aditya

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Edgecov() term quest and interpreting gwidegree
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

This is my first attempt with ergm and I have a couple of questions:

1. Is there any term equivalent to the edgecov() that accepts values from categorical variables? I am asking this because one of my edge list variables is "distance" (in km) of a shipment between two villages (my nodes). Distance values range from 0 to 328km (IQR=13.9), thus, I standardised this variable (and the model runs OK!). However, I am finding it very difficult to interpret the coefficient. Therefore, I decided to categorise "distance" in 3 categories (dist.c) and try to run the model with edgecov(dist.c), getting the following error:

Error in sum(c(xm)[c(xm) < 0]) : invalid 'type' (character) of argument

In addition: Warning message:

In (function (nw, arglist, ...)  : NAs introduced by coercion



2. I am also trying to interpret gwidegree. I have read Hunter 2007, Harris 2003<https://us.sagepub.com/en-us/nam/an-introduction-to-exponential-random-graph-modeling/book237737> and checked this<https://statnet.org/trac/raw-attachment/wiki/FrequentlyAskedQuestions/gwtermsNotes.txt> and this<https://statnet.org/trac/attachment/wiki/Resources/GWDegree.xlsx> links. However, I am still a bit confused on how to interpret my results. I set my decay parameter to 0.55 (I chose this value by running the model with the fixed option=FALSE and then exponentiating the resulting coefficient: gwidegree.decay = -0.588563, thus, exp(-0.588563) = 0.55). When running the final model (see below), I get a significant (p-val=0.02) and negative gwidegree coefficient of -0.65114; aka: exp(-0.65114) = 0.521451.

mf<- ergm(netg5~edges+edgecov(netg5, attrname = "dist.s")+

             nodematch("region",diff=F)+nodefactor("region")+nodecov("fpv.s")

             gwidegree(0.55, fixed = TRUE)+mutual,

           estimate="MLE",

           control = control.ergm(seed = 1,

           MCMLE.density.guard = exp(5),

           MCMC.interval = 5000,

           MCMC.burnin = 50000,

           MCMC.samplesize = 50000)

 )



The way I am thinking of interpreting this coefficient is that my network follows a preferential attachment process. Following, I would say that [assuming that nothing else changes in the model] the odds of trade decrease by 0.52 when adding an edge between villages with low indegrees. Similarly, the odds of trade increase by 1.48 when adding an edge between villages with high indegrees... However, my network has a marked declining degree distribution (most of the villages only trade with one or two other villages, and only a few villages have a high indegree value), so my interpretation of the gwidegree term contradicts my descriptive results! Which probably means that I am very wrong somewhere. Any comments on the interpretation of gwidegree would be very welcomed!

On another note that may be relevant, my network is sparse (network density= 0.023; simplified network density= 0.008).

Thanks,

Esther Kukielka,
PhD student Graduate Group in Epidemiology,
CADMS, UCDavis.
http://www.vetmed.ucdavis.edu/cadms/

Center for Animal Disease Modeling and Surveillance: Vet ...<http://www.vetmed.ucdavis.edu/cadms/>
www.vetmed.ucdavis.edu
Our overarching goal is to develop systems that can be used to prevent, control, or eradicate animal diseases and their associated adverse economic impacts.

> That's why I am wondering if something in my syntax (see below) is wrong?
> Actually, I want to measure to what extent actors with a specific
> (quantitative) attribute tend more to be involved in reciprocal ties than
> the whole of actors (whether they have a high value in the attribute or
> not). I understood from the specifications of ergm-terms that the right
> parameter to use was mutual(by="attribute")?

> Hi Natalie,
>
> I don't know about the mutual term in PNet, but the mutual term in the ergm
> package is kind of a misnomer. Intuitively, I would understand mutuality to
> be
>
> h(N) = N_{ij} * N_{ji} * [X_{ij} == X_{ji}] + (1 - N_{ij}) * (1 -
> N_{ji}) * [X_{ij} == X_{ji}]
>
> (i.e., reciprocation of ties and non-ties), while reciprocity should be
> merely the first part, i.e.,
>
> h(N) = N_{ij} * N_{ji} * [X_{ij} == X_{ji}].
>
> However, the ergm-terms help page indicates that the mutual term is actually
> based on this second definition. Just guessing, but perhaps that's the
> difference between the two implementations?
>
> You could try to include the corresponding change statistic as a dyadic
> covariate (using an edgecov term) and check if that gets you closer to PNet.
> I think the change statistic would be
>
> \delta^{<ij>} = N_{ji} * [X_{ij} == X_{ji}] - (1 - N_{ji}) * [X_{ij} ==
> X_{ji}],
>
> but you may want to double-check. That is, you could include an edgecov term
> with a covariate matrix that has values of 1 if the reciprocal tie exists
> and the attribute matches and -1 if it doesn't exist and there is a match
> (instead of including the mutual term). Just a thought, but maybe I'm wrong.

        na.action = na.fail,
        do.fit = TRUE)
Does the ?na.action=na.fail? mean the model will fail with missing values? How do the ergm.ego handle the missing values? 

Thank you very much.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] STERGM under TERGM
messages.body_plain:
Dear members,

I'm working with  STERGM under TERGM package but the model get stuck and
stop running after a while.
Here is my model:

samp.fit1 <- stergm(  net,  formation=
~edges+mutual+cyclicalties+transitiveties+nodematch('Job'),  dissolution =
~edges+mutual+cyclicalties+transitiveties+nodematch('Job'),  estimate =
"CMLE",  times=c(1:50))

My data contains 50 longitudinal networks with an average of about 180
nodes and 500 edges.

The number of nodes and arcs are changing between networks and I'm working
with networkDynamic package.

I have access to a server with 720 GB RAM and 64 cores (although I think my
code doesn't utilize it)

My questions are: (1) What can I do in order to be able to run my model?
(2) How can I make use of my server capabilities?

(3) When I run the code several times with a time interval of 5 weeks (i.e.
time=c(1:5),  time=c(6:10), time=c(11:16),.......time=c(45:50) ) I get good
results

Is it OK to make conclusions based on the produced models (as they all
have similar coefficients)?

Thanks,

Shiran Cohen
Ph.D. Candidate

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Add dependence terms to check model fit of undirected network
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

I was modeling an undirected network with covariates by adding dependence terms and use MCMC estimates to check model fit (start from alpha=0.1). But then errors came up: 

> gwict1 <- ergm(g7cnet1~edges+nodefactor('gender')+nodecov('fbintensity')+nodecov('ictintensity')+nodecov('ictskill') + gwdegree( .1,T) + gwesp( .1,T ) + gwdsp( .1,T ),control=control.ergm(MCMC.samplesize=100000, MCMC.burnin=1000000, MCMC.interval=1000, seed = 567), eval.loglik = T, verbose = T )
Evaluating network in model
Initializing Metropolis-Hastings proposal(s): ergm:MH_TNT ergm:MH_listTNT
Initializing model.
Using initial method 'MPLE'.
Fitting initial model.
MPLE covariate matrix has 190 rows.
Error in solve.default(real.cov) : 
  Wired in system calculation: Inverted condition number=9.18355e-26
Warning messages:
1: In ergm.mple(Clist, Clist.miss, m, MPLEtype = MPLEtype, init = init,  :
  GLM model may be separable; restarting glm with zeros.
2: glm.fit: fitted probabilities numerically 0 or 1 occurred 

Any hints to fix the problem?? Thanks in advance!

Best,
Shupin

messages.subject: [statnet_help] STERGM under TERGM
messages.body_plain:
On Tue, 26 Jul 2016, Philip Leifeld wrote:

> That said, perhaps others can comment on why the STERGM gets stuck. I would 
> assume that the STERGM is estimated by MCMC-MLE, and MCMC-MLE is just 
> prohibitively slow when the normalizing constant in the denominator of the 
> ERGM equation gets blown up by the 50 time points.

I think the problem may be the way stergm stores the data for 50 time 
points, rather than the MCMC-MLE estimation itself.  MCMC-MLE scales 
reasonably well for large sparse nets in ergm, and 50x180=9000 is a size 
we have worked with before.  But it's a different thing for stergm, 
because stergm needs to condition on the fixed dyads in each process 
(formation and dissolution), so this info is kept for all dyads, and the 
current code does not do that very efficiently.

Pavel, if I've miss-stated this, please correct as needed.

best,
mm

> Best,
> Philip
>
> PS: If you'd like to read a paper that reports both a TERGM and a STERGM 
> side-by-side, take a look at this: http://dx.doi.org/10.1093/jopart/muu043.
>

messages.body_plain:
Dear listserv members,

I'm trying to test a hypothesis about tie strength and similarity of
cultural attitudes (i.e., the stronger the tie between nodes, more similar
their attitudes would be).
I have tie strength as edge value (range 0-6), and cultural attitudes
measured with 5-point scale (so 1-5).
I'm using ergm terms like edgecov and nodematch to test that, and used
reference = ~Binomial(6). Am I doing it right?
Although the model did not converge, I'm getting most parameters
significant and very low AIC and BIC values.

Also, when I got this message "MCMLE estimation did not converge after 20
iterations. The estimated coefficients may not be accurate. Estimation may
be resumed by passing the coefficients as initial values; see 'init' under

interval, but seemed to keep getting the same message. Can anyone tell me
what I can do better? or should I give up since it's a model degeneracy?

My network visualization (attached below) gave me some confidence about the
hypothesis, but maybe I'm doing something wrong.

Your advice/help will be greatly appreciated.

Sunny

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] question on ERGM using egocentric data
messages.body_plain:
Ya,

I'm guessing you're trying to fit a model that has too many parameters 
for the little data you have available, and your data collection forces a 
constraint that max(degree)=5 that needs to be included.

I'd suggest you try fitting the degree constraint with 
constraints=~bd(maxout=5) (see ?"ergm-constraints"), and then dropping 
the degree terms.

Then try starting with simpler models (nodefactor terms only), and 
adding the nodematch terms, each one separately, with diff=F (the 
default), before putting them all in together.

But the bottom line here is that you have very little data, so you may not 
be able to identify all the effects of interest.

best,
mm

if you are dealing with AH), but does employ the directed data:

Wang, Cheng; Butts, Carter T.; Hipp, John R.; and Jose, Rupa; and Lakon, 
Cynthia M. (2016). ``Multiple Imputation for Missing Edge Data: A 
Predictive Evaluation Method with Application to Add Health.'' Social 
Networks, 45, 89-98.

Cheng Wang has spent a lot of time on data wrangling with the full 
version of AH, so you might want to follow up with him if you have 
detailed data-related questions on the above.  Martina, Steve, Mark, and 
others have obviously been thinking very deeply about this data set for 
many years, so I'm sure they will have further suggestions.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] TERGM
messages.body_plain:
Shiran,

There is no detailed book or online course at this point.  But one of the 
benefits of the STERGM approach is that each component of the model, 
formation and dissolution, is an ERGM.  So to interpret the dissolution 
model coefficients, you can use the conditional logit interpretation, 
as you would for a regular ERGM (refer to the ERGM tutorial).  The only 
thing to keep in mind is that the dissolution model is parameterized in 
terms of *persistence* of partnerships -- so positive coefficient values 
imply that the term increases the conditional odds of a partnership 
persisting.  As always, you need to keep in mind the other terms in the 
model when you interpret any individual terms.

If you have more specific questions, let us know.

best,
Martina

messages.subject: [statnet_help] layout algorithm that takes into account node characteristics for x or y coordinates
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] layout algorithm that takes into account node characteristics for x or y coordinates
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Franziska -

There's not a standard built-in for that, but there are various 
approaches that might work for you.  The most natural would be to 
compute distances between vertices on your attribute(s) of interest, and 
the use a scaling of a linear combination of that and the geodesic 
distances among vertices to define your coordinates. Here's an ad hoc 
example:

library(sna)
library(network)
data(emon)
s<-emon[[5]]%v%"Sponsorship"  #This is a categorical variable, BTW
s.dist<-outer(s,s,"!=")                  #Get distances with respect to s
g.dist<-geodist(symmetrize(emon[[5]]))$gd  #Get geodesic distances
library(MASS)                                 #Needed for non-metric MDS
coord<-sammon(g.dist+0.5*s.dist)$points  #Weight the graph more heavily
plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Sponsorship",coord=coord)

You will note that the vertices with similar sponsorship are now 
co-located.  Adjusting the relative weights of the geodesic distances 
and the attributes will let you tune the importance of each factor in 
the final solution.

A simple function generalizing this can be used to automate the process:

#Demonstration layout function for plot.network that combines attribute 
value scaling and
#scaling by geodesic distances.  layout.par arguments are as follows:
#
#  categorical - Vector of categorical vertex attributes (one value per 
vertex)
#  numeric - Vector or matrix of numeric attributes (one value or row 
per vertex)
#  weights - Numeric vector of length 2 with weights to be used for 
geodesic distances
#    and attribute distances (respectively) in the final solution
#
#Within network, this can be selected by adding mode="geoandattrdist" to 
your plot
#call; note that layout.par=list(...) must be used to specify attributes.)
#
network.layout.geoandattrdist<-function(nw, layout.par){
   require(sna)
   require(MASS)
   g.dist<-geodist(symmetrize(nw))$gd          #Get geodesic distances
   g.dist[!is.finite(g.dist)]<-network.size(nw)   #Substitute a large 
value for Inf
   cat.dist<-matrix(0,network.size(nw),network.size(nw)) #Categorical 
distances
   num.dist<-matrix(0,network.size(nw),network.size(nw))  #Numeric distances
   if(!is.null(layout.par$categorical)){                 #Categorical 
attribute
     at<-layout.par$categorical
     cat.dist<-outer(at,at,"!=")
   }
   if(!is.null(layout.par$numeric)){                     #Numeric attribute
     at<-layout.par$numeric
     num.dist<-as.matrix(dist(at))
   }
   at.dist<-cat.dist+num.dist #Attribute distances
   if(is.null(layout.par$weights))                        #Get weights
     weights<-c(1,0.2*max(g.dist)/max(at.dist))
   else
     weights<-rep(layout.par$weights,length=2)
    #Scale the combination of distances and return
coord<-sammon(weights[1]*g.dist+weights[2]*at.dist)$points
    coord
}

Once this is defined, we can easily use it, like so:

plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Sponsorship",mode="geoandattrdist",
   layout.par=list(categorical=emon[[5]]%v%"Sponsorship"))

plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Location",mode="geoandattrdist",
   layout.par=list(categorical=emon[[5]]%v%"Location"))

Here's a more complex example (using two dimensions at once, which the 
above code supports for numeric attributes)

crs<-emon[[5]]%v%"Command.Rank.Score"
crs[is.na(crs)]<-0 #Orgs w/NA weren't in the initial response
drs<-emon[[5]]%v%"Decision.Rank.Score"
drs[is.na(drs)]<-0
plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Sponsorship",mode="geoandattrdist",
   layout.par=list(numeric=cbind(crs,drs), weights=c(1,0.1)))

We can also combine numeric and categorical attributes, albeit crudely:

plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Location",mode="geoandattrdist",
layout.par=list(categorical=emon[[5]]%v%"Location",numeric=cbind(crs,drs)/7, 
weights=c(1,0.5)))

Many more such strategies are possible, but hopefully this provides some 
useful ideas!

-Carter

On 04/24/2016 07:25 PM, John Burrett wrote:
> Aha. Now I realize what happened. Carter, you confused me with the 
> person who started the thread, who had just tried an ERGM with no 
> success, and innocently and reasonably wanted to ask why.  Someone 
> (Steve) replied very helpfully and kindly.  I thought that was great

>>> On Apr 24, 2016, at 8:18 PM, martina morris 
>>> <morrism@u.washington.edu <mailto:morrism@u.washington.edu>> wrote:
>>>
>>> And just in case Carter's answer isn't long enough for you :)
>>>
>>> It's worth making a distinction between the general form of the 
>>> Markov model, and the homogeneous reduced form that most folks are 
>>> familiar with.
>>>
>>> The general specification allows for each configuration (edge, 
>>> k-star or triangle) to have it's own coefficient.  That model is not 
>>> identifiable. In fact, you run out of degrees of freedom on the 
>>> edges terms alone, since each edge would have its own coefficient.
>>>
>>> Hence the "simpler" 3 parameter model we've come to know and hate: 
>>>  the edges+2star+triangle model.  It imposes both homogeneity 
>>> constraints (each configuration now has a single coefficent, node 
>>> labels don't matter anymore) and a reduced form from k-stars to 2-stars.
>>>
>>> This homogenous reduced form Markov is, we now know, just a bad 
>>> model. It doesn't produce interesting graphs, and it wouldn't 
>>> produce any of the networks we're likely to analyze. Frank and 
>>> Strauss committed the original sin, but the entire field is still 
>>> learning this lesson.
>>>
>>> But I don't think that means the Markov class as a whole is bad. 
>>>  The heterogeniety is there in the class to exploit.  But the way to 
>>> do it is with other effects, like homophily, that introduce 
>>> interpretable heterogeneity into the configurations, and declining 
>>> marginal returns (as Carter notes).
>>>
>>> best,
>>> mm
>>>
>>> On Sun, 24 Apr 2016, Carter T. Butts wrote:
>>>
>>>> Hi, John -
>>>> You asked for our opinions on the issue of degeneracy, and you 
>>>> obtained one: (1) building good models
>>>> in any complex system is a challenging task that requires knowledge 
>>>> of how the model class operates;
>>>> (2) ERGMs are no exception; and (3) if you put together a bad model 
>>>> (e.g. the example that was offered)
>>>> you will get poor results.  My comments regarding the necessity of 
>>>> learning and practice were made in
>>>> response to your own claims to be a newcomer, your evident concern 
>>>> at the behavior of a very
>>>> well-studied model class (see, e.g. Snijders's 2002 JoSS paper for 
>>>> details on the edge/k-star family),
>>>> and your apparent concern that failure to obtain a good model on a 
>>>> first try implies that the whole
>>>> approach is broken.  I would be inclined to take those comments 
>>>> positively - i.e., this _is_ a
>>>> learnable task, and indeed there are many exciting and intriguing 
>>>> things to discover - but they are
>>>> relating a basic fact that you can celebrate or decry as you choose.
>>>> Substantively, Steve and Martina have made some very excellent 
>>>> comments on the modeling issues, which
>>>> underscore some of the things to which one needs to attend in 
>>>> building good models. The many threads
>>>> in the current literature regarding model parameterization are an 
>>>> outgrowth of these important and
>>>> hard-won lessons, and to understand this new work it is likewise 
>>>> necessary to know something about the
>>>> foundational challenges that all such modeling efforts face.  (This 
>>>> knowledge is also important for
>>>> sorting out the sometimes dubious claims that are made regarding 
>>>> what constitutes an "extension" or a
>>>> fundamentally alternative approach - caveat emptor.)  These are as 
>>>> much substantive theoretical
>>>> challenges as they are technical ones, as Martina, Steve, and many 
>>>> others have frequently emphasized:
>>>> "bad" models generate unrealistic behavior because they posit 
>>>> social mechanisms that are themselves
>>>> unrealistic.  As with any complex system, determining what is 
>>>> unrealistic in a network model is not
>>>> trivial, and indeed we are learning quite a lot about the social 
>>>> world by studying "bad' models and
>>>> mechanisms!  (I cut my teeth as an agent-based modeler, and my view 
>>>> was always that one learned more
>>>> from the models that failed than from the ones that succeeded: 
>>>> there are lots of "obvious" ways to
>>>> construct a system with specified behavior that do not in fact 
>>>> behave as you expect, usually for
>>>> reasons that are clear only after one has banged one's head against 
>>>> the proverbial or actual table many
>>>> times.)  To take the example of the edge/k-star/triangle family 
>>>> (which you raised), there were many
>>>> plausible a priori arguments that suggested that such families 
>>>> would provide a good characterization of
>>>> many classes of social networks.  (See, e.g., the classic 
>>>> dependence arguments of Frank and Strauss
>>>> (1986), although the thread goes back farther than that.)  When it 
>>>> was discovered that these models
>>>> tended to be ill-behaved (a phenomenon of which Strauss himself 
>>>> warned in his 1986 SIAM paper), this
>>>> meant that the underlying theoretical rationale for those models - 
>>>> that is, the ideas about how, when,
>>>> and how strongly one edge could affect another - had to be 
>>>> revisited.  This has led to a whole slew of
>>>> interesting proposals for alternative specifications, each of which 
>>>> is based on a substantively
>>>> different notion of the mechanisms behind triangulation.  This 
>>>> represents theoretical progress: the
>>>> early models helped us learn that the world didn't work as we 
>>>> naively expected, and we are now
>>>> investigating other ways that the world might work (with those 
>>>> proposals being guided by what we
>>>> learned from the initial effort).  As of right now, it appears that 
>>>> there are several classes of
>>>> factors that act in the real world to inhibit phenomena such as the 
>>>> density explosion, including (1)
>>>> decoupling of edges across social or physical barriers, (2) 
>>>> heterogeneity in opportunity structures,
>>>> and (3) diminishing marginal effects of closure on edge formation.  
>>>> The jury is still out on exactly
>>>> where, when, and how much these factors are active, but I expect 
>>>> that we will know more in the coming
>>>> years as more models get tried, more/better data is acquired, and 
>>>> the properties of different
>>>> specifications become better understood. It's an exciting time to 
>>>> be in the field.
>>>> Hopefully, the above provides further elaboration of why 
>>>> familiarizing oneself with some background
>>>> information is important for making progress with ERGMs (or any 
>>>> other modeling approach), and why I and
>>>> others typically give this advice to newcomers.  It's natural to 
>>>> wander into the field, throw together
>>>> some models that seem intuitively sensible (or are mentioned in old 
>>>> papers or more recent papers
>>>> studying pathological models), and accidentally rediscover 
>>>> degeneracy.  This can be a useful learning
>>>> experience (I suggest that everyone play with such models!) but can 
>>>> be frustrating if your proximate
>>>> objective is getting a good model for some substantive purpose.  
>>>> There's nothing unique about ERGMs in
>>>> this regard; for instance, when I first started dabbling in 
>>>> molecular dynamics (and I'm still a
>>>> neophyte in that domain), it took me a while to figure out that my 
>>>> proteins kept unfolding because I
>>>> hadn't properly specified the disulfide bonds that were stitching 
>>>> them together (oops).  The model
>>>> wasn't wrong per se - it was predicting what would really happen if 
>>>> those bonds got reduced - but it
>>>> certainly wasn't doing what I intended. (Ditto for getting 
>>>> protonation states right, something which
>>>> can require some significant homework.) In my experience, most 
>>>> folks readily expect that they will
>>>> need to learn about such things to model physical systems, but some 
>>>> are surprised that modeling social
>>>> networks also requires one to develop a deeper understanding of the 
>>>> underlying technical and
>>>> substantive issues.  Indeed, this is the case.  The good news, 
>>>> however, is that there _is_ more to
>>>> learn than there was say, 15 years ago. The science continues to 
>>>> advance.
>>>> Ultimately, you should choose the right tool for your problem, and 
>>>> that tool might or might not be a
>>>> stochastic network model in ERGM form.  If you elect to work with 
>>>> the latter, the discussion and
>>>> references posted here will hopefully provide you with information 
>>>> that can help you get started in
>>>> this rich and fascinating research area.
>>>> Hope that helps,
>>>> -Carter
>>>> On 04/24/2016 05:31 AM, John Burrett wrote:
>>>>      Wow, Carter, thanks for the pedantic and condescending answer. 
>>>> Fact is, researchers are
>>>>      working on SUGMs and SERGMs because ERGMs fail to be useful so 
>>>> often, and generally work
>>>>      for networks that are less than interesting in structure.   
>>>> Moreover, if you can?t even
>>>>      look for dyads and triangles/stars at the same time, including 
>>>> using GWESP, etc, then it?s
>>>>      a method that is problematic, per se. All I wanted was some 
>>>> thoughts on the matter, and not your opinion of my assumed ignorance.
>>>> John Burrett
>>>> haikuanalytics inc
>>>> clarity in data, power in presentation
>>>> jburrett@haikuanalytics.com <mailto:jburrett@haikuanalytics.com>
>>>> 613.818.2848
>>>>
>>>>      On Apr 23, 2016, at 11:26 PM, Carter T. Butts <buttsc@uci.edu 
>>>> <mailto:buttsc@uci.edu>> wrote:
>>>> The problem is not with ERGMs per se - the problem is that you 
>>>> chose a model that was
>>>> ill-suited to your system.  Poor specification is a problem in any 
>>>> context; try e.g.
>>>> putting multiple high-order polynomial terms in a typical OLS and 
>>>> see how that goes.  Of
>>>> course, learning how to specify better models takes some reading, 
>>>> and some practice, so one
>>>> should not be surprised if one's first efforts go poorly.  (And the 
>>>> field as a whole is
>>>> continuing to learn about how to specify improved models for 
>>>> different applications...it's
>>>> a very active area.)  But the bottom line is that parametric 
>>>> modeling of an entire social
>>>> network is a challenging problem that requires some expertise (!), 
>>>> and software tools can't
>>>> substitute for that.  Learning is required.
>>>> Vis a vis permutation methods, there are many clever things that 
>>>> can be done with those
>>>> approaches.  They do, however, have a lot of intrinsic limitations, 
>>>> and are never going to
>>>> be a general-purpose substitute for full probability models.  (By 
>>>> turns, there are things
>>>> that you can do very easily and robustly with permutation 
>>>> techniques that are very hard to
>>>> do in other ways.  As always, one wants to pick the right tool for 
>>>> the job.) -Carter
>>>> On 04/23/2016 04:41 PM, John Burrett wrote:
>>>>      Great info Steve, and thanks.  Seems to me that the utility of 
>>>> ERGMs is pretty
>>>>      restricted by this most of the time, and one is better off 
>>>> with the
>>>>      permutation-based correlation/regression models using both 
>>>> structure and
>>>>      attributes as described by Borgatti.  This is also why people 
>>>> are working on
>>>>      SERGMs, etc. Your thoughts would be helpful - am I too 
>>>> pessimistic about ERGMs? John
>>>> John Burrett
>>>> haikuanalytics inc
>>>> clarity in data, power in presentation
>>>> jburrett@haikuanalytics.com <mailto:jburrett@haikuanalytics.com>
>>>> 613.818.2848
>>>>
>>>>      On Apr 23, 2016, at 12:43 PM, Steven Goodreau 
>>>> <goodreau@uw.edu> wrote:
>>>> Hello Jesse-
>>>> Alas, it sounds like you have discovered the wonders of model 
>>>> degeneracy --
>>>> that is, you've specified a model where even the true maximum 
>>>> likelihood
>>>> estimates for the model would be so unlikely to produce the 
>>>> observed network
>>>> that the estimation algorithm is unable to converge. This is a 
>>>> challenge with
>>>> network models, where the intuition we bring from simple linear 
>>>> models is often
>>>> confounded by the complex dependence in our data and among our 
>>>> model terms. And
>>>> unlike in linear world, where starting with a simple model and building
>>>> complexity is generally guaranteed to work, here a simple model can 
>>>> often be
>>>> the source of the problem, because it doesn't capture the 
>>>> real-world processes
>>>> that offset one another to prevent our social worlds from going off 
>>>> in one
>>>> direction or another.
>>>> You might find it useful to go through the ERGM tutorial if you 
>>>> haven't before,
>>>> and see the advice we give for diagnosing degeneracy:
>>>> https://statnet.org/trac/wiki/Sunbelt2016#WorkshopMaterials
>>>> You could also read up a lot more in depth on the statistical 
>>>> underpinnings of
>>>> degeneracy if you wish, using resources pointed to on the statnet 
>>>> wiki.  I
>>>> suspect your more immediate concern is finding a model that fits - 
>>>> and this
>>>> group has a lot of built-up knowledge that they may offer.  I'd 
>>>> start by
>>>> suggesting the use of degree terms instead of star terms; there is 
>>>> a direct
>>>> mapping from one to the other, but the degree terms are generally 
>>>> far more
>>>> stable; they're also easier for most readers to interpret If you 
>>>> wish to stay
>>>> with stars, you might consider reading up about alternating k-stars.
>>>> Note that as you progress you might experience similar issues with your
>>>> triangle term - if so, I'd suggest reading up about GWESP.
>>>> Cheers,
>>>> Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Question about mutual term with vertex attribute
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Question about mutual term with vertex attribute
messages.body_plain:
Hey Natalie,

I understand your decision to incorporate them in one network. Comparing
parameters of network models with varying sample size and density is very
difficult, if not quite impossible.

First, could you take a look if all of these sub networks are not
degenerate or completely mutual? It could be that one of your groups has
only reciprocated ties. this could lead to computational problems.
Second, it might be an idea to add a general mutual term. Because mutual by
is an interaction of mutual and the covariate, and having interactions
without both main effects is rather odd (although I understand your
decision here, for there are no ties between groups). I have not used
mutual(by =) in ergm so I might be wrong about this...
Third, it might help if you fix your gwesp parameter and not estimate a
curved exponential random graph. E.g: gwesp(alpha = log(2),fixed = TRUE,
cutoff = 30)
Related, I found that triadic structures are better captured if next to
gwesp gwdsp is also included -> gwdsp(alpha = log(2), fixed = TRUE, cutoff
= 30)

Unfortunately these might nit fix your problem after all. To be sure, your
computer has enough free working memory?

It might be an idea to run the model without the control part. You might
not get a converging model, but if you do not encounter the error, we are
closer in finding where it comes from.


Best Regards,

Robert Krause

ICS Sociology, PhD Student
University of Groningen
Grote Rozenstraat 31,
Room B119
9712 TG Groningen, The Netherlands

plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Sponsorship",mode="geoandattrdist",

the weights are not the weights of crs vs. drs, but geometric distance vs
whatever else, correct? So c(1, 0.000001) would give me a layout that is
more or less identical to one purely based on geometric distance, correct?

> ---------- Forwarded message ----------
> From: Franziska Barbara Keller <fbkeller@nyu.edu>
> To: statnet_help@u.washington.edu
> Cc:
> Date: Tue, 10 May 2016 20:06:38 -0400
> Subject: [statnet_help] layout algorithm that takes into account node
> characteristics for x or y coordinates
> Dear statnet community,
>
> are there layout algorithms implemented in R that take into account node
> characteristics in addition to the adjacency matrix?
>
> I'm thinking of something like "ideology" when mapping co-sponsorship
> networks in the congress, to ensure that the Republican cluster ends up on
> the right, and the Democrats on the left side. Or a "formal rank"
> characteristic, which ensures that more highly-ranked nodes tend to be
> located at the top of the illustration.
> I know this is not how we usually think about the x and y axis, but it
> might make some illustrations more easily understandable. Especially if it
> is just about "breaking a tie", e.g. when determining the order of the
> outer nodes in a star network.
>
> One way I could think of how to achieve it is by setting x and y position
> of the nodes before running a layout algorithm, but I was wondering if
> there is a more principled approach to this?
>
> Best,
>
> Franziska
>
> --
>
> Franziska Barbara Keller
> PostDoctoral Fellow, Harriman Institute, Columbia University
> phone US: (+1) 646-829-5277 / phone CH: (+41) 78 808 66 62
> www.fbkeller.net
>
> Latest publication: Moving Beyond Factions
> <http://dx.doi.org/10.1017/jea.2015.3>, Journal of East Asian Studies
> 16:1.
>
>
>
> ---------- Forwarded message ----------
> From: "Carter T. Butts" <buttsc@uci.edu>
> To: statnet_help@u.washington.edu
> Cc:
> Date: Tue, 10 May 2016 18:43:21 -0700
> Subject: Re: [statnet_help] layout algorithm that takes into account node
> characteristics for x or y coordinates
> Hi, Franziska -
>
> There's not a standard built-in for that, but there are various approaches
> that might work for you.  The most natural would be to compute distances
> between vertices on your attribute(s) of interest, and the use a scaling of
> a linear combination of that and the geodesic distances among vertices to
> define your coordinates.  Here's an ad hoc example:
>
> library(sna)
> library(network)
> data(emon)
> s<-emon[[5]]%v%"Sponsorship"  #This is a categorical variable, BTW
> s.dist<-outer(s,s,"!=")                  #Get distances with respect to s
> g.dist<-geodist(symmetrize(emon[[5]]))$gd  #Get geodesic distances
> library(MASS)                                 #Needed for non-metric MDS
> coord<-sammon(g.dist+0.5*s.dist)$points  #Weight the graph more heavily
> plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Sponsorship",coord=coord)
>
> You will note that the vertices with similar sponsorship are now
> co-located.  Adjusting the relative weights of the geodesic distances and
> the attributes will let you tune the importance of each factor in the final
> solution.
>
> A simple function generalizing this can be used to automate the process:
>
> #Demonstration layout function for plot.network that combines attribute
> value scaling and
> #scaling by geodesic distances.  layout.par arguments are as follows:
> #
> #  categorical - Vector of categorical vertex attributes (one value per
> vertex)
> #  numeric - Vector or matrix of numeric attributes (one value or row per
> vertex)
> #  weights - Numeric vector of length 2 with weights to be used for
> geodesic distances
> #    and attribute distances (respectively) in the final solution
> #
> #Within network, this can be selected by adding mode="geoandattrdist" to
> your plot
> #call; note that layout.par=list(...) must be used to specify attributes.)
> #
> network.layout.geoandattrdist<-function(nw, layout.par){
>   require(sna)
>   require(MASS)
>   g.dist<-geodist(symmetrize(nw))$gd          #Get geodesic distances
>   g.dist[!is.finite(g.dist)]<-network.size(nw)   #Substitute a large value
> for Inf
>   cat.dist<-matrix(0,network.size(nw),network.size(nw))    #Categorical
> distances
>   num.dist<-matrix(0,network.size(nw),network.size(nw))  #Numeric distances
>   if(!is.null(layout.par$categorical)){                 #Categorical
> attribute
>     at<-layout.par$categorical
>     cat.dist<-outer(at,at,"!=")
>   }
>   if(!is.null(layout.par$numeric)){                     #Numeric attribute
>     at<-layout.par$numeric
>     num.dist<-as.matrix(dist(at))
>   }
>   at.dist<-cat.dist+num.dist                            #Attribute
> distances
>   if(is.null(layout.par$weights))                        #Get weights
>     weights<-c(1,0.2*max(g.dist)/max(at.dist))
>   else
>     weights<-rep(layout.par$weights,length=2)
>    #Scale the combination of distances and return
>    coord<-sammon(weights[1]*g.dist+weights[2]*at.dist)$points
>    coord
> }
>
> Once this is defined, we can easily use it, like so:
>
> plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Sponsorship",mode="geoandattrdist",
>   layout.par=list(categorical=emon[[5]]%v%"Sponsorship"))
>
> plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Location",mode="geoandattrdist",
>   layout.par=list(categorical=emon[[5]]%v%"Location"))
>
> Here's a more complex example (using two dimensions at once, which the
> above code supports for numeric attributes)
>
> crs<-emon[[5]]%v%"Command.Rank.Score"
> crs[is.na(crs)]<-0                                              #Orgs
> w/NA weren't in the initial response
> drs<-emon[[5]]%v%"Decision.Rank.Score"
> drs[is.na(drs)]<-0
> plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Sponsorship",mode="geoandattrdist",
>   layout.par=list(numeric=cbind(crs,drs), weights=c(1,0.1)))
>
> We can also combine numeric and categorical attributes, albeit crudely:
>
> plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Location",mode="geoandattrdist",
>
> layout.par=list(categorical=emon[[5]]%v%"Location",numeric=cbind(crs,drs)/7,
> weights=c(1,0.5)))
>

plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Sponsorship",mode="geoandattrdist",
label=emon[[5]]%v%"Decision.Rank.Score", label.pos=5,
     edge.col="grey", layout.par=list(numeric=cbind(crs,drs),
weights=c(1,0.000001))) # weight on network


>
> Many more such strategies are possible, but hopefully this provides some
> useful ideas!
>
> -Carter
>

messages.subject: [statnet_help] model selection in ergm
messages.body_plain:
I would say this is a pretty general question that applies equally to 
network modeling and any kind of regression modeling. Unless you are 
obsessed with prediction and don't care about theory, the choice of your 
model terms should be primarily theoretically informed. That said, there 
is one caveat here: if your theory (and especially the endogenous part 
of it) does not fit very well, you may encounter model degeneracy, which 
may prevent you from estimating the model in the first place. So in 
practice it is a mix of theoretical specification and inductive tweaks 
to your theory because it's relatively hard to come up with the perfect 
specification from scratch (if it were possible, we wouldn't need any 
goodness-of-fit measures, after all, because we would know the result 
from the outset). The way I understand your question, though, is that 
you are looking for an algorithm that tries all combinations of model 
terms and reports the one with the best AIC or BIC (i.e., something like 
a stepping algorithm). If that's what you are intending, I think this 
will be neither sensible as it is not theoretically informed (unless you 
do machine learning), nor will it be practical because degeneracy issues 
will not allow you to estimate most model configurations. At least when 
you use MCMC-MLE estimation. If your question is rather about good ways 
to come up with a network theory for a given phenomenon, I would suggest 
reading up on the literature that applies ERGMs and see how they do it. 
The statnet tutorials on the wiki also contain some nice examples.

Best,

Philip

messages.body_plain:
On Tue, 26 Jul 2016, Philip Leifeld wrote:

> I agree that a bipartite version of GWNSP is really missing badly in statnet. 
> I'd love to see it being added to the ergm package at some point! If possible 
> with an 'attrname' argument.

if someone wants to write it, we'll add it.

:)

> In principle, the current version of GWNSP can be used with bipartite graphs, 
> but it does not discriminate between having the multiple two-paths on the 
> second mode (with the unconnected base dyad on the first mode) and having the 
> multiple two-paths on the first mode (with the unconnected base dyad on the 
> second mode). Most of the time, however, this means the statistic mixes up 
> two relatively different NSP distributions, thus leading to a poor fit if 
> applied to a two-mode network.
>
> Philip

Hi --

Your second model is overspecified.  Since you have a maximum degree of 
5, you can either specify the model with edges + degree(1:4), or just 
degree(1:5).  The edges term is the sum of all the degree terms, so you 
can't put the whole sequence in the model along with the edges term. 
They're co-linear.

best,
mm

messages.body_plain:
Hi Kevin -

I don't know what work has been done on the directed AH networks (I 
haven't been following this literature lately), but I can say that the 
main methodological reason we did undirected was simply that back then 
we didn't have gwesp terms for directed networks available.  We do now.  
That said, the straight up gwesp term that appears in ergm, when used on 
directed networks, captures only one of the four types of directed gwesp 
terms, and I suspect you will need to have some larger combination of 
the four in there (and perhaps all four) to get model stability.

Since I rarely ever work with directed networks in my current research, 
I'm not sure of the syntax for the four terms, but Martina's grad 
student Li Wang is familiar with their current state, and I'm copying 
him here.

Cheers,
Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] directed networks in Add Health
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Quick question, short version: Has anyone had success modeling the full (directed) friend networks from Jefferson and Sunshine in Add Health (wave 1)?

Longer version: I'm aware that a number of publications have applied ERGMs to wave 1 Add Health data- but most (if not all) of these efforts have looked only at mutual friendships. I have a *vague* memory of asking someone about this ages ago, and it seemed, in addition to the theoretical motivation of looking at "stronger" (i.e. mutually validated) friendships, there was also a methodological backstory that folks were having a terrible time getting models for the full (directed) friend networks to converge. I am recently (and for the first time) diving into the data for these two schools myself- have spent some number of hours (unsuccessfully) pounding away at directed models- and am just wondering if this is a lost cause and I should use some undirected version (mutual or symmetrized) of the network instead. Or, if anyone has had success with it- advice would be appreciated! It's of course very possible I've missed a relevant publication or conversation.

Hope everyone is enjoying a great start to the summer.

Best wishes,
Kevin

P.S. Before sending, I did a quick search in the archives to make sure I'm not asking a dumb (i.e. already answered!) question. It looks like there was a similar exchange back in 2014 where, ironically, Martina and I were trying to help Karen figure out what was going wrong with her models for the exact same two schools. Karen/Martina, did you ever find a solution??! Could this have been just a directed/undirected issue, where for some reason the directed versions are especially slippery?

Kevin Lewis
Assistant Professor of Sociology
University of California, San Diego

Hey Natalie,

 

I understand your decision to incorporate them in one network. Comparing parameters of network models with varying sample size and density is very difficult, if not quite impossible.

 

First, could you take a look if all of these sub networks are not degenerate or completely mutual? It could be that one of your groups has only reciprocated ties. this could lead to computational problems.

Second, it might be an idea to add a general mutual term. Because mutual by is an interaction of mutual and the covariate, and having interactions without both main effects is rather odd (although I understand your decision here, for there are no ties between groups). I have not used mutual(by =) in ergm so I might be wrong about this...

Third, it might help if you fix your gwesp parameter and not estimate a curved exponential random graph. E.g: gwesp(alpha = log(2),fixed = TRUE, cutoff = 30)

Related, I found that triadic structures are better captured if next to gwesp gwdsp is also included -> gwdsp(alpha = log(2), fixed = TRUE, cutoff = 30)

 

Unfortunately these might nit fix your problem after all. To be sure, your computer has enough free working memory?

 

It might be an idea to run the model without the control part. You might not get a converging model, but if you do not encounter the error, we are closer in finding where it comes from.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Statnet for cellular network
messages.body_plain:
Dear statnet group,

First, I would like to congratulate you for this fantastic package I found
it very interesting. I'm a postdoctoral researcher about cellular
technologies (5G). Since I have been using R from last three years, I want
to use it for my future research. I wasn't sure to find a package to
simulate a network and then I have found your collection of packages. Thus,
I would like to use this package to simulate my research on cellular
networks. My research aims to reduce the connection delay when a user goes
from a small cell (base station) to another while he/she is connected to
avoid service failure (e.g. making a call). My scenario is formed by three
different nodes: Macro base stations, small cells and users. The macro
cells are connected to one or more small cells. the small cells are not
connected between them, the communication between small base stations must
be through the macro base station. Macro base stations and small base
stations are static nodes. The users are dynamic, they should move randomly
along the network and they are connected to the small base stations. Is it
possible to simulate such network?

Thank you for your help. Do not hesitate to contact me for further
information.

Sincerely,

Dr. Ra?l Parada

> On Apr 24, 2016, at 8:18 PM, martina morris <morrism@u.washington.edu> wrote:
> 
> And just in case Carter's answer isn't long enough for you :)
> 
> It's worth making a distinction between the general form of the Markov model, and the homogeneous reduced form that most folks are familiar with.
> 
> The general specification allows for each configuration (edge, k-star or triangle) to have it's own coefficient.  That model is not identifiable. In fact, you run out of degrees of freedom on the edges terms alone, since each edge would have its own coefficient.
> 
> Hence the "simpler" 3 parameter model we've come to know and hate:  the edges+2star+triangle model.  It imposes both homogeneity constraints (each configuration now has a single coefficent, node labels don't matter anymore) and a reduced form from k-stars to 2-stars.
> 
> This homogenous reduced form Markov is, we now know, just a bad model. It doesn't produce interesting graphs, and it wouldn't produce any of the networks we're likely to analyze. Frank and Strauss committed the original sin, but the entire field is still learning this lesson.
> 
> But I don't think that means the Markov class as a whole is bad.  The heterogeniety is there in the class to exploit.  But the way to do it is with other effects, like homophily, that introduce interpretable heterogeneity into the configurations, and declining marginal returns (as Carter notes).
> 
> best,
> mm
> 
> On Sun, 24 Apr 2016, Carter T. Butts wrote:
> 
>> Hi, John -
>> You asked for our opinions on the issue of degeneracy, and you obtained one: (1) building good models
>> in any complex system is a challenging task that requires knowledge of how the model class operates;
>> (2) ERGMs are no exception; and (3) if you put together a bad model (e.g. the example that was offered)
>> you will get poor results.  My comments regarding the necessity of learning and practice were made in
>> response to your own claims to be a newcomer, your evident concern at the behavior of a very
>> well-studied model class (see, e.g. Snijders's 2002 JoSS paper for details on the edge/k-star family),
>> and your apparent concern that failure to obtain a good model on a first try implies that the whole
>> approach is broken.  I would be inclined to take those comments positively - i.e., this _is_ a
>> learnable task, and indeed there are many exciting and intriguing things to discover - but they are
>> relating a basic fact that you can celebrate or decry as you choose.
>> Substantively, Steve and Martina have made some very excellent comments on the modeling issues, which
>> underscore some of the things to which one needs to attend in building good models.  The many threads
>> in the current literature regarding model parameterization are an outgrowth of these important and
>> hard-won lessons, and to understand this new work it is likewise necessary to know something about the
>> foundational challenges that all such modeling efforts face.  (This knowledge is also important for
>> sorting out the sometimes dubious claims that are made regarding what constitutes an "extension" or a
>> fundamentally alternative approach - caveat emptor.)  These are as much substantive theoretical
>> challenges as they are technical ones, as Martina, Steve, and many others have frequently emphasized:
>> "bad" models generate unrealistic behavior because they posit social mechanisms that are themselves
>> unrealistic.  As with any complex system, determining what is unrealistic in a network model is not
>> trivial, and indeed we are learning quite a lot about the social world by studying "bad' models and
>> mechanisms!  (I cut my teeth as an agent-based modeler, and my view was always that one learned more
>> from the models that failed than from the ones that succeeded: there are lots of "obvious" ways to
>> construct a system with specified behavior that do not in fact behave as you expect, usually for
>> reasons that are clear only after one has banged one's head against the proverbial or actual table many
>> times.)  To take the example of the edge/k-star/triangle family (which you raised), there were many
>> plausible a priori arguments that suggested that such families would provide a good characterization of
>> many classes of social networks.  (See, e.g., the classic dependence arguments of Frank and Strauss
>> (1986), although the thread goes back farther than that.)  When it was discovered that these models
>> tended to be ill-behaved (a phenomenon of which Strauss himself warned in his 1986 SIAM paper), this
>> meant that the underlying theoretical rationale for those models - that is, the ideas about how, when,
>> and how strongly one edge could affect another - had to be revisited.  This has led to a whole slew of
>> interesting proposals for alternative specifications, each of which is based on a substantively
>> different notion of the mechanisms behind triangulation.  This represents theoretical progress: the
>> early models helped us learn that the world didn't work as we naively expected, and we are now
>> investigating other ways that the world might work (with those proposals being guided by what we
>> learned from the initial effort).  As of right now, it appears that there are several classes of
>> factors that act in the real world to inhibit phenomena such as the density explosion, including (1)
>> decoupling of edges across social or physical barriers, (2) heterogeneity in opportunity structures,
>> and (3) diminishing marginal effects of closure on edge formation.  The jury is still out on exactly
>> where, when, and how much these factors are active, but I expect that we will know more in the coming
>> years as more models get tried, more/better data is acquired, and the properties of different
>> specifications become better understood.  It's an exciting time to be in the field.
>> Hopefully, the above provides further elaboration of why familiarizing oneself with some background
>> information is important for making progress with ERGMs (or any other modeling approach), and why I and
>> others typically give this advice to newcomers.  It's natural to wander into the field, throw together
>> some models that seem intuitively sensible (or are mentioned in old papers or more recent papers
>> studying pathological models), and accidentally rediscover degeneracy.  This can be a useful learning
>> experience (I suggest that everyone play with such models!) but can be frustrating if your proximate
>> objective is getting a good model for some substantive purpose.  There's nothing unique about ERGMs in
>> this regard; for instance, when I first started dabbling in molecular dynamics (and I'm still a
>> neophyte in that domain), it took me a while to figure out that my proteins kept unfolding because I
>> hadn't properly specified the disulfide bonds that were stitching them together (oops).  The model
>> wasn't wrong per se - it was predicting what would really happen if those bonds got reduced - but it
>> certainly wasn't doing what I intended.  (Ditto for getting protonation states right, something which
>> can require some significant homework.)  In my experience, most folks readily expect that they will
>> need to learn about such things to model physical systems, but some are surprised that modeling social
>> networks also requires one to develop a deeper understanding of the underlying technical and
>> substantive issues.  Indeed, this is the case.  The good news, however, is that there _is_ more to
>> learn than there was say, 15 years ago.  The science continues to advance.
>> Ultimately, you should choose the right tool for your problem, and that tool might or might not be a
>> stochastic network model in ERGM form.  If you elect to work with the latter, the discussion and
>> references posted here will hopefully provide you with information that can help you get started in
>> this rich and fascinating research area.
>> Hope that helps,
>> -Carter
>> On 04/24/2016 05:31 AM, John Burrett wrote:
>>      Wow, Carter, thanks for the pedantic and condescending answer. Fact is, researchers are
>>      working on SUGMs and SERGMs because ERGMs fail to be useful so often, and generally work
>>      for networks that are less than interesting in structure.   Moreover, if you can?t even
>>      look for dyads and triangles/stars at the same time, including using GWESP, etc, then it?s
>>      a method that is problematic, per se. All I wanted was some thoughts on the matter, and not your opinion of my assumed ignorance.
>> John Burrett
>> haikuanalytics inc
>> clarity in data, power in presentation
>> jburrett@haikuanalytics.com
>> 613.818.2848
>> 
>>      On Apr 23, 2016, at 11:26 PM, Carter T. Butts <buttsc@uci.edu> wrote:
>> The problem is not with ERGMs per se - the problem is that you chose a model that was
>> ill-suited to your system.  Poor specification is a problem in any context; try e.g.
>> putting multiple high-order polynomial terms in a typical OLS and see how that goes.  Of
>> course, learning how to specify better models takes some reading, and some practice, so one
>> should not be surprised if one's first efforts go poorly.  (And the field as a whole is
>> continuing to learn about how to specify improved models for different applications...it's
>> a very active area.)  But the bottom line is that parametric modeling of an entire social
>> network is a challenging problem that requires some expertise (!), and software tools can't
>> substitute for that.  Learning is required.
>> Vis a vis permutation methods, there are many clever things that can be done with those
>> approaches.  They do, however, have a lot of intrinsic limitations, and are never going to
>> be a general-purpose substitute for full probability models.  (By turns, there are things
>> that you can do very easily and robustly with permutation techniques that are very hard to
>> do in other ways.  As always, one wants to pick the right tool for the job.) -Carter
>> On 04/23/2016 04:41 PM, John Burrett wrote:
>>      Great info Steve, and thanks.  Seems to me that the utility of ERGMs is pretty
>>      restricted by this most of the time, and one is better off with the
>>      permutation-based correlation/regression models using both structure and
>>      attributes as described by Borgatti.  This is also why people are working on
>>      SERGMs, etc. Your thoughts would be helpful - am I too pessimistic about ERGMs? John
>> John Burrett
>> haikuanalytics inc
>> clarity in data, power in presentation
>> jburrett@haikuanalytics.com
>> 613.818.2848
>> 
>>      On Apr 23, 2016, at 12:43 PM, Steven Goodreau <goodreau@uw.edu> wrote:
>> Hello Jesse-
>> Alas, it sounds like you have discovered the wonders of model degeneracy --
>> that is, you've specified a model where even the true maximum likelihood
>> estimates for the model would be so unlikely to produce the observed network
>> that the estimation algorithm is unable to converge. This is a challenge with
>> network models, where the intuition we bring from simple linear models is often
>> confounded by the complex dependence in our data and among our model terms. And
>> unlike in linear world, where starting with a simple model and building
>> complexity is generally guaranteed to work, here a simple model can often be
>> the source of the problem, because it doesn't capture the real-world processes
>> that offset one another to prevent our social worlds from going off in one
>> direction or another.
>> You might find it useful to go through the ERGM tutorial if you haven't before,
>> and see the advice we give for diagnosing degeneracy:
>> https://statnet.org/trac/wiki/Sunbelt2016#WorkshopMaterials
>> You could also read up a lot more in depth on the statistical underpinnings of
>> degeneracy if you wish, using resources pointed to on the statnet wiki.  I
>> suspect your more immediate concern is finding a model that fits - and this
>> group has a lot of built-up knowledge that they may offer.  I'd start by
>> suggesting the use of degree terms instead of star terms; there is a direct
>> mapping from one to the other, but the degree terms are generally far more
>> stable; they're also easier for most readers to interpret If you wish to stay
>> with stars, you might consider reading up about alternating k-stars.
>> Note that as you progress you might experience similar issues with your
>> triangle term - if so, I'd suggest reading up about GWESP.
>> Cheers,
>> Steve

messages.body_plain:
I agree that a bipartite version of GWNSP is really missing badly in 
statnet. I'd love to see it being added to the ergm package at some 
point! If possible with an 'attrname' argument.

In principle, the current version of GWNSP can be used with bipartite 
graphs, but it does not discriminate between having the multiple 
two-paths on the second mode (with the unconnected base dyad on the 
first mode) and having the multiple two-paths on the first mode (with 
the unconnected base dyad on the second mode). Most of the time, 
however, this means the statistic mixes up two relatively different NSP 
distributions, thus leading to a poor fit if applied to a two-mode network.

Philip

messages.subject: [statnet_help] STERGM under TERGM
messages.body_plain:
Hi Shiran,

This is precisely the kind of scenario where bootstrapped MPLE is both 
unbiased and fast. Try the btergm function in the xergm package, which 
has the same syntax as the ergm function in statnet and takes care of 
node composition change automatically. If you'd like to read up on the 
bootstrap approach, I recommend this paper: 
http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.physa.2011.10.018. If you need help setting 
it up, I may be able to assist with troubleshooting.

180 nodes is about the size of the international system of states, and I 
have previously run analyses on international conflicts or alliances 
(with similar densities as you are describing) over more than 50 years 
without any problem and in less than an hour. xergm implements TERGMs, 
not STERGMs, but ultimately this is just a matter of data 
transformation. The btergm function can also run in parallel on your 64 
cores via the MPI protocol, so estimation should be super fast. Only a 
fraction of your RAM should be required; I have run my models and done 
goodness-of-fit assessment with only 16 GB of RAM and that was no problem.

That said, perhaps others can comment on why the STERGM gets stuck. I 
would assume that the STERGM is estimated by MCMC-MLE, and MCMC-MLE is 
just prohibitively slow when the normalizing constant in the denominator 
of the ERGM equation gets blown up by the 50 time points.

Best,
Philip

PS: If you'd like to read a paper that reports both a TERGM and a STERGM 
side-by-side, take a look at this: http://dx.doi.org/10.1093/jopart/muu043.

messages.body_plain:
I need some help understanding gwesp and cycle terms for directed networks.
My outcome is a network of threats (nodes are countries, if there is a
military threat between them edge=1). The direction of the edge goes from
aggressor to target of the threat. I want the ergm to speak to several
theories:


   1.

   If a dyad A-B has any shared partners C, meaning there are threats A-C
   and B-C, but either direction for threats with C is acceptable, which ergm
   term do I use? Triangle?

   2.

   Similar to (1), but I want the number of 4-cycles including A and B.
   Again, I don?t care about direction. How do I add a term for the number of
   undirected 4-cycles in a directed network?

   3.

   I have an additional network of wars using the same countries. In
   theory, if there is a shared partner in the undirected wars network (e.g.
   A-C and B-C at war), it will reduce the likelihood of a threat A -> B or B
   -> A. Is there a way to do that?

Thanks
Jeff Carnegie

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] layout algorithm that takes into account node characteristics for x or y coordinates
messages.body_plain:
Dear statnet community,

are there layout algorithms implemented in R that take into account node
characteristics in addition to the adjacency matrix?

I'm thinking of something like "ideology" when mapping co-sponsorship
networks in the congress, to ensure that the Republican cluster ends up on
the right, and the Democrats on the left side. Or a "formal rank"
characteristic, which ensures that more highly-ranked nodes tend to be
located at the top of the illustration.
I know this is not how we usually think about the x and y axis, but it
might make some illustrations more easily understandable. Especially if it
is just about "breaking a tie", e.g. when determining the order of the
outer nodes in a star network.

One way I could think of how to achieve it is by setting x and y position
of the nodes before running a layout algorithm, but I was wondering if
there is a more principled approach to this?

Best,

Franziska

Dear Statnet community,

I am working on a simulation study that involves simulating and estimating
a large amount of ERGMs. I encountered some weird behavior in the
estimation that I cannot explain.
While estimating 100 networks (30 nodes, average degree 8, reciprocity
~.30, transitivity ~.3, 70% homopholous ties) with the exact model that I
used to simulate them, about 45 of the networks gave an error:
"Unconstrained MCMC sampling did not mix at all. Optimization cannot
continue."

I took one of the networks giving the error and estimated it 100 times with
100 randomly selected random number seeds. Of those 100 estimations, 21
gave the same error.

Is there a way to avoid this problem, other than catching it with
tryCatch() and letting the code re-run with a different random number seed?

Best Regards,

Robert Krause

messages.body_plain:
Yes, that's correct: in this example, the attribute component of the 
layout will be driven by the Euclidean distance between vertices in the 
two dimensional (crs,drs) space.  If you wanted crs vs. drs, you'd want 
to use something like e.g. crs-drs as your numeric attribute.  And 
setting the second weight parameter to a very small value (including 0) 
should give you layout based only on the network.  (Setting the first 
parameter to 0 will similarly give you a layout that depends only on 
attributes.)

Hope that helps!

-Carter

>     Hi, Franziska -
>
>     There's not a standard built-in for that, but there are various
>     approaches that might work for you.  The most natural would be to
>     compute distances between vertices on your attribute(s) of
>     interest, and the use a scaling of a linear combination of that
>     and the geodesic distances among vertices to define your
>     coordinates. Here's an ad hoc example:
>
>     library(sna)
>     library(network)
>     data(emon)
>     s<-emon[[5]]%v%"Sponsorship"  #This is a categorical variable, BTW
>     s.dist<-outer(s,s,"!=")                  #Get distances with
>     respect to s
>     g.dist<-geodist(symmetrize(emon[[5]]))$gd #Get geodesic distances
>     library(MASS) #Needed for non-metric MDS
>     coord<-sammon(g.dist+0.5*s.dist)$points #Weight the graph more heavily
>     plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Sponsorship",coord=coord)
>
>     You will note that the vertices with similar sponsorship are now
>     co-located.  Adjusting the relative weights of the geodesic
>     distances and the attributes will let you tune the importance of
>     each factor in the final solution.
>
>     A simple function generalizing this can be used to automate the
>     process:
>
>     #Demonstration layout function for plot.network that combines
>     attribute value scaling and
>     #scaling by geodesic distances.  layout.par arguments are as follows:
>     #
>     #  categorical - Vector of categorical vertex attributes (one
>     value per vertex)
>     #  numeric - Vector or matrix of numeric attributes (one value or
>     row per vertex)
>     #  weights - Numeric vector of length 2 with weights to be used
>     for geodesic distances
>     #    and attribute distances (respectively) in the final solution
>     #
>     #Within network, this can be selected by adding
>     mode="geoandattrdist" to your plot
>     #call; note that layout.par=list(...) must be used to specify
>     attributes.)
>     #
>     network.layout.geoandattrdist<-function(nw, layout.par){
>       require(sna)
>       require(MASS)
>       g.dist<-geodist(symmetrize(nw))$gd #Get geodesic distances
>     g.dist[!is.finite(g.dist)]<-network.size(nw) #Substitute a large
>     value for Inf
>     cat.dist<-matrix(0,network.size(nw),network.size(nw)) #Categorical
>     distances
>     num.dist<-matrix(0,network.size(nw),network.size(nw)) #Numeric
>     distances
>       if(!is.null(layout.par$categorical)){         #Categorical attribute
>         at<-layout.par$categorical
>         cat.dist<-outer(at,at,"!=")
>       }
>     if(!is.null(layout.par$numeric)){ #Numeric attribute
>         at<-layout.par$numeric
>         num.dist<-as.matrix(dist(at))
>       }
>       at.dist<-cat.dist+num.dist                           #Attribute
>     distances
>     if(is.null(layout.par$weights)) #Get weights
>     weights<-c(1,0.2*max(g.dist)/max(at.dist))
>       else
>         weights<-rep(layout.par$weights,length=2)
>        #Scale the combination of distances and return
>     coord<-sammon(weights[1]*g.dist+weights[2]*at.dist)$points
>        coord
>     }
>
>     Once this is defined, we can easily use it, like so:
>
>     plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Sponsorship",mode="geoandattrdist",
>     layout.par=list(categorical=emon[[5]]%v%"Sponsorship"))
>
>     plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Location",mode="geoandattrdist",
>     layout.par=list(categorical=emon[[5]]%v%"Location"))
>
>     Here's a more complex example (using two dimensions at once, which
>     the above code supports for numeric attributes)
>
>     crs<-emon[[5]]%v%"Command.Rank.Score"
>     crs[is.na <http://is.na>(crs)]<-0 #Orgs w/NA weren't in the
>     initial response
>     drs<-emon[[5]]%v%"Decision.Rank.Score"
>     drs[is.na <http://is.na>(drs)]<-0
>     plot(emon[[5]],vertex.col="Sponsorship",mode="geoandattrdist",

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Question about mutual term with vertex attribute
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Question about mutual term with vertex attribute
messages.body_plain:
Hi Natalie,

I don't know about the mutual term in PNet, but the mutual term in the 
ergm package is kind of a misnomer. Intuitively, I would understand 
mutuality to be

h(N) = N_{ij} * N_{ji} * [X_{ij} == X_{ji}] + (1 - N_{ij}) * (1 - 
N_{ji}) * [X_{ij} == X_{ji}]

(i.e., reciprocation of ties and non-ties), while reciprocity should be 
merely the first part, i.e.,

h(N) = N_{ij} * N_{ji} * [X_{ij} == X_{ji}].

However, the ergm-terms help page indicates that the mutual term is 
actually based on this second definition. Just guessing, but perhaps 
that's the difference between the two implementations?

You could try to include the corresponding change statistic as a dyadic 
covariate (using an edgecov term) and check if that gets you closer to 
PNet. I think the change statistic would be

\delta^{<ij>} = N_{ji} * [X_{ij} == X_{ji}] - (1 - N_{ji}) * [X_{ij} == 
X_{ji}],

but you may want to double-check. That is, you could include an edgecov 
term with a covariate matrix that has values of 1 if the reciprocal tie 
exists and the attribute matches and -1 if it doesn't exist and there is 
a match (instead of including the mutual term). Just a thought, but 
maybe I'm wrong.

Philip

messages.body_plain:
Hi Statnet group,

I am curious if there is a simple way to import "node list" or "adjacency
list" data into statnet as a network object. I cannot seem to figure out a
way to do this.

Here is an example data set

>
dat2<-read.csv("articleList_bipartite.csv",header=FALSE,fill=TRUE,sep=",",na.strings="");dat2

    V1                  V2            V3              V4            V5
       V6           V7           V8          V9         V10           V11
    V12       V13
1 art1            Chen. DJ        Hu. MP          Guo. Y  Dahlgren. RA
     <NA>         <NA>         <NA>        <NA>        <NA>          <NA>
   <NA>      <NA>
2 art2     Srinivasarao. C      Kundu. S     Shanker. AK      Naik. RP
Vanaja. M  Venkanna. K  Sankar. GRM    Rao. VUM        <NA>          <NA>
   <NA>      <NA>
3 art3 Clermont-Dauphin. C  Suvannang. N  Pongwichian. P    Cheylan. V
 Hammecker. C  Harmand. JM         <NA>        <NA>        <NA>
 <NA>      <NA>      <NA>
4 art4              Hok. L       Sa. JCD     Boulakia. S      Reyes. M
  Leng. V      Kong. R    Tivet. FE  Briedis. C  Hartman. D  Ferreira. LA
 Magno. T  Pheav. S
5 art5            Chen. DJ        Hu. MP          Guo. Y  Dahlgren. RA
     <NA>         <NA>         <NA>        <NA>        <NA>          <NA>
   <NA>      <NA>
6 art6     Srinivasarao. C      Kundu. S     Shanker. AK          <NA>
     <NA>         <NA>         <NA>        <NA>        <NA>          <NA>
   <NA>      <NA>
>

as you can see it is a bipartite citation network with the articles 1:6
listed in rows of the first column and authors of each article following.
NAs are used to pad the rows to make each row have the same number of
entries.

I have tried bringing the data in as a incidence matrix but that does not
seem to work as I suspect incidence looks for an adjacency matrix (i.e.
node IDs in rows and columns, values in cells) as opposed to a list (i.e.,
node in column 1 with neighbors listed after)

network(dat2, bipartite=TRUE, matrix.type = "incidence")

I have also tried

network.incidence(as.matrix(dat2), network.initialize(6,directed=FALSE))

but this gives an error:

"Error in add.edge.network(g, tail, head, names.eval = en, vals.eval = ev,
 :
  (edge check) Attempted to add multiplex edge where multiple==FALSE in
addEdge_R.  Exiting."


Any advice would be welcome
Thank you and best wishes
Jesse


-- 

Jesse Sayles, PhD


*Postdoctoral Fellow*


*Department of Geography*

*McGill University  *

*saylesunchartedwaters.com <http://saylesunchartedwaters.com>*

Hi Jesse, I don't think there is yet a native function in 'network' to 
construct networks from nodelist format, perhaps there should be. Below 
is a draft function that seems to work OK for your example data.

best,
  -skye



testData<-as.data.frame(matrix(c(
c('art1', 'Chen. DJ', 'Hu. MP', 'Guo. Y', 'Dahlgren. RA', NA, NA, NA, 
NA, NA, NA, NA, NA),
c('art2', 'Srinivasarao. C', 'Kundu. S', 'Shanker. AK', 'Naik. RP', 
'Vanaja. M', 'Venkanna. K', 'Sankar. GRM', 'Rao. VUM', NA, NA, NA, NA),
c('art3', 'Clermont-Dauphin. C', 'Suvannang. N', 'Pongwichian. P', 
'Cheylan. V', 'Hammecker. C', 'Harmand. JM', NA, NA, NA, NA, NA, NA),
c('art4', 'Hok. L', 'Sa. JCD', 'Boulakia. S', 'Reyes. M', 'Leng. V', 
'Kong. R', 'Tivet. FE', 'Briedis. C', 'Hartman. D', 'Ferreira. LA', 
'Magno. T', 'Pheav. S'),
c('art5', 'Chen. DJ', 'Hu. MP', 'Guo. Y', 'Dahlgren. RA', NA, NA, NA, 
NA, NA, NA, NA, NA),
c('art6', 'Srinivasarao. C', 'Kundu. S', 'Shanker. AK', NA, NA, NA, NA, 
NA, NA, NA, NA, NA)),ncol=13,byrow=TRUE),stringsAsFactors = FALSE)


as.network.nodelist<-function(x,bipartite=FALSE,...){
   x<-as.matrix(x)
   # construct a table of ids
   vertex.names<-unique(as.vector(x))
   vertex.names<-vertex.names[!is.na(vertex.names)]
   if(bipartite){
     # permute so that the first elements appear as events
     vertex.names<-c(x[,1],vertex.names[!vertex.names%in%x[,1]])
     bipartite<-nrow(x)
   }
   rows<-lapply(1:nrow(x),function(r){
     i<-match(x[r,1],vertex.names)
     j<-match(x[r,which(!is.na(x[r,]))[-1]],vertex.names)
     cbind(i,j)
   })
   edgelist<-do.call(rbind,rows)
   net<-network(edgelist,matrix.type='edgelist',bipartite=bipartite,...)
   network.vertex.names(net)<-vertex.names
   return(net)
}
