al., 2013 book), and in SAOM that you have mentioned (interactions of ties
in endowment and creation of ties across time). However, I lack statistical
knowledge to write my own multiplex analyses in ergm. But to put the latter
circumstance aside, I would like to understand your point better for future
reference. Namely, If I understood you correctly, only a multiplex analysis
(i.e. being able to treat all networks as endogenous) would open up the
possibility to have an imputation model as the actual model
(notwithstanding the lack of possibility to preserve relationships between
networks properly)? In the latter context, can you please expand on the
following sentence of yours, for future reference?

*If you cannot run a multiplex ERGM but you are "just" using the other
networks as covariates, it is possible to write your own multiplex analyses
for Bergms.*

I am asking this also because Koskinen et al (2013) present a method for
augmentation of missing data for covariates, but this probably does not
include dyadic covariates such as my case.

Best regards and thanks,
Marko

P.S. Btw, I have run the bergmMis function you kindly provided and it
worked like a charm for a specification without network covariates (i.e.
without missing data for the covariates).

P.P.S. For present purposes, I think I will resort to your last comforting
paragraph and references therein when presenting the results :D







2017-09-14 10:16 GMT+02:00 Krause, R.W. <r.w.krause@rug.nl>:

> Dear Marko,
>
> Your suggestion is in line with the work by Wang et al 2016 (attached). It
> has the caveat that these imputations are not "proper" imputations, because
> all imputed data sets are imputed with the same parameters. For proper
> imputation you need to draw the parameters from an estimated posterior (in
> non network settings you could also do bootstrapping). Otherwise you will
> underestimate the between imputation variance (obtaining the proper
> standard errors for the effects after multiple imputation is a bit more
> complicated than taking the mean of the estimated models - see the attached
> paper by Schafer and Graham, 2002, page 19/20).
> You can solve this problem by utilizing the method by Koskinen et al.
> (2013) that you mentioned.
> It is available in the PNet software. I attached an adaptation of it for
> R. It requires the packages Bergm and igraph. (Please note that this is NOT
> Johan Koskinen's R script but an adaptation of his R-script, in which I
> implemented the missing data treatment within the normal Bergm estimation.
> I do not know where, you can find his script on the web, but you can get it
> from him via email.)
>
> However, you are absolutely right, that you still have the problem that
> your actual model would not be the imputation model and that the
> imputations might not preserve the relationships between the networks
> properly.
> I have never run a multiplex ERGM. If you can run a multiplex ERGM with
> the ergm package in R, then it should be straight forward to adapt the
> Bergm code to impute all of the networks properly.
> If you do this and your interest is in the model parameters, you will not
> need multiple imputation. The estimated posteriors that you will get from
> the Bergm estimation should be (asymptotically) identical to multiple
> imputation. The procedure imputes the missing data at every iteration and
> uses the new imputed network for the next parameter estimation. Running 50
> or so additional ERGMs or BERGMs will not provide you with better parameter
> or standard error estimates. If you cannot run a multiplex ERGM but you are
> "just" using the other networks as covariates, it is possible to write your
> own multiplex analyses for Bergms.
>
> Lastly, if you can run the analysis without treating the missing data
> (like Handcock & Gile, 2007 - which is the default in the ergm package),
> then you will probably be not to far off of the "true" parameter estimates.
> You should investigate whether your data is missing at random. E.g. have a
> look at the average in-degree of missing actors and non-missing actors. If
> the actors are missing randomly, the Handcock & Gile method should not be
> too far off. You do not have a large percentage of missing actors. If you
> have a look at the work of Smith, Moody and Morgan (2013/2017 - also
> attached) you will see that with such small percentages of missing data
> most descriptive statistics are only weakly biased. I am working on a paper
> estimating bias for parameter estimation, but unfortunately I have not
> analyzed this part of the data yet. A quick glance suggests (and this comes
> with a big warning, this is really just a quick glance!) that the biases at
> 10% missing data are quite low and interpretation of the model would not
> change. This is also in line with the results from Huisman & Steglich 2008
> on SAOMs, you can see there that with 20% missing data, the bias in
> parameter estimation is quite low. Of course SAOMs and ERGMs are a
> different model family, but they are both network models...
>
>
> Best Regards,
>
> Robert Krause
>
> ICS Sociology, PhD Candidate
> University of Groningen
> Grote Rozenstraat 31,
> Room B119
> 9712 TG Groningen, The Netherlands
>
> On Thu, Sep 14, 2017 at 1:29 AM, Marko Luci? <marko.lucic15@gmail.com>
> wrote:
>
>> Hello statnet,
>>
>> In our research, we need to establish the association of three networks
>> (socialization, perceived competence and perceived value homophily) with
>> tie-formation in the "focal" network of task advice in an organization (so,
>> the four networks contain the same node set). We apply ERGMs, to account
>> for other tie-formation regularities besides the associations of interest.
>>
>> The problem at hand is missing data: unit non-response, by Huisman's
>> terminology (2009), i.e. three of 43 actors did not respond to our survey
>> (they have no outgoing ties recorded), but they were in the survey roster
>> (so, we do have their incoming ties).
>>
>> Having in mind that the "covariate networks" have missing data, a "tacit
>> imputation method" implemented in ergm (statnet) is a no-go for my final
>> models, since this method assumes no missing information on the fixed
>> covariates' part.
>>
>> My question is then how should I approach the missing data imputation, a
>> priori assuming some ERGM-based imputation is a way to go? More precisely:
>> am I on the right track with the strategy outlined below, and do you have
>> some pointers regarding the specific question in the end of the following
>> section of this message?
>>
>> I guess I could build four separate ERG models for each of the four
>> above-mentioned networks (utilizing the tacit imputation method), with all
>> the usual caveats of model selection and examining GOF. Then I could run
>> some arbitrary number of simulations constraining the observed edges to
>> remain unchanged (as described in Section 6, p.15 of PolNet 2011 tutorial
>> on modeling missing data). I could then use those simulated networks in
>> further modelling. The problem then is, how to choose which of the
>> simulated networks should I use out of each set of simulated networks (per
>> each of the four observed networks)?
>>
>> What comes to mind is to run ERGMs for all combinations of, let's say, 50
>> "partly simulated" (imputed) graphs per each of the four networks, and take
>> mean parameter estimates and standard errors as "true", but this would take
>> a very long time, and I am not so sure of ERGM statistical underpinnings to
>> vouchsafe this approach.
>>
>> What may complicate things even further is that we know (from the
>> truncated models) that the three covariate networks have some effect on
>> ties of the focal network, and some of the covariate networks are
>> themselves "correlated" (we ran separate ERGMs to establish that). It seems
>> to me that this would in the ideal case call for an imputation procedure
>> that takes these "associations" into account.
>>
>> In conclusion, I get the feeling of "trying to use a sledge-hammer to
>> kill a fly on the wall". Perhaps some simpler (single) imputation methods
>> would still be viable, having in mind that outgoing ties of not more than
>> 7% actors are missing?
>>
>> Kind regards,
>> Marko Luci?
>>
>> P.S. Not entirely related to the problem above, I saw that Koskinen,
>> Robins and Pattison (2013) mention some "freely available software" to
>> illustrate their Bayesian approach to data augmentation. I wasn't able to
>> find this software on the web, so can any of you please provide me with a
>> link if it is available?
>>
>>
>>
>> _______________________________________________
>> statnet_help mailing list
>> statnet_help@u.washington.edu
>> http://mailman13.u.washington.edu/mailman/listinfo/statnet_help
>>
>>
>

GreifOlution: Greifswald Summer School for PhD-students, PostDocs and advanced graduate students from 16/09/2018 to 22/09/2018 in Greifswald, Germany

As part of the "Year of Mathematical Biology" we proudly announce GreifOlution, the 1st Greifswald Summer School on Mathematics of Evolution (kindly funded by the DAAD, the German Academic Exchange Service).
The main focus of this summer school will be on mathematical models and methods for reconstructing phylogenetic trees and networks, but upon request we might also include some sessions on other related topics, e.g. from population genetics.
 
So if you are a mathematician or computer scientist with a strong interest in biology or a biologist who aspires to a deeper understanding of mathematical or statistical methods and  models, this summer school is what you need! 
 
Greifswald University is one of the hotspots of mathematical phylogenetics and biomathematics in Germany - as the only German university which has been offering a biomathematics study program already for 20 years, the small town located directly at the Baltic Sea has attracted lots of renowned researchers over the years!
So why not benefit from the presence of all these experts? Come and spend a week in summer at the beautiful Baltic Sea and deepen your knowledge on mathematical phylogenetics!

This summer school aims at bridging the gap between mathematics and biology and providing both a broad introduction to various fields of biomathematics (e.g. biostatistics, bioinformatics and mathematical phylogenetics) as well as insights into state-of-the-art research. 
 
We invite applications from PhD students, PostDocs and advanced graduate students of Mathematics, Computer Science or Biology (and related areas of study) who have a great interest in Biomathematics, in particular in Mathematical Phylogenetics.
The school is free of charge. There are also no costs for the social dinner, the excursions and lunch during the summer school, but participants must cover their own accomodation and travel expenses. Foreign participants, however, may be eligible for funding (see the below for the DAAD reglementation concerning foreign participants).

For more details, please visit https://math-inf.uni-greifswald.de/institut/ueber-uns/mitarbeitende/fischer/greifolution/ 

or contact us at greifolution@uni-greifswald.de


We would be pleased to welcome you in Greifswald in September 2018!

Kind regards,
Mareike Fischer

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ergm-terms for ergm.count
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Shane,

On Sat, 2017-12-09 at 11:44 -0700, Shane Gleason wrote:
> Hello-
> 
> I've been working with the ergm.count package and am having a hard
> time 
> getting my model to converge. I suspect part of the problem is in
> the 
> network terms I am using (e.g. nonzero, mutual, etc). The
> documentation 
> directs me to help("ergm-terms").  

Also, it might be worth keeping in mind that valued ERGMs often have
slower mixing, so you might need to increase MCMC sample size and
interval, or use MCMLE.effectiveSize mechanism to try to get them
adaptively.

> However, this file only contains one 
> term.
> 
> Looking through the help file entitled, "Modeling valued networks
> with 
> statnet" (04/16/16) from the Sunbelt 2016 conference ( 
> https://statnet.org/trac/raw-attachment/wiki/Sunbelt2016/Valued.pdf
> ), I 
> am able to come up with a few other terms.  However, I am curious if 
> there is a full list of all the  ergm-terms avaiable for the
> ergm.count 
> somewhere?
> 

Most of the valued terms are usable for data other than counts (though
what they mean might be a work in progress), so they are actually in
the ergm package. help('ergm-terms', package="ergm") will get you the
list of terms implemented, and some of them will be tagged "(valued)".

					I hope this helps,
					Pavel

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Weird summary behavior after loading the "network" package
messages.body_plain:
It's not a bug: the package happens to provide a summary method for a 
class that didn't already have one, and you just happen not to like how 
that method behaves.  This was implemented in the first place because 
yet other parties did not like how the default summary method treated 
character data (which was relevant to how the network package was being 
used), and wanted this behavior. Preferences can, and do, vary.

That said, I'm not personally wedded to this particular approach.  If 
enough folks dislike the current behavior, then we can take a look at 
modifying it in the future.

Hope that helps,

-Carter


On 06/10/2017 02:29 AM, Matteo Gagliolo wrote:
> Hello Carter,
>
>    that is exaclty the issue: loading network changes the behavior of 
> UseMethod("summary") globally for character vectors.
>
> Before loading network, summary.default is called, which produces a 
> result that has names, and can be integrated in the global result of 
> summary.data.frame. After loading network, summary.character is used 
> instead, producing a result with a NULL name, hence the issue.
>
> I think this qualifies as a bug, as loading the package changes the
> behavior of a base function. Also, the change stays after detaching
> the package, until R is restarted.
>
> Is there any way to fix this?

> Matteo

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Question about directed shared partner terms
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Question about directed shared partner terms
messages.body_plain:
Dear statnet team,

I apologize in advance for the long intro. I thought it was important to 
give some background to what I am trying to do.

*Intro:*

I have been 'playing around' a lot with the statnet ergm package 
recently. What I am currently interested in is to explore the 
possibility of applying erg modeling to event graphs. That is, directed 
graphs where the nodes are events, and where the edges (in my case) 
indicate which events (tails) occurred in response to which other events 
(heads). I have been using the idea of representing social processes as 
event graphs for a while now, but I have never been able to really go 
beyond using this as a visual aid in a largely qualitative, interpretive 
analysis. I hope that ergms of event graphs can help me get more out of 
this approach. Just as a note on the side, I am also aware of, and 
exploring other approaches to studying social dynamics, including 
relational event models and stochastic actor-oriented models (especially 
those adapted for events [e.g., Stadtfeld's work]), but I am very keen 
to explore the idea of 'social processes as event graphs' as well, 
because I think it could lead to complementary insights. I am also aware 
that the interpretation of the modeling terms, and of the models 
themselves changes by applying ergms to event graphs. One thing that I 
am doing is thinking about the meaning of statistics like ostars, 
twopaths, transitive triads, shared partners, nodemix, nodematch and so 
on in the context of event graphs.

An important difference between the event graphs that I am trying to 
model, and the social network graphs that ergms are usually applied to, 
is that the nodes in event graphs are ordered in time. That is, edges 
can only point from nodes (events) that occur later in time, to nodes 
(events) that occur earlier in time. This also means that edges can, for 
example, never be reciprocal, and that only a limited number of 
triangles can exist (transitive triangles can occur, but cycles cannot). 
So basically, I am working with Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs), although 
the acyclic nature of the graphs is a consequence of the chronological 
order of the nodes, rather than being at defining feature of event 
graphs. Simply put, all edges in event graphs obey the rule that an edge 
i->j cannot exist if i happened before j. The random graphs that are 
considered by the ergm package (under normal circumstances) of course do 
not obey this rule. To impose this rule on my models, I use the 
ergm-constraints function. I wrote a simple script for R that steps 
through all the dyads in a network, and if the dyad breaks the rule, it 
puts a 1 in a new adjacency matrix for the corresponding dyad. I then 
turn this adjacency matrix into a network object, and then tell the 
ergm-constraints function to keep all the edges in this network fixed as 
absent. This seems to work, at least to some extent, because all 
simulations of models that I created with this constraint obey the 
appropriate rule (edges never point forward in time).

*My puzzle:*

However, *and here comes my question/puzzle*, I was wondering if this 
rule also appropriately translates into the way that statistics are 
calculated. It seems to do so for the edges term. If I translate the 
coefficient for the edges term to a probability, it gives me a measure 
of density that respects the fact that certain edges can never occur. 
However, I was unsure whether the rule is also respected when I look at 
statistics like dyad-wise shared partners. If I understand it right, the 
gw versions of shared partner statistics also consider the number of 
dyads for which the number of shared partners is 0. When counting the 
number of dyads for which this is true, does the algorithm respect the 
fact that certain dyads should be excluded from the count? In other 
words, is it enough to include the constraints that I discuss in the 
intro above, or should I also consider developing adapted versions of 
some of the statistics? (I am not that experienced in statistical 
modeling, but I am fairly experienced in programming in C++, which is 
very similar to C).

*Another, related point:
*While looking into the characteristics of the various terms for shared 
partner distributions, I also encountered something I did not fully 
understand. I saw that there are directed version for the shared partner 
distributions (e.g., desp, ddsp, dgwesp, and so on), which are very 
interesting to me because of their potential meaning in the context of 
event graphs. I also understood (correct me if I am wrong) that, for 
directed networks, the esp.OTP term should essentially be the same as 
the original esp term (OTP is the default choice). However, the 
summaries for these statistics seem to be different.

Consider the following example. I created a simple network of 4 nodes 
and 4 directed edges (see attached file): A->B, A->C, B->D, C->D. If I 
load this network into R, I get the following results if I study their 
dyadwise shared partner distributions:

 > summary(net~dsp(0:3))
dsp0 	dsp1
	dsp2
	dsp3
11
	0
	1
	0


 > summary(net~ddsp(0:3, type = 'OTP'))
dsp0 	dsp1
	dsp2
	dsp3
-1
	0
	1
	0


I have the impression that something goes wrong here. Is it a mistake on 
my side?

Unfortunately, I am not that experienced in statistical modeling, 
although I am very keen to learn more about it, and I am currently 
investing a lot of time and energy in that. However, there are still 
plenty of things that are hard for me to get my head around. I really 
appreciate any help.

Apologies again for the long email. And many thanks for your time and 
patience if you have gotten this far. :)

With kind regards,

Wouter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Valued ERGMs with highly skewed edge weights
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Valued ERGMs with highly skewed edge weights
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Devin -

As always, one's first step is to consider what the weights mean (i.e., 
what is being measured?) and make sure that the model one is positing 
makes sense in that light.  There are relatively few relational 
quantities (binding affinities?) I can think of that vary over 4-5 
orders of magnitude, so this is presumably not a typical social system; 
including edge values over such a wide range would seem to imply either 
that they are being normalized by interacting with similarly large 
coefficients as part of some other process (e.g., molar substrate 
quantities in a chemical system, firing events over a long period of 
time in a neural system) or that the response to the edge weight is not 
on the same scale (i.e., a unit increase in edge weight yields much less 
than a unit increase in response at high weight levels).  In the former 
case, one might consider dichotomizing the data (since the low-weight 
edges might as well be zero weight), while in the latter case it might 
be more reasonable to transform the data into a phenomenologically 
reasonable scale.  But it's hard to know how to proceed further without 
knowing more about what the network represents, and what you want the 
model to accomplish.

Hope that helps (by spurring productive questions, at least!),

-Carter

When transforming to log-space, it seems to converge much more reliably (I *think* because the reference parameter doesn?t expect distributions like mine?). Is there a way to either A. ensure convergence for such highly skewed edge weights or B. reasonably interpret a log transformed edge weight?
>
> Devin

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Using GPU processing for ERGMs
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Juan,

I am aware of some work trying to parallelise various aspects of ERGM MCMC sampling (beyond the trivial one of running multiple independent chains in parallel), but I am not aware of any resounding successes thus far, and none with GPUs. Part of the problem is that while it's often possible to split up the space of possible Metropolis-Hastings proposals in such a way that their acceptances and rejections are mutually independent,

  *   this is only possible to do efficiently if there is a Markov conditional dependence structure (which often leads to bad models);
  *   for less restrictive structures, there would be significant overhead in calculating what is independent of what; and
  *   after every acceptance or rejection, all the results would need to be collated, so the pipeline for each GPU would be very short.

Best,
Pavel

On Wed, 2017-09-20 at 20:13 -0400, Juan Arroyo Flores wrote:
Does anyone know a way of using GPU instead of CPU processing power for doing ERGMs of large networks? As far as I can tell, using GPUs for data processing is getting more and more popular, and seem to be faster. I know there are several packages that make use of GPUs, but I am not sure if I can or how to implement them with statnet. I have a NVIDIA 1070GTX GPU and an i5 (quad-core).

Best,

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Weird summary behavior after loading the "network" package
messages.body_plain:
Hello again,

I found a turnaround this, by defining a function 
"format.summary.character" that restores the expected behavior of the 
code inside summary.data.frame. The function is inspired by format.factor:

format.summary.character <- function(x, ...) {
     s <- summary.default(as.character(x), ...)
     format(structure(as.character(s), names = names(s), dim = dim(s),
                      dimnames = dimnames(s)), ...)
}

After defining this function, the output of summary for character vector 
is still controlled by summary.character, but the output for 
summary.data.frame goes back to normal.

summary(test$a) # still calling summary.character

##   char   many   some vector   with  words
##      1      2      1      1      1      1

summary(test)   # back to normal

##       a                   b
##  Length:7           Min.   :1.0
##  Class :character   1st Qu.:2.5
##  Mode  :character   Median :4.0
##                     Mean   :4.0
##                     3rd Qu.:5.5
##                     Max.   :7.0
##

Hope it helps other users in the same situation.

Cheers,

Matteo

On 2017-06-10 11:29, Matteo Gagliolo wrote:
> Hello Carter,
>
>     that is exaclty the issue: loading network changes the behavior of
> UseMethod("summary") globally for character vectors.
>
> Before loading network, summary.default is called, which produces a
> result that has names, and can be integrated in the global result of
> summary.data.frame. After loading network, summary.character is used
> instead, producing a result with a NULL name, hence the issue.
>
> I think this qualifies as a bug, as loading the package changes the
> behavior of a base function. Also, the change stays after detaching
> the package, until R is restarted.
>
> Is there any way to fix this?
>
> Thanks a lot,
>
> Matteo
>
> On 2017-06-10 00:56, Carter T. Butts wrote:
>> Hi, Matteo.  The network package has a summary.character function, which
>> is presumably being called by summary.data.frame. The different behavior
>> would be due to having this function loaded.
>>
>> -Carter
>>
>>
>> On 06/09/2017 02:30 PM, Matteo Gagliolo wrote:
>>> Dear statnet list,
>>>
>>>     I have been having a weird bug lately when calling summary
>>> on data frames containing character columns, and it seems to be
>>> related to the network package.
>>>
>>> The following code is sufficient to reproduce the bug, after calling
>>>
>>> R --no-restore
>>>
>>> ---
>>> test <- data.frame(a=c("some", "char", "vector", "with", "many",
>>> "many", "words"), b=1:7, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
>>> summary(test)
>>> summary(test$a)
>>> library("network")
>>> summary(test)
>>> summary(test$a)
>>> ---
>>>
>>> The output for the first summary(test) is:
>>>
>>>       a                   b
>>>  Length:7           Min.   :1.0
>>>  Class :character   1st Qu.:2.5
>>>  Mode  :character   Median :4.0
>>>                     Mean   :4.0
>>>                     3rd Qu.:5.5
>>>                     Max.   :7.0
>>>
>>> as expected, while the same command after loading network gives:
>>>
>>>     a                b
>>>  NULL:some     Min.   :1.0
>>>  NULL:char     1st Qu.:2.5
>>>  NULL:vector   Median :4.0
>>>  NULL:with     Mean   :4.0
>>>  NULL:many     3rd Qu.:5.5
>>>  NULL:many     Max.   :7.0
>>>  NULL:words
>>>
>>> Notice the repetition: *every* line is printed, prepended by "NULL:",
>>> and it becomes impossible to read when there are thousands of lines.
>>>
>>> In both cases, summary(test$a) gives the expected output.
>>>
>>> The prepended NULL comes from these three lines in summary.data.frame:
>>>
>>>         sms <- format(sms, digits = digits)
>>>         lbs <- format(names(sms))
>>>         sms <- paste0(lbs, ":", sms, "  ")
>>>
>>> It's inside a for loop over columns, where sms is the output of
>>> summary for the current column. For character columns, names(sms) is
>>> NULL, hence the issue.
>>>
>>> I'm on R version 3.3.3 (2017-03-06), using network

> No problem. You are right. Rsiena is used mainly for formation. But 
> Rsiena is the only method that i know for modeling longitudinal data!
>

TERGMs (with e.g. STERGMs as an important special case), dynamic latent 
variable models (e.g., dynamic latent space models, DRIFT, etc.), REMs, 
etc. would all be examples of non-SAB families for longitudinal 
relational data.  If one is interested in exploratory analysis (rather 
than modeling per se), one could add time series analysis of network 
descriptives, multidimensional scaling of Hamming or structural 
distances, etc.  There are quite a lot of alternatives, whose 
applicability depends on what you are willing to assume, and what you 
want to achieve.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Valued ERGMs with highly skewed edge weights
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Valued ERGMs with highly skewed edge weights
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Devin.  Pavel provided one useful approach.  Since you are dealing 
with transition matrices, another natural approach would be to 
row-normalize: your i,j cell is then the probability of posting on j 
next, given that one has previously posted on i.  (I would also consider 
using a simple local posterior mean for those probability estimates, 
treating the counts in each row as multinomial and using a minimally 
informative prior - this will give you some shrinkage for extremes in 
the case of small sending groups, and will pull your probability 
estimates away from 0 in the no-observed-transition case.  It's also 
extremely easy to do.)  It would then be natural to work on the logit 
scale, and obvious controls would be column effects (you don't need row 
effects, obviously) and reciprocity.  In principle this can be fit with 
ergm() using the StdNormal reference, although Pavel may want to comment 
on how thoroughly this has been tested to date. Another approach would 
be to fit a latentnet model with receiver effects to control for 
popularity, and then use a permutation test to see if political 
subreddits are closer than would be expected in the residual space.  
(You could put the homophily effect in the model directly, but given the 
issues with accurately estimating the latent versus manifest components 
of latent space models, it's probably just as well to map the subs into 
the latent space and then assess proximity after the fact.)

Hope that helps,

-Carter


On 04/17/2017 06:18 PM, Devin Gaffney wrote:
> Ah yes, the nodes-and-edges question. This is part of a study on how people move around on Reddit (i.e. why people post on some subreddit and then another and so forth). The network is a snapshot of the transition matrix of dominant subreddits, where nodes are subreddits and edges are the number of people who posted on subreddit A and then subsequently posted on subreddit B (I?m assuming some familiarity with Reddit as a forum, correct me if I?m wrong in assuming that!). The problem is that, when considering the largest subreddit transitions (such as people posting on AskReddit and then posting on videos, for example, the number of people moving in that direction could be, for some snapshot, many thousands of people, while transitions between two much smaller subreddits may have only a dozen or so people moving that direction. The goal of fitting this into an ERGM is to see if there is a topical homophily effect (i.e. do people move between political subreddits more often than chance). I?m controlling for sum+nonzero+mutual+edges as a first pass, and am adding nodecov on the number of people posting on each subreddit to attempt to control for subreddit size - any and all advice/productive-question-asking is definitely sought!
>
> Devin
>
>> On Apr 17, 2017, at 8:49 PM, Carter T. Butts <buttsc@uci.edu> wrote:
>>
>> Hi, Devin -
>>
>> As always, one's first step is to consider what the weights mean (i.e., what is being measured?) and make sure that the model one is positing makes sense in that light.  There are relatively few relational quantities (binding affinities?) I can think of that vary over 4-5 orders of magnitude, so this is presumably not a typical social system; including edge values over such a wide range would seem to imply either that they are being normalized by interacting with similarly large coefficients as part of some other process (e.g., molar substrate quantities in a chemical system, firing events over a long period of time in a neural system) or that the response to the edge weight is not on the same scale (i.e., a unit increase in edge weight yields much less than a unit increase in response at high weight levels).  In the former case, one might consider dichotomizing the data (since the low-weight edges might as well be zero weight), while in the latter case it might be more reasonable to transform the data into a phenomenologically reasonable scale.  But it's hard to know how to proceed further without knowing more about what the network represents, and what you want the model to accomplish.
>>
>> Hope that helps (by spurring productive questions, at least!),
>>
>> -Carter
>>
>> On 04/17/2017 03:39 PM, Devin Gaffney wrote:
>>> Hello all - I have highly skewed edge weights for a 50 node network. Most edges have values in the single or maybe double digits, while several edges have values in the 10^4->10^5 region. In other contexts I would log-transform the data during a regression and then talk about coefficients in reference to the log value of the variable, but I?m not sure how to do that with valued ERGMs. In other words, I have a highly skewed edge weight distribution, and models often fail to converge. When transforming to log-space, it seems to converge much more reliably (I *think* because the reference parameter doesn?t expect distributions like mine?). Is there a way to either A. ensure convergence for such highly skewed edge weights or B. reasonably interpret a log transformed edge weight?
>>>

Hi Rachael -

It seems likely to be one of a few factors:

- nearly all ties in the network are homophilous on pasture, so the 
estimate is very high and causing instability

- there is very high correlation between pasture and one of the other 
attributes (breed or use).

Follow these commands, and send the results just to me.? Once we 
diagnose the issue for sure, we can update the list with the final 
insights, for those who are interested.

mixingmatrix(new1, pasture)
mixingmatrix(new1, breed)
mixingmatrix(new1, use)

pasture <- new1%v%'pasture'
breed <- new1%v%'breed'
use <- new1%v%'use'

xtabs(~pasture+breed)
xtabs(~pasture+use)

HTH,

Steve

As you suggested, the issue came from the one of the combinations that was
not represented in my dataset (women having 1 main and 2 casual partnership

this item makes the model run smoothly.

 

Concerning the type of model, I decided to go for a model with a nodematch
term on sex to stay as general as possible (and be able to target both
heterosexual and homosexual partnership).

Damien

summary(your.network.name ~ edges + nodefactor(c('sex',"deg.main",

including the model estimation line.  let me know what results you get, as
that will also help pinpoint this.

steve

Damien - 

My guess is that in the network that you created to do the estimation on,
one of the 12 possible (sex x deg.main x deg.pers) combinations is not
actually represented by anybody in the network.  The tools can't tell that
there are some combinations that are theoretically possible in your model
but don't actually appear, so they don't include a term for them.

to me with some reproducible code and I can check further.

Also, out of curiosity, since you are doing two sexes - have you set the
model up as bipartite or do you just have a nodematch term on sex? I don't
think that would affect this issue here, but perhaps there's something I'm
not thinking of.

Cheers,

Steve

> Dear statnet list,
>
>     I have been having a weird bug lately when calling summary
> on data frames containing character columns, and it seems to be
> related to the network package.
>
> The following code is sufficient to reproduce the bug, after calling
>
> R --no-restore
>
> ---
> test <- data.frame(a=c("some", "char", "vector", "with", "many", 
> "many", "words"), b=1:7, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
> summary(test)
> summary(test$a)
> library("network")
> summary(test)
> summary(test$a)
> ---
>
> The output for the first summary(test) is:
>
>       a                   b
>  Length:7           Min.   :1.0
>  Class :character   1st Qu.:2.5
>  Mode  :character   Median :4.0
>                     Mean   :4.0
>                     3rd Qu.:5.5
>                     Max.   :7.0
>
> as expected, while the same command after loading network gives:
>
>     a                b
>  NULL:some     Min.   :1.0
>  NULL:char     1st Qu.:2.5
>  NULL:vector   Median :4.0
>  NULL:with     Mean   :4.0
>  NULL:many     3rd Qu.:5.5
>  NULL:many     Max.   :7.0

messages.body_plain:
Only thing I would add is that lowering alpha towards gwesp(0) becomes 
problematic in dense networks, where every edge is likely to be involved 
in at least one triangle (thx to Steve Goodreau for reminding me of this 
yesterday).

With a density of 11% that may be reaching that threshold.  So I would 
suggest looking at summary(netw ~ edges + gwesp(0, fixed=T) + ...) to 
see whether the summary statistics for the gwesp(0) term is almost equal 
to the number of dyads.

best,
mm

> If you are using gwesp() and still having issues, this can suggest that you 
> are trying to model clustering associated with an underlying source of 
> heterogeneity (e.g., homophily or propinquity on unobserved variables) with a 
> homogeneous mechanism (here, the ESP effects that go into the GWESP term). 
> Adding more covariate effects, or looking more carefully at how they are 
> parameterized, can often make a huge difference.? (In essence, the issue is 
> that GWESP and friends are trying to capture the pattern of triadic closure 
> by positing a uniform tendency towards closure that affects the entire 
> network equally.? If what is really going on is that your clustering is the 
> result of some inhomogeneous process, then the model is stuck between the 
> Scylla of not producing enough triangulation in the high-density portions of 
> the graph and the Charybdis of producing too much triangulation in the 
> low-density portions of the graph.? The way the model resolves this untenable 
> situation is not always to one's liking.)
>
> Lowering the alpha coefficient towards 0 (which damps out the marginal effect 
> of additional shared partners more aggressively) can also help.? But I would 
> start by doing some exploratory analysis of the network, and asking whether 
> it is plausible that you are leaving out some important sources of 
> heterogeneity. Control for that first, then worry about homogeneous sources 
> of dependence.
>
> Hope that helps,
>
> -Carter

messages.body_plain:
Hello Carter,

    that is exaclty the issue: loading network changes the behavior of 
UseMethod("summary") globally for character vectors.

Before loading network, summary.default is called, which produces a 
result that has names, and can be integrated in the global result of 
summary.data.frame. After loading network, summary.character is used 
instead, producing a result with a NULL name, hence the issue.

I think this qualifies as a bug, as loading the package changes the
behavior of a base function. Also, the change stays after detaching
the package, until R is restarted.

Is there any way to fix this?

Thanks a lot,

Matteo

messages.subject: [statnet_help] extending lnam with "snow" or "parallel"?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Mark.  Your question seems to conflate lnam and netlm.  In what 
analysis are you actually interested?  (I would note that neither 
currently has a parallel implementation, but the issues involved in 
parallelizing each are very different.  Also, there are other 
optimizations for large, sparse matrices that can in principle be 
employed for network autocorrelation models that cannot be used for 
netlm, and vice versa.)

As a general matter, just setting aside cores is not going to result in 
performance enhancement for most computation: you have to actually have 
and specifically employ a parallel implementation.  Depending on the 
problem, the difficulty of parallelization can vary from trivial to 
impossible (and it always involves engineering tradeoffs).  But it's 
something that has to be actively designed in.

-Carter

Hi, Shupin -

If you are using gwesp() and still having issues, this can suggest that
you are trying to model clustering associated with an underlying source
of heterogeneity (e.g., homophily or propinquity on unobserved
variables) with a homogeneous mechanism (here, the ESP effects that go
into the GWESP term).  Adding more covariate effects, or looking more
carefully at how they are parameterized, can often make a huge
difference.  (In essence, the issue is that GWESP and friends are trying
to capture the pattern of triadic closure by positing a uniform tendency
towards closure that affects the entire network equally.  If what is
really going on is that your clustering is the result of some
inhomogeneous process, then the model is stuck between the Scylla of not
producing enough triangulation in the high-density portions of the graph
and the Charybdis of producing too much triangulation in the low-density
portions of the graph.  The way the model resolves this untenable
situation is not always to one's liking.)

Lowering the alpha coefficient towards 0 (which damps out the marginal
effect of additional shared partners more aggressively) can also help.
But I would start by doing some exploratory analysis of the network, and
asking whether it is plausible that you are leaving out some important
sources of heterogeneity. Control for that first, then worry about
homogeneous sources of dependence.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Weird summary behavior after loading the "network" package
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Weird summary behavior after loading the "network" package
messages.body_plain:
Dear statnet list,

	I have been having a weird bug lately when calling summary
on data frames containing character columns, and it seems to be
related to the network package.

The following code is sufficient to reproduce the bug, after calling

R --no-restore

---
test <- data.frame(a=c("some", "char", "vector", "with", "many", 
"many", "words"), b=1:7, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
summary(test)
summary(test$a)
library("network")
summary(test)
summary(test$a)
---

The output for the first summary(test) is:

       a                   b
  Length:7           Min.   :1.0
  Class :character   1st Qu.:2.5
  Mode  :character   Median :4.0
                     Mean   :4.0
                     3rd Qu.:5.5
                     Max.   :7.0

as expected, while the same command after loading network gives:

     a                b
  NULL:some     Min.   :1.0
  NULL:char     1st Qu.:2.5
  NULL:vector   Median :4.0
  NULL:with     Mean   :4.0
  NULL:many     3rd Qu.:5.5
  NULL:many     Max.   :7.0
  NULL:words

Notice the repetition: *every* line is printed, prepended by "NULL:", 
and it becomes impossible to read when there are thousands of lines.

In both cases, summary(test$a) gives the expected output.

The prepended NULL comes from these three lines in summary.data.frame:

         sms <- format(sms, digits = digits)
         lbs <- format(names(sms))
         sms <- paste0(lbs, ":", sms, "  ")

It's inside a for loop over columns, where sms is the output of summary 
for the current column. For character columns, names(sms) is NULL, hence 
the issue.

I'm on R version 3.3.3 (2017-03-06), using network
Version 1.13.0 created on 2015-08-31. I'll be happy to upgrade if
this is a known bug.

Thanks a lot for your help!

Matteo

On Thu, 16 Nov 2017, Carter T. Butts wrote:

> Hi, Shupin -
>
> If you are using gwesp() and still having issues, this can suggest that you
> are trying to model clustering associated with an underlying source of
> heterogeneity (e.g., homophily or propinquity on unobserved variables) with a
> homogeneous mechanism (here, the ESP effects that go into the GWESP term).
> Adding more covariate effects, or looking more carefully at how they are
> parameterized, can often make a huge difference.  (In essence, the issue is
> that GWESP and friends are trying to capture the pattern of triadic closure
> by positing a uniform tendency towards closure that affects the entire
> network equally.  If what is really going on is that your clustering is the
> result of some inhomogeneous process, then the model is stuck between the
> Scylla of not producing enough triangulation in the high-density portions of
> the graph and the Charybdis of producing too much triangulation in the
> low-density portions of the graph.  The way the model resolves this untenable
> situation is not always to one's liking.)
>
> Lowering the alpha coefficient towards 0 (which damps out the marginal effect
> of additional shared partners more aggressively) can also help.  But I would
> start by doing some exploratory analysis of the network, and asking whether
> it is plausible that you are leaving out some important sources of
> heterogeneity. Control for that first, then worry about homogeneous sources
> of dependence.
>
> Hope that helps,
>
> -Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Clarification requested on summary.statistics()
messages.body_plain:
Just a quick additional comment.

You can think of the GW terms as weighted sums (of either degree 
sequences for the GWD terms, or of shared partner sequences for the 
GW*SP terms).  The weight is

{1 - (1-exp{-decay})^i}

where i is the degree (or shared partner) value

>From this you can see why the weighted sum will (often) produce 
non-integers.

best,
mm

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Power analysis for ERGM
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Michael -

Power analysis in the context of dependent data is not trivial, and 
indeed a lot is unknown; ERGMs are no exception.  However, here are some 
practical suggestions:

- In the special case of edgewise independent data, ERGMs reduce to 
logistic network regression, which is nothing more than logistic 
regression where the variables have been expressed as matrices rather 
than vectors.  Standard logistic regression results apply here, and you 
can employ them in the event that you happen to be in this regime.  (In 
particular, note that in this case you have N(N-1)/2 data degrees of 
freedom in the undirected case, and N(N-1) in the directed case, 
assuming no loops.)

- Likewise, dyad (but not edgewise) independent models are akin to 
multinomial logit models on the dyad states, and can be treated accordingly.

- In the more general case, your best bet is probably simulation.  There 
are various ways to proceed, depending on what you want to know - it's 
hard to tell from your description what the specific complaint was, but 
I would look at what, specifically, it is claimed that you would not 
have the power to detect and attempt to assess that by conditional 
simulation.  So, e.g., if you don't find an effect for statistic t, then 
one way to assess how large/small a value t_obs would have been needed 
(holding all else constant) to obtain a significant result at p<k is to 
(1) simulate draws from your model (w/out the t effect), (2) calculate t 
for each draw, and (3) examine the 1-k simulation interval.  (This 
mirrors the type of test for which ERGMs were initially introduced - see 
the later part of Holland and Leinhardt's 1981 JASA paper, on testing 
for triadic effects using p1 as a baseline.)  Other types of questions 
require other procedures, of course.

Hope that helps!

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] expanding the size of the network
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] expanding the size of the network
messages.body_plain:
Hi Lin,

When changing the network size, the key is to update the edges 
coefficient in your model.? The basic idea is to take the edges 
coefficient and add the natural log of the old network size and then 
subtract the natural log of the new network size. Equivalently, one can 
think about partitioning the edges coefficient into two parts: one an 
offset based on the network size and another the remainder, and then 
update the offset. Without this update, ergms will preserve density as 
one changes network size, but with this update, they preserve mean 
degree. Although the former may seem reasonable on first pass, for most 
social phenomena the latter makes muc more sense and matches observed 
behavior much more closely. Note that you do *not* have to update any 
other coefficients besides the edges.

All this is explained in:

Pavel N. Krivitsky, Mark S. Handcock, and Martina Morris (2011). 
Adjusting for Network Size and Composition Effects in Exponential-Family 
Random Graph Models. Statistical Methodology, 8(4): 319?339.

and is also talked about in our Network Modeling for Epidemics course: 
http://statnet.github.io/nme/

Note, however, that Kirivitsky, Handcock and Morris have - in the paper 
below, and in subsequent explorations - proven that this works perfectly 
for dyadic independent terms, and behaves reasonably for some common 
dyadic dependent terms, but haven't proven it works exactly for the 
latter. (Co-authors - correct me if I'm wrong on that!!!)

It's not actually 100% clear (at least to me) what the expected behavior 
should be for something like GWESP when networks change in size - how do 
we believe explicit triangle closure behaves as networks scale in size, 
such that the background probably of a triangle being closed declines 
for the same density? Will the magnitude of the force stay the same, or 
will people exert more effort to close trinagle in order to get back to 
the same prportion of their triangles being closed as in a smaller 
network?? It's tricky stuff, but very intersting, for someone who wanted 
to explore it in depth with comparative empirical data, like Add Health.

Nevertheless, I believe this simple method should get you close to where 
you want to be.

Here is some basic example code using a network of size 100 with mean 
degree of 1, then simulating a network of size 1000 that also has a mean 
degree of 1, by updating the coefficient form the first model. You 
should be able to use this as a base, and add in you GWESP and other terms.

library(statnet)
smallnet <- network.initialize(100, directed=F)
smallnet <- san(smallnet~edges, target.stats = 50) # mean deg = 1
smallergm <- ergm(smallnet~edges)

largenet <- network.initialize(1000, directed=F)
largecoef <- smallergm$coef[1] + log(100) - log(1000)
largenet <- simulate(largenet~edges, coef=largecoef)

Cheers,

Steve

I have collected  friendship network data for *multiple classes* in
different schools.

who didn?t took it, controlling for some variables and baseline indegree
using MRQAP.

?*Course*? is an attribute of each node and is equal to ?1? for those who
took the course, ?0? for those who didn?t took it and ?NA? for those who
didn?t know about it.


*However, the problem is that:*
*A)* since students were asked to nominate only classmates I have multiple
networks not a single big network.
*B)* in some of them I have just one student who is either part of the
?course group? or the ?non-course group?. Therefore, I don't think running
MRQAP for each class and then using meta-analysis will work.


The other option that I found is to use "structural zeros" to create a
single big matrix and run MRQAP, but since I?m very new in R and I couldn?t

success

mynet %v% "class"<-class

mynet %v% " course "<- course

list.vertex.attributes(mynet)


Thanks in advance for your support,

dynfit<-stergm(sim.edges[[1]],

First, am I allowed to do smth like that?

messages.subject: [statnet_help] extending lnam with "snow" or "parallel"?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mark,

I don't think the underlying optim function permits parallelization, and 
I can't of any good ways to do this task in parallel. However, it may be 
possible to speed up computations by employing a canned GLM routine that 
is optimized for speed, such as the speedglm package. If you are willing 
to use the tnam package instead of the lnam function, you can use its 
tnamdata function to prepare a data frame with the relevant terms and 
then hand it over to some fast GLM implementation like speedglm. But 
this is experimental, so make sure you compare your findings to lnam 
with a smaller dataset.

Best,

Philip

--
Dr Philip Leifeld
Senior Lecturer in Research Methods
Director of Postgraduate Research Training
School of Social and Political Sciences
University of Glasgow

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Predicting changes in node network centrality over time
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Chris.  If your nodal attributes are constant, then what do you mean 
by their having an effect on centrality over time?  This can be made 
meaningful, but only in the context of a more specific class of 
assumptions.  (For instance, if you posited a growth model for 
centrality whose parameter was putatively related to the covariate, you 
could test that.)

Without such additional clarifications, your problem is ill-posed: you 
are asking for the relationship between a vector of real numbers and a 
vector of time series.  (In this case, the fact that your time series 
come from a network is a red herring.)  There are many kinds of 
relationships that one could seek, but you will need to be more specific 
about what you want to know in order for us to be of much help...

-Carter

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] error with induced subgraph, edge IDs
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Jesse -

Your problem appears to stem from using 
which(expNets[[1]]%e%"effect"==3) to get the edge IDs.  This will only 
work if your edge IDs happen to be exactly the same as their ordering 
(1, 2, 3...).  This is usually the case for newly created network 
objects, but it does not have to be true in general: e.g., your edge IDs 
could be 2, 5, 10, 31, 127, and so forth.  Such "gaps" in edge ID 
sequence usually arise from edges having been deleted from a network 
object at some stage.  As you discovered, the safe way to select edge 
IDs is to use valid.eids() to obtain the ordered list of valid edge IDs, 
and then to subset this list by the output of %e%.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGM
messages.body_plain:
Dear Shiran,

Could you explain what you mean with grow?


If you want to add, say 250 more nodes and simulate the ties between the
old and new nodeset and within the new nodeset but keeping the ties within
the old nodeset fixed, then this can be easily done with the ergm package.

#1) Add the new nodes to the old network - I assume a simple adjacency
matrix:

# first we create the new bigger network.
#oldNet = your current network with the 300 nodes

newNodes <- 250 #number of new nodes
newSize <- nrow(oldNet) + newNodes

newNet <- matrix(NA, newSize , newSize )
newNet[nrow(oldNet),nrow(oldNet)] <- oldNet

# Now we have and adjacency matrix of the desired size with the former
network between the 300 original nodes and missing data for all other ties

#2) Simulate the new ties -I do not know if you used simulate in R to
simulate the network you have, so I write the script with sufficient
detail, if you have not used it.
# If you are familiar, just set: constraints = ~observed, to keep all old
ties as they are and only simulate the new ones.


newNetSim <- sim (newNet ~ ... , #insert your model parameters here
                               coef = ..., #insert a vector with the
parameter values here
                               statsonly = FALSE,  #to return the simulated
network(s)
                               nsim = 1, # the number of simulated networks
you want
                               constraints = ~observed, #this leaves all
observed ties (here your original network) as they are - the function will
only simulate missing ties
                               control = control.simulate(MCMC.burnin =
1,000,000 #given that your network is very big, I would give the algorithm
enough time to simulate

                                        #through all the cells multiple
times. Maybe your model is quite simple, then a smaller

                                        #value will be fine. Best have a
look at the network statistics of the simulated networks,

                                        #if there are multiple and see if
the simulation is converged

 MCMC.interval = 1,000,000)) # if you sample multiple networks ensure that
they are spaced out far enough in the

                                             # sampling process. Otherwise
your network statistics will be highly correlated.

                                             # Best monitor the auto
correlation of the simulated networks and increase the interval if
necessary.


I hope this helps.

Best Regards,

Robert Krause

9712 TG Groningen, The Netherlands

Shupin,

The edges+triangle model is well known in the field for being a
"degenerate" model specification.  There is a substantial literature on
the problem of degeneracy in specifying models for ERGs -- it's not a
problem with the method, it is a problem of model specification.
Essentially, this result means "that model would never have produced
the network you observe"

Try using the gwesp terms instead. And if you're not familiar with them I
suggest you take a look at the following papers:

Snijders TAB, Pattison PE, Robins GL, Handcock MS. New
specifications for exponential random graph models. In: Stolzenberg RM,
editor. Sociological Methodology 2006, Vol 362006. p. 99-153.

Hunter DR. Curved Exponential Family Models for Social Networks.
Social networks. 2007;29(2):216-30. doi: 10.1016/j.socnet.2006.08.005.

best,

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Check for correlation between predictors
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Yes, as with linear and logistic regression, multicollinearity can be a problem. The effects on interpretation are similar, but correlation can also interfere with estimation.

To examine it once you've successfully fit the model, mcmc.diagnostics() will show you which statistics are the most correlated. Before fitting the model, you can look at the variance-covariance matrix of the MPLE estimates (vcov(ergm(nw~model, estimate="MPLE")), which should give a pretty good idea (especially for dyad-independent predictors) as well.

I hope this helps,
Pavel

messages.subject: [statnet_help] 答复: Error in MCMC
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Shupin -

If you are using gwesp() and still having issues, this can suggest that 
you are trying to model clustering associated with an underlying source 
of heterogeneity (e.g., homophily or propinquity on unobserved 
variables) with a homogeneous mechanism (here, the ESP effects that go 
into the GWESP term).? Adding more covariate effects, or looking more 
carefully at how they are parameterized, can often make a huge 
difference.? (In essence, the issue is that GWESP and friends are trying 
to capture the pattern of triadic closure by positing a uniform tendency 
towards closure that affects the entire network equally.? If what is 
really going on is that your clustering is the result of some 
inhomogeneous process, then the model is stuck between the Scylla of not 
producing enough triangulation in the high-density portions of the graph 
and the Charybdis of producing too much triangulation in the low-density 
portions of the graph.? The way the model resolves this untenable 
situation is not always to one's liking.)

Lowering the alpha coefficient towards 0 (which damps out the marginal 
effect of additional shared partners more aggressively) can also help.? 
But I would start by doing some exploratory analysis of the network, and 
asking whether it is plausible that you are leaving out some important 
sources of heterogeneity. Control for that first, then worry about 
homogeneous sources of dependence.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGM warning
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Replying to this publicly, in case anyone has a similar question. The reason for the problem in this case is that one of the "employer" levels has 0 relationships, which is the smallest attainable value in the sample space and therefore has MLE at -?. For binary ERGMs, this would be detected, but for valued ERGMs, this type of detection doesn't work, because 0 is not the smallest value for nodefactor(..., form="sum") in all possible sample spaces (e.g., signed edges).

Also, because there are 31 distinct employers, I recommend increasing the MCMC.samplesize and/or MCMC.interval.

I hope this helps,
Pavel

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Comparing levels of homophily between subsets of edges in the same network
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Comparing levels of homophily between subsets of edges in the same network
messages.body_plain:
Hello Timoth?e --


One idea for something to try here would be to code up one or more new 
ERGM terms for the count of homophilous ties that appear within your 
higher-order configurations of interest.? You could then fit a model 
that had both a basic nodematch term in it and your more specific 
nodematch term in it, and you could see if the latter was positive and 
significant even when the former was in the model. This would give you 
the amount of homophily "boost" associated with the configurations.? The 
trick, of course, is that it requires writing up a new term -- this is 
often not a lot of work, but when your configurations of interest are 
slightly larger -- e.g. cliques of size 4 or above -- them the change 
statistics are less straightforward.? Still doable, though, and starting 
with an existing term /cycle, /and borrowing code from nodematch to put 
into it,//would simplify things dramatically. .? Note that this does 
require a small knowledge of C, although I've been able to mostly fake 
it by combining code from existing terms in most cases. And we have a 
few sets of resources to help, all linked to from 
https://statnet.csde.washington.edu/trac/wiki/Resources. These include a 
dedicated CRAN package (ergm.userterms), and a workshop offered at past 
Sunbelts (see "Archive of previous workshop materials") and tutorial 
(under "statnet User's Guide: JoSS papers on statnet") that both provide 
guidance for that package.

HTH,
Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Comparing levels of homophily between subsets of edges in the same network
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Comparing levels of homophily between subsets of edges in the same network
messages.body_plain:
Dear Statnet users,


I work on (ethnic) homophily in social networks. An hypothesis I want to test is whether the ties that are embedded in higher level structures are more homophilic, on average, than the ones who are not.


>From my original network, I can extract only those edges that are reciprocated (ie, symmetrizing the network); then that are part of a full triad ; that are part of a clique of size 4, 5 and so on. In each case, I am interested in comparing the levels of homophily ("nodematch" term) among the edges of the subset with that of the whole network.


How can I do this using ERGMs ? Extracting a subset of my network  and estimating an ERGM model with the "nodematch" term for that subset is pretty easy, but how to make sure that the increase in homophily that I may observe in the new subset is not a mechanical result produced by the extraction itself ? For e.g., I guess that if you symmetrize a random network, the homophily rates observed in the symmetrized graph will always be higher than that of the original graph. Is there a way to assess the statistical significance of the increase in homophily that I observe in symmetrical links ?


Below is an example using statnet built-in data. I only show it for reciprocal as opposed to all links, but I ask myself the same question about links within triads or cliques.

library(statnet)
library(stargazer)

data("faux.dixon.high")
net <- faux.dixon.high

net.s <- as.sociomatrix(net)
net.s <- symmetrize(net.s, rule = "strong")
net.s <- network(net.s,directed = F)

net.s%v%"race" <- as.character(net%v%"race")

m1 <- ergm(net ~ edges + nodematch('race'))
s1 <- ergm(net.s ~ edges + nodematch('race'))

stargazer(m1,s1,type="text")

# The nodematch coefficient is greater ! Does it mean reciprocal ties are more often homophilic ?

summary(net ~ edges + nodematch('race'))
summary(net.s ~ edges + nodematch('race'))

912/1197
180/219

# There is indeed a greater proportion of symmetric ties that are homophilic. But is it significant ?

At some point I thought that it may be done using interaction effects (modelling the interaction effect between the "mutual" and "nodematch" term in an ERGM model applied to the full network) but I don't know whether the ERGM package can do this. Do you have any ideas or suggestions on how to work around that problem ?


Many thanks for the help !


Best Regards


---------------------------------

Timoth?e Chabot

PhD Researcher

European University Institute

On Tue, Oct 31, 2017 at 4:32 PM, Micha? Bojanowski <michal2992@gmail.com>
wrote:

> Hi Shiran,
>
> Your seemingly simple question actually touches many quite fundamental
> issues, both statistical and substantive. Let me give you my take, I hope
> others in this list will chip in if I miss something.
>
> From the purely technical point of view, you can fit an ERGM to your
> 300-node network, take the parameter estimates, and then sample 400-node
> networks from an ERGM with the same parameter estimates. HOWEVER, the BIG
> question is:
>
> Is it reasonable to assume that the generated 400-node networks can be
> thought of as a result of the same real-world process that governs the
> observed 300-node network?
>
> The answer is not obvious because it depends how the real-world processes
> shaping the network scale with network size. That's a substantive question
> and answer depends on what the network represents.
>
> ERGMs with "standard" parametrisation scale with network size preserving
> the density, i.e. networks of different sizes sampled from the same ERGM
> model (terms and coefficient values) will have on average the same density.
> Sometimes this might be what you want, but sometimes it is not. For
> example, if you study social network within a school class of 20, kids
> might report on average 3 friends. It is not  reasonable to assume that
> average number of friends for a kid in a class of 40 will be a double of
> that. The average degree will be rather similar. In other words, the
> befriending process scales with network size such that average degree
> should stay the same and density, as a consequence, decrease. Naive
> sampling of bigger networks from the same ERGM will give unrealistically
> dense networks. To overcome that offset terms were developed, see:
>
> Krivitsky, Pavel N., Mark S. Handcock, and Martina Morris. "Adjusting for
> network size and composition effects in exponential-family random graph
> models." *Statistical methodology* 8.4 (2011): 319-339.
>
> Kolaczyk, Eric D., and Pavel N. Krivitsky. "On the question of effective
> sample size in network modeling: An asymptotic inquiry." *Statistical
> science: a review journal of the Institute of Mathematical Statistics* 30.2
> (2015): 184.
>
> ... and section 5.3 of
>
> Schweinberger, Michael, Pavel N. Krivitsky, and Carter T. Butts.
> "Foundations of Finite-, Super-, and Infinite-Population Random Graph
> Inference." *arXiv preprint arXiv:1707.04800* (2017).
>
> You can use offsets with ergm(). I don't have a good code snipet with an
> example at this very moment but have a look at ?ergm and arguments `offset`
> and `offset.coef`.
>
>  Of course the issue of scaling may not be limited to density vs average
> degree (essentially the `edges` term), but may in principle apply to other
> terms as well.
>
>
> hth,
> Michal
>
>
>
>
>

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] expanding the size of the network
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Lin and Steve,

Somewhat belatedly, adjusting the density alone will not help with triadic effects. What might help (although only very approximately) is a triadic offset of the form

offset(edges)+offset(gwesp(0, fixed=TRUE))

with

offset.coef=c(-1,+1/3) * (log(Nsim)-log(Nfit))

where Nsim is the network size you are simulating and Nfit is the network size you estimated from.

More details can be found in
Krivitsky, P. N. & Kolaczyk, E. D. (2015) On the Question of Effective Sample Size in Network Modeling: An Asymptotic Inquiry. Statistical Science, 30(2): 184-198.
I hope this helps,
Pavel
On Thu, 2017-12-07 at 08:29 -0800, Steven M Goodreau wrote:

Hi Lin,

When changing the network size, the key is to update the edges coefficient in your model.  The basic idea is to take the edges coefficient and add the natural log of the old network size and then subtract the natural log of the new network size. Equivalently, one can think about partitioning the edges coefficient into two parts: one an offset based on the network size and another the remainder, and then update the offset. Without this update, ergms will preserve density as one changes network size, but with this update, they preserve mean degree. Although the former may seem reasonable on first pass, for most social phenomena the latter makes muc more sense and matches observed behavior much more closely. Note that you do *not* have to update any other coefficients besides the edges.

All this is explained in:

Pavel N. Krivitsky, Mark S. Handcock, and Martina Morris (2011). Adjusting for Network Size and Composition Effects in Exponential-Family Random Graph Models. Statistical Methodology, 8(4): 319?339.

and is also talked about in our Network Modeling for Epidemics course: http://statnet.github.io/nme/

Note, however, that Kirivitsky, Handcock and Morris have - in the paper below, and in subsequent explorations - proven that this works perfectly for dyadic independent terms, and behaves reasonably for some common dyadic dependent terms, but haven't proven it works exactly for the latter. (Co-authors - correct me if I'm wrong on that!!!)

It's not actually 100% clear (at least to me) what the expected behavior should be for something like GWESP when networks change in size - how do we believe explicit triangle closure behaves as networks scale in size, such that the background probably of a triangle being closed declines for the same density? Will the magnitude of the force stay the same, or will people exert more effort to close trinagle in order to get back to the same prportion of their triangles being closed as in a smaller network?  It's tricky stuff, but very intersting, for someone who wanted to explore it in depth with comparative empirical data, like Add Health.

Nevertheless, I believe this simple method should get you close to where you want to be.

Here is some basic example code using a network of size 100 with mean degree of 1, then simulating a network of size 1000 that also has a mean degree of 1, by updating the coefficient form the first model. You should be able to use this as a base, and add in you GWESP and other terms.

library(statnet)
smallnet <- network.initialize(100, directed=F)
smallnet <- san(smallnet~edges, target.stats = 50) # mean deg = 1
smallergm <- ergm(smallnet~edges)

largenet <- network.initialize(1000, directed=F)
largecoef <- smallergm$coef[1] + log(100) - log(1000)
largenet <- simulate(largenet~edges, coef=largecoef)


Cheers,

Steve

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] dyadic dependent model: is it a real effect or an artefact ?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jaber,

The choice of null model depends on the substantive theoretical context.

If your context is known to have hubs -- i.e., there's a pre-existing 
explanation for their presence -- then yes, there's no reason to test the 
hypothesis that they exist.  In that case, it would be appropriate to 
include them in the "null" model, to control for their effects when 
testing any additional terms.  I can imagine an example would be internet, 
telephone or airline routing networks, where we know the network has 
been explicitly designed with a hub structure.

If there is no such exogenous process at work, then testing for the 
presence of degree effects would make sense.  An example might be 
friendship networks.

hth,
Martina

messages.body_plain:
Dear Subhasree,

There is your problem. Your network has 100% reciprocated ties. Thus the
parameter tends to infinity and is therefore impossible to estimate.
It seems that you have an undirected network and thus a mutual parameter is
unnecessary for your model, but you should specify the network as
undirected.

If this level reciprocity is just a "coincidence" and the network is truely
undirected and could have unreciprocated ties, then I think your best
option would berunning a Bayesian ERGM and specify a weakly informative
prior for the reciprocity parameter (e.g mean = 0, SD = 3). By doing so
your model will estimate a strongly positive reciprocity parameter, but
will not run into degeneracy problems.
Of course it would be much easier to just make it undirected, exclude the
mutual paramter and stick to ERGM.

Best Regards,

Robert Krause

University of Groningen

The workshop focuses on epidemics, but the methods and software (based on

############################################################################

Network Modeling for Epidemics
Summer short course at the University of Washington
20-24 August, 2018

Network Modeling for Epidemics (NME) is a 5-day short course at the University 
of Washington that provides an introduction to stochastic network models for 
infectious disease transmission dynamics, with a focus on empirically based 
modeling of HIV transmission. It is a ''hands-on'' course, using the EpiModel 
software package in R (www.epimodel.org). EpiModel provides a unified framework 
for statistically based modeling of dynamic networks from empirical data, and 
simulation of epidemic dynamics on these networks. It has a flexible 
open-source platform for learning and building several types of epidemic 
models: deterministic compartmental, stochastic individual-based, and 
stochastic network models. Resources include simple models that run in a 
browser window, built-in generic models that provide basic control over 
population contact patterns, pathogen properties and demographics, and 
templates for user-programmed modules that allow EpiModel to be extended to the 
full range of pathogens, hosts, and disease dynamics for advanced research. 
This course will touch on the deterministic and individual-based models, but 
its primary focus is on the theory, methods and application of network models.

The course uses mornings for lectures, and afternoons for labs with students 
working in small groups. On the final day, students have the option of 
developing an EpiModel prototype for their own research projects, with input 
from the instructors, which includes the lead EpiModel software developer, Dr. 
Samuel Jenness.

Returning students: We encourage previous attendees with active modeling 
projects to apply to return for a refresher course. The EpiModel package has 
been significantly enhanced over the last few years. Returning students with 
active projects will have the opportunity to work with course instructors to 
address key challenges in the design of their network model code.

Dates and location:

The course will be taught from Monday, August 20 to Friday, August 24 on the 
University of Washington campus in Seattle.

Costs:

Course fee is $600. Travel and accommodation costs are the responsibility of 
the participant, although discounted hotel rates are available. We offer a 
limited number of fee waivers for pre-doctoral students or for attendees from 
low income countries.  These cover waiver of the registration fee only; travel 
and accommodation are still the responsibility of the fee waiver recipient.

Application dates and decision dates:

*    Apr 1: Fee-waiver application deadline. Decisions will be made by Apr 15, 
and response required by May 1.

*    May 1:  General application deadline. Decisions will be made by May 15 and 
a response required by June 1. A waitlist will be established with rolling 
admission through June 30.

Application:

Apply online at https://catalyst.uw.edu/webq/survey/morrism/347069

Course website and more information: http://statnet.github.io/nme

Please free to share widely!

Yours,
Martina Morris, Steve Goodreau and Samuel Jenness

messages.body_plain:
Hi Lin -

The good news is that, if it fits sometimes and simulations look good, 
then you know your model is indeed generally estimable, and not 
degenerate. That said, it sounds like your estimation algorithm 
sometimes wanders into degenerate or near-degenerate territory. I'd try 
varying some of the ergm control parameters from their defaults to add 
more stability to the estimation procedure - it'll take longer, but 
hopefully lead more consistently to successful estimation.? Common ones are:

- increasing MCMLE.maxit, MCMC.interval, MCMC.burnin, and/or MCMC.samplesize

- decreasing MCMLE.steplength

And there are many more to explore at ?control.ergm.

If you wish a deep theoretical dive into this concept of stability, one 
place to start is Schweinberger 2011 
(https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3405854/). Not for the 
statistically faint of heart though! :-)

HTH, Steve
