messages.subject: [statnet_help] Model choice for Temporal ERGMs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Timoth?e,

I'll try to offer my perspective on this. I assume you have consulted
the following forthcoming paper, which will appear very soon (in fact, I
have just returned the proofs):

Leifeld, Philip, Skyler J. Cranmer and Bruce A. Desmarais (2018):
Temporal Exponential Random Graph Models with btergm: Estimation and
Bootstrap Confidence Intervals. Journal of Statistical Software 83(6):
1-36. http://dx.doi.org/10.18637/jss.v083.i06

The DOI is not working yet, but you can download a copy here for now:
https://www.philipleifeld.com/cms/upload/v83i06.pdf

About your questions:

1. STERGM takes the changes between t_1 and t_2 and models them using an
ERGM. Since there are two transition matrices -- a matrix with new ties
and a matrix with disappearing ties -- you necessarily have to estimate
two separate models. This can be good if you have separate theories on
tie formation and dissolution and if the two processes do not interact.
A TERGM, in contrast, models t_2 and can include temporal dependencies
that encompass changes from t_1 to t_2 as model terms. So it is fair to
say that changes are accommodated in both model types, but in a
different way: in the dependent variable in the STERGM and in the
independent variables in the TERGM.

This also means that dependencies over more than two consecutive time
points can in principle be included in the TERGM, for example triadic
closure over three time points or autoregressive lags of more than one
time point or temporal trends or breaks, depending on what makes sense
theoretically.

Since the TERGM models network states (even if as a function of changes
and thereby possibly as a temporal process), it would be wrong to say
that it can only model formation but not dissolution since both go into
the state that is being modeled.

You can also say that both the TERGM and the STERGM are essentially
pooled ERGMs over multiple time points, but the STERGM would be more
precisely characterized as a pooled ERGM of the transition matrices
while the TERGM is a pooled ERGM of the list of networks. At least in
its simplest form if you do not include any temporal dependencies like
delayed reciprocity or triadic closure, autoregressive memory terms,
temporal trends etc.

Whether you should use a STERGM or a TERGM depends likely on the
following questions:

a. Are you theoretically interested in explaining the transition
matrices (e.g., the transitions from not sitting together to sitting
together and from sitting together to not sitting together) or in the
network matrices (e.g., sitting together or not sitting together)? In
the former case, use a STERGM; in the latter case, use a TERGM.

b. Do you have theoretical reasons to think that the act of
transitioning from sitting together to not sitting together is
independent of the transitioning from not sitting together to sitting
together, or are they a joint process that should be modeled in the same
equation? In the former case, use a STERGM, in the latter a TERGM.

c. Do you have reason to believe that your data-generating process is a
Markov process in the sense that the network at t_3 is only affected by
the network at t_2 but not by the network at, say, t_1 or t_0, or can
there be longer-term dependencies? In the former case, either model is
fine, in the latter case the TERGM can do this.

d. Do you have many consecutive networks and are these networks large,
such that MCMC-MLE estimation is not feasible, or is MCMC-MLE a feasible
estimation strategy in terms of degeneracy and computation time? If this
is an issue, the btergm procedure is your friend. If not, use mtergm for
MCMC-MLE or use a STERGM.

e. Do you need to model time trends? For example, does your network get
denser or sparser over time (linearly, with a polynomial function of
time, as a step function etc.)? Do you need to interact these time
trends with covariates, for example for modeling differential effects of
covariates before and after some event? If so, the timecov term in the
btergm package can do this.

2. I'm not sure about data requirements in the tergm package, but in the
btergm package you can supply consecutive matrices or networks with
different dimensions as long as the matrices or networks have (node)
labels. The package will automatically take care of composition change.

I don't have a good solution for choosing the optimal duration of the
time window for aggregating your events into time slices, but you could
play with different aggregation rules and check if there is a massive
difference or if the results are relatively robust with regard to the
length of the time window.

The problem you are describing with on-off-on relationships can either
be solved by aggregating into larger time windows or, possibly, by
increasing K in the TERGM. This means you would condition not just on
the previous time point, but possibly on (functions of) the pre-previous
time point or interactions between that and the current or previous time
point. For example, you could add a list of covariate matrices that
specify a temporal lag of the relationships at t over the last three
time points t_-1, t_-2, and t_-3, with a geometric temporal weight, such
as x_ij^t = N_ij^t_-1 + (0.5 * N_ij^t_-2) + (0.25 * N_ij^t_-3) or
something like that. It depends on what you think captures your temporal
dependence best, and you can test this through goodness-of-fit measures.
On top of these temporal specifications, you can then include other
temporal or within-time-step effects, both endogenous and exogenous.

As far as I know, valued-edge ERGMs (e.g., GERGM) and TERGMs have not
been combined so far, but I may be wrong.

Best regards,

Philip

--
Dr Philip Leifeld
Senior Lecturer (Associate Professor) in Research Methods
Director of Graduate Training
School of Social and Political Sciences
University of Glasgow
http://www.philipleifeld.com

On Jan 31, 2018 2:39 AM, "Krause, R.W." <r.w.krause@rug.nl> wrote:

Dear Juan,

I would estimate an ERGM on the network that you have observed with
parameters for all the statistics of interest (excluding edges) and then
use those parameters in your simulate() function.
If the goal is to simulate 100 networks, then I would simulate a lot of
networks, say 2000, and from these select those networks that are closest
to the target statistics.
E.g. by calculating all statistics for each network and then calculate the
distance between the statistic vectors of the simulated networks and the
observed statistics. Further, I would exclude deviations you consider too
far.
Another option is to go through every statistic and except say a 2.5%
deviation and exclude all networks that do not meet this criterion for all
statistics.
If 2000 is not enough to get you 100 networks that you like, you can just
add more by simulating with another random number seed. Be careful when
simulating a lot of networks as they tend to be rather big when saved as
network objects in R and several thousand might exceed the RAM of your
machine.

Lastly, if you estimate your ERGM with an edges parameter your other
parameters are estimated conditional on this parameter. Thus, the other
parameters correspond to different statistics, if you exclude the parameter
or fix its statistic to a certain value. This holds of course for every
paramter, but I think the edges parameter, as a sort of intercept, is most
influential here. So, if you use the parameter estimated in mod.e to
simulate, your statistics will not be met. You should condition the
estimation of mod.e also on the number of edges, as you do the
simulation: constraints
= ~edges. That is why I said "excluding edges" above.

The ERGM experts might have a more efficient way how to do it, but this
should work.

Best Regards,

Frank,


I am not sure if these measures can be generated from nodal information because they rely on data that is not available in the network. For instance, one of the measure is the euclidean distance between pairs of nodes measured in the network of previous years.

On Mon, Feb 26, 2018 at 11:35 PM, Pavel Krivitsky <pavel@uow.edu.au<mailto:pavel@uow.edu.au>> wrote:
Dear Frank,

TL;DR: The edgecov() terms are very memory-inefficient. I don't know what these mg/m4/mt matrices represent, but if they can be generated from, say, nodal information, you can implement a custom ergm term that gets passed nodal information and generates them on the fly.

Technical explanation: Internally, ergm concatenates covariate vectors and passes them on to the C code, where they get unpacked. Each edgecov() term passes an n*n matrix, and in your case, each of these matrices is 270000^2 elements long. Three of them add up to a vector of length 2187000000<tel:(218)%20700-0000> which is longer than the greatest integer that can be represented using the basic integer type (2147483647<tel:(214)%20748-3647>). Now, R can handle vectors like that, but not through the .C() interface.

I hope this helps,
Pavel

On Mon, 2018-02-26 at 17:19 +0100, FRANK VAN DER WOUDEN wrote:
Dear listers,

I'm examining a series of 140 annual networks. In more recent years the networks get very large (more than 27,000 nodes) and sparse (21,000 edges):

> netx
 Network attributes:
  vertices = 27123
  directed = FALSE
  hyper = FALSE
  loops = TRUE
  multiple = FALSE
  bipartite = FALSE
  total edges= 21570
    missing edges= 0
    non-missing edges= 21570

 Vertex attribute names:
    position club vertex.names

 Edge attribute names not shown

When I estimate an ERG model for such a large network, I run into the following error:

> modelx <- ergm(netx ~ edges + edgecov(mg) + edgecov(m4) + edgecov(mt))
[1] "Warning:  This network is allowed to contain loops"
Error in ergm.getglobalstats(nw, model, response = response) :
  long vectors (argument 13) are not supported in .C

I believe this error message occurs because R is trying to pass a long vector via .C, which doesn't support long vectors.

Did anyone else run into similar issues? If so, how did you engage with this issue?

Any help is much appreciated. Thank you!

Best wishes,

Frank van der Wouden

        Lin that is one of the known (classic) degenerate specifications.  you 
        really need to read some of the literature here if you are going to use 
        ERGMs...
        
        see, for example:
        
        Snijders TAB, Pattison PE, Robins GL, Handcock MS. New 
        specifications for exponential random graph models. In: Stolzenberg RM, 
        editor. Sociological Methodology 2006, Vol 362006. p. 99-153.
        
        bottom line: we do not use this specification for ERGMs any more.
        
        > Today I tried the model ~ edges + degree(1:4) + gwesp(decay = 0.5, fixed 
        > = TRUE) + nodefactor("gender") + nodefactor("hcv") + absdiff("age")+ 
        > ("degree") + nodemix("gender").
        
        > I did this model a few days ago, it converged but the result was bad (a 
        > pic of simulated network from the model degeneracy attached). But today 
        > it fitted well once(not that good but looks normal, a pic for the normal 
        > fit attached too), but when I tried one more time it became degeneracy 
        > again. When I used decay=0.4 a few days ago, it fitted well, but now I 
        > suspect it might produce degeneracy too if I try more times. Please let 
        > me know if any additional information if needed.
        
        1. I would start by fitting the model without the gwesp term, and looking 
        carefully at the GOF plot for the ESP.  How well does this model fit the 
        observed ESP distribution?  If well, then you do not need a gwesp term.
        
        2. If (1) indicates a poor fit to the ESP distribution, then you need to 
        assess what the pattern in the lack of fit implies for a gwesp 
        parameterization.  In general, decay=0 specifies that only the first 
        shared partner influences the odds of a tie.  Decay > 0 faster decline in 
        the right tail of the distribution relative to that predicted by a model 
        without gwesp.  The larger the decay, the faster the decline

> Dear Subhasree, 
> 
> There is your problem. Your network has 100% reciprocated ties. Thus the parameter tends to infinity and is therefore impossible to estimate. 
> It seems that you have an undirected network and thus a mutual parameter is unnecessary for your model, but you should specify the network as undirected. 
> 
> If this level reciprocity is just a "coincidence" and the network is truely undirected and could have unreciprocated ties, then I think your best option would berunning a Bayesian ERGM and specify a weakly informative prior for the reciprocity parameter (e.g mean = 0, SD = 3). By doing so your model will estimate a strongly positive reciprocity parameter, but will not run into degeneracy problems. 
> Of course it would be much easier to just make it undirected, exclude the mutual paramter and stick to ERGM.

Thx Lin --

The ESP GOF suggests the decay param is a bit too high.

But I think the real issue here is the sampled/missing data.  You need to 
address that both to properly model the network with ERGM, and to make the 
kind of diffusion inferences that are your ultimate goal.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Long vector support for large networks
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Long vector support for large networks
messages.body_plain:
Dear Frank,

TL;DR: The edgecov() terms are very memory-inefficient. I don't know what these mg/m4/mt matrices represent, but if they can be generated from, say, nodal information, you can implement a custom ergm term that gets passed nodal information and generates them on the fly.

Technical explanation: Internally, ergm concatenates covariate vectors and passes them on to the C code, where they get unpacked. Each edgecov() term passes an n*n matrix, and in your case, each of these matrices is 270000^2 elements long. Three of them add up to a vector of length 2187000000 which is longer than the greatest integer that can be represented using the basic integer type (2147483647). Now, R can handle vectors like that, but not through the .C() interface.

I hope this helps,
Pavel

On Mon, 2018-02-26 at 17:19 +0100, FRANK VAN DER WOUDEN wrote:
Dear listers,

I'm examining a series of 140 annual networks. In more recent years the networks get very large (more than 27,000 nodes) and sparse (21,000 edges):

> netx
 Network attributes:
  vertices = 27123
  directed = FALSE
  hyper = FALSE
  loops = TRUE
  multiple = FALSE
  bipartite = FALSE
  total edges= 21570
    missing edges= 0
    non-missing edges= 21570

 Vertex attribute names:
    position club vertex.names

 Edge attribute names not shown

When I estimate an ERG model for such a large network, I run into the following error:

> modelx <- ergm(netx ~ edges + edgecov(mg) + edgecov(m4) + edgecov(mt))
[1] "Warning:  This network is allowed to contain loops"
Error in ergm.getglobalstats(nw, model, response = response) :
  long vectors (argument 13) are not supported in .C

I believe this error message occurs because R is trying to pass a long vector via .C, which doesn't support long vectors.

Did anyone else run into similar issues? If so, how did you engage with this issue?

Any help is much appreciated. Thank you!

Best wishes,

Frank van der Wouden
University of California, Los Angeles

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Network Modeling for Epidemics -- Summer short course at the University of Washington -- 20-24 August, 2018
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Network Modeling for Epidemics -- Summer short course at the University of Washington -- 20-24 August, 2018
messages.body_plain:
Network Modeling for Epidemics (NME) is a 5-day short course at the
University of Washington that provides an introduction to stochastic
network models for infectious disease transmission dynamics, with a focus
on empirically based modeling of HIV transmission. It is a ''hands-on''
course, using the EpiModel software package in R (www.epimodel.org).
EpiModel provides a unified framework for statistically based modeling of
dynamic networks from empirical data, and simulation of epidemic dynamics
on these networks. It has a flexible open-source platform for learning and
building several types of epidemic models: deterministic compartmental,
stochastic individual-based, and stochastic network models. Resources
include simple models that run in a browser window, built-in generic models
that provide basic control over population contact patterns, pathogen
properties and demographics, and templates for user-programmed modules that
allow EpiModel to be extended to the full range of pathogens, hosts, and
disease dynamics for advanced research. This course will touch on the
deterministic and individual-based models, but its primary focus is on the
theory, methods and application of network models.


The course uses mornings for lectures, and afternoons for labs with
students working in small groups. On the final day, students have the
option of developing an EpiModel prototype for their own research projects,
with input from the instructors, which includes the lead EpiModel software
developer, Dr. Samuel Jenness.

Returning students: We encourage previous attendees with active modeling
projects to apply to return for a refresher course. The EpiModel package
has been significantly enhanced over the last few years. Returning students
with active projects will have the opportunity to work with course
instructors to address key challenges in the design of their network model
code.

Dates and location:

The course will be taught from Monday, August 20 to Friday, August 24 on
the University of Washington campus in Seattle.

Costs:

Course fee is $600. Travel and accommodation costs are the responsibility
of the participant, although discounted hotel rates are available. We offer
a limited number of fee waivers for pre-doctoral students or for attendees
from low income countries.  These cover waiver of the registration fee
only; travel and accommodation are still the responsibility of the fee
waiver recipient.

Application dates and decision dates:

*    Apr 1: Fee waiver application deadline. Decisions will be made by Apr
15, and response required by May 1.

*    May 1:  General application deadline. Decisions will be made by May 15
and a response required by June 1. A waitlist will be established with
rolling admission through June 30.

Application:

Apply online at https://catalyst.uw.edu/webq/survey/morrism/347069

Course website and more information: http://statnet.github.io/nme

Please free to share widely!

Yours,
Martina Morris, Steve Goodreau and Samuel Jenness

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Lin -

It sounds like you have a number of complex issues going on with respect 
to sampling and missing data.?There are ways to deal with these, some of 
which are implemented in statnet's ergm, but to figure out exactly the 
right approach for your specific data source and research questions you 
may need to dig more deeply into the underlying theory and methodological 
literature surrounding fitting ERGMs with these kinds of complex designs 
(and measurement error).?Some papers that might help you as you work this 
out include (but are not limited to):

Gile, K. J. and Handcock, M. S. 2017. Analysis of networks with missing 
data with application to the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent 
Health. J. R. Stat. Soc. C, 66: 501?519. doi:10.1111/rssc.12184

Gile, K. J. and Handcock, M. S. 2015. Network model-assisted inference 
from respondent-driven sampling data. J. R. Stat. Soc. A, 178: 619?639. 
doi:10.1111/rssa.12091

Krivitsky, P.N.; Handcock, M.S.; and Morris. 2011. Adjusting for Network 
Size and Composition Effects in Exponential-Family Random Graph Models. 
Statistical Methodology, 8(4): 319?339.

Lee, F. and Butts, C.T.?2018.?Mutual Assent or Unilateral Nomination? A 
Performance Comparison of Intersection and Union Rules for Integrating 
Self-reports of Social Relationships.?arXiv:1802.07838

Wang, C.; Butts, C.T.; Hipp, J.R.; and Jose, R.; and Lakon, C.M. 2016. 
Multiple Imputation for Missing Edge Data: A Predictive Evaluation Method 
with Application to Add Health. Social Networks, 45, 89-98. DOI: 
10.1016/j.socnet.2015.12.003

Good luck with your analysis!

       Hi Martina,

       Thank you so much for all the advices, they are super useful. I have a few explanations and follow-up
       questions for each point:

       1. Yes we do have missing data. First, the data was from respondent-driven sampling, so the
       participants could list 24 partners, but for the partners they listed, some were found and recruited
       into the study, some were not. And the "original network" we are using now are all participants who got
       interviewed in the study, and we removed all the ties connected to people who were not interviewed for
       this study, only ties between the participants were kept. Our assumption is that, the confirmed network
       we got here is a random piece of the whole network. So after we fit the ERGM with this confirmed
       network, we can then simulate bigger network preserving the density, then the ties removed will grow
       back. We also calculated the mean degree that included those being reported but not interviewed, and
       it's about twice the mean degree of the confirmed network, so once we grow the network to a double
       size, the mean degree would match that one, then the simulated bigger network would be !
       the real network. Does this make sense to you?

       A second consideration is the under-reporting of ties within the confirmed network. We are using
       undirected network because we don't care the direction (and the ties are "share with" ties, not "give
       needle to" or "be given needle" ties), but in the data, some ties were reported by both, and some ties
       were reported by only one node. So it indicates that there are under-reporting of ties, otherwise all
       ties should be reciprocal. With the proportion of reciprocal ties/non-reciprocal ties, we estimated
       that we only observed about half of the ties in this confirmed network. However, by comparing the
       reciprocal ties and non-reciprocal ties, the reciprocal ones have higher sharing frequency etc., so a
       big proportion of ties we are missing are low frequency ties which are less important for transmission.
       We thought about how to add back the un-observed ties, but didn't get an answer, so now we are using
       the observed ties only.

       Is there a way the package can add back those un-observed ties?

       2. I tried a formula without gwesp (only has edges and degree(1:4), and the GOF of shared partner was
       not as good. But I'll try again with the homophily terms together. The reason we still included gwesp
       is that, from literature, there should be high transitivity in drug using networks, so there should be
       triangles, by the same under-reporting theory, there should be may un-observed triangles, and the
       extent should be even greater than ties.

       3. The mixing pattern of gender was complicated, there was a very weak heterophily in males, and a very
       strong heterophily in females, i.e. there were slightly more males sharing with females than with
       males, but for females, most of them were sharing with males. In this case, should I use nodemix? And
       good to know the mixingmatrix function, I analyzed the data by hardcoding it...

       4. By analyzing the data, I found there were no disproportion of ties in age, the distribution of
       number of ties within each age is very similar with the distribution of number of nodes within each
       age. Should I still add nodecove in this case?

       5. I tried a formula without degree term when I first tried without the homophily terms. The GOF of
       degree distribution of 0 to 3 was not good without the degree term. I also tried degree(1:3) and
       degree(1:2) and they made the network very weird, so I finally selected degree(1:4). However, actually
       I began to think about this term because eventually I'll have to grow the network to a bigger size and
       mean degree, so yes, depending on whether our approach in the first point is feasible, I'll have to
       deal with the degree term.

       but didn't come to a satisfactory solution. It would be super helpful to hear your opinions. If there
       are other ways you prefer than writing emails, please feel free to let me know. I really appreciate it.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Model choice for Temporal ERGMs
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am currently trying to fit a temporal ERGM to a dataset containing information on the sitting of teenagers during their meals in a holidays? summer camp. The data is made of 30 waves (=meals); for each of those, I know who sat next to who out of the 60 teenagers. I also have various vertex attributes (gender, age, SES etc). I have worked with ERGMs before, but never temporal ones. Therefore, I have 2  questions:

  1.  What is the difference between stergm and btergm? From what I got reading various introduction papers, the former allows to specify two different formulae for edge formation and dissolution, while the latter is in its simplest form a pooled ERGM over the time steps, which can then take time-dependent terms to model longitudinal processes (e.g. persistence of ties and/or non-ties from one time-step to another). In practice, how should I decide which one to use? Do I need strong theoretical reasons to model formation and dissolution independently? Is btergm unable to differentiate between formation and dissolution ? meaning it only considers formation? Conversely, are there features of btergm that stergm cannot reproduce?
  2.  Do you have suggestions on how I should format the data? Strictly speaking, each single-time network does not represent relations, but rather events (sitting next to certain persons on a given meal). I do not know whether passing directly these 30 networks to the model would bias the estimates; for e.g., if A and B sat together on day 3 and 4, but not on day 5 and then again on day 6, I guess the model will assume a tie has disappeared and then appeared again. In effect, A and B probably remained friends over the time period, they just did not sit together on one particular meal for some reason ? friendship dissolution would probably result in not-sitting-by over several meals. To put it otherwise, the data concerns co-sitting but what I am really interested in are the underlying friendship relations. Does the model (either btergm or stergm) handle this kind of data structure well? Or should I rather cluster the data on longer time lengths to get fewer networks, with friendships inferred from the mean occurrence of co-sitting over the time period? E.g. I could group meals 6 by 6 (resulting in 30/6=5 networks) and treat these as pseudo friendship networks, with the number of co-sitting denoting the strength of the friendship tie.

In this latter case, can I compute valued tergms, or should I just discretise the data with some arbitrary cut-off on the number of co-sittings?

Many thanks for your help !

Best Regards

Timothee Chabot
PhD Researcher
European University Institute, SPS department

messages.subject: [statnet_help] different ergm fitting results
messages.body_plain:
To underscore Steve's comments, this is usually (though not always) an 
MCMC issue: you probably need a longer and/or higher quality chain.? If 
you look at the online ERGM tutorials, you can find information on how 
to assess your Markov chain to verify that it is mixing well and has 
adequately burned in.? The defaults are reasonably good, but are built 
for speed rather than for quality: you should expect to carry out 
refinement runs, especially on large graphs, with models that have 
substantial dependence, etc. If tightening the MCMC using the control 
parameters Steve mentioned doesn't help, then looking more closely at 
your model specification may be helpful - but the very first thing to 
check should be your Markov chain.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Constraining metrics for simulated graphs (degcor) ERGMs
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Constraining metrics for simulated graphs (degcor) ERGMs
messages.body_plain:
Dear Juan,

I would estimate an ERGM on the network that you have observed with
parameters for all the statistics of interest (excluding edges) and then
use those parameters in your simulate() function.
If the goal is to simulate 100 networks, then I would simulate a lot of
networks, say 2000, and from these select those networks that are closest
to the target statistics.
E.g. by calculating all statistics for each network and then calculate the
distance between the statistic vectors of the simulated networks and the
observed statistics. Further, I would exclude deviations you consider too
far.
Another option is to go through every statistic and except say a 2.5%
deviation and exclude all networks that do not meet this criterion for all
statistics.
If 2000 is not enough to get you 100 networks that you like, you can just
add more by simulating with another random number seed. Be careful when
simulating a lot of networks as they tend to be rather big when saved as
network objects in R and several thousand might exceed the RAM of your
machine.

Lastly, if you estimate your ERGM with an edges parameter your other
parameters are estimated conditional on this parameter. Thus, the other
parameters correspond to different statistics, if you exclude the parameter
or fix its statistic to a certain value. This holds of course for every
paramter, but I think the edges parameter, as a sort of intercept, is most
influential here. So, if you use the parameter estimated in mod.e to
simulate, your statistics will not be met. You should condition the
estimation of mod.e also on the number of edges, as you do the
simulation: constraints
= ~edges. That is why I said "excluding edges" above.

The ERGM experts might have a more efficient way how to do it, but this
should work.

Best Regards,

Robert Krause

ICS Sociology, PhD Candidate
University of Groningen
Grote Rozenstraat 31,
Room B119
9712 TG Groningen, The Netherlands

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] dyadic dependent model: is it a real effect or an artefact ?
messages.body_plain:
Hi guys,
I have a reviewer's comment running through my head lately. I was hoping
you guys can help me understand his concerns and perhaps figure out a
solution.

I am running a dyadic dependent model. I am looking at factors (specific to
the node, edge and network ) that might affect the presence of an edge in
my network. I am using an exponential random model with just the count of
edges as a null model.
One of the reviewers is wondering if some of the network factors that I
found significant in my final model  (indegree and outdegree for example)
might just be an artificial consequence of the presence of hubs (i.e. they
help to improve the fit for nodes of high degree) or if they correspond to
a real effect.  The reviewer is proposing to rerun the model with
significant network variables only as a null model instead of the count of
edges model.

The way I see it ( please, correct me if I am wrong) is that by adding
particular network factors (indegree and outdegree for example) we are
somehow controlling for them in the model similarly to how we address for
confounders in a regular logistic regression model.

I will be happy to give more details if needed.

Thank you all,
Jaber

messages.body_plain:
On Thu, 22 Feb 2018, Zhu, Lin wrote:

> Hi Martina,
>
> Sorry for having so many questions and thank you for your time answering all my questions. I'm still fitting my model to the injection drug user network (I sent emails yesterday and a few days ago).
>
> One model I had this issue is ~edges +kstar. It converged for a few times but the simulated networks have many big cycles, and then it didn't converge for many times so I gave up on the kstar term.

Lin that is one of the known (classic) degenerate specifications.  you 
really need to read some of the literature here if you are going to use 
ERGMs...

see, for example:

Snijders TAB, Pattison PE, Robins GL, Handcock MS. New 
specifications for exponential random graph models. In: Stolzenberg RM, 
editor. Sociological Methodology 2006, Vol 362006. p. 99-153.

bottom line: we do not use this specification for ERGMs any more.

> Today I tried the model ~ edges + degree(1:4) + gwesp(decay = 0.5, fixed 
> = TRUE) + nodefactor("gender") + nodefactor("hcv") + absdiff("age")+ 
> ("degree") + nodemix("gender").

> I did this model a few days ago, it converged but the result was bad (a 
> pic of simulated network from the model degeneracy attached). But today 
> it fitted well once(not that good but looks normal, a pic for the normal 
> fit attached too), but when I tried one more time it became degeneracy 
> again. When I used decay=0.4 a few days ago, it fitted well, but now I 
> suspect it might produce degeneracy too if I try more times. Please let 
> me know if any additional information if needed.

1. I would start by fitting the model without the gwesp term, and looking 
carefully at the GOF plot for the ESP.  How well does this model fit the 
observed ESP distribution?  If well, then you do not need a gwesp term.

2. If (1) indicates a poor fit to the ESP distribution, then you need to 
assess what the pattern in the lack of fit implies for a gwesp 
parameterization.  In general, decay=0 specifies that only the first 
shared partner influences the odds of a tie.  Decay > 0 faster decline in 
the right tail of the distribution relative to that predicted by a model 
without gwesp.  The larger the decay, the faster the decline

messages.body_plain:
Dear Philip,


many thanks for this (great) answer ! As you suggest, I think that extending K in the tergm would help a lot with my data. I will try it out.


All the best,

Timothee

________________________________
De : Philip Leifeld <Philip.Leifeld@glasgow.ac.uk>
Envoy? : vendredi 16 f?vrier 2018 02:24:43
? : Chabot, Timoth?e Pierre Jules; statnet_help@u.washington.edu
Objet : Re: [statnet_help] Model choice for Temporal ERGMs

Hi Timoth?e,

I'll try to offer my perspective on this. I assume you have consulted
the following forthcoming paper, which will appear very soon (in fact, I
have just returned the proofs):

Leifeld, Philip, Skyler J. Cranmer and Bruce A. Desmarais (2018):
Temporal Exponential Random Graph Models with btergm: Estimation and
Bootstrap Confidence Intervals. Journal of Statistical Software 83(6):
1-36. http://dx.doi.org/10.18637/jss.v083.i06

The DOI is not working yet, but you can download a copy here for now:
https://www.philipleifeld.com/cms/upload/v83i06.pdf

About your questions:

1. STERGM takes the changes between t_1 and t_2 and models them using an
ERGM. Since there are two transition matrices -- a matrix with new ties
and a matrix with disappearing ties -- you necessarily have to estimate
two separate models. This can be good if you have separate theories on
tie formation and dissolution and if the two processes do not interact.
A TERGM, in contrast, models t_2 and can include temporal dependencies
that encompass changes from t_1 to t_2 as model terms. So it is fair to
say that changes are accommodated in both model types, but in a
different way: in the dependent variable in the STERGM and in the
independent variables in the TERGM.

This also means that dependencies over more than two consecutive time
points can in principle be included in the TERGM, for example triadic
closure over three time points or autoregressive lags of more than one
time point or temporal trends or breaks, depending on what makes sense
theoretically.

Since the TERGM models network states (even if as a function of changes
and thereby possibly as a temporal process), it would be wrong to say
that it can only model formation but not dissolution since both go into
the state that is being modeled.

You can also say that both the TERGM and the STERGM are essentially
pooled ERGMs over multiple time points, but the STERGM would be more
precisely characterized as a pooled ERGM of the transition matrices
while the TERGM is a pooled ERGM of the list of networks. At least in
its simplest form if you do not include any temporal dependencies like
delayed reciprocity or triadic closure, autoregressive memory terms,
temporal trends etc.

Whether you should use a STERGM or a TERGM depends likely on the
following questions:

a. Are you theoretically interested in explaining the transition
matrices (e.g., the transitions from not sitting together to sitting
together and from sitting together to not sitting together) or in the
network matrices (e.g., sitting together or not sitting together)? In
the former case, use a STERGM; in the latter case, use a TERGM.

b. Do you have theoretical reasons to think that the act of
transitioning from sitting together to not sitting together is
independent of the transitioning from not sitting together to sitting
together, or are they a joint process that should be modeled in the same
equation? In the former case, use a STERGM, in the latter a TERGM.

c. Do you have reason to believe that your data-generating process is a
Markov process in the sense that the network at t_3 is only affected by
the network at t_2 but not by the network at, say, t_1 or t_0, or can
there be longer-term dependencies? In the former case, either model is
fine, in the latter case the TERGM can do this.

d. Do you have many consecutive networks and are these networks large,
such that MCMC-MLE estimation is not feasible, or is MCMC-MLE a feasible
estimation strategy in terms of degeneracy and computation time? If this
is an issue, the btergm procedure is your friend. If not, use mtergm for
MCMC-MLE or use a STERGM.

e. Do you need to model time trends? For example, does your network get
denser or sparser over time (linearly, with a polynomial function of
time, as a step function etc.)? Do you need to interact these time
trends with covariates, for example for modeling differential effects of
covariates before and after some event? If so, the timecov term in the
btergm package can do this.

2. I'm not sure about data requirements in the tergm package, but in the
btergm package you can supply consecutive matrices or networks with
different dimensions as long as the matrices or networks have (node)
labels. The package will automatically take care of composition change.

I don't have a good solution for choosing the optimal duration of the
time window for aggregating your events into time slices, but you could
play with different aggregation rules and check if there is a massive
difference or if the results are relatively robust with regard to the
length of the time window.

The problem you are describing with on-off-on relationships can either
be solved by aggregating into larger time windows or, possibly, by
increasing K in the TERGM. This means you would condition not just on
the previous time point, but possibly on (functions of) the pre-previous
time point or interactions between that and the current or previous time
point. For example, you could add a list of covariate matrices that
specify a temporal lag of the relationships at t over the last three
time points t_-1, t_-2, and t_-3, with a geometric temporal weight, such
as x_ij^t = N_ij^t_-1 + (0.5 * N_ij^t_-2) + (0.25 * N_ij^t_-3) or
something like that. It depends on what you think captures your temporal
dependence best, and you can test this through goodness-of-fit measures.
On top of these temporal specifications, you can then include other
temporal or within-time-step effects, both endogenous and exogenous.

As far as I know, valued-edge ERGMs (e.g., GERGM) and TERGMs have not
been combined so far, but I may be wrong.

Best regards,

Philip

--
Dr Philip Leifeld
Senior Lecturer (Associate Professor) in Research Methods
Director of Graduate Training
School of Social and Political Sciences
University of Glasgow
http://www.philipleifeld.com

>     which can then take time-dependent terms to model longitudinal
>     processes (e.g. persistence of ties and/or non-ties from one

Hi Martina,

Thank you again for your advices!

1. Without gwesp, the GOF of ESP was not good (gof3, attached, producing much less triangles/ESP), but with gwesp (decay around 0.4) it's much better (gof11, attached). Thank you for the suggested paper, I need to systematically read more ergm literature, also about missing data, and the MCMC process Steve and Carter suggested too.

All your advices are very helpful and inspiring. Thanks all!

Best,
Lin


?On 2/23/18, 5:59 PM, "martina morris" <morrism@u.washington.edu> wrote:

    On Thu, 22 Feb 2018, Zhu, Lin wrote:
    
    > Hi Martina,
    >
    > Sorry for having so many questions and thank you for your time answering all my questions. I'm still fitting my model to the injection drug user network (I sent emails yesterday and a few days ago).
    >
    > One model I had this issue is ~edges +kstar. It converged for a few times but the simulated networks have many big cycles, and then it didn't converge for many times so I gave up on the kstar term.
    
    Lin that is one of the known (classic) degenerate specifications.  you 
    really need to read some of the literature here if you are going to use 
    ERGMs...
    
    see, for example:
    
    Snijders TAB, Pattison PE, Robins GL, Handcock MS. New 
    specifications for exponential random graph models. In: Stolzenberg RM, 
    editor. Sociological Methodology 2006, Vol 362006. p. 99-153.
    
    bottom line: we do not use this specification for ERGMs any more.
    
    > Today I tried the model ~ edges + degree(1:4) + gwesp(decay = 0.5, fixed 
    > = TRUE) + nodefactor("gender") + nodefactor("hcv") + absdiff("age")+ 
    > ("degree") + nodemix("gender").
    
    > I did this model a few days ago, it converged but the result was bad (a 
    > pic of simulated network from the model degeneracy attached). But today 
    > it fitted well once(not that good but looks normal, a pic for the normal 
    > fit attached too), but when I tried one more time it became degeneracy 
    > again. When I used decay=0.4 a few days ago, it fitted well, but now I 
    > suspect it might produce degeneracy too if I try more times. Please let 
    > me know if any additional information if needed.
    
    1. I would start by fitting the model without the gwesp term, and looking 
    carefully at the GOF plot for the ESP.  How well does this model fit the 
    observed ESP distribution?  If well, then you do not need a gwesp term.
    
    2. If (1) indicates a poor fit to the ESP distribution, then you need to 
    assess what the pattern in the lack of fit implies for a gwesp 
    parameterization.  In general, decay=0 specifies that only the first 
    shared partner influences the odds of a tie.  Decay > 0 faster decline in 
    the right tail of the distribution relative to that predicted by a model 
    without gwesp.  The larger the decay, the faster the decline
    
    > Thank you so much!

Hi Frank - '

When Pavel talks of writing a custom term, he means the process described in this paper:

https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v052i02<https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__www.jstatsoft.org_article_view_v052i02&d=DwMDaQ&c=Nd1gv_ZWYNIRyZYZmXb18oVfc3lTqv2smA_esABG70U&r=YJkZt1Kj_3QEpjIbPMsRKhBuYwzSaheXr32WdroNv8KZnumyWGDZR6ngZyRvUjOz&m=9Bcxyrt9GOMTLBo7pRbY3z1tsm66cyMoYplT498pymk&s=tMijxvlnIsTP9Qk7s_Kpq-aFCtYosjkXGTUrNViiAeI&e=>

which involves the R package ergm.userterms.

I haven't worked through it in a long long time, so I cant say for sure if any of the explanations are now out of date, but perhaps others on the list--developers and/or those who've developed their own terms recently--can weigh in.

A term that measures Euclidean distance on attributes that represent coordinates is an obvious choice for a statistic to be added to the pot, and I wouldn't be surprised if someone in our user base has already done this, and might be willing to share.  Anyone?

If you do take on the task, and were willing to share the results, then we'd be open to adding it to ergm or to the ergm.userterms repository on Github.

Thanks,

Steve

On Mon, Feb 26, 2018 at 11:35 PM, Pavel Krivitsky <pavel@uow.edu.au<mailto:pavel@uow.edu.au>> wrote:

Dear Frank,

TL;DR: The edgecov() terms are very memory-inefficient. I don't know what these mg/m4/mt matrices represent, but if they can be generated from, say, nodal information, you can implement a custom ergm term that gets passed nodal information and generates them on the fly.

Technical explanation: Internally, ergm concatenates covariate vectors and passes them on to the C code, where they get unpacked. Each edgecov() term passes an n*n matrix, and in your case, each of these matrices is 270000^2 elements long. Three of them add up to a vector of length 2187000000<tel:%28218%29%20700-0000> which is longer than the greatest integer that can be represented using the basic integer type (2147483647<tel:%28214%29%20748-3647>). Now, R can handle vectors like that, but not through the .C() interface.

I hope this helps,
Pavel

On Mon, 2018-02-26 at 17:19 +0100, FRANK VAN DER WOUDEN wrote:
Dear listers,

I'm examining a series of 140 annual networks. In more recent years the networks get very large (more than 27,000 nodes) and sparse (21,000 edges):

> netx
 Network attributes:
  vertices = 27123
  directed = FALSE
  hyper = FALSE
  loops = TRUE
  multiple = FALSE
  bipartite = FALSE
  total edges= 21570
    missing edges= 0
    non-missing edges= 21570

 Vertex attribute names:
    position club vertex.names

 Edge attribute names not shown

When I estimate an ERG model for such a large network, I run into the following error:

> modelx <- ergm(netx ~ edges + edgecov(mg) + edgecov(m4) + edgecov(mt))
[1] "Warning:  This network is allowed to contain loops"
Error in ergm.getglobalstats(nw, model, response = response) :
  long vectors (argument 13) are not supported in .C

I believe this error message occurs because R is trying to pass a long vector via .C, which doesn't support long vectors.

Did anyone else run into similar issues? If so, how did you engage with this issue?

Any help is much appreciated. Thank you!

Best wishes,

Frank van der Wouden
University of California, Los Angeles

Hi Martina,

It's good that there are ways to deal with these issues. Thank you so much for taking time to write down all the papers from different aspects of this issue! I'll do more research on these and hopefully we can get a better model soon.

Lin

?On 2/26/18, 6:41 PM, "martina morris" <morrism@u.washington.edu> wrote:

    Hi, Lin -
    
    It sounds like you have a number of complex issues going on with respect 
    to sampling and missing data. There are ways to deal with these, some of 
    which are implemented in statnet's ergm, but to figure out exactly the 
    right approach for your specific data source and research questions you 
    may need to dig more deeply into the underlying theory and methodological 
    literature surrounding fitting ERGMs with these kinds of complex designs 
    (and measurement error). Some papers that might help you as you work this 
    out include (but are not limited to):
    
    Gile, K. J. and Handcock, M. S. 2017. Analysis of networks with missing 
    data with application to the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent 
    Health. J. R. Stat. Soc. C, 66: 501?519. doi:10.1111/rssc.12184
    
    Gile, K. J. and Handcock, M. S. 2015. Network model-assisted inference 
    from respondent-driven sampling data. J. R. Stat. Soc. A, 178: 619?639. 
    doi:10.1111/rssa.12091
    
    Krivitsky, P.N.; Handcock, M.S.; and Morris. 2011. Adjusting for Network 
    Size and Composition Effects in Exponential-Family Random Graph Models. 
    Statistical Methodology, 8(4): 319?339.
    
    Lee, F. and Butts, C.T. 2018. Mutual Assent or Unilateral Nomination? A 
    Performance Comparison of Intersection and Union Rules for Integrating 
    Self-reports of Social Relationships. arXiv:1802.07838
    
    Wang, C.; Butts, C.T.; Hipp, J.R.; and Jose, R.; and Lakon, C.M. 2016. 
    Multiple Imputation for Missing Edge Data: A Predictive Evaluation Method 
    with Application to Add Health. Social Networks, 45, 89-98. DOI: 
    10.1016/j.socnet.2015.12.003
    
    Good luck with your analysis!
    
    
           ---------- Forwarded message ----------
           Date: Wed, 21 Feb 2018 19:41:19 +0000
           From: "Zhu, Lin" <lzhu@hsph.harvard.edu>
           To: martina morris <morrism@u.washington.edu>
           Subject: Re: [statnet_help] ERGM term for my network
    
           Hi Martina,
    
           Thank you so much for all the advices, they are super useful. I have a few explanations and follow-up
           questions for each point:
    
           1. Yes we do have missing data. First, the data was from respondent-driven sampling, so the
           participants could list 24 partners, but for the partners they listed, some were found and recruited
           into the study, some were not. And the "original network" we are using now are all participants who got
           interviewed in the study, and we removed all the ties connected to people who were not interviewed for
           this study, only ties between the participants were kept. Our assumption is that, the confirmed network
           we got here is a random piece of the whole network. So after we fit the ERGM with this confirmed
           network, we can then simulate bigger network preserving the density, then the ties removed will grow
           back. We also calculated the mean degree that included those being reported but not interviewed, and
           it's about twice the mean degree of the confirmed network, so once we grow the network to a double
           size, the mean degree would match that one, then the simulated bigger network would be !
           the real network. Does this make sense to you?
    
           A second consideration is the under-reporting of ties within the confirmed network. We are using
           undirected network because we don't care the direction (and the ties are "share with" ties, not "give
           needle to" or "be given needle" ties), but in the data, some ties were reported by both, and some ties
           were reported by only one node. So it indicates that there are under-reporting of ties, otherwise all
           ties should be reciprocal. With the proportion of reciprocal ties/non-reciprocal ties, we estimated
           that we only observed about half of the ties in this confirmed network. However, by comparing the
           reciprocal ties and non-reciprocal ties, the reciprocal ones have higher sharing frequency etc., so a
           big proportion of ties we are missing are low frequency ties which are less important for transmission.
           We thought about how to add back the un-observed ties, but didn't get an answer, so now we are using
           the observed ties only.
    
           Is there a way the package can add back those un-observed ties?
    
           2. I tried a formula without gwesp (only has edges and degree(1:4), and the GOF of shared partner was
           not as good. But I'll try again with the homophily terms together. The reason we still included gwesp
           is that, from literature, there should be high transitivity in drug using networks, so there should be
           triangles, by the same under-reporting theory, there should be may un-observed triangles, and the
           extent should be even greater than ties.
    
           3. The mixing pattern of gender was complicated, there was a very weak heterophily in males, and a very
           strong heterophily in females, i.e. there were slightly more males sharing with females than with
           males, but for females, most of them were sharing with males. In this case, should I use nodemix? And
           good to know the mixingmatrix function, I analyzed the data by hardcoding it...
    
           4. By analyzing the data, I found there were no disproportion of ties in age, the distribution of
           number of ties within each age is very similar with the distribution of number of nodes within each
           age. Should I still add nodecove in this case?
    
           5. I tried a formula without degree term when I first tried without the homophily terms. The GOF of
           degree distribution of 0 to 3 was not good without the degree term. I also tried degree(1:3) and
           degree(1:2) and they made the network very weird, so I finally selected degree(1:4). However, actually
           I began to think about this term because eventually I'll have to grow the network to a bigger size and
           mean degree, so yes, depending on whether our approach in the first point is feasible, I'll have to
           deal with the degree term.
    
           I apologize for the long questions, especially for the first point, we discussed about it extensively
           but didn't come to a satisfactory solution. It would be super helpful to hear your opinions. If there
           are other ways you prefer than writing emails, please feel free to let me know. I really appreciate it.
    
           Best regards.
           Lin
           On 2/20/18, 4:38 PM, "martina morris" <morrism@u.washington.edu> wrote:
    
               ok, thx, i didn't realize that.
    
               1. most important:  do you know if you have missing data on ties?  if so,
               then some of the non-ties may actually be ties, if you had observed them.
    
               if so, then you need to address that in the modeling.  the ergm package
               allows you to specify missing ties, and it handles these correctly.
    
               assuming there are no missing data then:
    
               2. i don't see many triangles in this network, so there may be no need for
               a gwesp term.  but if you do use one, you may want to set the decay
               parameter to 0.  in any case, i'd start with no gwesp term and look at the
               GOF plot for ESP
    
               3. you probably want to use nodematch, not nodemix.  but first take a look
               at the mixing pattern using the mixingmatrix() function
    
               4. if you're going to use absdiff("age"), you should also include
               nodecov("age") -- main effects should be included with interactions
    
               5. try it without the degree term, and then look at the GOF plot for
               degree to see if you really need to include this.
    
               best,
               mm

if any of the explanations are now out of date, but perhaps others on 
the list--developers and/or those who've developed their own terms 
recently--can weigh in.

A term that measures Euclidean distance on attributes that represent 
coordinates is an obvious choice for a statistic to be added to the pot, 
and I wouldn't be surprised if someone in our user base has already done 
this, and might be willing to share. Anyone?

If you do take on the task, and were willing to share the results, then 
we'd be open to adding it to ergm or to the ergm.userterms repository on 
Github.

Thanks,

Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Valued models with missing edges
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Meredith -

Based on your description, it sounds like those edge variables should be 
structural 0s, not NAs.? (NA would mean that you don't know the value of 
the edge.? A structural 0 is a null that is fixed by something exogenous 
to the network generating process. Since the monkeys here could not have 
interacted, you would want - if I understand your situation correctly - 
to treat those cells as structural 0s.)? To do that, you will want to 
leave the network as is (i.e., set the edges as absent, not missing) and 
use the constraints argument to ergm() to tell the model that those 
edges are constrained to be absent; see the constraints help page for 
details on how to do that.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] ERGM: Error in rbind (using edgecov term)‏
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben -

If I understand correctly, netdel is a binary network that has a 0 
everywhere fullnet has a 0, and has a 1 everywhere that fullnet has a 
value >1.? Is that right?? If so, then you can't really use fullnet as a 
predictor of whether or not there is a tie in netdel, as there will be 
collinearity between the two.? The error you got is not very clear, I 
realize, but I do suspect that that is the underlying problem. Can you 
clarify (off group if you wish) what it is you are aiming to show by 
having fullnet as a predictor of netdel?? Knowing that may help to 
figure out what would be an appropriate analysis. Depending on the 
answer, one good option may be to use valued ergms with fullnet as your 
outcome. See the valued ergm tutorial at: 
https://statnet.org/trac/wiki/Sunbelt2016.

HTH,

Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Valued models with missing edges
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Meredith,

This is because that constraint combination is not implemented in the current ergm and ergm.count releases. There are two options:
1) If you are comfortable installing packages from GitHub (https://github.com/statnet/ergm), a pre-release version implements it.
2) A slightly less elegant option is to forbid those ties by adding offset(nodeocov("absent")) + offset(nodeicov("absent")) terms (where "absent" is a 0-1 vertex attribute indicating whether the monkey is absent) and setting offset.coef=c(-Inf,-Inf).

I hope this helps,
Pavel

On Fri, 2018-03-30 at 11:09 -0700, Meredith Lutz wrote:

Hi Carter,

Thanks so much - you are correct that the edges in question should be structural 0s. When I implemented that using the constraints argument, I got the following error message though:

Error in MHproposal.formula(constraints, weights = control$MCMC.prop.weights,  :

  The combination of class (c), model constraints (fixedas), reference measure (Poisson), and proposal weighting (default) is not implemented. Check your arguments for typos.

I tried using the constraint in a binary version of the same model, and didn't get the same error message (although the model is degenerate). Are fixedas constraints not currently implemented for valued ERGMs (Poisson reference)? If so, any advice for an alternative, aside from making it a binary outcome?


Thanks again,

Meredith


Model code: model1 <- ergm(plynet ~ sum + mutual(form = 'min') + transitiveweights('min', 'max', 'min') + nodematch('sex', form = 'sum') +

edgecov(plynet, 'agemat', form = 'sum') + nodecov('age', form = 'sum') + edgecov(plynet, 'elomat', form = 'sum') +

nodecov('elo', form = 'sum') + edgecov(plynet, 'kin', form = 'sum') + edgecov(plynet, 'numaff', form = 'sum') + edgecov(plynet, 'obsmat', form = 'sum'),

  response = 'numply', estimate = 'MLE', reference = ~Poisson, constraint=~fixedas(present = plynet, absent = missingEdges),

control = control.ergm(MCMC.interval = 1000, MCMLE.maxit = 200,

init.method = 'CD', MCMC.samplesize = 1000, seed = 32164))


---------- Forwarded message ----------
From: "Carter T. Butts" <buttsc@uci.edu<mailto:buttsc@uci.edu>>
To: statnet_help@u.washington.edu<mailto:statnet_help@u.washington.edu>
Cc:
Bcc:
Date: Thu, 29 Mar 2018 17:21:22 -0700
Subject: Re: [statnet_help] Valued models with missing edges

Hi, Meredith -

Based on your description, it sounds like those edge variables should be structural 0s, not NAs.  (NA would mean that you don't know the value of the edge.  A structural 0 is a null that is fixed by something exogenous to the network generating process.  Since the monkeys here could not have interacted, you would want - if I understand your situation correctly - to treat those cells as structural 0s.)  To do that, you will want to leave the network as is (i.e., set the edges as absent, not missing) and use the constraints argument to ergm() to tell the model that those edges are constrained to be absent; see the constraints help page for details on how to do that.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

I'm struggling with incorporating missing edges into several valued-ERGM models trying to understand how monkeys choose their play partners (directed network). The problem is that some of those 21 animals weren't in the group at the same time (due to birth's and deaths) so there are 20 edges that should be NA's. I currently have a working model that incorporates everything except the NA's (they are just 0's in the dataset):

messages.subject: [statnet_help] NAs in Bipartite ERGMs
messages.body_plain:
Hello Statnet Team,

I am writing to seek your help with an NA issue in bipartite ergms.  My aim
is to assign attributes to primary and secondary nodes and then calculate
bipartite ergms with these.  My valued network includes 787 primary nodes
and 45 secondary nodes.

So far I have been working with both
1) a complete csv. file including all attributes for primary and secondary
nodes (with NA's) and, also
2) as recommended by Skye Bender de-Moll in a statnet help post (
http://mailman13.u.washington.edu/pipermail/statnet_help/2014/001663.html)
with two separate csv. files for each node set (thus without NA's).

Problem: With both attribute lists I receive an error about NAs after
running ergms.  Any idea what could be wrong?  Here is the code I have been
working with and the error I received.

 net <- network(el, matrix.type="edgelist", bipartite=787, directed=F,
ignore.eval=FALSE,names.eval='Value')

 ## Primary node attributes
pna <- read_csv("Primary node attributes 1492_Bipartite network.csv")
net <- set.vertex.attribute(net, attrname = 'Capital', value=pna$ValueSum,
v=pna$ID)

 ## Secondary node attributes
sna <- read_csv("Secondary node attributes 1492_Bipartite network.csv")
net <- set.vertex.attribute(net, attrname = 'Distance',
value=sna$Greatcircledistance, v=sna$ID)

# ERGM with Error
model1 <- ergm(net ~ edges + b1cov('Capital') + b2cov('Distance'))
Error in ergm.getglobalstats(nw, model, response = response) :
  NA/NaN/Inf in foreign function call (arg 13)

Sorry in case this problem is too trivial for this community.  Any help
would be much appreciated.

I would also be very happy about any further information, literature
suggestions about how to do and work with bipartite ergms, interesting
applications etc.

Best wishes,
Bernd



-- 

Bernd Wurpts, M.A. (Magister Artium)
Graduate Student, Ph.D. Candidate
Department of Sociology
University of Washington
http://www.soc.washington.edu/faculty-details/wurpts

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Hypergraph/hyperedge modeling?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tyler,

I asked Carter for some help answering your question, and he responded 
with this:

There are lots of things that you can do with hypergraphs in statnet, but 
it all depends on what you want/need to accomplish.?There are few if any 
very specialized hypergraph tools at the moment, but that is mostly 
because there is very little work on decent methods for hypergraphs per 
se, and very little demand.?(There is a bit more for two-mode networks, 
which are not exactly the same as but often thought of as hypergraphs. 
Again, many things can be done with the standard tools.)?BTW, it is 
certainly possible to model two-mode networks in ergm(), and has been for 
a long time....these aren't general hypergraphs, but can stand in in some 
cases.

Again, the issue isn't "can you do things with hypergraphs."?Sure, you 
can.?The question is, "what do you want to do with hypergraphs that you 
can't currently do?"?Slapping a "hypergraph friendly" label on a routine 
just to do it has never been a priority, but a request for a specific 
feature could get traction....


hth,
mm


On Wed, 28 Feb 2018, Tyler A Scott wrote:

> 
> Greetings statnet cognoscenti,
>
> ???? The ergm package has a setting in the as.network() function for whether or not hyper-edges are allowed, but this
> setting is currently ignored (in version 3.8.0). Is this an area of active development? Is anyone on the mailing list
> aware of other resources which might be useful for those interested in modeling hypergraphs? I am aware of the hypergraph
> package (https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/hypergraph.html), but not of any tools at this point
> that go beyond this. 
>
> 
> 
> Best,
> 
> -tyler

> *TL;DR:* The edgecov() terms are very memory-inefficient. I don't know
> what these mg/m4/mt matrices represent, but if they can be generated from,
> say, nodal information, you can implement a custom ergm term that gets
> passed nodal information and generates them on the fly.
>

>
> *Technical explanation: *Internally, ergm concatenates covariate vectors
> and passes them on to the C code, where they get unpacked. Each edgecov()
> term passes an n*n matrix, and in your case, each of these matrices is
> 270000^2 elements long. Three of them add up to a vector of length
> 2187000000 <%28218%29%20700-0000> which is longer than the greatest
> integer that can be represented using the basic integer type (2147483647
> <%28214%29%20748-3647>). Now, R can handle vectors like that, but not
> through the .C() interface.
>
>
>
> I hope this helps,
>
> Pavel

messages.subject: [statnet_help] weighted networks dynamics with TERGMs
messages.body_plain:
Dear Sebastian,
tergm the package only handles binary networks at this time. However,
you can use the previous time step's network as a predictor to the
current time step's in ergm, and that would give you a temporal ERGM
over one transition (two networks). The version of ergm currently on
GitHub (in the master branch) can also apply a block-diagonal
constraint, and that would let you fit multiple transitions.
							Best,		
					Pavel

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Valued models with missing edges
messages.body_plain:
Hi Carter,

Thanks so much - you are correct that the edges in question should be
structural 0s. When I implemented that using the constraints argument, I
got the following error message though:

Error in MHproposal.formula(constraints, weights =
control$MCMC.prop.weights,  :

  The combination of class (c), model constraints (fixedas), reference
measure (Poisson), and proposal weighting (default) is not implemented.
Check your arguments for typos.

I tried using the constraint in a binary version of the same model, and
didn't get the same error message (although the model is degenerate). Are
fixedas constraints not currently implemented for valued ERGMs (Poisson
reference)? If so, any advice for an alternative, aside from making it a
binary outcome?


Thanks again,

Meredith


Model code: model1 <- ergm(plynet ~ sum + mutual(form = 'min') +
transitiveweights('min', 'max', 'min') + nodematch('sex', form = 'sum') +

edgecov(plynet, 'agemat', form = 'sum') + nodecov('age', form = 'sum') +
edgecov(plynet, 'elomat', form = 'sum') +

nodecov('elo', form = 'sum') + edgecov(plynet, 'kin', form = 'sum') +
edgecov(plynet, 'numaff', form = 'sum') + edgecov(plynet, 'obsmat', form =
'sum'),

  response = 'numply', estimate = 'MLE', reference = ~Poisson,
constraint=~fixedas(present = plynet, absent = missingEdges),

control = control.ergm(MCMC.interval = 1000, MCMLE.maxit = 200,

init.method = 'CD', MCMC.samplesize = 1000, seed = 32164))


---------- Forwarded message ----------
From: "Carter T. Butts" <buttsc@uci.edu>
To: statnet_help@u.washington.edu
Cc:
Bcc:
Date: Thu, 29 Mar 2018 17:21:22 -0700
Subject: Re: [statnet_help] Valued models with missing edges

Hi, Meredith -

Based on your description, it sounds like those edge variables should be
structural 0s, not NAs.  (NA would mean that you don't know the value of
the edge.  A structural 0 is a null that is fixed by something exogenous to
the network generating process.  Since the monkeys here could not have
interacted, you would want - if I understand your situation correctly - to
treat those cells as structural 0s.)  To do that, you will want to leave
the network as is (i.e., set the edges as absent, not missing) and use the
constraints argument to ergm() to tell the model that those edges are
constrained to be absent; see the constraints help page for details on how
to do that.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

On 03/29/2018 01:19 PM, Meredith Lutz wrote:

Hi all,

I'm struggling with incorporating missing edges into several valued-ERGM
models trying to understand how monkeys choose their play partners
(directed network). My nodes are individual monkeys (21 in total in the

The problem is that some of those 21 animals weren't in the group at the

On Mar 15, 2018, at 3:15 PM, martina morris <morrism@u.washington.edu<mailto:morrism@u.washington.edu>> wrote:

Hi Tyler,

I asked Carter for some help answering your question, and he responded with this:

There are lots of things that you can do with hypergraphs in statnet, but it all depends on what you want/need to accomplish. There are few if any very specialized hypergraph tools at the moment, but that is mostly because there is very little work on decent methods for hypergraphs per se, and very little demand. (There is a bit more for two-mode networks, which are not exactly the same as but often thought of as hypergraphs. Again, many things can be done with the standard tools.) BTW, it is certainly possible to model two-mode networks in ergm(), and has been for a long time....these aren't general hypergraphs, but can stand in in some cases.

Again, the issue isn't "can you do things with hypergraphs." Sure, you can. The question is, "what do you want to do with hypergraphs that you can't currently do?" Slapping a "hypergraph friendly" label on a routine just to do it has never been a priority, but a request for a specific feature could get traction....


hth,
mm

> target statistics and find it very hard to match the absdiff(?age?). 
> Even I first simulate a network without this term, and then use the 
> value of absdiff(?age?) of that network to be the target statistics, 
> it still tells me ?Unable to match target stats? once I add the 
> absdiff(?age?) term. Are there any tricks to make the target 
> statistics to simulate a hypothetical network?

I was intrigued by your questions so just wrote code to give it a try 
myself. (You caught me over morning coffee when I had just enough 
time!)? It seemed to work perfectly on my end.? I'm using the latest 
ergm (3.8.0).? My code is here, followed by a few thoughts:

library(ergm)
mynet <- network.initialize(100, directed=FALSE)
mynet <- set.vertex.attribute(mynet, "age", sample(1:80,100,replace=TRUE))
mynet %v% 'age'
myergm1 <- ergm(mynet~edges, target.stats=200)
mynet <- simulate(myergm1)
myformula <- mynet~edges+absdiff("age")+gwesp(0.5, fixed=TRUE)
mystats <- summary(myformula)
myergm2 <- ergm(myformula, target.stats=mystats)
mynet <- simulate(myergm2)
mystats
summary(myformula)

- The "unable to match target stats" sometimes appears as a warning, not 
an error, letting you know as a courtesy that the algorithm cannot get 
the target stats exactly matched in the initial network.? This is 
especially true when your target stats are not integers but any 
individual network can only have integer values for those target stats. 
However, this is actually not a problem since the estimation algorithm 
used when supplying target stats is able to work just fine, even if the 
starting network for estimation is not exactly on the target stats.? 
That's why it is a warning only, not an error.? I expected this to be 
what I saw when I tried recreating your example. However, I didn't even 
get this warning.? Is this showing up for you as a warning or an error?? 
Is the estimation algorithm proceeding after it gives you the message?

- Are you trying to get the final simulated network to match the target 
statistics exactly?? That is not likely to happen, by design.? Each 
individual network simulated from an ergm is a stochastic process - they 
will only match the target statistics on average over many simulations.? 
If you need to match an exact set of target statistics in a single 
network, you can try using the san command; however this typically only 
works on relatively simple models.? Actually getting an individual 
network to be guaranteed to match a set of target stats for arbitrarily 
complex model is a difficult (impossible?) problem.

- If my code doesn't help you answer your question, can you send me 
yours so I can take a look?

Cheers, Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] conversation networks
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Teresa -

If you have a very large collection of sparse dyadic networks without 
much meta-data (e.g., individual attributes), you may find it easiest to 
store them as a list of sna edgelists (see the help in the sna package 
for more details).? They are simple, lean, can encode values, and can be 
interconverted into other forms if needed.? If you need a richer format, 
lists of network objects (which you have considered previously) are 
often very effective; if you only have thousands of networks, then the 
length of the list should not be a concern.? (It could be a problem if 
you have more than, say, 1e8 conversations.? But that's probably not the 
case.)

In terms of encoding numbers of contacts between pairs, storing this as 
a value associated with each edge will probably prove easiest for most 
conventional network analyses.? That said, if you are really interested 
in things like conversational interaction then you are probably not 
interested in conventional network analysis - you are really looking at 
relational event sequences.? Rather than trying to find a way to 
shoehorn your question into a network analytic framework, you might want 
to consider an approach that considers such a process on its own terms 
(e.g. a REM model or sequence analysis).? That said, there are lots of 
things that can be learned by "flattening" an interaction sequence 
across time and treating it as an aggregated network, and I find that to 
be a useful exploratory step in such analyses; there's no single 
approach that answers all questions.

Anyway, hope that helps!

-Carter

messages.body_plain:
Dear statnet community,

I?m quite new to network analysis, so I apologize in advance for any inconsistencies. And the lengthy email :)

I?m building thousands of networks of conversations, and I have a couple of questions about how to build them/calculate some relevant statistics:

1. First, I tried two different approaches to building these networks. One is to build a list of network objects, so that each conversation has its independent network. Each conversation is built from a subset of the full edgelist identified by a specific conversation ID (this is added to the edgelist as a third column). The problem with this approach may be that the list becomes extremely big.

The second approach is to build a single large network object g from which later on subgraphs will be obtained iteratively by accessing only the subset of edges identified with a specific id, which I previously added as an edge attribute

get.inducedSubgraph(g, eid = which(g%e%"my_convo"== convo)

but I eventually want to be able to calculate network statistics independently for each conversation, and with this second method I?m not sure whether a given subgraph would be assessed independently should one (or more) of its nodes be also part of other subgraphs (given that it is possible that one actor could have participated in many conversations).

Which method should I follow, and are there any other considerations I haven?t thought of?

2. Since I?m working with conversational data, it is often the case that two nodes start a mutual exchange within a thread, creating redundant ties. This is actually very meaningful information that I would like to consider when  calculating several network measures. Once again, I?ve taken two approaches: one, I have built the network from the weighted edgelist mentioned above. It would look something like this:



In this case, only unique edges will be counted (7) on the network summary, and weight is an edge attribute. 

The second approach is to build the network with an edgelist containing redundant ties. The above case would then look like:

user6	user7	5
user6	user7	5
user6	user7	5
?
user7	user6	5
user7	user6	5
?

and so on. A summary of this network will count all edges (24). So the approach I take changes how some measures are going to be calculated and ought to be interpreted. I?ve looked online and it seems that reciprocity and density are not very reliable measures for weighted networks. How should one proceed when such redundancies actually matter and should be taken into account when evaluating, for example, the overall level of reciprocity in a conversation?

Thank you so much for any help; looking forward to reading your answers.
Sincerely,
Teresa

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Hypergraph/hyperedge modeling?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Tyler.  I?d second the message below, and in particular I?d point out that I?ve come across a few papers lately on hypergraphs that could be viewed as two-mode/bipartite/affiliation networks whose authors seemed unaware of this fact (and of course this means they also weren?t aware of the sizable literature relevant to their work).  So if your problem happens to be of the hypergraph-that-can-be-viewed-as-bipartite-network type, then you might be able to make considerable headway in statnet by using bipartite networks.

Good luck!
Dave


> On Mar 15, 2018, at 3:15 PM, martina morris <morrism@u.washington.edu> wrote:

> Hi Tyler,
> 
> I asked Carter for some help answering your question, and he responded with this:
> 
> There are lots of things that you can do with hypergraphs in statnet, but it all depends on what you want/need to accomplish. There are few if any very specialized hypergraph tools at the moment, but that is mostly because there is very little work on decent methods for hypergraphs per se, and very little demand. (There is a bit more for two-mode networks, which are not exactly the same as but often thought of as hypergraphs. Again, many things can be done with the standard tools.) BTW, it is certainly possible to model two-mode networks in ergm(), and has been for a long time....these aren't general hypergraphs, but can stand in in some cases.
> 
> Again, the issue isn't "can you do things with hypergraphs." Sure, you can. The question is, "what do you want to do with hypergraphs that you can't currently do?" Slapping a "hypergraph friendly" label on a routine just to do it has never been a priority, but a request for a specific feature could get traction....
